Processing Text: The Mg-4Sn (at.%) alloy ingot was produced by induction melting using a steel crucible under the protection of an argon atmosphere, and then cast into a steel mold. The cast alloy was homogenized at 400 °C for 6 h and cooled in the furnace. The homogenized sample was machined into cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 10 mm and a length of 14 mm for UP treatment in a modified CS-IB type hexahedral anvil apparatus. The sample was wrapped with tantalum foil and inserted in a boron nitride capsule. The hydrostatic pressure was obtained by the press along three axes. The samples were treated for 30 min at temperatures from 600 to 1100 °C under UP treatment under 4 GPa. The heating rate and time to boost pressure were 6 °C/s and 2 min, respectively. After UP treatment, the samples were cooled to room temperature by circulating water before unloading pressure. The UP-treated sample was subjected to aging heat treatment in a silicone oil bath at 200 °C, which was denoted as UPA. As a comparison, the cast alloys underwent solid solution treatment at 500 °C for 8 h, followed by aging heat treatment in a 200 °C silicone oil bath, denoted as T6. The UP-treated sample was machined into sheet specimens with the dimensions of 13 mm × 7 mm × 2 mm, and then the oxide was removed from the surface using the SiC paper. The sheet was connected to a direct current pulse power supply through Cu wires. The JT experiment was conducted at a current density of 4.5 × 10 3A/cm 2, with a voltage of 100 V, a pulse width of 80 μs and a frequency of 500 Hz. The sample was recorded by quenching every 60 s. The duty cycle is one of the main factors influencing the heat generation of the sample. Considering systematic errors, the duty cycle has been calculated to be 3-5 % in this work. Moreover, during the JT experiment, fans were utilized for supplementary air cooling, while the temperature was monitored using an infrared thermometer and maintained at about 50 °C. The JTed sample after a UPed treatment under 4 GPa at 800 °C was denoted as an ultrahigh-pressure treatment followed by Joule-heat treated (UPJTed). Processing Text: In this study, combined nanoprecipitation and gradient grain structure were introduced into a Co-Cr-Ni-based multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) using surface mechanical attrition treatment (SMAT). The alloy with low local stacking fault energy provides sufficient flow stress to reach the critical value for twinning, a phenomenon rarely observed in MPEAs with high-density L12 nanoprecipitates under quasi-static tensile conditions. The bulk ingot of CoCrNi 2(Al 0.2Nb 0.2) alloy, weighing 3 kg, was produced using electromagnetic levitation melting, as detailed in our previous work. The alloy underwent a series of treatments including homogenization, cold-rolling, recrystallization annealing, and aging to achieve the L12-strengthened structure. Subsequently, the aged CoCrNi 2(Al 0.2Nb 0.2) plate with dimensions of 55 mm × 25 mm × 1 mm was subjected to SMAT, as illustrated schematically in Fig. 1(a). During SMAT, 3 mm diameter bearing steel shots were activated at a vibrating frequency of 20 kHz, impacting each side of the alloy plate for 10 min. Samples were prepared using laser-powder bed fusion (L-PBF) from commercial gas-atomized powders of FeCoCrNi. These powders were mixed with AlSi10Mg powders for 10 h in a three-dimensional powder mixer with a mass ratio of 94:6, vacuum-dried for 4 h, and subsequently processed on a Renishaw RenAM 500E machine using a 316 L stainless steel substrate. For each layer, a scanning strategy involving 5 mm stripes was adopted, with a 67° rotation angle applied between consecutive layers. Different laser powers, ranging from 80 to 200 W, and scanning speeds, varying from 400 to 1800 mm/s, were used to prepare 32 test block samples. Based on these measurements, the processing parameters that resulted in the highest-density sample were selected: laser power was set to 200 W, scanning speed to 1400 mm/s, scanning hatch spacing to 80 µm, and thickness of each powder bed layer to 30 µm. Samples were then subjected to heat treatment at 1000 and 1200 °C for 1 and 10 h, respectively, in an argon atmosphere, followed by water quenching to investigate the thermal stability of the L-PBF (HEA) alloy. High-temperature tensile tests of the as-built alloys were conducted at 300, 600, 700, 800, 900, and 1000 °C. Annealing Condition: 1000 °C/1 h

The Fe-Ni based alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting with a nominal composition of 30Ni-15Cr-2.0Ti-0.3Al-1.3Mo-0.2Si-Fe bal. (wt.%). The ingot was homogenized at 1160 °C for 20 h, then forged and rolled into a bar with a diameter of 15 mm. After that, the bar was solutionized at 980 °C for 1 h followed by water cooling, to obtain a fully solid solution coarse-grain (CG) structure with an average grain size of 32 µm (referred to as SS-CG). Cylindrical SS-CG samples with an initial height of 15 mm were subjected to multiple dynamic plastic deformation (DPD) impacts at room temperature to obtain a nanograin (NG) structure (referred to as SS-NG). The final height of the sample was 3 mm after an 80% thickness reduction. To achieve their peak aging state, the SS-CG sample was aged at 740 °C for 8 h followed by water cooling (referred to as Aged-CG), while the SS-NG sample was aged at 680 °C for 30 min followed by water cooling (referred to as Aged-NG). Processing Text: The equiatomic CoCrNi alloy was produced by melting a mixture of high-purity raw metals (99.95 wt.% or higher) using induction melting. To prevent oxidation and minimize evaporation of elements, the furnace chamber was evacuated and then filled with high-purity argon gas to achieve a slightly positive pressure of 0.02 Pa. The melting and flipping process was repeated at least four times to ensure chemical homogeneity before drop-casting the alloy into a copper mold with a rectangular cavity (40 mm × 40 mm × 25 mm). To reduce compositional inhomogeneity, the ingots were homogenized at 1250 °C for 24 h in an argon-filled furnace. Processing Text: C4, C10, and C16 RMPEAs were synthesized by vacuum arc-melting in a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. High-purity (99.9 wt%) refractory metals W, Ta, Mo, Nb, and powdered graphite were utilized as raw materials. To ensure chemical homogeneity, each ingot was remelted at least 8 times. Subsequently, rods with a dimension of Φ20 mm × 8 mm were obtained by suction casting. Specimens for mechanical testing and microstructure analysis were then prepared from the rods by electrical discharge machining. RT compressive tests were conducted on an Instron machine at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1 with a strain gauge. The specimens had a diameter of 2 mm and a height of 4 mm, and each alloy was tested at least three times. HT compression tests at 1600 °C were conducted in a vacuum furnace using a Zwick KAPPA 100 dynamic thermal simulation testing machine. The samples with a dimension of Φ4 mm × 8 mm were initially heated to 1600 °C at a rate of 20 °C min−1 and held for 15 min under a load of 5 N, and then compressed at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. For a long time, the large loss of the strength and toughness of fusion welded joints for thick near β titanium alloys has largely hindered their engineering application, which results from the few precipitations of the strengthening α phase during welding cooling. In this study, double annealing treatment was designed for electron beam welded joints of 30-mm-thick near β Ti-5Al-5Mo-5V-1Cr-1Fe alloy, with the aim of regulating the proportion of multi-level lamellar microstructures and enhancing the joint properties. Among various annealing temperatures (first annealing at 750-880 °C + second annealing at 580 °C), the 750 °C + 580 °C annealed joint exhibited simultaneously enhanced strength and toughness, with the increase in tensile strength and impact energy from 844 MPa and 8.8 J for the as-welded joint to 1129 MPa and 14.5 J for annealed joint, respectively, which were superior to those of the joints of Ti-5Al-5Mo-5V-1Cr-1Fe alloy as reported. The good coupling of α p phase and α s phase improved the precipitation strengthening and the resistance to crack propagation. The modified strengthening mechanism models were proposed by introducing the thickness and proportion parameters of the precipitated phase. This study provides a novel method via designing proper multi-level lamellar microstructures to simultaneously improve the strength and toughness of near β titanium alloy joints. Processing Text: The Mn and trace amounts of V and Nb were added to the original 300 M composition. The quenching temperature for the newly developed material was ultimately determined to be 820 °C, which is higher than the Ae 3point, ensuring the refinement of the original austenite structure. V-precipitates start form at 1048 °C and Nb-precipitates form at 1234 °C, providing precipitation and grain refinement strengthening during hot rolling and quenching processes. The material was cast into 50 kg pieces using a vacuum induction melting furnace, homogenized at 1200 °C for 6 h, and then forged into ingots measuring 80 mm × 80 mm at approximately 1050 °C. The hot rolling process involved heating the billet to 1200 °C for 2 h, hot rolling it to a thickness of 40 mm at 1100-1200 °C, further reducing it to 14 mm at 920-950 °C, and finally air cooling to room temperature. After hot rolling, the samples underwent various treatments: the hot-rolled sample was tempered at 200 °C for 1 h (denoted as sample L); the hot-rolled sample was cryogenically treated at −196 °C for 20 min and then tempered at 200 °C for 1 h (denoted as sample D-L); the hot-rolled sample was austenitized at 820 °C for 1 h and then tempered at 200 °C for 1 h (denoted as sample Q-L); the hot-rolled sample was austenitized at 820 °C for 1 h, cryogenically treated at −196 °C for 20 min, and then tempered at 200 °C for 1 h (denoted as sample Q-D-L). All cooling processes are air-cooled due to the high hardenability of the designed alloy. Processing Text: The Ti64 alloy powder with a spherical shape (between 45 and 325 µm in diameter) had an average chemical composition (wt%) of 6.15Al, 4.05 V, 0.089Fe, 0.15O, 0.01 N, 0.05C, 0.004H, and balance Ti. Deposited parts (140 mm × 70 mm × 90 mm) were produced via a high-power (8 kW CO 2) laser solid forming (LSF) equipment (LSF-V machine), a kind of laser-directed energy deposition additive manufacturing. Laser processing parameters are as follows: laser power 7.6 kW, beam diameter 6 mm, scanning velocity 900 and 1500 mm/min, powder feed rate 500 g/h, overlap 40 %, and Z-axis increment 0.8 mm. These deposition parameters have been optimized. Solution treatment and aging (STA) was further conducted on the deposited samples at 950 °C for 2 h followed by air cooling (AC) and 550 °C for 4 h followed by AC. STA was performed in the air. After STA, the oxidative layers at the surface of the deposits were removed. The C(T) specimen in different directions from the deposited specimens after heat treatment was cut by wire electronic discharge machining. The notch direction and detailed dimensions are shown in Fig. 1(c, d). Pre-fabricated fatigue crack conditions are as follows: at the beginning, the maximum loading force is Fmax=17,000 N, and the minimum loading force is Fmin=1000 N; at the final stage, Fmax=16,000 N, Fmin=1000 N. The total number of cycles is from 18,000 to 24,000 cycles, the pre-fabricated fatigue crack length is ∼4.5 mm. Finally, fracture toughness tests were conducted in tension at a displacement speed of 1 mm/min until the C(T) specimen failed. The plane strain fracture toughness ( KIc) tests were conducted according to the Chinese standard GB/T 4161-2007, corresponding to the ASTM E399-12standard. Specimens for the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) characterization were prepared by pre-mechanical polishing and a Leica multifunctional ion thinning instrument (Leica EM RES102) at a voltage of 6 kV for 2 h with an angle of ion beam machining of 6°. The steel was then precision cut into 10 mm thickness rectangular plates using electrical discharge machining (EDM). The plates were homogenized for 2 at 1200 °C, followed by hot rolling through 6 passes at 1050 °C, with each pass lasting 5 min in the furnace after each rolling, subsequently quenched in water to room temperature, resulting in a final thickness of 3 mm after rolling. The quenched samples were annealed at temperatures of 700 °C and 800 °C respectively. For clarity, these samples are referred to as A0 (post quench), A7 (annealed at 700 °C), and A8 (annealed at 800 °C) in the following discussions. Processing Text: The Al-5.0Mn-1.5Mg-0.82Sc-0.76Zr (wt.%) alloy powder with a standard composition was prepared by gas atomization (Panxing New Alloy Materials Co., Ltd., China). The powder was spherical in shape, with the particles less than or equal to 22.3 µm accounting for 10% while 90% of the particles were less than or equal to 63.4 µm, as shown in Fig. 1(a, b). All the LPBF samples investigated in this work were manufactured using a BLT S210 LPBF machine equipped with a 400 W fiber laser. Constant laser power (350 W), scanning spacing (90 µm), and layer thickness (30 µm) were used with scanning velocities ranging between 450 and 1450 mm/s. Two different substrate temperatures, 25 and 200 °C, were used for each condition. The samples with the optimized process parameters had a relative density higher than 99.8 %. A bilinear scanning strategy with a scan rotation of 67° was used between the layers. The samples were printed in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the samples were heat-treated at 200 °C for 1 h to remove residual stresses before evaluating their microstructures and mechanical properties. The LPBF samples were prepared for microstructural characterization by mechanical grinding and polishing following a standard metallographic procedure recommended in ASTM E3-11. After polishing, the microstructural features were revealed using an etchant consisting of HNO 3(2.5 mL), HCl (1.5 mL), HF (1.0 mL), and distilled water (95 mL). The wire-cut electro-discharge machine was used to slice samples with the following dimensions: ∼5 mm long, ∼5 mm wide, and ∼1 mm thick. Prior to the EBSD characterization, the sheet samples were first mechanically polished with 400 #, 1000 #, 2000 #, and 3000 # SiC water abrasive paper, then electropolished to remove the surface deformation layer generated by mechanical grinding. Electropolishing was performed at −30 °C, with: 7 % perchloric acid, 93 % ethanol; a voltage of 25 V, and a current density of 450 mA/cm 2for about 1 min. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed using the CMT4105 universal testing machine. The gauge length and cross-sectional area of the tensile specimens were 22 mm and 1.5 mm × 4 mm. All the tensile samples were tested perpendicular to the build direction at a constant strain rate of 1 mm/min, following the standard ASTM E8. Fatigue test samples with the dimensions 60 mm × 12 mm × 1.5 mm were tested on an MTS370.02 fatigue testing machine. All samples were mechanically ground and polished prior to fatigue testing to ensure similar surface roughness. The uniaxial fatigue tests were conducted in a load control mode at a frequency of 40 Hz and stress ratio of R= 0.1, following the standard ASTM E466. The samples were tested until fracture or exhaustion till 10 7cycles. Processing Text: Six ultrahigh-strength DP steels with varying microstructure but comparable tensile strength (>1400 MPa) were prepared via tailoring the heat treatment process after cold rolling. The experimental steel, with a composition of Fe-0.19C-0.26Si-3.2Mn-0.16V-0.19Mo (wt.%), underwent melting, forging, hot rolling, and cold rolling processes. The related process parameters matched those in Ref. [ 11]. The final cold-rolled sheet thickness is 1.8-1.9 mm. Then the cold-rolled sheets were heated in a tube furnace under the specified heat treatment process. Fig. 1 shows the thermomechanical processing routes. Various DP steels with different matrix phases, grain sizes, and ferrite morphologies were produced through these six routes. In this context, 'F-' and 'M-' denote ferritic matrix and martensitic matrix, respectively. 'CG' and 'FG' represent coarse-grained microstructure and fine-grained microstructure, respectively. 'P' indicates a plate-like ferrite morphology. The microstructure was examined by scanning electronic microscopy (SEM, Zeiss Sigma 300) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Thermo Scientific 153 FEI Talos F200X). Metallographic samples for SEM were mechanically ground and polished and then etched in a solution of 4 % (volume fraction) nitric acid. Samples for TEM were mechanically ground to a thickness of 200 µm and then electropolished in a twin-jet machine in a solution of 5 % perchloric acid in 95 % alcohol at 20 °C. Tensile tests were performed on a 100 kN Servo-Hydraulic Testing Machine equipped with an Epsilon extensometer at a strain rate of 10 -3s -1 at room temperature (20 °C). All tensile specimens are the standard subsize ones with a 25 mm gauge length and 6 mm width, machined along the rolling direction (RD) of the sheet (ASTM-E8 M). In addition, the hole expansion test was conducted on a hole expansion machine (SAS-200DT-01), with specimens being thin plates measuring 110 mm × 110 mm and featuring a central circular hole with a diameter of 10 mm (GB/T 15,825.4-1995). Compact-tension (CT) specimens were cut with a thickness (B) of 1.8 mm, and a width (W) of 18 mm. A straight-through notch was cut with a length of 8 mm, with the crack direction perpendicular to the RD. Prior to the fracture toughness measurement, fatigue pre-cracking was produced in force control with a stress ratio ( R) of 0.1, and the length of the final pre-crack was about 9 mm. Grain size: 1.06 µm (martensite); UE: 7.2%; EtF: 9.8%

Al-Mg-Mn-Sc-Zr alloy powder with high content of Sc and Zr elements was prepared by vacuum induction gas atomization. The powder granularity was 10-60 μm. The chemical composition of the Al-Mg-Mn-Sc-Zr alloy powder is shown in Table 1. The content of Sc/Zr elements is almost twice that of conventional alloys. The Mg/Mn element is also added to the alloy mainly because of its excellent solid solution strengthening. In particular, Mg element can also inhibit recrystallization to a certain extent and prevent grain growth. To avoid the influence of harmful elements such as H and O on the forming sample, drying treatment was applied to the powder and oxygen level of the forming chamber was strictly controlled to a low value. Before the LPBF forming experiment, the powder was placed in a vacuum heating furnace with a vacuum level super than 10 −1Pa for preheating to prevent the moisture in the powder from affecting the forming quality. The holding temperature was 120 °C and the holding time was 4 h. A BLT-S210 selective laser melting system from Xi'an Bright Laser Technologies Co., Ltd. was used to achieve the fabrication of Al-Mg-Mn-Sc-Zr alloy samples. Before the forming experiment, the surface of the substrate was cleaned to remove surface impurities and fouling. During the forming process, the argon with 99.999 % purity was filled into the forming chamber continuously to control the oxygen content below 100 ppm throughout the entire forming process of the samples. The forming process parameters were selected after the orthogonal test, and the reasonable process parameter was determined by a higher relative density and fewer metallurgical defects. An overview of the as-built samples is shown in Fig. 1(d), and the optimized forming process parameters are shown in Table 2. According to the above alloying principle, from the point of view of improving the strength of the LPBFed Al-Mg-Mn-Sc-Zr alloy, direct aging treatment was adopted during the post-heat treatment process to facilitate the precipitation of the secondary Al 3(Sc,Zr) phase and maintain the fine-grain structure. In the pre-experiment, we obtained the aging response by microhardness test the samples with different aging temperatures and aging times. The peak aging treatment process of the LPBFed Al-Mg-Mn-Sc-Zr alloy is holding at 330 °C for 4 h. The fabricated samples were intercepted along the building direction for microstructure characterization, with a size of 10 mm (length) × 10 mm (width) × 5 mm (height). After grinding and polishing, the samples were etched by Keller's reagent (2.5 ml HNO 3+1.5 ml HCl+1 ml HF+100 ml H 2O) for 20 s, and then the microstructure was observed by a SU151 scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The samples were treated by ion polishing before the electron back-scatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis with a MIRA3 EBSD probe. The sample was further cut to a thickness of 0.5 mm, polished and made into 100 μm sheet and then prepared using an ion thinning instrument before it was analized in a Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). The second phase of the LPBFed Al-Mg-Mn-Sc-Zr alloy was characterized by an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) system during the TEM observation. The room-temperature tensile test was carried out on a WDW-200D testing machine with a displacement rate of 1 mm/min. The loading direction is perpendicular to the deposition direction. After the tensile test, the cross section and longitudinal section were observed by a KYKY-EM8100 scanning electron microscope. The Instron 8801 tensile machine was used for the LUR tensile test of the samples, and the displacement rate was 1 mm/min. Processing Text: The as-received (AR) standard UNS N07718 (Alloy 718) alloy was utilized. A high-energy Nd-YAG laser (Tyrida YS120-R200A) with an 18 ns pulse width and 1064nm wavelength was employed for LSP. The 10.9 J laser pulse of 4 mm spot size produced a peak power density of 4.82 GW/cm 2. Peening was performed in a ring-wise pattern along the gauge area of the dog bone samples. Each ring consisted of 13 overlapping laser spots. Successive rings were 1.2 mm apart vertically. The calculated overlap in both the circumferential and axial directions was 70%. A thin layer of deionized water was used as the tamping medium without any ablative coating, a technique which is often referred to as LSP without coating (LSPwC) or uncoated LSP. The ex-situ hydrogen charging process was performed using a three-electrode electrochemical charging cell, incorporating a platinum foil as the counter electrode and a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode, in line with ASTM G148. The electrolyte used for hydrogen charging was a 0.5M H 2SO 4solution containing 1g/L of thiourea to act as a recombination agent for enhanced hydrogen absorption. The electrochemical charging process was carried out at room temperature with a current density of 590 mA/cm 2for both 2 and 24 h, utilizing an Autolab PGSTAT302N potentiostat. TiZrAlMn alloy ingots were produced by melting in a vacuum non-consumable electric arc furnace. Titanium, acting as an oxygen absorber, effectively prevented oxidation. The ingots were turned and re-melted at least eight times under a pure argon atmosphere to ensure a uniform composition. Each alloy ingot, weighing approximately 65 g, displayed a coarse Widmanstätten structure composed of lamellar αphase and residual βphase. The phase transition temperatures of TiZrAlMn alloys were using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) by ASTM F2004-05 (2010) at a heating rate of 10 °C/min. The onset and end temperatures of the alloy were determined to be 785±4 °C and 869±10 °C, respectively, using the tangent method on the DSC curves. To optimize the coarse Widmanstätten structure, hot rolling was performed at different phase transition temperature regions (900 °C, 850 °C, 800 °C and 750 °C). Each TiZrAlMn alloy ingot was held in the muffle furnace for 40 min before rolling to ensure uniform heating and reaching target temperature. Button ingots, approximately 14 mm thick, were rolled to 2 mm using two-high rolls mill, achieving a total deformation of 85.7%. Between each rolling pass, the ingots were reheated in the furnace for 6 min, with a rolling reduction of 1.5 mm per pass (rolling speed: 0.5 m/s). Air cooling was used after rolling. The rolled specimens were labeled as 900-AC, 850-AC, 800-AC and 750-AC, according to their respective rolling temperatures. To obtain fully recrystallized microstructures, the specimens were then annealed at 1373 K for 6 h and quenched in water. Compression and tensile specimens with a gauge section of 2 × 2 × 5 mm3 were cut by electrical discharge machining. Surfaces of specimen were polished mechanically and then electronically in a solution of 1 : 2: 7 perchloric acid, n-butanol and methanol by volume prior to mechanical testing. Condition: 77 K

The IN718 components were fabricated using SLM Solutions 280HL machine, Germany. The powders were spread on the platform and melted layer by layer to generate the cylindrical specimens of dimensions 13 mm diameter and 80 mm length. An argon atmosphere was maintained in the chamber throughout the process to avoid oxidation during SLM process. A hatch style rotation of 67° was employed between the layers. The parameters utilized for SLM process like laser power of 200 W, scan speed of 1200 mm/s, hatch spacing of 90 μm and layer thickness of 30 μm. To maintain proper heat dissipation during the printing process a support structure were maintained for the samples with the same material and the supports were removed from the platform using wire cut electric discharge machine, once the printing process completed. The cylindrical specimens generated by SLM were friction welded by continuous drive KUKA friction welding (FW) machine. A facing operation was performed for the faying surfaces to remove any contaminations or oxides if present. The parameters employed for FW process such as, heating pressure of 50 bar, upset pressure of 60 bar, heating time of 6 s, upset time of 3 s and a rotary speed of 1125 rpm. An infrared thermographic (IR) camera (FLIR-make) was used to measure the temperature distribution at the interface during FW. Two cylindrical rods were considered whereas one was at stationery position and other was rotated with constant rpm during FW. The workpieces generate the frictional force in between the faying surfaces and an upset force was applied to forms the welds. The SLM samples after FW were examined for the microstructural characterization. The cross section of samples was grounded and polished with standard metallography practices to obtain scratch free surfaces. After etching with an etchant of HCl -10 ml and H 2O 2-3 ml for 10 s, the microstructures were observed under Olympus BX51 optical microscope (OM) and for higher magnification, scanning electron microscope (SEM) of Zeiss EVO MA 15 was used. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed using Rigaku ultima IV with Cu-Kα radiation of wavelength 0.1542 nm. The step size of 0.02° was used during diffraction analysis at an angle ranging from 40° to 100°. For micro-texture analysis, a FEI TMQuanta 3D-SEM with TSL-EDX TMEBSD (electron back scatter diffraction) system was utilized. OIM Analysis TM(version 8.1) post processing software was used to analyse EBSD data. The Vickers microhardness tests were carried out with 500 g load and a dwell time of 10 s using Buehler Micromet indenter. The measurements were performed along the cross section of the specimen to cover all the zones present in the specimen. Room temperature tensile tests were conducted using Instron 8516 with a strain rate of 10 -4s -1for the as-built SLM and welded samples. The strain hardening behaviour was analysed using Kocks-Mecking plots from the tensile tests data and fracture analysis was performed on the tensile samples to evaluate the fractography features. The strength contribution from the various strengthening mechanisms were calculated for both the SLM as built and weld conditions of IN718 components. A master alloy with nominal composition of Ni 49Fe 20Al 17Cr 8V 6(at. %) was prepared by arc-melting Ni, Fe, Al, Cr and V elements with high purity (99.99 wt%). Each ingot was remelted at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity. Subsequently, the molten liquid was drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold with dimension of 70 × 10 × 10 mm. The as-cast alloys were cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of ∼90 % and then annealed at 775 °C for 2 h. Here, based on the equilibrium phase diagram of Ni 49Fe 20Al 17Cr 8V 6EHEA, we have performed a series of annealing treatment within a range temperature of 750∼900 °C for 2 h on the cold-rolled samples to achieve a superior mechanical performance. The as-cast, cold-rolled and annealed at 775 °C for 2 h were denoted as AC and CR-775 EHEAs, respectively. Processing state: as-cast; Microstructure: dual-phase lamellar structure with soft FCC/L12 and hard B2 phases

Processing Text: The ingot was prepared using vacuum induction melting, and then homogenized at 1180 °C for 4 h, followed by hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 11 ± 1 mm at 1150 °C. Subsequently, the plates were annealing at 720 °C for 1.5 h with air cooling to room temperature, and then several 70 × 10 × 10 mm samples were obtained from the pates using wire cut electrical discharge machining (WEDM). The phase transformation temperatures Ac 1 and Ac 3 were determined using a thermal expansion analyzer and JMatPro, resulting in values of 780 °C and 860 °C, respectively. The HAZ simulation utilized a heating rate of 100 °C/s, The Gleeble-3500 thermal simulator was used to simulate the welding HAZ microstructure of the novel martensitic heat-resistant steel G115. Thermal simulation tests were conducted using the Gleeble system under various heat input conditions. As the heat input increases from 8.64 kJ/cm to 14.4 kJ/cm, the fraction of low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) in the FGHAZ rises from 56.9 % to 60.9 %, and the grain size distribution becomes more uniform. Sample: 1320-A; UTS: 1043 MPa; EL: 13.7%

Processing Text: Initially, we prepared ten button ingots by arc-melting the different constituent elements with a purity of over 99.9 wt% under a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. Each ingot was remelted at least four times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The next step involved remelting these ingots in a vacuum induction furnace to create a large cylindrical master alloy with dimensions of Ø29.3 mm × 55 mm (Fig. S1a). This master alloy was then vacuum-sealed in a steel sleeve under an argon atmosphere and homogenized at 1423 K for 24 h, followed by water quenching. Processing Text: The Al 0.25CoCrFeNi ingot about 8 kg was prepared by a mixture of high-purity (99.9 wt%) Al, Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni powders followed by induction melting under an argon atmosphere. The ingot was repeatedly melted at least 5 times to homogenize the composition. Furthermore, a cylinder ingot of Al 0.25CoCrFeNi was obtained by pouring the liquid Al 0.25CoCrFeNi into a ceramic mold with an inner diameter of 160 mm and a height of 70 mm. The 20 plates with dimensions of 45 mm × 20 mm × 15 mm were cut from the alloy ingot by electric spark cutting followed by ∼85 % cold rolling (CR) along the longitudinal ingot direction. Then, the sheets were of a final thickness of approximately 2.25 mm. To obtain fully recrystallized equiaxial structures with three different grain sizes, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at 1000 °C, 1100 °C, and 1200 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching, which were denoted as CR-1000, CR-1100, and CR-1200, respectively. The crystalline structures of the as-prepared Al 0.25CoCrFeNi HEA were characterized by X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Shimadzu, MAXima XRD-7000, Japan) using Cu Kα (λ = 1.5418 Å) radiation. The voltage and current applied to the Cu target were 40 kV and 30 mA, respectively. Then the microstructure was studied on the three principal planes (perpendicular to RD (rolling direction), TD (transverse direction), and ND (normal direction) directions) of the sample by a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Helios G4 CX) equipped with energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometry (EDS, Helios G4 CX) and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detectors. The grain size of the alloy was measured and calculated by the EBSD statistics. The samples used for SEM and EBSD characterization were mechanically polished and then electropolished in a mixture of C 2H 5OH (90 %) and HClO 4(10 %). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and selected area electron diffraction (SAED) were carried out on an FEI Tecnai G2 F30 microscope at a voltage of 300 kV for deformed samples. Dog-bone-shaped specimens with a gauge length of 20 mm, width of 4 mm, and thickness of 2 mm were prepared from annealed samples by electrical discharge machining. Uniaxial tensile tests were carried out with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1at 25 °C and −196 °C. The cryogenic tension tests were performed with the specimens completely immersed in liquid nitrogen. Three samples were measured for each condition. Temperature: 25 °C; Grain size: 217 μm

Processing Text: The as-received material was acquired by cold rolling and subsequently annealed, the final thickness is 0.8 mm. To obtain different initial phases for the cold rolling experiment, two treatment temperatures of 600 °C and 700 °C were selected in the heat treatment experiments, which are higher than 456.5 °C to ensure the α phase can be covert to the β phase. The holding time of the heat treatment was 1 h and followed by air cooling. Subsequently, the cold rolling experiments for the two specimens with heated treatments were carried out with a rolling mill (BF-YP-50P) at room temperature. The rolling speed was 10 mm/s and the single thickness reduction was 0.05 mm. The two treatment temperatures of 600 °C and 700 °C specimens were directly cold rolled from 0.8 mm thickness to 0.55 mm, 0.4 mm, and 0.2 mm thickness respectively, with a thickness reduction of 31 %, 50 %, and 75 %. The corresponding true strains were 0.37, 0.69, and 3.39, respectively. The metallographic specimens were cut with a width of 5 mm and a length of 5 mm and then mounted in epoxy resin. The surface of each specimen was mechanically polished by the machine (AutoMet 250 Pro, Buehler) and then etched with the solution made by 50 mL HCl, 10 mL H2O, and 5 g FeCl3. Initial state before rolling

Processing Text: Disc-shaped specimens with a diameter of 30 mm and a thickness of 0.80 mm sliced from the ingots were provided for the HPT process. The HPT was performed at a rotation speed of 0.2 rpm under a compressive pressure of 6 GPa at room temperature. The homogeneous liquid melt was quickly cast into a water-cooled copper crucible to form ingots of the alloys, each with a thickness of 15 mm. High-purity nickel, cobalt, and vanadium (all >99.9 % purity) were selected for the preparation of the VCoNi MPEA. The alloy was smelted using the arc-melting method under an argon atmosphere and cast into the mold of 130 mm in diameter and 150 mm in height. To ensure chemical homogeneity, the ingot was turned upside down and re-melted five times. Subsequently, the ingot was hot-forged and hot-rolled at 1423 K to form a plate with dimensions of 12 × 100 × 600 mm³. The plate underwent annealing in a vacuum at 1373 K for 2 h, followed by water quenching. Finally, cold rolling (CR) was performed with a thickness reduction of 90 % to produce sheets with a thickness of 1 mm. The samples were annealed at a temperature of 1153 K for 1.3 min, 1.6 min, 5 min, 10 min, 20 min, 1 h, 5 h, 20 h, and 50 h, respectively, followed by water quenching. Processing Text: Heterogeneous laminated Al matrix composites reinforced by 5, 10 and 20 wt% CrCoNi medium entropy alloy lamellas were fabricated by a powder metallurgy approach with two-step ball-milling process. Spherical pure Al powders (99.9 % purity, 10 μm average particle size, Henan Yuanyang Powder Technology Co., LTD.), and spherical equiatomic CrCoNi powders (99.9 % purity, 20 μm average particle size, Beijing Yanbang New Material Technology Co., LTD.) were used as the raw materials. Firstly, the CrCoNi powders were ball milled in an attritor (Qingdao Union Process Precision Machinery Co., Ltd.) at a speed of 450 rpm in pure ethanol for 15 h, with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 20:1. The CrCoNi slurry was then vacuum-suction filtered and vacuum dried at 333 K for 24 h to obtain CrCoNi flaky powders. Next, flaky CrCoNi powders and Al powders were mixed with 1 wt% stearic acid in a glovebox with a highly purified argon atmosphere to minimize the oxidation of Al powders. Composite powders were then ball milled in a planetary mill (QM-DY2 Nanjing NJU-instrument Co., LTD.) at 300 rpm for 8 h with the ball-to-powder weight ratio of 20:1, followed by degreasing at 673 K for 0.5 h in a muffle furnace inside the glovebox to remove the residual stearic acid. Subsequently, the composite powders were hot pressed under 900 MPa at 723 K for 0.5 h and hot extruded with the extrusion ratio of 9:1 at 573 K to obtain CrCoNi-Al composites. According to the CrCoNi content in the composite (5 wt%, 10 wt% and 20 wt%), the as-fabricated composites are designated as 5CrCoNi-Al, 10CrCoNi-Al, and 20CrCoNi-Al, respectively. Processing Text: 321 stainless steel wire with a diameter of 1.2 mm was applied as the deposition material. A 304 stainless steel plate with 150 × 300 × 6 mm 3 dimensions was used as a substrate. In the deposition process, the Fronius TPS4000 CMT welding machine was applied. Considering the deposition quality and impact requirement, a single-layer deposition with a relatively flat and smooth surface was selected to keep the process stable and ensure the impact effect. A single-point impact mode was conducted to treat the top part of the deposition after the deposition was cooled to room temperature. The process parameters were set to obtain a noticeable impact effect on the basis of ensuring the stability and sustainability of the UIT process. The impact load was applied and controlled through the KUKA robot based on the pressure sensor during this process. The UIT was applied to the single-layer deposition to better compare inter-layer thermal effects on microstructure evolution and recrystallization behavior after UIT. After obtaining 321 stainless steel bulk fabrications, samples were machined from X, Y, and Z directions to compare the impact toughness, tensile properties, and anisotropy of the fabrications with and without inter-layer UIT strengthening. Before the EBSD experiment, 10 % perchloric acid was used for electrolytic polishing of the samples. The EBSD equipment type was C-Swift manufactured by Oxford Instruments, with an accelerating voltage of 20 kV, a working distance of 15 mm, a scanning step of 1.3 μm for the macroscopic region of 0.5 × 0.5 mm 2, and 0.25 μm for the microscopic region of 0.1 × 0.1 mm 2. The macroscopic region was sampled in an area 0.5 mm away from the treated surface of the deposition to avoid the influence of interlayer remelting. The microscopic regions were located in the macroscopic region from top to bottom, with an interval of 0.1 mm. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed using a FEI Scios 2 HiVac microscope. Samples were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB) to ensure precise thinning of the regions of interest. The TEM analysis was conducted at an accelerating voltage of 200 kV, and high-resolution images were captured to examine dislocation structures and grain boundaries. The Microhardness of the bulk fabrication was tested along the Y-Z cross-section at intervals of 1 mm to analyze the microhardness distribution in different regions. The impact toughness at room temperature was conducted using the ZBC2452-C pendulum impact testing machine from MTS Industries in the USA. The AG-X plus electronic universal testing machine with a maximum load of 100 kN produced by Shimadzu Corporation from Japan was used for the tensile property testing at room temperature. Three typical temperatures (1050 °C, 1150 °C, and 1250 °C) are selected to simulate in-situ microstructure evolution influenced by UIT and inter-layer thermal effects using an ultra-high temperature laser confocal microscope. Direction: X; Before UIT

Four melts were prepared by using a medium frequency induction furnace and the chemical compositions of these prepared samples are given in Table 1. The produced stainless-steel alloys were subjected for solution treatment at 1100 °C for about 1 h, followed by water quenching. Samples were prepared through grinding and polishing sequence and etched by using 100 ml Hcl, 33 ml HNO 3, and few drops of H 2SO 4. The etched surface has been observed at high magnification using SEM in attached with EDS. Cu Kα-target diffractometer with wavelength 1.54184 A° has been used for determining the constituent phases of the observed austenitic stainless steel. Round tensile specimens are machined according to the specification of the ASTM E8 − 16b of 6 mm diameter and 32 mm gauge length. The tensile test is carried out using a 300 kN Shenzhen Wance Testing Machine at room temperature with constant crosshead velocity of 1 mm/min and strain rate 0.1 S -1. Ultimate tensile strength, 0.2 % yield strength, and elongation to fracture were estimated throughout the tensile test. Standard Charpy V-notch specimens were prepared according to the specification of ASTM A370 and tested at room temperature on PKP450 impact-testing machine to measure the energy transferred to the stainless-steel samples and the average of two tests was adopted. Specimens were corrosion tested using cyclic anodic polarization technique. The samples were prepared with mirror surface and were involved as working electrodes in 3 electrodes system, which contains saturated calomel electrode (SCE) (reference electrode) and Pt wire (counter electrode). The samples exposed area to the solution were fixed (1 cm 2) during the investigation in 3.5 % NaCl solution at the room temperature. The cyclic anodic polarization measurements were carried out starting from −0.3 V. Processing Text: High-purity Fe, Mn, Co, Cr, and C (≥99.8 wt%) were utilized as raw materials. Initially, these materials were melted in a vacuum arc furnace to produce an ingot with a nominal composition of Fe 49.5Mn 30Co 10Cr 10C 0.5(at.%), forming a metastable interstitial high-entropy alloy (iHEA). The ingot was hot-rolled at 900 °C with a thickness reduction of 50 %. Following this, it was homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h in an argon-protected tube furnace. The alloy was then cold-rolled at room temperature with a 60 % thickness reduction. After cold rolling, the alloy sheet was cut into dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a specified gauge length. At this stage, the material exhibits a high yield strength of 1110 MPa, but its fracture strain is significantly limited to only 8 %, indicating relatively severe embrittlement. Consequently, in the final processing step, the cold-rolled Fe 49.5Mn 30Co 10Cr 10C 0.5iHEA specimens were annealed in the temperature range of 850 °C-1050 °C (with 100 °C intervals) for 3 min, producing the iHEAs with various grain sizes. Processing Text: The 5Ni alloy ingot was meticulously cast in an argon (Ar) atmosphere using the arc-melting technique. After casting, the ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 1 h in a high-temperature muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. The homogenized ingot was then subjected to a hot and cold rolling process, reducing its thickness to approximately 1 mm. Dog-bone-shaped tensile samples, with a gauge length of 10 mm and a cross-sectional area of 3 × 1 mm 2, were fabricated using wire cutting. Annealing of the cold-rolled (85 % thickness reduction) MEA at 900 °C produced a partially-recrystallized, L12-type nanoparticle-hardened MEA containing recrystallized grains with an average size of 3.2 μm, a geometrically-necessary dislocation (GND) density of 1.9 × 1014 m−2 and a {110}<112> texture, while the unrecrystallized grains show an average size of 7.6 μm, a GND density of 8.9 × 1014 m−2, and a {110}<111> texture. Subsequently, one as-cold-rolled MEA sample was aged at 900 °C for 24 h to produce a refined microstructure. All the heat treatment of samples was cooled by water quenching. An MEA ingot Ni 42.4Co 24.3Cr 24.3Al 3Ti 3V 3(at.%) of 10 kg was cast using a magnetic suspension melting technique, where a mixture of Ni, Co, Cr, Al, Ti, and V pieces with purity higher than 99 % and dimensional size smaller than 10 mm are used. During the magnetic suspension melting, a voltage of 550V and a current of 450A was adopted, which was remelted by 2∼3 times to ensure compositional homogeneity. A 10 mm thick piece was cut off via electrical discharge machining from the as-cast ingot and homogenized at 1150 °C for 4 h followed by water-quenching, which was followed by cold-rolling to a total thickness reduction of 85 %. It is worth noting that a thickness reduction rate of 5 % was adopted for each pass of cold-rolling to avoid cracks. The five equiatomic four-element alloys were manufactured using induction melting and yielded cylindrical ingots with a diameter of approximately 60 mm. Macroscopic observation showed the presence of dendrites in these as-cast materials. Therefore, the alloys were homogenized at 1150 ⁰C for 24 h inside stainless-steel bags to minimize oxidation and promote chemical homogenization. The cylinders were subsequently sliced into four sections longitudinally. The smaller segments were deformed to a nominal compressive strain of −0.3 in an Enerpac machine with a 100-ton capacity. The deformation could not be conducted at ambient temperature because the samples cracked; therefore, they were preheated to 400 °C. The samples were subsequently heat treated at 900 ⁰C for 1 hour in order to ensure recrystallization following deformation. These temperatures were selected due to their successful use in previous studies to ensure the homogenization of chemical elements and recrystallization. Fully recrystallized; Grain size: 70 μm

Processing Text: The five equiatomic four-element alloys were manufactured using induction melting and yielded cylindrical ingots with a diameter of approximately 60 mm. Macroscopic observation showed the presence of dendrites in these as-cast materials. Therefore, the alloys were homogenized at 1150 ⁰C for 24 h inside stainless-steel bags to minimize oxidation and promote chemical homogenization. The cylinders were subsequently sliced into four sections longitudinally. The smaller segments were deformed to a nominal compressive strain of −0.3 in an Enerpac machine with a 100-ton capacity. The deformation could not be conducted at ambient temperature because the samples cracked; therefore, they were preheated to 400 °C. The samples were subsequently heat treated at 900 ⁰C for 1 hour in order to ensure recrystallization following deformation. These temperatures were selected due to their successful use in previous studies to ensure the homogenization of chemical elements and recrystallization. Processing Text: Hybrid manufactured components were made by depositing TC11 alloy on the rolled TC11 plates. The rolled TC11 substrate with dimensions of 225 × 40 × 100 mm3 was chosen as the substrate, and it was polished and washed with acetone and anhydrous alcohol in order to remove the oil and oxide layer. The optimized laser DED processing parameters were set as follows: the laser power of 3.5 kW, the scanning velocity of 16 mm/s, the powder feeding rate of 1000 g/h, and using the crosshatching scanning strategy along the short side. During the whole forming process, the oxygen content was always kept below 50 ppm. The TC11 titanium alloy powders with a spherical morphology for the deposition experiment were prepared by the plasma rotation electrode process method. After deposition, the hybrid manufactured TC11 sample was then immediately annealed at 530 °C for 2 h in order to eliminate residual stress and it was labeled as as-deposited sample. Three different double annealing heat treatments were conducted on the as-deposited hybrid manufactured TC11 sample. As displayed in Fig. 1d, in this study, 990 °C (below the TβSZ), 1013 °C (between the TβSZ and TβLDZ) and 1035 °C (above the TβLDZ) were chosen as the first step high annealing temperature and the second annealing temperature was all 530 °C. The soaking time for the first and second step annealing treatments were 1 h and 6 h, respectively. They both followed by air cooling to room temperature. The samples were placed directly in a furnace at the target temperature to prevent any possible changes in the microstructure during heating. These heat treatments were denoted as the 990HT, 1013HT and 1035HT in turn. The metallographic samples of the as-deposited, 990HT, 1013HT and 1035HT hybrid manufactured TC11 alloy were taken from the transverse section. These specimens were prepared using standard mechanical polishing methods and etched using Kroll's reagent (1 ml HF + 6 ml HNO3 + 43 ml H2O). Annealing temperature: 990°C; Processing state: heat-treated

A series of CoCrFeNi(B 4C) x(x = 0, 0.01, 0.05, and 0.1) HEAs composites were fabricated via vacuum arc melting of high-purity metal elements (purity >99.95 wt%) and B 4C ceramic particles in a water-cooled copper crucible under a high-purity argon atmosphere. Each sample was remelted at least five times to ensure uniform chemical composition. The samples were defined as B0, B0.01, B0.05, and B0.1, respectively. The samples were mechanically polished to a mirror finish, followed by vertical mechanical polishing and etching with aqua regia (HNO 3:HCl = 1:3). The samples for TEM observation were mechanically thinned to approximately 50 μm, punched into 3 mm diameter discs, and electro-polished in a solution of 10 vol% HClO4 + 90 vol% CH3OH at −20 °C, applying a voltage of 20 V. The ingots were precisely machined into cylindrical compression specimens (Φ 3 × 6 mm) using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Compressive properties were evaluated using an INSTRON-5982 universal testing machine equipped with a mechanical tensile tester, at a constant strain rate of 0.48 mm/min. Vickers hardness measurements were conducted on the samples using an FM-ARS 9000 micro-hardness tester. Nano-indentation tests were performed with a Hysitron TI-900 triboindenter integrated with an in-situ atomic force microscope (AFM). The tests were performed with the following conditions: an 8000 μN load, a loading rate of 1000 μN/s, a 2 s hold time, and an unloading rate of 4000 μN/s, using an indenter with an effective diameter of approximately 450 nm. Processing Text: The WNbTaVTi RHEA was successfully synthesized by spark plasma sintering (SPS) technology. The raw materials for ball milling were high-purity W, Nb, Ta, V and Ti powders. The powder was ball milled using a planetary ball mill (QM-3SP2, Nanjing Chishun Technology Co., Ltd.) with zirconia balls as the grinding media. In the process of ball milling, the ball-to-powder ratio was maintained at 5:1, and the equipment ran at a speed of 300 rpm, and alcohol was introduced as auxiliary grinding medium to promote the crushing and mixing of powders. The whole milling process was performed for 24 h with intermittent cooling to avoid excessive temperature rise. Post-milling, the powder was sieved through a 200-mesh screen to ensure a uniform particle size. The SPS process was carried out using a LABOX-350 spark plasma sintering system. The powder was loaded into a 13 mm diameter graphite die and then evacuated to a vacuum level of less than 10 Pa. A uniaxial pressure of 30 MPa was applied using a hydraulic press prior to sintering. The samples were first heated at a rate of 100 °C/min to 1200 °C and then held for 10 min to increase the solid solubility. Afterwards, the samples were heated to the target temperatures (1400, 1500, and 1600 °C) and held for 5 min. The temperature was monitored using an infrared pyrometer focused on the surface of the die. After sintering, the samples were allowed to cool naturally in the low vacuum atmosphere. Once cooled, the samples were carefully extracted and any flash or excess material was removed by gentle grinding. Sintering temperature: 1500 °C; Peak yield strength and compressive strength

Processing Text: Gas atomization, which includes free fall gas atomization (FFGA) and confined gas atomization (CGA), is a high-speed, high-pressure technique that uses gases such as helium, nitrogen, or argon to break down molten metal. In this process, inert gas is forcefully sprayed from a dedicated device or reservoir into the atomization chamber under high pressure. The forceful impact of the gas causes vigorous deformation, primary breakup, and secondary breakup of the molten metal, leading to the formation of small spherical particles. A gas atomizer system comprises essential components such as the gas storage system, metal tundish, atomizer system, spray system, and powder collection system. Research has consistently shown that gas atomization produces spherical metal powder with high production efficiency. GA offers broad applicability, excellent powder characteristics, controllable processes, and high production efficiency. The size of powders decreases with the increase of atomization pressure, gas velocity, GMR and superheat of melt. The material selected for the test was 45CrNiMoVA ultra-high-strength steel. The received materials were cylindrical bars with a diameter of 52 mm and a length of 200 mm. The cylindrical bars have undergone two heat treatment processes (normalizing heat treatment, quenching and tempering treatment). Slow wire cutting was used to cut a ϕ21 mm × 150 mm cylindrical sample from the cylindrical rod. After grinding the center hole, fine turning, and fine grinding, the sample is processed into a sample with a gauge length of ϕ12.5 mm × 30 mm. The cylindrical sample was electrothermally inlaid, polished, and corroded for 15 s with a 4 % nitric acid alcohol solution, and the microstructure of the cross section after roller rolling was observed on TESCAN MIRA 3 (SEM). Vickers hardness (MHVS-30AT) tester is used to hold for 15 s under 0.5 kg preload, measure the surface hardness of 10 different positions on the sample, and take the average value. In addition, a 3D laser scanning electron microscope (VK-X100, Kenyence) is used to measure the surface morphology of the sample at two ends and in the middle of the cylindrical surface. Surface morphology measurements were made using a 20× objective lens. The residual compressive stress on the specimen surface is measured by PROTO-LXRD X-ray. 1 mm aperture collimator is used. The diffraction angle is {211} Kα = 156.413°. Maximum beta is 25°. The number of beta angles is 5. Exposure time is 2 s. The surface normal residual stress was measured three times and the residual stress along the depth of the layer was measured one time. The cylindrical samples were inlaid, ground, and polished with argon ions, and the grain characteristics of the surface layers of the strengthened specimens were analyzed by using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, JSM 7200F). The microstructure morphology of different processes was also analyzed by transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI Talos F200X). The fracture morphology was observed using TESCAN MIRA 3 (SEM). The strengthening mechanism of the PT-DR process sequence on the surface modification of 45CrNiMoVA steel was revealed. The PT-DR process provides an effective surface strengthening method for the key structural parts with weak cold plastic deformation. The main chemical elements of the steel are shown in Table 1. The tensile yield strength of the material reaches 1639 MPa, the compression yield strength reaches 1813 MPa, and the torsional shear yield strength reaches 1249 MPa after heat treatment. The DR strengthening is carried out through the workpiece rotation speed ndrof 350 r/min, feed fof 0.028 mm/r, rolling cutter amount apof 0.8 mm, and each sample is rolled twice, as shown in Fig. 1c. A roller with arc profile is used, and the hardness of the roller is greater than that of the sample. The PT strengthening and torsional fatigue tests were conducted on the MTS 809.25 torsional fatigue testing machine, as shown in Fig. 1d. The sample was subjected to 5 repeated pre-twists with an angle of 13.7° ( θpre), a torsion loading rate of 8°/min and an unloading rate of 200 N·m/min, releasing to zero torque each time. Each group of samples was treated according to the process sequence. Under the temperature of 19 °C, three samples of each group in the final state after strengthening for the fatigue test. The maximum shear stress level τ maxis 1200 MPa with a sine waveform, the stress ratio R= 0, and the frequency is 7 Hz. The microstructure and grain characteristics of the material is characterized on the circular cross section of the sample, and the microhardness is characterized on the surface of the specimen, as shown in Fig. 1b. Processing Text: Using vacuum induction melting, a 50-kg ingot of steel with the composition Fe-24Mn-8Al-1C was produced. The ingot was heated to 1200 °C for two hours before being hot-forged into a slab that measured 35 mm × 100 mm in section. The slab was swan into several chunks with a length of 150 mm. The pieces were hot-rolled to 5 mm thick plates after being homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h. Following air cooling to room temperature, the hot-rolled plates were further rolled into 1-mm-thick sheets. Some cold rolled samples were annealed at 750 °C for 5 min and then water quenched to produce heterogeneous microstructures. Besides, for comparison, other cold rolled samples were annealed between 750 and 1150 °C for 30 min respectively and subsequently water quenched in order to produce homogeneous microstructures. In order to study the effect of aging strengthening, all above annealed samples were aged at 550 °C for 30 min and then water quenched. Besides, in order to explore the potential of aging strengthening in these investigated steels, the 750-30 samples have been aged at 550 °C for 4, 6 and 8 h, respectively. Processing Text: Pure metals (>99.99 wt%) of Ni and Nb were used to fabricate Ni-Nb alloy targets with nominal composition Ni 60Nb 40(at.%) using a vacuum arc melting furnace and a vacuum casting machine in a high-purity Ar gas atmosphere. All ingots were remelted four times to ensure chemical homogeneity. The cast ingot was then sliced and polished into targets of ∼2 inches in diameter and ∼3 mm in thickness. The amorphous thin films were prepared on clean (100)-Si wafers in an ultrahigh vacuum direct current MS system (TA16-10D) with a base pressure of ∼2 × 10 −6Pa at different deposition power ranging from 15 W to 180 W at room temperature. The alloy target was placed directly underneath the substrate without an oblique angle, and the distance from the target to the substrate was 45 mm. During the sputtering process, the deposition pressure, substrate rotation speed, and flow rate were kept at 1.5 Pa, 3 rpm, and 40 sccm, respectively. The film thickness was controlled to be 1.0 ± 0.1 μm by changing the deposition time under various power conditions with an average deposition efficiency of ∼0.017 nm/J. The substrate temperature was measured by fixing a Ni-Cr thermocouple on the Si substrate surface (the film growth plane) to monitor the real-time temperature variation. To avoid unexpected oxidation and contamination, annealing treatments were performed in the MS chamber directly (without venting the chamber) under a base vacuum of 5 × 10 −4Pa at 613 K, 713 K, 804 K, and 843 K for 1 h. Selected Ni-Nb thin films were immersed in 0.5 M hydrochloric acid solution in water for up to 8 h. The topography of these sample surfaces was measured after different immersion durations by tapping mode AFM with stiff single crystalline Si tips (type: NCHR, manufactured by NanoSensors, Switzerland). After 8 h of immersion in an acidic solution, the chemical composition of the film surfaces was measured and compared to their composition before corrosion treatment by X-ray photoelectronic spectroscopy (XPS, K-Alpha +system, ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The XPS measurements were recorded with a monochromated Al Kα source (1486.6 eV, 12 kV) and a spot size of 400 μm 2in ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) conditions (base pressure below 5 × 10 −7Pa). Besides, angle-resolved XPS (ARXPS, Axis Supra +, manufactured by Shimadzu, Japan) was adopted to evaluate the thickness and structure of the oxidation layer on the film surface. The measurements were performed with Al Kα radiation. The X-ray spot had an elliptical shape with a long axis of 0.7 mm and a short axis of 0.3 mm. Estimated from micropillar compression test; Deposition power: 15 W

Processing Text: This work presents the fabrication of a metastable non-equiatomic Co45Cr25(FeNi)30 MEA using PBF-LB. The alloy was printed using EOS M100 PBF-LB machine equipped with 200W Yb-fiber laser. Extensive design of experiments (DOE) was performed to optimize the printing parameters for high density. Based on the DOE results, the samples used in this study were produced with 90W of laser power, 1010 mm/s of scan speed, 0.07 mm of hatch distance, 20 μm of layer thickness, with a stripe scan strategy and a stripe width of 5 mm with 67° scan rotation between subsequent layers. The as-printed samples were metallographically prepared for microstructural characterizations by first grinding the samples using SiC emery sheets from 500 grit to 4000 grit. The ground samples were then electrochemically polished using the Struers A2 electrolyte to achieve a mirror-like finish. The preparation of TEM samples involved a two-step process. Initially, samples of approximately 1 mm thick were extracted along both vertical and horizontal cross sections from the as-printed bulk material. These extracted samples were then thinned down to a thickness of approximately 120 μm and punched into discs of 3 mm diameter. The final stage of the preparation involved twin-jet electrochemical polishing of the discs using Struers A2 electrolyte performed at −2 °C and 30 V until the hole is formed at the center of the sample. Tensile samples of 4 mm in gauge length, 1.2 mm in thickness, and 2 mm in width were extracted from the as-printed samples, using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Miniature dogbone shaped tensile samples were extracted from the as-printed samples, with a gauge length of 7 mm and thickness of 1.2 mm, using EDM. The extracted samples were then carefully mechanically ground and polished, finishing with colloidal suspension of 50 nm sized silica solution (OPS, Struers) to ensure that there was no deformed layer induced by grinding. The in-situ tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4s−1 to a maximum nominal strain of 40 %. Ex-situ tensile testing was performed on the Kammrath & Weiss tensile stage to obtain mechanical properties of the alloy in the as-printed state, using the displacement control mode equivalent to a strain rate of 2.5 × 10−4s−1. In-situ EBSD combined with tensile testing was performed in GEMINI 1550 SEM equipped with the velocity detector. The in-situ EBSD and tensile tests were performed using a Kammrath & Weiss tensile stage mounted inside the SEM and at a strain rate of ∼2.5 × 10−4s−1. Firstly, a carefully polished tensile sample was mounted onto the tensile stage inside the SEM and the EBSD data from the as-printed state was obtained at zero load. During the tensile testing, the loading was stopped at nominal strains of 15 %, 25 %, and 40 % to acquire EBSD data. Building direction: Horizontal; Processing state: as-printed

Processing Text: Two types of base metals (BMs) were utilized in this study: 6082-T6 aluminum alloy and WHS-T6 aluminum alloy, both provided as 2 mm thick plates. The WHS alloy represents a novel aluminum alloy, distinguished from the 6082-T6 aluminum alloy primarily by minor differences in its copper content and the composition of other alloying elements. Prior to welding, the BMs were mechanically polished to eliminate the surface oxide layer, followed by cleaning with acetone and ethanol to remove any residual contaminants. A NIR-blue hybrid laser welding system was employed to join the two BMs. This system primarily consists of a NIR laser, a blue laser, a hybrid laser head, and a dedicated welding platform. The NIR laser utilized was the Raycus RFL-C3000S, characterized by a Gaussian energy density distribution, a maximum output power of 3000 W, a fiber core diameter of 25 μm, and an emission wavelength of 1064 nm. The blue laser source was the Raycus RFL-B500D, featuring a flat-top energy density distribution, a peak power of 500 W, a fiber core diameter of 400 μm, and a wavelength of 450 nm. During welding, 99.99 % purity argon was supplied at a flow rate of 25 L/min as a shielding gas to prevent oxidation. The principal parameters used for hybrid laser welding are presented in Table 2. Welded joints were initially sectioned utilizing a wire-cut electrical discharge machine. The resulting metallographic samples underwent a systematic polishing procedure using SiC paper. Subsequently, they were refined further with diamond paste and colloidal silica solution to achieve a smooth, mirror-like surface devoid of scratches. Following these preparatory steps, the samples were subjected to chemical etching with 0.5 % HF for a duration of 25 seconds. A subset of these samples was then anodized using Barker’s reagent, a solution consisting of 7 ml of 48 % HBF 4 and 93 ml of distilled water, with the anodization current meticulously regulated between 200 and 300 mA for 30 seconds. The metallographic samples were chemically polished for 40 seconds under an electrolysis voltage of 20 V using a high-chloride ethanol solution. Processing Text: The experimental material consisted of 316L austenitic stainless steel rods with a diameter of 30 mm. The material was hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness, followed by solution treatment at 1050 °C for 1 h. Before each rolling pass, the initial material was immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min. The thickness reduction per pass was kept below 5 %. Surface cracks developed when the total thickness reduction reached 70 %. Consequently, the final thickness was reduced by 70 %, resulting in a thickness of 1.2 mm for the cryo-rolled sample, which was labeled as CryoR sample. After cryo-rolling, the samples were subjected to annealing at 700 °C 20 min, 750 °C 6 min, and a sequential 700 °C 20 min + 750 °C 6 min process, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled as 700A, 750A, and 700A-750A, respectively. All heat treatment processes were performed in a muffle furnace without a protective atmosphere. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (5105, SSANS-CMT) at room temperature (24 °C) and liquid nitrogen temperature (−196 °C) with a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. All tensile samples were cut along the rolling direction into dog-bone shapes with a gauge length of 34 mm, width of 10 mm, and thickness of 1 mm. Each test was repeated at least three times to ensure accuracy. To evaluate inhomogeneous deformation, load-unload-reload (LUR) tests were also performed under the same conditions as the tensile tests to quantify the back stress (σ B) component. The microstructural evolution of the samples along the rolling direction (RD) was characterized. XRD analysis was conducted to examine phase transformation with a diffraction angle range of 40°-100° and a scanning speed of 2°/min, using Cu-Kα radiation at 40 kV and 150 mA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford) was employed for quantitative analysis of the phase microstructure. After mechanical polishing, samples were electropolished using a 10 % perchloric acid solution at 20 V for 20-25 s. EBSD measurements were performed on a Zeiss Auriga scanning electron microscope with a step size of 100 nm at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV. Processing state: Two-step annealing (700A-750A); Test temperature: Room Temperature

The specimens were initially homogenized at 1200 °C for 1 h and air-cooled to room temperature, followed by a double-step aging process: held at 720 °C for 8 h, furnace-cooled to 620 °C, and maintained at this temperature for an additional 8 h before air-cooled to room temperature. Processing Text: A powder metallurgy (PM) AA6061-10Cu hybrid material was fabricated by a thermomechanical consolidation technique involving hot extrusion of the compact of an AA6061 aluminum alloy and Cu powder blend. The blended powder was die-pressed uniaxially with a pressure of 750 MPa and a holding time of 5 min to produce two cylindrical powder compacts with dimensions of 52 mm in diameter and 55 mm in height. The powder compacts were induction heated to 450 °C at a heating rate for 30 °C/min, held at the temperature for 5 min, and then extruded with extrusion ratios of 9:1 and 25:1, respectively. Part of the as-extruded rod with an extrusion ratio of 9:1 was solution heated at 500 °C for a very short time of 10 min to mitigate the Kirkendall effect at the interfaces between the aluminum matrix and Cu particles, water quenched and then aged at 170 °C for 8 h to achieve a tailored-T6 heat treated state. Part of the as-extruded rod with an extrusion ratio of 25:1 was solution heated at 450 °C for 10 min to avoid excessive reactions at the interfaces between the aluminum matrix and Cu particles, water quenched and then aged at 170 °C for 8 h to also achieve a tailored-T6 heat treated state. Extrusion ratio: 9:1; As-extruded state

Processing Text: In this experiment, CuCrZr metal powder with a size of 15-53 μm was prepared by gas atomization method. The chemical composition and content of CuCrZr alloy powder are shown in Table 1. The LPBF process was used to prepare CuCrZr alloy samples, and the process parameters included a laser power (P), scanning speed (V), scanning spacing (H), and layer thickness (L). The volume energy density (Ea) was calculated using the formula: Ea = A P / (V H L). The cubes, cylinders, and tensile specimens were printed for subsequent microstructure characterization and performance testing. The samples were preheated at 150 °C before use, and the scanning strategy was a chessboard, with each layer rotated by 67°. The forming process adopted an argon atmosphere, and the oxygen content was controlled below 100 ppm. The samples were cut using an electrical discharge machining (EDM) process. The phase composition of the original powder and the sample was characterized by an X-ray diffractometer (XRD). The morphology of the original powder and the microstructure of the printed sample were studied by optical microscope (OM) and scanning electron microscope (SEM). The microstructure and phase composition of the samples were characterized by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The density of all 10 × 10 × 10 mm³ printed samples was measured by the Archimedes method, and each sample was measured seven times. Tensile tests were carried out to study the mechanical properties of printed transverse specimens at room temperature using a universal tensile machine. The conductivity of a wafer with a diameter of 10 mm was measured using a Sigma 2008 digital eddy current metal conductivity meter. The thermal diffusivity of the sample was accurately measured by a laser thermal conductivity meter, and the specific heat capacity was detected by a specific heat capacity device. The actual density ρ of the sample was measured according to the Archimedes drainage method. Processed with optimized construction parameters; Relative density: 98.07%; Mechanical properties: good

Processing Text: The nominal composition of the Co-based superalloys studied in this paper is Co-30Ni-9Al-2W-4Ti-xTa (at.%), where x is 0, 1, and 2, respectively. The raw materials used were of purity above 99.9 wt %. Alloy ingots were prepared using a vacuum arc melting furnace and cooled in a water-cooled copper crucible in an Ar atmosphere. Each ingot was remelted at least four times to ensure uniform alloy composition. The alloys were solutionized in a vacuum furnace at 1250 °C for 10 h, followed by aging at 900 °C for 100 h, and then air-cooled. The resulting samples are referred to as 0Ta, 1Ta, and 2Ta. Samples prepared by spraying in a perchlorate ethanol solution at −20 °C with a voltage of 40 V. Condition: room temperature

Cu/Ti composite plates with shuttle-heterostructure (SH) were prepared by accumulative roll bonding (ARB) process. Before the first ARB process, industrial pure copper and industrial pure titanium surfaces to be laminated were mechanically polished and wiped by a louver blade and industrial alcohol, respectively. Then, an 11-layer laminated billet was obtained by alternately stacking in the order of Cu/Ti. After that, the first pass of ARB at room temperature was carried out, and an intermediate billet was obtained. Subsequently, the intermediate billet was cut from the center and the surface to be laminated of intermediate billets was mechanically polished with the louver blade. After stacking, the second pass of ARB at room temperature was carried out. Repeat the above surface treatment and ARB process until 3 passes ARB at room temperature were completed, and an ARB Cu/Ti composite plate was obtained. In order to achieve interfacial microalloying of heterostructures, ARB Cu/Ti composite plates were held at 100 °C for 1 h to complete the vacuum diffusion heat treatment. Afterwards, water cooling to room temperature was carried out to obtain heat-treated Cu/Ti composite plates. Condition: After 3 passes ARB at room temperature

Processing Text: AZ91 (an alloy composed of 9 % aluminum, 1 % zinc, and Mg) is chosen as the matrix material because of its distinct advantages, including high specific strength, affordability, and excellent corrosion resistance. Homogenization heat treatment was conducted on both the base and composite materials, leading to the suspension of the β-Mg17Al12 secondary phase into the primary α-Mg matrix. This heat treatment significantly improved mechanical properties, enhancing strength and ductility by 38 % and 136 % in base material and by 25 % and 145 % in composite, respectively. The mechanisms underlying these enhancements were elucidated through detailed analysis of fractographs and microstructures, highlighting the potential of homogenized in-situ composites for advanced engineering applications. Processing Text: The Al-Zn-Mg-Cu-TiC/Ti alloy samples were subjected to microstructural characterization using SEM, TEM, EBSD, and XRD techniques. The samples were mechanically ground and polished. The phase composition of the samples under various heat treatment conditions was analyzed using a Bruker D8 Focus X-ray diffractometer (XRD), utilizing Cu Kα radiation and a scan step size of 0.02°. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) images were obtained using a Thermo Scientific TMApreo 2 C field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an Oxford Nordlys Nano EBSD system. Backscattered electron (BSE) images and compositional analysis were conducted using a Coxem EM-30AX+ SEM equipped with an EDAX-APEX energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) system. The TEM samples were sectioned into 5 × 5 × 0.1 mm³ thin foils and ion-thinned for 3 hours using an ion thinning system. A FEI Technai G2 F20 transmission electron microscope (TEM), fitted with a high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) detector, was utilized for selected area electron diffraction (SAED) and high-resolution TEM (HRTEM) phase analysis. The size and distribution of grain boundary precipitates (GBPs), precipitate-free zones (PFZ), and matrix precipitates (MPs) were statistically evaluated using ImageJ software. The study utilized AA2195 Al-Cu-Li alloy test plates in the T8 state. The test plate was prepared through four processes: vacuum furnace smelting, semi-continuous casting, hot rolling, and heat treatment. Subsequently, wire electrical discharge machines were used to cut the material into a plate measuring 150 mm × 50 mm × 6 mm. Before welding, the oil on the surfaces of both the test plate and the welding wire was removed using acetone. The surface oxide film was then eliminated by pickling in a mixed acid solution (10 % HF, 10 % HNO 3, 20 % H 2SO 4, and 60 % H 2O) at 60 °C for 10 min. Finally, the test plate and welding wire were rinsed in flowing water and placed in a drying oven at 80 °C for 30 min. Notably, the test plate did not require the cutting of a groove. An I-shaped groove was utilized for direct butt welding. During the VPPA welding process, argon with a purity of 99.99 % was employed as both the plasma gas and the shielding gas. The ultrasonic power supply outputted a frequency of 28 kHz, with an amplitude range of 1-12 μm. A pneumatic system was used to press the ultrasonic head on the test plates with a certain pressure. Condition: ultrasonic amplitude of 6 μm (UWJ 1)

Processing Text: C and N were added into the base alloy by using pure carbon and Fe 2N, and the two alloys were referred to as C-HEA and N-HEA, respectively. The two alloys were cast in a vacuum induction furnace, followed by wet chemical analysis to control the exact composition after casting. The nominal composition of the interstitial contents is 0.5 at%. However, doping N is more difficult to maintain, and the actual composition of N doping is 1 at%. The cold-rolled HEAs were notated as C-CR and N-CR for carbon-doped and nitrogen-doped HEA, respectively. To minimize significant grain growth during recrystallization and compare the effect of grain refinement and interstitial types with previous work [8,15], short-duration annealing was performed under three conditions: 800 °C for 5 minutes, 800 °C for 10 minutes, and 900 °C for 5 minutes, respectively. Henceforth, the carbon-doped TRIP alloys after annealing are designated as C800-5, C800-10, and C900-5, corresponding to the annealing conditions at 800°C for 5 minutes, 800°C for 10 minutes, and 900°C for 5 minutes, respectively. O was added to the MEAs in the form of ZrO2 granules of 1 mm in diameter. The alloy ingot plates with dimensions of 8 × 2 × 70 mm3 were melted under an argon atmosphere in a water-cooled copper crucible furnace, flipped and remelted six times, and then suction cast using a water-cooled copper mold.
