A novel high strength Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 HEA was developed in this work. The spherical powders were prepared by the dual process of mechanical alloying and high temperature remelting spheroidization (DP) since such technology has combined effect of mechanical milling (plastic deformation) and temperature lifting (atomic diffusion) to achieve the composition homogenization. At the same time, the powder prepared by gas atomization (GA) method is compared, and the printed parts are compared under the same parameters of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). The yield strength (YS), ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and average elongation (ε) of the samples measured by DP-SLM were 953 MPa, 1159 MPa and 14.8 %, respectively. The hot compression test of Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 was carried out with Gleeble-3800 thermal simulation machine. The thermal processing diagram of the alloy under different stress variables was drawn by establishing the thermal deformation constitutive equation. The DP-SLM material recovers when the deformation temperature is 1000 ℃ with deformation rate stays at 0.01 s−1. Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 alloy processed at 1050-1150°C and a strain rate of 0.005∼ 0.1 s−1 shows high power dissipation efficiency (up to 37 %) and better dynamic recrystallization structure. Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 can be considered widely used in the engine combustion chamber, guide, turbine blade and turbo disk four hot end components. The RHEA spherical powders with uniform composition were prepared by mechanical alloying (MA) and High temperature remelting spherification technology (HTRS). MA technology achieves the composition uniformity of RHEA powder through the combined action of mechanical milling (plastic deformation) and temperature raising (atomic diffusion). Nb3Cr2Ti0.9W0.4Fe6 HEA powders were prepared by mechanical alloying process. After the alloyed powder was dried sufficiently, high temperature remelting equipment was used to prepare spherical powder, provided by Shaanxi Zhiqi Kaiwu Co. The printing parameters were set: laser power reached up to 550 W with 3200 mm/s scanning speed. laser wavelength is 1.06 μm, the thickness of each layer is 0.02 mm and spot diameter is 0.1 mm. 316 steel was regarded as the basic materials (BM) and its composition is shown in Table 3. In conclusion, MA can promote the alloying of refractory elements, while HTRS could change the powder morphology (spheroidization). Processing Text: Ti-1Fe feedstocks were prepared by mechanically mixing 1 wt% of Fe powder into a gas-atomised CP-Ti powder with spheroidal morphology (TILOP-45, Osaka Titanium). Two types of Fe powders were used: a fine Fe powder of ∼5 μm (FEE16PB, Kojundo Chemical) and a coarser Fe powder of ∼25 μm (300 M, Kobe Steel, pre-sieved <45 μm mesh). Mixing was performed by rocking mill (AV-2, Asahi Rika) in 500 g batches for 1 h at a setting of 60 Hz. To promote mixing, ⌀5 mm zirconia balls were added to each mixture at a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 1:10. The prepared feedstocks were consolidated into rectangular test coupons (10 mm × 10 mm × 60 mm) using a commercial laser powder bed fusion system (TruPrint 1000, TRUMPF). Test coupons were built directly onto a pure-Ti substrate, using build parameters including laser power fixed at 160 W, layer thickness fixed at 20 μm, and varied energy densities and hatch spacings (60-S, 60-W, 120-S, 120-W, 180-S, 180-W). Tensile test specimens were extracted from the centre of each test coupon by wire electrical discharge machining with the tensile direction oriented orthogonal to the build direction and parallel to the long edge of the rectangular test coupon. The oxygen (O), nitrogen (N), and hydrogen (H) contents in the powders and built materials were evaluated by inert gas fusion analysis. The mechanical properties were evaluated by uniaxial tensile testing. Prepared from 3 to 8 μm Fe powder at higher volumetric energy densities; Satisfies ASTM requirements for PBF-LB/M Ti-6Al-4V

Processing Text: TiCp/Ti6Al4V composites were prepared by low energy ball milling in a QM-3SP2 ball mill with a ball-to-powder ratio of 3:1, and a mixing time of 6 h was used to ensure the powders were evenly mixed. Samples without UIT (LMD sample) and with UIT (LMD-UIT sample) were prepared by the controlling variable method to study the effect of UIT. The experimental procedure was carried out using a one-way scanning strategy and in a chamber filled with argon atmosphere to prevent the melt pool from oxidation. The LMD and UIT processes were operated synchronously. The laser equipment (RFL-c6000x, Raycus Co., Ltd., China) had a laser beam diameter of 3 mm and a center wavelength of 1080 ± 5 nm. The UIT equipment equipped with the GS-S series ultrasonic generator with an ultrasonic frequency of 20 kHz and amplitude of 16 μm was employed in this work. Samples were grinded, mechanically polished, and then etched with Kroll's solution (2 mL HF, 4 mL HNO3, and 94 mL H2O). The cross-section in the vertical scanning direction was obtained by wire cutting for microstructure analysis. TEM foils were prepared by mechanical grinding followed by ion milling. Tensile specimens were cut parallel to the scanning direction, and each group consisted of three specimens with dimensions shown in Fig. 3(b). Processing Text: Samples were manufactured using EOS Ti-6Al-4V grade 23 powder on an EOS M290 (EOS GmbH, Germany) LPBF machine housed at the ISO 13485 certified Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) of the Central University of Technology in South Africa. Specimens were produced in three batches, and a representative portion of each batch and specimen type was selected to measure the oxygen content to ensure this was kept below 0.013 wt%. The base plate was preheated to 80 °C, and a high-speed steel blade was used as a scraper. The process parameters consisted of a 40 μm layer thickness, 280 W laser power, 1300 mm/s scan speed, 100 μm spot size and a hatch distance of 120 μm. Bidirectional scanning was used, and the scan direction was rotated by 67° between layers. This set of process parameters results in a material with less than 0.01 % porosity [ 23 ]. For tensile specimens, cylinders with a diameter of D = 10 mm and a length of L = 100 mm were produced in the vertical (Z) and horizontal (X) directions relative to the axis of the LPBF machine (and according to ASTM 59200) that is aligned with the direction in which the load is applied. For fracture toughness specimens, Compact Tension (C(T)) specimens were produced as rectangular blocks to allow for the final dimensions of a width of W = 25 mm. C(T) specimens were produced in three orientations, with the first letter indicating the direction in which the load is applied and the second letter indicating the direction in which the crack propagates, that is, ZX, XZ and XY [ 6 ], as shown in Fig. 1 . After printing, the specimens were stress-relieved (SR) at 650 °C for 3 h in a TSH 15/50/180 vacuum furnace (Elite Thermal Systems, England) and then wire-cut from the build plate. The SR treatment was chosen to allow comparison with the literature [ 15 ]. Subsequent heat treatments were conducted at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in atmospheric air using a box furnace (Ultrafurn, South Africa). Therefore, at least 1 mm was removed by wire cutting or machining from all the heat-treated specimen surfaces to remove any α-case and oxide scale that may have formed. The heat treatment schedules, detailed in Table 1 , included the SR, an anneal (AN) heat treatment, chosen due to its simplicity combined with good tensile properties, and a duplex anneal (DA) heat treatment, chosen based on optimal tensile properties reported in the literature [ 6 , 25 ]. Furthermore, the heat treatments above T β (selected based on values available in the literature [ 9 , 15 ]) were combined with the stress relief (BtSR) and anneal (BtAN) heat treatments to mimic how SR or AN specimens would perform if the PBGs were equiaxed c . c It is acknowledged the above T β heat treatment is at the cost of PBG growth. Comparison to specimens with elongated PBGs is only based on orientation effects. After heat treatment, the specimens were machined and wire-cut to their final dimensions. Processing Text: The CuCrZr alloy powder used in the experiment was prepared by the plasma rotating electrode atomization process. Specimens were prepared by EB-PBF equipment (Xi'an Sailong Additive Technology Co., Ltd., China). The maximum forming size of EB-PBF equipment is 150 × 150 × 210 mm, and the maximum vacuum degree is 5 × 10 −3Pa. In order to imitate the aging heat treatment process of CuCrZr alloy in-situ to precipitate nano-precipitates, the powder bed temperatures were controlled to 300 °C, 400 °C and 500 °C during the EB-PBF process. The specific forming parameters refer to our previous research [ 14]. The powder bed temperature of the EB-PBF sample is 200 °C, the conventional sample without CPBT is labeled as EB-PBF. When printing EB-PBF samples, the powder is melted directly after the powder coating is completed. When printing CPBT samples, an electron beam is used to heat the entire powder bed after the powder spreading is completed. The thermocouple used to measure the powder bed temperature is installed under the base plate. The powder bed temperature fluctuates and cannot be controlled very accurately at present. When the powder bed temperature is too high or too low, the electron beam current will be dynamically adjusted. The samples with the CPBT at 250-350 °C are marked as 300 °C, and the samples with the CPBT at 350-450 °C and 450-550 °C are marked as 400 °C and 500 °C respectively. In this way, the sample is always maintained in the aging heat treatment temperature range during the entire printing process. This special thermal history is controlled similar to traditional aging treatment. The thermal history of different samples is shown in Fig. 1c, and the printing process parameters are shown in Table 1. The powder particle size distribution is 15-106 μm, where D50 is 43 μm and D90 is 67 μm. The elemental content of Cr and Zr in the powder was determined by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES), while the elemental content of O was determined by pulse heating inert gas fusion intrinsic absorption method. Impurities such as Fe, Si, and P were determined by ICP-AES. As-built sample with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 60 mm 3 to determine the microstructure, phase composition and mechanical properties. A Shimadzu universal testing machine AGS-X 10 KN was used to conduct uniaxial tensile experiments at a strain rate of 1 mm/min on flat dog-bone shaped samples with a gauge length of 25 × 6 × 2 mm 3 to evaluate room temperature mechanical properties. Tensile specimens were cut from the same position of the as-built specimen for comparison. All specimens were polished before tensile to ensure smooth surfaces. An eddy current metal conductivity meter (Sigma 2008B, China) was used to measure the conductivity of the specimens with a resolution of 0.01 %IACS and a measurement range of 0.8-110 %IACS. Before the conductivity was tested, the surface was polished with sandpaper to ensure that there were no large scratches. Then the surface was polished with 2.5 μm and 0.5 μm diamond spray polishing agents. Finally, the sample was cleaned and dried. Each sample was tested 3 times, and the remaining values were averaged. Optical microscopy (GX51, OM), scanning electron microscopy (Gemini SEM 300, SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopic mapping (EDS), and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) were used to characterize the sample microstructure. Among them, the scanning step size in EBSD experiment is 1.5 μm, and the scanning area is 600∗450 μm. The mixed solution (FeCl 3/1 g, HCl/2 ml, H 2O/20 ml) was used to etch the sample surface. After etching, the samples were cleaned in C 2H 5OH and dried for observation of microstructure. The samples were prepared into thin slices with a thickness of less than 60 μm and a diameter of 3 mm, and then underwent ion beam thinning at a low temperature of 100 K. All prepared thin platinum samples were observed on a transmission scanning electron microscope (Talos F200s, TEM) operating at 200 keV. Finally, the TEM data were analyzed and processed by Digital Micrograph (DM) software. EB-PBF sample; Tensile properties tested perpendicular to the build direction

A novel Al-9.5Ce-0.6Mg/0.7GNPs (wt. %) composite with a network co-continuous Al/(Al, Mg)11Ce3 eutectic structure was fabricated using laser powder bed fusion. The spherical Al-Ce powder with a particle size distribution of 15∼53 μm was fabricated using the gas atomization method. Commercially irregular-shaped flake-like GNPs, with a lateral size of ∼200-300 nm and a thickness of ∼5-10 nm, were used as raw materials. A low-energy ball-milling was conducted to uniformly distribute the GNPs within the Al-Ce powder while maintaining the sphericity of the Al-Ce powder particles. The ball-milling process was performed using a planetary ball milling machine (Nanjing Nanda Instrument Group Co., Ltd., China) at a rotation rate of 200 rpm for 6 h with a ball-to-powder ratio of 2:1. The as-mixed Al-Ce/0.7 wt% GNPs powder was firstly heated to 60 °C and maintained at that temperature for 6 h with a vacuum of 10−2Pa in a vacuum drying oven to evaporate residual H2O on the powder surface. A SLM 125HL machine (SLM Solutions Group AG, Germany) was used to fabricate Al-9.5Ce-0.6Mg/0.7GNPs samples with dimensions of 35 mm × 20 mm × 10 mm. The parameters used were: laser power of 330 W, laser scanning speed of 1200 mm/s, hatch spacing of 30 μm, layer thickness of 30 μm. A scanning strategy with a rotation of 67° per layer was adopted. The aluminum substrate was preheated to 200 °C before printing. Subsequently, the as-built Al-9.5Ce-0.6Mg/0.7GNPs composite was subjected to post-heat treatment. The heat treatment (HT) was operated at 400 °C for 1h followed by water quenching. Condition: room temperature; Additional properties: UTS of 452 ± 3 MPa, elongation of 5.6 ± 0.2 %

The Fe-Cr-Mo-Mn steel used in this study are first heated by oxidation in an electric arc furnace, then decarbonized and desulphurized, with argon stirring to achieve deoxidation and desulphurization during the refining process. Subsequently, the steel ingot was subjected to multi-pass forging on a servo-hydraulic press. The forging process was initiated at an initial temperature of 1220 °C, with the final temperature reaching 800 °C, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The H1 sample undergoes QT based on the forged state, while the Ac1 and Ac2 temperatures for Fe-Cr-Mo-Mn steel are determined to be 710 °C and 780 °C, respectively. The H2 sample is subjected to an initial high-temperature normalization at 950 °C, followed by a near-Ac3 normalization at 770 °C, before proceeding to QT. In contrast, the H3 sample receives two successive high-temperature normalizations at 950 °C prior to the QT treatment. Following a single normalization, the resulting microstructure exhibits a combination of ferrite and pearlite. However, a significant refinement in both phases occurs after double normalization, as depicted in Fig. 1. The high-temperature tempering process engenders the formation of TS, characterized by the homogeneous dispersion of carbides within a ferritic matrix. The acicular martensite formed during the quenching process undergoes decomposition into a finer TS, which is uniformly distributed within the ferrite matrix during high-temperature tempering. Moreover, the elevated tempering temperatures facilitate enhanced diffusion of carbides, promoting the coalescence and growth of precipitated carbides within the ferrite matrix into a more uniformly dispersed granular morphology. Prior to the fatigue crack propagation tests, the initial microstructures of the H1, H2, and H3 specimens of Fe-Cr-Mo-Mn steel under varying heat treatment conditions were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Following the fatigue crack propagation tests, the three groups of samples underwent characterization using SEM and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to provide a comprehensive analysis of the microstructure evolution. Processing Text: NiCoFeCr HEA ingots were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure metals (purity > 99.9 wt.%) in a high-purity argon atmosphere. After the raw materials were loaded in the arc melter, the chamber was first evacuated to ∼5 × 10−2Pa and then backfilled with pure Ar and evacuated twice to dilute the residual air inside the chamber, finally backfilled at a pressure of ∼5 × 104Pa. Before the materials were melted, a small piece of pure Ti was melted to getter any residual air that might be present in the chamber. The buttons were remelted and flipped seven times to ensure chemical homogeneity before they were suction-cast into a rectangular copper mold with the dimensions of 8 mm × 17 mm × 70 mm. After solidification, the ingots were cleaned and dried, encapsulated in evacuated quartz tubes, and homogenized for 48 h at 1250 °C to minimize any casting-related segregation and then annealed for 1 h at 800 °C in air with water quenching. The samples were cut by electric discharge machining (EDM) from the suction cast ingot and annealed sheets and then ground with SiC adhesive papers to a grit size of 7 μm and polished with diamond suspension down to 1 μm. After mechanical polishing, the microstructure and phase composition of the alloys were investigated using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron-backscattered diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) techniques. Strain rate: 10^-3 s^-1; Temperature: 1073 K

The gas-atomized Haynes 230 powders with the chemical composition shown in Table 1 are used as material. The LPBF manufacturing process of the Haynes 230 alloy is completed using the SLM100-N2 system equipped with a fiber laser, the maximum laser power is 450 W, the maximum forming size is 100 mm × 100 mm × 100 mm, and the double cylinders feed powders in one direction. The process parameters used are the same as in our previous study [9]. Among them, the scanning speed, laser power, thickness, and rotation angle are 2500 mm/s, 260 W, 35 µm, and 90°, respectively. Before UIT, the tensile and wear samples are grounded by a grinding machine, and the processed dimensions after the process are shown in Fig. 1(d). Then, the surface is ground step by step with SiC sandpapers until smooth, and further polished to a mirror surface. The ultrasonic impact machine (UIT-500) is used to impact treat the LPBFed Haynes 230 samples. The amplitude, out current, impact frequency, pin diameter, and overlap rate of the UIT experiment are 27 µm, 1.0 A, 20 KHz, 3.0 mm, and 50 % respectively. In this experiment, the effects of repeated impact layer times (n=1, 2, and 3) on the pore closure, microstructure, mechanical, and wear properties are emphatically analyzed. Before internal porosity and microstructure characterization, the surface is grounded step by step with SiC sandpapers (180#, 400#, 600#, 800#, 1000#, 1500#, and 2000#) until smooth and further polished to hardly any tiny scratches by nylon polishing cloth. Then, electrolytic polishing is carried out, wherein the electrolytic polishing solution is 20 mL HClO4+ 80 mL C2H5OH, the voltage of electrolytic polishing is 20 V and the polishing time is 3-5 s. In addition, electrochemical corrosion is to observe the morphology of the melt pool and sub-grain structure. The electrochemical etching solution is 15 g CuSO4+ 50 mL HCl + 3.5 mL H2SO4, the voltage is 3-5 V and the etching time is 10 s. Before tensile and wear properties tests, the top surface of all samples is slightly polished with 1500 mesh sandpaper until smooth to eliminate impact caused by rough surfaces on performance. The tensile tests are performed by employing the universal testing machine (Instron 5582, Instron Systems Corporation, America), in accordance with the GB/T 228.1-2010 standard. Three tensile samples are manufactured for each group with a strain rate of 1 mm/min, all tensile tests are conducted at room temperature and fracture morphology is observed using SEM. Furthermore, the wear tests are performed by the high-frequency reciprocating tribometer (MGW-001, Jinan Yihua Tribology Testing Technology Co., Ltd, China) at room temperature, in accordance with the ISO12156-1:1997 standard. In the wear test process, the wear ball is Si3N4 with a diameter of 5 mm, and the load force, test duration, and reciprocating distance are 20 N, 15 min, and 5 mm, respectively. The wear tests are repeated three times. Processing state: LPBF + UIT1; Uncertainty: ± 17.9 MPa

Processing Text: A Cu-Ni-Si-Ca alloy was melted using a vacuum medium-frequency induction furnace and cast in a spheroidal graphite cast iron mold, resulting in a 30 mm-thick ingot, with the chemical composition listed in Table 1 obtained by using an Inductively Coupled Plasma-Atomic Emission Spectrometer (ICP-AES). The ingot was then hot rolled at 850 °C into a plate with a thickness reduction of 90 %. The steel plate was solution-treated at 980 °C for 4 h, water quenched, and cold rolled with a 90 % thickness reduction. The plate was then cut into several 11 mm (parallel to the rolling direction) × 13 mm specimens, for the aging treatment in the temperature range from 450 °C to 550 °C for 15-1440 min. The addition of only 0.05 % Ca in this alloy is used to purify the alloy during the melting and casting process as a refinery. The DP process combined with thermomechanical treatment was exploited to expedite the precipitation kinetics, whilst the competition between DP and CP was utilized to inhibit the nucleation and growth of continuous precipitation phase (CPP). Cold deformation was conducted to further increase the nucleation rate by providing potential nucleation sites, such as dislocations and stacking faults. The growth of classic discontinuous precipitation phase (CDPP) was restricted due to the high nucleation rate of spherical discontinuous precipitation phase (SDPP) and the deformed microstructure. The aging time can be substantially shortened to introduce these metastable ordered t-Ni 3Si precipitates in the alloy. Processing Text: ER55-B2 low-alloy steel wire with a diameter of 1.2 mm was used to remanufacture a high-strength low-alloy steel 42CrMo motor shaft with a size of Φ140 × 1000 mm. The rolling temperature was maintained within the ferrite phase region. An optimal processing window was identified with a rolling temperature of 600-700 °C and 23 % rolling strain. The interlayer temperature was controlled at 180 ℃ during deposition. The deposition power source is a Lincoln direct current pulsed Tungsten Inert Gas (TIG) welding machine INVERTEC CC400-TP. Before deposition, the surface of the motor shaft was polished and cleaned with acetone. The deposition parameters are: arc current of 220 A, arc voltage of 14.3 V, wire feed rate of 175 cm/min, deposition speed of 360 mm/min, and overlap rate of 0.15. A commercial pure argon shielding gas was used with a flow rate of 15 L/min. The optimal processing window for HR-WAAM was identified by adjusting the rolling temperature (500-600 ℃ and 600-700 ℃) and rolling force (0, 20 and 25 kN). For convenience, the HR-WAAM samples subjected to rolling temperatures within the ranges of 500-600 ℃ and 600-700 ℃ were designated as RT600 and RT700, respectively. The rolling strain is determined by calculating the percentage change in layer thickness, measured before and after hot rolling. To investigate the effect of in-situ hot rolling and thermal cycling on microstructures and mechanical properties of the cladding layer, we prepared the single-layer, double-layer and multi-layer samples by HR-WAAM with a rolling force of 25 kN and rolling temperature in the range of 600-700 ℃. The width and height of the multi-layer sample are 11 mm and 12 mm, respectively. All microstructural characterization samples were sectioned along the axial direction and sequentially grounded using 240#, 400#, 800#, 1200#, and 2000# grit SiC sandpaper and polished with 1.5 µm diamond paste. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) samples were further etched in a solution of nitric acid and ethanol with a ratio of 10:90 to reveal the microstructures. The electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) samples were subsequently vibrationally polished using 20 nm colloidal silica suspension. Microhardness tests were conducted using an INNOVATEST FALCON 500 Vickers hardness tester under 4.9 kN load with a dwell time of 10 s. 40 points were measured radially from the top of the sample across the cladding layer, the interface, and the base metal. Residual stress measurements on the specimen surface were conducted using an Xstress DR45 X-ray diffractometer, with a collimator diameter of 2 mm and an exposure time of 1 s. Measurements were conducted in both the rolling and axial directions. Prior to measurement, the specimen surface was electro-polished with a saturated NaCl solution using a VWEP-X1 electrolytic polishing machine. Stress-controlled rotating-bending fatigue tests were conducted at room temperature using a QBWP-10000 machine under various stress amplitudes. The stress ratio (R) of the tests was −1, while the waveform was sinusoidal with a nominal frequency of 100 Hz. The fatigue tests were stopped for specimens that were completely fractured (failed) or loaded for 10 7cycles (passed). For each set of process parameters, a total of 24 fatigue specimens were fabricated, with their dimensions illustrated in Fig. 2c. Among these, 15 specimens were selected to determine the fatigue limit using the staircase method. Three to five stress levels were applied, with each stress increment set at 3 %-5 % of the estimated fatigue strength, which was defined as 0.3-0.5 times the tensile strength. The remaining specimens were utilized to measure the high-stress region by the grouped-test method, with three to four elevated stress levels selected. Subsequently, the experimental data obtained from both methods were integrated to fit the fatigue curve (S-N curve). Sample condition: Unrolled

Processing Text: A 2200 MPa PHS with a chemical composition (wt%) of 0.40 %C, 0.40 %Si, 1.46 %Mn, 1.99 %Cr, 0.052 %Nb and 0.17 %V was melted in a vacuum inductive furnace. Then, the molten metal was poured into square ingots for casting. The slab was annealed at 1200 °C for 1 h to homogenize the composition. Afterwards, it was hot-rolled into a plate with a thickness of 3.0 mm between 1200 °C and 870 °C. The plate was rapidly cooled from the finish rolling temperature (870 °C) to the coiling temperature (660 °C) by laminar cooling. Then, the simulated coiling process was carried out, that is, the plate was transferred to a muffle furnace, which was heated to 660 °C in advance for 1 h, and finally, furnace cooling to room temperature. After pickling, the plate was cold-rolled to a final thickness of 1.5 mm. Subsequently, the cold-rolled sheet was austenitized at 900 °C for 15 min, followed by oil quenching to room temperature. For comparison, the as-quenched specimens were subsequently tempered in a salt bath at 170 °C and 300 °C for 20 min followed by air cooling to room temperature. Processing Text: In this work, high performance TiB2/M142 composites were prepared by powder metallurgy and hot extrusion. The results show that TiB2 particles can effectively refine the grain and the second phase, and induce more intragranular intermetallic phases. With the increase of TiB2 content, the strength increased continuously, but the ductility increased first and then decreased. The improvement of the strength of the composites are mainly attributed to thermal mismatch strengthening. The first increase in ductility is mainly due to the capture and pin of the dislocation by intragranular intermetallic phases, which makes the grains have stronger dislocation accumulation and storage capacity. The subsequent reduction in ductility is mainly attributed to the local stress concentration in the TiB2 agglomeration region, which eventually leads to the rapid failure of the composites. The starting powders used in this work were near-spherical M142 alloy powder with a size distribution of 15-53 μm (Bao-Hang New Materials Co., Ltd., Jiangxi, China) and irregular shape TiB2 powder with a diameter of about 2 μm (Macklin Bio-Chem Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). First, the weighed M142 alloy powder and the TiB2 powder (the content of TiB2 particles was 1, 3, 5 and 7 wt%, respectively) were put into a stainless steel jar filled with Ar atmosphere. The grinding medium was stainless steel ball with diameter of 10 mm, and the ball-to-material ratio was 10:1. TiB2/M142 composite powder was obtained by grinding at 200 rpm for 10 h. Secondly, the ball-milled powder was put into a Φ30 mm graphite mold and compressed at a uniaxial stress of 10 MPa through the punches. After that, the composite powder was sintered at 480 °C for 15 min by LABOX-650F spark plasma sintering (SPS) system under a vacuum pressure of less than 10 Pa. The pressure applied during sintering is 30 MPa. After cooling in the furnace, the sintered samples with a diameter of 30 mm and a thickness of 15 mm were obtained. Next, all sintered samples were hot extruded at 500 °C with an extrusion ratio of 25:1. Finally, the TiB2/M142 composite rod was subjected to T6 heat treatment (solid solution at 490 °C for 3 h, then water quenching, artificial aging at 180 °C for 6 h). The same procedure was employed to fabricate M142 alloy for comparative analysis. The effects of TiB2 particle content on the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of the TiB2/M142 composites were investigated. The Al 5Ti 8(FeCoNi) 86.9B 0.1 (at.%) ingots were fabricated by melting high-purity (>99.9 wt.%) raw materials (Al, Ti, Fe, Co, Ni, and B) in a vacuum arc furnace under a protective argon atmosphere. Each ingot underwent 5 melting cycles and was then cast into a copper mold with dimensions of 50×15×10 mm 3. The samples were subsequently heated to 1200 °C and held for 2 hours to achieve homogenization. Next, they were cut using an electrical discharge machine (EDM) to dimensions of 50×15×5 mm 3 along the thickness direction. These samples then underwent multiple cold-rolling passes to achieve a 70% deformation (reducing the thickness from 5 to 1.5 mm), followed by annealing at 1050 °C for 50 s to develop a fully recrystallized microstructure, abbreviated as CRSA alloy. Finally, the samples were aged at temperatures of 765 °C and 800 °C for varying durations: 0.1, 0.3, and 4 hours for 765°C, and 4 hours for 800°C. They were labeled as 765-0.1, 765-0.3, 765-4, and 800-4 according to their aging temperature and time. After each heat treatment, the samples were rapidly cooled to room temperature by water quenching. TEM samples before deformation were first thinned to 50 μm with sandpaper, followed by punching into 3 mm discs. Deformed TEM samples were directly mounted onto a molybdenum grid after thinning to 50 μm. Finally, these TEM samples were subjected to electrochemical twin-jet thinning to obtain the desired thin areas. Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 8 mm and a cross-sectional area of 2 × 1.5 mm 2 were obtained through EDM along the rolling direction. Tensile tests were conducted on a Zwick/Roell 5 kN tensile testing machine at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3 s −1, with a video extensometer employed to capture the real-time deformation of the gauge section. Processing Text: MAR-M247, a nickel-based superalloy, offers excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures but suffers from poor printability due to severe cracking. This study demonstrates the successful fabrication of MAR-M247 using electron-beam powder bed fusion (EPBF) with pre-heating at 1000 °C, achieving a high relative density (>99.5 %). Pre-heating suppressed the typical solidification microstructures observed in AM-fabricated alloys and minimised residual stress, resulting in reduced cracking. The as-printed alloy exhibited superior mechanical properties, with yield strengths of 820 MPa at room temperature and 640 MPa at 871 °C, outperforming conventionally cast MAR-M247. Atom probe tomography (APT) confirmed a high volume fraction (73.1 %) of γ' precipitates, including fine secondary precipitates near grain boundaries, enhancing mechanical strength by restricting dislocation motion. However, ductility decreased at elevated temperatures due to liquation cracking along grain boundaries, driven by solute segregation (Mo, B, and Cr). Creep behaviour analysis using the Larson-Miller Parameter (LMP) indicated that the as-printed alloy exhibited a rupture life comparable to post-processed cast alloys despite the presence of liquation cracks. Primary γ' precipitates (0.2-1 μm) were the main contributors to creep resistance, while fine secondary precipitates (∼30 nm) near grain boundaries provided additional resistance. Processing Text: To obtain a metastable phase microstructure, the alloys were hot-rolled at 850 °C within the β phase region. Inorganic silica coating was applied to prevent oxidation and control cooling. In order to eliminate the defects to the greatest extent and prevent the generation of cracks, the hot-rolling process was strictly selected. Specifically, the alloy ingots were held at 850 °C for 30 min in a muffle furnace, followed by multiple rolling passes with a 2 mm reduction per pass (rolling speed: 9 m/min). After each pass, the alloys were held at 850 °C for 3 min to maintain temperature uniformity. After reaching a final deformation of 80 %, the alloys were held at 850 °C for 3 min and then quenched. Processing Text: The alloys were manufactured using vacuum induction melting (VIM) from high-purity industry grade melt stock. The melt charges weighted 8 kg and were loaded in an alumina crucible for VIM under 200 Torr (26.7 kPa) partial pressure of argon. Once melted, the liquid metal was brought to a 50 °C superheat and poured into a cylindrical graphite mold to form 75 mm diameter ingots. The ingots were homogenized in a vacuum heat-treatment furnace with high-vacuum capabilities and utilizing a 50 Torr (6.7 kPa) argon partial pressure once the heat treatment temperature reaches 800 °C. A computationally optimized heat treatment schedule was determined based on chemistry and microstructure to reduce residual elemental inhomogeneity to below 1 %. Hot working was performed at 1100 °C and consisted of steps of forging followed by hot rolling with reheating between each step. Doing so, the ingots were processed into ∼10 mm thick plates. Processing Text: The alloy with the composition of Al-6Cu-1Ni-1Zr-1Ti(wt%) was adapted in the present work. For this purpose, the gas-atomized 2 wt% NiTi and 0.8 wt% Zr powders was added to AA2219 powder. Then, the powders were blended by mechanical mixing. To ensure homogeneity, a mixer was used to blend the powders at 100 rpm for 3 hours, changing the direction of rotation every half hour. The SLM process was conducted using an SLM 125 HL machine, which is equipped with a 400 W laser power. All SLM experiments were conducted under an argon atmosphere with the concentration of oxygen controlled below 0.1 vol%. The samples were fabricated on an Al substrate with a preheating temperature of 200 °C, using a scan strategy with a laser beam rotation of 67° between consecutive layers. The Al-Cu-Ni-Zr-Ti alloy were processed using different processing parameters, the laser power was selected within the range of 140 W to 260 W, and the scanning speed was varied between 850 ymm/s and 1750 mm/s. According to the forming quality, the optimized forming parameters were: laser power of 200 W, scanning speed of 1500 mm/s, hatch spacing of 90 μm and layer thickness of 30 mm, respectively. Cubic samples with the dimension of 10 × 10 × 10 mm 3was fabricated for the microstructure analysis, all samples for microstructural investigation were cut along the XOZ plane and mechanically ground and polished using SiC papers. The as-built samples were heat treated at 150 °C, 200 °C, 300 °C, 350 °C, 400 °C and 450 °C in the air furnace. To investigate the heat resistant of the alloy, the exposing time at 300°C and 350 °C was 200 h. Samples with the gauge dimensions of 60 mm (length) × 10 mm (width) × 1.5 mm (thickness) were machined from SLMed parts using electro-discharge machining (EDM). TEM samples cut from the SLMed Al-Cu-Ni-Zr-Ti alloy were mechanically ground and polished from ∼ 0.8 mm to 0.09 mm, followed by finally ion milling into thin foils in a Gatan Precision Ion Polishing System (PIPS). Condition: as-built

Ingots weighing 100 g of Al1Ti5Zr4Nb3Ta3 were fabricated in the vacuum arc-melting furnace under an argon atmosphere. Commercially pure metallic ingredients (the purity of metal elements: 99.99 wt%) were used as raw materials. Moreover, an ingot weighing 2.5 kg were melted and subsequently cast into an electrode bar with a length of 180 mm, upper inner diameter of 60 mm, and bottom inner diameter of 50 mm. Powders with different sizes in a range of 53 − 120 μm was prepared using the plasma rotating electrode process (PREP). To ensure the fluidity of powder feeding during AM process, the powders with approximately 160 mesh were selected through sieving. Pre-alloyed powders were heated up to 393 K for 2 h and cooled down to RT in a vacuum chamber to remove water vapor before use. The processing chamber was filled with high-purity argon and the oxygen content was maintained below 1000 ppm in the fabrication process, while the powder was delivered in to the laser molten on a Zr substrate through a coaxial powder delivery system. During the fabrication process, ytterbium-doped fiber laser unit with a wavelength of 1070 nm and a spot diameter of 1.8 mm was used as the power source. Before fabricating the single-wall samples, single-track experiments were carried out with a wide range of process parameters to determine the optimum process window. Optical micrographs of the transverse section of single-tracks specimens fabricated according to the Table 1 orthogonal experiment parameters are shown in Fig. 1(b). As a result, the moderate laser power P= 1400 W and laser scanning rate V= 500 mm/s are sufficient to obtain perfect molten pool morphology with the track height (Δh) of 0.36 mm and the track width (Δx) of 5 mm. The single-wall alloy with uniform distributed equiaxed grains along the deposition direction was fabricated successfully under the optimized process parameters. Then, the microstructures and mechanical properties of the LMD-fabricated alloy are characterized and tested, respectively. In comparison, a detailed analysis of the microstructures and mechanical properties of the as-cast alloy was also provided. Subsequently, the formation of microstructures mechanism and the strengthening mechanism of the LMD-fabricated alloy was discussed. Processing state: as-cast; Measured at Room Temperature (RT)

Commercially pure metallic ingredients (the purity of metal elements: 99.99 wt%) were used as raw materials. Moreover, an ingot weighing 2.5 kg were melted and subsequently cast into an electrode bar with a length of 180 mm, upper inner diameter of 60 mm, and bottom inner diameter of 50 mm. Powders with different sizes in a range of 53 − 120 μm was prepared using the plasma rotating electrode process (PREP). To ensure the fluidity of powder feeding during AM process, the powders with approximately 160 mesh were selected through sieving. Pre-alloyed powders were heated up to 393 K for 2 h and cooled down to RT in a vacuum chamber to remove water vapor before use. The processing chamber was filled with high-purity argon and the oxygen content was maintained below 1000 ppm in the fabrication process, while the powder was delivered in to the laser molten on a Zr substrate through a coaxial powder delivery system. During the fabrication process, ytterbium-doped fiber laser unit with a wavelength of 1070 nm and a spot diameter of 1.8 mm was used as the power source. Before fabricating the single-wall samples, single-track experiments were carried out with a wide range of process parameters to determine the optimum process window. Optical micrographs of the transverse section of single-tracks specimens fabricated according to the Table 1 orthogonal experiment parameters are shown in Fig. 1(b). As a result, the moderate laser power P= 1400 W and laser scanning rate V= 500 mm/s are sufficient to obtain perfect molten pool morphology with the track height (Δh) of 0.36 mm and the track width (Δx) of 5 mm. The single-wall alloy with uniform distributed equiaxed grains along the deposition direction was fabricated successfully under the optimized process parameters. Then, the microstructures and mechanical properties of the LMD-fabricated alloy are characterized and tested, respectively. In comparison, a detailed analysis of the microstructures and mechanical properties of the as-cast alloy was also provided. Subsequently, the formation of microstructures mechanism and the strengthening mechanism of the LMD-fabricated alloy was discussed. Processing Text: Alloys with atomic nominal compositions of Fe 40Mn 20Cr 10Ni 20Al 5Si 5 were prepared by arc melting under a high-purity argon atmosphere in a water-chilled copper crucible. The purity of each raw material was at least 99.9 weight percent (wt%). Ingots were remelted five times to ensure chemical homogeneity and then cast into a rectangular plate with dimensions about 60 mm × 10 mm × 3 mm. To compensate for Mn losses due to evaporation during melting, an additional 5 wt% of Mn was added. All ingots were homogenized at 1200 ℃ for 5 h, named homogeneous alloy. To increase the density of nucleation sites of the precipitated phases during the annealing process, cold-rolling was conducted with a total thickness reduction ratio of 70 % at room temperature before annealing. The thickness decreased from 3 mm to 0.9 mm. Finally, annealing treatments were carried out at 800 ℃ for 1 h. Annealing temperature are determined by phase diagram ( Fig. S1). They are all small size specimens (5 mm × 3 mm × 0.9 mm), so 10 min is enough for reaching the target temperature and homogenizing the temperature. Water quenching (WQ) was used as the cooling method for the above heat treatment. The Al5Si5 and Al3 alloys were electrolytically polished using 10 vol% perchloric acid-ethanol solution at a temperature of 298 K, with applied voltages of 15 V and 20 V for 50 s and 1 min, respectively. Processing Text: Experimental 2.1 Alloy fabrication Using metals with a purity greater than 99.9 %, composed of Cr 30 Co 30 Ni 30 Al 5 Ti 5 (at.%), a primary alloy ingot was obtained through vacuum arc melting in an argon-protected atmosphere. To ensure chemical homogeneity, the ingot was remelted five times. The remelted ingot was then subjected to solid solution homogenization annealing at 1100 °C for 3 h, followed by water quenching. To further refine the microstructure and enhance properties, a multistep cold-rolling process was employed on the homogenized annealed sample, resulting in an 85 % reduction in total thickness. The cold-rolled alloy was then subjected to a 1.5 min recrystallization annealing at 1100 °C, followed by quenching in water. Finally, the recrystallized annealed samples were subjected to isothermal aging treatment at 600 °C for 2 h, followed by quenching in water. The TiVNbTaAlx alloys (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, corresponding to Al0, Al0.1, Al0.2, Al0.3) were prepared by arc melting under a high-purity argon atmosphere. After homogenization, the HEA samples were annealed at 400°C, 600°C, and 800°C for 100 hours. All heat treatments were performed in a quartz tube under argon protection to prevent oxidation of the samples, followed by rapid water quenching to room temperature. The coating comprises two types of powder materials. One is spherical 316 L stainless steel powder, with a particle size ranging from 50 μm to 150 μm. The other material is YSZ (Jinggao Advanced Materials Technology). Its particle size range is 50 μm to 100 μm, with a purity of 99.9 %. The chemical composition of the YSZ powder is provided in Table 2. Firstly, 316 L stainless steel powder was mixed thoroughly with YSZ powder using a ball mill for approximately 4 h, resulting in mixtures containing 2.5 wt% and 5 wt% ZrO₂. The mixed powder was subsequently placed in a vacuum drying oven and preheated at 150 °C for 2 h to remove moisture and enhance flowability. The powder was then deposited as desired coating using a self-built LDED equipment equipped with a laser of 4 KW and 1060 nm wavelength (Raycus RFL-C4000). The LDED technology utilizes a coaxial powder feeding method to ensure the stability of coating properties. The optimal parameters were identified as a laser power of 1700 W, a scanning speed of 10 mm/s, a spot diameter of 4 mm, a powder feed rate of 1.2 r/min, and an overlap ratio of 50 %. With these optimized parameters, the 316 L composite coating was fabricated via multi-layer, multi-track laser processing, yielding a well-formed surface. After completing the coating process, the uneven top surface of the coating was removed using an electrical discharge wire cutting, and then cut into samples measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm and 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm for subsequent tests. The metallographic samples were sequentially ground with SiC sandpaper with grades from 240# to 2000#, followed by polishing with 2.5μm diamond polishing paste. Aqua regia (HCl:HNO 3=3:1 V:V) was employed to etch the sample surface for 10-15 s, followed by ultrasonic cleaning with alcohol. The polarization test samples were mechanically polished and subsequently ultrasonically cleaned with alcohol to remove any residual polishing paste and surface impurities. Composite with 5 wt% YSZ addition

Processing Text: Six alloys with varying compositions were produced by melting pure metals of aluminum, molybdenum, niobium, titanium, vanadium, and zirconium, each with a purity of no less than 99.99 %. During refining, evacuate the arc furnace chamber to a pressure below 5 × 10 −3 Pa, then fill it with high-purity argon gas to 0.02 MPa to guarantee the alloy is not oxidized during the melting process. To further reduce the oxygen concentration inside the furnace, Ti is melted once for 5 minutes to eliminate leftover oxygen in the electric arc furnace. Due to the high content of refractory elements in RHEA, increasing the current intensity and flipping times during melting is necessary. Repeated remelting ensures that any segregation or compositional inhomogeneities are minimized. The alloy ingot is melted 10 times in an electric arc furnace, each lasting 3–5 minutes, and the current is increased to 380–400 A to ensure sufficient mixing of refractory metal elements. Processing Text: These samples were built using the Laser Powder Directed Energy Deposition (LP-DED) process. The gas-atomized spherical shape powder utilized in this study demonstrated a particle size distribution ranging from 45 to 75 μm, with chemical compositions provided in Table 1. Sieve analysis, conducted in accordance with ASTM B214 on powder sampled following ASTM B215, indicated that no powder was retained on the +140 and +170 sieves, 0.2 % of the powder was retained on the +200 sieve, and 2.4 % of the powder was passed through the −325 sieve. The powder was delivered through a co-axial nozzle from an Oerlikon twin powder hopper, with argon gas serving as both the carrier and shielding gas at a flow rate of 10 L/min, and subsequently blown into the melt pool. The powder converged at a laser focal point initiating its controlled fusion and the creation of a distinct melt pool protected from atmospheric contamination by argon shielding gas. A wrought SS316 plate of dimensions 6″ length x 3″ width x 1″ thick was used as the substrate with the surface prepared by machining, followed by sandblasting. The Design of Experimentation (DOE) consisted of seven distinct configurations of DED process parameters including laser power, powder flow rate, and scan speed as shown in Table 2. Each sample, comprising six layers in height with dimensions of 2 inches in length and 1 inch in width, was fabricated in a single direction. Parameters such as layer offset (0.4 mm), hatch distance (with a step-over of 70 %), and dwell time between layers (set at 6 mins) remained constant. The implemented dwell time allowed each layer to cool adequately before the next layer was deposited, effectively minimizing the risk of overheating and reducing material variations due to uneven cooling. Additionally, to prevent any potential proximity effects, each sample was deposited with at least 1 inch of spacing between them. After AM, the entire build plate was subjected to a stress relief heat treatment at 1650 F for two hours in a vacuum furnace, a sufficient temperature to enable stress relief and the precipitation of δ phase. Each of the seven samples was then removed from the build plate using wire Electro Discharge Machining (EDM). SPT samples were extracted from each of the 7AM builds as shown in Fig. 1. After SPT samples were excised using wire EDM to an approximate thickness of 400 µm, each sample was polished on both sides with a 1200 grit polishing pad for one minute with a loading of 15 Newtons to remove the EDM recast layer. To reveal a pristine microstructure surface for Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), each sample was progressively ground for two minutes at 150 rotations per minute and 25 Newton loading on a Struers auto-polisher with 800-, 1000-, 1200-, 2400-, and 4000 grit sandpaper. After grinding, the samples were polished for five minutes using the same auto-polisher and parameters with a 3 µm suspension followed by a 1 µm suspension. A colloidal silica polishing step followed and utilized the same parameters apart from a change to a twelve-minute duration. Finally, the samples were subjected to vibropolishing in a Buehler VibroMet Polisher using a colloidal silica/water mixture for three hours at 3 rotations per minute. Processing Text: The binary Ti-12 wt. % Mo alloy was prepared by self-consumable vacuum arc melting. The ingot was re-melted three times in order to promote chemical homogeneity. It was hot forged into square bar and then cut into several plates of 10 mm in thickness. These plates were cold rolled and followed by homogenization at 900 °C for 30 min and water quenching to obtain Ti-12Mo samples of fully β phase. These as-homogenized specimens were subsequently cold rolled at room temperature with thickness reductions of 10 %, 20 %, 40 %, respectively. The cold-rolled-40 % specimens were aged at 300 °C, 400 °C, 500 °C for 60 min, respectively, and then water quenched for modifying their microstructures via phase transformation and partial recrystallization. Processing Text: LPBF-fabricated 316L stainless steel typically exhibits a high yield strength of approximately 600 MPa due to its high dislocation density. The raw material used in this work was commercially available gas atomized 316L stainless steel powders. The average size was 42.3 μm for 316L powder. The steels were fabricated using a commercial LPBF machine, the ProX DMP 300 (3D Systems, US). Specifications of the laser are as follows: full power = 500 W, wavelength = 1.07 μm, spot size = 75 μm. Oxygen level in the printing chamber was maintained below 300 ppm using high purity Argon gas. The laser scanning direction was rotated by 90° between consecutive layers. The printing parameters are presented in Table 2. Grinding, polishing, and etching were conducted to the samples for microstructural analysis. We used gradually finer SiC sandpapers from 180 grit to 2500 grit. We used a suspension with 40 nm SiO 2particles (OPS, Struers) to polish the samples. We used a self-mixed acid solution (HF:HNO 3:H 2O = 1:4:15) to etch the samples. Various microscopes were employed to observe and study the microstructures, including a Ziess Axioskop 2 MAT optical microscope, a JEOL JSM-7600F filed-emission electron scanning microscope equipped with backscatter electron (BSE) mode. The SEM observation was conducted at the accelerating voltage of 10 kV. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Nordlys, Oxford Instruments, Oxford) and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS, Oxford Instruments, Oxford) were acquired using the same SEM machine at the accelerating voltage of 20 kV. A step size of 0.6 μm was used for EBSD measurements. A smaller step size of 0.2 μm was used for a higher resolution EBSD measurement. X-ray diffraction (XRD, D8 Advance, Bruker) was conducted at 40 kV and 40 mA using a 0.6° divergence slit and a step size of 0.02°. Nanoindentation tests were carried out using Nano Indenter G200 equipped with a Berkovich tip (Agilent Technologies, USA) at a strain rate of 0.05 s −1. The maximum depth of the nanoindentation was 1000 nm. A 12 by 12 array of nanoindentation with an spacing of 20 μm was performed on 316L-1TiB 2. For each LPBF-processed material, three tensile samples were tested at room temperature using an Instron 5982 universal tensile testing machine, with a constant strain rate of 10 −3s −1. Tensile strain was recorded using a non-contact Instron AVE 2 extensometer. The tensile samples, with a dog-bone shape, were machined using wire cutting. After wire cutting, careful grinding using SiC sandpapers up to 1000 grit was conducted. The gauge size was 14 × 4 × 2 mm 3, and the total length was 50 mm. The synergistic interaction of Ti and B elements and 316L matrix was found to drive the formation of a distinctive core-shell structure. The core is filled with fine equiaxed grains and the shell is filled with columnar grains. A detailed microstructure characterization was further carried out using SEM BSE mode before and after etching the sample. It can be concluded that no diffraction peaks belong to the TiB 2phase. By incorporating 3 wt% TiB 2, the melt pool edge became narrower. Significant grain refinement has been achieved in LPBF-fabricated 316L by doping TiB 2particles. By incorporating just 1 wt% TiB 2, the grain size was reduced to about 1 μm. The mechanism behind the enhanced efficiency of TiB 2particles in grain refinement warrants further discussion. During the LPBF process of 316L-TiB 2composites, micronsized TiB 2particles dissolve and react with the 316L matrix. The Ti released from the decomposition of TiB 2is primarily responsible for the observed grain refinement. Additionally, the B from the decomposition forms a complex network of M 2B borides (M = Fe, Cr). These borides are distributed along the grain boundaries and the cellular structure boundaries. Additionally, Ti, resulting from the decomposition of TiB 2, acts as a potent solute for further grain refinement. Processing Text: Non-equiatomic Ti4VHf2.5Ta2.5 RHEA was fabricated by high-vacuum arc-melting using high purity raw materials (≥ 99.95 %). Before melting, high-purity Ti was first melted to absorb residual oxygen. Meanwhile, magnetic stirring was employed during the melting process to ensure uniform mixing of the liquid metal. The casted rods with a 20 mm diameter obtained by melting were directly subjected to 45 % and 90 % cold rolling individually. During cold rolling, the axis of the round rod was perpendicular to the rolling direction (RD), resulting in a final thin sheet with a thickness of 2 mm. The thin sheet obtained after 90 % cold rolling was annealed separately at 800 °C and 1000 °C for 1 h in air atmosphere. As shown in Fig. 1(a), all samples used for microstructure and mechanical properties characterization were extracted from the thin sheet using electro-discharging machine and then polished with silicon carbide paper to remove oxide layers. Processing Text: Spherical powders with a nominal composition of Co 18Cr 15Fe 50Ni 10Mo 6.5C 0.5(at%) in a particle size range of 10-55 µm were manufactured by gas atomization (Hot gas atomization system, PSI Ltd.). A commercial LPBF machine (Mlab, Concept Laser GmbH) was utilized to build cuboidal samples from the powders in a meander scanning pattern with a 180° rotation in a layer-by-layer process. A laser power of 90 W, a hatch distance of 77 µm, a scanning speed of 500 mm/s, and a layer thickness of 25 µm were applied. The printed sample was subsequently annealed at 900 °C for 10 min, which is hereinafter denoted by A900. The temperature was determined based on our previous works on alloys with similar compositions [ 8, 10], where annealing at 900 °C promoted precipitation of carbides and μ phase. The annealing duration was limited to 10 min to avoid grain growth or excessive coarsening of precipitates. Processing state: as-built; Microstructure: cell boundaries decorated by Mo segregation

Under argon protection, a cast Al 0.3CoCrFeNiTi 0.3HEA with a composition purity of 99.9 % was produced using the vacuum induction levitation melting method. Cylindrical specimens with dimensions of φ4 × 6 mm were obtained using electrical discharge machining (EDM) and subjected to quasi-static compression at room temperature with a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The samples underwent mechanical grinding and polishing, followed by electro-polishing in a solution of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol at −25 °C, applying a current of 0.5-0.6 mA for 30 s. Subsequently, in situ DIC-assisted quasi-static compression tests were performed at room temperature at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The tests were interrupted at applied strains of 3 %, 6 %, and 9 % to conduct microstructural characterization via SEM. Processing Text: Ingots with a diameter of 70 mm were prepared using a vacuum induction melting furnace. A 3.5 kg ingot underwent homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h to eliminate non-uniform microstructures formed during solidification, followed by multi-pass hot rolling with a finishing temperature of 860 °C, achieving a thickness reduction of 94.6 % (from 70 mm to 4 mm), and subsequently air-cooled to room temperature (RT). The hot-rolled steel was heated to 890 °C and held for 1 h before being furnace-cooled to 590 °C and then air-cooled. The plates were then cold-rolled in multiple passes down to 1.6 mm. Finally, the plates underwent quenching and tempering (QT) treatments. They were held at gradient temperatures (950 °C, 990 °C, 1030 °C, 1070 °C) each for 5 min and quenched in water; followed by tempering at 250 °C for 30 min and air-cooled, with the corresponding samples labeled QT950, QT990, QT1030, and QT1070, respectively. The microhardness of samples subjected to different heat treatment processes was measured using an HVS-1000 tester under a load of 0.98 N and a dwell time of 10 s. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM; ZEISS ULTRA 55) was employed to examine the microstructure, impact fracture morphology, and crack propagation path on the RD-TD plane for all samples. X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku Dmax2500) experiments were performed on samples subjected to different heat treatment processes. The Cu-Kα radiation with a wavelength of 1.54056 Å was employed, with diffraction patterns recorded at a step rate of 2°/min over a 2θ range from 40° to 110°. Further characterization of the martensite microstructure was carried out using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, ZEISS ULTRA 55). The samples were electro-polished in an ethanol solution containing 10 vol% HClO 4for 30 s, and data were collected under conditions of a step size of 0.05 μm, an acceleration voltage of 20 kV, and a tilt angle of 70°, and then processed using Channel 5 software. The phase composition and the interaction between carbides and dislocations during the impact strain process in all samples were investigated by transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEOL-F200). TEM samples were prepared by mechanically thinning to 40 µm, and then the TEM sample with a diameter of 3 mm was twin-jetted in a 10 vol% HClO 4ethanol solution at −30 ℃. A near-α Ti-6Al-2Sn-4Zr-2Mo-0.1Si-0.5Y (wt%) alloy with two distinct types of microstructures was fabricated using a powder metallurgy (PM) method involving thermomechanical consolidation (TMC) and subsequent heat treatments. The first heat treatment involved annealing at 960 ℃ for 1 h, followed by air cooling (AC), and the resulting sample was designated as 960-A. The second heat treatment consisted of annealing at 960 ℃ for 1 h, followed by water quenching (WQ), and subsequent aging at 580 ℃ for 6 h with air cooling. High temperature tensile tests at 600 °C were conducted using flat, dog-bone-shaped specimens with dimensions of 3 mm (width) × 2 mm (thickness) × 15 mm (length) at an initial strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1 on an AG-XPLUS 100 KN universal testing machine. The creep tests at 600 °C under applied stresses ranging from 150 to 350 MPa were performed using an ECM-100 creep testing machine. The creep specimen dimensions were 3.5 mm (width) × 2.5 mm (thickness) × 20 mm (length). Prior to loading, creep specimens were held at 600 °C for 1 h to ensure uniform temperature distribution. The temperature accuracy was maintained within ± 1 °C. Microstructure: Type 2; Condition: 600 °C; Sample designation: 960-STA

Processing Text: Specimens were cut along the diameter of the forged bar and vacuum-packaged. After solution treatment at 900°C, the specimens were cooled at a rate of 1 °C/min using temperature control equipment to temperatures between 725°C and 500°C in 25 ℃ intervals, holding at each temperature for 60 minutes, followed by water quenching to room temperature. For simplicity, these samples are referred to by their cooling temperatures (e.g., 725°C, 700°C, etc.) in the thereafter text. Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 18 mm were used for tensile testing. The tests were conducted on a universal testing machine at a rate of 0.5 mm/min, corresponding to a theoretical tensile strain rate of 4.6 × 10−3s−1. Microstructural analysis was performed using an optical microscope (OM), scanning electron microscope (SEM), and transmission electron microscope (TEM). For electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) characterization, samples were mechanically polished and then electropolished in a mixture of 60 % methanol, 34 % n-butanol, and 6 % perchloric acid at 30 V, −30°C for ∼60 s. The metallographic structure observation was performed using a modified Kroll reagent (5 % HF + 10 % HNO₃ + 85 % H₂O) to etch the electropolished surface. Transmission specimens were wire-cut to a thickness of about 500 μm and subsequently ground with SiC abrasive paper from coarse to fine, reducing the thickness to ∼50 μm. The samples were then twin-jet electropolishing using the same electropolishing solution. Heat treatment at 725°C; αS content: 14.6%

The Co-Cr-Fe-Ni powders were arranged in equiatomic ratio. A 5.1 g mixture of elemental powders and 1 wt% of stearic acid as a process control agent (PCA) to prevent excessive cold welding during mechanical alloying was mixed in a hardened steel vial. The powder preparation was performed in a glove box, where oxygen and humidity levels were maintained below 0.5 ppm by continuous circulation of high-purity argon gas through a purification system. The mixture was first milled for 30 min. Next, the vials were opened inside the glove box, and 440 C stainless steel balls with a powder-to-ball radio of 1:10 were added. The vials were then sealed in the glove box, and the mechanical alloying process was carried out at room temperature for 20 h using a SPEX 8000 M/D high energy ball miller. To minimize cold welding without the need for additional PCA, the sealed vials were placed in liquid nitrogen for 5 min after every 150 min of mechanical alloying period to reduce their temperature. After mechanical alloying, the vials were placed back inside the glove box, where the as-milled HEA powders were removed and stored until sufficient milling runs were completed to generate enough powder. This was followed by annealing in an argon atmosphere at 500 °C for 1 h to remove the PCA from the as-milled HEA powders. The cold-pressed pellets were then annealed at 700 °C for 1 and 24 h, and at 900 °C for 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h in an argon atmosphere, followed by in-furnace cooling. The consolidated and annealed samples were ground using 800, 1200, and 2500 grits, and then polished to achieve a mirror-like surface for subsequent testing and characterization. Processing Text: In this study, (CoCrCuFe)100-xNix (x = 5, 20, 35, 50 at%) high entropy alloys (HEAs) were fabricated by vacuum arc melting technique and characterized in their as-cast condition to control microstructure and mechanical behavior via Ni alloying. The Fe, Co, Cr, Cu, and Ni elements with high purity (>99 wt%) were used as raw materials for the production of (CoCrCuFe)100-xNix (x = 5, 20, 35, 50 at%) HEAs using a vacuum arc melter with a water-cooled copper hearth. The oxidation was prevented by repeatedly evacuating and refilling the melting chamber with high-purity (>99.99 %) Ar gas. The alloys were remelted at least 5 times, and the ingots were flipped upside-down between melting runs to achieve the chemical homogeneity in the as-cast alloys. Then, the alloys were cast into the 5 mm cylindrical copper mold. Samples were ground with 600, 1200, and 2000 SiC papers and polished with 6 µm, 1 µm diamond suspension, and 50 nm colloidal silica, respectively. Freshly prepared aqua regia solution (3HCl:1HNO3) was used as an etchant for 30-50 s. Each sample was investigated before and after etching to obtain microstructural and compositional micrographs by SEM-EDS analyses. It should be noted that all the HEAs were investigated in their as-cast states. A quasi-static compression test was performed to determine the macro mechanical properties of the samples. The compression test was carried out by the Shimadzu AGS-X universal test machine under the constant strain rate (10-4s-1), which was calculated after measuring the size of each cylindrical sample under ambient temperature according to the ASTM E9-09 standard. Three samples, which have parallel surfaces with the same compositions, were tested for compression, and averaged values were used for each set of samples. Yield strength was determined by using 0.2 % offset values after the test. The Vickers microhardness test machine (Emcotest, Durascan G5) was utilized to determine the hardness values of HEAs with a load of 4.905 N (HV0.5). The average hardness values were calculated from five different points on the surface of the samples. Micromechanical properties of samples with different Ni content were determined by using iNano® system (KLA Instruments, Milpitas, CA, USA). Mechanical property mapping was obtained quickly using the NanoBlitz® 3D technique (Nanomechanics, Inc.) Firstly, the target load was determined based on a single indentation on each sample to calculate the desired indentation spacings, accounting for the overlapping of the plastically deformed zone. After the pretest, a 10 mN target load was used for 15 indentations 45 × 45 array (225 indentations) for mapping. The same regions of the indented HEAs were then investigated under SEM by backscatter electrons and EDS mapping to correlate the microstructure and indented points. The recrystallization annealing experiment was carried out on the sample after the experiment. Annealed time /min is 30

Processing Text: This paper develops corrosion-resistant high-strength Al-Cu matrix composites (Na2MoO4@CNT/2024) by combining a new strategy of incorporating Na2MoO4 precipitant into bulk metals using the inner cavity of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and the heat treatment. The results show that as compared to the natural aging and peak aging treatments, the double aging (DA) and regression and re-aging treatments (RRA) can result in higher elongation (>10 %) with slightly decreased but still high strength (∼585 MPa, similar to ∼595 MPa of conventional CNT/2024 composite). This is attributed to the DA- or RRA-induced formation of precipitates and precipitation-free zone with proper sizes and distribution. Moreover, the Na2MoO4@CNT/2024 composite in any heat-treated state has excellent resistance to exfoliation corrosion (level N), intergranular corrosion (IGC depth < 8 μm) and corrosion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (corrosion rate < 0.02 mm/y), superior to all the other previously reported Al-Cu alloys. More preparation details can be found in our previous work [12]. For comparison, the 2024 Al alloy and CNT/2024 composite reinforced with 4 wt% purified CNTs were prepared by the same powder metallurgy process and underwent the same heat treatment. The Al0.5CrNi1.5Fe2 multi-principal element alloy was designed by completely replacing Co with Fe, and partially replacing Al with Ni to avoid the formation of excessive brittle phases. The alloy was prepared using a non-consumable vacuum arc furnace. The alloying materials employed were pure metals (Al, Cr, Fe, and Ni) with a purity greater than 99.95 wt%. The alloy was remelted four times under an argon atmosphere to ensure homogeneity, with electromagnetic stirring applied to accelerate the diffusion of elements. The alloy underwent thermal mechanical treatment to induce partial recrystallization, resulting in a multi-phase, multi-scale heterogeneous microstructure. After cold rolling the Al0.5CrNi1.5Fe2 alloy to 80 % reduction and annealing at 800°C for 1 hour, a heterogeneous structure predominantly consisting of “fine-grained recrystallized regions and nano-grained un-recrystallized regions” was formed. The phase compositions of both regions included a disordered FCC matrix and dispersed ordered BCC (B2) precipitates enriched in Al and Ni, as well as disordered BCC precipitates enriched in Fe and Cr. The Al0.5CrNi1.5Fe2MPEA samples were cold-rolled at room temperature using a two-roll mill. The rolling process was carried out in multiple passes, with the rolling direction maintained constant along the length of the samples. The reduction in thickness was 80 %, and the alloy obtained after this process is referred to as CR80 in this study. To regulate the microstructure of the Al0.5CrNi1.5Fe2MPEA, the CR80 samples were annealed at 600 °C and 800 °C. The heat treatment was performed in a box-type resistance furnace under an argon protective atmosphere. During the heat treatment, the cold-rolled samples were heated along with the furnace at a rate of 20 °C/min and held at the set temperature for one hour. Processing state: Annealed at 800°C for 1 hour after cold rolling to 80% reduction

Processing Text: The Al-5356 alloy deposits were fabricated using the P-FSAM technique. The process optimization focuses on the ratio of actuator reciprocating frequency to tool traverse speed, ensuring adequate heat generation and particle filling for high-quality deposition. Through the implementation of an optimized stirring pin and spiral groove design, the technique facilitates Z-direction flow of thermoplastic material, resulting in enhanced interfacial bonding and material flow characteristics. During the stable deposition of single-pass multilayers of this alloy, P-FSAM requires about 1 kN thrust force, with a maximum steady-state temperature exceeding 435°C. The deposits exhibit refined grain structures due to dynamic recrystallization, nearly complete dissolution of the Al3Mg2 phase, while maintaining grain stability during thermal cycling. The deposits achieve favorable mechanical properties, with yield strength exceeding 210 MPa, ultimate tensile strength surpassing 350 MPa, and elongation over 20 % in both build and traverse directions, outperforming fusion-based additive manufacturing counterparts. The wire was first straightened and then artificially sheared to less than 1.5 mm by a high-speed rotating blade, and the shapes and statistical sizes of the particles obtained are shown in Fig. 4. Most of the particles were close to cylindrical and the statistical mean of the maximum particle size was about 1.37 mm. A commercial 6061 aluminum alloy plate was selected as the substrate to facilitate the analysis of mixing behavior between the deposited material and the substrate through post-chemical-corrosion cross-sectional observations. The substrate dimensions were 200 × 400 × 15 mm. The P-FSAM deposited components were used on a wire cutting machine to prepare samples for microstructure characterization and mechanical properties testing. The sampling area is shown in Fig. 5. The surface of the cross-sectional sample and particles was first ground and polished to a mirror finish using standard procedures, followed by etching it with weck etchant (40 %HF+45 %C3H8O+H2O). The cross-section surface was photographed on an OLYMPUS-BX53M optical microscope (OM) using a low magnification lens, and the complete cross-sectional morphology was reconstructed by synthesizing the images using Photoshop (PS) software. Microstructure samples at different heights of the component were examined in detail for grain characteristics by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) using FEI Apreo 2 C after electrolytic polishing. The EBSD analysis was conducted with a step size of 0.2 μm. The phase composition of both the particles and the as-deposited material was identified using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, SmartLab SE, Rigaku) with a scanning rate of 2°/min. The microstructure sample surfaces of the as-deposited materials, as well as the tensile fracture morphology, were observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, JSM 7200 F, JEOL). All microstructural test samples were extracted from the locations labeled ①, ②, and ③, as illustrated in Fig. 5. Nine non-standard uniaxial tensile specimens were prepared along the transverse and building directions, with their sampling locations and dimensions shown in Fig. 5. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed at room temperature on an MTS-E45 testing machine at a displacement rate of 0.5 mm/min. Vickers hardness (HXS-1000AC) was tested at a load of 100 g with a dwell time of 15 s. Processing Text: The alloys underwent a processing sequence of casting, homogenization, hot deformation, annealing, cold deformation, solid solution treatment, followed by optional steps of cold deformation and pre-aging, and finally peak-aging. The alloys were melted under an argon atmosphere and cast into an iron mold with a size of 20 mm × 20 mm × 100 mm. The as-cast ingots were homogenized at 430 °C for 6 h and then 470 °C for 24 h, followed by hot- and cold-rolled into 2 mm thick sheets. Solid solution treatment was performed at 490 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching to room temperature. Subsequently a two-step aging process (90 °C for 24 h followed by 140 °C to peak aging) was employed. Dog-bone-shaped specimens of the alloys in the peak-aged state were prepared with a gauge length of 9.5 mm, and tensile tests were conducted using AGS-X tensile testing machine at a tensile rate of 0.572 mm/min at room temperature, with at least three repetitions for averaging. Hardness tests were conducted to observe the aging behavior of the designed alloys, while tensile tests were performed on the alloys in their peak-aged or near-peak-aged state. Composition: Al-5.68Mg-2.25Zn-0.71Ag-0.38Mn-0.29Sc-0.25Cu-0.09Ti; Processing state: peak-aged

In this study, the low-carbon ultra-high-strength steels with precipitation-free were prepared using quenching processes, and the co-precipitation strengthening of multi-scale Cu-rich and NiAl were designed to enhance fatigue performance through quenching-tempering (QT) and quenching-partitioning-tempering (QPT) processes respectively. The designed experimental steel billet of 150 kg was melted in a vacuum furnace, and the actual chemical composition of the billet was presented in Table 1. In order to obtain sufficient multi-component Cu-rich nanoparticles during the subsequent heat-treatment process, 1.65 wt.%Cu, 5.04 wt.%Ni and 0.94 wt.%Al were added to the steel billet. The tube billet was heated to 1280 °C for 30 mins to homogenize in a rotary heating furnace, and then air-cooled to 1150 °C for rotary piercing with a reduction rate of ∼74%. Subsequently, the pierced tube billet was air-cooled to 1000 °C and continuously rolled through 5 passes to obtain a raw tube with a reduction rate of ∼46%. The rolled raw tube was reheated to 850 °C in a circulating heating furnace, and then the stretch reducing process was performed at 850 °C through 7 passes with a total reduction rate of ∼20.6%. In order to achieve a substantial improvement in fatigue strength, martensite was designed as the ideal matrix microstructure, and a two-step quenching-tempering (QT) and a multi-step QPT processes are used to precipitate multi-component nanoparticles. The one-step quenching process requires the rolled tube was heated to 900 °C for 30 min to austenitized treatment, and then water quenched to obtain sufficient martensite. Processing Text: The SS 316L powder, which was produced through gas atomization, was provided by EOS in Germany. The Hall flow rate of the powder is 12.1 s/50g, and its chemical composition is presented in Table 1. The power morphology and particle size distribution are illustrated in Fig. 1(a) and (b), respectively, showcasing a highly spherical shape (≥99 %) with a D50 size of 34.3 μm, which makes it well-suited for LPBF technology. The SS 316L was fabricated using an HBD-80 machine (Shanghai Hanbang United 3D Tech Co., Ltd., China), equipped with a YLR-500 fiber laser operating at a wavelength of 1064 nm and a beam diameter of approximately 33 μm. The schematic diagram of LPBF technology is shown in Fig. 2(a), while Fig. 2(b) depicts the laser scanning strategy. The selection of process parameters was based on Ref. [ 16], which include laser power ( P), scanning speed ( v), scanning spacing ( h), and volumetric energy density ( VED = P/hvt) [ 33], as shown in Table 2. In this work, a total of 108 tensile specimens were examined, divided into 36 groups with each group consisting of 3 replicate specimens. The 3D model, as shown in Fig. 2(c), was printed via LPBF technology. The lower section of the model was used to evaluate its relative density and microstructure. While, the upper portion of the model was divided into specimens specifically designed for conducting tensile tests and its dimensions are illustrated in Fig. 2 (e). The microstructure of the alloy parallel to the BD orientation is characterized in Fig. 2(d). The specimen density was measured using Archimedes' theory with a MAY-D80 automatic testing balance. The macrostructure of specimens was observed using a Zeiss 40MAT metallographic microscope. EBSD pictures were obtained using the Zeiss Gemini 300 scanning electron microscope with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Previously, the specimens were electrochemically polished using a solution of HClO 4and C 2H 5OH in a 1:9 ratio, followed by Ar ion polishing with a Gatan Precision Etch Coating System (PECS) II 685. Finally, EBSD testing was performed with a step size of 1 μm. The EBSD data was processed using AZtecCrystal 2.1 software. Specimen S1; VED = 55.6 J/mm³; Relative Density = 99.91%
