The high pure metal powder (≥99.95 wt%) of Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni with equal atomic ratio was milled for 20 h in a planetary ball mill under an argon atmosphere to produce HEA powders. To prevent severe welding of the metal powders, 1 wt% N-heptane was added to the ball mill tank. The collected HEA powders were then transferred to a vacuum hot-pressing sintering system (HPS, FUJIDEMPA HIGH-MULTI 5000). The entire sintering process was conducted under a low vacuum of 10-1 Pa and cooled with the furnace after holding at 1050 °C and 50 MPa for 1h. The sintered bulk HEAs were immersed in liquid nitrogen and cooled to its temperature before being deformed under a hydraulic press. The overall thickness was reduced by 10 %. The deformed HEA samples were then annealed at 500 °C, 600 °C, 700 °C, and 800 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching. These samples were labeled A500, A600, A700, and A800, respectively. Before analysis, the samples were prepared through mechanical and electrolytic polishing. For transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis, the samples were wire-cut, mechanically polished to 50 μm, and subsequently thinned using an ion beam. Processing Text: Here, the single-phase body centered cubic (BCC) structured Ti3Zr1.5NbVAl0.25 RHEA with superior specific strength and ductility were developed by laser direct energy deposition and cold-rolling. The structures of RHEA were treated by various annealing temperatures ranging from 600 °C to 900 °C for an hour. The RHEA with a recrystallized equiaxed crystal annealed at 900 °C exhibited excellent mechanical properties such as yield strength of 976 MPa and tensile strength of 986 MPa. The elongation of 22.5 % is three times higher than original state and the specific strength of 173.1 MPa cm3·g−1 surpassed those of most RHEAs. More importantly, the enhanced yield strength can be attributed to the contributions among solution strengthening, grain boundary (GB) strengthening and dislocation strengthening. Moreover, emerging much rich dislocation microstructures make for improving strain hardening and preventing early necking for enhanced plasticity. Processing Text: The two HEAs with nominal compositions of (Cr 20Mn 24Fe 30Co 20Ni 6) 99C 1(at.%) and (Cr 20Mn 24Fe 30Co 20Ni 6) 99N 1(at.%), were cast using a vacuum induction furnace. Chromium nitride and iron-carbon were added as N and C element sources, respectively. The as-cast ingot has a cuboid shape in the dimension of 130 × 50 × 50 mm 3. Thin slices with a thickness of ∼10 mm were cut from the as-cast ingots and subsequently hot-rolled at 950 °C with a thickness reduction of 80 %. Each rolling pass reduces the thickness of 0.5-1 mm, and after every rolling pass, the sample is kept at 950 °C for 5 min. Further homogenization was conducted in an Ar atmosphere at 1200 °C for 2 h, followed by water quenching. Rectangular dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens were obtained from the as-homogenized materials using electrical discharge machining. The specimen had a total length of 130 mm and a thickness of 2 mm. The gauge area measured 50 mm in length and 10 mm in width. Tensile tests were conducted at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1using a screw-driven Zwick/Roell test rig (Z250 model) equipped with a cold chamber controlled by liquid nitrogen. The testing temperatures were set at dry ice-alcohol mixture temperature (200 K) as well as room temperature (298 K). To ensure data reproducibility, three tests were performed for each alloy state. As for the initial state, alloys were characterized using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD) machine equipped with a Cu-Kα radiation anode in order to determine the phase constitution and the lattice parameters. The samples were scanned at a 2θ angle ranging from 30° to 130°, with a scanning rate of 2°/min. To prepare specimens for electron channeling contrast (ECC) and EBSD analyses, initial grinding using silicon carbide paper was followed by polishing using a diamond suspension with a particle size of 2.5 μm. Subsequent finer polishing was carried out with oxide suspension (OPS) containing silica particles (approximately 50 nm in size). The remaining OPS particles were removed through soap polishing. Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) analysis was conducted using a ZEISS Gemini SEM300 equipped with an electron backscatter diffractometer and an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), at a voltage of 20 kV, scanned with a step size of 0.15 μm and a tilt angle of 70°. For ECC characterization, a ZEISS Gemini Crossbeam 340 instrument was utilized, and optimal imaging conditions were achieved at a voltage of 30 kV and a working distance of 6.5 mm. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was carried out for detailed characterization of the deformed microstructure using a JEOL JEM-F200 field emission high-resolution transmission electron microscope. For TEM foil preparation, the samples were polished to a thickness of approximately 80 μm using sandpaper and standard disk with a diameter of 3 mm was then punched out. Double-jet electron-polishing was employed to prepare for the TEM foils, and electron-transparent TEM foils can be obtained by utilizing 5 % perchloric acid in acetic acid at a temperature of 17 °C and a voltage of 32 V. Condition: Low Temperature (200 K); Phase: Single FCC phase

Processing Text: The specimens were obtained first by vacuum melting. The as-received rod-shaped samples had a diameter of 50 mm and length of 350 mm. After multi-pass rolling at 600 °C, the diameter became 16 mm. The final specimens were obtained by further annealing at 600 °C for 1 h. Some of them were irradiated at the High Flux Engineering Test Reactor (HFETR) at 350 °C with helium and argon as the atmospheric medium. Two neutron fluences of 2 × 10 19n/cm 2and 8 × 10 19n/cm 2(E > 1 MeV) were achieved for the following tensile tests. The corresponding displacement per atom (dpa) values are 0.11 dpa and 0.43 dpa, respectively. Under the standard of ASTM E8/E8M and ASTM E21, theun-irradiated and post-irradiation specimens were tensioned at room temperature (300 K) and 380 °C (653 K) using an MTS 810 tensile machine. The loading rate was 1 mm/min and the tensile axis is parallel to the rolling direction (RD). Engineering stress and engineering strain were recorded. Neutron fluence: 0; Temperature: 300 K

A high-strength Co-free triple-phase Al10Cr12Fe35Mn23Ni20 high-entropy alloy (HEA) was successfully fabricated using Friction Surface Layer Deposition (FSLD), a bulk manufacturing method. Multiple single-layer deposits were produced by varying forging force (F) and traverse speeds (Tr) to optimize the process parameters. The optimized conditions (F = 40 kN & Tr = 200 mm/min) were then applied to manufacture a scaled-up multi-layer specimen. During FSLD, the FCC-matrix underwent continuous dynamic recrystallization due to high-temperature severe plastic deformation, forming finer equiaxed grains. Simultaneously, the BCC-dendrites fractured into smaller fragments, some of which experienced partial growth and coarsening under applied stress, resulting in an hourglass morphology. In contrast, the small B2-precipitates within the BCC-fragments dissolved during the elevated temperatures of FSLD and reprecipitated as substantially finer precipitates during continuous cooling post-FSLD. Vacuum induction melted cylindrical bars of Al10Cr12Fe35Mn23Ni20 HEA were procured from Sophisticated Alloys Inc. 25.4 mm diameter and 152.4 mm length feed rods were sectioned from the As-Received HEA bars for FSLD. A constant rotation rate of 500 rpm was used in this work to allow comparison of microstructural evolution with similar heat generation rates. The microhardness measurements were performed using a CLARK CM-802AT automatic hardness tester, and a load of 500 gf and a dwell time of 10s were used. SEM analysis has been performed on the as-received cylindrical bars of the HEA to evaluate the initial microstructure. EBSD and EDS scans were performed to identify the three different phases present in the microstructure of AR HEA. Detailed microstructural characterization has been performed on the optimized condition of the FSLD Al10Cr12Fe35Mn23Ni20 HEA to understand the microstructural evolution during processing. A multi-layer deposit of Al10Cr12Fe35Mn23Ni20 HEA comprising 7 layers was deposited consecutively layer-by-layer over the SS 304 substrate via FSLD. The optimized process parameters (condition #1: F = 40 kN and Tr = 200 mm/min) were used for this deposition. Condition: #1; Estimated from Vickers Hardness: 278 ±3.9 HV

Processing Text: The Fe50.2-Mn30.0-Co5.0-Ni3.0-Cu2.0-Al9.0-C0.8 (mass%) alloy was prepared by induction melting for about 30 min in an alumina crucible under an argon atmosphere (99.9995 % purity). Later it was subsequently cast into a massive Cu mold forming an ingot of 20 × 50 × 100 mm in size. After homogenization for 4 h at 1100 °C in air and subsequent water quenching to avoid precipitation of carbides a slab of 20 × 20 mm in cross-section was subjected to hot dual axial forging (DAF) at 1050 °C in two steps. After the initial dual axial hammering out using a forging hammer the sample size was reduced to 16 × 16 mm size. Subsequent rolling using a caliber rolling mill produced the slabs of 10 × 10 mm in cross-section. Then, the sample cut in a longitudinal direction forming a 6 × 10 mm cross-section sample was subsequently cold rolled (CR) to 0.5 mm corresponding to 92 % thickness reduction (true/equivalent strain e= 2.5) in about 100 passes (∼0.1 mm size reduction per pass) at the linear passage speed of 1 cm/s. CR was performed between two stainless steel plates to protect the rolls. Then, aging temperatures of 550-600 °C, typical for Fe-Mn-Al-C alloys were applied. The samples were also aged at 200-300 °C. After homogenization, DAF and cold rolling, the chemical composition of the produced alloy was verified by the inductively coupled plasma emission spectroscopy with ARCOS FHM22 MV130 spectrometer made by SPECTRO Analytical Instruments (for metallic elements), combustion infrared absorption method with LECO CS-844 analyzer (for carbon) and helium transport melting infrared absorption method with LECO ONH836 (for oxygen). Cold-rolled sample; Tensile elongation of 4%; Annealed samples exhibited higher values.
Processing Word: Cold-rolled sample; Tensile elongation of 4%; Annealed samples exhibited higher values.

It was then underwent cold rolling to 6 mm after annealing at 360 °C for 5 h and 420 °C for 2 h. Following this, the cold-rolled plates were subjected to various annealing treatments with different temperatures and cooling rates. A subset of cold-rolled plates was annealed at temperatures of 300 °C, 325 °C, 350 °C, 375 °C, and 400 °C for 2 h, followed by faster cooling (FC) down to 250 °C at a cooling rate of approximately 3.65 °C/min, and then air cooled to room temperature. These samples were labeled as X-FC, with “X” indicating the specific annealing temperature. Another subset of the cold-rolled plates was annealed at 400 °C for 2 h and subsequently cooled with a slower cooling rate (SC) of about 0.5 °C/min down to room temperature, which is designated as 400°C-SC. All annealed specimens were underwent a solid solution treatment (SST) at 505 °C for 60 min before being quenched in ambient water. To determine the engineering mechanical properties, the materials were ultimately aged at 152 °C for 38 h following a 5 % pre-stretch deformation. Both cold-rolled and APC specimens were annealed at 300 °C-400 °C for 30 s-3600 s. Subsequently, rapid quenching in ambient water and HV testing were performed. For the HV testing, a 500 g load was applied for 15 s with an average of 10 measurements per sample. To further explore the recrystallization kinetics of the annealed samples during SST at 505 °C, samples previously annealed at 300°C-FC, 350°C-FC, and 400°C-FC were exposed to SST at 505 °C for durations of 15 s, 30 s, 45 s, 60 s, 180 s, and 3600 s. The specimens for EBSD observation were prepared through twin-jet electropolishing on MPT-1 electrolytic double sprayer. The AZtecCrystal software was employed to process the EBSD data. Processing Text: Cylinder ingots with nominal compositions of Co 25Cr 25Fe 25Ni 25 were prepared via levitation melting, in which the purity of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al, and Ti was 99.9 % (wt. %). The ingots were remelted five times to ensure its chemical homogeneity, followed by electrical discharge machining to produce cubic samples with dimensions of 60 mm(length) × 20 mm (width) × 10 mm (thickness). The cubic specimen was subjected to homogenization treatment at 1200 °C for 24h, followed by water quenching. To prevent sample oxidation during the homogenization, the samples were sealed into a quartz tube filled with argon gas. Cylindrical specimens of φ4✕4 mm were prepared via electrical discharge machining (EDM) for dynamic compression tests. The surface of the samples was mechanically polished using SiC sandpaper to eliminate surface defects. Dynamic compressive tests were performed at room temperature using a standard SHPB system (ZDSHPB-20), with strain rates ranging from 1000 s−1-4000 s−1. Processing Text: A hybrid nanostructured surface layer has been produced on interstitial-free steel by means of surface mechanical rolling treatment and subsequent chromizing treatment. As-received billets were first annealed at 850 °C for 120 min to obtain a CG structure with an average grain size of ∼200 μm, and then cut by electro-spark discharge machining to prepare cylindrical tensile specimens (for both experimental and controlled groups) with a gauge section of 4 mm in diameter and 10 mm in length. SMRT was applied to prepare a GNS surface layer on tensile specimens. After SMRT, a pure Cr layer of ∼0.30 μm in thickness was electroplated onto treated surface in an aqueous solution of 25.0 CrO 3and 0.25 H 2SO 4(in wt.%). Subsequently, Cr-coated and as-prepared (i.e. Cr-free) SMRT samples were annealed together in vacuum at 500 °C for 720 min. To preclude the possible influence on tensile properties from any residual Cr, annealed Cr-coated samples were gently polished by using an abrasive paper (5000 grit) and a surface layer of ∼0.50 μm in thickness was removed before tensile testing. Processing state: Surface Mechanical Rolling Treatment and subsequent chromizing treatment; Microstructure: Hybrid nanostructured surface layer with GBZ-UFG structure in near-surface layer and gradient structured subsurface layer

Processing Text: In this study, a TiZrHf RMPEA (Ti 33.3Zr 33.3Hf 33.3, in at%) was produced using vacuum arc melting, followed by rapid solidification. Initially, high-purity Ti, Zr, and Hf metals were mechanically polished to remove surface oxides, then pre-treated by soaking in organic solvents and vacuum dried. A small quantity of high-purity Ti ingot was added to act as an oxygen-getter. The vacuum chamber was evacuated to 10 −3Pa using a mechanical and molecular pump, then filled with 0.05 MPa of high-purity argon gas for protection. During the melting process, a current of 150-350 A was applied to heat and fully melt the metals, while magnetic stirring ensured chemical homogeneity. Multiple melting cycles (5-6) were conducted to eliminate any unmelted residues. Finally, the melt was suction-cast into a copper mold (10 × 10 × 70 mm). After cooling, a cylindrical as-cast TiZrHf sample was obtained. Before each experiment, both the flyer plate and the TiZrHf sample (Φ10 × 2 mm) were ground and polished to a mirror finish. Condition: quasi-static loading, Strain rate: 10^-4 s^-1

Processing Text: Round bar tensile samples with a diameter of 6 mm and a gauge length of 30 mm were machined from a φ20 mm-rod, which was solution-heat-treated at 1080 °C for 2 min followed by water-quenching. To obtain sufficiently averaged neutron diffraction patterns across the sample's gauge part, a uniformly hydrogen-charged (H-charged) sample was prepared via thermal exposure. The sample was subjected to a hydrogen gas atmosphere at 100 MPa and 270 °C for 200 h. The hydrogen concentration (CH) was quantified using Thermal Desorption Spectroscopy (TDS) coupled with a gas chromatography having a thermal conductivity detector (JTF-20A, J-SCIENCE LAB Co., Ltd., Japan). The analysis was conducted with a time step of 5 min, spanning a temperature range from 25 °C to 800 °C. Argon gas was used as the carrier with a heating rate of 100 °C/h. In situ neutron diffraction experiments during tensile tests were conducted at the Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility (MLF) of the Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex (J-PARC), utilizing the Engineering Materials Diffractometer, TAKUMI. During the plastic deformation, the crosshead speed was set at 0.05 mm/min, corresponding to an initial strain rate of 3×10−5 sec−1. The microstructures of the deformed samples, as well as that of the undeformed ones, were analyzed using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) technique, equipped with a field-emission (FE-) scanning electron microscope (SEM), Sigma Zeiss, Germany. Condition: H-charged sample; Measurement: 0.2% proof stress

Processing Text: Austenitization was conducted by holding the annealed steel at 880 °C for 40 min. Subsequent water quenching resulted in a fully martensitic microstructure. Tempering treatments were performed by holding the as-quenched steel at subcritical temperatures of 500 °C, 550 °C, and 600 °C for durations of up to 2 h to initiate microstructural evolution followed by air cooling. The specimen preparation involved grinding with 400∼3000 grit sandpaper, followed by a 10-s electropolishing step in a solution of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol. The specimens were extracted from 5 mm-thick heat-treated sheets utilizing a spark wire-cutting machine. Subsequently, the tensile specimens were abraded with 2000 grit emery paper and polished using 1 μm diamond paste. The specimens were then subjected to electrochemical charging to incorporate hydrogen atoms using an aqueous solution containing 0.05 mol L−1 H2SO4 and 3 g L−1 NH4SCN. A current density of 1.0 mA cm−2 was consistently maintained for 12 h at ambient temperature. To confirm that the gauge section of the specimens was exposed to hydrogen charging, the remaining components were thoroughly coated with a layer of silica gel to prevent any contact with the electrolyte solution. Immediately following the electrochemical charging, a layer of zinc was electroplated onto the surface to prevent hydrogen escape from the hydrogen-charged specimens. The protective zinc coating was applied using an aqueous solution containing ZnCl2 powder (64.3 g L−1), KCl (334.3 g L−1), H3BO4 (30.8 g L−1), and C12H25SO4Na (0.71 g L−1) at the current density of 25 mA cm−2 for 30 min. The Al-1.52 Mg-1.84 Mn-0.03 Si-0.05 Fe (wt%) alloy was processed in a Nabertherm electric resistance furnace using a 99.99 %Al, 99.95 %Mg, and Al-10 %Mn master alloy and was solidified at a casting cooling rate of ∼10 K/s. A mean grain size was 170 ± 30 µm for as-cast alloy. Samples with dimensions of 9 × 9 × 18 mm and 28 × 28 × 56 mm cut from the as-cast ingot were subjected to MDF for a cumulative strain of ∑e = 14.4 (6 cycles) and strain per pass of 0.8 at temperatures of 300 and 350 °C with a strain rate of ∼10 −2 s −1. Small samples were used to analyze stress–strain behavior, bulk samples were used to study mechanical properties, the microstructure was controlled for both. The MDF process details and the stress–strain curve recalculation method are described in [18]. The room-temperature mechanical properties were determined for MDF-treated samples and MDF-treated and annealed at 300 °C samples according to ASTM E8/E8M standard using a Zwick Z250 universal testing machine with a tensile rate of 5 mm/min. Three samples with a gage size of 25 × 6 × 1 mm were tested. Processing state: MDF-treated at 300 °C; Strengthening mechanisms: I-phase precipitation strengthening and grain boundary strengthening

Processing Text: Equimolar CoCrNi MEA was prepared by arc-melting Co, Cr, and Ni mixtures with 99.99 % purity in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted more than five times before the drop-cast process to ensure homogeneity. Subsequently, the as-cast CoCrNi MEA ingot was cold-forged by a 50 % reduction in thickness. Afterward, the alloy was annealed at 1173K for 1 h to reduce deformation-induced defects and promote recrystallization. Quasi-static compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^−1 s^−1 were performed on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 6 mm using an Instron 5969 testing machine. Dynamic compression tests with strain rates ranging from 2.6 × 10^3 s^−1 to 6.2 × 10^3 s^−1 were carried out on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 3 mm using a SHPB system. Stop-ring technology was introduced to control the strain during the dynamic compressions. The ramp wave and shock compression experiments were conducted using the CQ-4 magnetically driven system, delivering a pulsed current with a peak value of 4 MA and a rising time of 500 ns, developed by the Institute of Fluid Physics, China Academy of Engineering Physics. Multi-level characterizations were conducted to explore the intrinsic mechanisms of CoCrNi MEA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed using a JEOL JSM-7100F field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). An acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a specimen tilt angle of 70°, and a working distance of 15 mm were used in the EBSD observations. A JEM-2100F transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV to uncover microscopic deformation mechanisms. Strain rate: 10^-3 s^-1; Loading method: Quasi-static

Processing Text: lightweight (B4C)p/2024Al-T6 composites with varying volume percentages (30 vol.%, 50 vol.%, and 70 vol.%) were fabricated using pressure infiltration technology. The mold was filled with a certain powder gradation of (B4C)p and then placed in a furnace and pre-heated at the temperature 873-923 K for 4 h. Afterward, the molten 2024Al at 800 °C was poured into the prepared perform, and pressure was applied to form a sound interface between the Al matrix and ceramic particles until the solidification was complete. Finally, the composites and 2024Al were subjected to a solution treatment at 495 °C for 1 h and aging treatment at 190 !°C for 8 h to obtain excellent strength as T6 heat treatment. The densities of (B4C)p/2024Al-T6 composites were measured by the Archimedes method. The compressive yield stress of the composites was measured using an Instron-5569 electronic compress testing machine at 0.5 mm/min. The Young's modulus of (B4C)p/2024Al-T6 composites with volume fractions of 70 %, 50 %, and 30 % was determined using a dynamic elastic modulus tester (EMT-01). Dynamic stress-strain curves for the composites at a strain rate of 1500 s -1 were obtained using a 12.7 mm SHPB system. Composite with 30 vol.% B4C particles; measured using an Instron-5569 electronic compress testing machine at 0.5 mm/min.

Processing Text: Inconel 625 spherical powder from Sailong Metal Company (China) were used for the bulk HL-DED Inconel 625 and coated specimens. The powders were dried in an oven at 100 ℃ for 120 min to ensure good fluidity and to remove moisture. Bulk HL-DED Inconel 625 and coated specimens were manufactured using the ultra-high-speed laser cladding system (ZKZM-4000, ZKZM Co., China), which includes 4 kW laser, a central powder feeding system, and a computer numerical control stage. The deposition parameters were 1.8 kW laser power, 22 g/min powder feeding rate, 4 m/min laser scanning velocity, 80 % deposition tracks overlap, and 0.5 mm interlayer elevation. A single-layer Inconel 625 coating was produced moving the laser beam from left to right, while the double-layer coating was produced by laser beam passed from left to right, and then from right to left. For the double-layer coating, the endpoint of the first layer deposition served as the starting point for the second layer deposition. Based in the Inconel 625 coating defects and tensile properties discussed later, the optimal deposition parameters were 1.8 kW laser power and 4.6 Hz rotation frequency. The coating deposition rate is controlled by the rotation frequency in our experiments. The powder feeding rate was 34 g/min. The laser power was varied along with the rotation frequency. Although higher rotation speeds improve coating preparation efficiency, the maximum frequency of the computer numerical control equipment is limited to 5 Hz. Coating: Single-layer; Laser power: 1.6 kW

In the second set of experiments, the solution-treated alloy underwent a first-stage cold rolling with a deformation of 50 %, followed by aging treatments at temperatures of 400 °C, 450 °C, 500 °C, and 550 °C for holding times of 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, and 8 h. Following this, a second-stage cold rolling was performed with another 50 % deformation, ensuring the total deformation matched that of the R1 process. Processing Text: A series of 10 mm diameter bars were cut from the ingot using an electric discharge wire cutting machine (DK7735) as the initial sample for the whole process. A number of as-cast 7075 Al alloy bars were placed in a vacuum high temperature heating furnace (SGL-1700C). In order to reduce microstructure inhomogeneity and then improve room temperature deformability, a double-stage homogenization (DTH) 738K-24h+748K-4h was conducted on as-cast 7075 Al alloy, based on previous studies [30,41]. Subsequently, water quenching to room temperature was used and the sample transfer time was controlled within 3 s to avoid the effect of air cooling, resulting in supersaturated solid solution (SSS). Then, 7075 Al alloy was immediately placed into ECAP dies with inner angles of 120° and outer angles of 30°. At room temperature, the alloy was deformed by one ECAP pass using a four-column hydraulic press (YT-160T) at a descending rate of 3 mm/s, with each pass resulting in an effective strain of 0.622. Molybdenum disulfide (MoS 2) was used as a lubricant throughout the process to reduce the friction between the specimen and the mold. After ECAP, 7075 Al alloy was placed in CU dies and formed into fasteners, called ECAPed-CU samples. Finally, the ECAPed-CU samples of 7075 Al alloy fasteners were put into a vacuum high-temperature heating furnace (SGL-1700C) to be artificially aged (AA) at temperatures of 353 K, 383 K and 423 K at a heating rate of 283 K/min and for times of 10, 20, 60, 120 and 180 min, respectively, with specific experimental parameters and expressions shown in Table 2. The electrical discharge wire cutting machine (DK7735) was used to prepare dog-bone tensile specimens measuring 30 mm ×6 mm ×1.2 mm (with a gauge length of 10 mm) from the specimens. The specimens were ground and polished using sandpaper and polishing paste, followed by cleaning and drying using an ultrasonic cleaning machine (G-040S). The specimens were then subjected to uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature using a universal tensile testing machine (JVJ-50s) at a rate of 5 mm/min. Each specimen was tested three times to ensure the accuracy of the results. The microhardness test specimens were ground and polished to a mirror finish on a mechanical polishing machine (MP-2B). The prepared samples were subjected to microhardness testing at room temperature using a microhardness tester (MHVD-1000IS) with a load of 300gf and a holding time of 15 s. Each sample was tested 12 points independently, removing 4 points that were significantly different and taking the average of the remaining 8 points as the microhardness value to ensure the accuracy of the microhardness. DSC test samples were cut from the ECAPed-CU specimens using a wire cutter (DK7733). The samples were then machined on a mechanical grinding and polishing machine (MP-2B) to obtain a sample of approximately 3 mg. The specimens were placed in a differential scanning calorimetry (METTLER TOLEDO, DSC 3) and heated linearly in the range 303-773 K under nitrogen protection at a constant heating rate of 283 K/min to determine the order of phase precipitation during subsequent aging. X-ray diffraction (XRD, Smartlab3KW) was used to identity phases characterization and determine the dislocation density of all samples. After surface finishing, the samples were irradiated with a Cu kα (λ = 1.5418 Å) and the diffraction signals of 10-90° were collected from the samples at a scan rate of 5°/min and a step size of 0.02° at 40 KV and 30 mA. The microstructure evolution of the samples in terms of dislocations, grain boundaries and precipitation phase changes in different treatments were observed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-F200) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM). Meanwhile, the samples were observed by dark field imaging using high-angle annular dark field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM). For TEM observation, the samples were first mechanically ground to 60μm, followed by further ion thinning of the samples using an ion thinning system (GATAN) in an argon ion atmosphere. After ECAP

Samples were manufactured using an MLab 200R L-PBF machine (GE Additive) equipped with a 200 W Nd:YAG fibre laser (wavelength: 1064 nm) with a 75 µm spot size. Nine parameter sets were trailed with four samples for each parameter (totalling 36 samples simultaneously fabricated). The specimens had dimensions of 10 × 10 × 25 mm 3( X-Y-Z, where Zis the build direction (BD)) and were fabricated with a support structure on top of a 316 L stainless steel build plate. An alternating 90° rotation of the laser raster direction was employed between build layers. A 25 µm layer thickness ( t) and 75 µm hatch spacing ( h) were maintained for all specimens. The following process parameters were applied: laser power ( P) between 95 and 195 W and scanning speed ( s) between 360 and 860 mm/s. A Pof 195 W and sof 860 mm/s led to the highest material density of 99.90 ± 0.07 %, as measured by using Archimedes’ principle. The middle section of the samples was sectioned using an Accutom-50 diamond saw (Struers) to prepare cross-sections in two planes: the XZplane (parallel to BD) and the XYplane (perpendicular to BD). Specimens from the XZplane were mounted in epoxy and mechanically polished to a 0.25 μm surface finish, using a combination of silicon carbide papers followed by diamond suspension polishing. Subsequently, the samples were further polished using a VibroMet 2 vibratory polisher (Buehler) with 0.04 µm colloidal silica surface finish followed by broad Ar-ion surface polishing using a PECS II system (Gatan) at 4 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed using a Spectra and Themis-Z (Thermo Fisher Scientific), both operated at an accelerating voltage of 300 kV, coupled with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDXS). Site-specific TEM samples were prepared by standard lift-out techniques from polished EBSD specimens using a Helios G4 plasma focused ion beam (PFIB) SEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Atom probe tomography (APT) was conducted using an INVIZO 6000 (CAMECA) equipped with a dual 257.5 nm UV laser system. Site-specific APT specimens were also lifted-out from polished EBSD specimens via standard APT lift-out techniques in the Helios G4 PFIB SEM. APT was performed at ∼50 K and ∼2.6 × 10 -11Torr. A laser power of 400 pJ and laser pulse repetition rate of 200 kHz with a detection rate of 2 % were used. Processing state: as-built; Compressive test result

Processing Text: The Ti-5411 alloy ingot was melted with high-purity sponge Ti, Zr, and Mo, Cr, V bulk raw materials by vacuum arc melting furnace. To ensure the uniformity of the composition, the ingot was turned over and melted under magnetic stirring 8 times. The β phase transformation temperature ( Tβ) of the Ti-5411 alloy was analyzed by metallographic method to be about ∼745°C. The ingot was processed in two stages, the first stage of which was multi-pass hot rolling at 800 °C to 4 mm thick plates. In the second stage, the 4 mm-thick hot-rolled sheet was kept at 800 °C for 20 min and then water-cooled, while the 0.8 mm thick sheet was obtained by multi-pass unidirectional cold rolling. The total deformation of the cold-rolled sheet was 80%. The cold-rolled sheet was held at 780 °C for 20 min and then water-quenched to obtain the microstructure of the equiaxial β-phase. The sheet was placed in a tube furnace (argon atmosphere) to prevent oxidation of Ti-5411 alloy during heat treatment. Uniaxial tensile tests were implemented on a universal testing machine (GOTECH, AI-7000-LAU10) at a tensile speed of 0.5 mm/min. In-situ tensile tests were implemented at tensile speed of 0.033 mm/min on a Gatan loading system accessory with maximum load capacity of 1800 N installed on SEM (Zeiss 300). The in-situ tensile specimens were mechanically and electrolytically polished to remove residual stresses and improve the surface quality of the tensile specimens. Electropolishing was carried out at a voltage of 40 V for 45 s in an electrolytic polishing solution at −20 °C. The electrolytic polishing solution was formulated with 5% perchloric acid, 60% methanol and 35% n-butanol (volume proportion). Metastable β titanium alloy; Water-quenched state

Processing Text: FeCoNiCr high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are often prepared by casting, resulting in a coarse-grained (CG) microstructure and low yield strength. The synthesis of FeCoNiCr HEA through mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS) results in finer grain size, leading to high yield strength but low fracture strain. FeCoNiCr HEAs are often prepared by conventional casting, casting after purifying melts with B 2O 3, and occasionally by severe plastic deformation (SPD). Conventional casting of FeCoNiCr HEAs produces grain sizes ranging from 30 to 500 μm, yielding low strength (202 MPa) but high fracture strain (> 60 %). SPD processing of FeCoNiCr HEA can decrease the grain size to 50 μm, resulting in higher yield strength of 280 MPa and a lower fracture strain of 35 %. Casting after purifying melts with B 2O 3 causes supercooling, leading to a finer grain size of 7-20 μm, higher yield strength of 455 MPa, and a lower fracture strain of 16.8 %. FeCoNiCr HEA synthesized by MA and SPS techniques (MA-SPSed-FeCoNiCr HEA) leads to a grain size of 0.8 μm and significantly higher yield strength of 657 MPa. FeCoNiCr HEA containing 5 wt% nanoscale Y 2O 3 particles synthesized by MA and SPS techniques can even result in a grain size of 0.1 μm, leading to extremely high yield strength (1754 MPa), albeit with a low fracture-strain (5.8 %). CG FeCoNiCr (in equimolar ratio) HEAs were made via arc-melting a mixture of four elemental metal fragments. CG FeCoNiCr HEA was remelted five times to ensure uniformity and was made into an ingot weighing approx. 30 g in an electric arc furnace (Shenyang Jinyan JVAM-1B). Powders of FeCoNiCr HEA were prepared by mechanically alloying elemental Fe, Co, Ni, and Cr powders in a SPEX 8000D shaker mill for 24 h. A CS-IB cubic-anvil press was used to consolidate the as-milled powders into a bulk specimen for 30 min at 1000 °C and 4 GPa pressure. Processing Text: Al 0.7CoCrFeNi (at%) HEA ingot was prepared by levitation melting. In this study, pure metals of Al, Co, Cr, Fe and Ni (purity ≥ 99.9 %, wt%) were used as raw materials and loaded into a vacuum levitation melting furnace. Prior to the melting, the furnace was evacuated to 1 × 10⁻³ Pa to remove gases and volatile impurities from the alloy. During the whole melting process, the melt was electromagnetically stirred to ensure a uniform distribution of heat and thus the composition. Then the melt was cast into a graphite mold with dimensions of 200 mm × 200 mm × 25 mm. The alloy was set into a resistance heating furnace (SX-G 1300 ℃) holding at 1000 °C for isothermal and at 1050 °C to 1250 °C for non-isothermal treatments, followed by water quenching. Flat dog-bone-shape specimens with a dimension of 49 mm (in length) × 9 mm (in width) × 1 mm (in thickness) were cut by wire electric discharge machining for the test of mechanical properties. The tensile tests were carried out through a universal testing machine (Shimadzu AGX-V 100 KN) at room temperature with a nominal strain rate of 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. The Vickers hardness was measured using a micro-hardness tester (3S-1000QZ) with a loading force of 500 g/N for 10 s. Prior to microstructure characterizations, HEA samples were prepared by the standard metallographic method. After grinding with SiC sandpaper up to 7000 grit and polishing with diamond paste. The X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D/max-2200) and the scanning electron microscopy (SEM-5000Pro) were employed to examine the microstructure and composition. The XRD analysis was performed using Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å, 40 kV, 40 mA) with the range (2θ) of 20° to 100° at a scanning speed of 8°/min, and a step size of 0.026°. To observe the microstructure, samples were etched with aqua regia (HCl: HNO₃ = 3:1) and then characterized utilizing the SEM equipped with an energy-dispersive (EDS) detector, operating in the back-scatter electron (BSE) mode at a working voltage of 15 kV and a working distance of 6 mm. The phase volume fraction, average lamellar thickness, and precipitation phase size were assessed using Image-J software. The isothermal treatment at 1000 °C indicates that the prolonged holding time promotes the transformation of the BCC/B2 phases to the FCC phase. The heat-treatment duration was strictly regulated to be within 3 h. In the initial stage of exploring the combined effects of the lamellar structure and B2 precipitates, the temperature interval for non-isothermal heat treatment was precisely set at 50 °C. Subsequently, with the intention of accentuating the influence of the lamellar-strengthening effect on the mechanical properties by highlighting the variances in the morphological distribution of the lamellar phase, the temperature interval was further augmented to 100 °C. The ingots were inverted and remelted five times to ensure chemical homogeneity, followed by casting into a copper mold with dimensions of 8 × 20 × 60 mm 3. Then the CR sheet was partially annealed at 700 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling. The reason for choosing the partial annealing temperature of 700 °C is shown in Supplementary Text 2. Interrupted tensile tests at specific strains of 5 % and 15 % were also performed on the PR sample to evaluate microstructural evolution upon tension. TEM slices were cut from undeformed and deformed samples, mechanically grounded to ∼30μm, and then twin-jet polished in a solution of 5 vol% perchloric acid and 95 vol% ethanol at around −20 °C. Processing Text: An alloy with a nominal composition of Al-3.80Ni-0.50Cr-0.15Zr (all in atomic %) was prepared by arc melting constituent elements with 4 N purity (99.99 at %) under an argon atmosphere at a vacuum level of ∼10⁻⁵ mbar. The molten button was chill cast into a split copper mold to produce a rod with a diameter of 3 mm and a length of 80 mm. After confirming the absence of solute microsegregation and verifying the bulk alloy composition using wavelength dispersive spectroscopy (WDS) in a field emission gun (FEG) electron probe microanalyzer (EPMA, JEOL JXA-8530F) operating at 30 kV, the cast alloy was sliced into small pieces and subjected to aging heat treatment at 375 °C and 400 °C for various durations, followed by water quenching. TEM samples were prepared by manually grinding 3 mm discs to a thickness of 30 µm, followed by argon ion milling using a precision ion polishing system (PIPS II, Gatan) to obtain electron-transparent regions. The preliminary aging response was confirmed by measuring the Vickers hardness (HV) using a microhardness tester (Future Tech, FM-800) at a 100 g load and a dwell time of 10 s. The yield strength of the peak-aged alloys was evaluated using a screw-driven uniaxial testing machine (Zwick/Roell) at a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹ and test temperatures of 25 °C (room temperature, RT), 200 °C, and 250 °C. Compression test specimens, with dimensions of 3 mm diameter and a height of 5 to 6 mm (1.5 ≤ h⁄ d≥ 2.0), were prepared from the peak-aged rod. Maraging 250 steel wire was used as a feedstock material and remotely fed under the electrode to coincide with the plasma arc during printing. Before printing bulk samples, 12 single tracks were printed as a preliminary study to identify optimized printing parameters. The optimized printing parameters were set as: welding current 182 A, voltage 30 V, welding speed 5 mm/s and wire feed speed 50 mm/s. During printing, argon (99.99% purity) was applied as both shielding and welding gas. Using these parameters, thin walls of about 80 mm (length) × 20 mm (height) × 10 mm (width) with a layer thickness of 1.2 mm were printed with different interlayer dwell times of 0 min, 1 min, and 3 min to exploit the effects of thermal history on the microstructure evolution and mechanical properties of the printed maraging 250 steels. By introducing a dwell time between adjacent layers, the maraging 250 steel is cooled below the martensite start temperature, triggering thermally-driven martensitic transformation during the printing process. Thermal cycling during subsequent layer deposition results in the formation of reverted austenite which shows a refined microstructure and induces elemental segregation between martensite and reverted austenite. The reverted austenite is metastable during deformation, leading to strain-induced martensitic transformation under loading. Specifically, a 3 min interlayer dwell time produces a maraging 250 steel with approximately 8% reverted austenite, resulting in improved work hardening via martensitic transformation induced plasticity during deformation. Meanwhile, the higher cooling rate and refined prior austenite grains lead to substantially refined martensitic grains (by approximately fivefold) together with an increased dislocation density. With 3 min interlayer dwell time, the yield strength of the printed maraging 250 steel increases from 836 MPa to 990 MPa, and the uniform elongation is doubled from 3.2% to 6.5%. This intermittent deposition strategy during PAW-DED allows us to achieve an outstanding strength-ductility synergy that outperforms conventional wrought and other additively manufactured maraging steel counterparts. Processing Text: The commercially available TC4 titanium alloy bars in an annealed state with the dimensions of Ф50 mm× 200 mm were used in this experiment. The annealing process was heating at 750 ℃ for 1.5 h and then air-cooled. The rectangular billets with dimensions of 35 mm × 35 mm × 37 mm were cut from the centre of the long bar for the subsequent MDF process. The relationship between DRX behavior and strain rate was determined by hot compression experiment. The deformation temperature was selected to be 940 ℃, 880 ℃ and 820 ℃. MDF was conducted on a four-column hydraulic press. The sample was rapidly heated in the furnace to the deformation temperature and then was soaked at this temperature for 5 min. Each forging pass was involved in three steps, and the forging axis was rotated by 90° step by step (i.e. Z to X to Y to Z). The true strain for each step was 0.22, calculated from ln(h 0/h 1), where h 0and h 1were the blank height values before and after forging, respectively. Therefore, the cumulative strain per pass was approximately 0.66. The samples were re-heated in a resistance furnace to the deformation temperature after each forging pass to compensate for the temperature loss during the MDF process. The microstructures of the alloys were characterized by optical microstructure (OM, Leitz MM-6), X-ray diffraction (XRD, D/MAX2500PC), scanning electron microscope (SEM, FEI Quanta 200), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Titan G2 F20). The samples for OM observation were etched in a solution of 0.5 ml hydrofluoric acid, 1 ml nitric acid and 25 ml deionised water. TEM and EBSD foils were firstly ground to 80 µm and then further prepared with a twin-jet electropolisher (a solution of 6 % perchloric acid+34 % normal butanol+60 % methyl alcohol, vol%). Mechanical properties of the alloys were characterized by tensile tests. The room temperature tensile tests were conducted on an Instron 3369 electronic universal testing machine at a constant cross-head speed of 1 mm/ min. Processing Text: Raw Cu, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al and Ti blocks with purity>99.8 wt % were selected to prepare the 3.5 kg CuCrFeNiTi0.8Al1.2 HEA via magnetic levitation induction melting under high purity argon atmosphere. The purity of the alloy is guaranteed by removing the oxide scale on the surface of the crude material and cleaning it in acetone by ultrasonic wave for 20 min. The melting process was repeated 4 times to achieve chemical homogeneity. In order to better study the organizational transformation behavior and solidification process during annealing, the obtained specimen was then annealed at 800 °C and 1000 °C for 24 h, followed by water quenching. Upon the introduction of annealing process, significant grain refinement was achieved. Additionally, the increase of annealing temperature led to the presence of secondary precipitated particles within the alloy. The annealed CuCrFeNiTi0.8Al1.2 HEA displays similar microstructure compared to the as-cast state. Following annealed at 800 °C, there are much more precipitates generated in the grains and several structures transformed from spherical to short-rod. Besides, note a great deal of micron-particles are precipitated from matrix. As increase the annealing temperature to 1000 °C, relatively large quantities of secondary nano-particles precipitated from α phase not just the micro-particle from DR matrix. Room temperature compressive properties and Vickers hardness of CuCrFeNiTi0.8Al1.2 HEAs were tested to study the mechanical properties. Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: The cast AlZnCuMgSi alloy was prepared using high-purity Al (99.999%), Cu (99.90%), Si (99.90%), Mg (99.90%), and Zn (99.50%) through a melting-casting method. When the melt reached 830 °C, Si was added and thoroughly mixed into the molten Al, then allowed to stand for 15 min to ensure complete dissolution. At 800 °C, Cu was introduced, stirred well, and left to stand for 10 min. When the melt cooled to 780 °C, Zn was added, followed by Mg, which experienced an approximate loss of 10%. The ingot was kept at 490 °C for 12 h, and then water cooled to achieve homogenization. Before extrusion, the ingot and the heating sleeve were heated to 250 °C, 300 °C, and 350 °C, respectively, for 30 min. Extrusion was then carried out using a 600-ton hydraulic press at speeds of 0.3 mm/s, 0.6 mm/s and 1.0 mm/s. During the extrusion process, the extrusion ratio was 16:1, and oil-based graphite was used as a lubricant. Extrusion temperature: 250 °C; Extrusion speed: 1.0 mm/s

The ingots of the alloy were prepared by melting pure magnesium, zinc, copper, and Mg-30Ce Master alloy in a high-temperature resistance furnace, and SF 6and CO 2mixed gas were introduced for protection. Processing Text: The material was subjected to melting in a vacuum induction furnace to yield a 50 kg ingot, followed by homogenization at 1050 °C. Subsequently, the material was forged into a 45 mm × 45 mm square bar through a process of upsetting and drawing at temperatures ranging from 1150 to 850 °C, repeated three times. Subsequent to the forging process, the material was allowed to cool in a ambient atmosphere. Cylindrical specimens (Φ3 mm × 10 mm) were extracted from the forged bar using electrical discharge machining. All the samples were austenitized at 920 °C for 2 h, and then quenched with different cooling media (water, oil, air, and furnace) to ambient temperature. Some of the water-cooling quenched specimens (Q920) were then tempered at between 560 ◦C and 700 °C. For convenience, the samples after tempering at the different temperatures of 560, 600, 640, 660, 680, and 700 °C are designated T560, T600, T640, T660, T680, and T700 respectively. After heat treatment, the specimens were processed into standard tensile samples with dimensions of Φ5 mm × 10 mm and standard Charpy V-notch impact samples with dimensions of 55 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm. They were subjected to a tensile test using a Z-150 universal testing machine and Charpy -60 °C impact test using a PIH-752H pendulum impact tester. Metallographic specimens (10 mm × 10 mm) were cut, then mechanically ground, polished, and etched with 4 % (volume fraction) nital. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) samples were prepared using a twin-jet electropolishing device. Firstly, the thickness of the thin slice specimen was reduced to less than 50 μm. Then, the specimen was punched into a 3 mm diameter disc using a punching instrument. Finally, the thin-film specimen was prepared using a twin-jet electropolishing device. The twin-jet solution contained anhydrous ethanol and 10 % (volume fraction) perchloric acid solution. Processing Text: The target nominal hypoeutectic composition of Fe–4.85Ti–0.78B (wt.%) was designed, which is equivalent to 5 vol%TiB2 (equivalent to 2.4 wt%TiB2) in an α–Fe matrix. The feedstock is a powder mixture of commercially available raw materials of gas–atomized Fe (99.99%, 15–53 μm), Ti (99.99%, 1–3 μm) and TiB2 (99.8%, 3–5 μm). The raw materials at the predesigned ratio were mechanically blended with a planetary ball mill (QM–3SP4, NANDA INSTRUMENT, China) at 200 rpm for 2 h to obtain a uniformly mixed mixture. Processing Text: The maraging steel employed in this study was Fe-18Ni-8.5Co-5Mo-0.7Ti-0.2Al (wt.%). The steel was produced using a vacuum induction melting furnace and cast into ingots with a diameter of 50 mm and a weight of 2 kg. Before melting, the furnace chamber was evacuated to 10−3Pa and filled with 0.05 MPa of high-purity argon as a shielding gas. The steel ingot was remelted five times to ensure uniform distribution of the alloying elements and subsequently homogenized at 1100 °C for 2 h to eliminate compositional segregation. Specimens for testing and observation were subjected to two different heat treatments. The first heat treatment process was solid solution treatment (SST) at 840 °C for 1 h, followed by single aging treatment (SAT) at 480 °C for 4 h. The second heat treatment process was SST at 840 °C for 1 h, followed by aging at 370 °C for 2 h (DAT-1) and at 480 °C for 4 h (DAT-2), which was denoted by duplex aging treatment (DAT). The heat treatment processes used to produce the SAT and DAT samples in this work are displayed in Fig. 1. The dog-bone shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 20 mm and a gauge diameter of 3 mm were machined from heat-treated samples. Room temperature tensile tests were conducted on the Instron 5969 testing machine with a laser extensometer at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. More than three independent tensile tests were performed for each sample. The fracture toughness was assessed by ASTM Standard E1820 using compact tensile C(T) specimens with a thickness of B= 4 mm and a width of W= 8 mm. All specimen surfaces were ground and polished to enable the measurement of crack length using a Leica DM4 long-distance optical microscope. Before the fracture toughness measurement, all the C(T) specimens were fatigue pre-cracked to a crack length with 0.45 W< a <0.55 Wrange using an Instron E300 electro-dynamic test instrument at a frequency of 40 Hz with a load ratio Fmin/ Fmaxof 0.1. The in-situ synchrotron experiments with a gauge size of 20 × 4 × 0.4 mm3were performed at Beamline BL22XU in Spring-8, Japan. The wavelength of the high-energy X-ray beam was 0.4131 Å. The beam size was 0.2 × 0.2 mm2. The sample-to-detector distance was 207.6 mm. A uniaxial tensile machine (Yonekura, Osaka, Japan) with a maximum loading of 2 kN was utilized for the tensile test, and the tensile strain rate was 1 × 10−3s−1. The diffraction profiles (2-D Debye rings) were recorded during the tensile deformation of the samples using a high-speed CCD camera with a dwell time for each profile of 1 s. Then, the recorded images were analyzed using Image J software. X-ray diffraction (XRD) characterization was employed on a Bruker D8 X diffractometer. Data collection was performed using Cu-Kαradiation in the 2θrange of 30-100° at a scan step interval of 0.02°. The microstructure and fracture topography were observed using the Tescan Clara S8151 scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). Simultaneously, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) mapping was conducted using the Tescan Clara S8151 SEM equipped with a fully automatic Oxford Instruments Aztec 2.0 EBSD system (Channel 5 software). The operating voltages of SEM and EBSD were 20 kV and 10 kV, and the scanning step size of EBSD was 0.05 μm. The EBSD sample was mechanically polished and electropolished in an electrolyte of 95 vol% glacial acetic acid and 5 vol% perchloric acid at −25 °C and 30 V. The transmission electron microscope (TEM) observations were conducted in an FEI-Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN microscope operating at 200 kV. The samples for TEM characterization were prepared by mechanical polishing down to a thickness of 50 μm and then punching them into discs with a diameter of 3 mm. Finally, the discs were electropolished by twin-jet electro-polishing in an electrolyte of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% glacial acetic acid performed at −30 °C and 20 V. The Mo-enriched particles precipitated after solid solution treatment due to the low solubility and diffusion rate at low temperatures. The aging treatment conducted at 370 °C enhances the density of the Mo-enriched particles and inhibits the formation of Ni3Ti. The pre-formed precipitates act as heterogeneous nucleation sites for Ni3Ti during aging at 480 °C, increasing the nucleation rate and reducing the size. As aging continues, Mo segregates to the interface of Ni3Ti and the matrix, inhibiting the growth of Ni3Ti and forming Fe7Mo2 precipitates. Processing Text: TiAl composites with Ti-rich region were prepared by hot-pressing sintering using Ti powders and Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb alloy powders as raw materials. Ti-48Al-2Cr-2 Nb powders and pure Ti powders were used as raw materials. Ti powders were adhered to Ti-48Al-2Cr-2 Nb powders by ball milling to ensure that the powder is evenly dispersed inside the TiAl composite, and the TiAl composite with Ti-rich region was successfully prepared via powder metallurgy. The TiAl composite was prepared by vacuum hot-pressing sintering technology. The process involved the following steps: First, the powders were mixed by a planetary ball mill at 250 r/min for 1.5 h. Second, the mixed powders were heated and pressed at 1200 °C and 30 MPa for 1 h in a vacuum hot-pressing sinter furnace (ZT-40-21Y, Shanghai Chenhua Co., Ltd. China). Third, to obtain the compact structure and reduce the porosity of the TiAl composite, the hot extrusion is performed at 1100 °C with a strain rate of 1 × 10 −4s −1and a deformation amount of 10 %. Tensile tests were carried out at 1 × 10 −4s −1under 800 °C, 900 °C, and 1000 °C in air atmosphere, respectively. Temperature: 800°C

Thermo-mechanical processing, including extrusion, has resulted in alloys with high ultimate tensile strength values, representing the largest proportion of the database. Other valid processing methods include casting + high-temperature heat treatment and forging. In general, the maximum values of yield and ultimate tensile strengths can be obtained through three process routes: extrusion, casting + high-temperature treatment, and deformation. The highest ductility values in this database were also obtained under forging and extrusion processing conditions, suggesting that the combination of thermal and mechanical processing is the key to alloy strengthening. The compositions of the alloys and the processing in the new experimental data are detailed in Table 4. The newly generated high tensile strength magnesium alloys were analyzed in comparison with the tensile strength data of magnesium alloys in the training dataset. The recommended newly generated magnesium alloys are compared with the data of magnesium alloys in the database, and the results show that the newly generated data effectively fills the vacancy of yield strength greater than 440 MPa in the database. Afterwards, through the solubility-based stochastic generation algorithm, combined with the A-SMOTE technology and gradient-enhanced regression (GBR) model, the inverse design and prediction of the composition ratio of the new magnesium alloy was successfully realized, striving for the magnesium alloy to have high yield strength and tensile strength under the condition of high ductility. A Cu-4Ti-0.5Cr-0.5 Mg alloy, specifically designed to achieve superior strength and conductivity, was subjected to pre-aging, cold rolling, and final aging to improve its mechanical and electrical characteristics. Cu-4Ti-0.5Cr-0.5 Mg (wt. %) ingots measuring 120 × 150 × 25 mm were produced by casting pure copper, titanium, magnesium, and chromium in an intermediate frequency furnace. After addressing surface defects, the ingot underwent hot rolling at 830 °C, reducing its thickness from 6.7 mm to 2 mm. Subsequently, the hot-rolled samples of the Cu-4Ti-0.5Cr-0.5 Mg alloy were subjected to solid-solution treatment at 900 °C for 240 min and quenched in water to obtain a supersaturated solid solution (ST). The first group was pre-aged at 450 °C for different durations (referred to as the SA group). Subsequently, the ingot was cold rolled with a total deformation of 40%. Finally, the samples were subjected to a final aging treatment at 380 °C and 450 °C for various periods (referred to as the SARA group). The second group was directly cold-rolled with a total reduction in thickness of 40% without pre-aging and ultimately aged at 400 °C and 450 °C for different times (referred to as the SRA group). Pre-aging was suggested to increase the strength and electrical conductivity of the samples prior to cold rolling. The impacts of pre-aging, cold rolling, and final aging treatment on the microstructure and mechanical performance were thoroughly examined. Through process optimization, both the strength and the electrical conductivity of the alloy were enhanced. Pre-aging, cold rolling, and final aging treatments were implemented to enhance the overall performance of the sample. Process: SARA; Temperature: 380°C; Time: 120 min

Mg-Al-Ca alloys processed via extrusion, hot-rolling and subsequent annealing were examined, focusing on microstructures and mechanical properties. Processing Text: The FeCoCrNiCu HEA ingot with an equal atomic ratio was prepared from metals with >99.9 % purity by vacuum arc smelting under argon protection. To ensure chemical homogeneity, an ingot was remelted five times and then poured into the copper mold to prepare the HEA plate. The prepared plate was further rolled at 1150 °C to reduce the thickness by 50 %, and the rolled plate was cut into a plurality of blocks with a dimension of 5 mm × 5 mm × 4 mm by the slow wire cutting. Ulteriorly, the blocks were divided into three batches for annealing at different temperatures. Specifically, the first batch of blocks was annealed at 300 °C, which was recorded as Specimen B. The second batch of blocks was annealed at 700 °C and was recorded as Specimen C. The third batch of blocks was annealed at 1100 °C and was recorded as Specimen D. All the above blocks were annealed in a vacuum tube furnace at a temperature-rise rate of 8°/min for 4 h. Meanwhile, the as-cast specimen without rolling and annealing treatments was recorded as Specimen A, as a control experimental group. Subsequently, the dynamic compression with a strain rate of 1.8 × 10 3s −1 was carried out on four types of specimens using a SHPB device. Processing Text: Cu-0.5Cr-0.05Zr-0.15Sc alloys were prepared by vacuum melting. The hot-forged samples were cut into 5 mm thick plates and subjected to 80% reduction room-temperature rolling. Afterward, the rolled samples were vacuum aged at 350 °C-550 °C for 0-12 h. To ensure the complete dissolution of solute atoms and eliminate potential micro segregation in the as-cast structure, homogenization annealing was performed at 930 °C-990 °C (with 20 °C intervals) and at 900 °C-1050 °C (with 50 °C intervals). For the Sc-doped alloy, homogenization annealing processes of 970 °C × 2 h were applied to eliminate the micro segregation caused by Sc. Considering that some second phases precipitate after hot forging at 870 °C, both alloys were subjected to solution treatment at 1000 °C for 1 h to ensure the complete dissolution of residual second phases. For TEM sample preparation, after mechanical grinding, electro-polishing was performed at −30 °C using a solution of 70% HNO 3+ 30% CH 3OH, followed by ion milling with argon ions. EBSD samples were taken from the center of the same position on the sheet under different aging conditions, and for EBSD sample preparation, the cold-rolled samples were cut and polished on the TD plane using diamond polishing paste, followed by electro-polishing with a solution of 50% H 3PO4 acid +25% C 2H 5OH + 25% water at a current of 0.1A. Processing state: Solution treatment + 80% rolling + 450 °C × 1 h aging treatment

The materials were melted in a vacuum induction furnace and cast into 20 kg ingots. As shown in Fig. 1, after being subjected to homogenization at 1250 °C for 5 h, the ingots were cooled down to 1150 °C and held for 2 h prior to being forged into the Φ30 mm round bars to obtain a uniform composition and fine microstructure. The samples were held at 1000 °C for an hour to ensure complete solid solution of alloying elements, followed by water quenching to achieve a fully martensitic microstructure. Next, the samples were tempered at 600 °C for 2.5 h to facilitate the complete precipitation of MC-type nano-carbides, after which they were naturally cooled to room temperature. Thereafter, standard cylindrical tensile specimens with a threaded section diameter of 10 mm and a parallel section diameter of 5 mm were processed in the tempered samples along the forging direction. Afterwards, the 700 °C high-temperature tensile tests were performed on the MTS E45.105 tensile machine at a strain rate of 0.00007s−1/0.0014s−1 before and after yielding (GB 228.2-2015). The sample microstructures before and after high-temperature tensile tests were observed using a JSM-7000F field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectrum analysis (EDS) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). In terms of SEM observation, the samples were etched using 4% (V/V) nitric acid alcohol solution. Regarding EBSD analysis, the samples were etched using a solution which contained 10% HClO4 and 90% C2H5OH for 30 s. The EBSD measurements were performed at a step size of 150 nm. The nano- and micro-sized carbides in samples were observed by TEM (Titan ETEM, FEI) operating at 300 kV. The TEM thin foils (diameter, 3 mm) were prepared by twin-jet electropolishing with the 5% (V/V) perchloric acid alcohol solution. Calculated theoretical yield strength at 700 °C; Strengthening mechanisms include solid solution, grain boundary, dislocation, and MC nano-carbide strengthening.

Binary Mg–5Y (wt%) alloy ingots were prepared by a multi-step process. First, high purity Mg (99.99%) and Mg–25Y (wt%) master alloys were melted within a crucible resistance furnace at ∼750 °C. This casting process was carried out under the safeguard of a protective atmosphere comprised of SF 6 and CO 2 mixed gas, with a volume ratio of 1:100. The as-cast ingots were subsequently subjected to solution treatment in a vacuum tube furnace at 530 °C for a duration of 12 h, under the protective cover of argon gas, before being cooled in ambient air. Subsequently, cylindrical billets, processing a diameter of 90 mm, were machined from the solution-treated Mg–5Y alloys by a commercial lathe. Prior to the extrusion process, these billets were preheated at 300 °C for 2 h. The extrusion procedure includes following parameters: a mold temperature was 400 °C, an extrusion temperature was 300 °C, and an extrusion ratio of 9:1. To obtain a fully dynamic recrystallized structure, the samples were air-cooled subsequent to extrusion. Ultimately, extruded Mg–5Y sheets, featuring a cross-sectional dimension of 80 × 8 mm 2 were finally fabricated. Strain rate: 800 s−1; Processing state: extruded fine-grained

The heat treatment procedure for the experimental steels involved subjecting them to austenitization at a temperature of 980 °C for a duration of 30 min, followed by water quenching. The samples were prepared using mechanical alloying and microwave sintering methods. Powders of Fe, Co, Ni, Cr, and Mn with a purity of 99.9 wt% were employed as raw materials, possessing an average particle size smaller than 45 μm. The FeCoNiCrMn HEAs was synthesized using an equimolar atomic ratio. Initially, steel balls with a mass ratio of 1:2:4 were utilized as the grinding medium. The ball-to-material ratio was established at 10:1, and the ball milling process was conducted for a duration of 48 h at a rotational speed of 300 revolutions per minute (r/min). Subsequently, the HEAs powder was dried in a vacuum environment at 80 °C for 48 h, after which the powder was extracted. In this procedure, 50% absolute ethanol was employed as the ball milling agent. The milling was conducted at a speed of 200 r/min for a duration of 6 h to ensure thorough mixing. Subsequently, the milled powder was dried at 80 °C. The dried Al 2O 3p/FeCoNiCrMn powder was subjected to cold isostatic pressing at 300 MPa for 2 min to create a cylindrical blank. This blank was subsequently sintered using microwave technology in a Muffle furnace. The sintering process was conducted at a temperature of 1000 °C, with a heating rate of 10 °C per minute and a holding time of 40 min. Condition: after addition of 2 wt% Al2O3

The CuCrZr alloy powder used in the experiment was prepared by the plasma rotating electrode atomization process. Specimens were prepared by EB-PBF equipment (Xi'an Sailong Additive Technology Co., Ltd., China). The maximum forming size of EB-PBF equipment is 150 × 150 × 210 mm, and the maximum vacuum degree is 5 × 10 −3Pa. In order to imitate the aging heat treatment process of CuCrZr alloy in-situ to precipitate nano-precipitates, the powder bed temperatures were controlled to 300 °C, 400 °C and 500 °C during the EB-PBF process. The specific forming parameters refer to our previous research [ 14]. The powder bed temperature of the EB-PBF sample is 200 °C, the conventional sample without CPBT is labeled as EB-PBF. When printing EB-PBF samples, the powder is melted directly after the powder coating is completed. When printing CPBT samples, an electron beam is used to heat the entire powder bed after the powder spreading is completed. The thermocouple used to measure the powder bed temperature is installed under the base plate. The powder bed temperature fluctuates and cannot be controlled very accurately at present. When the powder bed temperature is too high or too low, the electron beam current will be dynamically adjusted. The samples with the CPBT at 250-350 °C are marked as 300 °C, and the samples with the CPBT at 350-450 °C and 450-550 °C are marked as 400 °C and 500 °C respectively. In this way, the sample is always maintained in the aging heat treatment temperature range during the entire printing process. This special thermal history is controlled similar to traditional aging treatment. The thermal history of different samples is shown in Fig. 1c, and the printing process parameters are shown in Table 1. The powder particle size distribution is 15-106 μm, where D50 is 43 μm and D90 is 67 μm. The elemental content of Cr and Zr in the powder was determined by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES), while the elemental content of O was determined by pulse heating inert gas fusion intrinsic absorption method. Impurities such as Fe, Si, and P were determined by ICP-AES. As-built sample with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 60 mm 3 to determine the microstructure, phase composition and mechanical properties. A Shimadzu universal testing machine AGS-X 10 KN was used to conduct uniaxial tensile experiments at a strain rate of 1 mm/min on flat dog-bone shaped samples with a gauge length of 25 × 6 × 2 mm 3 to evaluate room temperature mechanical properties. Tensile specimens were cut from the same position of the as-built specimen for comparison. All specimens were polished before tensile to ensure smooth surfaces. An eddy current metal conductivity meter (Sigma 2008B, China) was used to measure the conductivity of the specimens with a resolution of 0.01 %IACS and a measurement range of 0.8-110 %IACS. Before the conductivity was tested, the surface was polished with sandpaper to ensure that there were no large scratches. Then the surface was polished with 2.5 μm and 0.5 μm diamond spray polishing agents. Finally, the sample was cleaned and dried. Each sample was tested 3 times, and the remaining values were averaged. Optical microscopy (GX51, OM), scanning electron microscopy (Gemini SEM 300, SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopic mapping (EDS), and electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) were used to characterize the sample microstructure. Among them, the scanning step size in EBSD experiment is 1.5 μm, and the scanning area is 600∗450 μm. The mixed solution (FeCl 3/1 g, HCl/2 ml, H 2O/20 ml) was used to etch the sample surface. After etching, the samples were cleaned in C 2H 5OH and dried for observation of microstructure. The samples were prepared into thin slices with a thickness of less than 60 μm and a diameter of 3 mm, and then underwent ion beam thinning at a low temperature of 100 K. All prepared thin platinum samples were observed on a transmission scanning electron microscope (Talos F200s, TEM) operating at 200 keV. Finally, the TEM data were analyzed and processed by Digital Micrograph (DM) software. Original sample; 0.2% offset yield strength

In this work, Hastelloy C276 alloy with exceptional strength and ultra-high elongation is fabricated using laser and arc hybrid additive manufacturing (LHAM). The specimen undergoes solution treatment at 1177 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching. Further heat treatment (LHAM-HT) results in reduced texture strength, equiaxed grains with annealing twins and no precipitates detected. A Hastelloy C276 alloy wire (Atlantic China Welding Consumables, Inc.), 1.2 mm in diameter, was used for the deposition onto the substrate. The system comprised an IPG YLS-6000 fiber laser, a Fronius 500i welding machine, and a KUKA six-axis robot operating at 30 Hz, which were utilized for WAAM and LHAM processing of Hastelloy C276 alloy. The laser beam spot size is 0.2 mm. During the additive manufacturing process, the laser leaded, positioned at a 20° angle from the vertical to prevent reflective damage to equipment, while the CMT trailed. To manage heat accumulation, each deposited layer was cooled below 100 °C before subsequent layers are added, with the final specimens reaching a height of 40 mm. The entire process was conducted in a 99.999% pure argon atmosphere to prevent internal defects from atmospheric contamination. After deposition, the LHAM specimen underwent solution treatment, where the heating rate was set to 600 °C/h until reaching 1177 °C, followed by a 30-min hold and water quenching. For convenience, the specimens fabricated using CMT are referred to as WAAM, that fabricated by laser and arc hybrid additive manufacturing as LHAM, and the LHAM specimen after heat treatment as LHAM-HT. Processing Text: The intermetallic compound FeV alloy and high purity (>99.8 wt%), and Cr and W metal powders, were used to produce the as-cast (FeCr2V)1−xWxRMEAs using arc melting. First, the powders were proportioned according to the different alloy compositions and mixed evenly using physical blending. Then, the mixed metal powders were melted using arc melting technology to produce a casting ingot of approximately 30 g. The arc melting process was carried out in an atmosphere of argon to reduce the potential impact of oxidation on the sample during the process. Finally, the melting process was repeated three times to improve the uniformity of the microstructure and composition. The melted as-cast (FeCr2V)1−xWx sample was sliced into cross-sections using Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM) for observation and study of the microstructure. The standard metallographic sample preparation procedure was then followed for grinding and polishing. X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) testing was conducted on the cross-sectional sample using a CuKα radiation (λ = 1.5418 Å) with a PANalytical X’PERT PRO X-ray diffractometer to study the phase composition of the (FeCr2V)1−xWx alloy. In addition, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with an Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) testing was conducted using a JEOL® JSM-7001F for observation of the microstructure. The JEOL® JSM-7001F and an EDS detector operated at an acceleration voltage of 15 kV were used for elemental quantification analysis. Mechanical properties of the RMEAs were evaluated through a Hysitron TI 950 Triboindenter, Struers Durascan-70 hardness tester and a Gleeble 1500 thermo-mechanical simulator. The nano-indentation tests, with an indentation load of 7 mN and a step size of 7 µm, were conducted on distinct phase areas observed in the metallographic specimens, namely the dominant phase and the minor phase regions. Vickers microhardness was measured four times for each sample using a load of 1 kg and a duration of 10 s by the Struers Durascan-70 automatic hardness tester. The compression tests were conducted on cylindrical samples (Φ6.5 mm × 8 mm), which were ground and polished according to standard metallographic sample preparation procedures using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Each alloy composition was tested under ambient conditions using a Gleeble 1500 thermo-mechanical simulator, with an engineering strain rate of 0.001 s−1. The 5356 aluminum alloy samples were fabricated utilizing WAAM and U-RE-WAAM processes, respectively. Prior to additive manufacturing, the substrate surface was mechanically polished and cleaned with alcohol to remove any oxide films and oil contamination. Deposition was conducted using three distinct processes: WAAM, RE-WAAM, and U-RE-WAAM. In each process, the filler wire was melted by an electric arc under a protective atmosphere of 99.99 % argon. The torch and the molten wire moved horizontally in the Y deposition direction to form the deposited layers. By elevating the torch height in the Z building direction, subsequent layers were deposited onto the previous ones. The specific parameters for the additive manufacturing process are listed in Table 2. The parameters for the ultrasonic rotating extrusion system are specified in Table 3. In the initial layer of the additive manufacturing process, a wire feed speed of 7.5 m/min is utilized. Subsequently, the wire feed speed is decremented by 0.5 mm/min with each additional layer, down to a minimum of 5.0 mm/min. This gradual reduction in wire feed speed is necessitated by the proximity of the initial layers to the substrate, where the melting pool experiences rapid cooling and limited spread, thus requiring a higher feed rate to ensure adequate deposition width. As the number of deposited layers accumulates, the cooling rate of the melt pool decreases, necessitating a reduction in wire feed speed to 5.0 mm/min to prevent the collapse of deposited layers. The additive manufacturing process incorporates a single stack path, with interlayer temperatures strictly controlled below 50°C to maintain material integrity and process consistency.
