The ingot, prepared by the vacuum melt casting method, was heated to 1200 °C for 2 hours and then forged into 100 mm × 100 mm × 80 mm forgings. Once cooled to room temperature, the forgings were cut into 50 mm × 20 mm × 8 mm slabs using wire-cutting technology. Subsequently, the slab underwent homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 hours. Then, its thickness was reduced to 4 mm (50% reduction) through six hot rolling passes conducted within a temperature range of 1010 - 1150 °C, starting at 1150 °C and ending at 950 °C. After hot rolling, the sheet underwent dephosphating and was then cold rolled through ten processes, ultimately resulting in a thickness of 2.2 mm (45% reduction). Lastly, the cold-rolled sheet was annealed at approximately 1173 K for 15 mins. All heat treatments were conducted in an inert gas (argon) atmosphere to ensure material purity and prevent oxidation. A rectangular sample measuring 10 mm × 30 mm was cut from the rolled and annealed billet and then finely polished with 1500 grit silicon carbide sandpaper to achieve a uniform thickness of 2 mm. Compression testing of these thin sheet samples was conducted using the CMT5305 microcomputer-controlled universal material testing machine along the normal direction (ND), with a strain rate of 0.001 s−1. To ensure precise control of deformation, dual means of stroke and pressure control were employed in the experiments. Thickness measurements were taken at three different locations before and after the compression test, with the average values documented to reflect the initial and final thicknesses. The average thicknesses of the four samples before compression were 1.98 mm, 2.02 mm, 2.00 mm, and 2.00 mm, respectively, and they changed to 1.80 mm, 1.62 mm, 1.48 mm, and 1.34 mm after compression. Uniaxial micro-tensile tests were conducted at 298 K (room temperature) on an in-house miniature-testing machine with a load cell of 5000 N and a nominal strain rate of 0.001 s−1. The samples were cut by EDM from the pre-compressed sheet material with gauge dimensions of 5 mm × 2 mm × 1 mm. The tensile direction of the samples was strictly aligned with the rolling direction (RD). Before testing, all samples underwent mechanical grinding to ensure a smooth surface without any obvious defects. To accurately determine the tensile strain value, random speckle patterns were uniformly sprayed onto the sample surface. During the tensile process, deformation images were captured in real-time using a high-resolution camera. Subsequently, MATLAB software was utilized for image processing and analysis. Initially, the images were converted into monochrome. Then, based on the center point of the sample gauge area, a virtual extensometer was constructed from the two preset solid lines. Finally, the sample's strain was determined by calculating the displacement of pixel points between the virtual extensometers over time. In this study, two types of micro-tensile tests were conducted: in-situ tests and interrupted tests, both loaded by displacement control. The in-situ tests were designed to obtain the stress-strain curve of the sample up to fracture, and back stress was also assessed through a LUR cycle test. To ensure reproducibility, three independent tensile tests were conducted for each pre-compressed sample. During the LUR test, a strain rate of 0.001 s−1 was used for strain control during loading, while unloading was force-controlled at 25 N/s. Reloading began when the force was unloaded to 25 N. The interrupted test was designed to study the microstructure evolution, with interruptions at specific points or continuation until fracture. Additionally, to accurately characterize the microstructure evolution of the pre-compressed sample at the same position before and after tensile deformation, hardness markers were placed in the center of the target region. These markers served as reference points, facilitating accurate analysis of the microstructure evolution during subsequent EBSD characterization. Microstructure characterization was performed using EBSD on a Nova Nano SEM 230 ultra-high resolution field emission SEM. The sample preparation consisted of coarse grinding and fine grinding followed by electrolytic polishing at -20 °C using an electrolytic polishing solution of 4 vol% perchloric acid mixed with 96 vol% ethanol at a voltage of 30 V and a polishing time of 30 s. For EBSD analysis, the operating voltage was set to 20 kV, and the step size was 0.25 μm. In addition, the TEM sample was prepared from the specified sample using a focused ion beam (FIB) technique at an acceleration voltage of 30 kV. In this study, a total of two TEM observations were performed. The first observation was performed on the sample with a compressive strain of 0.4, and the second TEM test was conducted on the pre-compressed sample after stretched to 0.2. The FIB slice was taken from the central region of the sample, with the slice plane perpendicular to the RD and the slice size of 10 μm × 8 μm. The TEM sample was mechanically polished to a thickness of 30 μm, then thinned by double injection at -25 °C with an electrolyte of 10% perchloric acid and 90% alcohol at 15 V, and finally cleaned by ion grinding at 3 kV at a 2 °C angle for 10 min. Finally, the samples were observed by the TALOS F200X field emission transmission electron microscope under a 200 kV acceleration voltage. Condition: quasi-static loading; Type: tension

IN718 alloy produced by additive manufacturing (AM) displays significant anisotropy due to its unique microstructure. SLM-fabricated IN718 was analyzed in detail using the crystal plasticity method. Statistical analysis of SLM IN718 data identified microstructural descriptors to describe the heterogeneous microstructural characteristics adequately. A representative volume element (RVE) is constructed for CP simulations. A dislocation-based crystal plasticity constitutive model, combined with a spectral solver, is developed to elucidate the anisotropic behavior of SLM IN718 under uniaxial tension. The constructed EM-ET RVEs were subjected to uniaxial tensile deformation along the BD and TD under quasi-static loading rates ε̇=10-3s-1 and room temperature T=298 K. A 20 % strain is applied in the TD (BD). Tensile simulations were conducted on the EM-RT RVEs and RM-ET RVEs. Columnar grain morphology significantly influences the yield strength and strain-hardening behavior, especially under loading perpendicular to the BD. Loading direction: TD; Microstructure: columnar grains; Context: EM-RT RVE

Processing Text: AA7050 forgings with a longitudinal (L), long transverse (LT), and short transverse (ST) length ratios of approximately 26:4:1 were fabricated through direct-chill-casting, homogenization, multiple high-temperature (440 °C) upsetting and cogging processes. Subsequently, the forgings were solution-treated (Sol.) at 471 °C for 9 h and then water-quenched. Rectangular (15 × 15 × 5 mm 3) and dog-bone-shaped tensile samples (gauge: diameter 6 × 25 mm) were machined from the forged and solution-treated alloys. To eliminate the natural aging effect, the samples were solution-treated again in an electric furnace at 471 °C for 1 h and then water-quenched at room temperature. The solution-treated samples were first aged (FA) at 121 °C for 16 h (peak aging condition) and secondary-aged (SA) at 177 °C for different times up to 192 h, and then water-quenched. After the specimens were mechanically polished and electrically etched using a 5 % fluoroboric (HBF 4) solution with a power supply (TOYOTECH, TDP-605B) of 20 V for ∼120 s, the α-Al grain structure was observed using optical microscopy (OM; Nikon, EPIPHOT) under polarized light. Condition: Solution-treated; Direction: LT

Processing Text: The original TA4 pure Ti was cut into round bar samples measuring Φ25 mm × 150 mm, then annealed in a muffle furnace at 750 °C for 1.5 h, followed by air-cooling to room temperature. Samples underwent pretreatment, with a graphite and MoS 2 serving as lubricant. TA4 pure Ti samples with the size of Φ25 mm × 150 mm were processed using a YJ160B1 four-column hydraulic testing machine. The ECAP deformation parameters were as follows: the die channel angle was Φ = 135°, and the outer angle was ψ = 20°. Samples were pressed at a rate of 2.5 mm/s for four passes along route C. After four passes, the samples underwent CR using a Φ160 × 170 two-roll mill, with reductions set to 30 and 50 %. This process produced fine-grained TA4 pure Ti samples with dimensions of 20 mm × 20 mm × 180 mm and 12.5 mm × 12.5 mm × 250 mm. EBSD samples were prepared through an electrolytic polishing process. Thinning of samples for transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed using a MTP-1A double-jet electrolytic thinning instrument, with an electrolyte composed of 60 % methanol, 35 % n-butanol, and 5 % perchloric acid by volume. The voltage of thinning was 50 V and the current was 50 mA. Mechanical properties were evaluated using a WDW-300 electronic universal testing machine at a strain rate of 1 ×10 −3s −1. For microhardness testing, a 15 mm × 15 mm × 5 mm block sample was cut from the middle of each cross-section (rolling direction or RD surface) of the samples subjected to ECAP and combined ECAP-CR deformation. Testing was conducted using an HVS-10Z Vickers hardness tester with an applied load of 200gf and a holding time of 10s. Processed by combined ECAP-CR (50 %) deformation; Schmid factors for basal and prismatic slip were 0.248 and 0.363, respectively.

Processing Text: The Al-12Ce-3Mg-0.45Sc (wt.%) alloy was prepared using squeeze casting at Loukus Technologies. Plates measuring 380 mm (length) × 280 mm (width) × 15 mm (thickness) were cast by pouring molten alloy at 750 °C into platens preheated to 400 °C. The cooling rate during squeeze casting was measured using fast response thermocouples placed near the center of one of the cast plates. The average cooling rate between 1025 K (the temperature where squeeze was applied) and 800 K (below the solidification temperature) was measured to be approximately 50 K/s. The squeeze cast alloys were processed by additive friction stir processing (AFSD) technique using a MELD B8 machine (MELD Manufacturing). The AFSD technique utilizes a hollow rotating tool to feed the material, which undergoes localized plastic deformation and shear deposition. The feedstock, a rod with a square cross-section of 9.5 mm × 9.5 mm × 150 mm long, was prepared by sectioning the squeeze cast plates using electrical discharge machining. Before deposition, the feedstock rods were lubricated with graphite spray to minimize friction during processing. The deposition process employed a tool made of H13 tool steel, featuring a 38.1 mm diameter shoulder with four teardrop-shaped protrusions. Two protrusions were 2 mm in height, while the other two measured 1 mm. The vacuum induction melting inert gas atomization (VIGA) process was employed to produce the high-quality CCM alloy powders. The particle size of the obtained spherical-shaped powders was sieved into the size range of 15-53 μm. The chemical compositions of the powders were examined by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometer (ICP-AES). The alloy powders were dried at 120 °C for 8 h in vacuum environment prior to LPBF fabrication. The building substrate was set at 80 °C and argon gas was filled in the building chamber to prevent oxidation. Based on our previous work, a set of optimized process parameters with the laser power of 300 W, scanning speed of 950 mm/s, hatching space of 110 μm and the layer thickness of 40 μm were chosen to ensure the sample relative density above 99.5 %. A continuous 67° rotation scanning strategy was adopted between the successive building layers. In this study, the commercial EP-M150 Plus LPBF machine equipped with a 500 W fiber laser was utilized for sample fabrication. Rectangular plate-shaped samples were fabricated with its longitude axis inclined 0°, 45°, 60°, 75° and 90° from the base substrate, which are named as V0, V45, V60, V75 and V90 samples in this context, respectively. Sample: V0; Building angle: 0°

Processing Text: The steel was prepared using a vacuum induction melting furnace under an argon protective atmosphere, maintaining a vacuum level of approximately 5 MPa, and was eventually cast into a 30 kg ingot. The hot rolled plate is cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of 20 %, 40 %, 60 % and 80 %, which are referred to as CR20, CR40, CR60 and CR80, respectively. Processing Text: Non-equiatomic CoNiMo alloys with nominal compositions of (CoNi) 88Mo 12, (CoNi) 85Mo 15, and (CoNi) 82Mo 18 (designated as M12, M15, and M18, respectively) were fabricated by vacuum induction melting (MC100V, Indutherm, Germany) using high-purity (99.95%) elements under Ar atmosphere. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h under Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching, and subsequently cold-rolled with an 80% reduction at room temperature. The HPT process was then performed on the cold-rolled sheets to significantly impose strain energy for recrystallization and the formation of a UFG structure. A total of ten turns of HPT were conducted at 1 rpm under 6 GPa on disc-shaped specimens with a diameter of 10 mm, machined from the cold-rolled sheets. To ensure sufficient ductility, the annealing temperatures predicting a high volume fraction of FCC phase were selected ( Fig. 1b-d), specifically 800 °C, 900 °C, and 975 °C for M12, M15, and M18, respectively, with a duration of 120 s. Processing Text: The samples were prepared using a Renishaw AM250 printer with a molding space of 250 mm × 250 mm × 300 mm (X, Y, Z). The layer thickness was adjustable between 0.02 mm and 0.10 mm, and the laser spot diameter was 70 μm. After each layer was deposited, the grating pattern was rotated by 67° to minimize overlap between adjacent laser vectors. Samples with thicknesses of 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm, 1.5 mm, and 2.0 mm were printed perpendicular to the substrate. Adjacent samples were kept parallel, with the build plane oriented at a 45° angle to the substrate. Additionally, a block sample with a thickness of over 1 cm was printed. Pores and melt pool morphology of the treated samples were observed using optical microscopes (OM, PME3, Olympus), and dendrite structures of the samples were examined with scanning electron microscopes (SEM, LEO 1530vp and VEGA 3 LMU). A high-resolution scanning electron microscope (SEM, Mira 3, TESCAN) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, NordlysMax2, Oxford) probe was used to analyze grain structure, and vibratory polishing was performed to relieve surface stresses prior to characterization. Physical phase was analyzed using X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D8 DaVinci). The samples for the tensile test were prepared as flat dog-bone specimens with dimensions of 55 mm in length and 10 mm in width. Block samples were cut to a thickness of 1.2 mm. The mechanical properties of the tensile specimens were conducted using a Zwick universal mechanical testing machine with a tensile speed of 1 mm/min. The reported mechanical property data for each thickness represent the average of three valid test results. Aged at 873 K for 4 h

High-purity (>99.9 %) Fe, Co, Ni, Cr, and Ti metals were arc-melted in argon atmosphere to produce ingots with the (FeCrCoNi) 95Ti 5composition. After flipping and melting five times, an ingot (diameter = 50 mm, weight = 150 g, height = 10 mm) was obtained. The ingots were hot-rolled to a thickness of 2 mm in five passes after homogenization at 1373 K for 12 h, followed by solid-solution treatment at 1373 K for 1 h and water quenching. Finally, the hot-rolled plate was aging at 873, 973, and 1073 K for 4 h, followed by water quenching. After the surface of the tensile specimen was sanded with sandpaper, its mechanical properties were tested using a universal testing machine (Zwick Z2.5 TH) at a deformation rate of 10 −3/s −1. After polishing the surface with sandpaper, the damping performance was measured using a Q800 DMA dynamic thermomechanical analyzer. Standard condition

The as-cast ingot was first homogenized at 1373 K for 6 h, and then hot forged to a bar with section size of 45 mm × 45 mm at around 1273 K. Subsequently, the bar was further cold-rolled to sheet with thickness of 15 mm and then annealed at 1073 K for 5 min, followed by water-quenching. The recrystallization and non-crystallization regions of BCC and FCC phases in A5 were analyzed. The corresponding KAM maps of BCC and FCC phases were studied. The statistical results of KAM values were obtained. Flat dog-bone shape specimens with gauge dimensions of 10 mm × 2.5 mm × 2 mm were cut from the sheets. Rectangular Charpy impact samples with a size of 10 mm × 10 mm × 55 mm were cut along the rolling direction. A 45° V-notch was machined in the middle of the sample with a depth of 2 mm and a radius of 0.25 mm at the root. Vacuum arc melting was conducted under an argon atmosphere using metal raw materials with a purity exceeding 99.9 %. The ingot was subjected to at least three flips to ensure a relatively homogeneous Fe 57.88(CrNi) 32.08Al 10.04MEA. The heat treatment process was carried out in an electric resistance furnace under an argon atmosphere, with a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The heat treatment schedules for the Fe 57.88(CrNi) 32.08Al 10.04MEA are detailed in Table 1. The selection of 1300 °C and 850 °C as the solution and aging temperatures, respectively, was based on the results of Thermo-Calc calculations. According to these calculations, the chosen solution temperature of 1300 °C exceeded the alloy's solution temperature but remained below its melting temperature. Furthermore, the aging temperature of 850 °C was primarily aimed at precipitating sufficient strengthening phase while maximizing the proportion of the alloy's soft phase (FCC phase). For simplicity, the as-cast Fe 57.88(CrNi) 32.08Al 10.04MEA was designated AC, while the heat-treated alloys were denoted 1300-HT and 850-HT, respectively. In this heat treatment process, the alloy underwent a 2-h solution treatment at 1300 °C, followed by furnace cooling. Subsequently, an aging treatment of 10 h at 850 °C, followed by water quenching, was performed. This process primarily enabled the complete precipitation of all phases within the alloy at this temperature. After annealing at 1300 °C for 1 h, followed by aging at 850 °C for 10 h, the as-cast alloy exhibited notable changes in phase composition: the FCC phase decreased from 83.66 ± 2.00 % to 78.80 ± 2.03 %, the BCC phase increased from 0.20 ± 0.05 % to 2.61 ± 0.01 %, and the B2 phase increased from 16.1 ± 0.25 % to 18.6 ± 0.01 %. Processing Text: The preparation of x wt.% Al2O3-added Ti-25V-15Cr alloys involved using commercial pure metals and Al2O3 particles, including pure Ti particles (purity >99.95 wt.%), pure V particles (purity >99.95 wt.%), pure Cr particles (purity >99.95 wt.%), and pure Al2O3 particles (purity >99.99 wt.%). Al2O3-added Ti-25V-15Cr ingots were fabricated via vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper crucible under an argon atmosphere. After placing the raw materials and titanium sponge in the crucible, the chamber was evacuated to below 2 × 10−3Pa. Subsequently, high purity argon gas (99.999 %) was repeatedly used to purge the air for three times. Before smelting, the argon gas was pressurized to 0.05 MPa as a protective gas. Each ingot underwent at least eight flipping and remelting cycles to ensure chemical homogeneity and eliminate composition segregation. Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: The composition used in this study was Cu46Zr46Al8 (at.%), prepared from pure metals with a purity exceeding 99.99 %. The master alloy underwent five repeated melting cycles in a vacuum arc remelting furnace under a protective atmosphere of argon gas (purity of 99.999 %), with titanium gettering, to ensure homogeneity. BMG rods of Ø3 mm × 70 mm were produced via suction casting in a water-cooled copper mold and then cut into 1.25 mm thick disks. Samples were polished using an automatic polishing system (LMP-3S, China) to reduce disk thickness to 1.0 mm, ensuring parallelism of top and bottom surfaces. BMG rods of Ø2 mm × 70 mm were prepared and cut into cylindrical compression test samples with a length of 3 mm, ensuring parallel and orthogonal ends to minimize geometric constraints. UV treatment involved an ultrasonic vibration setup consisting of a transducer, booster, and horn connected to a control unit for parameter adjustment. During the process, the horn made contact with the sample's top surface under a preset pressure, and 20 kHz vibrations were applied. Various UV energies ranging from 50 to 400 J were employed, resulting in processing times of ∼0.6 to 1.95 s and powers of ∼83 to 205 W. The vibration amplitude and static stress were maintained at low values, specifically 40 µm for vibration amplitude and 400 kPa for static stress, to ensure the elastic nature of cyclic strains imposed by horn. The infrared imaging camera (Fotric 280d, China) with data-acquisition frequency of 30 Hz was used to capture thermal images from the BMG sample during UV treatment. AnalyzIR software analyzed temperature changes during treatment. Additionally, due to the continuous pressure applied between the horn and the sample, a K-type thermocouple with a sampling frequency of 1000 Hz was put on the struck surface to monitor temperature fluctuations throughout the process on the struck surface. Two samples were immersed in liquid nitrogen for different durations, 60 h and 10 s, respectively, followed by exposure to UV energy of 400 J. Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: The WE43 magnesium alloy powder was obtained from cast rods using a plasma rotating electrode process (Weihao Co., Tangshan, China). The powder nominal composition was Mg-4%Y-3.3%(Gd, Nd)-0.5%Zr in units of mass fraction. In order to enhance the safety of storage and use, the powder surface was passivated to reduce the activity of the powder based on the high oxygenophilicity of Y. Prior to the LPBF experiments, the powder was held in a vacuum oven for 3 h to remove moisture and improve the flowability of the spreading powder. An HK-M300 (Huake 3D Co., Wuhan, China) commercial machine was used to fabricate samples, which equipped with an IPG 500 W fiber laser and a focused laser spot diameter of about 100 µm. In order to obtain the optimum process parameters, the LPBF printing experiments were carried out with various laser powers and scanning speeds. Based on the average particle size of the powder, the printing layer thickness was set to 30 µm to obtain a good powder spreading effect. A hatch space of 80 µm was used to minimize the Plateau-Rayleigh capillary instability and thus reduce surface roughness. A scanning strategy of 67° rotation in the scanning direction of each layer was conducted along the build direction (BD), which aimed to enhance the isotropy of the microstructure and mechanical properties. During the LPBF process, the AM50 magnesium alloy substrate was preheated to 200 °C to minimize thermal stresses caused by temperature gradients. The fabrication chamber was continuously ventilated with high-purity argon gas to reduce the risk of samples oxidation and explosion. With the process described above, the representative cubic block samples (10 × 10 × 10 mm3), dog-bone tensile samples and porous lattice structures (10 × 10 × 10 mm3) were printed. The samples were extracted from the substrate using wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM). The cubic sample densities at different process parameters were measured using the Archimedes' drainage principle. Prior to the measurements, six surfaces of the samples were mechanically ground using 400# SiC sandpaper. Pore defects were examined using an optical microscope (OM, Leica DM750M, Germany). The x-y top and y-z side surfaces were mechanically ground using 500#, 1000#, 2000#, 3000#, and 5000# SiC sandpapers in sequence, and then polished on a polyurethane pad using a diamond solution with a grit size of 50 nm to obtain a smooth surface without scratches. To facilitate the examination of the microstructure using OM and SEM, the polished surfaces were metallurgically etched with a 4% solution of nitric acid in alcohol. The crystal structure and phase composition were determined using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD-7000S, Shimadzu, Japan) with Cu-Kα radiation (λ= 1.5406 Å) operating at 40 keV and 30 mA. Morphology, distribution and size of precipitated phases were observed by backscattered electron (BSE, Quanta650 FEG, FEI, USA). The grain size, grain orientation and texture were determined via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, GeminiSEM300, German) and the collected data were post-processed by AztecCrystal software. Prior to EBSD testing, the mechanically polished surfaces were first electrolytically polished at 30 V for 20 s, and then etched on an argon ion beam instrument (PECS II 685, USA) for 30 min to remove surface residual stresses. To elucidate the sequence of phase precipitation during the non-equilibrium solidification, thermodynamic calculations were conducted using the PanMg database within the Pandat software. Furthermore, the nano-precipitates and dislocations were identified using a field emission transmission electron microscope (FTEM, Tecnai G2 F30, Netherlands) at an accelerating voltage of 300 keV. The nano-structure were identified with the selected area electron diffusion (SAED) patterns, high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). The TEM thin-foil specimen was obtained by argon ion beam thinning on PECS II 695 equipment. Uniaxial quasi-static tensile tests were performed on a material mechanical properties tester (MTS-647 Hydraulic Wedge Grip, USA) at a constant strain rate of 4 × 10−4s−1 at room temperature. Elongation changes were recorded using a contact extensometer with a 20 mm scale. Tensile samples were tested at least three times to obtain the average yield strength (σy), ultimate tensile strength (σUTS) and elongation at break. The fracture morphologies were observed using SEM. Furthermore, loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) cyclic tensile tests were conducted to reveal the grain size-induced Bauschinger effect. Samples were first loaded to 1.5% strain at a strain rate of 10−3s−1, then unloaded to 20 N at an unloading rate of 100 N/min, and subsequent cycles were performed per 1% of the strain. Processing Text: The WE43 magnesium alloy powder was obtained from cast rods using a plasma rotating electrode process (Weihao Co., Tangshan, China). The powder nominal composition was Mg-4%Y-3.3%(Gd, Nd)-0.5%Zr in units of mass fraction. In order to enhance the safety of storage and use, the powder surface was passivated to reduce the activity of the powder based on the high oxygenophilicity of Y. Prior to the LPBF experiments, the powder was held in a vacuum oven for 3 h to remove moisture and improve the flowability of the spreading powder. An HK-M300 (Huake 3D Co., Wuhan, China) commercial machine was used to fabricate samples, which equipped with an IPG 500 W fiber laser and a focused laser spot diameter of about 100 µm. In order to obtain the optimum process parameters, the LPBF printing experiments were carried out with various laser powers and scanning speeds. Based on the average particle size of the powder, the printing layer thickness was set to 30 µm to obtain a good powder spreading effect. A hatch space of 80 µm was used to minimize the Plateau-Rayleigh capillary instability and thus reduce surface roughness. A scanning strategy of 67° rotation in the scanning direction of each layer was conducted along the build direction (BD), which aimed to enhance the isotropy of the microstructure and mechanical properties. During the LPBF process, the AM50 magnesium alloy substrate was preheated to 200 °C to minimize thermal stresses caused by temperature gradients. The fabrication chamber was continuously ventilated with high-purity argon gas to reduce the risk of samples oxidation and explosion. With the process described above, the representative cubic block samples (10 × 10 × 10 mm3), dog-bone tensile samples and porous lattice structures (10 × 10 × 10 mm3) were printed. The samples were extracted from the substrate using wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM). The cubic sample densities at different process parameters were measured using the Archimedes' drainage principle. Prior to the measurements, six surfaces of the samples were mechanically ground using 400# SiC sandpaper. Pore defects were examined using an optical microscope (OM, Leica DM750M, Germany). The x-y top and y-z side surfaces were mechanically ground using 500#, 1000#, 2000#, 3000#, and 5000# SiC sandpapers in sequence, and then polished on a polyurethane pad using a diamond solution with a grit size of 50 nm to obtain a smooth surface without scratches. To facilitate the examination of the microstructure using OM and SEM, the polished surfaces were metallurgically etched with a 4% solution of nitric acid in alcohol. The crystal structure and phase composition were determined using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD-7000S, Shimadzu, Japan) with Cu-Kα radiation (λ= 1.5406 Å) operating at 40 keV and 30 mA. Morphology, distribution and size of precipitated phases were observed by backscattered electron (BSE, Quanta650 FEG, FEI, USA). The grain size, grain orientation and texture were determined via electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, GeminiSEM300, German) and the collected data were post-processed by AztecCrystal software. Prior to EBSD testing, the mechanically polished surfaces were first electrolytically polished at 30 V for 20 s, and then etched on an argon ion beam instrument (PECS II 685, USA) for 30 min to remove surface residual stresses. To elucidate the sequence of phase precipitation during the non-equilibrium solidification, thermodynamic calculations were conducted using the PanMg database within the Pandat software. Furthermore, the nano-precipitates and dislocations were identified using a field emission transmission electron microscope (FTEM, Tecnai G2 F30, Netherlands) at an accelerating voltage of 300 keV. The nano-structure were identified with the selected area electron diffusion (SAED) patterns, high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). The TEM thin-foil specimen was obtained by argon ion beam thinning on PECS II 695 equipment. Uniaxial quasi-static tensile tests were performed on a material mechanical properties tester (MTS-647 Hydraulic Wedge Grip, USA) at a constant strain rate of 4 × 10−4s−1 at room temperature. Elongation changes were recorded using a contact extensometer with a 20 mm scale. Tensile samples were tested at least three times to obtain the average yield strength (σy), ultimate tensile strength (σUTS) and elongation at break. The fracture morphologies were observed using SEM. Furthermore, loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) cyclic tensile tests were conducted to reveal the grain size-induced Bauschinger effect. Samples were first loaded to 1.5% strain at a strain rate of 10−3s−1, then unloaded to 20 N at an unloading rate of 100 N/min, and subsequent cycles were performed per 1% of the strain. Processing Text: The 3 wt.% SiC/ZA63 (SiC/ZA63) composites were prepared by the semi-solid stirring casting method. The Mg-6Zn-3Al alloy (wt.%, all in wt.% otherwise stated) was selected as the matrix alloy, and SiC particles (provided by Shanghai Xiangtian Nano Co, China) with the average size of 8 µm, 30 µm, and 50 µm, respectively, were selected as the reinforcement phase. Before the addition of SiC particles, the SiC particles were cleaned by 5% hydrofluoric acid solution for 24 h to remove the contaminants on the surface of particles. Firstly, the pure Mg (99.95%) was melted at 720 ℃ in a steel crucible using a resistance furnace. The Zn (99.995%) and Al (99.995%) were added into the melt when the temperature of the Mg melt reached 720 ℃, and then the melt was stirred by a graphite rod for 2 min and held for 10 min to homogenize the composition. Secondly, the melt was cooled to 600 ℃, at which the Mg-6Zn-3Al alloy was in a semi-solid condition. Subsequently, the preheated stirring paddle was inserted into the melt for stirring. After the formation of stable eddy, the SiC preheated 450 ℃ was added into the melt at a constant rate by a vibrating powder feeder. The melt was reheated to 720 ℃ after stirring and then poured into an H13 mold preheated at 500 ℃. The ingot was solidified under a pressure of 200 MPa. Afterwards, the composite ingot was homogenized at 350 ℃ for 10 h followed by quenching in water at ∼20 °C. Before extrusion, each ingot with a size of φ35 ×70 mm 3was pre-heated at 300 ℃ for 30 min, and the extrusion process was conducted at this temperature with an extrusion ratio of 12.5:1 and a ram speed of 0.1 mm/s. The diameter of extruded composite was 10 mm. Particle size: 30 µm; Decreased mechanical properties compared to MMC8; Average grain size: 6.72 µm

Processing Text: The validity and accuracy of the model are verified using titanium alloy as a case study, followed by an analysis of the microstructure and process properties of the as-deposited. Following optimization, the average grain size in the deposited state reached 245.1 μm; the deposition efficiency increased to 22.35 mm³/s; and the energy consumption decreased to 0.41 kWh. The optimized deposited state achieved an average tensile strength of 951 MPa, an average yield strength of 869 MPa, and a microhardness of 338.3 HV1, meeting the objectives of high performance, high efficiency, and low energy consumption. Microstructure and mechanical properties remain important indicators for large-scale structural components in aerospace ( Ren et al., 2017). For the high-power/high-efficiency LDED process of titanium alloys, research hotspots mainly focus on the microstructural and properties ( Zhang et al., 2019), including the non-uniformity of microstructure, grain refinement mechanism, anisotropy of properties, and the improvement of mechanical properties ( Song et al., 2023). Through the use of the pulsed LDED process, it has become possible to produce a fully equiaxed grain structure in TC4 titanium alloy, with an average grain size of 139 μm ( Zhang et al., 2023). However, the drawback is that the tensile elongation is only 4.09%, indicating insufficient toughness ( Chen et al., 2024). Meanwhile, the introduction of external energy fields also contributes to grain refinement ( Tan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022, 2023). Applying high-frequency ultrasonic vibration during the deposition process can transform coarse columnar grains into fine equiaxed grains, thereby refining the grain structure and effectively enhancing tensile properties ( Todaro et al., 2020). In the LDED deposition of TC4 titanium alloy, the introduction of a transverse static magnetic field can refine the primary β grains and produce a discontinuous grain boundary α phase, thereby improving tensile ductility and reducing the anisotropy of tensile properties ( Yuan et al., 2021). Processing Text: AA7075 is widely utilized in aerospace and transportation due to its high specific strength, specific stiffness, and corrosion resistance. Hot forging is an efficient and cost-effective method for manufacturing AA7075 cylindrical rings. During hot forging, AA7075 cylindrical ring undergoes complex metal flow, resulting in anisotropy in both microstructure and mechanical properties. The present study investigated the anisotropic behaviors of microstructure and mechanical properties in AA7075 cylindrical rings along three directions: rolling direction (RD), transverse direction (TD), and normal direction (ND). The results indicated that the microstructural anisotropy contributed to anisotropy in mechanical properties both before and after hot forging. In the present study, an AA7075 extruded bar ( Table 1), measuring ø300 × 520 mm, was held at 435°C for 12 h before the initial upsetting was completed. Following the first upsetting, the material was held at 435°C for 1 h prior to the second upsetting. Following the second upsetting, the bar diameter was adjusted to ø415 mm after another hour at 435°C. Finally, the material underwent hot forging in a hot forging mold after being held at 435°C for one more hour. Fig. 1shows the hot forging die and the resulting AA7075 cylindrical ring. The tensile strength and elongation at break of AA7075 cylindrical ring were evaluated in RD, TD, and ND using uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature. Fig. 2a illustrates the relative positions of the tensile samples within the cylindrical ring, while Fig. 2b provides the detailed dimensions of these samples. Each tensile testing was performed according to the same standard procedure. Three tensile tests were conducted for each group of samples at room temperature, using a strain rate of 2 mm/min, to obtain the average values of the samples' tensile strength and elongation at break. The microstructures of three planes - RD-TD, RD-ND, and TD-ND - were examined using a scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. Before microscopic analysis, the samples were ground and polished to achieve a suitable surface finish. This process involved three stages: grinding with sandpaper with roughness of 800, 1200, 1500, 2000, and 2500, respectively; polishing with a 1μm diamond suspension; and electrolytic polishing with electrolyte (10 % HClO 4+90 % C₂H₅OH). The SEM and EBSD test were conducted on the JSM-7800F electron microscope equipped with the EBSD detector at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV and a scanning step of 1.4 μm. Direction: RD-TD plane; Mechanism: dislocation strengthening

Powder assembly and alloying process including elemental alloying and shift-speed ball milling is applied in fabrication of CNT/Al-xMg (x = 0, 2.5, 5, wt.%). Pure Al powders (mean diameter ∼30 μm), pure Mg powders (mean diameter ∼10 μm) and graphitized raw CNTs powders (30-50 nm in diameter and <10 μm in length, 1.5 wt.% added, Chengdu Organic Chemistry Co., Ltd.) are mixed together and then ball milled at 135 rpm for 10 h and 270 rpm for 2 h, respectively. The mass ratio of stainless-steel milling balls to powders is controlled to be 20:1. Low speed ball milling (LSBM) at 135 rpm flake the powders and provides sufficient surface areas for uniform dispersion of CNTs. High speed ball milling (HSBM) at 270 rpm assembles the powder flakes by cold welding. To avoid massive oxidation and cool down the planetary ball milling system, the ball milling jars are filled with Ar atmosphere and take rest for 30 min after every 2 h of working. The cold-welded particles and pure Al powders (∼10 μm in diameter) with mass ratio of 7:3 is further ball milled together at 135 rpm for another 2 h and then assembled under pressure of 70 T to form green compacts. Subsequent vacuum sintering at 813 K promotes their densification and the diffusion of Mg in Al matrix. The heating rate of the sintering furnace is 4 K/min. After cooling down at ∼0.67 K/min to room temperature, the as-sintered samples are preserved in Muffle furnace of 653K for 2h and then extruded at 653 K under pressure of 80 T. The extrusion ratio is 25:1 and the diameter of the extruded rods are ∼8 mm. After cooling down by water quenching, the extruded rods showing surface temperature of ∼300 K are preserved in freezers (∼273 K). Specimens for tensile tests, EBSD, XRD, TEM and Raman tests are cut from the extrusion rods of CNT/Al, CNT/Al-2.5 Mg and CNT/Al-5Mg. Processing Text: In the present study, a novel dual-heterogeneous structure with a bimodal grain distribution in both ferrite and austenite phases was fabricated via cold rolling and partial recrystallization annealing on solution-treated 2205 duplex stainless steel (DSS). The received hot-rolled DSS 2205 was treated with TSS treatment to obtain "TSS" samples. This process involves an initial solution treatment at 1380 °C (1653 K) for 20 min, followed by rapid water quenching, and a subsequent solution treatment at 1000 °C (1273 K) for 20 min, followed by water quenching. The comparative sample was subjected to 90 % cold rolling deformation after TSS pretreatment, and then held at 930 °C (1203 K) for 1 min, followed by quenching to room temperature, resulting in the formation of bimodal grain heterostructured 2205 DSS ((hereinafter referred to as "CRA" sample). Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 16 mm (//RD), a width of 4 mm (TD), and a thickness of 1 mm (ND) were cut along the rolling direction (RD: rolling direction, TD: transverse direction, ND: normal direction). The sample size for tensile testing was based on a laboratory standard. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted on a Shimadzu AG-X100KN testing machine with a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1at room temperature. Additionally, cyclic loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests were performed on the same equipment. In the LUR tests, specimens were initially loaded to an assigned strain at a rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1, subsequently unloaded with the unloading rate of 500 N min −1to 80 N, and then reloaded to the specified strain at the same rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. To ensure the reliability of the results, three parallel tensile tests were repeated for each sample at the same strain rate. Electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD) mapping of undeformed samples was conducted on an Apreo field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with a NordlysMax2 EBSD detector from Oxford instrument. The accelerating voltage was set at 15 kV, and the scanning step size was 0.2 µm. Microlattices are 3D-extruded with inks containing a blend of precursor Ti + Nb + TiAl3 powders, and their struts are then densified through a series of heat treatments to eliminate organic binder, sinter porosity, and achieve compositional Ti2AlNb homogeneity. The phase evolution of an as-printed filament (representative of a microlattice strut) is examined using in-situ X-ray diffraction, revealing a series of steps: (i) TiAl3 decomposition, starting at 710 °C and ending at 780 °C, to form TiAl; (ii) Nb and Al interdiffusion, initiating at 820 °C, accompanied by the formation of Nb2Al and Nb3Al phases; (iii) the α→β Ti phase transformation and (iv) Ti3Al formation, starting at 870 °C. Fully-homogenized Ti2AlNb microstructures with low residual porosity, comprising a B2 matrix and two types of α2 and O (orthorhombic) secondary phases, are achieved after sintering at 1300 °C for 5 h. The as-printed microlattices and heat exchanger were subjected to a three-step heat-treatment: (i) debinding at 450 °C for 30 min to decompose PS and remove residual DCM; (ii) pre-sintering at 750 °C for 2 h to remove any remaining organic materials; and (iii) sintering at 1300 °C for 5 h, followed by furnace cooling at a rate of 10 °C/min. Both the debinding and pre-sintering steps were carried out in an MTI GSL-1500 tube furnace with Ar (99.999 % pure) flowing at a rate of 500 sccm, with a Ti foil as an oxygen getter. For the sintering step, the pre-sintered microlattice was wrapped with Mo foil and vacuum-encapsulated in a quartz tube (OD: 19 mm, ID: 15 mm, residual Ar pressure: 190 mbar). Test temperature: 1000 °C; Compressive measurement; Ductility: 48%

The Al x(CoFeNi 1.5) 100-xHEA in atomic fraction was designed and a button ingot of 100 g was fabricated using an arc melting furnace in a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. The ingot was flipped, melted and electromagnetically stirred for six times, in order to ensure chemical homogeneity. Samples were cut from the as-cast button (designated as AC) and cold rolled down to 80 % reduction (designated as CR). The CR samples were recrystallized in a muffle furnace at 1010 °C for 15 minutes followed by water quenching (which is denoted here as CRR) to achieve the full FCC microstructure. Subsequently, these samples were annealed at 500, 550, 575 and 600°C for 36, 54, and 72 hours, respectively, to achieve nano-lamellar structure. The schematic diagram of heat treatment with sample dimensions are shown in Fig. 1(a-b). The samples are denoted as, for example, CRR500-36 and CRR550-72, in which the first number from the left indicates the aging temperature and the second number indicates the aging time. The microstructures of these samples were examined via scanning electron microscope (SEM; ZEISS, SUPRA 55) and transmission electron microscope (TEM: FEI Talos F200X). The samples for SEM were prepared by grinding with SiC papers (grit sizes: 240-2500), polishing with 0.01μm colloidal silica solution, and finally etching in a 300 mL solution containing 25 % HNO 3, 25 % HF, and 50 % H 2O. The chemical composition was measured using energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) coupled with SEM. The samples for TEM imaging were prepared by using the Gatan ion thinner method and TEM investigation was performed at a voltage of 250 kV. Flat dog-bone tensile specimens were machined on a wire-cut electric discharge machine, with dimensions of 6 mm × 2 mm × 1 mm (length × width × thickness). All tensile specimens were ground to 1200 grit emery paper and then cleaned with acetone to remove surface defects. Tensile tests were performed using a universal double-column testing machine (Instron 45582 100KN) at room temperature with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. Two specimens were tested for each aging condition. The fracture surfaces after tensile testing were examined by SEM. Sample ID: CRR500-72; Aging at 500°C for 72 hours

The medium Mn steel used in this study was initially a hot-forged plate with a thickness of 35 mm. Before the cyclic treatment, the hot-forged plate was heated to 1200°C and held for 2 h before being hot rolled. The final rolling temperature exceeded 850°C, with a total of 7 passes. The final rolled thickness was 5 mm, corresponding to a reduction of 85.7 %. After hot rolling, the medium Mn steel was water-cooled to room temperature. For ease of reference, the hot-rolled medium Mn steel is referred to as HR in this study. The sequence includes the first intercritical annealing (denoted as I1), followed by the first cold rolling (C1), progressing to subsequent cycles of annealing and rolling—specifically, the second (I2, C2), third (I3, C3) as well as fourth (I4, C4) intercritical annealings and cold rollings. According to simulations using Jmatpro 7, the A1 and A3 temperatures for medium Mn steel were 500°C and 750°C, respectively. In this study, 700°C was selected as the intercritical annealing temperature. The entire process and the corresponding detailed parameters are presented in Table 2 and Fig. 1. As previously mentioned, medium Mn steel is prone to cracking during cold rolling. When the reduction exceeds 25 %, surface cracks develop, preventing further processing. Therefore, the cold rolling reduction was limited to 25 %. The microstructures of medium Mn steel in various states were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JSM-7100F), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, JSM-7100F, OIM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Tecnai F30). For SEM, samples were ground with sandpaper, mechanically polished, and electrolytically etched in a 10 % perchloric acid alcohol solution at 15 V for 25-30 s. SEM examination was performed at 15 kV. For EBSD, samples underwent mechanical polishing followed by electrolytic polishing using the same 10 % perchloric acid alcohol solution at 20 V for 15-25 s. EBSD was conducted at 20 kV. The scan parameters were as follows: 80 μm × 80 μm with a step size of 0.5 μm for HR; 8 μm × 8 μm with a step size of 0.1 μm for I2 and I3; and 40 μm × 40 μm with a step size of 0.2 μm for I4. For TEM, samples were thinned to below 50 μm, cut into 3 mm discs, and further thinned using an MTP-1A twin-jet electrolytic polisher in 4 % perchloric acid alcohol at −40°C with 75-100 V. TEM was conducted at 200 kV. Element distribution in the C3 sample after tensile testing was analyzed using electron probe microanalysis (EPMA, JXA-8530F). Samples were ground and polished. EPMA was conducted at 15 kV, with scan parameters as follows: 100 μm × 50 μm, step size 0.2 μm for HR and C1; 10 μm × 5 μm, step size 0.1 μm for I2; and 20 μm × 10 μm, step size 0.1 μm for I3 and C3. Phase content was analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku) with Cu Kα radiation. Samples were electrolytically polished to reduce residual stress using the same parameters as EBSD preparation. The scanning range was 40°-100° at 3°/min. The austenite volume fraction ( fγ) was calculated using Eq. (1)[32]. (1)fγ=1.4Iγ1.4Iγ+Iαwhere Iγis the integrated intensity of austenite and Iαis the integrated intensity of α or α’-phase, which were calculated based on the integrated intensities of (200)α, (211)α, (200)γ, (220)γ, and (311)γ diffraction peaks. Hardness measurements for each layer were conducted using a Vickers microhardness tester (TMVS-1). A load of 10 g and a dwell time of 10 s were applied, with at least five points tested per layer, and 5 layers per each type of multilayer structure. Tensile testing (UTM5105X) was performed on dog bone-shaped specimens, with an initial tensile speed of 1 mm/min. The longitudinal direction of the tensile test specimen was consistent with the rolling direction. The gauge length of the specimen was 10 mm, and the width was 2.4 mm. If the plate thickness exceeded 2 mm, the specimen thickness was 2 mm; otherwise, the specimen thickness matched the plate thickness. Three specimens of each parameter were tested in tensile test. The deformation behavior of the tensile specimens in various states was assessed using DIC. Images during the tensile loading process were captured using an Elphel NC353L camera, which provided high-resolution images of 1224 × 614 pixels, with a physical resolution of 0.021 × 0.021 mm/pixel. The camera's sampling frequency was set to 5 frames per second. Before conducting the tensile tests, the facet of DIC specimens was uniformly sprayed with black paint, followed by the application of white paint using a spray gun for contrast enhancement. Before the cyclic treatment, the hot-forged plate was heated to 1200°C and held for 2 h before being hot rolled. The final rolling temperature exceeded 850°C, with a total of 7 passes. The final rolled thickness was 5 mm, corresponding to a reduction of 85.7 %. After hot rolling, the medium Mn steel was water-cooled to room temperature. For ease of reference, the hot-rolled medium Mn steel is referred to as HR in this study. The sequence includes the first intercritical annealing (denoted as I1), followed by the first cold rolling (C1), progressing to subsequent cycles of annealing and rolling—specifically, the second (I2, C2), third (I3, C3) as well as fourth (I4, C4) intercritical annealings and cold rollings. According to simulations using Jmatpro 7, the A1 and A3 temperatures for medium Mn steel were 500°C and 750°C, respectively. In this study, 700°C was selected as the intercritical annealing temperature. The entire process and the corresponding detailed parameters are presented in Table 2 and Fig. 1. As previously mentioned, medium Mn steel is prone to cracking during cold rolling. When the reduction exceeds 25 %, surface cracks develop, preventing further processing. Therefore, the cold rolling reduction was limited to 25 %. The microstructures of medium Mn steel in various states were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JSM-7100F), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, JSM-7100F, OIM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Tecnai F30). For SEM, samples were ground with sandpaper, mechanically polished, and electrolytically etched in a 10 % perchloric acid alcohol solution at 15 V for 25-30 s. SEM examination was performed at 15 kV. For EBSD, samples underwent mechanical polishing followed by electrolytic polishing using the same 10 % perchloric acid alcohol solution at 20 V for 15-25 s. EBSD was conducted at 20 kV. The scan parameters were as follows: 80 μm × 80 μm with a step size of 0.5 μm for HR; 8 μm × 8 μm with a step size of 0.1 μm for I2 and I3; and 40 μm × 40 μm with a step size of 0.2 μm for I4. For TEM, samples were thinned to below 50 μm, cut into 3 mm discs, and further thinned using an MTP-1A twin-jet electrolytic polisher in 4 % perchloric acid alcohol at −40°C with 75-100 V. TEM was conducted at 200 kV. Element distribution in the C3 sample after tensile testing was analyzed using electron probe microanalysis (EPMA, JXA-8530F). Samples were ground and polished. EPMA was conducted at 15 kV, with scan parameters as follows: 100 μm × 50 μm, step size 0.2 μm for HR and C1; 10 μm × 5 μm, step size 0.1 μm for I2; and 20 μm × 10 μm, step size 0.1 μm for I3 and C3. Phase content was analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku) with Cu Kα radiation. Samples were electrolytically polished to reduce residual stress using the same parameters as EBSD preparation. The scanning range was 40°-100° at 3°/min. The austenite volume fraction ( fγ) was calculated using Eq. (1)[32]. (1)fγ=1.4Iγ1.4Iγ+Iαwhere Iγis the integrated intensity of austenite and Iαis the integrated intensity of α or α’-phase, which were calculated based on the integrated intensities of (200)α, (211)α, (200)γ, (220)γ, and (311)γ diffraction peaks. Hardness measurements for each layer were conducted using a Vickers microhardness tester (TMVS-1). A load of 10 g and a dwell time of 10 s were applied, with at least five points tested per layer, and 5 layers per each type of multilayer structure. Tensile testing (UTM5105X) was performed on dog bone-shaped specimens, with an initial tensile speed of 1 mm/min. The longitudinal direction of the tensile test specimen was consistent with the rolling direction. The gauge length of the specimen was 10 mm, and the width was 2.4 mm. If the plate thickness exceeded 2 mm, the specimen thickness was 2 mm; otherwise, the specimen thickness matched the plate thickness. Three specimens of each parameter were tested in tensile test. The deformation behavior of the tensile specimens in various states was assessed using DIC. Images during the tensile loading process were captured using an Elphel NC353L camera, which provided high-resolution images of 1224 × 614 pixels, with a physical resolution of 0.021 × 0.021 mm/pixel. The camera's sampling frequency was set to 5 frames per second. Before conducting the tensile tests, the facet of DIC specimens was uniformly sprayed with black paint, followed by the application of white paint using a spray gun for contrast enhancement. Processing Text: A356 matrix composites with dual-structured reinforcements (monolithic τ2-phase particles and core (Ti)-shell (τ2) structured particles) and matrix (Si-rich regions and Si-lean regions) were fabricated via solid-state sintering and subsequent die forging. The detailed process parameters for ball milling (4.875 wt% Ti + A356 alloy powders) and hot pressing are presented in Ref. [18]. The achieved green billets were subsequently sintered under vacuum at 555 °C for 3 h, 4 h, 5 h, and 6 h, respectively. Once the sintering was completed, the billets were swiftly moved to a preheated steel mold cavity (300 °C) positioned on a hydraulic machine, and forged at 190 MPa for 20 s to densify the microstructures, and finally formed cakes with dimensions of Ø50 mm × ∼10 mm. The starting materials for this study were a Ni single crystal of 99.999 % purity. The cylindrical Ni single crystal rod had 70 mm length and 15 mm diameter. The Ni single crystal was prepared using the standard Czochralski method. Cylindrical specimens were cut using an electrical discharge machine (EDM) in three different crystallographic orientations, namely [100], [110], and [111], from the Ni single crystal rod and annealed at 500 °C for 1 h. The specimens were prepared using standard metallographic procedures followed by polishing with colloidal silica and finally electropolishing (Struers LectroPol 5) using A2 solution (90 ml distilled water, 730 ml ethanol, 100 ml butoxyethanol, 78 ml perchloric acid) at 20 V for 15 s at ambient temperature. Compression samples were extracted from nickel single crystals such that the [111], [110], and [100] direction was parallel to the compression axis. All the samples were tested in a Dartec servo-hydraulic universal testing machine with an initial strain rate of 10−3s−1 at ambient temperature up to 10 % true strain. Processing Text: The starting materials for this study were polycrystalline Ni of 99.998 % purity. Polycrystalline Ni was in the form of 4 mm thick and 20 mm long electrodeposited plates with two different grain sizes (GS-1 & GS-2). The sample preparation method for the electrodeposited Ni is reported in Ref. [33]. GS-2 of Ni was annealed at 400 °C, 500 °C and 700 °C for 1 h to induce grain growth and obtain the larger grain sizes GS-3, GS-4 and GS-5, respectively. Cylindrical specimens were cut using an electrical discharge machine (EDM) in three different crystallographic orientations, namely [100], [110], and [111], from the Ni single crystal rod and annealed at 500 °C for 1 h. The specimens were prepared using standard metallographic procedures followed by polishing with colloidal silica and finally electropolishing (Struers LectroPol 5) using A2 solution (90 ml distilled water, 730 ml ethanol, 100 ml butoxyethanol, 78 ml perchloric acid) at 20 V for 15 s at ambient temperature. Samples for uniaxial compression were cut by using EDM from the electrodeposited plate as shown in Fig. 1. Compression samples were extracted from nickel single crystals such that the [111], [110], and [100] direction was parallel to the compression axis. All the samples were tested in a Dartec servo-hydraulic universal testing machine with an initial strain rate of 10−3s−1 at ambient temperature up to 10 % true strain. Quantitative analysis of microstructural parameters such as dislocation density, dislocation character (screw, edge, or mixed character) and dislocation arrangement parameter (denotes the strength of interaction between dislocations) was performed by analyzing the X-ray diffraction profile using CMWP fitting. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded on a diffractometer (Rigaku Smart Lab) using Cu-Kα radiation operated at 45 kV and 100 mA current, with a step size of 0.01° and a scan speed of 1°/min. A 50 kg ingot was cast in a vacuum induction furnace, reheated to 1200 °C for homogenisation annealing, and forged into billets with a cross-sectional area of 1500 mm × 20 mm at 950-1200 °C. The forged plates were hot-rolled (HR) at 1050 °C to a thickness of 5.5 mm and air-cooled to room temperature. The HR plates were further subjected to WR at 650 °C to a thickness of 1.6 mm. During WR, the HR plates were first heated to the target temperature, maintained for 15 min, and rolled five times, which decreased the total thickness by approximately 71 %. The WR plates were intercritically annealed (IA) at 620 °C for 5 h to soften the steel, and then cold-rolled (CR) to reduce the thickness by 15 % to 1.36 mm. Finally, the ART samples were annealed at 600-750 °C for 5 min and then air-cooled to enhance their ductility; the final samples were named WCR600, WCR675, and WCR750. Processing Text: Argon gas atomised Al-Ni-Sc-Zr powder was used for LPBF fabrication. The chemical composition of the powder determined by Inductively Coupled Plasma Atomic Emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES) was Al-5.61Ni-0.63Sc-0.09Zr (wt.%). The samples were fabricated using a commercial ProX DMP 200 machine (3D Systems, USA) equipped with a 300 W fibre laser with a laser spot size of 75 μm and wavelength of 1070 nm. After optimising the laser parameters, the components were built using a laser power of 285 W, scanning speed of 1500 mm/s, hatch space of 90 μm, layer thickness of 30 μm, and island scanning strategy with a 90° rotation between layers. The fabrication process was carried out in a high-purity argon atmosphere with an oxygen content of <200 ppm. After the LPBF process, the as-built alloys were separated from the base plate using electrical discharge machining. Subsequently, the as-built alloys were then subjected to direct ageing at temperatures ranging from 200 to 375 °C, with ageing times ranging from 1 min to 70 h. The samples were then cooled in the air. Condition: As-built

The test material was additively manufactured using the directed energy deposition (DED) method. DED system (MX-600; InssTek) was used to make a bulk sample using a 2 kW Yttrium fiber laser and pre-alloyed 304L stainless steel powder. The process parameters employed in this study were as follows: a laser power of 450 W, a hatch spacing of 0.5 mm, a layer thickness of 0.25 mm, and a scan speed of 14 mm/s with a scanning direction rotated by 90° between the adjacent layers. The as-built samples were annealed at various temperatures, i.e., 750 °C, 850 °C, 950 °C, 1050 °C, and 1150 °C for 2 h. Annealing was performed in an Ar gas using a laboratory tube furnace. Tensile tests were performed at room temperature with a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3/s by displacement control, following the ASTM E8standard using Zwick Roell Z005. Processing state: as-built

The vacuum arc melting device was used to prepare the Fe2NiCoCr-(VN)x (x= 0, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0) series of HEAs. Ultra-pure metals (Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) with a minimum purity level of 99.99 %, and the V-N alloy with a composition ratio of 4:1 for both vanadium and nitrogen was used as the raw material. After mass calculation, 70 g ingots of each alloy were obtained. In order to inhibit oxidation, the melting chamber underwent multiple evacuations and refillings with high-purity argon gas (99.99 %), and the titanium ingot was initially melted to purge residual oxygen from the chamber. To achieve uniform homogenization of the as-cast alloys, each alloy underwent remelting five times, with the melt being thoroughly mixed during each cycle. For simplicity, the alloys were named in terms of VN alloy doped molar ratios, and the casting alloys with VN alloy doped molar ratios of 0, 0.3, 0.5 and 1.0 were named VN0, VN0.3, VN0.5 and VN1.0, respectively. Processing Text: The experimental steel was prepared by smelting in a high-frequency vacuum furnace using high-purity raw materials. The cast ingot was hot forged into a plate of 30 mm thickness and then homogenized at 1100 °C for 2h. The Ac 3and Ms temperatures of the as-obtained steel were 818 °C and 170 °C, respectively, as determined by a DIL-805A quenching thermal dilatometer. The austenitization temperature and the first-stage austempering temperature were determined to be 910 °C and 240 °C, respectively. Thermal simulation experiments were conducted using cylindrical samples ( φ6 mm × 70 mm) on a Gleeble-3500 simulator. All samples were austenitized at 910 °C for 30 min. For the TA-4.5 treatment, samples were quenched to 240 °C immediately after austenitizing and held for 4.5h. When the bainite transformation had progressed to 30 %, the samples were rapidly cooled to 180 °C to continue the second austempering stage until the bainite transformation was complete (approximately 16h). For the TA-8.5 treatment, after 8.5h of the first austempering stage at 240 °C (when 70 % of the bainite transformation had occurred), the samples were immediately cooled to 150 °C and held for 3h. This holding time slightly exceeded the incubation period of bainite transformation, enabling the refinement of BRA through localized BF formation in carbon-depleted regions. According to the calculations from JMatPro software, the samples were held at 240 °C for 8.5h and 20h before being brought down to ambient temperature, designated as SA-8.5 and SA-20, respectively. An Al-1%Si alloy was prepared using high-purity aluminum (99.99 %) and an Al-20%Si alloy by melting in a clay graphite crucible at 730 °C in an electric furnace. The melt was stirred with a graphite rod, degassed using hexachloroethane, and then cast into a graphite mold preheated to 200 °C. The ingot was sectioned into plates for solution treatment and subsequent rolling deformation. The as-cast (AC) samples underwent solution treatment at 570 °C for 10 h, followed by water quenching. The solution-treated samples are called AS for short. Cold rolling (CR) was performed at room temperature on a two-high mill without lubrication, achieving an accumulative reduction of 97.5 % over 15 successive passes. The corresponding von Mises equivalent strain: ε=4.26. After rolling, the samples were annealed at temperatures from 100 °C to 350 °C for 1 h. Samples are designated by their annealing temperature, e.g., CR100 to CR350. Solution treatment was carried out in an air furnace, while annealing was performed in an oil bath. Processing state: cold rolled; Microstructure: heterogeneous lamella structure with dense Si nanoprecipitates

Processing Text: In this study, hierarchical heterostructures were introduced into CoCrFeMnNi HEA via an in-situ rolling (ISR) assisted laser cladding (LC) process. The coating was fabricated by overlapping individual tracks with a 30 % overlapping ratio. Following the preliminary testing, the distance D between the laser head and the roller was set to 13 mm. In this work, static pressures of 0 N, 1000 N, 2000 N, 3000 N, and 4000 N were applied, and the corresponding coatings were referred as un-ISR, ISR1, ISR2, ISR3 and ISR4, respectively. Annealed 45 steel with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm was chosen as the substrate. To minimize the interference of oxides and other impurities, an angle grinder was used to remove the oxide layer from the substrate surface, followed by cleaning with anhydrous ethanol. The powder used in this study was CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder with a particle size range of 45-105 μm, produced by high-temperature gas atomization. Before the experiment, place the powder in a vacuum drying oven (Shanghai Jiecheng Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd., DZF-6050) and dry it at 100 °C for 2 h to ensure its uniformity and fluidity. The coating was prepared by using a semiconductor laser (HWL-1500) with a wavelength range of 910-1050 nm and a DPSF scraper powder feeder to transport CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy powder coaxially. Laser spot diameter 2 mm, laser power 1500 W, scanning rate 3 mm/s, powder feed 7 g/min, overlapping ratio 30 %. High purity argon is used as melt pool shielding gas with a flow rate of 3 L / min. The prepared coating was cut into cuboid specimens with dimensions of 15 × 15 × 10 mm 3using a high-speed wire electrical discharge machining machine tool (Fangzheng CNC Machine Tool Co., Ltd., DK7720). The specimens were then hot - mounted using a metallographic specimen mounting machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., XQ-2B). Subsequently, the cross - section of the specimen was ground using SiC sandpapers of grit sizes 60 mesh, 400 mesh, 800 mesh, 1500 mesh, and 2000 mesh in a wet - grinding manner on a metallographic specimen grinding and polishing machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., MP-2B). After grinding, the specimens were polished with diamond polishing paste until no obvious scratches were visible under an optical microscope. The specimens were placed in anhydrous ethanol and cleaned in an ultrasonic cleaner for 5 min. To prepare the surfaces for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis, the specimen was pre-ground and polished using the metallographic pre-grinding machine (Hua Xing Test Instrument Co., Ltd.). The surface was then ion-polished with a precision ion thinning instrument (GATAN PIPS II 695) to remove the damage layer caused by mechanical polishing. The microhardness was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., NVM-1000 A). The load was set at 0.3 kg, and the dwell time was 15 s. Each value was measured three times to ensure accuracy. The tribological properties of the coatings at room temperature (25 °C) were evaluated by a ball-on-disk wear tester (Lanzhou Zhongke Kaihua Science and Technology Development Co., Ltd., HT-1000) with a Si 3N 4ball as the counterpart. The tests, performed under dry sliding conditions in accordance with the ASTM G99-17 standard, were repeated three times. The test parameters included a loading force of 10 N, a friction radius of 3 mm, a rotation speed of 600 r/min, and a wear time of 30 min. Condition: Untreated; Measurement: Room Temperature

Processing Text: Forged H13 steel, supplied in a spheroidized annealed state with dimensions of 100 × 100 × 50 mm 3, was used as the substrate for metal deposition in the WA-DED process. H13 wire with a diameter of 1.6 mm was used as the deposition material. Two different process routes were designed to fabricate the hybrid samples, as shown in Fig. 1. The WA-DED process was accomplished by a GMAW-based WA-DED system consisting of a YASKAWA AR1440 robot and a YASKAWA MOTOWELD-RD500 welding power source. H13 blocks with dimensions of approximately 80 × 80 × 60 mm 3were deposited on the forged substrate using the composite path of Contour + Zigzag. Adjacent layers use cross-over deposition paths (see Fig. 1). The detailed process parameters of the WA-DED process are shown in Table 2. Processing Text: The AFMAR alloys were prealloyed and gas atomized by CEIT (Spain). The powders were then sintered through Spark Plasma Sintering (HPD-25 equipment, FCT System GmbH, Germany) in a graphite die 20 mm in diameter. A tungsten foil of 25-50 µm was placed between the inner walls of the die and the powder, isolating the alloy from the graphite and preventing carbon contamination. A heating rate of 400 °C/min was used to reach a sintering temperature of 1100 °C and held for 5 min while applying a 50 MPa uniaxial pressure under a 10 -2mbar low vacuum. This sintering cycle was chosen because it had been previously optimized with the same die geometry for a similar alloy. AFMAR samples were cut into semi-circles of 20 mm in diameter and approximately 2 mm in thickness. All samples were grounded to a 1200-grit surface finish and cleaned with ethanol prior to the corrosion tests. The samples were placed in rectangular alumina crucibles with molten lead. Samples of commercial alloys 316 L and T91 were placed in a separate crucible from the AFMAR alloys and were used as reference. The lead exposure tests were conducted in a COSTA (COrrosion test STand for liquid metal Alloys) facility located at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, developed by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT). The alumina crucibles containing the samples, and the lead were positioned inside a sealed quartz glass tube. To control the oxygen concentration in the atmosphere inside the tube, one extreme had inlet and outlet gas tubes. Since the oxygen partial pressures needed for the test are much lower than what can be provided in commercial bottles (≅ 10 -18bar), a flowing gas mixture of Ar, H 2and H 2O is used. An Ar gas flow is bubbled through water, carrying water vapor as it moves. Then, the humidified-Ar flow is mixed with an Ar-5 %H 2gas flow at the inlet of the gas tube. By controlling the flow rate of both gases, it is possible to adjust the H 2/H 2O ratio and achieve the desired oxygen partial pressure of the gas phase inside the glass tube (p O2). A Zirox SGM5 oxygen analyzer placed at the gas outlet was used to monitor the p O2. Corrosion tests at 550 °C and 650 °C were performed, lasting up to 1000 h each. Condition: after 500 h in molten lead at 550 °C
Processing Word: Condition: after 500 h in molten lead at 550 °C

Processing Text: The alloy components were weighed according to the designed composition and thoroughly melted in a ZG-25-A vacuum induction furnace at a temperature of approximately 1450 °C. The molten alloy was then poured into a sand mold to form 12 kg Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 ingots. A portion of the original ingot was subjected to further melting process to improve material homogeneity, remove impurities, and obtain the cast sample (noted as C-1 sample). For the LPBF process, the remaining primitive initial ingots were processed into 32 mm bars. The pre-alloyed Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 powders were generated by the plasma rotating electrode process (PREP) (the schematic view is shown in Fig. 1(a)) from the prepared bars. The particle size ranges from 10 to 53 μm. The 3 × 3 × 3 mm3 cuboid samples (noted as 0A ∼ 9J) were built on a commercial machine (TruPrint 1000) with a build chamber of Φ100 mm*80 mm (Figs. 2(a ∼ b)). Employing a laser power (P) of 175 W, and a layer thickness (h) of 30 μm, the laser was rotated at a 67° angle (α) for each scanning layer (Fig. 2(d)) for homogenous microstructure. The argon atmosphere was maintained during the deposition with an oxygen environment below 100 ppm to prevent oxidation. Meanwhile, the hatching space (d) ranged from 30 to 70 μm and the scanning speed (v) varied from 500 to 2400 mm/s, corresponding to changes in laser volumetric energy density (E=Pvhd) from 33.7 to 388.9 J·mm−3 (Table S1). These parameters were meticulously selected to build Al0.3CoCrFeNiTi0.15 specimens. In addition, to reduce the effect of pore characteristics (including shape, size, location and number) on stress concentrations (Fig. S1), the remelting technology was undertaken to further enhance the performance, as depicted in Fig. 2(c) (noted as R-2). Finally, 33 × 17 × 7 mm3 samples were deposited under the same optimized laser conditions to analyze their mechanical properties (Fig. 2(d)). The tensile test specimens perpendicular to the building direction, with a gauge length of 12.5 mm, a width of 4.0 mm, and a thickness of 1.5 mm (Fig. 2(d)), were cut out by a wire-cut electrical discharge machine. Then the tensile tests at 20 °C and 700 °C were conducted on the INSTRON 5982 and ZWICK universal testing machine (Z250SH) with a tensile rate of 5 × 10−3 s−1. A digital image correlation sensor was used to measure the strain at RT, the displacement at 700 °C tensile testing was measured by a ceramic contact extensometer. The microhardness was conducted by an XHVT-10Z Vickers hardness tester with a load of 1 kg for a dwell time of 20 s. Each reported hardness value is the average value of five measurements. The metallographic specimen was cut in the middle zone of cuboid samples, as depicted in Fig. 2(d), which were first ground with SiC papers up to 5000 grit and then polished. Defects and morphology (aqua regia etching: 15 mL HCl + 5 mL HNO3) were observed by optical microscope (OM) (SOPTOP RX50M). The microstructures and grain orientation were achieved using a TESCAN MIRA3 scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). The grain size, texture, misorientation between grains, and Kernel average misorientation (KAM) map were investigated using EBSD analysis (MTEX). The microstructures and precipitations were also characterized by the FEI TALOS F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). The 3 mm foils (thickness less than 50 μm) were polished to electron transparency by a twin-jet electro-polisher (5 % perchloric acid +95 % ethanol) at −15 °C and 30 V. Processing state: Casting (C-1 sample); Condition: Room Temperature

Processing Text: The material is entirely melted in an electric furnace at roughly 720 °C, with a combination of protective gases (SF 6: CO 2= 1: 99) to avoid oxidation, then it is transferred into a hot steel mold and allowed to air-cool, producing cylindrical ingots 90 mm in diameter. Afterward, the ingot is heated to 500 °C for 24 h and then allowed to cool in the air to achieve homogenization. The alloy was extruded at 400 °C, maintaining a speed of 2 mm/s with extrusion gradient: T1. The temperature as a single variable adds 300 °C, 350 °C, and 450 °C, while other parameters remain unchanged according to the T400S2T1. Similarly, speed as a single variable additionally adds 1 mm/s and 4 mm/s, and gradient as a single variable additionally adds T0 and T2 (angle α is 0 and 2 respectively, as shown in Fig. 1). Different mixed grain structures can be achieved in this work by adjusting extrusion parameters like speed, gradient, and temperature. By altering extrusion parameters to influence the DRXed process, different proportions, distributions, and types of coarse grains in Mg-5Y-1Sn alloy were obtained. The extrusion gradient refers to the number of modulus angles α in the forming strip. Extrusion conditions: T450S2T1

Processing Text: The Mn0.3CoCrFeNi was prepared via vacuum-induction melting using elements that are over 99.9 % in purity. The Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni in equimolar ratio were first added to an alumina crucible in a muffle furnace and melted. Afterward, Mn was added in an upper funnel in its respective molar ratio; this was done to achieve the best possible uniform alloy composition since Mn has a smaller molar ratio compared to CoCrFeNi, and to avoid possible oxidation/evaporation of Mn since it has a lower melting point compared to CoCrFeNi or its constituent elements. The furnace was vacuumed to a pressure of 0.1 Pa, filled with argon up to 100000 Pa, and then the furnace was turned on to melt all elements at 1600 °C for 75 min and continuously stirred for uniform mixing. An additional 2 min was spent for refining (removing impurities and fully fusing), and then the mixture was cast into ingots of 300 × 200 × 20 mm plate for each alloy. Alloys were then air-cooled. For each of the alloys, the as-cast samples (hereafter called AC) were split into 200 × 24 × 12 mm coupons; one of them was homogenized and cold-rolled (hereafter called CR). The homogenization was conducted at 1250 °C for 4 h using a high-temperature Carbolite furnace followed by water quenching to ensure chemical homogeneity. The cold rolling was conducted using a 2HI Lab Rolling Mill (IRM MODEL #3350) to achieve ⁓30 % thickness reduction at a final dimension of ⁓270 × 25 × 8 mm. A portion of the CR plates for both HEAs were further split, and half was annealed at 1250 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching to ensure chemical homogeneity, recovery, and recrystallization (hereafter called CRA). Processing conditions: AC-Mn; Quasi-static compression

The TA15 alloy was fabricated using laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) technology. After annealing, L-PBF TA15 samples exhibit excellent mechanical properties at medium to high temperatures. Heat treatment was conducted in a resistance furnace, with the samples coated with a ceramic protective layer to prevent oxidation. The heating rate was set at 10 °C/min, followed by a 2-h dwell at a temperature of 850 °C, and then cooled by air. The fine needle-like αʹ martensite transitioned into lamellar α + β phases after annealing treatment. Samples were tensile tested in the range of 500-750 °C. The as-built TA15 alloy consists of αʹ phase, which can be decomposed into α + β after annealing treatment. The TA15 alloy processed by L-PBF demonstrates exceptional high-temperature tensile properties, with a tensile strength of 686 ± 12 MPa and an elongation of 18.5 ± 2.1 % at 500 °C. Temperature: 750 °C; Processing state: annealed

The plastic deformation introduced by in-situ rolling facilitated the recovery and recrystallization of the pre-solidified layers. The yield strength was significantly enhanced due to grain refinement strengthening and work hardening.
