Processing Text: The GH3535 nickel-based alloy, designed for molten salt nuclear reactors, was fabricated using wire arc additive manufacturing. Utilizing ERNiMo-2 welding wire with a diameter of 1.2 mm as the filler material and with GH3535 alloy serving as the substrate material, the nominal chemical composition is detailed in Table 1. Prior to the deposition process, the substrate undergoes meticulous surface preparation, which includes sanding to eliminate oxide layers and subsequent cleaning with acetone to remove any residual grease or dirt. A mixture shielding gas of Argon (Ar) and 50 % Helium (He) was used, with a flow rate of 15L•min−1. The deposition employed a reciprocating scanning strategy, with the torch rotated 90° between successive layers (Fig. 1c). An overlap rate of 35 % between adjacent weld beads was maintained to ensure consistent layer fusion. Throughout the deposition process, the inter-bead temperature was meticulously regulated to remain below 100 °C. The specific processing parameters are outlined in Table 2. Metallographic and tensile samples were extracted at three distinct vertical levels along the horizontal direction plane (as depicted in Fig. 1d), specifically from the bottom, middle and top, to evaluate the uniformity of the mechanical properties of the WAAM-fabricated GH3535 alloy. Specimens for tensile testing were meticulously prepared at deposition heights of 1 mm (representing the bottom layer), 25 mm (the middle layer) and 48 mm (the top layer), with three samples tested for each condition. Additionally, Vickers hardness tests were executed on the WAAM-fabricated GH3535 alloy samples, which were taken from various deposition heights with a consistent interval of 2 mm. Each hardness test was applied with a static load of 500 gf for a duration of 15 s, providing a comprehensive assessment of hardness variations throughout the build height. Processing Text: The (CoCrFeNi)84(AlTi)16 M/HEA system was fabricated using MA + SPS. The high purity (≥99.7 wt %) elemental powders of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al and Ti (particles size ≤10 μm) were used as raw materials in specific atomic ratios. The compositions (via at. %) were synthesized in the current work as shown in Fig. 1. To attain M/HEAs with a nanocrystalline structure, the elemental powders were mechanically alloyed by planetary ball mill machine using stainless bowl and balls. The ball milling was conducted at a rotation speed of 300 rpm under Ar atmosphere for 70 h after mixing of 0.3 wt% stearic acid as a process control agent to improve milling efficiency. The milled M/HEA powders were consolidated (Ø25 mm × 10 mm) in the graphite mold under pressure of 40 MPa at temperature of 1000 °C using SPS for 8 min in a vacuum. The morphologies and microstructures followed by chemical composition/elemental maps (micro sized areas) of the MA and SPS processed (CoCrFeNi)84(AlTi)16 M/HEAs were characterized via the field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM, Mira3 TESCAN) equipped with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX). Also, the morphologies of the fracture/worn surfaces and corresponding chemical compositions were determined using FESEM/EDX analyses. Topographies of the worn surfaces and the roughness of the M/HEAs were determined by atomic force microscopy (AFM, multiple mode RAR). The phase identification of the MA processed M/HEA powders and SPS processed M/HEA specimens was examined using X-ray diffraction (X-ray diffractometer (XRD), λ = 1.54056 Å, D8 ADVANCE, BRUKER) in a 2θ scanning range of 20-80°. The diffraction spectra were investigated using Xpert software to consider full width half maximum of the FCC/BCC Bragg peaks to estimate the crystallite size (C.S), lattice parameter (L.P), lattice strain (L.S) followed by dislocation density (D.D). The C.S and L.S values estimated from Eq. (1) were used to calculate D.D by following relationship [ 77]: (2)D.D = 2√3 (L S/(b × C.S)) where b is Burger's vector. The room temperature mechanical properties of the SPS processed (CoCrFeNi)84(AlTi)16 M/HEAs were considered by the Vickers micro hardness tester (Qv-1000DM) and a universal testing machine (Zwick 250/Roell). The Vickers micro hardness test was done on the polished surfaces with 200 g applied load for 10 s. Uniaxial compressive tests were done on the cylindrical specimens (Ø 3 mm × 6 mm) at an initial strain rate of the 10−3s 1 and the stress-strain curves and the strain hardening rate (SHR) versus true strain were also plotted. The wear tests were carried out in the wear testing machine (AMI, via rotating abrasive plate (Ø 70 mm with a Rockwell hardness of ∼ 60 Ra)). The tested M/HEA specimens (Ø 5 mm × 10 mm) were sliding under contact conditions with a normal load of 50 N for 1500 s and sliding velocity of 450 rpm without lubricant. Friction force was automatically recorded during the wear test. The friction coefficient was estimated via normal load and friction force, where the wear rate of the tested M/HEA specimens was determined using the volume loss method. Condition: compressive yield strength (CYS); System: 3 M/HEA system

Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with varying laser scan speed under constant power was utilized to manufacture specimens of 316L stainless steel containing keyhole (KH) and lack of fusion (LoF) flaws. Optimal fully dense (FD) specimens were also manufactured. Rods of 15 mm in diameter and 100 mm in length were built horizontally (Y) and vertically (Z) for making FD specimens and vertically (Z) for making KH and LoF specimens. To ensure consistent particle size distribution, the powders underwent a sieving process using a 75 μm mesh screen for 15 min, following the guidelines specified in ASTM B214 for sieving metallic powders. For the laser powder bed fusion process, an SLM 125HL system (SLM Solutions Group AG, Lübeck, Germany) equipped with continuous laser beam was employed. The system utilized a single 1070 nm wavelength fiber laser with a maximum power of 400 W and a beam diameter of approximately 70 μm (IPG Photonics, Oxford, MA, USA). A preheated 316 L SS build-plate at 100 °C was used to minimize potential thermal mismatch issues. Argon was chosen as the protective atmosphere to maintain an O2 content below 0.1 % during the laser powder bed fusion process. The study maintained consistent parameters throughout, including a laser power of 200 W, a hatch distance of 0.12 mm, a layer thickness of 0.03 mm, a stripe width of 10 mm, a stripe overlap of 0.08 mm, a scanning rotation of 67° between subsequent layers, and a stripe scanning strategy. Contouring, up-skin, and down-skin parameters were deactivated. Based on previous research findings, the laser scanning speed (mm/s) was adjusted to achieve different density levels. This adjustment allowed to produce specimens with keyhole (KH) flaws (speed of 400 mm/s) and lack-of-fusion (LoF) flaws (1500 mm/s). Additionally, near fully dense (FD) specimens (99.9 %) were produced using a scanning speed of 800 mm/s. Prior to grain and texture characterization, the samples underwent a series of preparation steps. These steps involved sectioning, mounting, grinding, and polishing. To begin, the samples were carefully sectioned and then mounted using a graphite-based conductive mounting powder. Next, a sequence of abrasives with varying grit sizes (320, 600, 800, and 1200), all based on Silicon-Carbide, was employed for grinding the samples. Subsequently, the samples underwent a polishing stage using glycol-based polycrystalline diamond suspensions from Allied High Tech, specifically with particle sizes of 3 μm and 1 μm. The polishing process was carried out on Buehler TexMet C polishing cloth. For the final polishing step, Allied High Tech products were utilized, including a 0.05 μm colloidal silica suspension and Chem-Pol polishing cloth. To perform the grinding and polishing procedures, an automated Buehler AutoMet 250 Pro Polisher Grinder was employed. Processing Text: Alloy ingots with nominal compositions of NbTa xTiV ( x= 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 in relative molar ratio) were fabricated using pure Ti, V, Nb, and Ta metals (purity ∼99.95 wt%) in a non-consumable vacuum arc melting furnace (HVAM-B, China) under a high-purity argon atmosphere. All ingots were subjected to a minimum of six flips and remeltings to guarantee chemical homogeneity. The dimensions of the as-cast ingots were approximately 25 mm in diameter and 7 mm in thickness. The as-cast ingots were rolled into 1 mm-thick sheets using a double-high rolling mill with a rolling speed of 150 mm s −1(JH-RZH-110, China) at room temperature. Subsequent cold rolling was performed in a multi-pass rolling process with consistent directionality and a per-pass deformation of 0.01 mm, culminating in plates approximately 1 mm in thickness. Multiple dog-bone-shaped samples were extracted from the cold-rolled sheets along the rolling direction using an electrical discharge machine (DK77, China) for subsequent tensile tests. The tensile samples had dimensions of approximately 16 mm in gauge length, 4 mm in gauge width, and 1 mm in thickness. The tensile samples were encapsulated within a quartz tube under a vacuum pressure of 0.005 Pa, followed by annealing at 1200 °C for 45 min to recrystallization and relieving residual stress. After annealing, the samples were quenched in water to preserve the solid solution phase. Subsequently, the annealed samples were polished prior to tensile testing. Tensile tests were conducted at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1at room temperature. Each alloy underwent at least three repeated tensile tests for consistency and reliability. The microhardness of the alloys was assessed using a Vickers hardness tester (MHV-1000, China) with a 0.3 kgf load applied for 15 s. Each sample underwent more than ten hardness tests to ensure statistical reliability. The dynamic elastic modulus and Poisson's ratio of the alloys were determined using an ultrasonic pulse-echo measurement system (Teclab UMS-100 system, France). The mass density of the alloys was measured utilizing the Archimedes drainage method (JHY-300W, China) in accordance with the international standard ASTM B962-17. The phase structure of the as-cast alloys was detected using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD) (Rigaku Smartlab SE, Japan) operating within a diffraction angle (2 θ) range of 20°-90° with Cu-Kα radiation ( λ= 0.15406 nm). Microstructural characterization was performed using a field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Tescan Amber, Czech) operating at 20 KV voltage and 10 nA current. The chemical compositions of the as-cast alloys were examined using an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) (Oxford Ultim Max 40, UK). The samples used for XRD and SEM testing were prepared using a mechanical lapping method. The samples were grinded successively with abrasive papers ranging from 300-grit to 3000-grit abrasive papers, followed by final polishing using polishing pastes. Grain orientation and misorientation were analyzed using an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) camera (Oxford Symmetry, UK) with a scanning step of 1.5 μm. The EBSD samples were polished using a broad argon ion beam system (Gatan 685 PECS II, USA) for approximately 2 h at 7 kV voltage prior to analysis. Ta content: Ta 0.0; Measurement: Yield stress

Processing Text: The Al-5.0Mn-1.5Mg-0.82Sc-0.76Zr (wt.%) alloy powder with a standard composition was prepared by gas atomization (Panxing New Alloy Materials Co., Ltd., China). The powder was spherical in shape, with the particles less than or equal to 22.3 µm accounting for 10% while 90% of the particles were less than or equal to 63.4 µm, as shown in Fig. 1(a, b). All the LPBF samples investigated in this work were manufactured using a BLT S210 LPBF machine equipped with a 400 W fiber laser. Constant laser power (350 W), scanning spacing (90 µm), and layer thickness (30 µm) were used with scanning velocities ranging between 450 and 1450 mm/s. Two different substrate temperatures, 25 and 200 °C, were used for each condition. The samples with the optimized process parameters had a relative density higher than 99.8 %. A bilinear scanning strategy with a scan rotation of 67° was used between the layers. The samples were printed in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the samples were heat-treated at 200 °C for 1 h to remove residual stresses before evaluating their microstructures and mechanical properties. The LPBF samples were prepared for microstructural characterization by mechanical grinding and polishing following a standard metallographic procedure recommended in ASTM E3-11. After polishing, the microstructural features were revealed using an etchant consisting of HNO 3(2.5 mL), HCl (1.5 mL), HF (1.0 mL), and distilled water (95 mL). The wire-cut electro-discharge machine was used to slice samples with the following dimensions: ∼5 mm long, ∼5 mm wide, and ∼1 mm thick. Prior to the EBSD characterization, the sheet samples were first mechanically polished with 400 #, 1000 #, 2000 #, and 3000 # SiC water abrasive paper, then electropolished to remove the surface deformation layer generated by mechanical grinding. Electropolishing was performed at −30 °C, with: 7 % perchloric acid, 93 % ethanol; a voltage of 25 V, and a current density of 450 mA/cm 2for about 1 min. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed using the CMT4105 universal testing machine. The gauge length and cross-sectional area of the tensile specimens were 22 mm and 1.5 mm × 4 mm. All the tensile samples were tested perpendicular to the build direction at a constant strain rate of 1 mm/min, following the standard ASTM E8. Fatigue test samples with the dimensions 60 mm × 12 mm × 1.5 mm were tested on an MTS370.02 fatigue testing machine. All samples were mechanically ground and polished prior to fatigue testing to ensure similar surface roughness. The uniaxial fatigue tests were conducted in a load control mode at a frequency of 40 Hz and stress ratio of R= 0.1, following the standard ASTM E466. The samples were tested until fracture or exhaustion till 10 7cycles. Testing temperature: Room Temperature; Heat-treated at 300 °C for 6h

Processing Text: A 50 kg ingot of the investigated steel was prepared by vacuum induction melting. The ingot was soaked at 1200 °C for 3 h and then hot-forged into a slab with a sectional dimension of 35 mm ×100 mm. Once the chunks were reheated to a temperature of 1200 °C for a duration of 3 h, they were then subjected to hot-rolling in order to form plates with a thickness of 5 mm. After the hot-rolled plates were air cooled to room temperature, they were directly rolled into 1 mm thick strips. It can be summarized as the following two steps: (1) First stage annealing: the cold-rolled samples were annealed at 700 °C for 45 min in order to obtain a micrometer-scaled granular ferrite/austenite and partially recovered austenite microstructure and subsequently water quenched. The first heat-treated samples with a partially recrystallized microstructure are referred to as “PRX”; (2) Second stage annealing: the PRX samples were annealed at 800 °C for 30min and subsequently water quenched to form heterogeneous microstructure. To elucidate the impact of heterogeneous microstructures on mechanical properties, some cold-rolled samples were annealed at 800 °C for 30 min to obtain homogeneous microstructures. When the cold-rolled samples were annealed at 700 °C (first stage annealing), the κ carbides, ferrite and austenite grains nucleated at the primitive grain boundaries. The microstructures consisted of the mixture of recrystallized and non-recrystallized matrix. After that, the PRX samples were annealed at 800 °C (the second stage annealing). Due to the pinning effect of the κ carbides, ferrites and the high stored dislocation energy, the heterogeneous microstructure possessed fine ferrite, fine austenite, and coarse austenite. Through cold rolling and subsequent annealing, Fe-24Mn-10Al-1C lightweight steel with a heterogeneous structure was produced. Homo800 sample; Homogeneous microstructure

Processing Text: The Mo-11%Hf alloy (also called Mo-11Hf) was produced in the form of ∼250 g button by mixing and arc melting high purity (>99.9 %) elements. The arc melter operated at ∼20 V and 600 A. To obtain homogeneous distribution of the alloying elements in the liquid state, the button was flipped over and re-melted 6 times, being in the molten state for ∼1-2 min between each melting stage. To heal casting defects and homogenize the cast microstructure, the alloy button was wrapped in Ta foil to minimize possible interstitial elements pickup during processing and hot isostatically pressed (HIP’d) at 1400 °C for 5 h under a hydrostatic pressure of high-purity argon of 207 MPa. The heating and cooling rates were controlled to 15 °C/min at temperatures above 600 °C during the HIP process. Several SC alloy samples were wrapped in a Ta foil, placed in two quartz tubes, which were pulled under vacuum and purged with high-purity argon several times, and sealed under the argon pressure of 0.179 Torr. The samples in one quartz tube were additionally annealed at 1400 °C for 1 h and water quenched and in the other quartz tube annealed at 1400 °C for 50 h and water quenched. The average alloy composition was measured after HIP processing using direct current plasma emission spectroscopy (ASTM E 1097-12) for metals, inert gas fusion (ASTM E 1019-18) for oxygen and nitrogen and combustion infrared detection (ASTM E 1019-18) for carbon, and the results are given in Table 1. Compositions of the alloys in WQ1 and WQ2 conditions were measured using SEM/EDS. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was conducted from polished surfaces of alloy samples using a Bruker D2 Phaser diffractometer operating with Cu-K α1radiation in the 2θ range of 20°-100°. Microstructure, phases and local chemical compositions were studied using a TFS Apreo C field emission scanning electron microscope (FEG-SEM) equipped with a backscatter electron (BSE) detector, forward scattered electron (FSE) detector, calibrated Oxford X-Max energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) detector and Oxford Symmetry electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. The average concentrations of the alloy samples in WQ conditions were determined by SEM/EDS from 10 randomly selected regions, with the total surface area of ∼10 mm 2per each condition. Local chemistries were determined using a point analysis at the dwell time of 60 s per point, electron probe current of 0.8 nA and accelerating voltage of 20 kV. In the work, cold rolling and annealing were applied to powder plasma arc additively manufactured (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 medium-entropy alloy (MEA) to efficiently attain different types of lattice defects and heterogeneous structures, thereby enhancing the strength of the alloy. The microstructure and mechanical properties of cold rolled samples (50 % thickness reduction) annealed at 1073-1273 K for 1 h are compared. It has been shown that the MEAs prepared by additive manufacturing accumulate a large amount of deformation energy within the grains during the cold rolling process. At annealing temperatures ≤1173 K, the recrystallized grain size has not been coarsened, the coarse and fine grains formed a heterogeneous grain structure, leading to significant back stress strengthening. The specimens were cold rolled (CR) at 50 % in the direction shown in Fig. 1(b) at room temperature with an electro-hydraulic universal testing machine. Subsequently, the cold rolled specimens were annealed (RA) at 1073, 1173 or 1273 K for 1 h, followed rapid by water quenching. The PPA-AM with subsequent a single-step cold rolling (CR) and annealing (RA) is used to produce different types of lattice defects, heterogeneous structures, and fine-grained structures in the (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 MEA. For the cold-rolled samples, short-time annealing treatment was carried out, and the evolution of the alloy's microstructure and mechanical properties was studied in detail. The (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 MEAs powders used in this study were composed of Co, Cr, Ni, Al, and Ti mono metal powders (the particle size of the mono metal powders is 150-250 mesh and the purity was over 99.5 %). The monolithic metal powders were configured according to the proportions and then processed for homogeneous mixing with a high-energy ball mill (YXQM-12L, MITR Ltd, Hunan, China) for 6 h. The (CoCrNi)94Al3Ti3 MEAs were prepared with PPA-AM equipment (PPA-AM, DML-VO3AD, Duomu Company, Shanghai, China). Condition: RA-1173; Microstructure: fine-grained microstructure (average grain size of 5.42 μm), heterogeneous microstructure formed by grain size

An ingot of Co 17.5Cr 12.5Fe 55Ni 10Mo 5 (atomic percent, at%) MEA was fabricated using a vacuum induction melting equipment (MC100V, Indutherm, Germany) under a high-purity argon atmosphere. The raw materials, with a purity exceeding 99.9 %, were used for casting. A rectangular ingot with dimensions of 100 x 35 × 8 mm 3 was homogenized at 1250 °C for 6 h in an argon atmosphere. The homogenized ingot was then milled precisely to a thickness of 7 mm to remove surface oxides and roughness. Afterwards, cold rolling was carried out, reducing the thickness from 7 mm to 1.5 mm. The laser surface treatment was performed on the cold-rolled plate using three distinct scanning patterns: single scan that covers the surface once, a single scan at low speed for long-term exposure of the laser heat source to the material's surface, and a triple scan that repeats the laser scanning three times over the same track. Laser scanning was performed with a laser power of 250 W and a beam diameter of 400 μm under argon atmosphere, using a laser module (YLR-300-MM-AC, IPG photonics, USA). The hatch space during laser scanning was 2 mm, with a scan speed of 10 mm/s for SS and TS and 5 mm/s for SSLS. Both surfaces of the plate underwent laser scanning under the same conditions. For comparison, a typical annealing treatment was carried out on the cold-rolled plate. The cold-rolled plate was annealed in a furnace at 900 °C for 1 h under an argon atmosphere and then quenched in water. Condition: Annealed

Processing Text: HEA ingots with a nominal composition of Al 0.5 Cr 0.9 FeNi 2.5 V 0.2 were melted in a vacuum electromagnetic induction furnace, and the ingots were remelted at least eight times to ensure compositional homogeneity. To reduce micro-segregation during the casting process, the samples were heated slowly to 1150 °C, held at this temperature for 24 h, and then water-quenched to room temperature. The samples were finally aged at 700 °C for 1 h, followed by furnace cooling. Plates with dimensions of 100 (length) × 20 (width) × 1 (thickness) mm³ were cut from the samples for remelting experiment. A fibre laser (FF-M180 machine, Fastfotm) was used to fulfill the remelting experiment. The direct spacing of each remelted track in the lamellar-structured samples was 750 µm. Processing Text: The experiments were conducted using SS316L as both the powder bed material and the substrate material. The powder particles had a size distribution of 15-53 µm. In the first stage, nine cubic samples with dimensions of 10 mm x 6 mm x 5 mm were fabricated using the L-PBF process with processing conditions specified in Table 2. In the second stage, half of the top surface of each sample was polished using the LR parameters specified in Table 3. The L-PBF and LR experiments were performed using a Tong-Tai AM-160 machine, which is equipped with Ytterbium Fiber Laser YLR-1070 (wavelength 1070 nm) in a chamber filled with nitrogen and an oxygen concentration lower than 2000 ppm. For each as-built samples shown in Fig. 8, the top surface topology was measured using a confocal laser-scanning microscope (as shown in Fig. 13). and the corresponding values of Sa was determined as shown in Fig. 14. The feasibility of the proposed L-PBF+LR method is experimentally demonstrated using SS316L powder as the feedstock material. Tensile test specimens fabricated using the optimal processing conditions show an overall tensile strength of 550 ±7.8 MPa and an overall yield strength of 420 ±5.9 MPa. Compared to a conventional L-PBF process performed with a layer thickness of 30 µm, the mechanical properties of the optimal printed specimens are improved by 96 %, while the fabrication time is reduced by approximately 48 %. Tensile test specimens with the configuration and dimensions shown in Fig. 10 were fabricated using the L-PBF and in-situ LR process to investigate the effect of the re-melting process on improving the mechanical properties of the built parts. Tensile testing was performed at room temperature on an HT-2420 system at a displacement speed of 1 mm/min. In this study, the main purpose of density measurement is to observe the relationship between the SR and density of the L-PBF processed part. Thus, for each cubic samples, the average SR of each sample was measured, and the samples were then cut into two separate specimens to determine the density. In accordance with the procedure described in [55], polished cross-sectional images with different SR values were acquired using an optical microscope. The topology of the top surface of each specimen was measured after both the L-PBF construction process and the LR operation using a confocal laser-scanning microscope (KEYENCE VK-200) at 10-x magnification. The values of Sa and Sq, i.e., the arithmetical mean height and root mean square height, respectively, were computed from the measured surface profiles using MATLAB software. The autocorrelation function showing the spectral relationship between the surface height and the separation distance between surface points was also extracted from the SR profile. The correlation length, Cl, was determined as the point at which the autocorrelation function declined to 1/e [41]. The accuracy of the CFD model was verified by comparing the simulated depth of the melt pool ( Fig. 11) for three combinations of the L-PBF parameters with the results reported in [56]. The corresponding results are presented in Table 4 and Fig. 12. The reliability of the trained ANN model was evaluated by conducting a regression analysis of the ANN predictions for the melt pool depth and the SR results obtained by the CFD model. Note that the initial surface roughness was assumed to be 12 μm in both cases. The melt pool depth results presented in Fig. 19 indicate that the RSME has a value of 0.695. In order to examine the relationship between the SR and density of the built parts, a series of L-PBF experiments were conducted using different printing parameters to fabricate cubic parts with a size of 10 mm x 10 mm x T x No, as indicated in Table 5. After completing the printing process, the SR of each part was observed and the density value was calculated. In the present study, the mechanical properties and manufacturing efficiency were evaluated for three different printing strategies: LPBF30 (powder layer thickness of 30 µm); LPBF60 (powder layer thickness of 60 µm), and LPBF+LR60 (powder layer thickness of 60 µm and LR processing). Fig. 32 shows the arrangement of the different samples on the build table. Table 6 lists the L-PBF and LR parameters used for the different sample types. Finally, when the L-PBF and in-situ LR experiment finished, the tensile parts were conducted mechanical tests. Tensile strength was examined and compared between parts produced through L-PBF and in-situ LR and conventional L-PBF process. The mechanical properties of the samples fabricated using the different L-PBF and LR methods were evaluated through tensile testing. The results obtained for the yield strength, ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and elongation of the various samples are shown in Fig. 33. Fig. 34 shows the stress-strain curves for different methods namely LPBF60, LPBF30, LPBF+LR60 and EOS60. Note that the results for an EOS60 (powder layer thickness of 60 µm) standard components given in literature [62] are also shown for comparison purposes. The results have shown that the specimens fabricated using the LR method have an overall tensile strength of 550 MPa and an overall yield strength of 420 MPa. The corresponding standard deviation values are less than 7.8 and 5.9 MPa, respectively. These values are close to those of the optimal LPBF30 sample with no LR, that is, 564 ± 3.5 MPa and 425 ± 18.5 MPa, respectively. The elongation value of the LPBF+LR60 sample is greater (27 %) than that of the L-PBF60 and EOS60 samples. Processing Text: The MEA ingot with a nominal composition of Ni 46Co 23Cr 23Al 2Ti 2Nb 4(at.%) was fabricated by arc melting in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was inverted and remelted five times before being cast into the copper mold with dimensions of 150 mm × 50 mm × 12 mm. The plate-shaped ingot was first homogenized at 1473 K for 5 h and then hot rolled at 1373 K to reduce its thickness to 7 mm. Subsequently, the hot-rolled sheet was annealed at 1373 K for 10 min and then cold rolled (CR) at room temperature to achieve a further 50 % thickness reduction. The cold-rolled sheet was annealed at 1423 K for 10 min for recrystallization, followed by annealing at 923 K for 24, 96, and 192 h to introduce the nanoprecipitates and modulate their precipitation behaviors (size, distribution, and volume fraction). The CRS samples are subjected to aging treatment at 923 K for 24, 96, and 192 h. A dual heterostructure, comprising of heterogeneous grain structure with heterogeneous distribution of the micro-scale Nb-rich Laves phases, is introduced in a CrCoNi-based MEA through thermo-mechanical processing. Additionally, a high-density nano-coherent γ' phase is introduced within the grains through isothermal aging treatments. The microscale plastic deformation inhomogeneity occurring during hot rolling induces varying defect densities in the fcc matrix, thereby initiating the heterogeneous nucleation and growth of the Laves phase. The resultant heterogeneously distributed Laves phase generates differing grain boundary migration resistance, facilitating the development of heterogeneous grain structures during solid solution treatment. Subsequently, isothermal aging at 923 K for 24 h introduces a high-density coherent γ' phase into the fcc matrix. With increasing aging time to 96 h and 192 h, a brittle η phase is formed at grain boundaries. Room temperature; Dual heterostructure with high-density γ' phase; Optimal mechanical properties

The alloy compositions involved in this study are shown in Table 1, and all the as-cast alloys used were fabricated through a vacuum arc furnace with a high purity argon atmosphere. To chemically homogenize and reduce elemental segregation of the as-cast alloy, the ingots were solution-annealed for 4 h at 1000 °C followed by quenching in water. Processing Text: In-situ titanium boride (TiB) reinforced titanium matrix composites (TMCs) were fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) technique. The Ti6Al4V alloy powders were mechanically mixed with 0.5 wt% and 1 wt% TiB 2nanoparticles, respectively, using a three-dimensional mixer (JXHY-2L). The mixing process included a speed of 80 rpm/min and a duration of 4 h. To avoid the adverse effect of energy on the properties of the alloy powders during the mechanical mixing process, the machine was paused for cooling at room temperature for 10 min after every 20 min of mixing, ensuring mixed uniformly. The process parameters for fabricating samples with Ti6Al4V powders and 0.5 wt% TiB 2/Ti6Al4V powders, respectively, were as follows: a laser power of 180 W, a scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, a hatching spacing of 120 μm, and a layer thickness of 30 μm; additionally, a short linear scanning strategy was implemented with an interlayer rotation angle of 67°. To alleviate residual stress accumulation during processing, the substrate was preheated to 180 °C. In comparison to Ti6Al4V, TiB 2exhibits a higher melting point and enhanced laser absorption characteristics, necessitating increased laser energy densities when fabricating samples with elevated TiB 2content. Consequently, when the TiB 2addition reached 1 wt%, adjustments to the process parameters were made: specifically, increasing the laser power to 200 W while reducing the scanning speed to 800 mm/s and modifying the hatching spacing to 100 μm. Prior to processing, the powders underwent drying in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 8 h; high-purity argon gas was introduced to maintain oxygen levels below 100 ppm to prevent oxidation within the melt pool. The substrate employed in this study is a Q235 steel plate measuring 70 mm × 70 mm × 30 mm. One is spherical 316 L stainless steel powder, with a particle size ranging from 50 μm to 150 μm. The chemical composition of the 316 L stainless steel powder is provided in Table 1. The mixed powder was subsequently placed in a vacuum drying oven and preheated at 150 °C for 2 h to remove moisture and enhance flowability. The powder was then deposited as desired coating using a self-built LDED equipment equipped with a laser of 4 KW and 1060 nm wavelength (Raycus RFL-C4000). The LDED technology utilizes a coaxial powder feeding method to ensure the stability of coating properties. The optimal parameters were identified as a laser power of 1700 W, a scanning speed of 10 mm/s, a spot diameter of 4 mm, a powder feed rate of 1.2 r/min, and an overlap ratio of 50 %. With these optimized parameters, the 316 L composite coating was fabricated via multi-layer, multi-track laser processing, yielding a well-formed surface. After completing the coating process, the uneven top surface of the coating was removed using an electrical discharge wire cutting, and then cut into samples measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm and 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm for subsequent tests. The metallographic samples were sequentially ground with SiC sandpaper with grades from 240# to 2000#, followed by polishing with 2.5μm diamond polishing paste. Aqua regia (HCl:HNO 3=3:1 V:V) was employed to etch the sample surface for 10-15 s, followed by ultrasonic cleaning with alcohol. The polarization test samples were mechanically polished and subsequently ultrasonically cleaned with alcohol to remove any residual polishing paste and surface impurities. Processing Text: A room-temperature strength-ductility matching Ti2AlNb intermetallic was successfully prepared with hot-pressing sintering and following by a single-step solution heat-treatment in O + B2 dual-phase region. As-sintered Ti2AlNb intermetallic mainly contained the O phase and a little of B2 and α2 phases, showing brittle characteristics. A solution treatment at 950℃ for 2 h and then water quenching was conducted. The brittle α2 at the grain boundaries transformed into O phase and the O phase dissolved into the soft B2 phase partially, resulting in a much higher increase in elongation with 10.4 % and its yield strength still remained at 867.3 MPa compared with the sintered ones. Along with the EBSD analysis, this strength-ductility matching mechanism was mainly attributed to the decrease of the brittle hexagonal α2 and orthorhombic O phase, and the increase of the soft cubic B2 phase. The spherical Ti2AlNb pre-alloyed powder (Particle size: 75-125 μm) with a nominal composition of Ti-22Al-25Nb (at%) fabricated by plasma rotating electrode process, and purchased form Xi'an Sailong Additive Technology Co., Ltd. The pre-alloyed powder was filled into high-strength graphite molds and then uniaxially hot pressed for 2 h at 1300℃ and 35 MPa under vacuum condition of 10 -2Pa, followed by furnace cooling to fabricate Ti2AlNb alloy billet. The HT samples were obtained by solution treatment at 950℃ for 2 h followed by water quenching. The phase constitution in the pre-alloyed powder and sintered alloy were analyzed using the X-ray diffraction (XRD, X’PERT) with a Cu-Kα radiation. The room-temperature tensile properties were tested on an electro-mechanical universal testing machines (AGXplus) with a speed of 0.5 mm/min and an electronic extensometer was used to measure the strain. Sample type: HP (hot pressing sintered)

Processing Text: Specimens with cylindrical shapes measuring 40 mm in diameter and 60 mm in height underwent carburization in an Aichelin carburizing furnace. The bottom face of the cylindrical specimens was carburized. In contrast, the other surfaces were treated to prevent carburization. A droplet carburizing atmosphere activated by methanol and isopropyl alcohol was used, and methanol and isopropyl alcohol were added successively during the carburizing heating process. The specimens were subjected to intensive carburizing treatment at 900 °C. Subsequently, diffusion carburization at 900 °C for 2 h was performed, followed by austenitization at 830 °C, quenching in oil, and tempering at 180 °C for 15 h. Then the carburized specimen was strengthened by USRP. USRP tests were carried out on carburized specimens under different static pressures (200, 300, and 400 N). The ultrasonic rolling ball was a silicon nitride (Si3N4) ceramic ball with a diameter of 8 mm and a hardness of 1500 HV. The rolling surface with static pressure of 500 N presented quality defects, poor surface morphology, and uneven surface processing. Because of the rolled-surface quality problem, the surface did not meet the expected smoothness and consistency standards. On the basis of these parameters, the effects of 200, 300, and 400 N static pressures on surface integrity and corrosion resistance were the primary focus of this study. Initially, the specimens were ground, polished, and chemically etched with a 4 % nitrate alcohol solution, then observation of the microstructure was conducted using optical microscopy (VHX-2000E, Keyence) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM; ZEISS Auriga). In addition, for a deeper examination of the specimens' microstructure, the specimens were observed by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD; Thermo Scientific/Helios G4 CX). The EBSD analysis was conducted at a voltage of 20 kV. Before the EDS experiment, the specimen was soaked in alcohol and placed in ultrasonic cleaning equipment for cleaning. Specimen: Combined-200 N

The study is carried out on a cold-rolled 304 stainless steel sheet. For the bulging simulations and experiments, a 304 stainless steel cold-rolled sheet with a nominal thickness of 0.80 mm and an out diameter of 200 mm is used. The uniaxial tension specimens are designed and processed in accordance with the GB/T 228.1-2021 standard. Mechanical properties are tested at angles of 0 °, 45 °, and 90 ° with respect to RD. In uniaxial tension tests, the strain is measured synchronously by GOM-ARAMIS at a strain rate of 0.01 /s. Using the plastic strain data from these uniaxial tension tests, the Lankford coefficient and the degree of in-plane anisotropy are calculated based on the GB/T 5027-2016 standard. In this model: the sheet metal is configured as a deformable shell, discretized into four-node curved shell elements (S4R) with dimensions of 1 mm × 1 mm, and the Hill48 yield criterion is employed to define the anisotropy of the sheet metal. The dies used in the experiment are identical to those in the simulation, with all dies having a radius fillet of 5 mm at the cavity entrance. The radius value is set according to ISO 16,808-2022. Consistent with the uniaxial tension test, the strain rate of the feature points in the bulging area is designed to be around 0.01/s in the bulging test. The pressure loading curve is pre-set to the hydraulic station with a linear increase of 0.5 MPa/s, and then gradually reduces in slope until it reaches the burst pressure. Angle: 0°

The austenitic steel in this study has a composition of 16 %Ni-8 %Mn-4 %Al-1 %C-Fe (in wt. %). The casted steel is hot-rolled above 1000 °C to produce strips with a thickness of 5 mm. Afterward, the hot-rolled strip is cold-rolled (CR) at room temperature down to 1.5 mm thick, labeled as CR steels. The first strip is annealed at 650 °C for 60 mins, referred to as the An sample. The second strip is put into an 850 °C furnace for 3 mins for partial recrystallization, referred to as the PRex sample. Some 650 °C-annealed samples are further heated at the 850 °C furnace for 3 mins, labeled as the An-PRex sample. For the tensile tests, dog-bone samples with a gauge dimension of 12 mm×4 mm×1.5 mm are cut from the heat-treated plates along the rolling direction. The quasi-static tensile tests are performed using an MTS810 machine at a quasi-static strain rate of 0.001/s under ambient temperature, with the strain measured by a 10 mm extensometer. For microstructure characterization, samples are ground with sandpapers to achieve mirror-like conditions and then electropolished using a mixture containing 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % glacial acetic acid. The polished samples are examined using a Zeiss Sigma 300 scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with an Oxford electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. Microscale digital image correlation (μ-DIC) characterization during tensile tests is performed on a Kammrath & Weiss in-situ tensile stage. Nanoindentation tests are performed within the SEM facility using a Hysitron PI-88 PicoIndenter under displacement-control mode, with a maximum force of 2 mN. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) samples are prepared by site-specific lift-out method with Thermo Scientific Helios 5 CX dual-beam focus ion beam (FIB). The TEM and electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) characterization are performed using a Thermo Fisher scientific Talos F200X STEM at 200 kV and an aberration-corrected Themis ETEM at 300 kV. The prepared TEM samples are also used for transmission-EBSD (T-EBSD) characterization with a voltage of 30 kV and a step size of 10 nm, using the same SEM and EBSD facilities. For atom probe tomography (APT), needled-shaped samples are prepared by FIB, and the measurements are performed using a local electrode atom probe (Cameca LEAP 6000XR) at 50 K in laser mode with 25 pJ pulse energy and 200 kHz pulse rate. Synchrotron-based X-ray diffraction (Sync-XRD) measurements with an energy of 22.7 keV are performed at the BL02U2 surface diffraction beamline of the Shanghai synchrotron radiation facility (SSRF). Processing Text: W/AlSi10Mg composite powders were prepared using a solvent-assisted dispersion method, followed by low-energy ball milling and drying processes. The procedure entailed dispersing W nanoparticles (average size ∼500 nm, 272 g, 6.4 wt%) onto the surface of spherical AlSi10Mg powders (average size ∼32 μm, 4 kg, 93.6 wt%) in an ethanol medium. Following this, low-energy ball milling was performed for 4 hours at 150 rpm, with a ball-to-powder ratio of 1:1. The composite powders were dried at 80°C and then sieved through a 200-mesh screen. W/AlSi10Mg composite samples were fabricated using an SLM 280 HL machine (SLM Solutions GmbH, Germany). This equipment, equipped with dual fiber lasers with a maximum power of 400 W and a spot diameter of 80 μm, enables high-precision and high-performance metal 3D printing. The forming chamber was evacuated and filled with high-purity argon, maintaining the oxygen content below 100 ppm to prevent material oxidation during fabrication. The substrate was preheated to 150°C to mitigate residual stress and deformation caused by rapid heating-cooling cycles. Considering surface quality, densification, and production efficiency, the following process parameters were determined: powder layer thickness (t) of 30 μm, hatch spacing (h) of 80 μm, and laser power (P) of 300 W. To investigate the influence of laser scanning speed on the microstructure and properties of the composites, three representative scanning speeds (v) were selected: 1800 mm/s, 2200 mm/s, and 2600 mm/s. A stripe scanning strategy was employed, with adjacent layers rotated 67° to improve the anisotropy of the fabricated parts. Based on these parameters, the volumetric energy density (Ev) was calculated using the equation Ev = P/(v·h·t). The calculated Ev values were 69.4 J/mm³, 56.8 J/mm³, and 48.0 J/mm³ for the three scanning speeds of 1800 mm/s, 2200 mm/s, and 2600 mm/s, respectively. Samples included standard tensile specimens for mechanical testing and 8 × 8 × 8 mm³ cubes for microstructural analysis. Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) provides an innovative solution for the additive manufacturing of Al-Zn-Mg-Cu alloys and composites with poor printability due to their high hot crack sensitivity. The fine grains exhibit excellent stability during heat treatment due to the pinning effect of dispersed TiB2 particles. After heat treatment, these non-uniform features can be eliminated, and the η-Mg(Zn,Cu,Al)2 precipitates dissolve into matrix. Numerous homogenous nano-sized precipitates (∼4.8 nm, GPII zone and η’ phase) form at grain interior, and the interface precipitates (η-Mg(Zn1.5Cu0.5)) form at the interface between TiB2 particle and Al matrix. In addition, the heat-treated composite achieves uniform mechanical properties across different height positions, with a hardness of 219 HV, tensile strength of 644-650 MPa, and ductility of 13-14.6 %. During AFSD, the material is deposited layer by layer at high temperature and high strain rate through severe plastic deformation. Unlike fusion-based AM, no solidification-related defects are generated because feedstock is performed in the solid state without re-melt process. Based on this thermomechanical processing nature, the alloys fabricated by AFSD show fine, equiaxed microstructure due to dynamic recrystallization, thereby behaving the enhanced mechanical properties. The feedstocks (3.5 wt% TiB₂/7055 composite) were fabricated by two steps, including the preparation of the as-cast composite by the in-situ mixed salt method and hot extrusion. Step 1: the pre-weighted mixture salts of KBF4 and K2TiF6 were added into Al melt to fabricate in-situ TiB2 reinforced Al composite ingot (master composite). Subsequently, pure Zn, pure Mg, and Al-50Cu master alloy were added into the re-melted master composite to fabricate as-cast composites. Step 2: the as-cast composites were homogenized at 470 °C for 24 h, followed by air cooling to room temperature. The as-homogenized specimens were extruded at 420 ℃ to rods (diameter: 20 mm) with an extrusion ratio of 30:1 and extrusion speed of 0.5 mm/s. The actual composition of the feedstock rods was measured by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission analysis as 8.23 wt% Zn, 2.10 wt% Mg, 2.33 wt% Cu, 3.60 wt% TiB2 (∼2 vol%) with balanced Al. The AFSD process was carried out by the solid-state friction-based deposition equipment which was developed by Tianjin University. The feedstock was softened by the friction heat generated between the feedstock and the surface of the substrate, and then deposited onto the substrate by moving the shoulder. Here, a multilayer deposit (25 layers) was prepared under the suitable parameters of stirring head, i.e. the rotation speed of 300 r/min and traverse speed of 100 mm/min. The preset layer thickness and deposition length were 2 mm and 250 mm, respectively. Additionally, the rods were added individually when preparing the final 25-layers deposit. The as-deposited composite (named as AD composite) was subjected to solution treatment at 477 ℃ for 1 h, followed by water quenching, and then aged at 120 ℃ for 24 h to achieve T6 heat treatment state (named as HT composite). Processing Text: Samples were cut into cylindrical shapes with dimensions of (Φ) 5 mm × 6.8 mm from cast ingot solidified under normal pressure. Subsequently, the samples were wrapped in an insulating layer and a graphite tube. The pressure device of the LPR1000 2-6-8 multi-stage high-pressure apparatus consists of an axially cylindrical pressure chamber, resembling to a piston-cylinder system. Pressure is applied to the octahedral talc sample assembly through primary and secondary pressure transmission modules, driven by the press. Graphite is used as the heating element, and the heating temperature is controlled by adjusting the heating power. The sample was heated to 1550 °C under an external pressure of 6 GPa for 60 minutes, after which the heating device was turned off and the pressure was released to atmospheric levels. The SSS and HPS alloys were subsequently aged at 400°C, 450°C, and 500°C in an argon atmosphere for varying durations up to 10 hours. The samples were ground using SiC paper and polished with diamond suspension. A solution with the composition of FeCl 3(2 g), HCl (3 ml), and C 2H 5OH (100 ml) was used as the etchant. The microstructure was observed using a HITACHI SU50000 field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) and an FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). Image Pro Plus 6.0 software was used to measure the area fraction and size of various precipitates based on TEM images. The foil thickness in the beam direction was determined by measuring the spacing of Kossel-Mollenstedt fringes in a {111} αreflection in a < 011 > αtwo-beam convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) pattern. X-ray diffraction (XRD, X’PERT X-ray, Holland) with diffraction angle (2θ) ranging from 30° to 100° and a scanning speed of approximately 1°/min was utilized to determine the crystal structure of the alloys. The DC conductivity measurement at room temperature (300 K) was conducted using the traditional four-probe technique. The samples measured are approximately 3 mm in length, 1 mm in width, and 0.3 mm in thickness. Four platinum wires were affixed to the samples using conductive silver paste. The DC resistance of the samples was initially measured using a physical property measuring system (PPMS, Dynacool-14T, USA) and subsequently converted to DC conductivity. Vickers hardness testing of the specimens was performed using a Huayin HV-1000A microhardness tester with a load of 200 g and an indentation time of 15 seconds. The reported hardness values represent the average of eight separate measurements. The compression test was conducted using a SANS CMT6000 universal testing machine with a compression speed of 0.5 mm/min. The compression specimen measured are 2 mm in diameter and 3 mm in length. At least three measurements were taken for each sample to minimize experimental errors. Peak aging state; Aged at 450 °C

The examined material is 6061-T4 aluminum alloy, which is employed in the fabrication of battery enclosures for electric vehicles due to its outstanding combination of both strength and weight. The 6061-T4 alloy’s chemical composition is shown in Table 1. The common heat treatment procedure entails solutionizing for one hour at 530 ∘C, followed by aging and water quenching at room temperature [22]. This treatment dissolves alloying elements, such as Mg and Si, into a supersaturated solid solution, which subsequently promotes the formation of fine precipitates, such as Mg 2Si, during aging. These precipitates play a critical role in enhancing the alloy’s strength and mechanical properties. The first type is 76 mm × 19 mm × 3 mm samples, which are cut with a water-cooled abrasive cutter and ground with SiC paper of 1200 grit to an average roughness of 5.39 μm. The second type is 10 mm × 5 mm × 3 mm samples, which are cut using wire electrical discharge machining and polished to a mirror finish using an electrochemical polisher. These samples are used for microstructure characterization and microhardness testing. The third type is 20 mm × 20 mm × 3 mm samples, which are cut with a water-cooled abrasive cutter and ground with 1200 grit SiC paper to an average roughness of 5.39 μm, used for surface roughness and residual stress measurements. Samples are ultrasonically cleaned in denatured alcohol for 10 min before UNP treatment to eliminate surface contaminants including dust and grease. Ultra-high bonding double-sided tapes placed on the edges of the samples provide strong adhesion on the robot work table. To provide sufficient UNP energy, the peening device remains perpendicular to the surface of the sample. The ultrasonic generator power is set at efficiencies of 50 % and 100 %, corresponding to vibration amplitudes of 21 μm and 35 μm, measured via laser Doppler vibrometer (brand: Sunny Optical Technology). These amplitudes are selected to provide significant peening intensities that can be exploited to form and strengthen metallic components in the automotive industry. In addition, such vibration amplitudes can induce the desired level of plastic deformation, ensuring surface strengthening while preventing excessive damage or cracking at higher amplitudes. Additional manipulated variables that are fixed during the UNP process include the air pressure (0.5 MPa) and the standoff distance (2 mm) between the needle tips and the sample surface [19]. In addition, 16 translational UNP passes both forward and backward are executed by the end effector over the sample with a 50 mm/s robot travel velocity to ensure that the sample gets sufficient penetration energy. Before performing the test, the samples are polished using a motorized polisher (brand: Struers Tegramin-25) deploying grit papers of several grades until only a few indents remain to test the highly deformed surface layer. 100 gf of load and a 10-s dwell time are used for the test. Five indentation spots have been taken at various positions on the specimen surface for every test sample, with a distance of 500 μm between neighboring indents. Furthermore, 10 indentation spots are carried out at various points throughout the sample cross-section, following the recommendation of previous studies [24], with a 50 μm distance between two neighboring indents. According to ASTM International, tensile tests have been conducted on three type-1 samples in a longitudinal direction using an electronic universal material testing machine (brand: Zwick/Roll Z100) to evaluate their mechanical properties. For samples that exhibited bending after the robotic ultrasonic multi-needle peening process, we carefully flattened them before tensile testing to ensure accurate measurement of their mechanical properties. This approach is consistent with established practices for testing materials like Almen strips post-peening, where flattening procedures are employed to minimize the influence of residual stress-induced curvature on the tensile results [24,27]. The residual stress profiles of the UNP-0, UNP-1, and UNP-2 samples have been investigated using the incremental hole drilling strain gauge method. According to ASTM International [25], the SINT MTS3000 measurement system is used for all measurements. To eliminate distortion and edge effects and produce more accurate and reliable data, residual stresses are measured in the center of the samples rather than on their edges. The arc heights of the UNP-1 and UNP-2 samples have been quantitatively determined by employing an electronic indicator with a resolution of 0.002 mm. To ensure the stability and repeatability of the procedure, three iterations are taken into account for each of the samples. To compensate for initial arc heights, measurements are taken at three positions on each sample: the center and two adjacent points, both before and after the UNP process. Processing Text: Ingots were meticulously crafted with a precise nominal composition of (FeCoNi)86-Al7Ti7 through the process of arc melting. This involved blending constituent elements of exceptional purity exceeding 99.9 % mass, within a meticulously controlled Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. Each ingot underwent no less than five times of melting to guarantee the utmost chemical homogeneity. Subsequently, the molten alloy ingot was cast into a copper mold, precisely crafted to dimensions of 60 mm × 15 mm × 3 mm. To ensure the accuracy of collected data, grinding and polishing, approximately 2 mm in depth, were carried out on the surrounding area of the characterization sample. The resulting as-cast sheet then underwent a homogenization process at 1150 °C for approximately 2 h, followed by a water quenching process. This was followed by cold rolling, reducing the thickness by approximately 65 %. The cold-rolled thin sheet was then subjected to a recrystallization process, achieved by heating at 1150 °C for approximately 1.5 min. Subsequent to this recrystallization, the samples were meticulously subjected to a 4-hour aging treatment, also followed by a water-quenched process, at a series of temperatures of 580 °C, 650 °C, 690 °C, 720 °C, 780 °C, and 820 °C. Processing Text: Samples of the (CoNiV) 97Al 3MEA were prepared with high-purity (> 99.99 at%) Co, Ni, V, and Al in a vacuum smelting furnace (argon enclosure). To obtain a homogeneous alloy, the ingot needed to be turned over and remelted four times, and then a strip alloy ingot with dimensions of 70 mm × 30 mm × 10 mm was prepared by casting and molding. The melted alloy ingot was encapsulated in a quartz tube protected by argon gas and homogenized at 1200°C for 24 h. Then, the as-cast alloy ingot was polished with sandpaper to remove the surface oxidized skin and a small amount of impurities. In this study, two novel Co-free medium entropy alloys (MEAs) with compositions of Cu20Cr10Fe35Ni35 (Cu20) and Cu10Cr20Fe35Ni35 (Cu10) were successfully prepared by a combination of mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). High-purity (>99 %) Cu, Cr, Fe, and Ni powders (purchased from Kojundo Chemical Lab. Co., Ltd., Saitama, Japan) were used as the starting materials, and their average particle sizes were 75 μm, 63 μm, 4 μm, and 3 μm, respectively. The alloy powders with nominal atomic ratios of Cu20Cr10Fe35Ni35 and Cu10Cr20Fe35Ni35 (hereinafter denoted as Cu20 and Cu10, respectively) were synthesized by MA under an argon atmosphere using a high-energy ball milling device (Zoz Simoloyer CMJ-02SS) equipped with a water-cooling system. Cr-steel balls with chemical compositions of 0.95-1.1 wt% C, 1.3-1.6 wt% Cr, 0.15-0.35 wt% Si, <0.5 wt% Mn, <0.025 wt% P, and <0.025 wt% S (JIS SUJ-2) were used as the milling media, and the ball to powder weight ratio was 15:1. The milling operations were carried out at optimized cycles of 1200 rpm and 700 rpm for 6 h with time intervals of 45 s and 15 s, respectively. The progress of milling was monitored by taking out a small amount of powder every 1 h and examining it using XRD analysis. The 6 h-MAed powder was consolidated by SPS in a graphite die at 1000 °C for 10 min under uniaxial pressure of 30 MPa in vacuum. Processing Text: Bulk samples of HEA matrix-MXene composites were prepared by spark plasma sintering (SPS) using a mixture of CrMnFeCoNi HEA powder that contained 2 wt%, 4 wt%, 6 wt%, 10 wt% of MXene phase. The microstructure evolution, phase structure, and compressive mechanical properties of the samples were investigated at room temperature. The fractions of the MXene phase played important roles in the nanostructural evolution and grain refinement of the HEA-MXene composites. The densities of SPS-processed (SPS-ed) CoCrFeMnNi-MXene composites were measured using the Archimedes method. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was used to characterize the phase and crystal structure of both the powder and bulked HEAs-MXene composites. The microstructure of the CoCrFeMnNi-MXene composites was characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), backscattered diffraction (EBSD) system attached to the field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The mechanical properties of the HEAs were evaluated using compression tests at an initial strain rate of 10−3, and the hardness of the gas-atomized and bulk samples was measured using a Vickers micro-hardness test with a load of 1000 g and a holding time of 10 seconds. The tribological characteristics of the SPS-ed CoCrFeMnNi-MXene composites were conducted at ambient conditions on a ball-on-disc tribometer. MXene content: 10 wt%; Condition: room temperature; Microstructure: FCC and HCP phases

Processing Text: In this study, hierarchical heterostructures were introduced into CoCrFeMnNi HEA via an in-situ rolling (ISR) assisted laser cladding (LC) process. The coating was fabricated by overlapping individual tracks with a 30 % overlapping ratio. Following the preliminary testing, the distance D between the laser head and the roller was set to 13 mm. In this work, static pressures of 0 N, 1000 N, 2000 N, 3000 N, and 4000 N were applied, and the corresponding coatings were referred as un-ISR, ISR1, ISR2, ISR3 and ISR4, respectively. Annealed 45 steel with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm was chosen as the substrate. To minimize the interference of oxides and other impurities, an angle grinder was used to remove the oxide layer from the substrate surface, followed by cleaning with anhydrous ethanol. The powder used in this study was CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder with a particle size range of 45-105 μm, produced by high-temperature gas atomization. Before the experiment, place the powder in a vacuum drying oven (Shanghai Jiecheng Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd., DZF-6050) and dry it at 100 °C for 2 h to ensure its uniformity and fluidity. The coating was prepared by using a semiconductor laser (HWL-1500) with a wavelength range of 910-1050 nm and a DPSF scraper powder feeder to transport CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy powder coaxially. Laser spot diameter 2 mm, laser power 1500 W, scanning rate 3 mm/s, powder feed 7 g/min, overlapping ratio 30 %. High purity argon is used as melt pool shielding gas with a flow rate of 3 L / min. The prepared coating was cut into cuboid specimens with dimensions of 15 × 15 × 10 mm 3using a high-speed wire electrical discharge machining machine tool (Fangzheng CNC Machine Tool Co., Ltd., DK7720). The specimens were then hot - mounted using a metallographic specimen mounting machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., XQ-2B). Subsequently, the cross - section of the specimen was ground using SiC sandpapers of grit sizes 60 mesh, 400 mesh, 800 mesh, 1500 mesh, and 2000 mesh in a wet - grinding manner on a metallographic specimen grinding and polishing machine (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., MP-2B). After grinding, the specimens were polished with diamond polishing paste until no obvious scratches were visible under an optical microscope. The specimens were placed in anhydrous ethanol and cleaned in an ultrasonic cleaner for 5 min. To prepare the surfaces for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis, the specimen was pre-ground and polished using the metallographic pre-grinding machine (Hua Xing Test Instrument Co., Ltd.). The surface was then ion-polished with a precision ion thinning instrument (GATAN PIPS II 695) to remove the damage layer caused by mechanical polishing. The microhardness was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (Laizhou Hengyi Test Instrument Co., Ltd., NVM-1000 A). The load was set at 0.3 kg, and the dwell time was 15 s. Each value was measured three times to ensure accuracy. The tribological properties of the coatings at room temperature (25 °C) were evaluated by a ball-on-disk wear tester (Lanzhou Zhongke Kaihua Science and Technology Development Co., Ltd., HT-1000) with a Si 3N 4ball as the counterpart. The tests, performed under dry sliding conditions in accordance with the ASTM G99-17 standard, were repeated three times. The test parameters included a loading force of 10 N, a friction radius of 3 mm, a rotation speed of 600 r/min, and a wear time of 30 min. Condition: room temperature (RT)

Processing Text: Alloys were prepared through cold crucible induction melting using high-purity elements. Ingots with masses between 300 and 2500 g have been first cast. Subsequently, a portion of each ingot was remelted under a nitriding atmosphere with controlled pressure and time to promote nitrogen absorption in the liquid alloy. In the case of the Y3 matrix, various nitrogen contents were introduced (ranging from 0.1 to 0.3 wt% N) by adjusting the time under the nitriding atmosphere. After casting, the ingots were homogenized at 1200 ∘C during 2 h and then hot forged at approximately 1000 ∘C to produce 14 mm diameter bars. Forged bars were annealed at 1100 ∘C during 90 min followed by air cooling to produce the reference state of the materials. For Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) observations and Energy-Dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) analyses, all the samples were ground with SiC papers down to 1200 grade. Final preparation was made by electropolishing (6 % HCl in ethanol, at 10-12 ∘C, at 25 V during 30 s). Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) samples were prepared from discs of around 100 μm in thickness and 3 mm of diameter, twin-jet electropolished with a Struers TENUPOL-5. The electrolyte is composed of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol cooled to − 4 ∘C while the voltage is set between 17 and 20 V. Nitrogen content: 0 wt%

Hastelloy X was additively manufactured using the LPBF technique, forming a vertical rod measuring 120 mm in length and 22 mm in diameter. The as-built material was stress-relieved at 1050°C for 1 h. Subsequent to stress relief, the material was subjected to heat treatment at two distinct temperatures isothermally, i.e., 800 °C and 950 °C, for the duration of 500 h. The specimen subjected to 800 °C for 500 h will be referred to as S1, while the specimen subjected to 950 °C for the same duration will be referred to as S2 hereafter. Micro tensile specimens, with gauge dimensions measuring 6 mm x 2 mm x 1 mm, were precision machined from the additive manufacturing (AM) rod along the build direction (BD) using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Tensile tests were carried out utilizing a universal testing machine (Zwick/Roell Z100) at a strain rate of 10−3s−1 under both ambient temperature (25 °C) and 800 °C conditions. Before each tensile test, the specimen underwent a heating process with a rate of 10 °C/min and was held at 800 °C temperature for 30 min to ensure specimen homogenization using a three-zone furnace. Spherical TC17 powder was prepared using the vacuum plasma rotating electrode atomization method, with a particle size ranging from 45 to 106 μm and a flowability of 19.7 s/50 g. To remove moisture from the powder, it was treated in an electric thermostatic drying oven at 110 °C for 1.5 h. TC17 specimens with dimensions of 60 mm × 50 mm × 12 mm were prepared on a TC4 substrate using an n-shape scanning strategy. The specimens were subjected to vacuum heat treatment in a TL1400 tube furnace. The heat treatment process referenced the heat treatment standard for titanium and titanium alloy parts (GB/T 37584-2019). Due to the limited effect of annealing and solution treatment on the strength-ductility balance, three aging treatments at varying temperatures were conducted after these treatments. The specific heat treatment procedures are shown in Table 3, with all cooling methods being furnace cooling. Samples with dimensions of 15 mm × 15 mm × 8 mm were cut from the specimens for wear testing, while the dimensions for other tests were 6 mm × 6 mm × 8 mm. The phase analysis was conducted using an X-ray diffractometer (D/MAX-2500, Cu target), with the experimental parameters set as follows: 2θ = 10-90°, a step size of 0.02°, and a scanning speed of 1°/min. The polished TC17 samples were chemically etched for 10 s using a mixed solution with a volume ratio of HF, HNO 3, and H 2O of 2:3:40. Measurements were taken every 100 μm under a load of 200 g and a dwell time of 10 s, with 30 points measured for each sample. Dry sliding wear tests were carried out using an MPX-3G pin-disc wear tester, with a 6 mm diameter GGr15 steel ball as the counterface. A normal load of 20 N was applied, the rotational speed was set to 300 r/min, the friction radius was 1.5 mm, and the wear time was 45 min. Annealing at 840 °C and solution treatment at 800 °C promoted the precipitation and growth of lath and plate-like primary α phase (α P), as well as continuous and discontinuous grain boundary α phase (α GB). Aging induced the preferential precipitation of secondary α phase (α S) around the grain boundaries, but it did not fully occupy the PFZ region. As the aging temperature increased, both the α P and α S underwent coarsening. Sample: Deposition

Ti-Ni-Fe multiphase intermetallic with nominal composition Ti 45Ni 50Fe 5 (taken from dashed red circle region in Fig. 1a) in at% was fabricated from pure Ti (99.99 %), Fe (99.99 %), and Ni (99.7 %) via vacuum arc melting (VAM) technique in an argon atmosphere (10−6Torr) using a non-consumable tungsten electrode. The eutectic Fe-B alloy with compositions of Fe-3.8B (wt%) was fabricated in a 10 kg-capacity vacuum induction furnace with the charge materials of pure iron, ferroboron (Fe-18.8 wt% B) and cast as ingots with the dimension of 200 × 150× 40 mm. Substrates of 150 × 100 × 10 mm in size were cut from the ingots via wire-electrode cutting for LR treatment, followed by surface grinding using a grinding machine, cleaned with acetone and dried. A Trumpf TruLaser Cell 7020 (TRUMPF SE + Co. KG, Germany) equipped with a TruDisk 3001 solid state laser was carried out for LR treatment. The specific laser process parameters are listed in Table 1. The interval spacing between the two scans was 1.5 mm, and Argon shielding gas (flow rate of 20 SCFH) was used during the LR process to prevent oxidation. To characterize the architectured nano-lamellar structure, TEM samples were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB) from specimen A3. STEM samples were lifted out using a ultra-high-resolution FIB/SEM system (GAIA3, TESCAN, Czech). The foils were thinned with a 30 kV Ga beam to about 250 nm and then polished at progressively lower voltages to gradually reduce the sample thickness to around 50 nm. Processing Text: The AA 2024 alloy was melted using susceptor-assisted microwave heating, and the molten alloy was then directionally solidified in-situ at five solidification rates (50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 μm/s) under microwave irradiation. The target alloy was exposed to microwave at 900 W for 1200 s with a 300 s stabilization period; duty cycle was adjusted as shown in Table 3. Upon melting, the target alloy gets self-poured in-situ into the preheated mould which is adequately connected to the cooling and withdrawal system. The mould withdrawal system was equipped with a CNC controller to effectively maintain the targeted solidification rate by providing the physical movement to the mould using a stepper motor arrangement. The cooling system was designed to extract heat from the bottom of mould using a water jet at 30 °C. Initially, water jet cooling was applied at the bottom of the mould to induce nucleation, followed by withdrawing the mold from the applicator to the ambient environment at a predetermined rate to facilitate the growth of the nuclei. The phase identification of directionally solidified samples was carried out using an X-ray diffractometer (Model: Smart Lab, Make: Rigaku) diffractometer with Cu-Kα X-radiation at a scan rate of 1° min−1 scanning from 10° to 120°. The hardness of transverse and longitudinal sections was determined using a microhardness tester (Make: Omnitech, Model: MVH-SAuto) using a 50 g load and 10 s of dwell time in accordance with the ASTM E384 standard. Elemental composition was analyzed using the SEM images scanning the EDS point spectra to observe the distribution of alloying elements of various phases within the AA 2024 alloy. The chemical composition and ingredients of different phases were analyzed using multiple characterization techniques. The mechanical properties were determined in terms of hardness and tensile strength. Solidification rate: ∼125 µm/s; Microwave interaction during solidification

A Fe35.4Ni24Cr21Co9Mo2Cu1.6Al3Ti4 multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) reinforced by L12 nanoprecipitates was fabricated with four different grain sizes (∼19, ∼50, ∼127 and ∼361 μm) to optimize mechanical and corrosion properties. In a high purity argon protective atmosphere, the Fe 35.4Ni 24Cr 21Co 9Mo 2Cu 1.6Al 3Ti 4(at%) MPEA ingots were prepared by vacuum induction arc furnace. The purity of each element was ≥ 99.9 wt%, and the ingots were remelted at least 6 times in a water-cooled copper cavity to ensure the uniformity of the chemical composition. Then, the ingots were homogenized at 1180 °C for 8 h in muffle furnace with high purity argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the ingots underwent multiple cold rolling, with a cold rolling reduction of ∼82 % (from a thickness of ∼8.3 mm to ∼1.5 mm). As shown in Fig. S1, the annealed temperature was initially determined based on the phase diagram, followed by preliminary experiments to identify the specific temperature and duration required to achieve the desired grain size. Thus, cold-rolled plates underwent recrystallization annealing at 1180 °C for durations of 60 s, 300 s, and 900 s, respectively, to obtain the MPEA with different grain sizes, and followed by aging at 700 °C for 2 h. Note that following aging, the samples were quenched into water. The resulting three samples were denoted as An60s-Ag2h, An300s-Ag2h, An900s-Ag2h, respectively. Meanwhile, an ingot without cold rolling underwent the identical homogenization and aging treatment, and this sample was named as Ag2h. Grain size: ∼50 μm; Microstructure: L12 nanoprecipitates embedded in the FCC matrix

Processing Text: A dual-phase (DP) Co-free HEA was manufactured by SLM and annealed at 900 °C in this work. Cube samples with a dimension of 10 × 10 × 10 mm, and dog-bone shape samples with a gauge length of 25 mm, width of 5 mm, and thickness of 2 mm, were fabricated under an argon atmosphere using a HANS-M-100 SLM machine (HAN’s Laser, Shenzhen, China). A 500 W fiber laser with a focused beam diameter of 50 μm and a wavelength of 1070 nm was equipped into the SLM machine. The following SLM parameters were used during the SLM process: laser power of 160 W, scanning velocity of 1000 mm/s, interlayer scanning angle of 67°, hatch spacing of 60 μm, and layer thickness of 30 μm, which resulted in the final specimens having a relative density higher than 99 %. Annealing samples were achieved in a SX2-5-12 furnace (LICHEN, Shanghai, China) after heat treatment at 900 °C for 1 h, then cooled in air. Previous research by our team has indicated that the as-printed dual-phase (DP) Co-free HEA Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 demonstrates high yield strength but low elongation [13]. So this work tries to increase the ductility of the SLM-processed dual-phase (DP) Co-free HEA Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 and heat treatment at 900 °C for 1 h was chosen. Thus, annealing at 900 °C for 1 h and then cooling in air was tried in this work. Gas atomization produced pre-alloyed Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 (at%) powder from vacuum induction melted ingots for SLM. The particle size has a characteristic of D50 = 32.7 μm, as shown in Fig. 1(b). In this study, the as-printed dual-phase Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 HEA was annealed at 900 °C for 1 h. During annealing, spinodal decomposition occurred with element redistribution. Processing Text: The Al-4Ni-0.4V-0.2Zr-0.2Ti (ANV-ZT) alloy was prepared from a commercial-purity Al ingot, an Al-10Ni master alloy, an Al-5V master alloy, and Al-5Zr and Al-5Ti master alloys. The alloy was melted in a ZnO-coated clay-graphite crucible in a resistance furnace at a temperature of 800 °C. Argon was used for degassing, and the alloy was allowed to settle for 10 min. The melted alloy was then poured into a permanent mold (cooling rate 7 °C/s) at 750 °C. The permanent mold was preheated to 220 ± 5 °C before the alloy was poured into it. Isochronous and isothermal annealing experiments were conducted on the ANV-ZT alloys. For isochronous annealing, the duration was 8 h, with temperature ranging from 200 to 500 °C, in 50 °C increments. After determining the optimum annealing temperature, isothermal annealing kinetics experiments were performed, varying the holding time from 2 to 120 h. The samples were positioned similarly to those used for microstructure observations. Sample dimensions were 8 × 8 × 8 mm. All annealing was carried out in air, and the samples were cooled in water at 60 °C after annealing. The sampling locations are shown in Fig. 1(a). After casting and annealing, the samples were ground, polished, etched with a 0.5 % HF aqueous solution. Their microstructures were observed using an optical microscope (DMM-580C, Caikon, China). The average grain size of the primary α-Al (as cast) was measured using a lineal intercept image analysis method (ImageJ), with the average calculated from ten visual fields for each sample. The eutectic Al 3Ni phases were observed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Nova Nano SEM 450, FEI, Netherlands), and the intermetallic compounds were analyzed using energy dispersive spectroscopy spectrometer (EDS). The samples were further etched with a 10 % HCl aqueous solution and the three-dimensional morphology of the eutectic Al 3Ni phase was observed using SEM. Multiple fields of view were selected for each sample, and at least 300 rod-like eutectic Al 3Ni phases from different eutectic colonies were measured using ImageJ software to determine the average diameter and spacing of the Al 3Ni phases. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Tecnai G2 F30, FEI, Netherlands) was used to observe the morphology and distribution of the precipitated phases. TEM samples were prepared from the ANV-ZT (isothermal peak annealing) alloy. The sample was initially to 50 μm and then thinned using a double-spray method (TenuPol, Struers, Denmark). The double-spray electrolyte was a nitrate methanol solution, with a voltage of 18-20 V, and a temperature of −25 °C. The microhardness of the alloys was measured under a load of 4.9035 N for 30 s using a Vickers hardness tester (430 SVD; Wilson, USA). Each sample had 10 measurement points selected randomly, and the average hardness value was calculated. Tensile tests were conducted using a universal testing machine (AG-IC/100kN, Shimadzu, Japan) at a loading speed of 1.0 mm/min, with a strain rate of 1.4×10 −6s −1. The positions and sizes of the tensile samples are shown in Fig. 1(b). The elevated-temperature tensile test tests were performed at 350 °C. The samples maintained at this temperature for 10 min before stretching, and the tensile strength and elongation were determined from the average of at least three samples. Condition: annealed at 350 °C for 8 h; Temperature: room temperature
