Processing Text: Heterogeneous lamella structures in m- & n-SiCp/2024Al composites were architected by assembling building blocks with different microstructures via planetary ball milling, mechanically mixing, hot pressing and extrusion, as schematically shown in Fig. 1. 57 wt% 2024Al powders and 3 wt% n-SiCps were first planetary ball milled at a rotational speed of 250 rpm for 6 h to uniformly disperse n-SiCps and refine substructures, by which brittle n-SiCp/2024Al UFG building blocks were obtained. Ball milling was conducted in stainless steel jars filled with Ar at 1 atm atmosphere and Φ6 mm steel balls at a ball to powder ratio of 20:1. 1 wt% stearic acid was also added as process control agent. Then, another 28 wt% raw coarse-grained 2024Al powders as ductile FG building blocks and 12 wt% m-SiCps were mechanically mixed with cold-welded n-SiCp/2024Al powders using nylon jars at a rotational rate of 120 rpm for 8 h. Φ6 mm ZrO 2balls following a ball to powder ratio of 5:1 were added. The above powder mixtures were hot pressed into billets at 853 K for 2 h using a uniaxial pressure of 300 MPa and a vacuum pressure of 10 −3Pa. To tailor differentiated heterogeneous lamella structures and study microstructure related strengthening and toughening behaviors, the sintered billets were hot extruded into rods at 673 K with extrusion ratio of 9:1, 16:1 and 25:1. Corresponding samples were abbreviated as E9, E16 and E25, respectively. Subsequently, the extruded rods were solid solution treated at 768 K for 2 h and quenched in water, followed by artificial aging treatment at 443 K for 4 h (T6 state). Finally, three heterogeneous lamella m- & n-SiCp/2024Al composites were fabricated. Sample: E25; Further increasing extrusion ratio with over-refinement of heterogeneous lamellas

Processing Text: The gas-atomized (FeCoNi) 86 Al 7 Ti 7 HEA powders (provided by Zhongyuan New Material Technology Co., Ltd., Ningbo, China.) were used as feed-stock powders in the present study. The sizes of the particles D 10 , D 50 , and D 90 are calculated to be ∼20.17, ∼34.73, and ∼57.53 μm, respectively. A selective laser melting HBD-100 printer (Hanbang United 3D Tech Co. Ltd., Shanghai, China) equipped with a fiber laser (wavelength of 1064 nm) was used to prepare the HEA samples. The laser offers an output power of 200 W, and a spot diameter of 60 μm. A 67° scan rotation between the successive layers was employed to minimize the thermal residual stresses generated during the PBF process. Condition: tested at 77 K (cryogenic temperature)

The SMAT samples were annealed under vacuum for 20 min at 300 °C, 320 °C and 350 °C. A 50 kg ingot of lightweight steel with a composition of Fe-18Mn-8Al-1C-5Ni (wt%) was prepared in a vacuum induction melting furnace (chemical composition analyzed by spark optical emission spectroscopy: Fe-18.20Mn-7.98Al-1.03C-5.02Ni wt%). The as-forged steel was hot rolled to 5 mm at 1200°C with a total reduction of 93 %, followed by water quenching (referred to as "WQ"). The hot-rolled steels were homogenized at 1200°C for 1 hour and then cold-rolled to a final thickness of 1 mm with a total reduction of 80 %. Three types of heat treatment schedules were applied to the cold rolled specimens in the present study, as illustrated in the Fig. 1. The cold-rolled strips were at 1000°C for 50 minutes to obtain full recrystallization (referred to as "AN50"), and annealed at 850 °C for 5 minutes to induce partial recrystallization (referred to as "AN5"), followed by WQ. Pre-straining was conducted in the AN5 specimen with several tensile strains of 0 %, 5 %, and 15 %. Subsequently, these AN5 specimens with different pre-strains were annealed at 850°C for 7 minutes with WQ. These pre-strained and sequent annealed specimens were denoted as "0 %-AN7", "5 %-AN7", and "15 %-AN7," respectively. Condition: aged specimen; Microstructure: optimized precipitation of GB-B2, IG-B2 particles, and coherent κ-carbides

To investigate the impact of new phase addition of Invar 36, B4C particles, known for their high melting point, were used as reinforcement phases to fabricate B4C/Invar 36 composites through laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technology, which offers high design flexibility. The Invar 36 powder (15-55 μm) and the B4C particles examined in this study were supplied by Shandong Lianhong New Material Technology Co., Ltd., China. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), the gas-atomized spherical Invar 36 powder is uniformly distributed, with a mean particle size of 26.24 μm, making it well-suited for the LPBF powder laying process. Fig. 1(b) presents the 99.9 % purity irregularly shaped B4C powders. The chemical composition (in wt.%) of the precursor powders is detailed in Table 1 and 2. To achieve a homogeneously mixed feedstock composite powder containing 2 wt% B4C, a ball-milling process was conducted using a QM-3SP4-1 planetary ball mill at a rotation speed of 150 rpm for 2 h. Following this optimized ball-milling duration, the B4C particles were nearly all firmly embedded within the relatively soft surface of the larger Invar 36 powders, without any significant alteration to the original spherical particle shape or size distribution (Fig. 1(c)). It is noteworthy that the composite powder was dried at 80 °C for 120 min prior to the experiment. The LPBF apparatus utilized was the Hans-M100, which was equipped with a YLR-200/500 YAG fiber laser, featuring a wavelength of 1060 nm, a laser spot size of 70 μm, and a maximum power output of 500 W. The layer thickness, stripe width, and stripe overlap were consistently maintained at 0.03 mm, 10 mm, and 0.08 mm, respectively. Additionally, after the construction of each layer, the scanning direction was rotated by 67°. The influence of laser scanning speed on the relative density, microstructural evolution, and mechanical properties of the B4C/Invar 36 composites was systematically examined. The results indicate that B4C/Invar 36 composites with nearly full density (99.32 %) were successfully produced at a laser power of 150 W and a laser scanning speed of 700 mm/s. B4C particles exhibited a strong heterogeneous nucleation effect on Invar 36 grains; the increase in nucleation sites contributed to grain refinement, ultimately enhancing the mechanical properties of the samples. The yield strength of the samples reached 410.17 MPa, while the ultimate tensile strength reached 729.27 MPa. Calculations reveal that grain refinement strengthening is the primary mechanism by which B4C enhances the Invar 36 matrix, with other strengthening mechanisms serving as auxiliary contributors to achieve synergistic strengthening. Laser scanning speed: 1100 mm/s

Processing Text: Commercial pure Zr having 98.5 % purity (other elements: 1.2 wt% Hf, 0.2 wt% Mo, 0.1 wt% O) was used for performing multi-axial cryo-forging (MACF) experiments. Before performing MACF experiments, samples were heat treated at 780 °C for 1.5 h to obtain strain-free equiaxed grains. MACF experiments were carried out at an equilibrium temperature of 77 K (boiling point of N 2) and a nominal strain rate of 1 s −1. Samples with initial dimensions of 15 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm were forged using a 500 kN capacity hydraulic UTM in a displacement control mode. A liquid N 2bath setup was prepared for carrying out forging at an equilibrium temperature of 77 K. Zr samples were multi-axially cryo-forged (MACF) using the forging sequence of A- B- A- C- A- Bto effective strains of 0.3 and 0.4 ( Fig. 1b) for bringing out the effect of strain on twin density and subsequent mechanical behaviour. MACF of Zr to effective strains of 0.3 and 0.4 (hereafter referred to as MACF-0.3 and MACF-0.4, respectively) resulted in hierarchical twins within the prior coarse-equiaxed grains ( Fig. 2c-f). The as-MACF samples were heat treated at 500 °C for 1 h to recover the dislocation substructure and relieve the internal residual stresses generated during MACF (dominant recovery temperature for Zr is between 400 and 550 °C, beyond which it undergoes recrystallization owing to enhanced boundary migration [ 36, 37]. Condition: MACF-0.3; Microstructure: dense and fine tensile twins

The ingots of Fe x(CoCrNi) 100-x (x = 25, 40, 50, 62, 64, 66, and 71, at.%) MEAs were produced using an arc-melting technique in a water-cooled copper mold under high-purity argon. The Ni 50Cr 20Co 15Al 10V 5(at. %) HEAs in this work were synthesized using an arc-melting furnace in a Ti-getter, high-purity Ar atmosphere. High-purity Ni, Cr, Co, Al, and V metals (>99.9 wt %) were melted to cast the alloys. To ensure compositional uniformity, the alloys underwent more than seven repeated melting cycles under electromagnetic stirring. The alloys were then cast into a water-cooled copper mold, producing ingots measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 80 mm. Subsequently, homogenization treatment was carried out at 1200 °C for 24 h in an Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching. The homogenized ingots underwent cold rolling, resulting in an 80 % reduction in thickness. Following cold rolling, the alloys were recrystallized at 1100 °C for 10 min and then water-quenched to room temperature. After that, the recrystallized samples were subjected to aging treatments at 700 °C for 1 h and 12 h, respectively. These alloys for the study were named as aged-1h, aged-12 h, and recrystallized samples, respectively. The samples for examination underwent initial sanding with SiC sandpapers ranging from 400# to 2000#, followed by polishing with a 50 nm oxide polishing suspension (OPS) solution to remove surface stress. Samples for TEM analysis were first ground with SiC sandpapers to a thickness of less than 100 μm. Following this, the samples were further thinned using a precision Ar ion-beam milling system (Gatan 691) to achieve electron transparency. Samples for tensile tests were obtained with a gauge length of 10 mm and width of 2 mm using electric spark cutting. Before testing, the surface of all samples was sanded with SiC sandpapers ranging from 400# to 2000#. For analyzing the deformed microstructure, samples were additionally polished with OPS solution for EBSD and ECCI measurements. Processing state: Recrystallized

FeCoCrNiMnP xHEAs were cast by arc melting in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The Fe, Co, Cr, Ni, and Mn particles were obtained in Kairui New Materials (Beijing) Technology Co., Ltd. P was added in the form of FeP (the P content is 22 wt%). The all particles were ultrasonically cleaned in alcohol and weighed according to their design ratios. The particles are then placed in a copper mold crucible in order of their melting point from lowest to highest. Before melting the alloys, the pure metal Ti is melted first in order to remove residual oxygen from the furnace chamber. To ensure uniform composition, the alloys were repeatedly melted five times in an argon atmosphere and subsequently cooled with the furnace. The ingot is homogenized at 1100 °C for 6 h respectively. The two alloys were denoted as P0-CG and P2-CG HEAs (CG: coarse grains). The geometric shape of an 8 × 15 × 25 mm 3block was cold rolled, reducing its thickness from 8 mm to 3.2 mm and resulting in an overall rolling reduction of 60 %. Then, the cold-rolled samples were annealed at 1100 °C for 30 s to obtain fully recrystallized fine grain microstructure, and they were denoted as P0-FG and P2-FG HEAs respectively (FG: fine grains). The matrix was BCC-structured ODS-FeCrAl alloy. Processing Text: The graphene/Ni composites with different Mo content were fabricated by the in-situ method described in our earlier research [ 10 , 19 ]. First, 3 g metal powder (Ni or NiMo particles) was added into the HCl solution of 0.01 mol/L. The mixtures were mechanically stirred for 30 min to completely remove the surface oxide layer of the metallic particles, and then rinsed with deionized water and anhydrous ethanol, respectively. The pre-treated metallic particles were poured into the PMMA/DMF solution (10 mL), stirred, and maintained at 80 °C to evaporate the DMF solvent. Thereafter the metallic particles were coated by a thin PMMA layer, and the core-shell PMMA@Ni composite particles were prepared. Second, the PMMA@Ni precursor was homogeneously mixed with the cleaned Ni or NiMo powder of the same quality (3 g). The mixtures were compacted into a square green body in the stainless mold with a length and width of 30 mm and 15 mm under 200 MPa. Third, the green body was transferred into a graphite mold and then processed by the vacuum hot-pressed sintering at 1050 °C for 30 min with a heating rate of 10 °C/min. A uniaxial pressure of 40 MPa was applied when the temperature reached 600 °C. Containing 3D graphene networks; Compared to pure Ni bulk

Commercial Zircaloy-4 tubes with a diameter of 9.5 mm and wall thickness of 0.57 mm were procured with a nominal composition in Table 1. The 2 µm and 7 µm geometries were prepared in the axial direction using a gallium ion FIB and plasma xenon FIB with two varying tensile geometries shown in Fig. 1. In addition to this, four 2 µm and seven 7 µm of the tensile bars were made from an irradiated tube of Zircaloy-4. This irradiated tube with an ID of “R-05″ was part of the Accident Tolerant Fuels 2 (ATF-2) experiment and was irradiated at the Advanced Test Reactor (ATR) Loop 2A at Idaho National Laboratory (INL). This rod was able to achieve a burnup of 9.27 GWd/tHM at temperatures ranging from 250 °C to 280 °C. Kamerman et al. calculates this rod's fast fluence as 1.98 х 10 25n/m 2using a coupled Monte Carlo N-Particle (MCNP) and ORIGEN methodology. Rough milling of the SSMT tensile samples was conducted at 30 kV and 60-2000nA while final cleaning used 30 kV and 0.5-10nA. The meso‑scale 80 µm tensile specimens were prepared from a 100 μm thick foil sample of Zircaloy-4 tubing which was sectioned using a high-speed diamond saw. The sample surface on both sides was polished from 600 grit sandpaper to a final solution of 1 μm diamond suspension. The foil was machined using an 8 W Spirit One fs-laser combined with a Newport microfabrication workstation to control movement. The laser system was run at a power of 3 W, a laser wavelength of 1040 nm, a pulse duration of 332fs, and a repetition rate of 50 kHz using a Mitutoyo NIR 10x objective lens which has a focused spot size of ∼10 μm. A compressed air gas flow was used to assist in removing ablation particles during cutting. Following laser machining, the tensile bars were quickly immersed in a bath of ethanol in an ultrasonic cleaner to remove excess ablation particles on the surface. Microstructural examination was performed using a Thermo Fisher Scios 2 DualBeam SEM equipped with an Oxford Symmetry S3 electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. Prior to examination the surface was mechanically polished from 600 grit sandpaper to a 0.02 μm colloidal silica solution and then cryo-electro polished at 0 °C for one minute. To ensure uniformity, the ingot was re-melted at least five times. Then, the as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h followed by air cooling. Processing Text: A solution-treated Cu-0.5Cr-0.05Zr-0.05Ti (wt.%) alloy was drawn into a large-depth cup implementing a two-stage deformation process in the present study, firstly using a ∅ 50 mm cylindrical punch and subsequently redrawn by a ∅ 34 mm punch. The redrawn cup wall was subjected to aging heat treatment up to 400 °C, 500 °C, and 600 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching to understand the microstructural evolution and its correlation with mechanical properties. The as-received sheets were solutionized at 950 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching to enhance the deep drawability. These solution-treated sheets were considered for the two-stage deep drawing experiment as illustrated in Fig. 1(a). The first stage involved the deep drawing of a circular blank into a cylindrical cup, followed by the second stage, which involved redrawing the fabricated cup to increase the cup height. The deep drawing experiment was performed using a deep drawing die setup comprised of a cylindrical punch of 50 mm diameter and a die of 55 mm diameter. Similarly, the redrawing test was carried out using a 34 mm diameter punch and a redrawing die. A maximum cup depth of 38.5 mm and 58.5 mm was achieved in the deep-drawn and redrawn cups, respectively, from an initial blank of 100 mm diameter. Before the experiment, 2.5 mm circular grid patterns were marked over the blank surface to determine the post-deformation strains. The major and minor strain distributions of the drawn-cups were evaluated by mapping the deformed circular grid dimensions using the circular grid analysis technique [ 25]. Therefore, the redrawn cups were subjected to aging treatment at different temperatures, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b), to analyze the microstructural and mechanical property variation in the deformed components under thermal exposure prior to the actual use in the space application. Microstructural characterizations of the redrawn cup wall and aged specimens (referred to as aged-redrawn cup, henceforth) were performed using SEM (ZEISS Merlin) equipped with EBSD and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) facilities. The specimens for microstructural examination were extracted from the redrawn cup wall as depicted in Fig. 1(b). The specimen surfaces were prepared using a standard metallographic procedure and then etched with an etchant containing 2 gm K 2Cr 2O 7, 8 ml H 2SO 4,and 100 ml distilled water. For the EBSD analysis, the surfaces were further electropolished at −5 °C using a solution of 25 ml HPO 3, 25 ml C 2H 5OH, and 50 ml deionized water at 6 V for 20 s. The EBSD scans were performed with a step size of 0.25 μm, and the data were processed in a commercially available TSL-OIM software to evaluate grain size, grain boundary characteristics viz., high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs with misorientation angle 15°-65°) and low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs with misorientation angle 2°-15°), grain orientation spread (GOS), and Kernel average misorientation (KAM). Further, a detailed investigation of precipitate characteristics was done using high-resolution TEM (HRTEM, JEOL3000) technique. The TEM specimens were prepared using mechanical thinning followed by focused ion milling for final thinning and dimpling. Further, X-ray diffraction (XRD) method was utilized to determine phase composition, micro-strain, and crystallite size in all the specimens using a diffractometer (Bruker D8, Germany) equipped with a Cu target. The mechanical properties of the redrawn and aged-redrawn cup specimens were evaluated to comprehend the effect of aging temperature. Hence, miniature tensile specimens were cut from the redrawn cup wall region using a wire electro-discharge machine, as per the dimension given in Fig. 1(b) [ 26]. These specimens were then subjected to aging, and uniaxial tensile tests were performed in a 50 kN universal testing machine at 2 mm/min. The tests were repeated on three specimens in each condition. Moreover, hardness variation in the cup was estimated along a curvilinear distance from the cup bottom center to the cup top edge, and compared with aged-redrawn cup specimens. A Vickers hardness tester was used to apply an indentation load of 100 gf. Condition: Solution-treated

Processing Text: The 2 wt.% Ti particle reinforced Mg-6 Zn alloy composites with different contents (0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2 wt.%) of Mn were prepared using semi-solid stirring assisted ultrasonic treatment followed by hot extrusion. Approximately 1 kg matrix alloy was melted in an electronic resistance furnace at 720 °C under the protective atmosphere of 99 vol. % CO 2 and 1 vol. % SF 6. Once the alloy was fully melted for 2 h, the floating slag was removed, and the temperature was lowered to 650 °C to achieve a semi-solid state. The pre-heated 2 wt.% Ti particles (200 °C for 2 h) were quickly added into the molten melt for 6-min mechanical stirring. After stirring, the mixed melt was reheated to 680 °C to reach a liquid state and subjected to ultrasonic treatment for 5 min. The ultrasonic power was 1.5 kW and the frequency was 20.1 kHz. Before water quenching, an additional 30 s of mechanical stirring was applied following the ultrasonic treatment. At last, the as-cast Ti particle reinforced Mg-6Zn- xMn composites were obtained. In order to eliminate the segregation of second phases, the ingot with a diameter of 80 mm was homogenized at 420 °C for 4 h. The composite ingots were extruded at 360 °C with an extrusion ratio of 25:1 with a speed of 0.5 m/min. Room temperature; Composite with 0.5 wt.% Mn addition

Processing Text: In the PBF [ 39 ], the material is deposited by melting a powder bed in a layer-by-layer pattern using a heat source ( Fig. 4 (a)). The main difference between the two main categories of PBF, SLM and EBM, is the heat source used to melt powder: the former uses a laser, and the latter uses an electron beam. Various scanning strategies and process parameters used in PBF are shown in Fig. 4 (b). The most popular scanning strategies include unidirectional, bidirectional, spiral, zigzag, and crosswise; in each instance, neighboring tracks are overwritten with a hatch spacing lower than the track width to ensure complete melting. The directional hatch policy is usually rotated in the subsequent layers by a 67 o rotation. Rotating scanning helps to break down the epitaxy of columnar growth [ 40 ]. These include the scan speed, power source density, scanning strategy and spacing, and layer thickness [ 41 ], which affect the microstructural phases formed inside material, layer patterns and orientations, type of defects, and residual stresses. Processing Text: This experiment utilized commercially available hot-rolled and annealed AZ31B magnesium alloy sheets. Strips with a thickness of 4 mm, a length of 130 mm, and a width of 100 mm were cut from the sheets for rolling. During the rolling process, the rolling speed for both passes was set at 50 mm·s−1, with a reduction rate of 25 % per pass. Prior to rolling, the sheets were heated to 350 °C and held at this temperature for 30 min before the first pass. After the first pass, the sheets were reheated to 350 °C and held for 15 min before the second pass. SR was performed using a two-roll synchronous rolling mill with a working roll diameter of 320 mm. ASR and AAR were conducted using a two-roll asymmetrical rolling mill with working roll diameters of 320 mm and 280 mm, respectively. The heated magnesium alloy sheet is placed on a conveyor roller table, and then the angle between the rolling centerline and the length direction of the plate is controlled by adjusting the pushing mechanism located on both sides of the sheet. Based on previous research on sheet shape, this study selected a rolling angle of 40° for the first pass and 80° for the second pass in the AAR process. Process: SR; Tension direction: 45°

Processing Text: The Al-Mg alloy plates used for the study were prepared by depositing AA5087 wire (1.2 mm in diameter) onto AA5A06 plates via the WADED system. The WADED system mainly includes an ABB six-axis robot and a Fronius CMT Advanced 4000R welding system. During the WADED process, the filler wire was melted by the arc in a protective atmosphere (99.99 % Ar), and the CMT torch moved horizontally (Y-depositing direction) with the molten wire to form a deposited layer. Deposition of the next layer was performed on the previous layer by raising the torch height (Z-building direction). The WADED Al components were finally removed from the substrate using electrical discharge machining (EDM) and double-side milling to 6 mm thickness. The LSP experiment was carried out in a self-built LSP system, which mainly included a Nd: YAG pulsed laser (with a wavelength of 1064 nm and a pulse duration of 15 ns) and a six-axis robot. WADED Al plate was ground and polished before LSP, and then fixed on six-axis robot to adjust position. The Al foil with a thickness of 100 µm and the flowing water layer were covered on the surface of WADED Al plate as absorbing layer and constraining layer, respectively. The front and back sides of the WADED Al plate were strengthened in turn. The pulsed laser with energy of 5 J was focused by a convex lens into a circular spot with a diameter of 2 mm. Both sides of sampling region were treated twice by LSP at a 50 % overlapping rate to prevent the distortion and obtain the unform residual stress distribution. The as-deposited samples after LSP treatment were further annealed at 200 °C for 1 h to study the effect of the LSP + annealing process on the WADED Al alloy. Processing state: as-deposited

Processing Text: The materials used in this study were commercial CuCrZr alloys (grade C18150). The commercial copper alloys had undergone cold deformation and annealing treatment, resulting in mostly deformed grains and a large number of precipitates. To improve the uniformity of the microstructure and composition of the copper alloys and minimize the dissolution of precipitates back into the matrix, the alloys were initially subjected to a solid solution treatment at 950 ℃ for 2 hours before cryogenic treatment. Subsequently, they were rapidly cooled using water as the medium to achieve a solid solution state. Cryogenic treatment was conducted using the SLX-30B cryogenic treatment box, developed by the Institute of Physics and Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, with nitrogen supplied from a pressure tank. It should be noted that the cryogenic box controlled the temperature and cooling rate by adjusting the flow rate of liquid nitrogen. In this study, the latent heat of vaporization of liquid nitrogen was used to cool the sample, and the cooling rate was set at 3 ℃/min. Processing Text: Disk-shaped ingots of the Co 40(CrFeNi) 60alloy with a thickness of 10 mm and a diameter of ∼ 40 mm were produced in a vacuum arc melter. Each ingot was flipped and re-melted five times to improve the chemical homogeneity. Several tensile specimens and specimens for microstructural examinations were annealed at 600 °C for 15 min, 1 h and 10 h to produce material at different stages of recrystallization. This plane was electrochemically polished and then examined using electron channeling contrast (ECC) imaging and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). Processing Text: Gas-atomized AISI 4140 powder was used as the additive material. The powder is spherical in shape, with an average particle size of approximately 40 μm. 95 % of the particles have diameters ranging from 25 to 53 μm. The experimental setup for conducting the LMD and EHLA processes is depicted in Fig. 2. The machine employed in this study consisted of a focusing optic PHFQ-H1-C, a coaxial powder nozzle, and a spindle. A diode laser with a maximum power of 4000 W was used as the beam source. Powder feed was accomplished through the coaxial powder delivery system of the laser head using a pneumatic twin powder feeder. Argon gas was used for powder delivery and specimen shielding to prevent oxidation, and the purity of argon gas is 99.99 %. A water-cooling system was implemented to cool the laser system and laser head. In the LMD process, the interaction time between the laser beam and the powder particles is short, resulting in a high ratio of laser energy being absorbed by the substrate. The powder particles melt in the melting pool, leading to a relatively large heat-affected zone. Conversely, in the EHLA process, the laser-powder reaction occurs along the powder delivery path. Consequently, most of the powder particles melt above the surface and enter the melting pool as liquid drops. The EHLA process employs higher laser power to ensure a pore-free, less-cracked, and metallurgical-bonded layer. We studied divergent parameter combinations for a single layer and investigated the microstructure (pores, cracks, bonding quality, thickness, etc.) of the cross-section of the deposition accordingly, and those results feeded back to the process parameters. Through trial and error, the process parameters for a single layer with low porosity, metallurgic bonding between the substrate and the layer, and without any cracks were finally selected. The parameters used for LMD and EHLA are presented in Table 2. In the process strategy, the workpiece rotates using a fixed lathe chuck while the powder nozzle moves horizontally above the substrate. The overlap ratio between two tracks in the same layer is approximately 70 %. All experiments were conducted using a meandering scan path. Case 1: a single layer with multiple tracks using LMD, following the process parameters outlined in Table 2(LMD process parameters). Case 2: a single layer with multiple tracks using EHLA, following the process parameters described in Table 2(EHLA process parameters). Case 3: a 3D structure using LMD on a cylindrical base material. The dimensions of the deposition were 10 mm in the thickness direction (BD, R) and 100 mm in the length direction (SD, Z). In order to mitigate potential hot cracking caused by high temperatures during continuous deposition and to conduct comparative IHT experiments, we fabricated a total of 22 layers (10 mm) and allowed a dwell time of 15 min for cooling the deposition to 60 °C. Case 4: a 3D structure using EHLA on a cylindrical base material. The dimensions of the EHLA deposition were identical to those of the LMD deposition. However, since the thickness of an EHLA layer is approximately one-fourth to one-fifth of an LMD layer, we deposited a total of 95 layers to achieve a structure with a 10-mm thickness. To study the IHT effect and compare the resulting microstructure with LMD, we implemented a cooling time of 15 min after each set of five continuous deposited layers in order to facilitate cooling to 60 °C. Due to the high-power input and limited time available for heat transfer, the EHLA deposited structure exhibited some burnt edges, with a zig-zag burnt position of 5 mm at a 45-degree angle to the horizontal direction at each edge. This phenomenon is primarily attributed to the zigzag scanning strategy, as it results in a brief period of secondary heating at both ends and insufficient time for heat dissipation. The as-built deposition was sectioned along the cross-sectional (R-Z) direction for microstructural characterization. The samples were carefully examined under a microscope (Axio Imager Objective A-Plan 50×) to ensure minimal pores, crack-free deposition, and a sound metallurgical interface. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, ZEISS Sigma 300) was used to analyze the microstructural composition after etching with a 2 % Nital etchant (97 % ethanol and 3 % nitric acid) for 10 s. Electron dispersive spectroscopy (EDS, ZEISS) analysis was conducted to determine the element distribution in selected regions. Prior to texture analysis, vibration polishing with Al2O3 powders was performed. Texture analysis was carried out using an electron backscattered diffraction detector (EBSD, Oxford C-Nano) for both single-layer and multi-layer samples. Nanoindentation tests (FISCHERSCOPE HM2000, Germany) were used to measure the nanohardness of single layers, while the hardness of multi-layer samples was determined using a Vickers hardness tester as per DIN EN ISO 6507-1. To mirror the measurement errors, the hardness test was performed on three 3 positions from the edge to the middle (along Z direction) of the cross section, and three lines was defined for each position. The mean value of each point at three lines was used for the final results. The Vickers test was performed with a force of 0.98 N and a dwell time of 10 s. The distance between the clad edge ZB and testing position Z1 was approx. 2 mm. The horizontal distance between two testing lines Z1 and Z2 was 50 μm, and the vertical distance between two testing points R1 and R2 was 25 μm. A total length of approx. 3.5 mm consisting of deposition, heat affected zone (HAZ) and part of the substrate were tested. Similarly, three replicates were performed, and the mean value was used for the nanoindentation test, and a force of 300 mN was applied with a dwell time of 25 s according to standard ISO 14577-1 Metallic materials — Instrumented indentation test for hardness and materials parameters. A volume with thickness of 10 mm and length of 100 mm for the manufacturing of tensile test samples was produced for both LMD and EHLA process. Tensile tests were performed according to the DIN EN ISO 6892 standard, and the round tensile samples adhered to the dimensions specified in DIN 50125. AlSi10Mg was typically employed as a primary material for components utilized in SLM manufacturing due to its favorable mechanical properties, heat resistance, corrosion resistance, and lightweight characteristics [7-10]. In order to further enhance the mechanical properties of AlSi10Mg and meet specific requirements, heat treatment can be used to modify its atomic structure and nature [11-16]. The heat treatment process was Solution Heat Treatment (SHT, 525 °C), and the heat treatment time includes 1 h, 2 h, and 3 h. Cooling methods consist of Refrigerant Cooling (RC), Water Cooling (WC), Air Cooling (AC), Oil Cooling (OC), and Furnace Cooling (FC). As the cooling rate decreases and the heat treatment time increases, the size of the formed Si phase particles varies from small to large, and the distribution deviates from inhomogeneous to homogeneous. In addition, the number of precipitated particles increases and then decreases. To investigate the impact of cooling rates and heat treatment time on the mechanical properties of AlSi10Mg alloys, quasi-static tensile and compression tests were performed. On the other hand, the tensile strength of the heat-treatment samples decreases while the ductility increases, and the Vickers hardness of the samples also decreases with decreasing cooling rate and increasing heat treatment time. The samples treated at 525 °C - 2 h - AC exhibited the highest tensile and compressive properties. Selective laser melting (SLM) was a form of additive manufacturing (AM) that employs metal powders to fabricate components. The experimental samples were fabricated using AlSi10Mg powder aerosol obtained from Beijing Research State Technology Company. SLM uses an EOS 280 3D printer (400 W, 100 μm) with a Yb fiber laser. To mitigate the risk of embrittlement caused by the reaction between oxygen and Al or magnesium during the manufacturing process, the sample specimens were produced in an air-free environment. Argon gas was employed to maintain the oxygen concentration below 0.6 %. The printer uses a laser power of 300 W, a scanning rate of 1000 mm/s per second, a layer thickness of 30 μm, and a hatch spacing of 120 μm. The AlSi10Mg specimens produced through SLM were subjected to various heat treatments, as outlined in Table 2. The primary heat treatment was Solution Heat Treatment (SHT), with a temperature of 525 °C [33-35]. One noteworthy method was RC, which employs a refrigerant spray to lower the temperature of the sample to ambient temperature. In the process of OC, the quenching oil was heated to 60 °C. Subsequently, the sample was submerged in the heated oil and allowed to cool to the ambient temperature. The cooling rates associated with the various cooling methods were ranked in descending order as follows: V (RC)> V (WC)> V (AC)> V (OC)> V (FC). Additionally, argon gas was employed to safeguard the samples against oxidation during the heat treatment. The solid block samples were subjected to heat treatment before polishing. After polishing, the samples were subjected to corrosion for 20 s using Keller's reagent (2.5 ml HNO 3, 1.5 ml HCL, 1.0 ml HF, and 95 ml H 2O). Condition: Fastest cooling rate after SHT (525 °C - 2 h)

Processing Text: The experimental material was a cylindrical ingot of Mg-12.8Gd-3.8Y-1.9Zn-0.5Zr (wt%) alloy, which was produced by semi-continuous casting process. The alloy ingot was homogenized at 520 °C for 16 hours and cooled at RT. Before the experiment beginning the homogenized alloy ingot underwent a series of pretreatment steps. Firstly, the alloy ingot underwent one pass of upsetting-extruding experiment. Subsequently, one pass of backward-extruding experiment was performed. Finally, the backward-extruded sample ring was cut into rectangular initial alloys of 70 mm × 56 mm × 120 mm. The deformation temperature for both the upsetting-extruding and backward-extruding experiments were 450 °C, and the dies were preheated at 450 °C × 8 h before the experiments. The size of the alloy after upsetting experiment was Φ465 mm, and the extrusion ratio was 1.9:1. Two passes of forging experiments were conducted on the initial alloy, with each forging direction perpendicular to the axial direction of the backward-extrusion experiment. The detailed experimental steps are as follows: Firstly, the initial alloy was pre-aged at 200 °C. Based on previous research, it was found that the sample was in peak aging state at 120 h. The first pass of forging was performed on the pre-aged samples. The die and initial alloy were preheated at 460 °C and 450 °C, respectively, and held for 30 minutes before the experiments, and cooled at RT after forging. The sample after the first pass of forging was defined as PF sample. The PF sample was treated with low-temperature solid solution at 460 °C for 8 hours. After the treatment, it was put back into the die for the second pass of forging. Prior to the experiment, both the die and sample were preheated and held at the same temperature and holding time as the first pass. The sample after the second pass of forging was defined as PFSF sample. The second pass of forging was performed directly on the PF sample, as well as the die and sample were also preheated and held at the same temperature and holding time before the experiment. The sample after the second pass of forging was defined as PFF sample. Initial state

Processing Text: In this study, low-density (< 6 g/cm3) AlCrFeTiX (x = Co, Ni, Cu) high-entropy alloys were produced by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS), and their structures and mechanical properties after SPS and annealing at 1000 °C for 24 h were reported. The commercial powders of Al (99.7 wt%, particle size < 30 μm), Cr (99.7 wt%, particle size in the range 10-30 μm), Fe (99.9 wt%, particle size < 75 μm), Ti (99.5 wt%, particle size < 45 μm), Co (99.8 wt%, particle size < 70 μm), Cu (99.97 wt%, particle size < 60 μm), Ni (99.9 wt%, particle size < 30 μm) were used as the precursors. 18 g batches of an stoichiometric Al:Cr:Fe:Ti:Co (1:1:1:1:1:1 mol), Al:Cr:Fe:Ti:Cu (1:1:1:1:1:1 mol), and Al:Cr:Fe:Ti:Ni (1:1:1:1:1:1 mol) mixtures were used for mechanical alloying at 694 rpm (jar rotated at 1388 rpm) for 60 min in a water-cooling double-station planetary ball mill (Activator 2S, Activator, Russia), which is high energy planetary ball mill and allows reaching centrifugal acceleration more than 90 g. Before the milling, a stainless steel jar of 250 ml capacity was vacuumed, filled with the 99.98 %-purity argon having a pressure of 4 atm and then sealed. The powders were unloaded from jars and loaded to graphite die for SPS in a glove box in an argon atmosphere. Cylindrical graphite die (the inner diameter of 30 mm) was filled with a desired amount of the mixed powders. Then, the powders were consolidated using a SPS apparatus (Labox 650, Sinter Land, Japan) using the following parameters: heated in vacuum (15-20 Pa) at the rate of 100 °C/min, the temperature of 900°C, under uniaxial loading of 50 MPa, and dwell time of 10 min. After sintering, the specimens were free cooled in vacuum; cooling time to room temperature was ∼15 min. Disc-shaped samples of 30 mm in diameter and 7 mm thick were obtained. The specimens measured 3 × 3 × 5 mm 3 were cut from the disc-shaped samples after SPS using electrical discharge machining. A part of the specimens were annealed at 1000 °C for 24 h with further air cooling. Prior to annealing, the specimens were sealed in a vacuumed (10 −2 torr) quartz tube filled with titanium chips to prevent oxidation. Temperature: 600 °C; State: after SPS

Processing Text: Buttons of CrFeNi are firstly prepared using vacuum arc melting in the water-cooled copper hearth utilising 99.9 % pure Fe, Cr, and Ni elements. The buttons were remelted 5 times at argon atmosphere for homogeneity. The casted buttons were cleaned and polished removing the oxide layer from the button surface. Further buttons of 48 gms for CrFeNi were cast into a rod of 10 ×10 x 50 mm 3 using suction casting. The suction casting was carried out at 10-7 mbar pressure. The rods were homogenised at 1100˚ C for 24 hours in an argon atmosphere followed by water quenching to attain a single-phase FCC structure. Consequently, the homogenised rods were cold rolled up to 50 % thickness reduction to minimise the casting defects. The rods were then further subjected to annealing at 1373 K for 2 hours to remove all the residual stress and attain a fully recrystallised microstructure in the rods before further processing. The rods were then rolled at room temperature (300 K) up to 90 % rolling reduction with a 5 % reduction in each pass. The samples at different rolling reductions of 20 %, 40 %, 60 % and 90 % were cut and kept for further characterisation. The rolled samples were prepared by polishing on SiC paper up to 2500 grade followed by alumina cloth polishing and vibromet polishing with colloidal silica. Condition: Annealed

Processing Text: Master alloys with nominal composition of Co 68Al xFe 24.7-xV 4.8Cr 2.5(x = 16.5, 17 and 18 at.%) were prepared by arc-melting high-purity (99.95 wt%) Co, Cr, Fe, V and Al, which was denoted as Al-16.5, Al-17 and Al-18 samples, respectively. Each master alloy was remelted five times to ensure chemical homogeneity, and the molten liquid was subsequently drop-cast into a water-cooled copper mold of 70 × 10 × 10 mm 3. The crystal structure was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Bruker AXS D8 Advance) with Cu Kα radiation with a scanning range of 20° ∼ 100°. The microstructure of the samples was characterized by field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM, FEI Quanta 250F). The samples were ground with 400-2000# SiC sandpapers until the surface was smooth, and finally polished with 0.25 μm diamond suspension. Then, the polished samples were electrochemically etched, and the corrosive solution was a diluted aqua regia solution of HNO 3: HCl:C 2H 5OH = 1:3:8 vol%. The phase structure and chemical composition were characterized by FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). For the TEM sample preparation method, the sample was first punched to circle sheets with radius of Ф3 mm and then ground to about 50 μm. Twin-jet electropolishing was performed at a temperature of about 233 K using a mixed solution of HNO 3:CH 4O = 1:4. An Oxford symmetry S2 detector was installed on the JEOL-JSM-IT800 instrument and electron back-scatter diffraction (EBSD) measurements were performed. Vickers hardness measurements were performed using a hardness tester (HVS-1000) at a load of 500 gf and a load time of 10 s. Average hardness was obtained after at least 5 measurements of each sample. A rectangular specimen with 2 × 2 × 4 mm 3was cut from the ingot with an electric discharge machine, and a room temperature compression test was performed at a strain rate of 2 × 10 −4s −1. Compression tests were performed on three samples of each material to confirm repeatability. Nanoindentation test (KLA-Nano Indenter G200) was measured at least four times to ensure data reliability. Processing Text: Master ingots of present HEA with a nominal composition of Al 0.3CoCrFeNi were fabricated by vacuum-levitation melting method. All elements (Al, Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni) used as raw materials have the purity higher than 99.9 wt%. The ingots were remelted four times to ensure chemical homogeneity. Original HEA plates with dimensions of 150 mm (length) × 60 mm (width) × 20 mm (thickness) were obtained by drop casting method using a steel mold. Then, the plates were annealed at 1150 °C for 24 h for homogenization and water-quenched. The homogenized plates were cold-rolled to sheets with a thickness of ∼2 mm (90 % reduction) and then cut into specimens with dimensions of 5 mm (length) × 5 (width) × 3 mm (thickness) for recrystallization annealing. To investigate microstructures at higher temperatures, additional specimens were annealed at 1000 °C, 1100 °C and 1200 °C for 1 h, and water quenched. The microstructural evolution of Al0.3CoCrFeNi high entropy alloy after cold rolling and annealing treatment (at 750 °C, 850 °C and 950 °C) was investigated by scanning electron microscopy and electron backscatter diffraction. Processing Text: A novel Ti35Zr35Nb15Mo5Fe5Cr5 complex concentrated alloy (CCA) with potential for biomedical application was developed by vacuum arc melting. Metal pieces of Ti, Zr, Nb, Mo, Fe, and Cr with high purity (greater than 99.95 %) were used to produce Ti 35Zr 35Nb 15Mo 5Fe 5Cr 5CCA in a vacuum arc melting furnace. The sample was melted in a high vacuum melting chamber (vacuum pressure ∼ 10 −6mbar) under a high-purity argon atmosphere using a Ti getter. It was then solidified on a water-cooled copper hearth. For chemical homogeneity, the sample was remelted five times, and each time, the sample was flipped before melting. In accordance with ISO 2738, the density of the as-cast CCA sample was determined by applying Archimedes' principle. For annealing treatment, the as-cast specimens were vacuum-sealed in a quartz tube and annealed at temperatures of 700˚C, 900˚C, and 1100˚C for a duration of 20 h using a muffle furnace. All the as-cast and annealed specimens were metallographically prepared for microscopy using emery papers for polishing and Kroll's reagent (6 ml HNO 3, 2 ml HF, and 92 ml H 2O) for etching. The (ZrNb) 100–x Ti x (x = 10, 15, 20; at.%) MEAs (denoted ZNT 10, ZNT 15, and ZNT 20, respectively) were prepared by arc melting of pure Zr, Nb, and Ti, all with 99.95% purity (Beijing Licheng Innovation Metal Materials Technology Co., Ltd., China). The CLAM steel, with a chemical composition (in wt.%) of Fe - 8.91% Cr - 1.4% W - 0.54 % Mn - 0.15% Ta - 0.15% V- 0.09% C - 0.06% Si, was melted in a vacuum induction furnace prior to casting an ingot with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 120 mm. The ingot was solution treated in an air furnace at 1200 °C for 2 h to homogenize the microstructure and completely dissolve primary carbides, prior to hot and then warm rolling to extensively elongate the prior-austenite grains along the rolling direction. With a starting hot rolling temperature of 1150 °C, the ultimate rolling temperature was 1050 °C with a deformation rate of 50%; with the starting warm rolling temperature as 850 °C, the ultimate rolling temperature was 800 °C with a deformation rate of 80%. During subsequent cooling, the austenite was completely transformed into martensite to form a laminated martensite microstructure. To prepare the lamellar grain structure in the CLAM steel, the steel was directly tempered at 700 °C for 15 min to transform the martensite into ferrite but to prevent the ferrite grains undergoing complete recrystallization. Evolutions of the mechanical properties for the top (a) and bottom (b) AlSi7Mg samples in relation to the direct-aged conditions (Table 2). The starting points at 0.1 and 70 h represent the as-built conditions for both the top (a) and bottom (b) samples. They indicate the different exposure times at the build platform temperature (150 °C). Variations of both the Vickers microhardness values and size of Si-eutectic particles in relation to the direct aging temperatures of top (dotted lines) and bottom (continuous lines) samples. Evolutions of the mechanical properties of the artificially aged AlSi7Mg (a) and AlSi10Mg (b) samples. When the as-built AlSi7Mg samples underwent a solution heat-treated for 4 h (Fig. 7a), the yield and ultimate tensile strengths reached (125±10) MPa and (285±12) MPa, respectively, due to the microstructural changes affecting of Si-eutectic and grain sizes (see Fig. 3 and Fig. 4). Following a similar heat treatment, Bosio et al. [46] demonstrated that the significant strengthening contributions related to the α-Al cell size decreased the strength by approximately 82 %. They further showed that the α-Al cells confer 52 MPa compared to only 11 MPa conferred by the grain boundaries, as describe the following Hall-Petch equation: (8)σHP=k(1dcell+1dgrain) where σHP is the strength ruled by the Hall-Petch law, k is a material constant (40MPam1/2), dcell and dgrains([μm]) are the average cell (Fig. 3c,d) and grain sizes. As also reported by [11, 47], softening effects were also caused by a reduction in the percentage of alloying elements within the crystal lattice, as discussed in the Introduction section. True elongations increased from 0.135 to 0.180. Both the artificial aging treatments at 150 and 175 °C restored the mechanical performance of each solution heat-treated sample, bringing them to the peak-aged conditions (see yellow rectangle in Fig. 7). Conversely, over-aging led to softening phenomena, resulting in values below those observed after solution heat treatment. The most pronounced softening effects occurred with artificial aging at 175 °C per 512 h, reducing the true yield strength values to (100±11) MPa for AlSi7Mg and (93±7) MPa for AlSi10Mg. Other intermediate conditions, including peak-aging at 200 °C (see Table 2), fell between the maximum (peak-aging) and minimum value (175 °C × 512 h). Samples artificially aged at 200 °C exhibited yield and the ultimate tensile strengths ranging from 195 to 230 MPa and 260-290 MPa, respectively. Condition: solution heat-treated for 4 h

Processing Text: The Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys ingots were purchased from Beijing Zhongnuo New Material Technology Co., Ltd. The actual chemical compositions of the as-cast Zn-xCu alloys were measured by ICP-OES, as listed in Table 1. The plates with a size of 100 mm × 60 mm × 20 mm were prepared from the as-cast Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys, and then were homogenized at 350 °C for 9 h. In order to crush coarse cast microstructure and obtain fine equiaxed grains, the as-cast Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys plates were rolled down to 8 mm by 15 % reduction in thickness per pass after preheating at 200 °C for 5 min. Subsequently, the rolled samples were annealed at 300 °C for 1 h. The annealed Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys plates were sequentially further rolled to 65 % rolling reduction in thickness by multi-pass after preheating at 250 °C for 10 min. The tensile specimens of the Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys with a gauge length of 20 mm and a width of 3 mm were prepared from the rolled samples. The tensile specimens were cut along the rolling direction. The thickness of tensile specimens was equal to that of the rolled sheets. Specimens for microstructure characterization were ground, polished and etched with an acid solution (20 g CrO3, 1.5 g Na2SO4 and 100 mL distilled water), then were characterized by the optical microscope. The microstructure at high magnification and the chemical compositions of phase were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive spectrometry (EDS). The phase compositions of the Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys were identified using an X-ray diffractometer analysis (XRD) with a Cu-Kα irradiation and the XRD patterns were collected over the 2θ range of 30-80° at a scan rate of 2° per min. Moreover, microstructure and texture evolution of the Zn-xCu (x= 0, 2, 4 and 8 wt%) alloys during hot-rolling were characterized by the electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) analysis. To further characterize the microstructures of Zn-xCu alloys after hot-rolling, TEM observations were carried out by a Tecnai G2 transmission electron microscope. The TEM samples were prepared by mechanical grinding to below 50 μm, and then ion thinning in a 4 wt% perchloric acid alcohol solution. Processing Text: A 2 kg ingot (20 × 40 × 300 mm) of the Cr40Co40Ni20 (at.%) alloy was produced with commercially pure elements (>99.7 %) by vacuum induction melting with non-forced cooling using an alumina crucible. The ingot was homogenized at 1100 °C for 2 h, and the thickness was gradually reduced by several hot rolling steps to a final thickness of ∼1.7 mm at around 1100 °C. The plate was cold rolled up to a final thickness of ∼1.0 mm (final cold rolling thickness reduction of ∼40 %). Tensile test specimens were obtained by electrical discharge machining and a schematic of the sample geometry is provided in the supplementary material (Section S1). Samples were recrystallized under four different conditions (1: 800 °C/20 min; 2: 900 °C/30 min; 3: 1000 °C/2 h; 4: 1100 °C/2 h) to obtain four different grain/crystallite sizes, followed by water quenching. The heat treatment conditions were chosen based on the grain growth kinetics of the Cr40Co40Ni20 alloy, studied by Bertoli et al. (2021). Samples with different grain/crystallite sizes were analyzed by in-situ SXRD during tensile testing. SEM-EBSD analysis were performed on the recrystallized and deformed samples, in the grip section and in the gauge length, respectively, after the tensile tests. Samples were carefully prepared according to standard metallographic preparation, up to a final stage of at least 15 h in a vibratory polisher with a 0.04 μm colloidal silica suspension. In-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (SXRD) was performed during uniaxial tensile testing at Sector 1-ID at the Advanced Photon Source (APS), Argonne National Laboratory, IL, USA, at room temperature with a constant strain rate of 2 × 10-4 s-1. A monochromated 71.6 KeV high-energy beam was used, with a corresponding wavelength of 0.1731 Å. CeO2 powder was used as a standard for the calibration of the instrument parameters and to determine the sample-to-detector distance, which was calculated to be 2129 mm. Four GE-41RT area detectors were used to capture the 2D raw Debbye-Scherrer rings at different stress/strain levels. Each diffraction pattern was obtained through the summation of 10 individual images with an exposure time of 0.3 s. A dark image was recorded before each test for background subtraction. The 2D Debye-Scherrer rings were converted into conventional 1D intensity vs 2θ diffraction patterns by integrating along the full azimuthal angle (φ range from 0 to 360°) and the 10° transverse direction (TD) (φ range from −5 to 5°) using the General Structure Analysis System (GSASII) software. The HCP phase fraction was quantified by two methods: via EBSD and via SXRD. SEM-EBSD analysis were performed on the recrystallized samples to assess their microstructure, phases and average grain/crystallite size. FCC average grain size: 17.0 μm; FCC average crystallite size: 6.8 μm; Annealing twin boundaries per grain: 1.50

Processing Text: The single-phase β coarse-grained (CG) specimens of metastable Ti25Nb (at.%) alloy were subjected to solution treatment in the β phase region, followed by aging at 300 °C for 60 min to obtain CG60. The resulting CG specimens were then subjected to low-temperature aging at 300 °C for 60 min, 660 min, and 1440 min, followed by water quenching to obtain CG60, CG660, and CG1440, respectively. The Ti 25Nb (atomic percent, at.%) ingot (length × width × thickness: 200 mm × 55 mm × 6.5 mm) was produced by arc melting pure titanium and niobium metals in an argon atmosphere, with at least three remelting cycles to ensure uniform distribution of elements. The ingot was then cold-rolled at room temperature to produce sheets with a thickness of 0.65 mm, resulting in a 90 % reduction from the original 6.5 mm thickness. The sheets were then cut into dog bone-shaped tensile specimens with dimensions of 10 mm in total length and 3 × 1 × 0.45 mm 3 (the gauge dimensions: length × width × thickness) using an electrical discharge wire cutting machine. To obtain specimens with coarse grains (hereafter referred to as CG), the dog bone-shaped specimens were first placed in a quartz tube furnace and annealed at 825 °C for 30 min, followed by water quenching. A heterogeneous lamella structure was produced in a single-phase Fe55Mn20Cr15Ni10 MEA via two-step rolling and annealing. The received Fe55Mn20Cr15Ni10 MEA was melted at least four times from the starting elements with a purity exceeding 99.9% in a magnetic levitation melting furnace. The ingots underwent homogenization at 1373 K for four hours under vacuum, followed by water quenching. Subsequently, a two-step rolling and heat treatment process was conducted. Initial room-temperature rolling (50% reduction) and annealing at 973 K for 10 min, followed by quenching, were carried out to obtain a refined grain structure. Subsequently, cryorolling was conducted with a reduction of 67%, followed by annealing at 923 K for 10 min and quenching. The samples thus obtained are denoted as T0. The samples annealed at 1023 K for 10 min after cryorolling were also prepared to achieve a coarse-grained (CG) structure for comparison. For cryorolling, the sheets were immersed in liquid nitrogen for 10 min before each pass and rolled immediately to minimize the increase in deformation temperature. The per-pass reduction was maintained below 0.1 mm, and final sheets with a thickness of 0.5 mm were obtained. Following the final annealing, dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with gauge dimensions of 3 × 22 mm were sliced along the rolling direction and ground with SiC papers up to 2000 grit. Cryo-pre-straining at varying degrees (6, 12, 21, and 36%) introduced hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase, high-density dislocations, twins, and stacking faults, leveraging the reduced stacking fault energy at cryogenic temperatures. The Shimadzu AGS-X 10 kN universal testing machine was employed for cryo-pre-straining at 77 K and subsequent tensile tests at 293 K. For the T0 samples, tensile experiments at 77 K with a crosshead movement speed of 0.75 mm/min were interrupted at plastic strains of 6, 12, 21, and 36% to obtain the cryo-pre-strained samples with different deformation amounts (denoted as T1, T2, T3, and T4, respectively). During cryo-pre-straining, the samples were fully immersed in liquid nitrogen, and the strains were determined by measuring the changes in the displacement of the Vickers microindents (300 gf) before and after loading. The annealed sample and cryo-pre-strained samples were further subjected to tensile testing at 293 K with a constant strain rate of 1 ×10−3s−1 until fracture, and the strains were measured using a digital video extensometer. Condition: uniform coarse-grained structure

Processing Text: CoCrFeNiMo0.2 HEA solid wire was prepared and used for WAAM based on cold metal transfer for the first time. Different deposition strategies (namely single-pass (SP), oscillation (OS), and multi-parallel pass (MPP)) were used to prepare metal wall samples of different thicknesses. The HEA samples' microstructure with different deposition strategies were explored by optical and scanning electron microscopy, as well as the electron backscatter diffraction method. Microhardness and tensile tests were used to evaluate the mechanical properties of different samples. CoCrFeNiMo0.2 HEA wire was used for CMT-WAAM. Three deposition strategies (single-pass (SP), oscillation (OS), and multi-parallel pass (MPP)) were adopted to prepare metal walls of different thicknesses. CoCrFeNiMo0.2 HEA solid wire with a diameter of 1.2 mm was used for WAAM. The chemical composition of the HEA is given in Table 1. According to previous research, the parameters of different deposition strategies were preset, as shown in Table 2. The heat input formula of the sample in the WAAM process has the following form: HI = ηUI/TS, where η is the thermal efficiency (set to 0.8 in this study), U is the welding voltage, I is the welding current, and TS is the torch travel speed. The hardness of the alloy was measured along the building direction (BD) using a Vickers hardness tester (Shimadzu HMV-2T) with a load of 1 kg and a dwell time of 10 s. Processing Text: Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2 EHEA was additively manufactured using the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technique. The pre-alloyed powder of Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2EHEA was prepared through vacuum induction gas atomization. The Ni30Co30Cr10Fe10Al18W2EHEA samples were fabricated using a TruPrint 1000 3D printer (TRUMPF, Germany). The printer is equipped with a Nd:YAG fiber laser, which can generate a maximum laser power of 200 W with a spot diameter of 80 μm. High purity argon gas was used as the protective atmosphere during fabrication to maintain minimum oxygen content (below 200 ppm) inside the printing chamber. A 5 × 5 mm2 checkerboard scanning strategy was employed to suppress cracking and reduce stress. An angle of 67° between successive layers was used to control the anisotropy. A polished 316 stainless steel with a diameter of 98 mm was used as the substrate. The volumetric energy density (VED) has been used as a direct parameter to describe the incident laser energy, which can be calculated as E=P/(νsht) where P is the laser power, νs is the scanning speed, h represents the hatch spacing, and t is the layer thickness. By conducting the parameters optimization process, the optimal combination (laser power: 120 W, scanning speed: 1100 mm/s, hatch spacing: 0.07 mm, layer thickness: 0.02 mm, VED: 77.92 J/mm3) was then decided based on the sample having the highest density of 99.73 %. These parameters were then used to build samples with dimensions of 30 × 14 × 5 mm3 for subsequent microstructural characterizations and mechanical tests. After printing, the samples were annealed at temperatures of 750, 800, 900, and 1000 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 20 °C/min, followed by water quenching. For SEM, specimens were all vibratory-polished to obtain mirror finish of surface and eliminate residual stress from mechanical polishing. For transmission electron microscope (TEM) sample preparation, selected specimens were mechanically polished to a thickness of less than 60 μm and then punched into 3 mm circular discs. The samples were further thinned to approximately 40 nm using ion milling. Tensile tests were performed using a servo-hydraulic 810 MTS testing machine (MTS Corp., USA). The tensile strain was measured using an ARAMIS v6.1 digital image correlation (DIC, GOM Optical Tech., Germany). Uniaxial testing was conducted at a strain rate of 10−3 s−1 at room temperature, with three repeated tests for each condition. Processing state: Heat-treated; Temperature: 750°C for 1 h

Processing Text: The raw materials are sponge titanium, vanadium blocks, molybdenum sheets, chromium particles, sponge zirconium and aluminum particles which the purity are exceeding 99.9 %. 300g ingots were melted in a vacuum non consumable electric arc furnace. In order to ensure uniform composition, the ingots were repeatedly melted three times. After sealing the melted alloy ingot with argon gas and annealing at 1000 °C/6h and water cooling for homogenization treatment, cut it into rectangular original specimens using a wire cutting machine. The sample was subjected to multiple passes of cold rolling (with a reduction rate of less than 10 % per pass), and the thickness reduction of the sample after cold rolling was 20 %, 60 % and 85 %, respectively. The alloy with a 60 % reduction is annealed at 800 °C for 30 min, while the alloy with an 85 % reduction is annealed at 800 °C for 20 min. This is because the time to complete recrystallization decreases with increasing deformation. After testing its organization as recrystallized equiaxed β grains, it was subjected to aging treatment at 550 °C for 5–10 h. After annealing and recrystallization

Processing Text: The designed alloys were prepared using constituent elements of 4 N (99.99 at %) purity. A 100 g batch of each alloy was produced using a laboratory-scale vacuum arc melting unit filled with argon and equipped with a water cooled copper hearth and a non-consumable tungsten electrode. The alloy was melted 6 to 8 times with flipping after each cycle to avoid macro-segregation of elements. The melted samples were subsequently cast into rods (ϕ × l- 3 mm × 80 mm) and slabs ( l× w× t- 80 mm × 10 mm × 6 mm) using a vacuum suction casting unit attached with a water-cooled split copper mould. The cast rods were solutionized at 1175 °C for 20 h and aged at 900 °C for 20 h followed by water quenching. Bulk composition determination and elemental mapping of the cast and solutionized alloys were performed in an electron probe micro analyzer (EMPA, JEOL, JXA-8530F) with both energy and wavelength dispersive detectors (EDS and WDS). The chemical in-homogeneity/segregation of the cast microstructure is removed by solutionizing heat treatment above the solvus temperature. The sub-solvus temperature was determined by thermodynamic calculations using Thermo-Calc. Backscattered SEM micrographs of the peak aged 5Fe alloy (aged at 900 °C for 20 h) show cuboidal shape precipitates distributed uniformly within the matrix. The Fe addition results in the slight change of average γʹ precipitate size (< r> ± σ) of 71 ± 1.1 nm. The Fe addition does not significantly affect the γʹ volume fraction (57 ± 3 (%) for the 5Fe alloy). The lattice misfit across the γ/γʹ interface is measured by performing synchrotron X-ray diffraction analyses on the 5Fe alloy aged at 900 °C for 20 h. The lattice parameter value of γʹ precipitates is measured to be 3.6052 Å for the 5Fe alloy. The lattice misfit values for the 5Fe alloy are measured to be +0.56. Atomic-scale compositional measurements were performed using atom probe tomography (APT, LEAP™ 5000XS, Cameca Instruments), operating in a laser pulsing mode. The laser pulse repetition rate of 250 kHz, a pulse energy of 40 PJ with base temperature of 30 K and 0.5 % detection rate were used for the measurements. The Ga ion milling was performed at 30 kV, with final cleaning at 2 kV and 8 pA current to remove the severely damaged regions. γʹ dissolution temperature of peak aged alloys was determined by heating 50 mg weighted samples in a differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, STA449F3 NETSCH). The sample was heated under an inert argon atmosphere at 10 °C/min till 1250 °C, followed by cooling to 50 °C at a cooling rate of 10 °C/min. Room temperature density measurement was performed using Archimedes principles, as described in ASTM 311-17. Room temperature mechanical property was evaluated by performing a uniaxial tensile test on the flat dog bone-shaped specimen with a gauge dimension of 10 × 1.2 × 1 mm 3in a Gatan micromechanical testing platform at a constant strain rate of 6.7 × 10 -4s -1. For high-temperature mechanical properties, uniaxial compression tests were carried out in a servo-hydraulic driven universal testing system (UTS, DARTEC) at a constant strain rate of 10 -3s -1. Cylindrical samples with dimensions of 3.1 mm in diameter (ϕ) and 5.5 mm in length (L), maintaining an L/ϕ ratio of 1.5-2.0, were used for the compression tests. The samples were heated at a rate of 100 °C/min in a split tube furnace, followed by an isothermal hold at the testing temperature for 10 min to ensure uniform temperature distribution. Processing Text: The Co-Cr-Fe-Ni powders were arranged in equiatomic ratio. A 5.1 g mixture of elemental powders and 1 wt% of stearic acid as a process control agent (PCA) to prevent excessive cold welding during mechanical alloying was mixed in a hardened steel vial. The powder preparation was performed in a glove box, where oxygen and humidity levels were maintained below 0.5 ppm by continuous circulation of high-purity argon gas through a purification system. The mixture was first milled for 30 min. Next, the vials were opened inside the glove box, and 440 C stainless steel balls with a powder-to-ball radio of 1:10 were added. The vials were then sealed in the glove box, and the mechanical alloying process was carried out at room temperature for 20 h using a SPEX 8000 M/D high energy ball miller. To minimize cold welding without the need for additional PCA, the sealed vials were placed in liquid nitrogen for 5 min after every 150 min of mechanical alloying period to reduce their temperature. After mechanical alloying, the vials were placed back inside the glove box, where the as-milled HEA powders were removed and stored until sufficient milling runs were completed to generate enough powder. This was followed by annealing in an argon atmosphere at 500 °C for 1 h to remove the PCA from the as-milled HEA powders. The cold-pressed pellets were then annealed at 700 °C for 1 and 24 h, and at 900 °C for 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h in an argon atmosphere, followed by in-furnace cooling. The consolidated and annealed samples were ground using 800, 1200, and 2500 grits, and then polished to achieve a mirror-like surface for subsequent testing and characterization. 3D-printed; No AlTi addition

The CoCrFeNi powder (Yijing New Material Technology Co., Ltd, China) with purity of 99.85 wt% and the AlTi powder (Zhongkeyannuo New Materials Technology Co., Ltd, China) were prepared by gas atomization. The size range of both powders is 13-53 μm. AlTi powders were added into CoCrFeNi powders in a ratio of 2.5, 5 and 7.5 wt% using a custom-made tumbling powder mixer. Each proportion was blended for 8 h to ensure uniform mixing. All powders were stored in the glove box to maintain purity. Before each printing, powders were heated to 80 °C for 2 h, which is aimed to reduce the moisture of the powders. A 50 × 50 mm 2 size 316L stainless steel substrate was used, and all the samples were fabricated in an argon protection atmosphere with a purity level of 99.98 %. The CoCrFeNi(AlTi) xwt%(x = 0, 2.5, 5 and 7.5) HEAs samples were produced using a 3D printer (SLM 125, SLM solution, Germany). The total printing process was divided into two stages. In the first stage, we printed the CoCrFeNi specimens for parameter optimization. Table 2 summarizes six groups of parameters for optimization printing. Each group was designed according to a different VED, which can be calculated by the following equation [ 26]: VED=pv.h.tWhere p, v, hand tare laser power (W), scan velocity (mm/s), hatch spacing (mm), and layer thickness (mm), respectively. Fig. 1(a) shows the 3D printed density blocks, which were tested the density by using Archimedes method [ 27]. Three density blocks were tested for each group to minimize the error of the measured density. For the second part, we used the parameters of group 2 to produce CoCrFeNi(AlTi) xwt%(x = 0, 2.5, 5 and 7.5) HEAs samples, because samples from group 2 showed the highest relative density of 98.3 %, which is shown in Fig. 1(b). Density blocks with a dimension of 5 × 5 × 6 mm 3 and dog-bone-shaped specimens with a dimension of 45 × 10 × 1 mm 3 were cut from the 316L substrate with wire-electrode cutting. All structural and phase characterization samples were sanded with 1500 grits and polished with diamond and magnesium oxide powders. The samples for scanning electron microscope (SEM) were etched for 10 s in aqua regia consisting of hydrochloric acid (75 vol%) and nitric acid (25 vol%). A model microhardness tester (HV-1000, Yanrunguangji Technology Co., Ltd, China) was used to measure the Vickers hardness with a testing load of 200 gf and loading for 10 s. Each sample was tested for three points to obtain the average microhardness values on the surface. A universal tensile tester (UTM5105, Keshen Electron Co., Ltd, China) was used to perform tensile tests at room temperature. The tensile rate is 10 −3s −1, the width of the specimen is 2 mm, the thickness is 1 mm, and the extensometer with a 10 mm gauge is used. 3D-printed; AlTi addition (x = 7.5)

Processing Text: The present study utilized gas atomized pre-alloyed HX powder as the feedstock for the LPBF process. A BLT-S320 LPBF system (Xi'an Bright Laser Technologies Co., Ltd., Xian, China) was employed, with optimized process parameters to produce nearly fully dense samples: laser power of 300 W, scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, hatch distance of 0.09 mm, and layer thickness of 0.06 mm. A strip scanning strategy with a rotation angle of 67° was employed to perform sequential layer-by-layer fabrication, as illustrated in Fig. 1a. Tensile cylindrical bars with dimensions of Φ14 × 80 mm were built in both horizontal and vertical orientations. Following the LPBF procedure, the tensile sample bars underwent full heat treatments, consisting of HIP followed by ST. The HIP was conducted at 1180 °C and 150 MPa for 3 h with furnace cooling. Then, the ST was conducted at 1180 °C for 1 h with argon quenching. Both HIP and ST were performed under a vacuum of less than 1 × 10 −2Pa. To investigate the effect of temperature on deformation behavior, a series of tensile tests were performed on dog-bone shaped specimens ( Fig. 1c) machined from fully heat-treated (HIP + ST) tensile bars. These tests were performed at temperatures ranging from −50 °C to elevated temperatures. The tensile tests were conducted at a rate of 0.5 mm/min to ascertain the yield strength and 2.5 mm/min to fracture, using a universal testing machine. Specimens were cooled or heated to the test temperature and soaked for 15 min prior to the application of tension. The initial stage of tensile tests (first 0.2 % strain) was measured using an extensometer to ensure precise yield strength (YS) calculations. The tensile tests were repeated three times to quantify the standard error for each type of samples. The specimen used to examine the initial microstructure was obtained from the extremity portion of the tensile bar before testing. The specimen for deformation microstructure analysis was extracted from the gauge section of the tensile specimen, specifically near the fracture region. Temperature: -50 °C; Condition: fully heat-treated (initial hot isostatic pressing followed by solution treatment)

Processing Text: Samples were subjected to a two-step partitioning heat treatment, comprising intercritical annealing (IA) followed by low-temperature partitioning (LTP). Pre-quenched samples were heated to 745 °C or 765 °C for an IA holding time of 40 min and then oil quenched, named as IA 745 or IA 765, respectively. IA 745 or IA 765 samples were reheated to 380 °C, held at this temperature for 30 min for LTP and then oil quenched. Thus, the samples subjected to 745 °C or 765 °C IA process followed by 380 °C LTP treatment are named as IA 745+LTP or IA 765+LTP. Choosing 745 °C and 765 °C as the IA temperature is based on the thermodynamic calculations in Fig. S1(c), which indicates that a sufficient amount of RA can be obtained at room temperature. The temperature for LTP, 380 °C, was selected to sufficiently partition C atoms while avoiding the precipitation of cementite (Fig. S1a). Before conducting the two-step partitioning heat treatment, all specimens were subjected to a pre-quenching treatment, i.e. austenitizing at 950 °C for 20 min and then oil quenched, to obtain a structure of full martensite. The steel was melt using a 25 kg vacuum induction furnace. After casting, the ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 12 h and hot-forged to square bars with a cross-sectional size of 40 mm × 40 mm. Sample: IA 745; Processing: Intercritical annealing (IA)

Processing Text: The experimental HN-TWIP steels, X1MnN30-0.3 and X2MnN30-0.6, were firstly smelted in an induction furnace under the high-pressure N2 atmosphere of 0.8 MPa and 1.5 MPa, respectively. Subsequently, the two steels were hot forged after holding at 1473 K for 2 h and then hot rolled into the 8 mm bars after holding at 1423 K for 1.5 h. Finally, all steels were solution treated at 1323 K for 1 h, followed by water quenching. For convenience, X2Mn30, X1MnN30-0.3 and X2MnN30-0.6 steels in the solution treated state were defined as 0 N, 0.3 N and 0.6 N, respectively. Plate-type tensile specimens were cut from bars with the central axis parallel to the rolling direction (RD), and the gauge dimension was 15 × 3 × 3 mm3 according to the standard GBT 228.1-2010. Deformed 0.3 N and 0.6 N steels with the true strains of 0.25, 0.40 and 0.55 were obtained by interrupting the stretching at a strain rate of 10-3s-1. The sample surfaces were mechanically polished and then electrochemically polished in an electrolyte of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % alcohol at 253 K and 39 V. The samples were mechanically ground to a thickness of about 50 μm, then thinned and polished in an electrolyte of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % alcohol at 243 K. Steel: 0.6N

Under argon protection, a cast Al 0.3CoCrFeNiTi 0.3HEA with a composition purity of 99.9 % was produced using the vacuum induction levitation melting method. Cylindrical specimens with dimensions of φ4 × 6 mm were obtained using electrical discharge machining (EDM) and subjected to quasi-static compression at room temperature with a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The samples underwent mechanical grinding and polishing, followed by electro-polishing in a solution of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol at −25 °C, applying a current of 0.5-0.6 mA for 30 s. To facilitate microscale digital image correlation (DIC) measurements, a random speckle pattern was generated on the specimen surface by first depositing a silver film via magnetron sputtering for 60 s, then immersing the sample in a 1 % NaCl solution for 50 min to ensure uniform adhesion of nanoscale silver speckles. Subsequently, in situ DIC-assisted quasi-static compression tests were performed at room temperature at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The tests were interrupted at applied strains of 3 %, 6 %, and 9 % to conduct microstructural characterization via SEM. Large grain size after long annealing at elevated temperature

Annealed 45 steel with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm was chosen as the substrate. The powder used in this study was CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder with a particle size range of 45-105 μm, produced by high-temperature gas atomization. Before the experiment, place the powder in a vacuum drying oven (Shanghai Jiecheng Experimental Instrument Co., Ltd., DZF-6050) and dry it at 100 °C for 2 h to ensure its uniformity and fluidity. The coating was prepared by using a semiconductor laser (HWL-1500) with a wavelength range of 910-1050 nm and a DPSF scraper powder feeder to transport CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy powder coaxially.
