Ingots of the nominal composition Fe3.75Cr1.25NiAl0.6-xTix (x = 0, 0.15, 0.30 and 0.40, molar ratio) with a weight of 100 g were prepared by arc-melting raw elemental metals (with purities ≥99.9 wt %) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. Each alloy was melted four times to ensure chemical homogeneity in an arc melter (Hotstar). The as-cast alloy plates with dimensions of 10 mm × 5 mm × 80 mm were prepared by copper mold pour casting (Edmund Bühler). The samples cut from the as-cast alloy plates were characterized by means of X-ray diffraction (XRD, Philips PW 1050, Cu-Kα) at a scanning speed of 10°/min, scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Zeiss Supra 55), transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Talos F200) attached with energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). The etching solution used for sample preparation for SEM observations contains 6 % HClO4+ 35 % CH3(CH2)3OH + 59 % CH3OH (volume fraction). TEM samples with a diameter of 3 mm were mechanically ground to a thickness of about 50 μm, thinned by twin-jet electro-polishing in a solution of 10 % HClO4+ 90 % C2H5OH (volume fraction) at a cryogenic temperature of 243 K, and then further ion-milled in a Gatan 691 device. Statistical analysis on the volume fraction of each phase and particle size of precipitates were performed with at least 3 SEM micrographs, using the Image J 1.52V software. Tensile tests were conducted on a universal testing machine (Instron 5582) at a nominal strain rate of 2 × 10−4s−1 at room temperature. The tensile samples were in dog-bone plate shape with a gauge dimension of 14 mm × 2 mm × 0.8 mm. An extensometer was used to measure directly the tensile strain, and at least three specimens of each alloy were tested. Processing Text: A novel NiAlCrFeMo high entropy superalloy was prepared using the vacuum arc melting method, followed by annealing at 800 °C, 1000 °C, and 1200 °C for 10 h. The NiAlCrFeMo high-entropy alloy ingot was prepared by melting bulk Ni, Al, Cr, Fe, and Mo metals of no less than 99.9 % purity using a non-consumable vacuum arc furnace. To ensure the homogeneity of the chemical composition, the alloy ingot was remelted at least four times on both sides before being suction-cast into a water-cooled copper mold. Prior to annealing heat treatment, the cast ingot was sectioned into cylindrical rods with a diameter of 10 mm and a length of 110 mm, as well as other cylindrical and thin sheet specimens, using a DK7735 electrical discharge wire cutting machine. The former was used for high-temperature tensile testing, while the latter were prepared for electron microscopy and XRD analysis. Various samples were first subjected to heat treatment at different temperatures. The annealing temperatures were set at 800 °C, 1000 °C, and 1200 °C, using an SGL-1700C heat treatment furnace, with a heating rate of 10 °C/min. Upon reaching the target temperature, the samples were held for 10 h, followed by water quenching to preserve the high-temperature microstructure. High-temperature tensile tests were conducted on the tensile specimens using a Gleeble-3800 thermal simulation machine, with a strain rate of 0.001 s⁻ 1 and a deformation temperature of 1000 °C. The heating rate was set at 10 K/s, and the specimens were held at the target deformation temperature for 4 min to ensure uniform heating before water quenching to maintain the high-temperature microstructure. During the tensile tests, the stress-strain curves were corrected for adiabatic heating effects to eliminate thermal influences on the results. A NiCr-NiSi thermocouple was welded to the center of each specimen using a spot welder to monitor the temperature in real-time during deformation. The true strain values were calculated based on the specimen's geometry and temperature variations. SEM samples were embedded in phenolic resin, polished to 2.5 μm by PRESI automatic polishing machine, etched in 30 ml HCL +30 ml HNO 3+ 1g CuSO4·5H 2O solution, and placed under Zeiss Sigma 500 SEM equipped with EDS for microstructure and chemical composition observation. The polished surface was subjected to microhardness testing for 15s under a load of 500g using an MHVD−1000IS Vickers microhardness tester. At least 50 measurements were taken for each sample to obtain an average value. The microstructure was further characterized using a JEM-F200 Japanese JEOL field emission transmission electron microscope (TEM). TEM samples were mainly mechanically polished to 30 μm and then ion thinned using a precision ion thinning instrument (Gatan 691). A near-dense LPBF CoCrFeNi HEA was manufactured by fine-tuning the parameters. The LPBF was conducted via the HY-M300 LPBF system (Huayang New Material Technology Co., Ltd.). The LPBF machine is mainly composed of a Yb-fiber laser (wavelength 1060-1100 nm; maximum output power 500 W; spot diameter 80 μm), a laser galvanometric scanning system with an available maximum scanning velocity of 7000 mm/s, an automatic powder delivery system, a building platform with an effective forming space of 300 × 300 × 450 mm 3. The 304 stainless steel plate was chosen as the building substrate upon LPBF with a preheating temperature of 373 K. To avoid excessive oxidation, the LPBF experiment was performed in a protective atmosphere (Ar) with an oxygen concentration below 100 ppm. Various printing parameters were investigated in the LPBF experiment. In this experiment, the samples were fabricated with varied laser power ( P: 220-420 W) and scanning speed ( v: 450-1350 mm/s) at a constant hatch spacing ( h: 90 μm) and layer thickness ( t: 50 μm) to investigate the effect of processing parameters on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the as-printed HEA specimens. The scanning strategy was chosen as the strip scanning strategy, keeping the interlayer rotation angle of 67°. The samples with two geometries were prepared by LPBF: cuboid samples with a dimension of 9 × 9 × 5.5 mm 3for microstructural analysis and cuboid samples with a dimension of 50 × 15 × 2.5 mm 3for mechanical test. Dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 12 mm were prepared via electro-discharge machining. For microstructural observation, the samples were first mechanically grounded by SiC sandpapers from 400 grit to 2000 grit, followed by electropolishing using 20 % nitric acid and 80 % ethanol at 20 V. The tensile test was performed on the HUALONG 50KN universal testing machine at a strain rate of 0.001 s −1at room temperature. The surface of the tensile specimens was grounded by 2500 grit SiC sandpapers before the tensile test. Condition: as-printed; Processing method: LPBF; Associated with superior mechanical properties including over 50% ductility

Processing Text: The 35Co-34Ni-24Cr-7Mo alloy, with the chemical composition presented in Table 1, was prepared as described previously [45]. The solution-treated plate was cold rolled to the thickness of 1.5 mm (88 % reduction in thickness) and annealed at 950 °C for 750 s in an electrical furnace with an ambient atmosphere. Based on the ASTM E8M standard, sub-size dimensions (gage length: 25 mm, width: 6 mm, thickness: 1.5 mm), were used for the tensile test samples, which were prepared along the rolling direction by a wire-cutting process followed by polishing to achieve a smooth surface. The tensile tests were performed with a computer-controlled GOTECH AI 7000-10 tones tensile tester machine at a constant speed of 3 mm/min. To provide different deformation temperatures, samples were pre-cooled for 5 min in liquid nitrogen (∼ 77 K), dry ice + ethanol (∼ 195 K), and an ambient (∼ 295 K) environment, and then tensile tests were performed in a chamber with the mentioned environments to keep the temperature stable during deformation. To observe the microstructure before and after deformation, the center of the gage in the tensile test sample (RD-ND plane) was electro-polished and, consequently, electro-etched by the electrolyte of 35 vol% H 2SO 4in methanol with the voltage of 6 V. The samples were mechanically polished up to 1200 grit SiC papers and subsequently electropolished with a 92 % HCl + 8 % CH 3COOH solution. For this purpose, samples with a diameter of 3 mm and a thickness of 60 μm were prepared using a jet polish technique with HNO 3acid. Condition: Cryogenic Temperature (77 K)

A Ti-4Al-6V-5Mo-3Cr-1Zr (wt%) cylindrical rod with a diameter of ∼150 mm was used in this work. The as-received alloy has a bi-modal microstructure and its β-transus temperature was determined to be 830 ± 5 °C through metallographic examination. A sub-transus solution treatment was performed at 820 °C for 30 min and the sample in this condition will be referred to as “ST820”. Afterwards, ST820 was subjected to a dual-step aging treatment where the first-step aging was conducted at 300 °C for 5 h, 10 h or 100 h, and the second-step aging at 520 °C or 600 °C for 2 h. Hereafter, the Ti-46531 alloy in these dual-aged conditions will be referred to as “300°C/Xh+520°C” or “300°C/Xh+600°C” (X = 5, 10, 100). In addition, single-step aging was also conducted at 300 °C for 5 h, 10 h or 100 h, respectively. These specimens will be denoted as “300°C/ Xh ( X= 5, 10, 100)”. To clarify the nucleation mechanism of the α-phase, further short-term aging experiments were performed or 5 min at 520 °C or 600 °C on the 300°C/100 h sample, and these two specimens will be accordingly referred to as “300°C/100h+520°C/5min” and “300°C/100h+600°C/5min”. Each sample was wrapped in pure titanium foil and encapsulated in an evacuated quartz tube (vacuum level ∼ 5 × 10 −3Pa) to minimize the oxidation during the heat treatment. All samples were water quenched by breaking the quartz tubes immediately after the heat treatment. Aged at 600 °C; Dual-aged sample

Processing Text: The RHEAs with nominal composition Ti50Nb(20-x)V20Al10Six (x=0, 0.5, 1, 1.5 at%) were fabricated by vacuum melting furnace using 99.95 % (wt%) purity raw materials under a Ti-gettered argon atmosphere. The Nb-V (melting current ∼500 A, melting time ∼90 s) and Ti-Al-Si (melting current ∼300 A, melting time ∼90 s) intermediate alloys were prepared separately to prevent the volatilization of Al and Si. These intermediate alloys were subsequently merged to obtain the final button ingots. All button ingots underwent a minimum of six remelting (melting current ∼450 A, melting time ∼90 s) to ensure chemical homogeneity. And then, the button ingots were drop-cast (melting current ∼450 A, melting time ∼90 s, cooling rate ∼103K/s) into copper molds measuring 40 mm × 20 mm × 5.5 mm under argon protection. The cast samples were cold rolled with a thickness reduction of 80 %, then they were annealed at 1000 ℃ for 24 hours, followed by air-cooled. Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: The EHESs ingots with nominal compositions of Ni70-xCo10Cr20Alx (x= 17, 18, 19 at%, denoted by Al17, Al18, and Al19, respectively) were prepared by vacuum arc-melting a mixture of pure metals (purity > 99.9 wt%) in Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingots were flipped and smelted at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity and then were drop-cast into water-cooled copper molds with dimensions of 10 ×10 ×65 mm3 and 13 ×13 ×50 mm3. Part of the cast bars were annealed at 750 ℃ for 7 d. The density of the EHESs is measured by the Archimedes drainage method. Phase identification was investigated by X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation (Rigaku Kmax 2500 V). The microstructure and chemical composition were characterized by using a ZEISS SUPRA 55 scanning electron microscope (SEM) in secondary electron (SE2) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) modes as well as an F20 transmission electron microscope (TEM). The SEM and EBSD samples were prepared by electrolytic polishing in the solution with 90 % ethanol and 10 % perchloric acid at 30 V. The TEM samples were thinned by ion-milling. Tensile tests at ambient temperature and 750 ℃ in air were carried out at a strain rate of 10−3s−1. The dog-bone-shaped specimens with gauge geometry of 15 ×3 ×2 mm3 were used in the test. An extensometer to directly monitor strain was employed in the ambient-temperature tensile test. For the 750 ℃ tensile test, strains were determined indirectly from the load displacement and were further confirmed by measuring changes in sample gauge length before and after testing. As for the tensile load-unload-reload tests, the unloading-reloading process began at an engineering strain of 1 % and then was unloaded in a load-control mode to 40 N at an unloading rate of 10−3s−1, followed by reloading whenever the engineering strain increases 1 % until the fracture. Condition: ambient temperature; Microstructure: lamellar FCC(L12) and B2(BCC) phases with nano-precipitates

Processing Text: The experiment utilized vacuum-atomized 15-5PH stainless steel powder produced by Oerlikon Metco, Switzerland. The powder exhibited good sphericity, with a smooth surface and uniform morphology. The particle sizes for D10, D50, and D90 were 19.4 μm, 33.2 μm, and 50.9 μm, respectively. The primary chemical composition of the powder (wt. %) was Fe-12.48Cr-3.55Ni-3.04Cu-0.18Nb-0.48Mn-0.46Si-0.0509C. Subsequently, the 15-5PH samples required for this experiment were fabricated using the HBD 280 metal LPBF system from Guangdong HanBang Laser Technology Co., Ltd. Each layer was printed with a 67° rotation relative to the previous one. Based on previous studies, the optimal process parameters were: laser power ( P) of 260 W, hatch space ( H) of 0.06 mm, scanning speed ( V) of 1200 mm/s, and layer thickness ( T) of 0.04 mm. The two heat treatment processes adopted afterwards were ST-AT (solid solution at 1040 °C for 40 min, water cooling, aging at 482 °C for 1 h, then air cooling) and AT (aging at 482 °C for 1 h, then air cooling), respectively. The chemical composition of the powder was analyzed using inductively coupled plasma emission spectroscopy, while the particle size distribution was measured with a Bettersize 2600 laser particle size analyzer. After the sample (10 × 10 × 10 mm 3) was polished and ground, it was corroded for 15 s at 25 V in a 15% HF (vol. %) aqueous solution. Utilizing a mixed solution of 5% HClO 4+95% CH 3COOH (vol%), the electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) sample was corroded for 30 s at a voltage of 25 V. The microstructure was then examined using a Leica DMI3000 M-type metallographic microscope (OM) and the crystal structure, texture analysis and dislocation characteristics were examined Gemini SEM 300 type scanning electron microscope (SEM). Tiny cylinders, 3 mm in diameter and less than 0.5 mm thick, were cut from a substrate via wire cutting, then manually ground to 60 μm. Finally, transmission electron microscope (TEM) samples were further thinned using the ion thinning method and examined using a JEOL JEM-2100F SEM. Phase analysis was performed with a SmartLab X-ray diffraction (XRD) system carrying Cu Kα. The V-notch impact test specimen (55 × 10 × 10 mm³, notch depth 2 mm, root radius 0.25 mm) underwent Charpy impact testing using a JBN500 metal pendulum impact tester. Rod-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge diameter of ϕ5 mm and the gauge length of 25 mm were subjected to room temperature tensile performance tests on a DN200 universal tensile testing machine at a strain rate of 1.3 × 10 −3s −1. The hardness was measured using an HRS-150 Rockwell hardness tester with a load of 1470 N and 10 s dwell time. The morphologies of the tensile and impact fractures were examined using SEM (Gemini SEM 300). Processing state: AT (heat-treated); Microstructure: dual-phase α-martensite and γ-austenite
Processing Word: Processing state: AT (heat-treated); Microstructure: dual-phase α-martensite and γ-austenite

Tensile tests were performed at room temperature using an Instron 5569 universal tensile tester with a tensile load of 100 kN and a strain rate of 0.5 mm/min. Processing Text: Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloys with flat surface, low porosity and excellent mechanical properties were prepared by Laser Metal Deposition (LMD) and annealed (A) using secondary recycled Al-Mg-Sc-Zr powders in an open environment. The optimal LMD parameters are laser power 1800 W, scanning speed 5 mm/s and scanning spacing 3 mm The Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy deposited by multi-layer multi-track under optimal parameters and subsequent annealing treatment displays a flat surface, porosity of 2.08%, hardness of 134 HV, ultimate tensile strengthen (UTS) of 348 MPa, yield strength (YS) of 235 MPa and uniform elongation (εu) of 16.71%. The in-situ heat treatment induced by the subsequent multi-layer multi-track deposition transformed the alternately distributed coarse and fine equiaxed grain structure into a homogeneous grain structure. The Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy, developed by adding Sc and Zr elements to the traditional Al-Mg alloy, has attracted much attention due to its high specific strength, corrosion resistance, and weldability. In order to eliminate the internal stresses generated during the manufacturing process, the LMD-prepared Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy was annealed (A) at 300 °Cfor 2 h. The initial powder is argon atomized HS5501 powder produced by Jiangxi Baohang New Materials Co., Ltd. This study is collected all unmelted the argon atomized HS5501 powder after LMD under a closed argon protective atmosphere. Then, this recycled powder was filtered through a 150 μm sieve to ensure the removal of spatter and powder agglomerates. Then put secondary recycled Al-Mg-Sc-Zr powders into a vacuum drying oven at 120 °C to be dried for 2 h. The LMD experiments were carried out in an open environment using a LMD facility equipped with a 2000 W semiconductor fiber laser with an argon protected airflow at the nozzle. The processing parameters are as follows: laser power (P) was 1200-1800 W, the scanning speed (v) was 3-5 mm/s, the scanning space (l) was 2-3 mm, the spot of the laser was 3 mm, the flow rate of the protective gas was 10 L/min, the flow rate of the powder feed gas was 15 L/min, and the scanning strategy was unidirectional reciprocating scanning. Since aluminum alloy has high reflectivity, in order to prevent the reflected laser from damaging the cladding head, the LMD process makes the laser beam at an angle of 80° to the substrate. Processing Text: An irregular shape of pure Cr powder (>99% purity, JFE Material, Japan) was supplied as a starting material. The average particle size was measured using a Mastersizer 3000E particle size analyzer (Malvern Panalytical, UK), and the laser absorption of powder was determined using an ultraviolet-visible near-infrared spectrophotometer (V-770, Jasco, Japan). In addition, a rotary-drum-type powder flowability measuring device (Revolution Powder Analyzer, Mercury Scientific, US) was used to measure the rest fractal, avalanche angle. As described in Fig. 1(b), an L-PBF machine (EOS M290, EOS, Germany) equipped with a 400 W Yb-fiber laser as the primary heat source was used to fabricate the samples with dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 5 mm along the x-, y-, and z-axes, respectively. Preheat temperatures of 80 °C and 200 °C were applied. The 80 °C preheat temperature was used to avoid unexpected temperature fluctuations caused by laser energy input during the manufacturing process and to maintain a constant fabrication condition. For the 200 °C preheat temperature, the maximum preheat temperature setting of the equipment used. Furthermore, shorter scan length samples were fabricated in size of 5 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm at a preheat temperature of 200 °C to maximize the heat accumulation effect. A bi-directional scanning with 90° rotation between layers was used to minimize the residual stress, and various input energy density (ED) conditions were attempted to optimize the process parameters. The densification of the as-built Cr samples was measured by the Archimedes principle using ethanol at room temperature. The theoretical density of 7.19 g/cm3 for pure Cr was used to determine the relative density. The specimens were then sectioned on the yz-plane representing the x-scan direction by wire electrical discharge machine, and prepared as mirror polish surface quality. The relative densities of specimens were additionally evaluated for representative samples using an optical microscope (OM; Eclipse LV-150, Nikon, Japan) and ImageJ software. In terms of the mechanical properties evaluation, hardness was assessed using Vickers (HMV-G, Shimadzu, Japan) and nanoindentation (ENT-1100a, ELONIX, Japan) tests. The former test was performed with a test force of 0.2 kgf, while the latter test was carried out using a Berkovich tip at a force of 10 mN. Furthermore, compression tests (AG-X, Shimadzu, Japan) at room temperature were conducted at a nominal strain rate of 1.7 × 10−4s−1 condition employing the rectangular shape of the test samples with dimensions of 2 × 2 × 5 mm. The laser heat source behavior of multi-scan tracks was estimated by using a finite element thermal model simulation (COMSOL Multiphysics 6.1, COMSOL Inc., Sweden). Processing Text: The deformation production of the ferrite in the wire is simply dislocation, which subsequently transforms to subgrain boundary and high angle grains boundary. The microstructural evolution of ferrite is simpler. The dominant deformation mode in ferrite is dislocation. Thus, the deformation structure at small strain is mainly manifested as the dislocation cells with LAGB. However, due to the higher drawing strain in this study, these subgrains with LAGB evolved into HAGB via continuous rotation, thus refining the ferrite grains. Therefore, when the drawing strain reaches ε= 6.65, the boundary spacing in the ferrite phase decreases to 56 nm in average. The contribution of yield strength is the sum of dislocation strengthening and grain boundary strengthening. Processing Text: The deformation product of stainless steel with different Md30 versus deformation true strain. The boundary spacing in ferrite and austenite versus the drawing strain. The deformation mechanism of austenite phase in single phase austenite stainless steel or duplex stainless steel has previously been well summarized to follow the steps: dislocation gilding, formation of stacking fault, formation of twinning or ε-martensite and finally formation of α′-martensite from ε-martensite or twinning. The microstructure characterization confirms that twinning plays the key role in the deformation mechanism of the austenite during the drawing process, while α- or ε-martensite phase is formed after cold drawing even at the drawing stain ε= 6.65. The formation of ε-martensite or deformation twinning depends on the stacking fault energy (SFE) of the austenite phase. For measuring the SFE of the austenite during drawing deformation, 2507 DSS rod was tensile strained to 2% strain at ambient temperature. A TEM experiment was employed to measure the SFE of the austenite at room temperature. The yield strength of the austenite phase in 2507 DSS can be calculated according to the Hall-Petch equation. Processing Text: The pre-alloyed Ti-45Nb powder used in this study was provided by Ningxia Orient Ta Ind Co. With a powder particle size of 15-53 μm, and the powder was vacuum-dried before use. A process parameter with a laser power of 380 W, a scanning speed of 550 mm/s, a layer thickness of 0.03 mm, and a hatch distance of 0.08 mm was selected for producing LPBFed Ti-45Nb specimens using a DiMetal-100 device under a protective argon (99.99%) atmosphere. Based on the phase diagram of the Ti-Nb alloy, five types of heat treatments (at temperatures of 250 °C, 500 °C, 750 °C, 1000 °C, and 1250 °C, respectively) were used to investigate the phase transition. The as-built specimens and heat-treated specimens were named RT, HT250, HT500, HT750, HT1000, and HT1250, respectively, and are listed in Table 1. The heating rate for all heat treatment processes was 2 °C/min. All LPBFed specimens were heated to the preset temperature, held at that temperature for 24 h, and then cooled to 25 °C in the furnace. Heat treatment was carried out in a vacuum tube furnace (KSL-1500X-S). The phase formation and microstructural features were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku MiniFlex 600, Cu Kα). Microstructure characterization was performed by scanning electron microscope (SEM, Phenom pro). Furthermore, grain orientation was characterized by using FE-SEM with an electron backscatter diffraction device (EBSD, EDAX-TSL system). Room temperature compression tests were carried out using a universal testing machine (E44.304, MTS Co., China) at a speed of 0.001 mm/s. To ensure the repeatability of the results, at least 5 specimens were measured for each condition, and an extensometer was also used to ensure the accuracy of the strain measurements. The slope of the linear portion of the stress-strain curve was used to determine the Young's modulus for each specimen, and the Young's moduli of all specimens was calculated 8 times to minimize errors. Microhardness testing was performed on different types of specimens using an indenter (FM-110, Future-Tech) with a maximum load of 100 gf and a 10 s dwell time; the distance between individual indents was 80 μm. Each specimen was tested for 36 indentations to ensure the accuracy of the data. Sliding wear tests were carried out by a pin-disc wear instrument (Rtec, MFT-5000, USA) at room temperature under dry conditions with loads of 20 N and 40 N, a test-disc speed of 400 rpm, a wear radius of 20 mm, and a wear time of 60 min. The annealed GCr15 plate, with a hardness of 58-62 HRC, was used for the grinding disk, while the tested specimens served as pins during the wear test, and its working principle is shown in Fig. 1. The coefficients of friction (COFs) were automatically recorded as a function of the time of the cycle. In addition, the average COF was measured using a separate load system in contact with the continuous lever arm and recorded using a Nanovea Tribometer system. All of the data (specific wear rate and average COF) were measured at least three times to ensure the accuracy of the results. Condition: RT (Room Temperature); Microstructure: mainly β-TiNb phase

Processing Text: Equimolar CoCrNi MEA was prepared by arc-melting Co, Cr, and Ni mixtures with 99.99 % purity in a high-purity argon atmosphere. The ingot was remelted more than five times before the drop-cast process to ensure homogeneity. Subsequently, the as-cast CoCrNi MEA ingot was cold-forged by a 50 % reduction in thickness. Afterward, the alloy was annealed at 1173K for 1 h to reduce deformation-induced defects and promote recrystallization. Quasi-static compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^−1 s^−1 were performed on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 6 mm using an Instron 5969 testing machine. Dynamic compression tests with strain rates ranging from 2.6 × 10^3 s^−1 to 6.2 × 10^3 s^−1 were carried out on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 3 mm using a SHPB system. Stop-ring technology was introduced to control the strain during the dynamic compressions. The ramp wave and shock compression experiments were conducted using the CQ-4 magnetically driven system, delivering a pulsed current with a peak value of 4 MA and a rising time of 500 ns, developed by the Institute of Fluid Physics, China Academy of Engineering Physics. Multi-level characterizations were conducted to explore the intrinsic mechanisms of CoCrNi MEA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed using a JEOL JSM-7100F field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). An acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a specimen tilt angle of 70°, and a working distance of 15 mm were used in the EBSD observations. A JEM-2100F transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV to uncover microscopic deformation mechanisms. Condition: Base material; Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: The high-Mn steel plates were produced using a blast furnace. The cast ingot underwent solution treatment, followed by hot rolling to a thickness of 20 mm and controlled cooling. A single-mode 20 kW fiber laser (IPG, YLS-20,000-S2T) was used for welding. The bead-on-plate process was applied to specifically focus on manganese vaporization behavior, using Ar shielding gas (20 l/min), a welding velocity of 8.3 mm/s, and laser power of 3 kW. The focusing lens had a focal length of 300 mm. The laser beam had a diameter of 200 μm, a wavelength of 1080 nm, and a beam parameter product of 8 mm mrad. The laser defocusing (LD) was set to 0, +10, and +20 mm above the surface; for convenience, these three conditions are referred to as ‘LD0’, ‘LD10’, and ‘LD20’ in the study. The heat input was 361 J/mm, and the energy density ranged from 188 to 2302 J/mm² with respect to the various LDs. The tensile specimens (Shimadzu, AG-X Plus 300 kN) with a 5 mm gauge length and 1.5 mm thickness were prepared in the transverse direction from the top surface of the laser-welded specimens. Processing Text: This research aimed to enhance the strength and ductility of spray formed (SFed) 7050 aluminum (Al) alloy through hot extrusion and subsequent heat treatment. The as-deposited samples were heated at (300°C@24h + 470°C@24h) and cooled in air (pre-treated state). Afterwards, the billets were axially extruded into rods at 420 °C using different ERs (5, 9, 16, 25) with an extrusion speed of 0.8 mm/s. The as-extruded rods were solution treated (477℃@1h) and quenched into water (as-quenched state). Then, the aging treatment was performed at 120°C@16 h to achieve peak-aged state according to previous works. Microstructures were analyzed by optical microscopy (OM, Zeiss Microscope Axio Imager A2), scanning electron microscopy (SEM, TESCAN MIRA 3) equipped with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Talos F200X) equipped with scanning TEM mode (STEM) and high resolution TEM (HRTEM) technology. Smooth rods of 18 mm diameter (Arithmetic Average Roughness − Ra = 0.8 μm) were produced by voestalpine Böhler Edelstahl GmbH & Co KG, Austria and re-fer AG, Switzerland. These rods are fabricated sequentially by a hot rolling process in several steps to the targeted diameter, followed by air cooling. Rods were machined to 4.5 mm diameter and 9 mm height cylindrical samples by mechanical lath for the compression experiments. Cylindrical specimens were placed in a modified Bähr DIL 805 A/D dilatometer. During creep tests, the samples were subjected to targeted load values with respect to the yield strength (0.7 σ YS= 337 MPa, 0.9 σ YS= 433 MPa, 1.3 σ YS= 625 MPa, 1.6 σ YS= 770 MPa). Compression creep and stress relaxation tests with High Energy X-ray Diffraction (HEXRD) were conducted at the P07 beamline, experimental hutch 3, PETRA III, Deutsches Elektronen Synchrotron (DESY) Hamburg, Germany. The high energy X-rays of 0.124 Å wavelength (∼100 keV) were incident on the specimen during the test, and the diffraction rings were captured using PerkinElmer XRD image-plate detector. The ingots of HEAs with a nominal composition of Al 0.4CoCrFe 2Ni 2/TiC were prepared using a vacuum arc furnace. Ceramic reinforcement phases were added to the alloy by mass percentage, including TiC (μm) at 2.5 wt%. TiC (μm) powder was mixed with Ni powder. These two groups of powders were blended thoroughly using a ball mill to ensure uniform dispersion within the alloy. The sphere to material mass ratio is 10:1. YLJ-15 T manual tableting machine was employed for mechanical pressing to obtain block preforms made from composite powder with the pressure holding time is 10 min. The total mass of the matrix alloy was 80 g. Al, Cr, Ni-TiC (μm), and Fe-TiC (nm) metal raw materials were placed inside a vacuum arc furnace and melted under protection from ultra-high purity argon gas at 1 × 10 -4Pa pressure level. The ingots underwent five repeated melting cycles to guarantee consistent chemical composition. The size of the tissue cut by the electric spark wire cutting machine was 10 * 10 * 10 mm. The tensile sample is shown as a dog bone in Fig. 3, and the size of the transmission test sample is 10 * 10 * 0.5 mm. The as-cast samples were ground, polished and electrolytically corroded. The transparent thin foil for transmission electron microscope (TEM) observation was prepared by mechanical grinding, polishing and double jet electrolytic polishing technology, after the sheet with a thickness of 500 μm was cutting from the alloy. The tensile samples like dog bone with a gauge length of 7 mm, a width of 4 mm, and a thickness of 2 mm were subjected to tensile tests at room temperature on a universal electronic testing machine (MTS-E45) with a strain rate of 10 −3mm·s −1. Processing Text: The Al 9.0Hf 30.3Nb xTa 30.3-xTi 30.3(x = 0,10,15 at.%) RMPEAs were prepared by vacuum arc melting using pure metals Al, Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti (purity higher than 99.9 wt.%). The cylindrical sample of Φ 3 mm × 6 mm was cut from the alloy ingot by wire cutting method, and the quasi-static compression test was carried out on the universal material testing machine. To evaluate the quasi-static tensile properties, dog bone specimens, with the gauge length, width and thickness respectively of 8 mm, 2 mm and 1 mm, were cut from the ingot using electrospark wire-electrode cutting. The hardness of the alloys was evaluated using Vickers hardness tester under 200 g for 15 s and each sample was measured at least 9 points. The EBSD samples were mechanically ground and then electro-polished in an electrolyte solution of 10 vol% HClO 4, 90 vol% CH 3OH with an applied voltage of 20 V for 40 s at −30 °C. The (FeCoNi)90Al10 MEA was produced in a 2-kg vacuum induction furnace using high-purity raw material of Fe (99.91 wt %), Co (99.98 wt %), Ni (99.98 wt %), and Al (99.7 wt %). The alloy ingots were kept at 1100 °C for 1 h, and then forged into 40 × 26 × 13 mm3 plates within the temperature range of 1000-1100 °C. The plates were solution treated at 1200 °C for 1 h, followed by water quenching, then cold rolled to 1.4 mm thickness (reduction rate 78 %). The cold rolled sheets were solution treated at 1210 °C for 3 min, followed by water cooling. Finally, the sheets were aged at 620 °C for 30, 45, 60, and 120 min, respectively, followed by water cooling. The heat treatment process was determined using the TCHEA4 database of Thermo-Calc software. The solution treatment at 1210 °C could ensure both 0C and 0.2C alloys exhibited a single FCC structure, and ageing treatment at 620 °C ensured a sufficient L12 phase and a few B2 phases. Processing Text: Samples were cut into cylindrical shapes with dimensions of (Φ) 5 mm × 6.8 mm from cast ingot solidified under normal pressure. Subsequently, the samples were wrapped in an insulating layer and a graphite tube. The pressure device of the LPR1000 2-6-8 multi-stage high-pressure apparatus consists of an axially cylindrical pressure chamber, resembling to a piston-cylinder system. Pressure is applied to the octahedral talc sample assembly through primary and secondary pressure transmission modules, driven by the press. Graphite is used as the heating element, and the heating temperature is controlled by adjusting the heating power. The sample was heated to 1550 °C under an external pressure of 6 GPa for 60 minutes, after which the heating device was turned off and the pressure was released to atmospheric levels. The SSS and HPS alloys were subsequently aged at 400°C, 450°C, and 500°C in an argon atmosphere for varying durations up to 10 hours. The samples were ground using SiC paper and polished with diamond suspension. A solution with the composition of FeCl 3(2 g), HCl (3 ml), and C 2H 5OH (100 ml) was used as the etchant. The microstructure was observed using a HITACHI SU50000 field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) and an FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). Image Pro Plus 6.0 software was used to measure the area fraction and size of various precipitates based on TEM images. The foil thickness in the beam direction was determined by measuring the spacing of Kossel-Mollenstedt fringes in a {111} αreflection in a < 011 > αtwo-beam convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) pattern. X-ray diffraction (XRD, X’PERT X-ray, Holland) with diffraction angle (2θ) ranging from 30° to 100° and a scanning speed of approximately 1°/min was utilized to determine the crystal structure of the alloys. The DC conductivity measurement at room temperature (300 K) was conducted using the traditional four-probe technique. The samples measured are approximately 3 mm in length, 1 mm in width, and 0.3 mm in thickness. Four platinum wires were affixed to the samples using conductive silver paste. The DC resistance of the samples was initially measured using a physical property measuring system (PPMS, Dynacool-14T, USA) and subsequently converted to DC conductivity. Vickers hardness testing of the specimens was performed using a Huayin HV-1000A microhardness tester with a load of 200 g and an indentation time of 15 seconds. The reported hardness values represent the average of eight separate measurements. The compression test was conducted using a SANS CMT6000 universal testing machine with a compression speed of 0.5 mm/min. The compression specimen measured are 2 mm in diameter and 3 mm in length. At least three measurements were taken for each sample to minimize experimental errors. Process: P1; Final peak-aged state

FeMnCoCr spherical powders were produced using gas-atomization (Arcast, Oxford, ME) and sieved to achieve particle sizes ranging from 15 to 45 µm. The printing was carried out on a FormAlloy X2 DED system equipped with an IPG Photonics Nd:YAG continuous wave fiber laser, operating at a maximum power of 500W and a spot size of 1.2 mm. To prevent oxidation, the build chamber was purged with argon to reduce the oxygen level below 100 ppm. Blocks with dimensions of 26 mm × 10 mm x 6 mm (WxLxH) were printed on a 304L stainless steel substrate using a rectilinear infill scan strategy. A hatch spacing of 0.6 mm, alternating layer angles of +67° and −67°, and a layer height of 0.2 mm were used. All compositions were printed under consistent processing conditions of a laser power of 250W, a scanning speed of 800 mm/min, and a powder feed rate of 0.5 rpm. Processing Text: Alloys with a nominal composition of Co 37Cr 14Ni 37Al 6Ti 6(at. %), hereinafter referred to as Al 6Ti 6, were prepared in a vacuum furnace by arc-melting a mixture of the constituent elements with a high-purity (>99.9% pure) supplied by Beijing Ryubon New Material Technology, LTD. All ingots were melted at least four times with magnetic stirring, then suctioned into a copper mold (10× 100 × 2 mm 3). The as-cast ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h to eliminate elemental segregation during solidification, followed by oil quenching. The samples were cold rolled along the longitudinal direction with ∼65 % reduction in thickness, followed by a recrystallization annealing (RA) at 1050 °C for 2 min, and oil quenching, hereinafter referred to as Al 6Ti 6-RA. Part of the RA sheets was subjected to aging (RAA) at 700 °C for 4 h, followed by water quenching, hereinafter referred to as Al 6Ti 6-RAA. The aging temperature of 700 °C was chosen because it facilitates the formation of a hierarchical precipitation microstructure. All the heat treatments were conducted under an argon atmosphere in a high-temperature vacuum Muffle furnace. Notably, the heat treatment conditions of Al 6Ti 6alloy include solution treatment, cold rolling, RA, and aging, which were widely used for L1 2phase alloys in the previous reports [ 8-10, 14]. In addition, it is noted that the concentration of Cr element in the Al 6Ti 6alloy is lower than that of Co and Ni since an excessive concentration of Cr can result in the precipitation of a brittle phase. Condition: tested at ambient temperature (298 K); Microstructure: hierarchical L1 2 precipitates

Processing Text: A Cu-Cr-Ni-Co-Si alloy was prepared in the vacuum induction furnace with the raw materials of electrolytic-grade copper (99.99 wt%, 4 N), pure nickel (4 N), pure silicon (4 N), pure cobalt (4 N) and Cu-10Cr alloy under argon atmosphere. The chemical composition of the Cu-Cr-Ni-Si-Co alloy (as shown in Table 1) was determined by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer (ICP-OES, SPECTRO Analytical Instruments GmbH, Kleve, Düsseldorf, Nordrhein-Westphalia, Germany). Prior to ECAP deformation, the solid solution alloys were treated at 950 °C for 1 h before quenching in water. ECAP samples with the dimensions of 80 × 10 × 10 mm 3 were cut from solid solution alloys along the hot rolling direction. As shown in Fig. 1(a), the ECAP die is designed as a two-piece split mold with a channel angle Φ = 90° and an outer curvature of Ψ = 37° [ 35]. The billet was subjected to ECAP processing up to 4 times through the processing route (Bc). The billet was rotated 90° in the same direction on the longitudinal axis between successive passes. Finally, the ECAPed samples were aged at 400 °C, 450 °C, and 500 °C for different durations, after which the micro-hardness tests were performed, intending to determine the appropriate aging temperature and time for the following experiments. Subsequently, the aged samples were directly cold-deformation (CD) by rolling with an 80 % reduction, then aging at 400 °C, 450 °C, and 500 °C for different durations. The scanning strategy, layer thickness (τ= 40 μm), hatch spacing (h= 90 μm), and laser power (P= 270 W) were kept constant for all samples. The scanning speed (V) was varied from 600 to 1400 mm/s to adjust the VED within a defect-free processing range. Three typical laser scanning speeds―600 mm/s, 1000 mm/s, and 1400 mm/s―were employed to investigate the effect of LPBF heat input on recrystallization behavior. According to VED= P/(V·τ·h), the VED values for the three scanning speeds are 125 J/mm3 (VED-125), 75 J/mm3 (VED-75), and 53 J/mm3 (VED-53), respectively. HIP treatment was conducted at a supersolvus temperature of 1210 °C, with a pressure of 180 MPa and a holding time of 3 h, to investigate recrystallization behavior. Subsequently, the HIP-treated samples underwent a SHT consisting of two stages: holding at 1120 °C for 2 h, followed by 850 °C for 24 h. The AB samples were electrolytically etched using a solution containing 12 ml H3PO4, 40 ml HNO3 and 48 ml H2SO4 at a voltage of 6 V for 5-10 s to observe the cellular structure and MC-type carbides. The heat-treated samples were etched using the Kalling's reagent No.2 (5g CuCl2 in 100 ml hydrochloric acid and 100 ml ethanol) to reveal the grain boundaries, carbides and γ′ phases. Samples for examination by TEM were prepared as 5 mm diameter discs with a thickness of 50 μm and milled using an ion beam with a Gatan 695 ion mill. All tensile samples were treated by HIP and subsequent SHT (i.e., HIP + SHT). Temperature: 23 °C; Recrystallization fraction: lowest

Processing Text: In this work, a high-strength-ductility Ti2AlNb alloy is fabricated by hot rolling the compact prepared by spark plasma sintering. The microstructure and tensile properties of the rolled sheets were controlled by changing the thickness reduction and rolling pass. The starting material was pre-alloyed Ti2AlNb powders, which were fabricated by gas atomization. The powders had a composition of 20.3 % Al, 24.7 % Nb and 55.0 % Ti. The powders were sintered in a ZLY-60 sintering furnace. High-strength graphite was used as the sintering die. A glass tube, with the main function of preventing the current from flowing through the sintering die, was assembled between the die and the powders. The graphite paper and TC4 slice were placed between the graphite electrode and the powders to prevent the diffuse of C element. The vacuum degree during sintering was below 10−3Pa. The sintering temperature, pressure and time were 1060 °C, 50 MPa and 10 min respectively. The sintered compact had a diameter of 40 mm and a height of 15 mm. After sintering, the compact was cut into square blocks with dimensions of 28 mm × 28 mm × 3 mm. Then, these blocks were coated with parting agent (ZrO2) before assembled in the packs. The packs were made of 304 stainless steel. It has two main functions. The first is protecting the block from oxidation. The second is providing a compressive stress, avoiding the edge cracking of the sheet. The rolling machine was 400 two-roll asynchronous hot rolling machine. Before rolling, the sealed pack was heated to 1030 °C in a high temperature furnace and kept for 15 min. A box-type high temperature furnace named MXX1400-40 was used during preheating and reheating. The rolling temperature was 1030 °C. The sealed pack was held at 1030 °C for 15 min before the first rolling and then reheated for 5 min between each rolling pass. The sheets were water cooled after each rolling pass, and their microstructures and properties were tested. The microstructure and tensile properties of the rolled sheets were controlled by changing the thickness reduction and rolling pass. The multiple rolling process causes the increase in ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and yield strength but decrease in elongation (EL). Reported in the work of Niu et al.

Processing Text: This study focuses on the fabrication of SiC p/A356 aluminum matrix composites (AMCs) through stir casting and hot rolling, with the objective of investigating the effects of reduction on microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of SiC p/A356 AMCs. The composites were subjected to hot rolling at 500 °C for varying reduction levels of 30%, 50%, 70%, and 90%. The as-cast AMC ingot was cut into block specimens with dimensions of 60 × 30 × 12 mm 3 using wire electrical discharge machining for the hot rolling process. To obtain a smooth initial surface, all faces of the block specimens were ground using 2000-grit paper. Subsequently, the specimens were subjected to multi-pass hot rolling on a two-roll mill with a roller diameter of 350 mm at a rolling speed of 35 m/min under 500 °C without lubricant, with reductions of 30%, 50%, 70%, and 90%, respectively. The thickness reduction of each pass was 15% of the thickness of the previous pass. The sheets were heat treated at 500 °C for 10 min before the following pass. After the rolling process, the composites were subjected to solution heat treatment at 530 °C for 1 h, followed by an aging treatment at 180 °C for 6 h. Reduction: 70%

IN738LC superalloy samples were fabricated using a Bright Laser BLT-S210 system equipped with a 500W IPG-YLR laser with a Gaussian spot size of 80 μm. The rectangular samples (20 mm × 20 mm × 40 mm) were fabricated under an argon atmosphere with oxygen content lower than 100 ppm using optimized processing parameters with a laser power of 280 W, a scanning speed of 1200 mm/s, a hatch distance of 80 μm, and a layer thickness of 40 μm. Two scanning strategies namely 67° rotation and chessboard 67° rotation between the adjacent layers were selected for producing the specimens. To investigate the effect of preheating platform temperature on microstructure evolution and mechanical properties, one batch of specimens was printed at a preheating temperature of 25 °C and 350 °C, respectively. The printed rectangular samples were cut from the substrate by electrical discharge machining (EDM). The use of a chessboard scanning strategy and substrate preheating was found to be beneficial for achieving a larger melting pool size, coarser dendrite/cellular arm spacing, and a larger volume of carbide precipitates due to enhanced heat accumulation during the LPBF process, which was verified by finite element analysis. The samples used for the present study were prepared by arc-melting a mixture of pure elements. The ingots were re-melted five times to ensure compositional homogeneity before being drop-cast into a copper mold. Subsequently, samples were homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, water-quenched, and then cold-rolled to a thickness reduction of approximately 75 %. In order to obtain samples with different grain sizes, the cold-rolled sheets were annealed at various temperatures ranging from 650 °C to 1250 °C for various time intervals. Specimens for EBSD characterization were initially mechanically ground, polished with aluminum oxide suspension, and then electrochemically polished in an electrolyte of CH 3OH:HNO 3= 4:1 at 20 V for 30 s at -40 °C. For TEM observation, specimens were firstly mechanically ground to about 30 μm, punched into 3 mm diameter disks, and finally thinned by an ion milling system (PIPS, Model 695, Gatan). Dog-bone-shaped samples with 35 mm gauge, 5 mm width, and 3 mm thickness were used for in-situ tensile loading experiments by neutron diffraction. Processing Text: The pipes possess an outer diameter and wall thickness of 6 mm, while the plates are sized at 100 x 100 × 6 mm. Nine unique experiments were planned using the Taguchi orthogonal array method, with the welding tool remaining constant. Three independent variables (travel speed, rotation speed, and shoulder diameter) were altered at three different levels for each variable. The joint's surface flange was FSW-welded. The plates were subjected to FSW on the face side, resulting in a weld depth of 5 mm. AA 6061 pipes with an outer diameter of 50 mm and a wall thickness of 6 mm are considered for the friction stir welding process. Pipe AA 6061 has been subjected to friction stir welding. The dimension of the plate is 100 × 100 × 6 mm. The rotational speed was set to 1800 rpm after several trial and error experiments, and the traverse speed was 5 mm/min. The weld quality has been assessed through visual inspection. Tensile and load bending tests have been done to determine the weld's mechanical properties. The pipes are bent after being broken in half to flatten them. Tensile testing specimens have been produced following ASTM-E standards. The mechanical characteristics of an Al 6061 weld under ASTM- E8 (or AWS) conditions must be specified. The welded sample was cut into the required size for the tests. Tensile testing was also used to evaluate the joint's strength. The operating limitations for each of the FSW parameters, such as travel speed, tool rotational speed, and shoulder diameter, were defined to decrease flaws and improve the tensile strength in the FSW joint. The pipes to the plate are first clamped in a specially made spindle-mounted apparatus for FSW that may rotate at various speeds. Welding is done with EG-85- FSW equipment. The foundational parts of the FSW equipment are depicted in Fig. 2, which also contains the base, motor, pulley, chuck for holding shafts, shaft with removable bolts, and tail. Fig. 2 depicts a fixture that comprises a shaft and bolts and displays the fixture's geometrical dimensions. The welding setup for friction stir welding (FSW) is depicted in Fig. 3. ER 2319 aluminum welding wire with a diameter of 1.2 mm was chosen as the fill wire, and a 2A12 plate with a thickness of 12 mm was used as the substrate. Before the WAAM process, the surface oxide layer and contaminants of the substrate should be removed by a weak alkaline solution and a special polishing wheel. Then, the treated substrate surface needed to be cleaned with alcohol and acetone and then dried for use. The WAAM system comprised a cold metal transfer heating source (TPS 400i, Fronius, Austria), a robot (ABB robot), a the wire feeding mechanism, and a control system. The welding wire was melted by the heat of the arc to form the molten pool, which solidified to build a deposition layer. Then, after forming a deposition layer, raising the torch, repeating the manufacturing process of the previous deposition layer to form the next deposition layer, and cycling the deposition layer by layer to fabricate the as-deposited wall of 150 mm × 220 mm in size. Finally, the as-deposited wall was milled on both sides into a thin plate with a thickness of 5 mm. The WAAM 2319 aluminum alloy underwent a T4 heat treatment process within the KSL-1200× muffle furnace prior to LSP, involving a solution treatment followed by natural aging. The sample was introduced into the muffle furnace at an initial temperature of 25 °C and then gradually heated to the solid solution temperature of 535 °C at a rate of 200 °C/h. Following a 60-min dwell time, the sample was extracted from the furnace and promptly immersed in a cooling medium for quenching, which consisted of water at a temperature of 20 °C. Subsequently, the sample was placed in a room temperature environment for a minimum of 48 h. LSP experiments were carried out by an SGR-Extra-15 Nd: YAG high power pulse laser (Beamtech, Beijing china) with a wavelength of 1064 nm, a pulse width of 10 ns, a frequency of 5 Hz, and a spot diameter of 3 mm. During the LSP experiment, a 100 um thick 3 M special aluminum foil needed to be pasted on the surface of the specimen as an absorptive layer. To raise the peak pressure of the laser shock wave, a confining layer of running water with a thickness of roughly 1-2 mm was applied to cover the peening area. Both sides of the thin plate should be subjected to LSP treatment. The other main experiment parameters used were: the number of impacts was 2 times, the laser energy was 5 J and 10 J, and the spot overlap rate of the longitudinal and transverse direction was 50 %. The tensile investigations of specimens before and after LSP with different energies were performed at room temperature with a constant strain rate of 10 −3s −1 and a tensile rate of 1.5 mm/min using the 8801 servo-hydraulic testing equipment (Instron, USA). The hole fatigue specimens were examined on a high-frequency fatigue machine (QBG-100, Qianbang, china) with a stress level of 130 MPa, a frequency of about 96 Hz, and a stress ratio of 0.1. Processing Text: The T42 RHEA sample was additively manufactured using a mixture of pure Ti, Hf, Nb, and V powders (all with purities exceeding 99.95 %). The particle size of the powder mixture was determined via a particle analyzer (Malvern Mastersizer 3000), giving an average particle size of ∼81 μm. X-ray diffraction (XRD, λ = 1.54 Å for Cu Kα) testing was applied, showing the phase structure of well-mixed elemental powders. During the LENS process, a remelting procedure involving ultra-high energy input was performed to maintain a uniform elemental distribution and prevent the presence of un-melted elemental powder. Argon was introduced into the LENS machine's (Optomec LENS MR-7) working chamber to maintain a low oxygen content (below 200 ppm). The fabrication process involved a scanning speed of 5 mm/s, hatching space of 381 μm, working laser power of 550 W, remelting power of 800 W, and a layer thickness of 200 μm. After the LENS procedure, a bulk RHEA sample measuring 70 × 12 × 5 mm was obtained for further testing. The tensile tests were conducted on the as-deposited samples at various temperatures, including RT, 673 K, 773 K, 873 K, and 1073 K, at a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The tests were carried out using a ZwickRoell Proline universal testing machine equipped with a heating chamber, and strain evaluation was performed using digital image correlation (DIC). The tensile bar used in the experiments had a gauge length of 6 mm and a thickness of 1 mm. Prior to the hot tensile experiment, the tensile bar was preloaded at 30 N to compensate for thermal expansion during the heating process. A heating speed of 10 K/s was employed to reach the target temperature, and the hot tensile test commenced after a 10-min thermal insulation period at the target temperatures in the heating chamber. An ingot of equiatomic CoNiV (at. %) multicomponent alloy was produced using a conventional laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)-printing method. Argon-atomized CoNiV pre-alloyed powders were used in the current study. A commercial 45# steel plate was used for the building substrate during the LPBF process. The substrate was sandblasted and then thoroughly cleaned using acetone before the printing, and then preheated to a temperature of 100 °C. A piece of alloy bulk with a dimension of around 90 mm × 40 mm × 15 mm was produced using an FS271 laser melting facility equipped with a 5000-W Gaussian beam fiber laser protected by an inert high-purity Argon atmosphere, and the oxygen level was kept below ∼0.04 % during the LPBF process. The laser spot size was ∼100 μm in diameter, and the laser melting was conducted at 160 W and 800 mm/s scanning speed. The powder layer thickness was controlled at ∼20 μm during printing, and the hatch spacing was set as ∼0.1 mm. The laser scanning direction was anticlockwise rotated by ∼67° between each adjacent printing layer to lower the internal stresses. The printed specimen was naturally cooled to room temperature inside the chamber with the Argon atmosphere. Subsequently, a piece of alloy specimen was cut from the as-printed MCA bulk and then sealed into a quartz tube with a vacuum state. After that, the sealed alloy plate in the quartz tube was then heated to 500 °C in an oven and aged for 24 h, followed by water quenching. Condition: aged; Temperature: ~298 K

Processing Text: Alloy rods, weighing approximately 500 g, were fabricated from constituent elements (>99.95 at.% purity) by arc melting in an argon atmosphere on a water-cooled copper vessel. Prior to alloy melting, the furnace chamber was evacuated, flushed and backfilled with high purity argon. Notably, cryogenic condition was actualized through immersion in liquid nitrogen, and sufficient time (at least 2 min) was allowed for recovery to the designated temperature between each rolling pass. Processing Text: A series of TiZrHfNbSi x(x = 0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00, molar ratios) HEAs, named Si0, Si0.05, Si0.10, Si0.25, Si0.50, Si0.75, and Si1.00, were produced using a vacuum arc melting system (NMS-DRⅢ, Chengdu Zhongke New Materials Technology Engineering Co., Ltd, China). High-purity raw materials with purities exceeding 99.95 % were employed, including Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, and Si. To prevent oxidation of the specimens during melting, the furnace chamber was maintained at a vacuum level of 3 × 10 −3Pa. Subsequently, the melting furnace was filled with argon protective gas, and pure Ti ingots were melted for a minimum of 5 min to eliminate residual oxygen from the furnace chamber. The samples, approximately 20 g, were melted in a water-cooled copper mold. To enhance the chemical homogeneity of the alloys, five melting cycles were performed under electromagnetic stirring, each lasting over 4 min per smelting cycle. The samples were flipped between cycles to ensure uniformity. The density of the alloys was measured using the Archimedes method. The phase components of the samples were analyzed using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D8 Advance, Bruker, Germany) with Cu-Kα radiation. Scanning was performed at a rate of 5°/min within the range of 20°-80°. The microscopic morphology of the sample was observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Crossbeam 350, Zeiss, Germany), and the cross-sectional analysis of chemical composition and element distribution was conducted using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) at an acceleration voltage of 15 kV. An SEM (Merlin, Zeiss, Germany) equipped with Oxford Symmetry software was employed to determine the grain size, grain orientation, and phase distribution of the sample through electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, C-nano, Oxford, UK). The surfaces of the samples for SEM and EBSD, dimensions of 10 mm × 10 mm × 2 mm, were mechanically polished after sequential sanding with 400-5000 grit sandpaper, followed by final argon ion polishing. The Vickers hardness of the samples was measured using a Vickers hardness tester (MHVS-1000AT, Shanghai Aolong Xingdi Testing Instrument Co., Ltd, China) with a 98 N load applied for 10 s. The Young's modulus was determined by measuring the sound velocity with a sample size of 10 mm × 10 mm × 2 mm. Room temperature mechanical properties of the surface-polished samples were evaluated under uniaxial compression conditions using an electronic universal mechanical testing machine (AGX-VD, Shimadzu, Japan) with a strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1. The compressed samples, wire-cut using electrical discharge machining (WEDA), had dimensions of 2 mm × 2 mm × 4 mm. To analyze crack propagation and fracture morphology during the compression process, SEM analysis was employed. Corrosion resistance evaluations of TiZrHfNbSi xHEAs in Hank's balanced salt solution at 310 K were conducted using an electrochemical workstation (Ivium-n-Stat, Ivium Technologies, Netherlands) with three-electrode electrolytic cell. Samples for electrochemical testing were cut and encapsulated with epoxy resin after connecting the wires with conductive adhesive to avoid crevice corrosion. The electrodes have a working area of 5 mm × 5 mm and grounded with 400-2000 grit sandpaper. The dynamic potential scan ranges from −0.5 V to +1.5 V relative to the open circuit potential. An 80 kg steel ingot was smelted using a high-frequency vacuum induction furnace, which was then forged into billets with the dimension of approximately 60 mm × 60 mm. The billets were heated to 1250 °C for 1.5 h and then hot rolled to 3 mm by 8 passes. The finished rolling temperature was approximately 900 °C. After undergoing laminar cooling, the hot-rolled plates were transported to an insulation furnace, which was pre-set and maintained at 660 °C. The power of the insulation furnace was turned off after that the plates had been insulated in the furnace for 1 h. The plates were, thereafter, slowly cooled to room temperature within the furnace. The plates were, thereafter, cold-rolled to a thickness of 1.5 mm. The critical temperatures of the cold-rolled sheets, A c1and A c3, were determined as 709 °C and 908 °C, respectively, using a thermal dilatometer. As the next step, the cold-rolled samples were subject to an austenite-reverted-transformation (ART) annealing process. The annealing process was performed in one step at the temperatures of 715 °C, 735 °C, and 755 °C for 0.5 h. The corresponding samples were labelled as ART715, ART735, and ART755, respectively. In addition, a two-step annealed sample was completely austenitized at 920 °C for 0.1 h, then quenched to room temperature, and finally reheated to 735 °C and kept isothermal for 0.5 h. This sample was labelled Q-ART735. Furthermore, tensile samples with a gauge length of 50 mm have been prepared along the rolling direction. Tensile tests were, thereafter, performed by using a CMT5105-SANS electronic universal testing machine at RT. Also, microhardness measurements were performed by using an FM-700 Vickers hardness tester with a load of 200 g and a holding time of 15 s. The reported hardness value for each annealing process was an average of ten measurements and the standard deviation was also presented. Furthermore, the TI 950 TriboIndenter, with a constant load of 2 mN, was used in a nanoindentation study. Also, the HER was measured using a ZWICK BUP1000 forming testing machine. Hole expansion samples, with a dimension of 100 mm × 100 mm and a 10 mm diameter hole in the center, were used for these tests. These holes were formed by punching or wire-electrode cutting, with a punching clearance of 5 %. All samples with punched holes have been tested in the burr-up position at a speed of 0.3 mm/s. After a through-thickness crack had been detected, the HER was calculated using a crack propagation monitoring system. The following equation was used for these calculations: (1)HER(%)=Dh−D0D0×100where D0and Dhare the hole diameters before and after the test, respectively. For each annealing process, the reported HER value was an average of the HER values for three samples. Furthermore, microstructure characterizations were performed by using field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) and electron backscattering diffractometry (EBSD). A microscope (Zeiss Ultra-55) equipped with an electron backscattering diffractometer was used for the EBSD analyses. Also, the micromorphology of the retained austenite was analyzed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM; Tecnai G 2F20), and the Mn content in the retained austenite was examined by energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) during TEM analysis. Moreover, X-ray diffraction (XRD; D/max2400) was used to measure the volume fraction of the retained austenite, before and after tensile deformation. The samples used for SEM analysis were polished and etched with a 4 vol% nital solution. Also, the samples used for EBSD and XRD analyses were electropolished with a perchloric acid alcohol solution, which had the following composition: alcohol: perchloric acid: distilled water = 14:1:1. The TEM samples, with a diameter of 3 mm and a thickness of 50 μm, were electropolished using a twin-jet machine. The electrolyte that was used in the experiments was an 8 vol% solution of perchloric acid in alcohol. Processing Text: In this investigation, graphene nanoplatelets reinforced pure titanium matrix (GNPs/TA1) composites were synthesized via short-term ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering. Spherical TA1 powder (with a diameter of 45-105 μm) was provided by Beijing Gongcheng New Material Technology Co., Ltd. Multilayer graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) with a purity of 99.9 % and a lateral diameter of 5-15 μm was obtained from Shanghai Yaotian New Material Technology Co., Ltd. The fabrication of graphene-reinforced pure titanium matrix composites is detailed in Fig. 1and comprises two primary stages: (1) Preparation of the mixed powder: Initially, 0.03g of aggregated graphene nanoplatelets is dispersed ultrasonically in 500 mL of anhydrous ethanol. After being uniformly dispersed for 1 h, the graphene solution is combined with 14.97g of spherical TA1 powder and introduced into a 500 mL tungsten carbide ball mill jar. The mixture was ball-milled at a ball-to-powder ratio of 1:10 and a rotation speed of 300 rpm for 2.5 h. The slurry was then transferred to a vacuum rotary evaporator and processed for 1 h to remove a small amount of anhydrous ethanol. Finally, the slurry was placed in a vacuum drying oven at 85 °C for 10 h to obtain the mixed drying powder. (2) Preparation of GNPs/TA1 composites via SPS technology: The mixed powder was placed into a steel mold and subjected to a pressure of 30 MPa. The temperature was increased at a rate of 100 °C/min up to 730 °C. The material is maintained under vacuum at this temperature and pressure for 10 min, followed by natural cooling to yield a cylindrical billet. Cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 5 mm and a height of 6 mm were fabricated from billets using an electric discharge wire cutting machine. These specimens were employed for both quasi-static and dynamic compression testing, as depicted in Fig. 2. Quasi-static compression tests were executed on a SUNS universal testing machine (maximum load capacity of 100 kN) at strain rates of 10 −3s −1, 10 −2s −1and 10 −1s −1. Dynamic compression tests were carried out at strain rates of 1730 s −1, 2480 s −1and 3000 s −1utilizing a standard split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) system. Spherical TA1 powder (with a diameter of 45-105 μm) was provided by Beijing Gongcheng New Material Technology Co., Ltd. Multilayer graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) with a purity of 99.9 % and a lateral diameter of 5-15 μm was obtained from Shanghai Yaotian New Material Technology Co., Ltd. The fabrication of graphene-reinforced pure titanium matrix composites is detailed in Fig. 1and comprises two primary stages: (1) Preparation of the mixed powder: Initially, 0.03g of aggregated graphene nanoplatelets is dispersed ultrasonically in 500 mL of anhydrous ethanol. After being uniformly dispersed for 1 h, the graphene solution is combined with 14.97g of spherical TA1 powder and introduced into a 500 mL tungsten carbide ball mill jar. The mixture was ball-milled at a ball-to-powder ratio of 1:10 and a rotation speed of 300 rpm for 2.5 h. The slurry was then transferred to a vacuum rotary evaporator and processed for 1 h to remove a small amount of anhydrous ethanol. Finally, the slurry was placed in a vacuum drying oven at 85 °C for 10 h to obtain the mixed drying powder. (2) Preparation of GNPs/TA1 composites via SPS technology: The mixed powder was placed into a steel mold and subjected to a pressure of 30 MPa. The temperature was increased at a rate of 100 °C/min up to 730 °C. The material is maintained under vacuum at this temperature and pressure for 10 min, followed by natural cooling to yield a cylindrical billet. Cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 5 mm and a height of 6 mm were fabricated from billets using an electric discharge wire cutting machine. These specimens were employed for both quasi-static and dynamic compression testing, as depicted in Fig. 2. Quasi-static compression tests were executed on a SUNS universal testing machine (maximum load capacity of 100 kN) at strain rates of 10 −3s −1, 10 −2s −1and 10 −1s −1. Dynamic compression tests were carried out at strain rates of 1730 s −1, 2480 s −1and 3000 s −1utilizing a standard split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) system. Processing Text: The smelting of high-Mn damping steel was carried out using a 50 kg-capacity vacuum induction furnace. After casting, the riser was cut off, and then forged at 900 °C-1050 °C to produce steel slabs with a cross-sectional size of 80 mm × 50 mm. The chemical composition of the high-Mn damping steel was Fe-0.05C-17.2Mn-0.45Si-0.36Cr-0.05V (in wt pct). After heating the forged slab to 1200 °C and holding for 2 h, the slab was rolled into a 2.5 mm thick plate using a two-roll hot rolling mill (ϕ450 mm). The starting rolling temperature was 1000 °C and the final rolling temperature was 820 °C. After rolling, it was air-cooled to room temperature. Three steel plates with a length of 100 mm were cut from the hot rolled sheet and then subjected to solution treatment at 1100 °C for 1 h and subsequent water quenching to room temperature. After that, three steel plates were pickled and cold rolled with reduction ratios of 10 %, 40 % and 50 %, respectively. The cold rolled sheets with reduction ratios of 10 %, 40 % and 50 % were annealed at 700 °C for 30 min and water cooled to room temperature, and the corresponding samples were denoted as CR10, CR40 and CR50, respectively. The specimens for tensile test were taken from the annealed sheets along the rolling direction and the gauge size was 25 mm × 6 mm. The tensile test was conducted on the AI-7000-LAU10 tensile testing machine at a tensile speed of 3 mm/min, and the deformation area was fully monitored using a laser extensometer. Room temperature damping test was carried out using Dynamic Mechanical Analyzer (DMA Q800, TA Instruments, USA) in single cantilever beam mode and the sample size was 35 mm × 5 mm × 1 mm. The in situ tensile specimen was mechanically grinded to 0.5 mm thick and then electrolytically polished at 25 V for 25 s in the mixture of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% alcohol solution. In situ EBSD test was conducted on Zeiss Gemini SEM 300 equipped with GATAN tensile testing machine. Microstructure characterization was characterized by scanning electron microscope (SEM, Zeiss Gemini 300, Germany) equipped with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford Instruments Symmetry, United Kingdom), transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI Tecnai G 2F30, USA) and X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Smart Lab diffractometer, Rigaku, Japan). The ϕ3 mm thin foil for TEM observation was mechanically grinded to 40 μm and electrolytically double-jet polished in the mixture of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% alcohol solution at −25 °C and 25 V. EBSD and XRD samples were subjected to electrolytic polishing after mechanical grinding. The Cu-10Al-5Fe-5Ni-xMn alloys (x = 0, 1.5, 4.5, 7 wt%) were prepared by a medium-frequency induction furnace. Ingredients of pure Cu, Al, Fe, Ni, and Mn elements with a purity of at least 99.9 wt% were used as raw materials. The surface of the molten alloy was covered with cryolite powder to prevent oxidizing. Each sample was cut off from the middle of the ingot to get consistency. The whole casting process is shown in Fig. 1. The samples with different Mn content were denoted as S1, S2, S3 and S4, respectively, as shown in Table 1. The chemical composition of the NAB-xMn (x = 0, 1.5, 4.5, 7 wt%) ingots were detected by X-ray Fluorescence (XRF, Shimadzu XRF-1800). X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis was performed by a Bruker D8 Focus diffractometer equipped with a Cu radiation target to identify the crystalline phase. To further analyze the microstructure evolution of NAB alloys, the samples were polished and then etched in a solution containing 95 ml C 2H 5OH + 2 ml HCl +3 g FeCl 3for microstructural observation and composition analysis. Microstructural observation was carried out on a scanning electron microscope (SEM, IT 800 HSL) equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), and a transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEM-2100F). The TEM samples were prepared by twin-jet electro-polishing in a solution containing 30 % HNO 3and 70 % CH 3OH at −30 °C. Tensile tests were carried out using a universal tensile machine (Instron 5569, Instron Corp., America) at room temperature. The Digital Image Correlation (DIC) system (NCM-2D) was used to accurately measure the strain of samples. Fig. 1shows the size of tensile samples, the gauge was 15 mm in length and the tensile rate was 5 × 10 −4s −1. To ensure the accuracy of the data, at least three tensile samples were tested for each condition. The hardness test was measured by using a Vickers hardness tester under a constant load of 500 g for 15 s. Each sample was tested 6 times and took the average value to decrease the error. Processing Text: Invar 36 alloy samples were fabricated using the in-situ rolling-assisted laser directed energy deposition (LDED) process, and the effect of in-situ rolling on the microstructure, mechanical properties and coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) was investigated. The plastic deformation introduced by in-situ rolling facilitated the recovery and recrystallization of the pre-solidified layers. The yield strength was significantly enhanced due to grain refinement strengthening and work hardening. The refinement of grains and the increase in residual stress induced by in-situ rolling enabled these samples to maintain an ultra-low CTE. Gas atomized Invar 36 alloy powders were utilized as raw material, and the HAM experiments were performed on an IR-LDED system. The deformation of the deposited material was achieved by adding a rolling unit next to the deposition head and ensuring the synergistic movement of the two, and the distance between the rolling unit and deposition head was 35 mm. The rolling load was obtained in real-time through a sensor, and can be adjusted by controlling the lifting amount of the rolling unit in each layer. The dimension of the rolling head was ϕ50 mm × 20 mm, and a detailed description of the IR-LDED procedure can be found in our previous publication [ 16]. The scanning speed of rolling unit and deposition head was 8 mm/s, and the laser power and overlap rate were 1300 W and 40 %, respectively. Samples with dimensions of 70 mm × 5 mm × 50 mm were fabricated by the IR-LDED process under loads of 0 kN, 5 kN and 10 kN, and the corresponding lifting amount of the rolling unit in each layer were 0.55 mm, 0.38 mm and 0.28 mm, respectively. Processing Text: Two types of steel (Fe-0.3 %C and Fe-0.7 %C wt.) used in the tensile armor of flexible ducts, differing in chemical compositions and thermomechanical treatments, were analyzed, both exhibiting HE in a hydrogen-rich environment. Sample A showed a decrease in yield strength from 810 MPa in air to 687 MPa after hydrogen charging, with total elongation reduced from 11.15 % to 7.38 %. For Sample A, the average YS was recorded at 810 ± 15 MPa, while Sample B showed a higher YS of 1216 ± 6 MPa, indicating a significant increase of approximately 50 % attributable to the higher carbon content. Similarly, the UTS for Sample A was measured at 876 ± 64 MPa, compared to 1311 ± 51 MPa for Sample B, revealing an enhancement of nearly 50 % as well. The elongation percentage, a measure of ductility, was inversely affected; it decreased from 11.15 ± 0.7 % in Sample A to 8.52 ± 1.7 % in Sample B, reflecting a reduction in ductility by approximately 24 % due to the increased carbon content. YS of sample A decreases under both hydrogen exposure conditions, highlighting its vulnerability to HE. These morphologies demonstrate distinct mechanical behaviors, where spheroidized cementite provided embrittlement, while lamellae provided resistance to HIC. Sample A has lower carbon content, presented 34 % of elongation reduction. Condition: Hydrogenated in aqueous solution of NaCl

The constituent elements Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and W powders with at least 99.9 wt% purities were melted in a water-cooled copper hearth via vacuum arc melting to synthesize the bulk CoCrFeNiW 0.2HEA ingot. The re-melted process should be repeated at least ten times to ensure chemical homogeneity. All the tensile specimens were electric-discharge machined into dumbbell-like shape with gauge dimensions of 20 mm × 4 mm × 2 mm, and then carefully polished to remove oxide layer and scratch with 2000 grit sand paper. Uniaxial tensile experiments were carried out in the temperature range of 298 K-1173 K with a constant strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1 using a WANCE TSE105D universal testing machine. For high temperature tensile testing, a three-zone split furnace was utilized to preheat the tensile specimens. The temperature of three different zones, including the upper, middle and lower parts, was controlled by separate controller module, and K-type thermocouples were tied to tensile round bar and the middle of specimen for monitoring the temperature variation. The experimental target temperature maintains 10 min before the tensile test to ensure the uniform distribution of temperature within ±2 K. To study the strain rate sensitivity, the tensile experiments were additionally performed at 773 K under different strain rates between 1 × 10−4s−1 and 5 × 10−3s−1. The crystal structures and phase evolution of the HEA at different temperatures were examined by Bruker D8 Focus X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu Kα radiation. JEOL JSM 7200F scanning electron microscopy (SEM) attached with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), back-scattered electron (BSE) and EDAX Velocity Super was used for the microstructural and fractographic analysis. Electron back-scattering diffraction (EBSD) was performed with a step size of 2.9 μm. The EBSD specimens were cut from near the facture surfaces and polished by argon ion beam polishing (Leica EM RES 102). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) microscopy was conducted using FEI Tecnai G2 F20. Thin foils for TEM were mechanically grind to obtain about 30 μm thickness and finally thinning using ion-beam thinning (Gatan 691). Temperature: 1173 K; Processing state: as-cast
