The high power laser cladding (HPLC) process with laser power of 15 kW was used for the first time to fabricate 17-4PH alloy coatings. The experiment utilized 17-4PH powder smelted through vacuum gas atomization technology as the laser cladding material. The powder particles' morphology are near-spherical and the size ranges from 40 μm to 220 μm. The powder was dried for 2 h in a vacuum oven at 100 °C before the experiment. The HPLC system and details of the coating preparation: the HPLC system, the laser spot size (20 mm × 2 mm), the top view morphology, transverse morphology, and transverse dimensions of a single-track coating, respectively, the preparation process and final morphology of multi-track and multi-layer coating, respectively. Under a cladding speed (VC) of 10 mm/s, the build rate (η) was calculated to be about 272 mm3/s via the formula. Based on the preparation process and the process parameters, a multi-track and multi-layer coating with dimension of 170 mm × 190 mm × 7.2 mm (length × width × thickness) were prepared on the 0Cr13Ni5Mo substrate. In order to facilitate the heat treatment, the coating was divided into five groups (A-E) along the overlapping direction (X+). The group A did not undergo heat treatment, while groups B to E were first uniformly solution-treated at 1040 °C for 1 h, followed by natural cooling in the air. Subsequently, they were subjected to aging treatment at corresponding temperatures of 300 °C, 400 °C, 480 °C, and 550 °C for 4 h each, followed by natural cooling in the air. The metallographic specimens were obtained from each coatings (A-E) using a wire cutting machine. After grinding and polishing the XOZ plane, the specimens were corroded for 5 s in a corrosive agent, and then the microstructures were observed via a scanning electron microscope (SEM). The ground and polished specimens (XOZ plane) were submerged in perchloric acid solutions with a volume fraction of 8 %, subjected to electrochemical polishing at 20 V for 40 s, and then etched for 30 min at 4 kV and 3° in a precision etching coating system. Crystallographic data of the coatings were analyzed by an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) probe. In addition, the phases were analyzed via X-ray diffractometry (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The micro hardness was tested along the direction of Z- with a spacing of 0.5 mm, a load of 0.5 kg, and pressure retention of 20 s. The tensile specimens (three specimens per group) were taken from the coatings (A-E) and the forged substrate (F) respectively. All tensile specimens were tested at a strain rate of 1.4 × 10−3s−1. The CE test specimens (three specimens per material) were taken from the coating and substrate material respectively. The heat treatment process of the coating CE specimens were consistent with the heat treatment process parameters of the tensile test specimen with the best plasticity. Subsequently, the tested surfaces were polished. The CE test was performed according to ASTM G32-16. Before testing, the specimens were cleaned, dried, and weighed. Subsequently, each specimen underwent a 4-hour CE test in deionized water with temperature of 25 ± 2 °C using a magnetostrictive induced cavitation facility resonating at 20 kHz with an amplitude of 60 μm. After the CE test, all specimens were cleaned, dried, and weighed again to calculate the mass loss. Finally, the surface and transverse morphologies of the CE specimens were observed by SEM. The elastoplasticity of the 17-4PH coating specimens for CE test was probed through an instrumented nanoindentation method using a Berkovich-type indenter. Processing Text: WCAWs were prepared by liquid phase sintering (LPS) and laser ultrashort-time liquid phase sintering (LULPS) respectively. The 93 wt% W-CoAlW cuboid samples prepared by laser ultrashort-time liquid phase sintering were denoted as LULPS WCAWs. A laser deposition system was adopted in this work, equipped with a 4 kW fiber laser system (RC-LDM4030, RAYCHAM Laser Technology Group Co., Ltd), a coaxial powder feeding nozzle, and a 3 mm diameter beam. The ingot was remelted more than five times before the drop-cast process to ensure homogeneity. Subsequently, the as-cast CoCrNi MEA ingot was cold-forged by a 50 % reduction in thickness. Afterward, the alloy was annealed at 1173K for 1 h to reduce deformation-induced defects and promote recrystallization. Quasi-static compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 10^−3 s^−1 to 10^−1 s^−1 were performed on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 6 mm using an Instron 5969 testing machine. Dynamic compression tests with strain rates ranging from 2.6 × 10^3 s^−1 to 6.2 × 10^3 s^−1 were carried out on CoCrNi MEA samples with a diameter of 3 mm and length of 3 mm using a SHPB system. Stop-ring technology was introduced to control the strain during the dynamic compressions. The ramp wave and shock compression experiments were conducted using the CQ-4 magnetically driven system, delivering a pulsed current with a peak value of 4 MA and a rising time of 500 ns, developed by the Institute of Fluid Physics, China Academy of Engineering Physics. Multi-level characterizations were conducted to explore the intrinsic mechanisms of CoCrNi MEA. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed using a JEOL JSM-7100F field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). An acceleration voltage of 20 kV, a specimen tilt angle of 70°, and a working distance of 15 mm were used in the EBSD observations. A JEM-2100F transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV to uncover microscopic deformation mechanisms. A novel Co-free Al0.7CrFeMnNi1.3 high-entropy alloy (HEA) was prepared and followed by annealing treatment at 400-1000℃ for 2 h to investigate the effect of microstructure evolution on compression and tribological properties. The as-cast alloy ingots of Al 0.7CrFeMnNi 1.3were prepared using the vacuum arc melting under high purity Ar atmosphere, remelted at least 5 times to reduce element segregation, and then water-cooled directly in the copper crucible. The as-cast alloy ingots were then placed in the muffle furnace for annealing treatment followed air cooling, and the annealing temperature is set to 400, 600, 700, 800, 900 and 1000℃for 2 h, which were marked the as-annealed alloy. Annealing treatment results in the reversible transformation of matrix phase, and the phase transformation mechanism is discussed based on experimental and thermodynamic calculation. Processing Text: Herein, a TiVNb medium-entropy alloy was prepared via vacuum arc melting. Commercial pure Ti, V and Nb were used as raw materials. Equimolar TiVNb medium-entropy alloys were fabricated by vacuum arc melting, after which the as-melted alloys were slowly heated (at an average heating rate of 8 °C/min) to 1300 °C and kept in an Ar atmosphere for 12 h, followed by cooling to RT using a furnace cooling system. The alloy maintained a body-centred cubic (BCC)-dominant phase following an annealing treatment at 1300 °C for 12 h. Herein, we prepared a TiVNb medium-entropy alloy by arc melting and subsequent homogenisation. TiVNb medium-entropy alloys were prepared and found to maintain almost a BCC solid-solution structure after high-temperature ageing and annealing treatments at 1300 °C for 12 h. Processing Text: The composition of high-Mn austenitic steel was carefully designed to make the twinning behavior sensitive to changes in strain. The high-Mn steel is chosen here for the easy-controlled SFE and twinning behavior. The SFE of high-Mn steel is adjusted to close to 20 mJ/m2 by designing the Mn and C content. According to the Olson-Cohen thermodynamic model, a steel composition of Fe-20Mn-0.9C-5Mo (all in wt%) was designed, with a calculated SFE of 24.7 mJ/m2. The steel was prepared via vacuum induction melting. The as-cast ingots underwent homogenization at 1473 K for 2 h and hot forged at 1300 K to produce a round bar with a diameter of 80 mm. The forged bar is finally processed into a hollow tube with an inner diameter of 56 mm and a wall thickness of 10 mm. Then, the tube billets were forward power spinning at room temperature using a spinning machine with two symmetrically distributed rollers. Artificial spray emulsion was used to fully cool the contact part between the spinning wheel and the workpiece. After three spinning passes, the wall thickness is reduced from 10 mm to 8.5 mm, and the total wall thickness reduction is 15 %. The rollers are R type, with a diameter of 446 mm and a tip radius of 12.5 mm. The mandrel was rotated at a speed of 55 rpm, and the feed rate of the rollers was 0.5 mm/r. Additionally, a plate with a thickness of 4 mm was cut from the forged bar and underwent cold rolling for comparison. Processing Text: WC spherical particles of x wt% (x=0,10,20,30) were added into CrFeNiB0.03Si0.03 medium entropy alloy (MEA) prepared by the laser direct energy deposition. Diverse compositions of CrFeNiB0.03Si0.03/WC metal matrix composite samples with weight percentages of 0 %,10 %, 20 %, and 30 % WC are prepared, denoted as 0WC-CFN 10WC-CFN, 20WC-CFN, and 30WC-CFN. The powder undergoes mechanical mixing, followed by a 1.5-hour drying process to eliminate absorbed water vapor. Subsequently, it undergoes screening using a 100-mesh screen. The LDED process uses a fiber output semiconductor laser RFLA3000D operating at a center wavelength of 915±10 nm, with a maximum power output of 3000 W and a spot diameter of 3 mm. The equipment also integrates a laboratory-developed dual-cylinder powder feeder, a three-channel coaxial powder-feeding laser head, the KUKA six-degree-of-freedom robot arm KR22-1610, inclusive of an integrated control center, a laser water cooler, and an argon tank. Comprehensive setup parameters for composite material preparation are detailed in Table 2. The LDED material samples underwent sectioning using wire cutting equipment. Subsequently, the samples underwent a series of sequential steps: grinding with sandpaper ranging from 80 to 2000 mesh, followed by polishing with a 2.5-0.5 μm diamond polishing suspension. For microstructural analysis, the samples underwent etching using aqua regia (comprising 75 % HCl and 25 % HNO₃). Microstructure and elemental composition were examined via scanning electron microscopy (SEM, ZEISS Sigma 300) and operating at 15 kV, equipped with an energy-dispersive spectrometer (EDS). Phase analysis was conducted using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Rigaku D/max2500), with scanning parameters including a speed of 4°/min and a scanning range of 2θ = 30° - 100°. The microhardness of the sample was measured using an HV-1000 Vickers microhardness tester with a loading load set at 200 g, and the loading time was 10 s. Measurements were taken from the top of the material at 50μm intervals between each measurement point. The compression properties of composite materials were tested using an universal material testing machine (ETM105D), with the compressed sample size being Ø6 × 9 mm, and the strain rate set to 0.15 mm/min. To ensure the reliability of the test results, a minimum of three tests were conducted. The tribological properties of the samples were evaluated using an friction and wear testing machine (M-2000). The sliding friction test was conducted at room temperature (RT, 298 K) with a grinding ring made of ZGCr15 with a diameter of 50 mm. The pressure load was set to 200 N, and the rotation speed of the grinding ring was 300 rpm. WC content: 30 wt%; Condition: Maximum compressive yield strength

Processing Text: Bulk CoCrFeNiCu-based high entropy alloy was fabricated using a combination of short-term high energy ball milling and rapid spark plasma sintering. Commercial powders of Co (99.7 % pure, mean particle size 3 µm), Cr (99.35 %, >71 µm), Fe (99.96 %, 10-20 µm), Ni (99.5 %, 45-60 µm), and Cu (99.5 %, 45-60 µm) were used as starting materials. The powders were mixed in equiatomic proportion Co+Cr+Fe+Ni+Cu, then 20 g of the mixture were placed in steel jar of the planetary ball mill Activator-2S («Chemical Engineering Plant» Ltd, Russia) together with 400 g of steel milling balls (each ball was 6 mm in diameter, mass of one ball was about 0.86 g). High energy ball milling (HEBM) was carried out in Ar atmosphere (4 bar), without any liquid agent addition. After 120 min of HEBM at rotating speed 694 rpm for Sun disk and 1388 rpm for the jar (in laboratory coordinate system), mechanically alloyed powder CoCrFeNiCu was obtained. The extremely high rotating speed in combination with permanent water cooling of the jars available in the Activator-2S mill, allowed relatively fast mechanical synthesis of the alloy: less than 2 h instead of 5 - 65 h required in the air-cooling mills with rotating speed 200-350 rpm. As-prepared alloy powders were SPS-consolidated in vacuum using a Labox 650 apparatus (Sinter Land, Japan). The powder mixture was placed into а cylindrical graphite die (inner diameter 30 mm) and uniaxially compressed at 50 MPa. The sample was heated at а rate of 100°С/min up to the preset sintering temperature ∼ 1073 K by passing rectangular pulses of electric current through the sintering media. The dwell time at sintering temperature was 10 min. SPS-produced disks were 5 mm thick and 30 mm in diameter. Room temperature; Compression test; Hierarchical microstructure with Cu-depleted fcc-solid solution and Cr2O3 nano-precipitates

The series were made from ternary master alloys of CuPdPt and AuCuPd to ensure their constant ratio. The two additional elements were further added to pieces of the master alloy in different concentrations. All masses were weighed according to the stoichiometric composition of the desired alloy and melted under Ar atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu plate in an arc furnace (Arc Melter AM 200 Edmund Buehler GmbH). To enhance the homogeneity of the samples, they were flipped over and melted again four times. Finally, the samples were cast into a graphite mould (4 mm in diameter and 75 mm in length). The samples were homogenized at a homologous temperature of approx. 0.9 in sealed quartz ampules under Ar atmosphere and quenched in ice water. Afterwards, the samples were deformed by rotary swaging (UR2–4, Heinrich Müller Maschinenfabrik, Pforzheim) up to a true strain of ε = 0.71 (ε = ln A i / A f, where A i and A f are the initial and final cross-section area, respectively), while the degree of deformation per step was ε ≈ 0.24. The SPD processes can be classified as bulk-SPD, surface-SPD and powder-SPD methods. In bulk-SPD, the goal is to modify the bulk microstructure of a material with reasonably large sizes. In surface-SPD, only surface and sub-surface layers are modified. In powder-SPD, the material is in the form of powder, and strain is introduced on the surface layer and core of the powder particles usually by ball milling methods. Different methods based on rolling, torsion, forging and extrusion can satisfy the required conditions for SPD processing of bulk material. The most known method for inducing SPD in powders is high-energy ball milling. Recent trends in SPD methods include hydrostatic pressure methods, upscaling disc samples to rods using HPTE, pipe sample processing using t-HPS, sheet processing using IF-HPS, cryogenic-SPD, and ultra-SPD. Condition: cold rolled by 60%

Processing Text: A straightforward processing route, involving hot rolling followed by annealing, was utilized to produce single-phase FCC HEAs. Experimental The powder for PBF-LB was obtained by atomization of the vacuum induction melted Fe 65 Co 12.5 Ni 12.5 Cr 9.5 C 0.5 alloy using a US35 atomizer from ATO LAB. Rods (Ø10 mm) of the alloy were atomized in an argon atmosphere. The obtained particles of the alloy had a spherical shape with an average size of 35 μm. PBF-LB of the alloy was carried out in an argon atmosphere using a 3D printer DMP Flex 200 (3D Systems Inc., Rock Hill, SC, USA); the laser power (P) was 200 W, the scanning speed (V) was 1600 mm/s; a 316L steel plate was used as the substrate. The flow rate of the shielding gas (argon) was 5 L per minute. To improve the quality of the workpieces, the direction of laser movement was changed by 67° during fusion of each subsequent layer [ 67 ]. The distance between tracks and the beam diameter were 50 μm and 70 μm, respectively. All the parameters of PBF-LB were selected based on our earlier trials [ 43 ]. Samples for heat treatment, microstructure analysis, and mechanical testing were cut out of the as-produced alloy using an electric discharge machine. The samples were annealed for 60 min in a muffle furnace in air in a temperature range 800–1100 °C; then the specimens were cooled in air. For the sake of convenience, the Fe 65 Co 12.5 Ni 12.5 Cr 9.5 C 0.5 alloy samples produced using PBF-LB were denoted hereafter as PBF-LB (as-sintered), PBF-LB - 800, PBF-LB - 900, PBF-LB - 1000, and PBF-LB - 1100 (annealed at 800, 900, 1000 or 1100 °C, respectively). Samples measured 20 × 10 × 11 mm 3 were cut out using the electric discharge machine and then cold rolled at room temperature. Unidirectional multi-pass rolling of the samples was carried out to a total thickness reduction of 80 % (from 11 to 2.2 mm) with a reduction of 3–5% per pass without intermediate annealing. After cold rolling, the specimens were cut from the sheets and annealed in the muffle furnace at 800 °C for 60 min followed by air cooling. The cold-rolled and annealed conditions were marked hereafter as PBF-LB - CR and PBF-LB - CR-800, respectively. Condition: Cryogenic Temperature (77 K); Processing state: Cold-rolled

This study employed LPBF to fabricate TiN/GH5188 Co-based superalloy composites with alternative TiN nanoparticle contents (0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5 wt%). A series of TiN/GH5188 composites were synthesized by incorporating nano-TiN particles (obtained from Guangdong Yinna Technology Co., Ltd., China, with an average particle size of ∼100 nm) into gas-atomized GH5188 powder from AVIC Metal Powder Metallurgy Technology Co., Ltd., China. The preparation process, depicted in Fig. 1a, involved premixing the powders, followed by high-energy ball milling using a planetary mill (Retsch, Haan, Germany) at a speed of 280 rpm for 8 h. Silicon dioxide (SiO 2) served as the milling media, with a powder-to-ceramic ball mass ratio of 1:4. Mixed powders were dried in an oven at 100 °C for 20 min to remove moisture before being ready for printing. An LPBF machine (DiMetal-100, Guangzhou Laseradd Additive Technology Co., Ltd., China) was used for sample fabrication, equipped with an IPG fiber laser (maximum output power of 200 W) and a galvanometer (Hurryscan20-1080 nm-XY2, SCANLAB GmbH, Puheim, Germany). GH5188 and TiN/GH5188 composite samples were fabricated on a #45 steel substrate using optimized process parameters. Apply a laser power and scanning speed of 180 W and 900 mm/s, respectively. The layer thickness is 0.03 mm, and the hatching space is fixed at 0.07 mm. Block-shaped samples and tensile specimens were created using an orthogonal scanning strategy with a 45° angle to the airflow and a 90° rotation between layers. The dimensions of the block-shaped samples are 8 × 8 × 8 mm³, while the shape and dimensions of the tensile specimens are shown in Fig. 2c. The block-shaped samples were polished according to standard metallographic procedures, etched by a mixed solution of concentrated HCl and 3.3 wt% H 2O 2in a volume ratio of 4:1 for 60 s to prepare metallographic samples. The surfaces paralleled to the building direction were subjected to argon ion polishing using an ion grinding instrument (IM4000plus, HITACHI, Japan) at a voltage of 4 kV, an angle of 3°, and a duration of 2 h. Processing Text: A lightweight steel having a chemical composition, in wt. %, of Fe-26Mn-8Al-3Mo-1.2C-0.02Nb (wt.%), was cast in an induction furnace under Ar atmosphere and then hot rolled into plates. Subsequently, after the plates were solution treated at 1050 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching, they were cold rolled to obtain a reduction in thickness of 55 %. Finally, the samples cut from the plates were annealed at various temperatures (750, 800, 825, 850, and 900 °C) for 1 h, and then cooled in water. The microstructure after annealing consists of heterogeneous recrystallized, unrecrystallized grains containing nanoscale Mo 2C precipitates, and intergranular Mo-enriched carbides. As the annealing temperature increases, the fraction of recrystallization grains, and average Schmid factor increase, while the average grain sizes and the volume fraction of Mo 2C decrease. Annealing at 825 °C results in a desirable heterogeneous structure with normal bimodal grain distribution and uniform dispersion of nanoscale Mo 2C particles. Annealed at 825°C

Processing Text: The ingot with nominal composition Fe40Ni30Cr20Al5Ti5 (at.%) HEA was fabricated by vacuum arc-melting technology under an argon atmosphere. All alloy ingots with a mass of about 120 g were then drop-cast into a copper mold to form plates with dimensions of 6 × 12 × 60 mm3, subsequently homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h, followed by water-cooled. And then cold rolled to ∼1.2 mm with a thickness reduction of ∼80 %. A two-step heat treatment scheme was applied on the cold-rolled sheets: annealing for 3 min at 1150 °C followed by water cooling (referred to as A0) to achieve fully recrystallized microstructure, the final aging treatment was carried out for 4 h at different temperatures (700 °C, 800 °C, 900 °C, referred to as A700, A800, A900), also followed by water quenching. The EBSD and SEM specimens were polished with 3000-grit SiC papers and followed by twin-jet electropolishing in a solution of 90 % ethanol and 10 % perchloric acid at −25 °C under a direct voltage of 20V. TEM samples with a diameter of 3 mm were first mechanically ground to a thickness of 50 μm, then twin-jet polished in a solution of 90 % ethanol and 10 % perchloric acid at around −25 °C under a direct voltage of 25V. For the tensile tests, the specimens were cut into dog-bone shapes with gage dimensions of 1 × 2 × 15 mm3 and were machined and polished. Room temperature tensile tests were performed on the Instron 5582 testing machine at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. Aging treatment: 800 °C for 4h; Phases: sigma and L21 co-precipitated in FCC matrix

Processing Text: Argon atomized equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi HEA powder and high purity Ni powder (>99.9 wt%) both with a particle size range of 15-53 μm were blended for 6 h at a rotation speed of 28 rpm in an argon atmosphere using a three-dimensional (3D) swing powder mixer to prepare AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA powder. The mixed powder was then processed by L-PBF under a modulated pulsed laser mode using a Renishaw AM 400 system equipped with a ytterbium fiber laser. The oxygen level in the building chamber was reduced to below 50 ppm prior to sample fabrication. A laser power of 325 W, a point exposure duration of 60 μs, a powder layer thickness of 50 μm, a point distance of 60 μm and a hatch distance of 90 μm were used for the sample building. A Meander scanning strategy was used for hatch scanning on each layer and the scanning direction was rotated by 67° after each layer. Some of the as-printed samples were subsequently subjected to an aging treatment at 500 °C, 600 °C, 700 °C and 800 °C for 5 h in vacuum (∼10−6Pa), respectively, followed by air cooling. The as-built samples and the L-PBF-processed plus aged samples were sectioned along the build height direction by electrical discharge machining (EDM) and ground using SiC papers from 320 grit up to 2400 grit before being polished using 3 μm diamond suspension and colloidal silica suspension (or OPS solution). The samples were then electrolytically etched in a solution containing 10 g Oxalic acid and 100 mL water for microstructural characterization by optical microscopy (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) via a SUPRA55 electron microscope. Prior to the TEM study, disc specimens of 3 mm in diameter were machined out of the materials, ground to a thickness of 40-50 μm and then electropolished in a solution made from 5 vol% perchloric acid and 95 vol% alcohol using a twin-jet electro-polishing system. Tensile specimens with a gauge length of 23 mm and a reduced section diameter of 4 mm were machined out of the horizontally built samples. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted at a nominal strain rate of 5 × 10−4/s. Processing state: laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF); Microstructure: dual-phase nanolamellae of FCC and BCC

Processing Text: A 3 Kg CoCrFeNiAl 0.5Ti 0.1HEA ingot, with elemental purity exceeding 99.9 %, was fabricated using the vacuum arc melting method four times. The alloy ingot was annealed at 1100 °C for 4 h. Subsequently, it was forged into a rod with a diameter of 21 mm using a 400 kg forging machine. The initial billet temperature was approximately 1050 °C, decreasing to about 900 °C by the end of forging. TEM samples were first mechanically ground to a thickness of 30 μm, then twin-jet electro-polished using a solution of HNO 3:CH 4O = 1:4. Cylindrical tensile specimens, 15 mm in gage length and 3 mm in diameter, were machined from forged rods. These specimens were then polished using SiC paper up to 2000 grit. The samples were initially sanded with SiC paper up to 2000 grit to ensure a smooth surface. Then samples were polished with a polishing machine using a sequence of decreasing abrasive sizes until the surface was scratch-free. The polished samples were cleaned with ethanol and dried to remove any debris or contaminants. For high-temperature tests at 873 K, 1073 K, and 1273 K, the samples were heated by convective heat transfer from an induction-heated stainless steel susceptor at a rate of 1 K/s. Once the desired temperature was achieved, it was maintained for 15 min to allow the material to equilibrate. Temperature: 77 K

Processing Text: Ti2NbVAl0.3Zrx (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) LRHEAs were prepared by the vacuum arc melting furnace under the protection of high-purity argon gas. Metal particles with purity >99.95 % were used as raw materials. In order to avoid melting losses and melting segregation, Ti-Al and Zr-V-Nb intermediate alloys were prepared. Finally, the intermediate alloys were combined and melted six times repeatedly. Before melting, the air pressure in the chamber was reduced to 3*10−3Pa and the chamber underwent five purging cycles with high-purity argon gas. This was followed by melting Ti ingots to remove residual oxygen in the chamber and prevent sample contamination. SEM samples were polished using a 0.3 μm alumina suspension, followed by metallographic etching using a solution of HCL, HNO3, and HF in a ratio of 10:3:1. TEM samples were mechanically ground to 50 μm and subsequently thinned using an ionic thinning machine (Gatan 695). Tensile tests were conducted on the specimens using an electronic universal testing machine (Instron 68 MT-55) at a quasi-static strain rate of 1*10−3S−1. The tensile samples were identified with a section size of 5mm × 2mm × 1.5 mm and were mechanically ground to 2000 mesh prior to the commencement of the experiment. Vickers hardness of the samples was measured using TMHV-1000Z with a load of 200g and a force holding time of 15s. The corrosion behavior of the current alloy system was tested using an electrochemical workstation (VersaSTAT 3F) in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. The sample size was 10mm × 10mm × 4 mm, with a test area 1 cm2, and was mechanically ground to 2000 mesh prior to testing. Electrochemical tests were conducted in a three-electrode electrolytic cell setup, with the sample serving as the working electrode, the saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode, and the platinum electrode as the auxiliary electrode. The open circuit potential was initially stabilized for 1800s, followed by potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests. The PDP test was conducted at a scan rate of 0.333 mV/s, starting from an initial potential of −0.3V SCE(vs. OCP) and ending at 2V SCE(vs. OCP). EIS measurements were carried out with an amplitude of 5 mV/s and a frequency range from 105Hz to 10−2Hz. Each sample underwent three tests under identical conditions to ensure result accuracy. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; Thermo Scientific K-Alpha) analyzed the oxide film formed on the sample surface. Fracture elongation: ∼9.4 %

Processing Text: Spherical and non-porous powders were prepared using the plasma rotating electrode method. The particle sizes ranged from 45 μm to 220 μm. To improve the powder's fluidity during the deposition process, the powder was dried in a vacuum environment at 100 ± 10 °C for 4 h. A TC4 sheet measuring 150 mm × 150 mm × 30 mm was selected as the substrate. Before testing, the upper surface was polished with a grinding wheel and cleaned with ethanol and acetone to improve the laser absorptivity. The LDED equipment consists of a laser system, a powder delivery system, a CNC motion system, and an argon gas protection chamber. The laser beam created a molten pool on the substrate's upper surface during deposition. Three coaxial nozzles powered by argon gas inject and melt the titanium alloy powder into the molten pool. The robot drove the movement of the laser head assembly to form a layer-by-layer molten metal track on the surface of the substrate. The serpentine reciprocating scanning strategy was adopted. Throughout the entire procedure, the sample was kept in a clean argon environment (O₂ < 0.02 %, H₂O < 0.05 %) to avoid oxidation. The near-α titanium alloy was annealed by standard heat treatment. Temperatures ranging from 650 to 850 °C were selected for stress relief annealing temperature. 950 °C was chosen for recrystallization annealing. The super-transformation treatment temperature exceeded the β-transformation temperature (1030 ± 5 °C). Consequently, the super-transformation annealing temperature was 1050 °C. The specimens were air-cooled after being annealed for 4 h in an SA2-9-12 TP air resistance furnace. Condition: As-deposited; Direction: H

The multi-component ingots, with a nominal composition of Fe2Ni2CrAlx (x =0.9, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3), was prepared through the vacuum arc melting technique. The elemental metals, with boasted a purity exceeding 99.9%, were melted within a water-cooled copper mold. Arc melting were conducted under an atmosphere of ultrahigh-purity argon (Ar). The ingots experienced at least 5 re-melting cycles. The microstructures of the alloys were analyzed using electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) measurements, which were carried out using a SEM equipped with a EDAX detector and TSL OIM data collection software. Density of the Fe2Ni2CrAlx MPEAs were measured by using the Archimedes method. Each sample underwent five measurements to obtain averaged values. The solidus and liquidus temperatures were determined using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The DSC scans encompassed a temperature range from 25 °C to 1500 °C, at a rate of 10 °C/min during the heating cycles. It maintains a continuous flow of argon (Ar) during the process. The mechanical properties of the samples were evaluated using compressive tests at elevated temperatures. The compression tests of Φ4mm×6mm cylindrical samples were performed on the AG-X Plus 250 kN/50 kN Electronic Universal Testing Machine. The initial strain rate was 2 mm/min and the temperature was 200 °C, 400 °C, 600 °C and 800 °C. The testing was performed until the fracture of the samples or reaching a reduction of 70%, whichever was earlier. Three compression tests were conducted to derive the average value. Temperature: 200 °C

The specimens were produced from a plate of S690QL steel with 20 mm of thickness. The S690QL steel is a high-strength structural steel compliant with the British Standard BS EN 10025-6: 2004+A1: 2009. The sample was grounded using silicon carbide papers #80, #180, #220, #400, #600, #800, #1200 and #2500 in succession and in this order, polished and then etched with Nital (2% nitric acid). The specimens were prepared by grinding them successively with silicon carbide papers #400, #800, #1000, and #2000, followed by cleaning in an ultrasonic bath with ethanol. This process served two crucial purposes: removing naturally formed oxides and degreasing, thus achieving uniformity across all specimens. The grips were safeguarded from corrosion by applying a coating of spray paint on both sides, a layer of black electrical tape followed by a coating of silicone on the side that would be immersed in the solution. The specimens were stored in a desiccator until testing to prevent premature corrosion. To induce pre-corrosion, the specimens were placed in a three-electrode cell setup consisting of: the working electrode, which is a specimen of the S690 QL steel; the platinum wire counter electrode; the silver chloride electrode (Ag/AgCl electrode) reference electrode; and a water-based solution of 3.5% sodium chloride (3.5%NaCl) as the electrolyte. The specimens were left for 30 min in open circuit to reach a more stable surface state. At the end of that period, a current of 0.25 A was applied to the system for 8745 s (≈2 h 26 min) using the potentiostat’s Galvanostatic Scan function. All tests were conducted at room temperature. After corrosion, the specimens were cleaned under running water and brushed with a light plastic bristle brush, followed by an ultrasonic bath in ethanol. Quasi-static tensile tests were performed on four round-type specimens complying with the standard ASTM-E8/E8M-22. An extensometer with a 50 mm gauge length was employed to measure strain, and the tests were performed under displacement control at a velocity of 1 mm/min. The S690QL steel is a high-strength structural steel compliant with the British Standard BS EN 10025-6: 2004+A1: 2009. The sample was grounded using silicon carbide papers #80, #180, #220, #400, #600, #800, #1200 and #2500 in succession and in this order, polished and then etched with Nital (2% nitric acid). The specimens were prepared by grinding them successively with silicon carbide papers #400, #800, #1000, and #2000, followed by cleaning in an ultrasonic bath with ethanol. This process served two crucial purposes: removing naturally formed oxides and degreasing, thus achieving uniformity across all specimens. The grips were safeguarded from corrosion by applying a coating of spray paint on both sides, a layer of black electrical tape followed by a coating of silicone on the side that would be immersed in the solution. The specimens were stored in a desiccator until testing to prevent premature corrosion. To induce pre-corrosion, the specimens were placed in a three-electrode cell setup consisting of: the working electrode, which is a specimen of the S690 QL steel; the platinum wire counter electrode; the silver chloride electrode (Ag/AgCl electrode) reference electrode; and a water-based solution of 3.5% sodium chloride (3.5%NaCl) as the electrolyte. The specimens were left for 30 min in open circuit to reach a more stable surface state. At the end of that period, a current of 0.25 A was applied to the system for 8745 s (≈2 h 26 min) using the potentiostat’s Galvanostatic Scan function. All tests were conducted at room temperature. After corrosion, the specimens were cleaned under running water and brushed with a light plastic bristle brush, followed by an ultrasonic bath in ethanol. Quasi-static tensile tests were performed on four round-type specimens complying with the standard ASTM-E8/E8M-22. An extensometer with a 50 mm gauge length was employed to measure strain, and the tests were performed under displacement control at a velocity of 1 mm/min. Processing Text: The EHEA with a nominal composition of Al 21Co 19.5Fe 9.5Ni 50 was prepared by arc-melting a mixture of constituent elements with a purity higher than 99.99 wt.% in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Before the melting process, the surfaces of each metal block were mechanically cleaned to remove surface oxides. Each alloy sample was melted five times for one minute and flipped over each melting to ensure complete mixing and chemical homogeneity. Solution treatment at 900 and 1100 °C followed by furnace cooling to room temperature leads to a significant precipitation of L1 2 phases within the FCC phases. Furthermore, solution treatment at the same temperature, followed by rapid water quenching, results in the appearance of numerous L1 0 phases within the B2 phases. After solid-solution treatments at 900 °C for 1 h, the samples were cooled to room temperature using three different cooling methods: furnace cooling (at a rate of 5 °C min -1), air cooling, and water quenching. These samples were named as 900F, 900A, and 900W, respectively. Subsequently, following a 1-h solid-solution treatment at 1100 °C, the specimens were cooled to room temperature using the same cooling methods, resulting in samples named 1100F, 1100A, and 1100W, respectively. Solution treatment: 900 °C/1 h/Furnace cooling (900F)

Both alloys were prepared firstly by gravity casting and then solution treated at 500 °C for 8 h. During these processes, the Mg-6Li-2Gd alloy was protected under the Ar atmosphere to avoid oxidation. Afterwards, the Mg-6Li-2Gd alloy was preheated at 300 °C for 30 min and warm rolled at 200 °C using six passes, each of ∼22 % reduction, with inter-pass annealing of 10 min at 300 °C. After rolling, a final thickness of ∼1.4 mm Mg-6Li-2Gd sheet was obtained. To achieve a completely recrystallized microstructure, the rolled Mg-6Li-2Gd alloy was then annealed at 350 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching. Both uniaxial and interrupted LUR tensile tests were conducted on the Zwick-Roell testing machine at room temperature and used the dog-bone tension samples parallel to the extrusion direction (ED) or rolling direction (RD). The tension samples were machined in the middle of the extruded bars or rolled sheets, with a gauge length of 18 mm and a cross-section area of 3 mm × 2 mm. The rate of the uniaxial and interrupted LUR tension tests was the same, i.e., the cross-head speed was 1 mm/min. During LUR testing, the tensile samples were firstly stretched to a strain of 0.5 % under strain-controlled mode, then unloaded under stress-controlled mode, and finally reloaded to the next unloading strain under strain-controlled mode. The strain interval was set as 0.5 % strain. Individual intrinsic strengths were investigated using a Nano Indenter XP with a Berkovich tip. A maximum 200 nm displacement was applied in each indent with a strain rate of 4 nm/s and a 10 s holding duration at the peak contact displacement. Processing Text: The equimolar CoCrFeNi HEA ingot used in this work was prepared by vacuum induction levitation melting from pure Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni metals with 99.9 wt.% purity constituent elements. The ingot was remelted four times to promote chemical homogeneity and then dropped into a rectangular cross-section copper mold with a length of 300 mm and an inner diameter of 25 mm. The ingot was cut to a rod of diameter 20 mm and length 200 mm, which was then homogenized at 1473 K for 24 h. The rod was first hot-rotary swaged to 8 mm in diameter along the longitudinal direction after preheating at 1173 K for 1 h, and then hot-drawn to 1 mm in steps at 1023 K. Subsequently, the HEA wires of diameter 1 mm was subjected to multi-pass cold-drawing at ambient temperature with an areal reduction of ∼10% followed by annealing at 1173 K for 1 h in each step, resulting in a final diameter of ∼70 μm with a length of more than 300 m. The CoCrFeNi microfibers were further treated by ECT. The electric current was applied parallel to the length direction of the treated microfiber using a precision direct current (DC) power supply for 480 s with various current densities of j= 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200 A/mm 2, and the corresponding specimens are labeled as ECT100, ECT120, ECT140, ECT160, ECT180 and ECT200, which reach a stable temperature of 623 K, 747 K, 850 K, 943 K, 1013 K, and 1075 K during the ECT, respectively, as measured by an FLIR A325sc infrared camera. For comparison, CHT was also performed on another batch of CoCrFeNi microfibers at 623 K, 747 K, 850 K, 943 K, 1013 K, and 1075 K for 480 s, with the samples labeled as CHT623, CHT747, CHT850, CHT943, CHT1013 and CHT1075, respectively. The AlNbTiVZr RHEA powder was prepared by plasma rotating electrode process (PREP), and the atomic percentages of each element are shown in Table 1. The morphology of the alloy powder is shown in Fig. 1(a). The XRD pattern shown in Fig. 1(b) reveals that the alloy powder is composed of the body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution phase. The process was conducted in a laser direct energy deposition system, as shown in Fig. 1(c). The deposition process was carried out on a TA15 substrate with the X scanning direction. A zigzag scanning strategy in XOY plane was adopted to deposit each layer. The zigzag scanning strategy was adopted and the reasons were as below: firstly, this path ensured that the laser beam evenly deposits energy on the surface, thus achieving uniform heating and alloying of the workpiece surface; secondly, the Z-shaped path could effectively reduce the residual stress and deformation of the material, thereby improving processing quality and accuracy [22,23]. The process parameters were as below: the diameter of the laser beam was 3 mm; the laser power was 1600 W; the powder feeding rate was 7 g/min; and the scanning speed was 10 mm/s. The entire preparation process was carried out in an argon-protected atmosphere with an oxygen content below 100 ppm. Cylindrical specimens with a diameter of 4 mm and a height of 6 mm were prepared by cutting the deposited block using the wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) technique. The surface of the compression samples were cleaned with sandpaper before conducting the hot compression tests at room temperature, 600 ℃, 700 ℃, and 800 ℃ using a DSI-Gleeble 3500 equipment. The samples were heated from room temperature to preseted temperature using a heating device with a ramp rate of 10 ℃/s and held for 300 seconds after reaching the preseted temperature. The compression tests were performed at a strain rate of 0.001 s -1 with a strain of 50%. Condition: Room Temperature; Processing state: synthesized by levitation melting

The principal consumable materials were synthesized in powdered form utilizing commercially available Fe-based flux-cored wire, denominated as G6. The investigated feedstock powder exhibited a nearly spherical morphology and was atomized using nitrogen gas atomization. The average particle diameter of the feedstock powder was determined to be 94.7 μm, with particle sizes ranging from 58.2 μm (D 10) to 139 μm (D 90), as shown in Fig. 1. The chemical composition of the G6 powder was analyzed using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES), which revealed a nominal composition of Fe-9.3Cr-2.3Si-0.4 C-0.38Mn in weight percent (wt.%). Five distinct laser power settings were selected based on their substantial influence on the energy density across various parameter sets, thereby affecting the average grain size in the central region of the deposit. Each deposited block consisted of 10 layers, with the deposition area maintained constant throughout all the deposition processes. The laser power was determined through a preliminary series of experiments conducted prior to this study, which yielded stable tracks with uniform geometry (see Fig. 2 (b)). The design of experiments for single parts included various laser powers ranging from 300 W to 900 W, with intervals of 150 W. The powder deposition rate, scanning velocity, and coaxial gas flow were consistently maintained at 5 g/min, 850 mm/min, and 8 L/min, respectively. A beam diameter of 1 mm and a layer thickness of 250 μm were consistently applied for the deposition of each layer across all specimens of the Fe-Cr-Si based hardfacing alloy. It was observed that surface quality at power settings of 750 W and 900 W was significantly inferior, whereas the surface quality and geometric accuracy improved markedly at the setting of 450 W. The highest hardness observed in an additively manufactured part was at 600 W, achieving an average hardness of 554 HV. It is evident that a laser power of 450 W facilitates a notably enhanced surface morphology, and thus, was selected as the optimized laser power condition for processing parameters during repair operations. For microstructural characterization, the laser repaired G6 were sectioned along the middle of the edge in the XZ plane. To minimize the influence of temperature, unintended phase formation, strain, and residual stress on the microstructures, the specimens were machined using wire electrical discharge machining (wire-EDM). Subsequently, metallographic specimens were subjected to a series of grinding steps utilizing SiC grinding papers up to a grit size of 4000. The specimens were then polished using colloidal silica with a particle size of 0.04 μm and rinsed with ethanol to remove any residual silica from the surface. To reveal the boundaries of the melt pools (MPBs) and examine the microstructure, Beraha's reagent was used to etch the deposits [ 51]. Microstructural imaging was conducted using a Zeiss A1 optical microscope (OM) and a JEOL 7800F field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM) equipped with Aztec Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS). The specimens were analyzed using a Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diffraction (XRD) instrument equipped with a Cu Kα anticathode (λ = 1.5412 Å). XRD was operated at 45 kV and 200 mA in a theta-2theta scan mode to identify the phases present. The diffraction angle ranged from 30° to 100°, with a scan rate of 2°/min. For the characterization of the surface microstructure in the XZ plane, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was employed using the FE-SEM equipped with an Oxford EBSD camera. EBSD maps were acquired with a step size of 0.75 μm and an accelerate voltage of 15 kV. The data obtained from EBSD analysis were represented in the form of pole figure (PF), inverse pole figure (IPF) maps and kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps. The EBSD data collected were processed using MTEX toolbox [ 52]. The reconstruction of parent austenite grains was achieved using the algorithm proposed by Nyyssönen et al. [ 53]. To investigate the mechanical performance of DED-printed G6, a tensile test was conducted along the build direction (BD) at room temperature (RT, 20 °C) using miniature tensile test bars with a gauge portion of 2.0 mm in thickness samples [ 55]. A total number of 15 miniature size tensile test samples were extracted from the 50 × 50 × 50 mm 3block parallel to the building direction with an electrical discharge machine (EDM) technique. Continuous uniaxial tests were performed at room temperature using a strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. A nanoindentation test was conducted using an Anton Paar nanoindentation equipped with a NHT 3(Nano Hardness Tester) to obtain stress-strain responses, as seen in Fig. 5 (a). This technique enables the measurement of local hardness (H) and elastic modulus (E) of different phases present in the deposited layer. Indents with a diamond spheroconical tip (R = 10 μm) was made employing force-controlled continuous stiffness measurements (CSM) [ 57]. A sinusoidal oscillation with a frequency of 15 Hz and amplitude of 15 mN was superimposed on a base load that increased at a constant strain rate of 0.1 s −1up to 300 mN. The spacing between indents in the vertical direction was 50 μm. Processing Text: To reduce the initial sheet thickness for both alloys to 3 mm, cold-rolling and solution treatment at a temperature of 1100 °C was performed, followed by water quenching. FSW was conducted on a research-type FSW apparatus. The rotational speed, travel speed, and tile angle of the stir tool were 500 rpm, 40 mm/min, and 2.5°, respectively. In addition, the plunge depth of the shoulder was set to be 0.25 mm. The N-HEA and N-steel sheets were positioned on the advanced side (AS) and retreated side (RS), respectively. The samples for metallography were cut perpendicular to the welding direction. First, the sample was etched using 6 ml of hydrochloric acid, 6 ml of hydrogen peroxide, 6 g of copper sulfate, and 12 ml of water. Subsequently, the sample was gently polished with a polishing machine to remove the corrosion products from the N-steel side. Finally, the sample was etched with a solution of 10 g of picric acid, 5 ml of hydrochloric acid, and 100 ml of ethanol. Using electrical discharge machining, flat dog-bone-shaped specimens with standard dimensions of 22 mm in length, 4 mm in width, and 3 mm in thickness were cut. Condition: 77 K

CoCrFeNi(SiC)x (x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3) HEAs were prepared through laser metal deposition. Highly pure powders (purity >99.5 %, particle size >100 μm) of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni in equal atomic ratios of 100, 90, 80, and 70 at.% were weighed on a JS20-01 electronic precision balance (accuracy ±0.1 g). Before the start of alloying, 0, 10, 20, and 30 at.% SiC particles (purity >99.9 %, particle size <30 μm) were added, and the resulting specimens were labeled as 0-SiC, 10-SiC, 20-SiC, and 30-SiC, respectively. The formulated powders were mixed in a high-energy ball mill (YXQM-12L, MITR Co. Ltd., Hunan, China) at 100 r/min for 300 min. During the grinding process, the mill is stopped sequentially for 5 min at 15-min intervals to minimize the occurrence of cold-welding. A stainless steel bottle and Al2O3 balls with a diameter of 3-5 mm were used as the grinding medium under argon atmosphere protection. The weight ratio of balls to powder was 2:1. The substrate material was 304 stainless steel with dimensions of 180 mm × 100 mm × 10 mm. AM was performed by using an LMD machine (RFL-A3000D, Wuhan Lijiang Laser Technology). The laser power was 1500 W, scanning speed was 4 mm/s, spot size was 2.7 mm, and overlap rate was 50%. Pure argon was used as the powder feeding and protection gas. The specimen deposition height was approximately 10 mm. Specimens were cut into 10 mm × 10 mm × 2 mm blocks by using an electric spark wire cutter. The sample blocks were gradually sanded with sandpaper. The prepared samples were corroded with copper chloride solution (CuCl2:HCl:C2H5OH = 1:1:1). Specimen: 10 at.% SiC; Ultimate tensile strength: 799.67 MPa; Elongation: 8.17%

Processing Text: Rods of polycrystalline Ni with a diameter of 10 mm were selected as raw material and the energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) analysis was carried out to measure the chemical composition of pure nickel (listed in Table 1). Before processing, the Ni rod was annealed at 1000 °C for 10 h to homogenize the microstructure with an average grain size of 50 μm. Then, the gradient lamellar microstructure of the Ni rod was fabricated by means of ultrasonic surface rolling treatment (USRT) technique, which was first proposed by A. The USRT technique illustrated in Fig. 1(a) combines deep rolling with ultrasonic impact, leading to the dual effect of cold extrusion and impact with a high frequency of rolling ball on the material surface [ 24-26]. Therefore, severe plastic deformation was produced on the surface layer of the Ni rod, thus forming a gradient lamellar microstructure from the surface to the interior of the cross-section. During the USRT processing, the annealed Ni rod was fixed on the lathe with a rotation speed of 250 r/min and a feeding speed of 10 mm/min. Besides, the ultrasonic vibration frequency and amplitude of the rolling ball was 17.7-18.8 kHz and 12.8 μm, respectively. Five different static loads were adopted to force pressure on the rod surface for 5 repeated times from a single feeding direction, which successively was 120 N, 135 N, 150 N, 165 N, and 180 N. Cross-section depth: 20 μm; Lamellar thickness: 185 nm; Strain rate: 0.05 s^-1

Processing Text: Three alloys were selected for experimental validation, including one non-equimolar counterpart with greater plasticity (V5 alloy). The three HEAs were prepared by vacuum arc melting using raw materials of purity greater than 99.9 % for pure Nb, Ti, V, and Zr metals in an argon gas atmosphere. The samples were electrodischarged machined cut into Φ 4 mm × 6 mm for subsequent compression tests, and then mechanically polished to remove machining marks. Processing Text: In this work, API X65 steel with lamellar grain (LG) structure is constructed through warm deformation techniques. The material employed in this study is commercial API X65 pipeline steel, characterized by a chemical composition of Fe-0.051C-0.24Si-1.52Mn-0.18Mo-0.19Cr-0.2Ni-0.04V (weight percent). A 120 kg cast was fabricated by vacuum-induction melting (length of 550 mm, width of 200 mm, and thickness of 130 mm). The dilatometric analysis was conducted using a Gleeble-3180 thermal simulation machine, and measured Ac1 and Ac3 temperatures of the steel were 724 °C and 835 °C, respectively. In order to obtain LG structure, the cast was subjected to forging at 650 °C with 73 % reduction, resulting in a billet with a dimension of 930 mm × 320 mm × 35 mm. Subsequently, the billet was reheated to 780 °C for 2 h and warm-rolled to dimensions of 1900 mm × 400 mm × 16 mm, with a rolling reduction of 54 %, as shown in Fig. 1a. Processing Text: The 24CrNiMoY alloy steel powder was prepared by vacuum induction melting gas atomization (VIGA), and the fine powder with a particle size of 15-53 μm was obtained by vibration sieving. The powder particle size distribution was measured by LA-920 laser particle sizer, and the powder morphology and particle size distribution are shown in Fig. 1. It can be seen that the powder particle size distribution ranges from 5 to 80μ m, and the average powder particle size is 34.3 μm, and the alloy steel powders are well sphericalized, which is suitable for the SLM printing block. The SLM 24CrNiMoY alloy steel samples with good surface formation and high tensile strength along with high elongation were printed by varying the laser power, i.e., energy density, using a 1000 W fiber laser SLM 3D printer with no change in other parameters. The SLM device used an AFS-M260 model equipped with a 1000 W fiber laser manufactured by Beijing Long yuan Company for sample preparation, and the standard x/y grating alternate scanning mode was used. In order to minimize porosity and further melt the upper layers of unfused powder and pore defects, a cross-scanning strategy was used, where the laser scanning direction was periodically rotated by 67° between adjacent layers. Q235 steel was selected as the substrate, which was preheated to 80 °C to reduce the temperature gradient. During the forming process, argon was continuously injected into the cavity as a protective gas to ensure that the oxygen content was less than200 ppm. Two kinds of samples were prepared, one of which was 10mm × 10mm × 10 mm for microstructure analysis and hardness testing, and the other was a tensile specimen of 30mm × 7mm × 1 mm for testing the mechanical properties. The wire-cut samples were ultrasonically cleaned with acetone solution, then sequentially sanded and polished, and then corroded using a solution of HNO3 (2 ml) and C2H5OH (48 ml) in conjunction for 3-5s. The cubic specimen blocks were ground and polished to reduce their surface roughness, and the microhardness of the samples was tested with a Qness Q10A + type microhardness tester under a load of 4.9 N and a holding time of 15S. The tensile specimens were designed according to the ISO 6892-1 standard, and the tensile tests were carried out at room temperature using an AG-X plus 100 kN electronic universal testing machine at a tensile speed of 0.5 mm/min, and the fracture morphology was observed using SEM equipment. The results show that with the optimized laser power over 400 W, the powder layer thickness can be increased to 60 μm, and the theoretical productivity reaches 7.2 mm3/s, which is more than two times of the normal SLM technology. As the laser energy density increases, the structure of melt pool changes from a thermal conduction mode to a keyhole mode, and the microstructure mainly consists of martensite, bainite and pre-eutectic ferrite, and the phase composition of the specimen is α-Fe phase and a small amount of Fe3C,with fine grain size and irregular orientation. When the laser energy density is 68 J/mm3, the microhardness of the specimen is 410HV0.2, the tensile strength reaches 1121 MPa and the percentage elongation after fracture is 11.5%, which realizes a good match between strength and ductility. The fine tempered martensite and lower bainite in the microstructure is the key to excellent strength and ductility. In order to avoid the keyhole mode of the molten pool, it is necessary to reduce the laser power or increase the powder thickness. The pristine powder was prepared by vacuum induction melting gas atomization (VIGA) technique and the powder quality was good. The relative density of 24CrNiMoY specimens shows a trend of increasing and then decreasing with the increase of EVD, and when the laser energy density is 68 J/mm 3, the density of the specimen is the highest, which reaches 98.42%, with the best surface molding quality and fewer internal defects. When the laser energy density reaches 72 J/mm 3, due to the high laser energy density, the "keyhole effect" appears at the bottom of the molten pool, which reduces the molding quality of the specimen. The microstructure of 24CrNiMoY specimen is mainly dominated by martensite, lower bainite and granular bainite, and with the increase of EVD, the HAZ area increases, and the proportion of bainite organization increases, which reaches the optimum when the laser energy density is 68 J/mm 3. At this time, the grain size is fine, the weaving strength is the weakest, and the orientation is irregular, thus obtaining a uniform specimen organization, which is conducive to improving the strength of alloy steel. Under the optimized scanning strategy, the best microhardness of 410 HV, tensile strength of 1121 MPa, yield strength of 1080 MPa, elongation after break of 11.5% were obtained for 24CrNiMoY specimens when the laser energy density was 68 J/mm 3. By increasing the layer thickness to 60 μm, not only can we obtain SLM specimens with good molding performance, but the molding rate also reaches 7.2 mm 3/s, which is 2 times higher than that of the low-layer-thickness molding. The microstructure and its relationship with the mechanical properties of an Inconel 718 superalloy fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM) technology were investigated under different post processes, including HT1, HT2, HT2+HIP and as-built conditions. Specifically, HT1 involved solution treatment at 960 °C for 1 h followed by air cooling (AC) and aging treatment at 720 °C for 8 h with furnace cooling (FC) to 620 °C for 8 h. HT2 involved solution treatment at 980 °C for 1 h followed by AC and aging treatment at 760 °C for 1 h with FC to 650 °C for 1 h. HT2+HIP included the same solution and aging treatments as HT2, with an additional Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1170 °C for 4 h at 100 MPa. The AM IN718 superalloy was fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM) of gas-atomized IN 718 superalloy powders produced by Höganäs Corporation. The SLM parameters were as follows: laser power of 300 W, scanning speed of 1150 mm/s, hatch spacing of 110 μm and layer thickness of 30 μm. Following HT2+HIP treatment, the rod-like γ″precipitates appears comparatively shorter and thicker in comparison to the HT1 condition, albeit with a slight decrease in dimensions as shown in the blue window in Fig. 5. During HIP treatment, the Laves phase located between dendrites dissolves into the matrix at elevated temperatures, liberating a substantial quantity of Nb element. Consequently, this process yields a notable augmentation in the γ″precipitates generated through the aging treatment as shown in Fig. 5 (b). Condition: as-built; Temperature: room temperature

The Al2O3P/CoCrFeMnNi composites were fabricated by mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The base matrix is prepared using Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, Ni pure metal powder with a purity higher than 99.5 wt% and the particle size less than 48 μm. The Al2O3 powder of different sizes was used as the reinforcement, which contains nano and micro Al2O3. The size of nano-Al2O3 is 20-30 nm with purity of 99.8% and the values of micron-Al2O3 powder are 20-30 nm and 99.9%, respectively. In the process of SPS, infrared thermometer was used to determine the sintering temperature of the material by adding holes to the graphite mold. A two-step ball milling method was selected during the preparation process of micron and bimodal-size particle reinforced HEA composites, that is, the HEA matrix was alloyed by high-energy ball milling for 30 h, followed by an additional 10 h milling with the micron-Al2O3P to ensure uniform particle dispersion. The Cu-20 wt% Fe alloy was produced in a conventional VIM (Vacuum Induction Melting) furnace. For that, commercially pure Fe (99.97 wt%) and Cu (99.92 wt%) elements were poured into a graphite crucible, followed 10 min of metallurgical homogenization of the molten bath before solidification. The Cu-Fe alloy was solidified in a stepped Cu mold using centrifugal casting so that rapidly solidified samples could be generated. Rods having 7, 9 and 11 mm were produced in duplicate so that more samples for microstructural and mechanical properties analyses could be examined. The alloy was melted in situ since the heating system was able to control it. After attaining the desired temperature of the melt, the heating system was turned off and the mold rotated. As such, the molten alloy filled the stepped cylindrical internal cavity of the Cu mold, before solidification naturally started. For metallographic examination of the different sectors along the rods, the samples were polished and etched with a solution (5 g of FeCl 3+ 50 ml of HCl + 100 ml of H 2O) for 10 s, and then examined using an optical microscope. Hardness tests were performed on the transversal sections of the different rod sectors using a test load of 200 gf and a count time of 15 s. Great attention has been paid to the hardness tests to ensure that the indentation size was sufficiently large to encompass all microconstituents, thereby enabling a comprehensive response from the entire microstructure. The average of at least 20 measurements was used to determine the representative hardness value for each sample. Uniaxial engineering compressive tests on the cylindrical rods were performed by using a universal testing machine (Instron model 5500R) at a strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1(with constant crosshead speed). The tested specimens’ geometry was 5 mm in diameter and 7.5 mm in length. XRD analysis was carried out to identify the formed phases, using a Bruker D8 Advance ECO, within an angular range varying from 5° to 90° (2θ) with a step size of 0.02° and a count time of 0.25 s per step. Processing Text: The tensile specimens were cut by electrical discharge machining (EDM) along the rolling direction (RD) of the steel plate with a gauge length of 25 mm, a thickness of 3 mm and a width of 7 mm. Tensile tests were performed at a crosshead speed of 3 mm/min in a Gotech electronic universal testing machine, where a laser extensometer was used to monitor the tensile strain. At least three tensile specimens of each steel were deformed to fracture to ensure reproducibility. To reveal the microstructural evolution during straining, interrupted tensile tests to engineering strains of 3% (or 5%) and 10% were performed. The microstructure was analyzed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron back-scatter diffraction (EBSD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). EBSD was performed in a Zeiss Ultra55 scanning electron microscope, and specimens were prepared by vibration polishing with 50 nm colloidal silica for 2.5-24 h in a Buehler-VibroMet 2. TEM was performed on a FEI Tecnai G2 F20 instrument operating at 200 kV. The TEM specimens were cut by EDM with a thickness of 1 mm and then first ground into foils with a thickness of <80 μm. Subsequently, the foils were further thinned using Struers TenuPol-3 electrochemical double-jet equipment, which was formed into an electrolyte of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% ethanol at a voltage of 20 V and a temperature of −30 °C. In the present work, the AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA was hot rolled in multiple passes at different temperatures and reductions. The hot rolling process of as-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA is shown in Fig. 1(b) , involving four rolling temperatures (800 °C, 900 °C, 1000 °C and 1200 °C). Among them, the condition of 1200 °C and 60% reduction was tested as a control group to further explore the improvement of the mechanical properties. Taking the deformation of hot rolling at 1000 °C as an example, the sheet is heat-treated by annealing for 10 mins at 1000 °C, and then hot rolling operated at ∼10% reduction. Upon successful completion of the rolling process (i.e., absence of sheet edge cracking and uniform sheet thickness), the 10% reduction sample is reintroduced into the furnace and annealing for 10 mins again. Subsequently, the ∼20% reduction rolling stage is initiated, and the process is repeated. The deformation achieved during the final successful rolling represents the hot rolling reduction at this temperature. After completing all the hot rolling tests, sheets with 10% reduction at 800 °C, 40% reduction at 900 °C, 60% reduction at 1000 °C and 60% reduction at 1200 °C are obtained (denoted as H81, H94, H106 and H126, respectively). The specific samples of SEM were first polished to 3000-grit SiC abrasive paper, and then electrolytically polished for 50 s in a reagent mixture (electrolyte is a mixed solution of 10% perchloric acid, 30% n-butanol and 60% methanol). After polishing, the samples were etched in a solution (etching solution is a mixed solution of 3% hydrofluoric acid, 7% nitric acid and 90% deionized water) for 3 s to complete the SEM sample preparation. The TEM specimens were prepared by means of ion milling on a GATAN 691. High purity elements (Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni with purity above 99.9%) were used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA ingots in a vacuum induction magnetic levitation melting furnace under high purity argon atmosphere. To ensure the chemical homogeneity of the ingots, the melting process was repeated for more than five times. The melt was cast into the water-cooled copper mold, and finally AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA ingots were obtained. The material with Φ74 × 100 mm was cut from the center of the ingot as the raw material used in the experiment. Subsequently, a circular sheet with a diameter of 74 mm and a thickness of 4 mm was fabricated as a hot-rolled specimen. Condition: H106; Processing state: Hot-rolled

A series of (FeCoCrNi) 100-XTi X(X = 0, 1, 3, 7, and 9 at. %) HEAs were synthesized via arc-melting followed by thermo-mechanical treatment. These samples were derived from high-purity element powders of Fe, Co, Cr, Ni, and Ti (> 99.95 wt. %). The raw powders were blended in stoichiometric proportions and ball-milled for 4 h. To mitigate splashing during the melting process, the mixed powders were compacted into cylinders (φ10mm × 12 mm) under 15 MPa pressure. Each ingot underwent four remelting cycles to ensure uniform mixing, resulting in button-like as-cast samples. The as-cast samples were heat-treated at 1000 °C for 2 h, followed by hot compression deformation and annealing treatments (1000 °C for 2 h), and quenched in water to achieve homogenization. The as-homogenized samples were subsequently cold-rolled to achieve approximately 70% thickness reduction, then annealed (1000 °C for 5 min) before being quenched in water, resulting in as-recrystallized samples for further analysis. Condition: Room Temperature; Phase: FCC + Cr-rich (σ) phase + (Co, Ni), Ti-rich (η) phase; Processing state: Ti doping enhances yield strength and ultimate tensile strength

Compression tests at elevated temperatures were employed using a dynamic thermal simulator (Gleeble-3180) in a vacuum environment (4 × 10 −3Pa). Processing Text: In this study, a Ti3Zr1.5NbVAl0.25 HEA was produced by DED. The experimental Ti 3Zr 1.5NbVAl 0.25HEA powder was prepared using the plasma rotating electrode process, with specific parameters such as an alloy rod rotation speed of 21,000 r/min, a plasma arc current of 1500 A, and an electrode movement speed of 1.4 mm/s ( Fig. 1(a) ). The effects of process parameters on single track cladding layer (STCL) were studied by response surface methodology (RSM), and the parameters were optimized accordingly. The ranges for P, v, and fare 1200-1800 W, 8-11 mm/s, and 0.7-1 r/min, respectively. The DED equipment comprises an ytterbium fiber laser system (YLS-4000-U-K, Germany), a multi-axis linkage robot arm (KUKA, Germany), a coaxial powder feeder, circulating water cooling equipment, etc. ( Fig. 2(a) ). The molten pool forming process is shown in Fig. 2(b), where the high energy laser melts and deposits the powder onto the substrate. During the printing process, the shielding gas flow is maintained at 15 L/min, and the laser spot diameter is 3.85 mm. The process is conducted under high-purity argon, with an oxygen concentration below 50 ppm throughout. A total of 20 groups of experiments were designed, each requiring the printing of a 30 mm STCL. Microhardness testing was performed using a Vickers hardness tester (Innovatest Falcon 500) with a load of 200 g and a dwell time of 13 s, measuring at intervals of 0.5 mm between adjacent points. Nanoindentation experiments of the molten pool and HAZ were carried out using an Agilent G200 instrument, with 10 measurement points in each region and a spacing of 30 μm between adjacent points. For microstructure and elemental distribution analysis, a field emission SEM (Tescan MIRA3-LMH) was utilized. Additionally, the crystal orientation of grains in the molten pool was determined using electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD). The EBSD sample was prepared through electrolytic polishing in an electrolyte solution (10 vol% HClO 4+ 90 vol% CH 3OH), using a voltage of 25 V and a temperature of −30 °C for 30 s. Resulting in optimal values of P= 1615.51 W, v= 8 mm/s, and f= 1 r/min. Considering the precision of the laser equipments, a laser power of 1600 W was selected for the next experiments. The mixture of element powders of Co, Cr, Ni and nano-TiC powders was used to alloy the CoCrNi-TiC composite in-situ by LPBF. To begin with, the mixed powders were tumble blended for 4h, and ball milled for 4h at a powder ratio of 4:1 at 300 rpm. Then, the obtained powders were alloyed in-situ by LPBF on the BLT s200 laser printing machine with a laser wavelength of 1070 nm and a laser spot diameter of 80 μm. The hatch space was set to 80 μm, and the scan direction rotated 67° between each building layer. The strip scanning strategy with a strip width of 10 mm was adopted to minimize the thermal stress within the sample during preparation. According to the nominal composition of CoCrNi-4wt%TiC, the nano-TiC particles with an average diameter of 40 nm and spherical elemental powders of Co, Cr, Ni with an average diameter of around 40 μm were mixed. The laser scanning strategy that combines high scanning speed and high laser power can effectively disperse the agglomeration of the nano-TiC particles. Also, the high times taken by remelting in each building layers facilitates the in-situ alloying of the blended elemental powders containing high melting point Cr powders. This high depression force applied during the keyhole mode melting leads to the heterogeneous distribution of nano-carbides with a higher number density and a smaller particle size at the bottom of the melting pool. The addition of high fraction nano-TiC particles significantly improves the strength of the composite to 1886 MPa at 77K, 1456 MPa at 298K, 528 MPa at 1073K, 300 MPa at 1173K, respectively. Meanwhile, plasticity is maintained at a reasonable level. Test temperature: 77 K; Strengthening mechanisms include lattice friction, second-phase, grain-boundary, and dislocation strengthening

Processing Text: Nano-lamellar structured Cu-0.1 at.% Zr alloys are prepared by the combination of equal channel angular pressing and subsequent cryogenic rolling. A vacuum induction furnace was used to produce a 5 kg ingot (> 240 mm length × 50 mm height × 50 mm width) of the Cu-0.1 at.% Zr material starting from the pure constituent elements (purity ≥ 99.9 wt.%). After homogenizing the cast samples at 1200 K for 6 h and removing the oxidation layer, equal channel angular pressing (ECAP) processing via route B C was applied at room temperature for 12 passes using a die with a channel angle of 90°. This processing treatment introduced an equivalent Von-Mises strain during each ECAP pass of about 1, which was expected to significantly refine the as-cast coarse grained microstructure after the total strain increased up to about 12 to an approximately saturated ultra-fine-grained microstructure. Rolling billets (60 mm length × 50 mm height × 25 mm width) were cut from the center of the ECAP-processed samples along the extrusion direction. The details and underlying principles of ECAP processing and subsequent rolling at cryogenic temperatures, namely cryogenic rolling (CYR), can be found in our previous work [ 21]. After multiple repeated cryogenic cooling and CYR processes, the rolling billet thickness was finally reduced to 5 mm. The total thickness reduction and equivalent Von-Mises strain were about 90 % and 2.3, respectively. Post-deformation annealing treatments were conducted at temperatures between 523 K and 823 K for various durations to obtain different LB spacings. Processing Text: These alloys were prepared from commercial pure Al, battery-grade pure Li, pure Mg, Al-Cu and Al-Zr master alloys under the protection of high-purity Ar. The melt temperature was 710 °C before being transferred into the steel molds, which had been preheated to 250 °C. The molds include a T-shaped mold for evaluating HTS, a spiral mold for measuring fluidity, and a regular bottom-injection permanent mold for subsequent mechanical performance optimization. Some of the alloy ingots (Alloys 1-4) were subjected to a well-designed double-stage solid solution treatment under the protection of Ar. Then, they were quenched in water and aged at 175 °C. According to our previous studies [ 1, 38], the first-stage treatment parameters should be set as 480 °C/32 h. The second-stage treatment parameters are closely related to the melting point of (Cu, Mg)-rich secondary phases at the grain boundaries, which was measured to possess a lower limit of ∼535 °C derived from the DSC curve. Hence, the temperature was set to 530 °C (∼5 °C lower than the melting points) and the time was set to 24 h based on our work on diffusion kinetics. Consequently, the solid solution treatment scheme was determined as 480 °C/32 h + 530 °C/24 h. The aging treatment scheme was determined to be 175 °C/64 h. Processing state: peak-aged; Strengthening phases: δʹ-Al3Li and T1-Al2CuLi precipitates

Processing Text: LPBF builds of pure Nb, with a relative density of 98 %, exhibited an YS of 490 MPa, UTS of 609 MPa, and ductility of 9 % with appreciable strain hardenability. Spherical Nb powders were acquired from Atlantic Equipment Engineers (AEE), and powder size distribution (PSD) analysis was performed using the Microtrac S3500 laser diffraction analyzer. The D 90 upon doing the PSD analysis was found to be 48 μm. The Nb powder was also tested for O contamination using the LECO ON736 infra-red analyzer. Based on the LECO elemental analyzer data, the O and N concentrations in the starting powders were found to be 316 ±11 ppm and 190 ±10 ppm respectively. Nb samples of dimensions 15 mm × 15 mm x 10 mm were printed on the Trumpf TruPrint 1000 equipped with a 55 μm laser beam diameter using the following parameters - laser power of 180 W and 200 W; laser scanning speeds of 200, 400, and 600 mm/s; hatch spacing of 60 μm; layer thickness of 50 μm. The depositions were carried out in an inert Ar atmosphere, and the oxygen in the chamber was maintained below 100 ppm during the process. The sub-sized tensile specimens with a gauge length of 5 mm, and thickness of 1 mm, were machined from 180 to 600 condition using a KENT USA (WSI-200) electron discharge machine. The bulk specimens were uniaxially tensile tested at room temperature at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1. Compression tests were performed using the MTS 322 load frame (MTS Systems Corp., Eden Prairie MN) equipped with a 500 kN load cell. Cylinders of diameter 8 mm and height of 10 mm were compression tested at a strain rate of 10 −3s −1 at room temperature. The tests were conducted up to deformation with ∼80 % height reduction. Three tests each for both tension and compression modes were performed on the build with the optimized parameter. Imaging and Electron Back-Scattered Diffraction (EBSD) was performed using the FEI Nova NanoSEM 230, and Apreo SEM using a step size of 0.25 μm. The EDAX-OIM Analysis™ software was employed to analyze the EBSD scans. Rigaku Ultima III XRD with a Cu Kα target was used for the measurements with a step size of 0.025°. A dual-beam focused ion beam milling system (FEI Nova 200 Nanolab FIB/SEM) was utilized for the preparation of atom probe tomography (APT) tips and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) foil. The foils prepared for TEM were analyzed using the FEI Tecnai G2 F20 ST TEM operating at 200 kV with scanning and transmission modes capability. The APT was operated in laser mode using the CAMECA LEAP 5000XS with the specimen's base temperature at 50 K, pulse rate of 200 kHz, pulse energy of 50 pJ, and a target detection rate of 5-10 ions detected every 1000 pulses. Data analysis was performed using the software package AP Suite 6.1.
