The two studied steels, Fe18Mn0.6C (medium carbon) and Fe18Mn1.0C (high carbon), were fabricated in a vacuum induction furnace. To ensure compositional homogeneity, the ingots underwent annealing at 1150 °C for 4 h under an inert argon atmosphere, then hot-forged into billets with cross-sectional dimensions of approximately 35 mm × 45 mm, and subsequently air-cooled to room temperature. To achieve comparable grain sizes, Fe-18Mn-0.6C and Fe-18Mn-1.0C steels were solution treated at 900 °C for 25 min and 15 min, respectively, and then followed by quenching in water. The initial microstructure of both steels exhibited a fully austenitic structure, with an average grain size of approximately 45 μm (excluding annealing twin boundaries), as illustrated in Fig. 1. Tensile tests were conducted at 298 K and 223 K using an MTS tensile machine at a strain rate of 2 × 10 −3s −1. To investigate the evolution of microstructures, the tensile tests were interrupted at engineering strains of 10 % and 30 % (corresponding to true strains of 9.5 % and 26.2 %, respectively) or continued until fracture. Dog-bone shaped tensile specimens were obtained from heat-treated plates via electrical discharge machining. The specimens had a total length of 65 mm, a gauge length of 15 mm, a width of 4 mm, and a thickness of 2 mm. The strain for all specimens was measured using a standard contact extensometer with a gauge length of 10 mm during the tensile tests. For the tensile tests conducted at 223 K, a low-temperature chamber was attached to the testing machine. This chamber was connected to a liquid nitrogen tank, and the temperature of the tensile test was regulated by the evaporative cooling process of the liquid nitrogen. Following the tensile tests were completed, microscopic observations were performed on the deformed specimens, to investigate their deformation behavior. X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were inspected on Rigaku D/max-2500/PC (Cu radiation). To ensure sufficient diffraction intensity, a slow scan rate of 1° min −1and a range of 40-100° were employed for detection. Prior to XRD analysis, specimens were mechanically grinding with SiC paper and polished with 3 μm and 1 μm diamond paste. The specimens for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) observation were selected from the deformed tensile specimens. Then, these specimens subjected to a series of mechanical grinding and polishing procedures, followed by ion milling to eliminate any damaged surfaces. The ion milling was performed using the Hitachi IM 4000, which was operated under the conditions of 75° for 15 min. Subsequently, EBSD maps were gathered using AZtec software in a Hitachi SU 5000 scanning electron microscope (SEM) with an operating voltage of 30 kV and a step size of 200 nm. For the microstructural examination of fractured specimens, a FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM) operated at 200 kV acceleration voltage was applied. TEM specimens with a diameter of 3 mm were cut from the near tensile fractures and then ground to a thickness of approximately 30 μm by SiC paper, followed by thinning to perforation via ion polishing in a Gatan 694 ion polishing system. Test Temperature: 298 K; SFE: 35.1 mJ/m²

The initial microstructure of both steels exhibited a fully austenitic structure, with an average grain size of approximately 45 μm (excluding annealing twin boundaries), as illustrated in Fig. 1. Tensile tests were conducted at 298 K and 223 K using an MTS tensile machine at a strain rate of 2 × 10 −3s −1. To investigate the evolution of microstructures, the tensile tests were interrupted at engineering strains of 10 % and 30 % (corresponding to true strains of 9.5 % and 26.2 %, respectively) or continued until fracture. The specimens had a total length of 65 mm, a gauge length of 15 mm, a width of 4 mm, and a thickness of 2 mm. The strain for all specimens was measured using a standard contact extensometer with a gauge length of 10 mm during the tensile tests. For the tensile tests conducted at 223 K, a low-temperature chamber was attached to the testing machine. This chamber was connected to a liquid nitrogen tank, and the temperature of the tensile test was regulated by the evaporative cooling process of the liquid nitrogen. Prior to XRD analysis, specimens were mechanically grinding with SiC paper and polished with 3 μm and 1 μm diamond paste. Then, these specimens subjected to a series of mechanical grinding and polishing procedures, followed by ion milling to eliminate any damaged surfaces. The ion milling was performed using the Hitachi IM 4000, which was operated under the conditions of 75° for 15 min. Subsequently, EBSD maps were gathered using AZtec software in a Hitachi SU 5000 scanning electron microscope (SEM) with an operating voltage of 30 kV and a step size of 200 nm. For the microstructural examination of fractured specimens, a FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM) operated at 200 kV acceleration voltage was applied. TEM specimens with a diameter of 3 mm were cut from the near tensile fractures and then ground to a thickness of approximately 30 μm by SiC paper, followed by thinning to perforation via ion polishing in a Gatan 694 ion polishing system. Processing Text: A simple two-step process including the ultrasonic dispersion of ceramic particles and the volatilization of liquid medium by stirring was employed to synthesize Y2O3 nanoparticle modified CoCrNi matrix (Y2O3/CoCrNi) composite powders, which were subsequently processed for L-PBF to make samples. Y2O3 particles were dissolved firstly into alcohol with a powder-to-alcohol weight ratio of 1:200, and then dispersed under ultrasound condition to eliminate the inherent agglomeration. The ultrasonic process was last for 20 min at an input power of 270 W. Afterwards, the CoCrNi powders were poured into the solution, and the mixture was continuously stirred at a constant temperature of 120 °C until the liquid phase medium was completely evaporated. Finally, Y2O3/CoCrNi composite powders were dried in a vacuum furnace at 80 °C for 10 h to remove the moisture. The samples (10 mm × 10 mm × 5 mm and 30 mm × 10 mm × 5 mm) were produced using an EP-M150 facility equipped with a fibre laser at a maximum power of 500 W and a spot size of 70 μm. The substrate was preheated to 70 °C prior to printing and the oxygen content in the building chamber was strictly maintained below 100 ppm with the protection of argon atmosphere. A short linear scanning strategy with 67° rotation between adjacent layers was applied. To determine the optimal parameters, the h was kept constantly (60, 90 and 120 μm) with varying P from 150 to 350 W. The layer thickness (t) was kept at 40 μm. The scanning speed (v) was optimized in advance and the constant value of 800 mm/s was applied. The volumetric energy densities Ev=P/vht were calculated to explore the effects of processing parameters on the printing quality and microstructural evolution. The surface defects and microstructural characteristics of the specimens were detected by optical microscope (OM) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Tescan Mira3) equipped with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS). Before observation, the samples were polished using 1-3 μm diamond and 40 nm colloidal silica suspensions, and followed by etched in a solution of 5 g CuCl2+10 ml ethanal +10 ml HCl for 60 s. Thin foil samples were prepared for TEM by the precision ion polishing system (PIPS) at a voltage of 5 kV/2 kV and an incident angle of 3-7°. The room-temperature tensile test using a universal tensile machine (MTS Alliance RT30) was performed on dog-bone-shaped samples with a gauge dimension of 25 mm × 7.5 mm × 1.5 mm, which were sliced by electro-discharge technique machining (EDM). The tensile direction was perpendicular to the building direction and the strain rate was set at 1 × 10−3s−1. Processing Text: The HfMoNbTaTi alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying (MA) and subsequent spark plasma sintering (SPS). Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, and Ti pure elemental powders (＞99.5 %) with 325 mesh particle size (＜45 μm) were selected as raw materials. The raw material powders were weighed by equal atomic ratio in a vacuum glove box filled with high-purity argon. The total mass of powders in each jar was 50 g. The stainless steel balls with diameters of 5 mm, 8 mm, and 10 mm (1:1:1 mass ratio) were selected as the milling medium. The powders and milling balls were filled into stainless steel jars according to the 10:1 ball-to-powder weight ratio and sealed. QM-3SP4 (Nanjing Nanda Instrument Plant) planetary ball mill was employed for high-energy ball milling to achieve alloying between different elements. The parameters of MA process were as follows: rotational speed: 265 rpm, autorotation speed: 400 rpm, and milling duration: 50 h. To reduce the introduction of impurity elements, no process control agent (PCA) was employed during the MA process. The pre-alloyed powders were taken out in a vacuum glove box and sealed for storage. The pre-alloyed powders were loaded into graphite molds with a diameter of 20 mm in the air. To facilitate demolding, graphite papers (thickness: 0.15 mm) were used to separate the powder from the mold. Subsequently, the combination of powder and mold was placed into a spark plasma sintering furnace (SPS-20T-10, Shanghai Chenhua Technology Co., Ltd.) and preloaded with an axial pressure of 10 MPa. Once the vacuum level reached 7.5 × 10−3Pa, the sintering procedure was started. The sintering procedure comprised the following steps: (1) Heating-up stage: The combination body was heated up to the target sintering temperature at a heating rate of 50 °C/min. The sintering temperature was set to 1400°C-1700 °C at 50 °C intervals. Simultaneously, the sintering pressure was uniformly increased to 50 MPa. (2) Holding stage: The combination body was maintained at the sintering temperature and pressure for 15 min. (3) Furnace cooling stage: At the conclusion of the holding stage, the sintering pressure was rapidly decreased. The combination body was cooled to room temperature within the furnace. The sintering temperature was detected by an infrared pyrometer. The as-sintered alloys were ground using a standard metallographic procedure to 2000# of SiC papers and mechanically polished with a diamond suspension. Cylindrical specimens of dimensions φ4 × 6 mm were randomly obtained from the as-sintered alloys using the electric spark cutting. The specimens’ axes were aligned parallel to the axis of the sintered block’s axis. The specimen’s surfaces were ground by 1500# SiC paper. Instron 5569 electronic universal testing machine was used to conduct the room temperature compression experiments at a strain rate of 10−3s−1. Sintering temperature: 1450 °C; Compressive yield strength with plastic strain of 26.44 ± 1.17 %

The microstructural features, including solidification grains, structural defects, and phase transformations, along with uniaxial tensile behavior in different orientations, were comprehensively studied. A quantitative assessment was carried out to evaluate the contribution of strengthening mechanisms through apprising stacking fault constant of 11362 MPa nm for the developed MEA, enrolling the impact of FCC to HCP crystal structure transition for the cobalt matrix after rapid cooling LAM solidification in the solid-state board. Interstitial atoms of B and N were added by the high-purity FeB and MnN compounds. The ingot was homogenized at 1100 °C for 6 h under an Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching. Cold-rolling was applied to the BN-HEA ingot with a thickness reduction ratio of ∼79 %. Processing Text: The precipitation behavior, mechanical properties, and strengthening mechanisms of FeCrNi-based medium entropy alloys fabricated by laser powder bed fusion and followed by aging treatment were investigated. Subsequently, precipitates were introduced into these LPBF-fabricated FeCrNi and (FeCrNi) 94Ti 3Al 3MEAs through post-heat treatment. LPBF was employed to fabricate the as-built FeCrNi and (FeCrNi) 94Ti 3Al 3alloys samples using a building substrate pre-heated to 100 °C under Ar atmospheres. The as-built samples were subsequently aged at temperatures of 800 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching. For the (FeCrNi) 94Ti 3Al 3alloy aged at 800 °C for 2 h, the discrete needle-shaped precipitates are observed in the FCC matrix. Meanwhile, fine bead-shaped precipitates are uniformly distributed within the FCC matrix for the (FeCrNi) 94Ti 3Al 3alloy. Furthermore, rod-shaped precipitates are distributed within BCC island phase. After aging 800 °C for 2 h, the vacancy density significantly decreases, and dislocations slip from inside the dislocation cellular structure towards the cellular structure boundary. Opposite-sign dislocations are then annihilated at the cellular structure boundary. Consequently, there is a reduction in dislocation density and a gradual formation of a low-energy dislocation network within the cellular structure boundary. Initial state before aging

Alloy ingots with the nominal composition of Ni66-xFe28AlxV6 (x = 16, 17, 18 at%), were prepared by vacuum arc-melting the mixtures of high-purity elements (Ni, Fe, Al and V; 99.99 wt%) in an argon-filled atmosphere. Each ingot was remelted as least five times to guarantee chemical homogeneity. Subsequently, the molten liquid was drop-cast in a water-cooled copper mold with dimensions of 70 × 10 × 10 mm3. The as-cast Ni66-xFe28AlxV6 (x = 16, 17, 18) alloys were denoted as Al-16, Al-17 and Al-18 alloys, respectively. TEM samples were first mechanically ground to 45 μm in thickness and then punched to Ф3 mm circle sheets, followed by a twin-jet electro-polishing with the voltage of 28 V and current of 60 mA. The mixed solution is HNO3:CH4O = 1:4. Microhardness of these as-cast alloys was determined by the nanoindentation tests (KLA-Nano indenter G200) with the maximum load of 500 mN. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. The shape and dimension of tensile sample possess the gauge length of ∼6.5 mm, width of ∼2 mm and thickness of ∼1.2 mm, respectively. In order to guarantee the experimental repeatability, each alloy (Al-16, Al-17 and Al-18) needs to be tested at least three times. Processing state: as-cast; Microstructure: dual-phase eutectic structure of alternating soft FCC and hard B2 nano-lamellae

The LPBF-built samples were fabricated by a commercially available laser powder bed fusion machine (LPBF, GE, M2 Series 5) under a nitrogen atmosphere. The processing parameters optimized for LPBF were used with a laser power of 370 W, hatch space of 0.09 μm, laser scan speed of 1350 mm/s, and layer thickness of 50 μm. During the deposition of powders, bidirectional laser-scanning was conducted, with a 67° rotation between (N) thand (N + 1) thlayers. HIP (American isostatic presses, AIP10-30H) was treated on the LPBF samples in an argon atmosphere at 1150 °C and with a pressure of 100 MPa for 4 h. To achieve surface heterostructure, UNSM treatment was utilized because the system offers versatility in processing conditions according to the substrate. Both surfaces of the LPBF-built and the HIP-treated samples were UNSM-treated as shown in Fig. 1. Before the UNSM treatment, the samples were sliced to a thickness of ∼1.2 mm and polished up to 1200-grit SiC paper. Subsequently, the UNSM was treated on the XZ plane, using the processing conditions given in Table 1. The processing parameters for UNSM were adopted based on Ref. [ 30]. To assess heterogeneity in mechanical properties, Vickers microhardness testing (FM-700) was performed on the cross-section of the samples. For reliability, five indents were made at each position using a load of 50 gf and a dwell time of 10 s. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted at least twice at a quasistatic strain rate of 10 −3s −1along the Z direction using an Instron 5582 machine ( Fig. 1). The tensile specimens were prepared with a gauge length of 1.5 mm and width of 1 mm. The surfaces of the LPBF and HIP samples were polished using 1200-grit SiC paper before tensile testing, while UNSM-treated samples were not polished to preserve the hardened surface. Firstly, the sample design and sample processing of the failure die with different depths and directions were carried out. The material composition, hardness and metallographic structure of the samples were analyzed, and the tensile and impact properties were tested by direct-reading spectrometer, Rockwell hardness tester, optical microscope, scanning electron microscope, MTS testing machine and impact testing machine, etc. Meanwhile, with the help of Deform-HT software and JMatPro software, the coupling simulation of hardness, temperature and structure of the heat treatment of NOS525 steel was realized, and the hardness change of the material after heat treatment was predicted and verified by heat treatment test. Direct reading spectrometer was used to analyze the chemical composition of the samples. The literature shows that the heat treatment quenching process of NOS525 material was 650℃ (1 h) + 850℃ (2 h) + 950℃ (2 h) + 1030℃ (3 h). The cooling method was oil cooling for 8 min and then air cooling for 5 min. The temperature of the die after quenching was about 120℃, and the die was tempered three times in succession. The tempering process temperature was 560℃ (6 h) + 600℃ (6 h) + 600℃ (6 h), and the three times of tempering were all air-cooled cooling, and the die temperature was reduced to below 50℃. By combining Deform-HT software and JMatPro software, the coupling simulation of hardness, temperature and structure of NOS525 steel heat treatment process was carried out, and then the mechanical properties were evaluated according to the results of hardness simulation, and finally the optimization of heat treatment process was guided. The quenching simulation temperature was set to 1000℃, 1030℃, 1060℃, and 1090℃, and other heat treatment parameters were maintained unchanged from the existing heat treatment scheme. According to the sample size, the heat treatment holding time was determined, the quenching holding time is 12 min, and the tempering holding time is 22 min. The heat treatment tests were carried out at different quenching temperatures, the quenching temperatures were 1000℃, 1030℃, 1060℃ and 1090℃ respectively, and the other parameters were consistent with the existing process. A heat treatment model is established to optimize the quenching temperature. Through the coupling simulation of hardness, microstructure and temperature of the die material, combined with the heat treatment test, the heat treatment process temperature of the die material was optimized, that is, the quenching temperature is 1090℃, the first tempering temperature is 560℃, the second tempering temperature is 600℃, and the third tempering temperature is 600℃. Processing Text: In this study, we fabricate near-fully dense and crack-free AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA samples with an alternating nano-scale eutectic lamellar structure composed of disordered face-centered cubic (FCC) and ordered B2 phases using the laser directed energy deposition (LDED) method. By using a novel and simple interlayer pause strategy, we have found that the eutectic lamellar structure can be significantly refined, achieving approximately 40% greater refinement compared to the case without interlayer pause. The optimized EHEA exhibits an exceptionally high strength of 1214 MPa and a sufficient uniform elongation of 16.3%, outperforming the non-interlayer-pause counterpart by 14% in strength and 47% in uniform elongation. Pre-alloyed AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA powders. The LDED processes were performed on a metal LDED AM machine (BLT-C400B) equipped with a laser system with a maximum output power of 1000 W and a focused laser spot diameter of 1 mm. Before printing, the raw atomized powder was dried in a furnace with a vacuum atmosphere at 80 ℃ for 4 hours to ensure excellent powder flowability during the LDED process. Meanwhile, to reduce the potential for oxidation, high purity argon gas was introduced during printing to ensure that the oxygen content in the chamber being less than 100 ppm. The schematics of the scanning strategy and the dimension of the tensile specimen are shown in Fig. 2(b) and (c), respectively. The optimum printing window was acquired through orthogonal experiments, and the specific parameters involved in the orthogonal experiments include laser power (750 W to 950 W) and scanning speed (400 mm/min to 600 mm/min). The optical images representing the average porosity rate of the samples along DD-TD direction are shown in Fig. 3, where the lowest porosity of 0.12 % was obtained with a power of 900 W and scanning speed at 600 mm/min. In line with previous studies, we generally selected a scan spacing equivalent to 40∼50 % of the melting pool width to ensure an ideal overlap. The interlayer rotation angle was carefully chosen according to previous investigations. Based on the powder feed rate contingent upon the motor speed of the powder reservoir, we quantitatively assessed the feed rate by conducting three separate measurements of powder output quality per minute. The argon gas flow rate was set in accordance with the recommendations provided by the equipment engineer. Accordingly, the final optimal process parameters are established: the laser power of 900 W, scanning speed at 600 mm/min, scanning spacing of 1 mm, powder feed rate of 4-6 g/min, interlayer rotation angle of 67° and lens-protecting argon gas flow rate of 8-12 L/min. The pause time between interlayers was changed to 0, 15, 30, 60, and 120 seconds to print EHEA blocks with dimensions of 50×20×5 mm 3 for tensile specimens. Sample without interlayer pause; tensile strength: 1070 ± 12 MPa; uniform elongation: 11.1 ± 0.6%; processing state: LDED (Laser Directed Energy Deposition).

Processing Text: The designed Ti-4.5Al-4.5Mo-7V-1.5Cr-1.5Zr alloy was fabricated by a vacuum arc melting furnace. After casting, the ingot was subjected to two different forging processes. The first one takes place in the β-phase region, followed by water quenching (WQ). By contrast, the second one was performed with a starting temperature slightly above Tβ and a finishing temperature below it (β trans forging), followed by air cooling (AC). The single reduction for both processes was set to be ∼40 %. After the forging process, the alloy underwent an aging treatment at 480 °C for 6 h, followed by AC. The whole thermomechanical process is shown schematically in Fig. 2. The present forged and aged Ti alloys were subjected to various microstructure characterization facilities, including scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi-SU6600), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford instrument), transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-F200), and scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM, Hitachi-HF5000). The specimens for SEM and EBSD were prepared following standard metallographic procedures. For TEM analysis, the samples were ground to a foil with a thickness of ∼50 μm and punched into 3 mm discs. To produce electron-transparent regions in these punched disks, twin-jet polishing was conducted at -30 °C and 50 V in a solution of 65 % methanol, 30 % butyl alcohol, and 5 % perchloric acid. The X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical X'Pert-PRO diffractometer) pattern was obtained using a Cu anode at 45 kV, the diffraction angular is in a range from 30° to 90°. The flat dog-bone tensile specimens with a gauge length of ∼12 mm and gauge width of ∼5 mm were cut using an electrical discharge machine (EDM). Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests were performed on an INSTRON 1195 testing machine with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min (corresponding to an initial strain rate of 1.4 × 10 -3) at room temperature. Tensile properties such as yield strength ( σ0.2), ultimate tensile strength ( σUTS), and total elongation at fracture ( ɛf) were measured using standard operation. Loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) cycles were conducted to measure the back stress evolution. In each cycle, the specimen was first stretched with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min to a designated strain ε, and then it was unloaded using the load-control mode to 20 N at a rate of 200 N/min, followed by reloading at a rate of 1 mm/min again to the next designated strain. At least three samples were performed to ensure the repeatability of the testing. Processing state: aged; Microstructure: multi-architectured α precipitates in β-domains

Processing Text: The ferrous medium entropy alloys (FeMEA) of Fe 63.5(CoNi) 26.5Cr 10 were fabricated using vacuum induction melting MC100V equipment (Indutherm, Germany) with pure elements in an argon atmosphere. The homogenization heat treatment was carried out on rectangular ingots at 1373 K for 6 h and followed by water quenching. The homogenized ingot was rolled at room temperature from 7 to 1.3 mm thickness (a reduction ratio of 81.4%). Three different groups of samples were investigated: as-rolled, as-annealed, and laser-treated samples. The as-annealed samples were obtained through recrystallization annealing the as-rolled plate at 1073 K for 10 min, followed by water quenching. To develop a dual-gradient structure, the as-rolled sheet was laser-treated on both surfaces along a rolling direction. Laser treatment was conducted under an argon atmosphere using a laser module (YLR-300-MM-AC, IPG photonics, USA) with a wavelength of 1.07 μm and a beam diameter of 400 μm. The processing parameters for the laser treatment are listed in Table 1. To establish the distribution of mechanical heterogeneity on the present samples, Vickers microhardness tests were performed with microindent equipment (FM-700, Future-tech) with 100 gf and a dwell time of 10 s on the cross-section. Processing Text: Samples were manufactured using EOS Ti-6Al-4V grade 23 powder on an EOS M290 (EOS GmbH, Germany) LPBF machine housed at the ISO 13485 certified Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) of the Central University of Technology in South Africa. Specimens were produced in three batches, and a representative portion of each batch and specimen type was selected to measure the oxygen content to ensure this was kept below 0.013 wt%. The base plate was preheated to 80 °C, and a high-speed steel blade was used as a scraper. The process parameters consisted of a 40 μm layer thickness, 280 W laser power, 1300 mm/s scan speed, 100 μm spot size and a hatch distance of 120 μm. Bidirectional scanning was used, and the scan direction was rotated by 67° between layers. This set of process parameters results in a material with less than 0.01 % porosity [ 23 ]. For tensile specimens, cylinders with a diameter of D = 10 mm and a length of L = 100 mm were produced in the vertical (Z) and horizontal (X) directions relative to the axis of the LPBF machine (and according to ASTM 59200) that is aligned with the direction in which the load is applied. For fracture toughness specimens, Compact Tension (C(T)) specimens were produced as rectangular blocks to allow for the final dimensions of a width of W = 25 mm. C(T) specimens were produced in three orientations, with the first letter indicating the direction in which the load is applied and the second letter indicating the direction in which the crack propagates, that is, ZX, XZ and XY [ 6 ], as shown in Fig. 1 . After printing, the specimens were stress-relieved (SR) at 650 °C for 3 h in a TSH 15/50/180 vacuum furnace (Elite Thermal Systems, England) and then wire-cut from the build plate. The SR treatment was chosen to allow comparison with the literature [ 15 ]. Subsequent heat treatments were conducted at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in atmospheric air using a box furnace (Ultrafurn, South Africa). Therefore, at least 1 mm was removed by wire cutting or machining from all the heat-treated specimen surfaces to remove any α-case and oxide scale that may have formed. The heat treatment schedules, detailed in Table 1 , included the SR, an anneal (AN) heat treatment, chosen due to its simplicity combined with good tensile properties, and a duplex anneal (DA) heat treatment, chosen based on optimal tensile properties reported in the literature [ 6 , 25 ]. Furthermore, the heat treatments above T β (selected based on values available in the literature [ 9 , 15 ]) were combined with the stress relief (BtSR) and anneal (BtAN) heat treatments to mimic how SR or AN specimens would perform if the PBGs were equiaxed c . c It is acknowledged the above T β heat treatment is at the cost of PBG growth. Comparison to specimens with elongated PBGs is only based on orientation effects. After heat treatment, the specimens were machined and wire-cut to their final dimensions. Processing Text: Fe60Ni25Cr15, Fe60Ni30Cr10, and Fe64Ni15Co8Mn8Cu5 alloys were fabricated using a vacuum induction melting (MC100V, Indutherm) with pure metal (> 99.99 wt%). The 150 g ingots, measuring 50 mm in length, 35 mm in width, and 7 mm in thickness, were subjected to homogenization treatment at 1100 °C for 6 h under an Ar atmosphere. These ingots were then cold-rolled to a final thickness of 1.5 mm, corresponding to a total thickness reduction of 78.5%. To obtain a single face-centered cubic (FCC) phase, the cold-rolled specimens were annealed at 800 °C for 10 and 30 min, and at 900 °C for 30 min, respectively. Processing Text: A series of y (TiC)-Fe 1.4Co 0.8Ni 0.8Cr (y = 0, 2.5, 5.0, 7.5 and 10.0 % in volume fraction, respectively.) composites were prepared by mechanical milling in combination with the vacuum induction melting. Firstly, commercial high purity Fe, Ti and C (size from 0 to 50 μm) powders were weighted and followed mechanically mixed using a planetary ball milling machine. For mechanical alloying, the rotational speed was maintained at 250 r/min, the ball-to-materials ratio was closed to 10:1 and the milling time was set to 8 h. The homogeneous mixed powders were dried in a vacuum drying oven at 110 °C for 90 min, and subsequently shaped into a thin block using a hydraulic press at 15 MPa. The thin block was mixed with Ni, Co and Cr metal particles in a ceramic crucible and then put them into the smelting furnace. As the mixture become melted solution, poured it into a water-cooled copper crucible and cooled in the furnace. The addition of Ti and C element cause lattice distortion of the fcc structure, which in turn boosts the solid solution strengthening in L7.5 composite. Room temperature; Microstructure: fcc phase with submicron/micron TiC; Strengthening mechanisms: grain refinement, dislocation strengthening, precipitation strengthening

Tensile tests were performed at RT using a smooth round bar, the SP test, and fracture toughness tests using single-edge notched tension (SEN(T)) and compact tension (C(T)) specimens. Two tensile tests using the smooth round bar specimen extracted from the longitudinal direction of the pipe were performed at a strain rate of 1 × 10−4/s. For the fracture toughness test, an SENT test using the specimen shown in Fig. 7(a) was conducted according to BS8571. In addition, a C(T) test using the 0.5T specimen was performed according to ASTM E1820 at RT under monotonic loading with a constant velocity of 1 × 10−4 mm/s. SP tests were conducted in air and hydrogen at various hydrogen partial pressures. The maximum load in the SP tests decreased with increasing hydrogen partial pressure and increased with decreasing temperature. Both the C(T) and SEN(T) tests were performed in air, and the C(T) test was performed in hydrogen (under two different hydrogen partial pressures). Specimen: #1; Test condition: Room Temperature

Nominal TiZr-based (MoTiZr, NbTiZr, MoTiVZr, NbTiVZr, and NbMoTiZr) alloys were prepared by arc melting under an argon atmosphere. Each ingot (∼60 g) was fabricated from pure elemental metal of over 99.9% purity and remelted six times to achieve a uniform distribution of the alloying elements. The specimens for cell cultivation were prepared by cutting into Φ14 mm × 1 mm pieces using electrical discharge machining. The surfaces of these samples were mechanically polished using SiC sandpapers with a maximum grit size of #5000. Prior to the cell cultivation experiments, the samples were washed with acetone and ethanol in ultrasonication, heated at 180°C for three hours, and then exposed to ultraviolet light for 24 hours to ensure their cleanness and sterility. Then the samples were placed into a 24-well plate (n=3). Condition: Room Temperature; Microstructure: Multiphase composition; Ductility: 21.66%

Nano-sized graphene powders obtained via the arc-discharge method were incorporated into Al and Cu powders in varying amounts (0-5 wt%) by applying a high-energy ball milling (HEBM) process for different durations. The consolidated composites were prepared by the succeeding uni-axial pre-compaction and pressureless sintering stages. The raw powders were mixed in a powder shaker for 2 hours to obtain more homogenous starting mixtures for the milling process, and they were named as as-blended or non-MAed powders. Stearic acid (C 18H 36O 2, ZAG, 99.5 % pure) was added to the powder blends as the process control agent (PCA). The milling vials were loaded with as-blended powders with a ball-to-powder weight ratio (BPR) of 8:1 under an Argon atmosphere in a glove box to avoid oxidation during the milling process. The removal of PCA before the sintering step was applied in an MSE tube furnace at 420 °C for 2 hours under an Argon atmosphere. Following the de-binding step, the pressureless sintering process was carried out in a Protherm PZF12/105/900 tube furnace under a flow of Argon gas with a 5 °C/min rate of heating and cooling at 600 °C for 2 h. Spherical powder of three alloy compositions was fabricated by nitrogen gas atomization and provided by Höganäs AB, Sweden with powder size distribution of 20-53 µm diameter. All three alloy variants were manufactured using an EOS M290 machine with a 100 µm spot size and 370 W nominal power Yb-fibre laser. Samples were processed in an inert argon atmosphere with a standard oxygen level set and controlled at a maximum of 0.1 %. The samples were printed at 370 W power, 1300 mm/s laser scanning speed, 0.13 mm hatch distance and 0.03 mm layer thickness to produce fully dense samples (>99.8 % relative bulk density). These parameters were selected based on previous work where process optimisation was done utilising a design of experiments approach [32]. Scan rotation of 67° between each layer of material deposition was applied. The heat treatments for all the samples were conducted in a radiation-controlled furnace with a temperature control of ± 2 K. The samples were heated to optimum heat treatment temperature (623/ 648 K) at 10 K/min. The optimum heat treatments are based on previous work [32]. After heat treatment, the samples were air-cooled. The samples for room temperature (RT) tensile testing were heat treated as per specifications summarised in Table 2and then machined to the final shape (see Fig. 1) from the original cylindrical shape. The samples for high-temperature tensile testing were heat treated as summarised in Table 2and then machined to the final shape (see Fig. 1). Processing Text: The surface of the 27SiMn steel substrate was prepared by grinding to remove the oxide skin, followed by cleaning with anhydrous ethanol to remove oil stains and dust. Processing Text: The GH4099 powder prepared by vacuum induction-melting inert gas atomization (VIGA) method was used as the experimental material, with powder particle sizes distributed in the range of 15-53 μm. Before the experiment, the powder was dried in a vacuum drying oven at 80 °C for 8 hours to remove moisture. The GH4099 samples were fabricated using commercial L-PBF equipment (3D Systems ProX-200) for microstructure observations and mechanical performance testing. The fiber laser has a maximum power of 300 W, a wavelength of 1070 nm, and a spot diameter of 75 μm. During the L-PBF experiment, a protective argon gas atmosphere (purity of 99.9 %) was introduced to reduce the oxygen content to below 500 ppm. The laser scanning vector between layers rotates by 90 degrees. Based on optimization based on densification, the processing parameters for the L-PBF of GH4099 blocks include the laser power of 290 W, scanning spacing of 50 μm, layer thickness of 30 μm, and various scanning speeds of 1100 mm/s, 1300 mm/s, 1500 mm/s, and 1700 mm/s. After the L-PBF process, the samples are directly removed from the building platform using wire EDM (electrical discharge machining), without additional stress-relieving heat treatment. For convenience, the L-PBF GH4099 samples fabricated at different scanning speeds of 1100 mm/s, 1300 mm/s, 1500 mm/s, and 1700 mm/s are designated as V1, V2, V3, and V4, respectively. Sample: V1; Scanning speed: 1100 mm/s; Microstructure: Cellular structure; Condition: Room temperature

Processing Text: This study describes a new nonequiatomic proportional cast Co40Cr20Ni30Al4.5Ti5Mo0.5 high-entropy alloy prepared by a vacuum induction melting technique. The samples were then cut into 10 mm × 10 mm × 4 mm blocks and annealed in a KSL1400 high-temperature chamber furnace at 700 °C, 800 °C, 900 °C, or 1000 °C for 2 hours. After annealing at 800 °C, the alloy demonstrates excellent corrosion resistance, characterized by a low passivation current density, a large passivation range, and a high corrosion potential. The microstructure of the alloy was examined using optical microscopy (OM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Furthermore, various corrosion evaluation methods, such as total immersion experiments, potentiodynamic polarization experiments, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, were employed to assess the corrosion performance of the HEA in a 3.5 % NaCl solution. The alloy composition and heat treatment process were carefully designed. According to this strategy, the selected alloy composition is Co40Cr20Ni30Al4.5Ti5Mo0.5. In this study, a Co40Cr20Ni30Al4.5Ti5Mo0.5 HEA was prepared by arc melting the raw materials under a vacuum argon atmosphere. Co, Cr, Ni, Al, Ti, and Mo metal particles with a purity of 99.99 wt% were used as the raw materials. To ensure the chemical homogeneity of the alloy, the button-shaped ingot was remelted six times before being cast into a mould. Subsequently, homogenization was conducted at 1200 °C for 2 hours to obtain rectangular bars measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 100 mm. Afterwards, the specimens were sanded and polished using SiC metallographic sandpaper and a polishing machine. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted on these specimens using an Instron 5569 universal testing machine equipped with an optical extensometer. The loading speed was set at 0.5 mm/min. Additionally, hardness measurements were performed using an HXD-1000TMC/LCD microhardness tester. Electrochemical testing was conducted using a PARSTRT 4000 A workstation. Prior to testing, wires were spot welded to the specimens using a HIMAX TW50 stacker welder. The samples were then sealed with resin, leaving a 10 mm × 10 mm working area. Subsequently, the samples were polished using 180-2000 mesh sandpaper and W2.5 diamond polishing paste until the surface was free of scratches and exhibited a mirror effect, signifying completion of the polishing process. Finally, the samples were rinsed with water and anhydrous ethanol and dried. For the electrochemical tests, a standard three-electrode system was employed. The SCE reference electrode was chosen, with a platinum sheet serving as the auxiliary electrode. A 3.5 % NaCl solution was utilized in the experiment, which was conducted at room temperature (25 °C). Initially, an open-circuit potential (OCP) test was performed for 1800 s. Subsequently, an electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) test was conducted under OCP conditions. The frequency range was set from 100 kHz to 10 mHz with an amplitude of 10 mV. Equivalent circuit diagrams were plotted and fitted using ZView software to obtain the fitted EIS data. Adopting the measurement rate of 0.5 mV/s, potentiodynamic polarization experiments were then carried out, starting from a potential of −1 V (vs. Ref) and ending at 1 V (vs. Ref). The corrosion potential (Ecorr), corrosion current density (icorr), and other relevant data were obtained by fitting the curve using Tafel analysis. Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: The material used in this study was commercial AISI 304 stainless steel. 304 stainless steel bars were solution heat-treated at 1100 °C for 60 min and subsequently quenched in water to obtain a coarse-grained (CG) full austenitic microstructure. The USRP process mentioned in previous work [27-29] was employed on CG rod samples to prepare surface gradient nanostructures. Based on the exploration of a large number of USRP parameters and orthogonal experimental results, the USRP parameters in this study were customized under the premise of avoiding surface spalling: the surface static pressure was 0.4 MPa, the rotational speed of the main shaft was 300 rev/min and the axial feeding velocity of the WC/Co impact ball was 36 mm/min. The samples were processed 10 passes to obtain a thick deformation layer, which was referred to as the USRP sample. Then, a set of USRP samples was welded to a thermocouple and placed in an induction coil, and heated to 700 °C, followed by air-cooling to obtain annealed USRP samples, and the corresponding samples were labeled USRP-700. To reveal the influence of USRP and annealing on the mechanical properties of the material, the Vickers microhardness (HV) test was carried out on the cross-section of all the samples by the HVS-1000 automatic microhardness tester with a load of 25 g and a holding time of 10 s. Uniaxial tensile tests of USRP, USRP-700 and solution-treated (SS) coarse-grained samples (diameter of 5 mm and gauge length of 25 mm) were carried out on a servohydraulic testing machine (MTS810) at a constant cross-head speed of 1 mm/min, and the high-resolution extensometer was used to accurately measure the elongation of the sample to calculate the yield strength of material during the tensile process. To obtain the back stress, loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tensile tests were performed at a strain rate of 1 × 10−4s−1 at room temperature, and the back stress was analyzed using Yang’s method [30]. Tensile fracture morphology and cross-sectional microstructures were characterized using a ZEISS SUPRA55 field emission SEM with electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) and cross-sectional backscattered electron (BSE) detectors, the step size of EBSD is 50 nm. The TEM specimens were sliced by electrical discharge machining, mechanically ground to a thickness of ∼ 50 µm, and then twin-jet thinned using a solution of 10 vol% perchloric acid and alcohol. Processing Text: Samples were built using a SLM280HL (SLM Solutions, Germany) machine equipped with a maximum power of 400 W fiber laser and a laser spot size of 80 µm. To minimize the thermal residual stress, the 316 L stainless steel substrate plate was pre-heated to 200 °C. The following parameters were applied: laser power of 320 W, layer thickness of 30 μm, hatch distance of 70 μm, and scanning speed of 1000 mm/s. A 67° rotation between layers was applied. The as-built samples were annealed for the duration of 12 h at 500 °C - 1000 °C, followed by water quenching. The nomenclature used for the heat-treated condition was AM-HT. Alloy with a nominal chemical composition of Ni 35Co 35Cr 25Ti 3Al 2 was also prepared in conventional vacuum arc melter under argon atmosphere. Repeated melting was carried out at least five times to ensure chemical homogeneity and then dropped into water-cooled copper molds with the dimensions of 50 × 10 × 5 mm 3. The cast ingot was cold rolled to ∼12 % total thickness reduction and thereafter isothermally annealed at 700 °C. The condition was called CR-12 %-HT. All samples for EBSD and electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI) were prepared by standard metallography plus electropolishing. The final electrochemically polishing was carried out using a 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % ethanol electrolyte solution with a voltage of 30 V for 30 s at ambient temperature. Samples for SEM studies were then electro-chemical etched in 10 % phosphoric acid water solution at a voltage of 2 V for 5 s. EBSD was employed to evaluate the recrystallized volume fraction and GB statistics with step sizes of 1 μm (scan area of 500 × 500 μm 2) and 150 nm (scan area of 100 × 100 μm 2), respectively. The smaller scanning step size was utilized for the accurate determination of TB content. TEM foils were first mechanically ground to ⁓50 µm in thickness and then punched into 3 mm diameter disks. Disks were electro-polished using 10 % perchloric acid in ethanol with a twin-jet polisher. The dislocation density analysis of the samples was carried out using X-ray diffraction (XRD; D8 Discover A25, Bruker, Co K α) based on the convolutional multiple whole profile fitting (CMWP) procedure. Hardness tests were carried out using a Vickers hardness tester with a load of 1 kg and a duration of 15 s. For tensile testing, a universal testing machine TSMT EM6.504 equipped with an extensometer was used. Tests were performed at room temperature under quasi-static conditions at a strain rate of 10 −3s−1 on dog-bone-shaped samples with the gauge dimensions of 12.5 × 3.2 × 2 mm 3. A mechanical extensometer was used to monitor the tensile strain. To investigate the microstructural evolution during deformation, interrupted in-situ tensile experiments were conducted using a Kammrath & Weiss tensile stage with an initial strain rate of 10 −3s−1. The in-situ tensile specimens with a gauge dimension of 8 × 2 × 1 mm 3 were fabricated by electrical discharge machining (EDM). For LPBF Ni 35Co 35Cr 25Ti 3Al 2 alloy, all tensile tests were conducted with the loading direction oriented perpendicular to the build direction. Processing state: as-built

The challenges in Wire Arc Directed Energy Deposition (Wire-DED) of super duplex stainless steels (SDSS) are the growth of large columnar grains and undesirably high austenite content. Here we report the additively manufactured SDSS with the addition of TiN inoculant via Wire-DED. Commercial ER2594 SDSS wire (Cr 24.851 wt%; Ni 9.651 wt%; Mo 3.778 wt%; Mn 0.465 wt%; Si 0.471 wt%; Al 0.022 wt%; Ti 0.008 wt%; N 0.264 wt%; C 0.010 wt%; Nb 0.018 wt%; Fe 60.297 wt%.) with a diameter of 1.2 mm was used for fabricating the SDSS thin-wall slabs, and the fabrication of the SDSS component was carried out using WAAM in conjunction with cold metal transfer (CMT) technology. Furthermore, a shielding gas consisting of 98% argon (Ar) and 2% carbon dioxide (CO 2) with a flow rate of 20 L/min was selected. The specific processing parameters were provided in Table 1. In more detail, three distinct as-deposited SDSS samples were identified as follows: i) WAAMed, which was prepared solely using ER2594 wire and served as the control reference; ii) WAAMed-AG, which was deposited with alcohol gel but without any inoculant powder; and iii) WAAMed-TiN, created by employing alcohol gel mixed with TiN powder. In this method, the TiN powder was initially blended with alcohol gel using ultrasonic stirring. Subsequently, a brush was employed to apply the TiN powder as a thin coating onto the surface of each deposited layer when the interlayer temperature was maintained below 120 °C. In comparison to the base material of the as-built SDSS part, the addition of TiN amounts to approximately 0.14 wt%. The anisotropy of the ultimate tensile strength and yield strength reduced from 9% to 3% and from 5% to 2%, respectively. Condition: Vertical Tensile (VT); Processing state: WAAMed-AG

Processing Text: The 304L γ-austenitic stainless steel with FCC structure was processed by the L-PBF technique. The L-PBF equipment was a BHGD-LM150 laser melting 3D printer equipped with a 200 W IPG fiber laser generator. The whole L-PBF process was performed in a pure argon (99.9%) atmosphere. The gas-atomized powders with nominal sizes ranging from 15 to 53 μm were used for the L-PBF process. The following L-PBF processing conditions were adopted: laser power of 140 W, scanning speed of 900 mm/s, hatch spacing of 50 μm, and layer thickness of 30 μm. Prior to the L-PBF process, the substrate was preheated to 100 °C. The chessboard scanning strategy with a size of 4 × 4 mm 2 was used, and the adjacent blocks were rotated by 90°. After scanning each layer, the scanning direction of the subsequent layer was rotated by 67°. Ten rectangular blocks with a geometric dimension of 140 mm (length) × 32 mm (width) × 3.5 mm (thickness) were prepared with the L-PBF process. Five rectangular blocks were heated isostatically pressed at 1365 °C and 130 MPa for 3 h. These HIP parameters were selected based on our previous results, which could achieve an isotropic microstructure similar to that of traditionally manufactured materials. The samples under two conditions were hereinafter referred to as “as-received” and “HIPed” samples, respectively. The crossbeam 550 focuses ion beam field emission scanning electron microscopy (FIB-FESEM) equipped with a symmetry electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector was used to investigate the grain characteristics, including grain shape, grain size, grain boundaries (GB), and crystallographic orientations. The voltage for gathering energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mappings was 15 kV. Before EBSD observation, the printed bulks were firstly prepared with the metallographic polishing process (400, 800, 1000, 1500, and 2000-grit sandpapers, as well as 2.5 and 1.5-μm diamond polishing pastes). The metallographically polished bulk samples were electroetched in a 10% oxalic acid solution using the following parameters: 15 V DC voltage, 15 s duration, room temperature, with a galvanized iron sheet as the cathode material. The step size for EBSD observation was 0.55 μm. The acquired EBSD data was processed and analyzed by Aztecrystal software. The grain interfaces with the misorientations of 2-15° and > 15° were classified as low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) and high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs), respectively. Based on Brandon's criterion, twin boundaries were defined as Σ3 coincidence site lattice (CSL) 60° rotations with a tolerance angle of 8.66° around the <111> crystallographic direction. The Σ3 CSL boundaries with <111> 60° ± 8.66° misorientation were defined as twin boundaries (TBs). An FEI Talos F200X transmission emission microscopy (TEM) equipped with a high-angle annular dark field (HADDF) detector and an X-ray EDS system was used to analyze the dislocation distribution and atomic structures. The TEM foils were prepared with the mechanical polishing process (2000-grit sandpaper), electrochemical polishing process (10% perchloric aid solution), and ion thinning process (Gatan 691 thinning equipment). The rectangular blocks were processed into dog-bone-shaped tensile samples by electro-discharge machining (EDM) and surface polishing. The geometric dimension of the dog-bone-shaped samples conforms to the ASTM E8 standard. The length direction, width direction (building direction), and thickness direction of the printed rectangular blocks were hereafter referred to as LD, WD (BD), and TD directions, respectively. The surface roughness of the dog-bone-shaped samples was <0.4 μm after surface polishing using up to 2000 grit sandpaper. Tensile tests were performed using a Shimadzu 200 kN fatigue testing machine with a strain rate of about 1.1 × 10 −3s −1. To eliminate the adverse effect of subsurface defects on the mechanical testing and fulfill the ASTM E8 standard requirement, an additional surface grinding process with a removal depth of 250 μm was undertaken. Sample type: HIP-1365

The as-received material was AISI 316 L stainless steel sheet (0.01C-17.3Cr-10.1Ni-1.0Mn-2.0Mo, wt%) with austenitic structure and an average grain size of 25 μm. Room-temperature multi-pass cold rolling with thickness reductions (r) in the range of 12.5 to 75% based on both UR and CR routes were used during rolling, where during the CR route the rolling direction was altered by 90° around the normal direction after each pass. In each pass, the reduction in thickness was ∼3% for each step in both UR and CR routes. Afterwards, annealing at 825 °C for different holding durations up to 135 min was applied for the purpose of reversion and recrystallization. The choice of this temperature was based on the results of Sohrabi et al. [27] for the successful reversion and recrystallization of AISI 316 L stainless steel. Metallographic sample preparation included grinding, mechanical polishing, electro-polishing (40 V, 50%H3PO4-50%H2SO4 solution), and electroetching (2 V, 60% HNO3 solution) to reveal the microstructures using an OLYMPUS VANOX optical microscope and a Zeiss Sigma field-emission scanning electron microscope. Using an MTS universal testing machine, tensile tests at room temperature with constant cross-head speed of 0.3 mm/min (initial strain rate of 6 × 10−4s−1) were applied to the subsize JIS Z 2201 specimens (rectangular specimens with a gauge length of 8 mm and gauge width of 3 mm), for which the repetition of tests was considered to ensure the reproducibility of results. Processing Text: CoFeNiCr xcomplex concentrated alloys (x = 0 - 25 at%) were fabricated using L-DED technique by systematically varying the Cr concentration. The AM deposits were fabricated using pre-alloyed equiatomic CoFeNi and CoFeNiCr powders as precursor materials. The depositions were made in a Optomec LENS-750 L-DED unit with 300 W laser power, 12.7 mm/s laser traverse speed, 0.5 mm beam size, and 0.25 mm beam track overlap (hatch distance). A multi-track, multi-layer scanning strategy was used to achieve a final deposit dimension of 5 mm × 5 mm x 5 mm on a 316 L stainless steel substrate. A bidirectional scanning strategy was employed within each layer and the laser head was rotated 90⁰ after each layer, i.e., 90⁰ rotation of scanning plane, for optimum thermal management during deposition. The Cr concentration of the AM deposits was monitored by adjusting the feed rate of the pre-alloyed powders from the hoppers. The AM printed deposits possessed relative densities between 98 % and 99.5 % and contained the mean Cr xcomposition of x = 6, 12, 18, and 24 at% respectively. Further detailed descriptions on the processing conditions and parameters are provided in Ref. [25]. To experimentally determine the lattice parameters of CoFeNiCr xalloys, X-ray diffraction on the L-DED printed samples was performed in a Rigaku Ultima III high resolution diffractometer operated at 40 kV/44 mA with Cu K αradiation. The diffraction patterns were obtained for 2θ angles between 40⁰ and 100⁰ with a step size of 0.2⁰ and scanning speed of 0.2⁰/min. Precise lattice parameters of L-DED printed CoFeNiCr xalloy samples were estimated from X-ray diffraction patterns using Nelson-Riley [26]method. The evolution of microstructures and phases in AM printed alloys were characterized using electron back scattered diffraction (EBSD) technique in a Thermo Fisher Apreo 2 C scanning electron microscope (SEM) attached with an EBSD detector. The orientation image (OIM) micrographs obtained from EBSD were analyzed using TSL-OIM 8 analysis software to estimate the dislocation density and grain size. Nanoindentation experiments were carried out to estimate the elastic modulus values of L-DED printed CoFeNiCr xalloy samples using a KLA iMicro nanoindenter in continuous stiffness measurement (CSM) mode with a maximum load of 50 mN and a diamond Berkovich indenter. The elastic modulus values were determined from the initial slope of the unloading segment of the load-displacement curve using Oliver-Pharr method [27]. For better statistics and consistency in determination of elastic modulus values, 20 indents were carried out on each alloy composition. The profilometry-based spherical indentation plastometry (PSIP) technique was employed to determine the nominal stress-strain behavior and yielding characteristics of the L-DED printed CoFeNiCr xalloys. The technique involved indenting the surface with a hard spherical ball indenter (indenter radius of 1 mm), measuring the profile of the indent with a contact-type profilometer and iterative finite element modelling (FEM) to fit the profile of the residual indent using Voce hardening equation ( Eq. 1) [28]. Additionally, another set of two B samples was processed using a modified version of the ASTM standard heat treatment, which included pre-heating at 850 °C for 20 min, followed by homogenization at 1200 °C for 20 min, and then water quenched. One sample from this heat treated pair was further treated using the same DCT process as the B-D sample, resulting in the labels BH (for the solely homogenized sample) and BH-D (for the homogenized and DCTed sample), respectively. The M0 and M7 LRHEAs ingots were prepared by vacuum suspension melting furnace in argon atmosphere using high-purity (99.95 wt%) Ti, Zr, V, Nb, Al and Mo. Before melting, the metal monomers were mechanically polished and ultrasonically cleaned to remove oxide skin and other impurities on their surfaces. The ingots were repeatedly melted four times to ensure a uniform composition. Afterward, all the ingots were sealed in a quartz tube filled with argon, and homogenized at 1150 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching. Then, to address the issue of large ingots spending more time in the 400-600 °C temperature range due to slower cooling rates and resulting precipitated phases, we conducted an aging treatment with a 5-h hold at 500 °C to study the effect of Mo on the phase stability of the alloy in the mid-temperature range. Sponge Ti (≥99.9 wt %), sponge Zr (≥99.7 wt %), industrially pure Al (99.9 wt %), and granule Mn (≥99.7 wt %) were used as raw materials to prepare Ti-25Zr-4Al-1.5Mn (wt. %) ingots. To prevent oxidation during the smelting process, the alloys were melted under an argon atmosphere using Zr as an oxygen absorber in a vacuum non-consumable electric arc furnace. The rolling temperature was raised to 750 °C, 800 °C, 850 °C, 900 °C separately. Each TZAM sample was then heated in the furnace at the corresponding temperature for 30 min before undergoing multi-pass rolling using a two-high mill. During rolling, the samples were re-heated at the corresponding temperatures for 4 min before the next pass of rolling. The pressure applied during each pass was approximately 1.2 mm, with the total deformation reaching 88.5 % of the original ingot thickness. Once the desired thickness was achieved, the ingot was placed in the furnace for 4 min and then rapidly quenched. An inorganic silica coating was used to protect the specimens from oxidizing and cooling. According to the different hot rolling temperatures, the prepared samples were defined as 750-WQ, 800-WQ, 850-WQ, 900-WQ. The prepared samples were cut into thin flake tensile specimens of bone rods, with an effective area of 2 × 3 mm in the middle and an effective length of 20 mm. Single-axis tensile tests were conducted at room temperature until failure using an Instron 5982 testing machine, and the strain was measured with an extensometer at an initial strain rate of 5 × 10 −4s −1. Tension was applied parallel to the rolling direction. To ensure accuracy, each set of tensile specimens was tested at least three times. The microstructure of hot-rolled TZAM alloy was observed by optical microscope (OM, Ax 200 MAT), electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD, equipped in Hitachi S3400 SEM), and transmission electron microscope (TEM, Talos F200x). For OM observation, samples were abraded with sandpaper until fine scratches appeared on the surface in a uniform direction, mechanically polished with 0.02 μm silica suspension and chemically etched by using a solution of 10 % hydrofluoric acid (HF), 20 % nitric acid (HNO 3) and 70 % distilled water. For EBSD observations, samples were sandpapered until no rough scratches remained, followed by electrolytic polishing at 19 V and −23 °C using a solution containing 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % methanol until the surface was smooth. The EBSD scanning utilized a step size of 0.2 μm, and three regions were sampled per specimen to ensure data fidelity. An X-ray diffractometer (XRD, D/max-2500/PC) equipped with Cu Kα emitters was used to analyze the phase composition and crystal structure of hot-rolled TZAM samples. XRD was performed in step scan mode with a 2θ range of 30-80° and a scan rate of 2° per minute. For TEM sample preparation, the thin slice was ground to 30 μm by twin-jet electrochemical polishing and thinned with a solution containing 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % methanol at 13.5 V and −23 °C. The thinning time was determined according to the hole transmittance value. Under vacuum conditions, the acceleration voltage is selected to be 200 KV. Processing Text: The Mg-2.9Y (wt.%) alloy, which was extruded and subsequently annealed, was selected as the initial material. The alloy was cut into rectangle blocks with a dimension of 14 mm × 14 mm × 15 mm with a long axis parallel to the extrusion direction (ED). Then the TCC processing was performed on the blocks. The compression was conducted at a strain rate of 10−3s−1 on the Shimadzu AG-Xplus 100 KN equipment and the processing route is schematically shown in Fig. 1(c). Three blocks with different strains in each single compression pass, i.e., 5 %, 7.5 %, and 10 %, were fabricated via the TCC processing for 5 cycles, respectively. Each cycle includes three compressions at different orthogonal directions. The first compression was conducted parallel to the ED along the a-axis. In other words, compression was initially applied to the A plane, followed by subsequent compressions on the B and C planes, respectively. Taking the material compressed with 5 cycles under 5 % strain in each pass as an example, we name it the “5 %-5 cycles” material. The accumulative equivalent true strains of 5 %−5 cycles, 7.5 %−5 cycles, and 10 %−5 cycles materials are 0.37, 0.72, and 1.01, respectively. Dog bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gauge length of 3 mm (// a-axis), a width of 2 mm (// c-axis), and a thickness of 1.2 mm (// b-axis) were prepared, with the coordinate system referred to Fig. 1(c). The room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests were conducted on the Shimadzu AG-Xplus 100 KN equipment equipped with a digital image correlation (DIC) equipment with a tensile rate of 10−3s−1. To ensure the repeatability of uniaxial tensile tests, more than 8 samples taken from a region above 3 mm away from the surfaces of the TCC processed blocks were tested, and these samples showed similar mechanical properties. The loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) testing was also conducted on this device. The samples were first loaded to one specified strain at a strain rate of 10−3s−1, and then unloaded to 60 N at an unloading rate of 200 N min−1 with the stress control mode, followed by reloading at the same strain rate of 10−3s−1 to the specified strain. Nanoindentation tests were conducted on the triboincenter equipment produced by Hysitron Company. Apply a maximum load of 1500 μN to the surface of the sample using a diamond indenter. The nano-indentation tests were performed in a 4 × 6 matrix with a spacing of 15 μm for the 10 %-5 cycles material. The samples for electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) mapping were also taken from the area at least 3 mm away from the block surfaces, with a sample size of 4 mm (// a-axis) × 3 mm (// c-axis) × 1.2 mm (// b-axis). Using 2000#, 3000#, and 5000# sandpaper, the oxide layer of the samples was removed. Subsequently, electrolytic polishing was performed in a solution with perchloric acid (5 vol.%) and ethanol (95 vol.%) to release residual stress on the sample surfaces and also to achieve a mirror-like effect. The polishing process was carried out on the LectroPol-5 equipment produced by Struers company. The polishing voltage and polishing time were set to 25 V and 25 s, respectively, and the temperature of the electrolytic polishing solution was maintained at 0 °C. EBSD tests were performed on Thermo Scientific Apreo scanning electron microscope (SEM) with an accelerating voltage of 15 kV and a scanning step size of 0.8 μm. Detailed microstructures of the materials are further characterized by the JEOL-2001F transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The samples were first mechanically polished to a thickness of 50-60 μm, followed by thinning using the TenuPol-5 automatic twin-jet electrolytic polishing equipment. The electrolyte was a solution of perchloric acid (3 vol.%) and ethanol solution (97 vol.%). The polishing voltage was set to 35 V, and the temperature of the twin-jet electrolyte was maintained at -25 °C. 10 %-5 cycles material; Comparison with initial alloy (76 MPa); Fracture elongation of 15%

Processing Text: Oxygen-rich 47Zr alloy reinforced by spherulite ZrO phase was prepared by in-situ semi-solid processing. The material used for the experiments was an as-forged oxygen-rich 47Zr-45Ti-5Al-3 V (47Zr-O, wt%) alloy with an oxygen atom content of 2280 wt. ppm. The XRD pattern and TEM images show that the as-forged alloy is composed of acicular α and β phases, which is a typical widmanstatten microstructure, and the average width of the acicular α phase is 53 nm. According to the calibration results of PDF cards (JCPDS cards 44-1294, 65-7479, 44-1288, and 20-0684), α'' and ZrO phase is generated in the alloy after SSP as well as the normal α and β phases. The phase fractions were quantitatively determined using software Jade 6.5 and the reference intensity ratio (RIR) method. The as-forged alloy contains 63 wt% and 37 wt% β and α phases, respectively. Subsequently, α'', β, and ZrO phase content first increases and then decreases with increasing semi-solid temperature, achieving maximum α'', β, and ZrO phase content at 1500°C. The tensile tests were performed at 500°C using an Inspekt Table-100KN universal testing machine at a set strain rate of 0.6 mm/min. Condition: As-forged; High temperature (500°C) mechanical properties

Processing Text: Spherical powders of high-purity grade-2 titanium (45–150 µm, AP&C, Canada), aluminium (45–150 µm, Alfa Aesar, Republic of Korea), and cobalt (150 µm, Alfa Aesar, Republic of Korea), along with irregular silicon (>90 µm, Alfa Aesar, Republic of Korea) powder were blended using a Turbula shaker mixer for 1 h. The mixed powder was dried at 100 °C for 5 h in a vacuum oven to remove any moisture before printing. DED technique was performed using an InssTek metal 3D printer (MX-450, Republic of Korea). Cuboid samples with dimensions of 45 × 8 × 8 mm 3 were horizontally deposited on a Ti-6Al-4 V alloy base plate. Deposition parameters were as follows: laser power of 380 W, scan speed of 0.85 m/min, layer thickness of 0.25 mm, and hatch spacing of 0.5 mm. Processing Text: The preparation involved arc-melting high-purity raw materials, including Ti, Al, Cr, and Nb ingots, and irregular-shaped ZrO2 powders under an Ar atmosphere in a water-cooled copper crucible. Before drop-casting into a water-cooled copper mold with a dimension of 5×12×100mm3, all ingots underwent six cycles of flipping and repeated melting. Subsequently, the as-cast specimens were cold-rolled with a thickness reduction of ∼80% along the long axis. Recrystallization was performed at 900 °C for 30 min under an Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching to ambient temperature. The alloy sheet was then machined into dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a gage length of 12.5 mm and a cross-section of 3.2×1.0mm2 along the rolling direction. Tensile properties were measured at room temperature using a universal testing machine (Instron, Series 3382 UTM System) with a strain rate of 1×10−3s−1. Processing Text: A high-strength crack-free TiN/Al-Mn-Mg-Sc-Zr composite was fabricated by laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF). The L-PBF process involved the partial melting and decomposition of TiN nanoparticles under high temperature, leading to the formation of L12-Al3(Ti, Sc, Zr) nanoparticles. The composite samples were manufactured by an EOS M290 L-PBF system (EOS GmbH, Germany), with a maximum laser output power of 370 W and a laser spot size of 100 μm. Before and during the L-PBF processing, the chamber was filled with high-purity argon to maintain a low level of O2 (lower than 0.1 vol.%) and the substrate plate was preheated to 200 °C. A 67° rotation scanning strategy was employed. Optimized L-PBF parameters used to produce dense alloy and composite samples are as follows: laser power P= 300 W and scanning speed v= 800 mm/s for specimen S 0; P= 200 W and v= 1200 mm/s for specimen S 1.5, S 3.0, and S 4.5. Other parameters are hatch spacing h= 100 μm and layer thickness t= 30 μm. Cubic specimens with a size of 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm were prepared for microstructure characterization. Specimens with dimensions of 30 × 7 × 1.5 mm were fabricated for tensile test. Containing 1.5 wt% TiN; Processing state: as-built

To investigate the effect of Nb addition on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the current iHEA, 0.5 wt.% Nb powder (99.95 % purity) was mixed with 99.5 wt.% iHEA powder. The particle morphology of elemental Nb powder is shown in Fig. S1(b). These two powders were mixed in the mixer of the powder feeder for 24 h. The LMD process was carried out using a 3 kW IPF Photonics fiber laser with a wavelength of 1.07 μm. The following optimized printing parameters were used for the fabrication of the iHEA-Nb bulk sample: laser power of 1500 W, scanning speed of 350 mm s-1, and overlap ratio of 50 %. A scanning pattern with 180° angle rotation between two consecutive deposition layers was applied, and ST37 carbon steel plates were used as the substrates. For both iHEA-Nb and iHEA reference samples, tensile specimens with gauge dimensions of 11.5 mm × 3.5 mm × 1 mm were obtained with the long axes parallel to the laser scanning direction using electrical discharge machining. Prior to the tensile tests, the specimens were sequentially ground using SiC sandpaper from 320 to 2000 grit. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted using a Kammrath-Weiss tensile module in displacement-controlled mode at the strain rate of 10-4 s-1, and the machine displacement was used to measure tensile strain. Tensile tests were repeated at least 3 times for each condition to ensure the reliability and repeatability of the results. In situ micropillar compression tests were performed on differently oriented grains ([001] and [111], respectively) to study the micromechanical properties of the as-built iHEA-Nb sample. The micropillars were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB) and the detailed preparation parameters can be found in our previous work [27]. Pillar orientation: [001]-Nb; Deformation mode: Twin

Processing Text: Inconel 718 pre-alloyed powder with a spherical morphology was produced via argon gas atomization. The D10, D50, and D90 values were equal to 23.1, 31.3, and 42.6 μm, respectively. The chemical composition (wt.%) of Inconel 718 powder was determined via inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry. A 316 L stainless steel plate with dimensions of 250 mm × 250 mm × 10 mm was used as the building substrate that was preheated to 100 °C before LPBF processing. All LPBF specimens (16 mm × 16 mm × 100 mm) were manufactured using an EOSINT M280 LPBF printing system (EOS, Germany) equipped with a Gaussian beam fiber laser source with a maximum power of 400 W under an argon atmosphere. A 67° rotation angle between the successive layers was adopted during LPBF processing. A schematic of the LPBF process and its main parameters are shown in Fig. 1(c). They include a layer thickness of 40 μm, hatch spacing of 110 μm, scanning speed of 960 mm/s, and laser power of 258 W. After LPBF processing, some specimens were subjected to annealing at 1200 °C for 10, 30, and 60 min followed by water cooling. To enhance the alloy properties for engineering applications, a double-aging treatment involving heating to 720 °C, 8 h/furnace cooling at 55 °C/h to 620 °C, and 8 h/air cooling were performed to precipitate the γ'' and γ' phases. The double-aging treatment did not influence the fraction of twins or alloy morphology because of its high-temperature stability. Thus, the directly heat-treated specimens were denoted as LPBF-HT-10, LPBF-HT-30, and LPBF-HT-60. Other LPBF-fabricated specimens were soaked in liquid nitrogen for 7 d (168 h), recovered at ambient temperature, and held for 1 h (“DCT specimens”), which ensures that more homogeneous stress can be effectively introduced into the matrix. Subsequently, the DCT specimens were subjected to the same annealing and aging treatments described above and denoted as DCT-HT-10, DCT-HT-30, and DCT-HT-60. A schematic of the heat treatment and DCT processes is shown in Fig. 1(d). Processing Text: Inconel 718 pre-alloyed powder with a spherical morphology was produced via argon gas atomization. The D10, D50, and D90 values were equal to 23.1, 31.3, and 42.6 μm, respectively. The chemical composition (wt.%) of Inconel 718 powder was determined via inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry. A 316 L stainless steel plate with dimensions of 250 mm × 250 mm × 10 mm was used as the building substrate that was preheated to 100 °C before LPBF processing. All LPBF specimens (16 mm × 16 mm × 100 mm) were manufactured using an EOSINT M280 LPBF printing system (EOS, Germany) equipped with a Gaussian beam fiber laser source with a maximum power of 400 W under an argon atmosphere. A 67° rotation angle between the successive layers was adopted during LPBF processing. A schematic of the LPBF process and its main parameters are shown in Fig. 1(c). They include a layer thickness of 40 μm, hatch spacing of 110 μm, scanning speed of 960 mm/s, and laser power of 258 W. After LPBF processing, some specimens were subjected to annealing at 1200 °C for 10, 30, and 60 min followed by water cooling. To enhance the alloy properties for engineering applications, a double-aging treatment involving heating to 720 °C, 8 h/furnace cooling at 55 °C/h to 620 °C, and 8 h/air cooling were performed to precipitate the γ'' and γ' phases. The double-aging treatment did not influence the fraction of twins or alloy morphology because of its high-temperature stability. Thus, the directly heat-treated specimens were denoted as LPBF-HT-10, LPBF-HT-30, and LPBF-HT-60. Other LPBF-fabricated specimens were soaked in liquid nitrogen for 7 d (168 h), recovered at ambient temperature, and held for 1 h (“DCT specimens”), which ensures that more homogeneous stress can be effectively introduced into the matrix. Subsequently, the DCT specimens were subjected to the same annealing and aging treatments described above and denoted as DCT-HT-10, DCT-HT-30, and DCT-HT-60. Processing Text: Three ingots weighed 500 g of non-equiatomic TiZrHfNb x (x = 0.5, 0.55, 0.6) alloys were prepared by levitation melting in a cold crucible under argon atmosphere. The purity of the raw materials of Ti, Zr, Hf, and Nb blocks was above 99.9 wt. %. The ingots were melted at least four times to achieve a homogeneous distribution of alloy elements. After the last melting process, the alloy melts were finally dropped to the bottom of the crucible and solidified into ingots. The ingots were annealed at 1300 °C for 10 h in a circulating argon atmosphere to homogenize the microsegregation, followed by water quenching. The cold rolling with a total thickness reduction of about 80 % (from 10 to 2 mm) combined with recrystallization treatments at 1000 °C for 30 min was used to acquire microstructures with equiaxed grains.
