IN738LC is now widely used in gas turbine and aero-engine turbine components due to its excellent high-temperature strength, creep resistance, and corrosion resistance. IN738LC has been widely used in hot-end components owing to its excellent high-temperature performance, while it has still suffered from metallurgical defects during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) due to its high crack sensitivity. This study investigated forming behavior, microstructure evolution and mechanical property of LPBF-processed IN738LC samples at different parameters (laser power of 150-300 W, scanning speed of 500-1500 mm/s). The IN738LC alloy powder used in this study was manufactured by aerosolization method. The particle size statistics of the powders are shown in Fig. 1(a), with the powder range from 13 μm to 60 μm. The D 10, D 50and D 90are 23.7 μm, 36.9 μm and 57.1 μm respectively. SEM images of the powders are shown in Fig. 1(b), where some of the powders were observed to have satellites. The flowability of the powder determined by the Hall method was about 15.4 s., proving the good roundness and flowability of the powder. The composition of the element of IN738LC powder is shown in Table 1. The LPBF forming experiments were performed with a system equipped with a 500 W continuous fiber laser. Five different laser powers and scanning speeds were selected for the 5*5 forming experiment. Substrates with different parameters were first fabricated to take over the fabrication of single tracks. LPBF processing uses an “island” scan strategy, with a thickness of 30 μm per layer of powder and a rotation of 67° between each layer, to obtain lower residual stress levels and finer grains, as shown in Fig. 1(c). The hatch space and layer powder thickness were 50 μm and 30 μm. The finished printed substrate was a bulk with 10 mm sides. Subsequently, a separate layer of powder was laid on the top surface of the bulk to print a monorail with the same parameters. The laser power and scanning speed in this study are given in Table 2. Fig. 1(d) shows the schematic diagram of the single tracks formation. The morphology of single tracks was directly investigated by metallographic optical microscope. The cross sections were sanded and polished. The MP geometry and cracks were observed by using a metallurgical optical microscope. Optical microscope was used to observe the pores and cracks of the samples and the porosity was counted to reflect the denseness of the samples. The porosities obtained were averaged over different areas of the same cross-section selected to ensure statistical significance. The phase compositions of the LPBF-ed IN738LC bulk samples were identified by using X-Ray diffraction (XRD) method with Cu radiation, which was conducted with a scanning rate of 5°/min in 2θ between 20° and 100°. The polished surface was etched and then a scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to photograph the surface quality and microstructure of the sample. Grain orientation analysis by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was also performed. Microhardness was tested by a Vickers hardness tester with a loading load of 3 N and a loading time of 20 s. Tensile tests were carried out in the direction perpendicular to the building. Room temperature tensile properties were tested using wick/Roell BT1-FB005TN.14 tester using the loading rate of 20 μm/s, and the fractures were further characterized by SEM. Fig. 2shows the morphology of single tracks produced at different laser powers and scanning speeds. The result indicated that the decrease in energy density caused the width and depth of the melt pool to decrease and eventually broke into droplets, leading to an increase in porosity. As the scanning speed increases, the microstructure changes from irregular columnar/cellular dendrites to all distributed as columnar dendrites, exhibiting epitaxial growth. An optimal process window was finally obtained at a laser power of 200 W and a scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, which achieved excellent forming quality (the porosity of 0.01 %) and mechanical properties (microhardness of 445.5 HV, ultimate tensile strength of 1335 MPa and elongation of 19.3 %). This study provides process basis for subsequent studies of IN738LC fabricated by LPBF. Temperature: 450°C

Two 5 kg ingots of IN738LC and Mo-IN738LC alloys were fabricated by vacuum induction melting. The ingots were subsequently re-melted to make cylindrical specimens measuring 13 mm in diameter and 80 mm in length. The cylindrical specimens were solution-treated at 1120 °C for 4 h, cooled to 843 °C, aged at that temperature for 20 h using a furnace with an argon atmosphere, and then air-cooled to room temperature. Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted on cylindrical dog-bone-shaped samples with a gauge length of 25 mm and a width of 6 mm, which were extracted from the center of the cylindrical specimens. The tensile tests were conducted at 450 ºC and 750 ºC at a strain rate of 1.0×10−3s−1 using an MTDI tensile testing machine (Model UT-100E, Korea) following ASTM-E8 standard. Temperature: 450°C

Processing Text: The MEA specimens were printed using a PPA-AM equipment (DML-VO3AD, Duomu Company, Shanghai, China). The following processing parameters were used: deposition current 110 A, scanning speed 25 mm/min, interlayer waiting time 4 min, torch to sample distance 10-12 mm, powder feeding gas (high purity Ar) flow 2.5 L/min and powder feeding rotor speed 20 r/min. The first group of experimental samples were untreated after AM deposition (As-built), the second group of samples were first heat-treated at 1200 °C for 10 h and quenched in water, then aging-treated at 700 °C for 1.5 h and quenched in water (HT-AT). The other two groups of samples were heat treated at 1200 °C for 10 h (HT-1200) and aging treated at 700 °C for 1.5 h (AT-700) and then quenched in water. The samples were ground using 320-2000# SiC sandpaper in sequence, polished using 0.25 μm diamond spray. The EBSD samples were electropolished in a solution of 20% perchloric acid and 80% alcohol for 60-80 s at a temperature of −30 °C and voltage and electric current were set at 30 V and 0.2-0.5 A, respectively. The Vickers hardness of different MEA samples was measured by a digital microhardness tester (HVS-1000 A) under 9.8 N applied load and 15 s loading time. Hardness tests were performed at 1 mm intervals along the build direction. The tensile properties of the dog-bone shaped tensile specimens were carried out by displacement rate of 0.6 mm/min in a universal testing machine (Instron 5900) at room temperature (RT), and each group of samples was repeated at least three times to ensure the accuracy. Processing state: HT-AT (two-step heat treatment); Strength and ductility improved; UTS: 1080 MPa; EF: 22.3%

Processing Text: The test steel used in this study is the continuous casting billet of S32101. Firstly, the billet with length of 90 mm, width of 50 mm and thickness of 10 mm is cut from the continuous casting billet along the rolling direction (RD) by using electric discharge wire cutting. The billet is treated with solid solution at 1080 C for 30 min in a box resistance furnace, quenched after being released. The surface scale is removed by a steel brush, and then cold-rolled for several times. The total cold-rolled reduction rate was 76%, and the cold-rolled sheet with a thickness of 2.4 mm is obtained. Then the 2.4 mm thick cold-rolled sheet is annealed for 15 min at 1050 C, and cold rolled with the reduction of 50%. Finally, the cold-rolled plate is annealed at 1050 C for 1 min, and then quenched. Temperature: -70 °C

In this study, vanadium microalloying was employed to prepare high-nitrogen austenitic stainless steel with excellent comprehensive mechanical performance. The high nitrogen stainless steel was prepared by high-purity iron, chromium, electrolytic manganese, molybdenum, vanadium, and chromium-nitrides within a vacuum induction furnace. The steel was synthesized at 1550 °C with a nitrogen pressure of 0.1 MPa. Then, the induction melting synthesized steel was subjected to a high-temperature austenization process at 1150 °C for 1 h. Then, the steel was hot-rolled 5 times within the temperature range between 1150 °C and 950 °C until the thickness of the steel was reduced to 2 mm, followed by water quenching down to room temperature immediately. Subsequently, the hot-rolled steel plates were subjected to solid solution treatment at high temperatures of 900 °C, 1000 °C, 1100 °C, and 1200 °C for 1 h, followed by a water quenching process, respectively. Processing state: hot-rolled

The tensile strength, yield strength, and electrical conductivity of Cu-Ni-Co-Si-Mg alloy can reach 894 MPa, 855 MPa, and 47.1 %IACS after a third-stage of thermomechanical treatment (TTMT). Processing Text: The commercial IN738LC alloy powder with the composition shown in Table 1 was prepared using the argon atomization method. The powder was approximately spherical with a few satellite spheres on the surface with D50 about 30.97 μm (Fig. 1(a and b)), meeting the basic requirements for the printing process. An EOSINT M290 machine equipped with a YLR-400GIA fiber laser was used for printing, and the printing process was executed under argon protection with an oxygen concentration of less than 0.1%. The substrate was preheated to 100 °C before printing, and the specific printing parameters were: laser power of 270 W, the spot diameter of 80 μm, scanning speed of 1437 mm/s, layer thickness of 40 μm, scanning spacing of 72 μm, and rotational scanning strategy of 67° within the layer (Fig. 1(c)). Sample blocks measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 3 mm were cut using EDM wire-cutting equipment for subsequent experimental studies of heat treatment and hot corrosion. Table 2 shows the heat treatment regime for the samples, which consists of super solution treatment and standard solution heat treatment followed by aging. To prevent oxidation, the heat-treated samples were enclosed in an argon-filled ampule and placed in an SK-G08163-2-600 tube furnace (Tianjin Zhonghuan Electric Furnace). The furnace was heated to the target temperature at a ramp rate of 5 °C/min and kept for a specified time, then air-cooled (Fig. 1(d)). Three sets of samples were cut into 10 mm × 10 mm × 3 mm specimens, polished to 2000 mesh, and then measured for surface dimensions using vernier calipers. The mass of each sample was obtained using an analytical balance (Lichen FA1004). The samples were then ultrasonically cleaned in alcohol for 5 min, degreased in acetone, and dried for later use. The spare samples were immersed in a sealed alumina crucible containing a corrosive medium of 25% NaCl+75% Na2SO4. Hot corrosion tests were conducted in a box furnace at a target temperature of 900 °C. Samples were removed at 10 h intervals and washed with boiling deionized water to eliminate surface molten salts. To prevent damage from washing to the oxide layer, the samples were wrapped in filter paper during the cleaning process. After cleaning, the samples were dried in a vacuum oven at 100 °C and weighed to record the final mass change. The samples underwent three rounds of testing and the results were averaged. According to the literature, salt-coating method experiments were also conducted for comparison, and the detailed description is as follows: three sample groups using the same measurements were heated at 250 °C in a box furnace. A saturated 25%NaCl+75%Na2SO4 aqueous solution until a uniform salt mixture of 1 ± 0.1 mg/cm2 was sprayed onto the surface of the samples for the hot corrosion experiments at 900 °C (The corrosion kinetics curves are shown in Fig. S1). The samples were removed and weighed at regular intervals, which resulted in a significant degree of oxide layer shedding, and this directly affected subsequent observation as well as characterization analysis. Thus, the same crucible full-impregnation method as described in the literature was employed for this experimental (see Refs. [38, 41, 42]). Processing state: as-built (AB) sample

Processing Text: Ingots of the (TiNbZr)89(AlTa)11 (at. %) RHEA were produced using a vacuum-melting furnace. The constituent metals, sourced commercially, had a purity level exceeding 99.9 %. During arc melting, a mixture of these constituent elements was melted in an atmosphere consisting of argon gas. The specific operational procedure for melting involves the amalgamation of the alloy’s source components within the crucible. The technique utilizes an arc current ranging from 60 to 70 A. When the arc is initiated, it is initially melted on a crucible holding pure Ti for a duration of 1-2 min. This step serves to eliminate the oxygen present in the furnace, hence preventing oxidation of the HEA during the melting process. Afterwards, the alloy is melted using a smelting current ranging from 200 to 300 A. The alloy samples underwent multiple cycles of melting, with a minimum of 10 repetitions, in order to achieve consistent melting and enhance their chemical uniformity. Following casting, a homogenization treatment was performed at 750 °C for 3 h and then at 1,050 °C for 4 h to achieve a consistent microstructure. Cylindrical specimens, measuring 4 mm in diameter and 4 mm in length, were prepared for dynamic and quasi-static-compression tests. The quasi-static-compression tests were conducted at room temperature. Dynamic-compression tests with strain rates ranging from 1.0 × 103 to 3.5 × 103 s−1 were carried out using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB). Following this step, a solution treatment was applied to the samples at 1,000 °C for 30 min, succeeded by water quenching. Subsequently, the alloy underwent ageing at 600 °C for varying durations: 0 h, 2 h, 4 h, 8 h, 12 h, 16 h, 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h. This heat treatment aimed to determine the maximum hardness for microstructure analysis utilizing an ISO 6507-standard HV-1000Z micro-Vickers hardness tester at 10 kg-force loads for 15 s. The hardness of the alloy was measured to assess the effect of the heat treatment. Strain rate: 1.0 × 10^3 s^-1

Processing Text: Gas atomized, spherical or near-spherical powders of the CrMnFeCoNi, which have the atomic ratio of 1: 1: 1: 1:1, and particle size range of 45∼105 µm is used as the raw material for this study. The substrate is ground and ultrasonically cleaned in ethyl alcohol before performing LMD. Builds are fabricated with laser powers of 1100, 1400, 1700, 2000, and 2300 W. The laser spot size, feeding rate and scanning rate are ∼3 mm, ∼12 g/min and ∼600 mm/min, respectively. Moreover, the hatch-overlap and layer thickness are 30 % and 0.5 mm, respectively. Processing Text: The heavy warm rolling promoted the transformation of metastable austenite (∼12.2 vol%) into hard domain α’ martensite. After 600 °C re-annealing, the hard domain α’ re-reversed to α + γ. The austenite content of WRA (71.9 %) significantly increased compared to WR. It was deduced that the hard domain α’ martensite was re-reversed into α + γ, and the heterogeneous microstructure disappeared during re-annealing. It was found that the austenite content (48.0 %) in WRT decreased slightly compared to WR, which was attributed to the decomposition of a small amount of metastable austenite into cementite and ferrite during tempering. In addition, the low temperature tempering further promoted C enrichment of soft domain γ without the re-reversion of α’ martensite (400 °C below Ae1 temperature point), thus further improving the thermal stability of soft domain γ while maintaining the heterogeneous microstructure. The microstructures of WR, WRA and WRT were characterized by the EBSD band slope (BS) images superposed by the inverse polar figure (IPF) maps of austenite. Austenite was represented by the color region. For WRA, the durable high-temperature re-annealing promoted the re-reversion of the hard domain α’ martensite into newly nucleated γ L, while the pre-existing γ Lin WR recrystallized and grew into globular grains (γ G) with random crystallographic orientations, the austenite size was also coarsened (0.45 → 0.57 μm). In addition, the internal stress was released after a durable re-annealing. Homogeneous microstructure; Heat treatment: high temperature annealing

HR was annealed at 600 °C for 15 min and then immediately warm rolled to 3 mm. The sample was then immediately placed back into the heat treatment furnace and hold at 600 °C for 15 min. Processing Text: The initial material was melted and cast, and then held at 1200 °C for 60 min, and then water cooled. The as-cast plates were subjected to cold rolling with a total reduction of ∼80 % to 5 mm by multiple passes. After cold rolling, the samples were annealed at different temperatures 630 °C and 740 °C, for 60 min each. The 630 °C annealing resulted in a co-precipitate microstructure, designated as "CP-17Mn". SEM samples were prepared by mechanical-polishing etched with a solution of 2-4 % nitric acid alcohol. EBSD samples underwent mechanically polishing followed by a 20-second electrolytically polish at 25 V in a 7 % perchloric acid solution, using HKL Channel 5 software for analysis. TEM specimens were prepared by a twin-jet electrochemical polisher (25 V in a 7 vol% HClO 4acetic acid electrolyte), and examined in a scanning transmission electron microscope (JEOL JEM 2100F field emission, STEM) operated at 200 kV. 3D atom probe tomography (APT) using a local electrode atom probe (LEAP 3000 HR) was employed to study the microstructure of nanoprecipitates, conducted at 50 K under ultra-high vacuum (4.5 × 10 −11Torr) with a pulse fraction of 0.2 and a pulse repetition rate of 200 kHz. All samples were fabricated by the SLM technique using a commercial EOS M290 machine and a Yb:YAG fiber laser in an Argon atmosphere. The precursor material was gas atomized AISI 316 L SS powder with spherical morphology and an average particle size of 15–55 µm. Samples with 50 × 50 × 50 mm³ dimensions were printed on a 10 mm thick AISI 316 L SS substrate. Fig. 1 (a–b) display the fabrication of specimens via SLM, with parameters detailed as: laser power (280 W), scanning speed (960 mm/s), layer thickness (40 µm), hatch spacing (110 µm), and scan angle (67° between layers). To study annealing–induced hardening, they were annealed at six temperatures from 400 °C to 900 °C, with a step size of 100 °C, and the step size of annealing time is carried out in a proportional sequence of 2 h. Then, these samples were quenched in water, obtaining samples with 24 kinds of heat–treated conditions. Before microstructural analysis, the samples were mechanically ground with SiC papers from 800 to 3000 grit, and then polished with water–based diamond suspensions from 9 µm to 1 µm, and finally vibratory polished using a 0.05 µm OP–S colloidal silica suspension for 5 h. Phase composition and microstructures were analyzed using X–ray diffraction (XRD) with a Rigaku Smart–lab diffractometer, employing Cu Kα radiation at 40 kV and 40 mA. Dog bone tensile sample (Fig. 2 (b)), annealed at 500 °C for 8 h, was polished before quasi–in situ EBSD analysis. Processing Text: The prototypical material used in this study is a binary metastable β-Ti alloy Ti-11V (wt.%), which was supplied as hot-rolled block by the Northwest Institute for Nonferrous Metal Research, China. The actual chemical composition of the block consists of 10.6 wt.% V and Ti in balance, while the β-transus temperature (T β) is ∼730 °C. The block was cut into sheets for heat treatment and subsequent cold working. The solution treatment (ST) was performed at 950 °C for 2 h following water quenched (WQ) to room temperature. After heat treatment, the ST sheets are divided into two groups for cold working. In the first group, a combination of cold forging (CF) and cold rolling (CR) was applied. The CF was first performed on the ST sheets at room temperature with a thickness decrease of 10 % to induce deformation kinking in microstructure. Subsequently, these CF sheets underwent cold rolling at room temperature with a thickness decrease of 30 %. For convenience, these cold-worked sheets will hereafter be referred to as the F+ R-40 % ones. To investigate the effects of larger thickness reduction during cold rolling on mechanical properties, several CF sheets were subjected to a thickness reduction of 60 %, henceforth referred to as the F+ R-70 % ones. In the second group, individual CF or CR was applied separately. Some ST sheets underwent cold forging with a thickness decrease of 10 % (referred to as the F-10 % sheets), while others were directly subjected to cold rolling with a thickness decrease of 40 % (referred to as the R-40 % sheets). Processing state: R-40 % (cold rolling with 40% thickness reduction)

Processing Text: The Co-Cr-Fe-Ni powders were arranged in equiatomic ratio. A 5.1 g mixture of elemental powders and 1 wt% of stearic acid as a process control agent (PCA) to prevent excessive cold welding during mechanical alloying was mixed in a hardened steel vial. The powder preparation was performed in a glove box, where oxygen and humidity levels were maintained below 0.5 ppm by continuous circulation of high-purity argon gas through a purification system. The mixture was first milled for 30 min. Next, the vials were opened inside the glove box, and 440 C stainless steel balls with a powder-to-ball radio of 1:10 were added. The vials were then sealed in the glove box, and the mechanical alloying process was carried out at room temperature for 20 h using a SPEX 8000 M/D high energy ball miller. Green pellets with a diameter of 10 mm were produced using a 25-ton manual press (Kimaya Engineers, India) at a pressure of 520 MPa. The compacts were sintered in a tube furnace (Swam Equip, India) under a continuous flow of 99.99 % pure argon gas. The green samples were subjected to a sintering temperature range of 560-650 °C, with a 30 °C interval, at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The duration of sintering was 90 min, followed by controlled cooling within the furnace. Bulk density measurements were performed using the Archimedes principle with a Sartorius Secura YDK03 instrument. Phase analysis was conducted using a Panalytical X-pert powder X-ray diffractometer (Make: Panalytical, Model: X-pert powder). The instrument was equipped with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm) for data profile acquisition. The process involved a voltage of 45 kV and a current of 30 mA, with a step size of 0.02 and a duration of 25s/step. Optical microscopy (Quasmo ISI Microscope) and scanning electron microscopy (VEGA 3 LMU TESCAN) were employed to characterize the microstructure. Quantification and mapping of elements were performed using a Field Emission Gun Scanning Electron Microscope (FEGSEM) (JEOL, model: JSM 7800F) equipped with an Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) detector. For TEM analysis, specimens were obtained by cutting 300-micron-thick discs from the sintered samples, followed by metallographic polishing to a thickness of less than 100 μm. Subsequently, ion beam milling was applied to the specimens. The crystal structure and lattice imperfections, such as stacking faults, dislocations, and precipitation and their boundaries at the atomic scale, were investigated using a High Resolution- Transmission Electron Microscope (HR-TEM) (Model: JEOL JEM 2100, at an operating voltage of 200 kV). Nanoindentation measurements were performed using a Berkovich diamond indenter with a radius of 150 nm, featuring an included angle of 142.30° and a half angle of 65.27°, within a NANOINDENTER device (BRUKER'S HYSITRON TI PREMIER). A 2 mN load was used for the nanoindentation study and the distance between the two consecutive indentations was 3 μm to evaluate the hardness and modulus. The load-displacement curves were used to generate hardness and elastic modulus profiles across the matrix, intermetallic, and particle interfaces. The room temperature and isothermal compressive strength (at 200 °C, 250 °C, and 300 °C) of the composite were assessed using cylindrical samples (φ10mm x l = 15 mm) with an aspect ratio (l/d) of 1.5. The test was performed using a Universal Testing Machine (Jinan, WDW-100S) following the ASTM E−09standard. For the isothermal compression test, a furnace setup was employed. All samples were sintered at 620 °C due to its verified superior density in line with our previous findings. All samples were subjected to a strain of 0.5 and then water-quenched to facilitate microstructural observation. The strain rate for both room temperature and isothermal tests was set at 10 −4S −1. Room temperature; Pressureless sintering without heat treatment

Processing Text: Different combinations of chemical composition and process parameters have an essential influence on the organizational and mechanical properties. The content of Zn, Sr, and Fe are the main influencing factors of mechanical properties relative to other input variables in the whole data set. The importance of Si on EL and UTS is estimated to be lower than that of YS, but Cr affected EL to a greater extent than UTS and YS. Si is the main element in most die casting Al alloys, improving fluidity, wear resistance, and reducing thermal cracking tendency and shrinkage. Cu is similar to YS in that increasing the copper content improves flow and UTS. Mg and YS and UTS look similar; a small amount of Mg can improve the strength and yield limit, too much Mg content leads to poor casting properties. Zn can improve the fluidity and UTS, but the thermal cracking tendency increases and the corrosion resistance decreases. Ti shows a negative correlation with YS and UTS, and trace amounts of Ti can improve mechanical properties. Reasonable pouring temperature can provide initial high-quality conditions for production, and less variation in metal liquid temperature regulation during production. MT shows a high negative correlation with YS and UTS, with the mold cooling system taking up more of the regulatory function. Application range selection example with UTS ≥ 295 MPa, EL ≥ 13%

Processing Text: The Co 44Ni 44Mo 9W 3alloy was synthesized by vacuum arc melting using high-purity metals (>99.9 %). The melt was drop-cast into a rectangular water-cooled mold with sizes of 60 mm × 30 mm × 10 mm. The as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1250 °C for 12 h followed by water-quenching, and then cold-rolling (CR, with a reduction of 75 % in thickness) at RT. In order to obtain fully-recrystallized FCC microstructure with various average grain sizes, the cold-rolled alloy was annealed at different temperatures (i.e., 900 °C, 1100 °C, and 1200 °C, respectively) for 70 s and then water-quenched. These temperatures were chosen to ensure a single-phase structure based on thermodynamic calculation results using Thermo-Calc software (with a TCNI9 database). Dog-bone shaped tensile specimens (with gage length, width and thickness of 8 mm, 2 mm, and 1 mm respectively) were machined by an electro discharge machine with the loading axis parallel to the rolling direction. Tensile tests were performed using an Shimadzu AGS-X universal testing machine equipped with a RVX-112 video extensometer. The tests were conducted in air at RT under a nominal strain rate of 1.0 × 10 −3s−1. To understand deformation mechanisms, the microstructural evolution was characterized by a Zeiss Sigma 300 scanning electron microscope (SEM, equipped with electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) detectors) and an FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). Samples for SEM and EBSD investigations were prepared by conventional mechanical grinding and electro-polishing. EBSD imaging was performed with a step size of 0.12 μm, and the data were analyzed using AZtecCrystal software. TEM samples were further prepared using a Twin-Jet electro-polisher with electrolyte of 95 % methanol and 5 % perchloric acid solution. Conventional bright-field (BF) and dark-field (DF) TEM imaging was conducted at 200 kV. Condition: Ambient temperature; Microstructure: FCC single-phase
Processing Word: Condition: Ambient temperature; Microstructure: FCC single-phase

The melt was drop-cast into a rectangular water-cooled mold with sizes of 60 mm × 30 mm × 10 mm. The as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1250 °C for 12 h followed by water-quenching, and then cold-rolling (CR, with a reduction of 75 % in thickness) at RT. In order to obtain fully-recrystallized FCC microstructure with various average grain sizes, the cold-rolled alloy was annealed at different temperatures (i.e., 900 °C, 1100 °C, and 1200 °C, respectively) for 70 s and then water-quenched. These temperatures were chosen to ensure a single-phase structure based on thermodynamic calculation results using Thermo-Calc software (with a TCNI9 database). Dog-bone shaped tensile specimens (with gage length, width and thickness of 8 mm, 2 mm, and 1 mm respectively) were machined by an electro discharge machine with the loading axis parallel to the rolling direction. Tensile tests were performed using an Shimadzu AGS-X universal testing machine equipped with a RVX-112 video extensometer. The tests were conducted in air at RT under a nominal strain rate of 1.0 × 10 −3s−1. To understand deformation mechanisms, the microstructural evolution was characterized by a Zeiss Sigma 300 scanning electron microscope (SEM, equipped with electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) and energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) detectors) and an FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). Samples for SEM and EBSD investigations were prepared by conventional mechanical grinding and electro-polishing. EBSD imaging was performed with a step size of 0.12 μm, and the data were analyzed using AZtecCrystal software. TEM samples were further prepared using a Twin-Jet electro-polisher with electrolyte of 95 % methanol and 5 % perchloric acid solution. Conventional bright-field (BF) and dark-field (DF) TEM imaging was conducted at 200 kV. Processing Text: Ni20Cr3Al and nano Ti powders were mechanically milled in an atmosphere of Ar+20%Air. Ti powder was partly oxidized to be TiO2 during the milling and spark plasma sintering. The others are dissolved into the nickel-based alloy and form coherent intermetallic phase of Ni3Ti. Owing to the higher affinity of Al than Ti to O, most TiO2 particles were transformed to be in-situ nano Al2O3 dispersoids with good coherency to the alloy matrix as well. Grain refinement and precipitates strengthening contribute largely to the greatly improvement of mechanical strength of the NiCrAl-2Ti alloy, of which the yield strength reaches 884 MPa and ductility is 10.72%. Besides, the refined grains promote the selective oxidation of Al, ensuring an extremely high oxidation resistance. Its oxidation rate constant (kp) is as low as 9.7 × 10−8 mg2 cm−4 s−1 at 900 °C. Commercially available powders of Ni20Cr3Al (28-50 μm, Institute of Metal Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences), Ti (≤60 nm, Tijo Co., Ltd, China), and TiO2(≤25 nm, Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd, China) were used as the original materials. Ensuring the same mass fraction of Ti elements in alloys (2 wt%), nano TiO2 and Ti powers were added to the Ni20Cr3Al alloy powder to get NiCrAl-3TiO2 and NiCrAl-2Ti, respectively. Then the mixed powders were placed in a vacuum glove box filled with Ar. The NiCrAl-TiO2 and NiCrAl-2Ti powders were pumped to −0.1 MPa and 0.02 MPa (i.e. 0.2 atm) by the air pump, respectively, then filled with Ar. Subsequently, powders were milled by a high-energy ball-milling (HBM) machine (XQM-4 L, Changsha Tencan Powder, China) with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 10:1 at 300 rpm for 4 h. Thereafter, the mixtures were sintered by a spark plasma sintering technique (HPD 250, FCT Group, Germany) at 1150 °C under a pressure of 40 MPa for 20 min in Ar atmosphere. Processing Text: Spherical 1060 pure aluminum (Al) powders (purity＞99.6 %) and CuO powders (purity＞99.9 %) were used as raw powders, whose average diameters were 5 μm and 1 μm, respectively. The mass ratio of Al: CuO powders was 95:5. The Al/CuO blended powders were mixed by a planetary ball milling machine (QM-3SP2, Nanjing University Instrument Plant) with a rotation velocity of 200 rpm. The milling time and ball-to-powder ratio were 10 h and 10:1, respectively. The milled powders were pre-compacted at 200 MPa for 60 s by a cold tubular mold. Then, the round preform was placed in the Al mold and was sheared and stirred by a processing tool. This severe plastic deformation (SPD) process was named deformation-driven metallurgy (DDM) [20,21], which is derived from friction stir welding [22]. The rotational velocity of the tool was varied during the preparation process to introduce more substructure in materials. The rotational velocity was initially set at 500 rpm and changed to 100 rpm when the sample was only 1.5 mm (h 1in Fig. 1) in thickness. Then, keep it until 1 mm (h 2in the Fig. 1) and hold for 10 s. The detailed schematic of the whole preparation process is given in Fig. 1. Al-5wt.%CuO prepared with a constant rotational velocity of 500 rpm was used as the control group. Fe-Cr-Al alloys, owing to their absence of allotropic transformation, require multiple cycles of rolling and recrystallization annealing processes to achieve substantial grain refinement, ultimately leading to the attainment of outstanding mechanical properties. Simply using warm rolling for an ultra-coarse-grained Fe-Cr-Al alloy to introduce lamellar kink bands (KBs) into the matrix, the mechanical properties can be significantly improved. To improve their mechanical properties, the alloys would experience multiple plastic deformation and heat treatments to regulate their textures, substructures, second phase, grain size, and other microstructural characteristics [3-10]. This was followed by a simple warm rolling process to introduce KBs into the matrix, obtaining a new microstructure composed of original ultra-coarse grains and their internal KBs. Table 1 shows the nominal composition of hot-rolled Fe-Cr-Al slabs with a thickness of 6 mm. A solution treatment at 1150 °C for 6 h was performed to dissolve the Laves phase and also coarsen the grains. The as-soluted plates were then warm rolled to a thickness of 2 mm (with 66 % thickness reduction) at 400 °C by four rolling passes. Finally, the plates were annealed at various temperatures (700, 750, 800, and 850 °C) for 0.5 h to investigate the effect of temperature on hetero-deformation induced (HDI) strengthening effect of KBs. The warm-rolled samples are annealed at different temperatures (700, 750, 800, and 850 °C) for 0.5 h to eliminate residual stress (named KBs-700 °C/0.5 h, KBs-750 °C/0.5 h, KBs-800 °C/0.5 h, and KBs-850 °C/0.5 h). In this work, substantial KBs were introduced into an ultra-coarse-grained Fe-Cr-Al alloy by warm rolling. Processing Text: The as-cast GZ151K alloy ingots were solution treated (T4) at 520 °C for 12 h, quenched into water at 90 °C, and then cut into 110 mm diameter, 2 mm thick semicircular pieces with a wire cutting machine. All GZ151K alloy sheets were accurately ground to get the same degree of roughness before USRP with air pressure and the amount of rolling set at 0.3 MPa and 0.2 mm, respectively. The rolled alloy sheets were then held in a high-temperature resistance furnace at 450 °C with different annealing time (5 min, 15 min, 30 min, 60 min) and then cool in water to room temperature, named RUed 450-5 min, RUed 450-15 min, RUed 450-30 min and RUed 450-60 min, respectively. For OM and SEM, the samples were first cut by a wire machine, and the ND-RD plane (ND: normal direction, RD: rolled direction) of the samples was selected as the surface to make mosaic samples. Processing Text: Plastic deformation at room temperature followed by post-annealing is one of the best methods to achieve fine-grained metals and alloys. In this research, the high-temperature annealing behavior of cold-rolled electrolytic tough-pitch (ETP) copper sheets was studied. 90 % asymmetric cold rolling followed by high-temperature post-annealing at 673 K for 1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 60, and 120 min were applied on the copper. The microstructure was significantly changed with increasing annealing time from 1 to 2 min owing to full recrystallization. With increasing the annealing duration, the grain size is increased. The formation of equiaxed grains with a smaller size (∼9 μm) compared to the full-annealed (initial) sample (∼68 μm) is observed after the longest time of post-annealing (120 min) due to the pinning effect of Cu2O particles. The post-annealed copper sheets processed by asymmetric rolling (in this work) exhibited a more homogeneous microstructure through the thickness compared to the symmetric rolling due to more uniform stored strain energy. The results showed that the first deformed grains that undergo recrystallization during post-annealing are Goss-oriented grains. With an increase in the post-annealing time, the S and Copper components were eliminated and a strong Cube and P texture orientations were formed. Interestingly, after 1 min of post-annealing, the yield and tensile strength enhanced to 410.2 MPa and 418.6 MPa owing to the annealing hardening phenomenon. The hardness and strength reached a constant value after the post-annealing for 10 min and above. With the increase of post-annealing time from 1 min to 120 min, the electrical conductivity was increased from 77.6 to 97.5 %IACS. From the obtained results, it can be concluded that the asymmetric cold rolling followed by high-temperature post-annealing is capable of strength improvement and maintaining electrical conductivity in copper. Processing Text: Samples were cut into cylindrical shapes with dimensions of (Φ) 5 mm × 6.8 mm from cast ingot solidified under normal pressure. Subsequently, the samples were wrapped in an insulating layer and a graphite tube. The pressure device of the LPR1000 2-6-8 multi-stage high-pressure apparatus consists of an axially cylindrical pressure chamber, resembling to a piston-cylinder system. Pressure is applied to the octahedral talc sample assembly through primary and secondary pressure transmission modules, driven by the press. Graphite is used as the heating element, and the heating temperature is controlled by adjusting the heating power. The sample was heated to 1550 °C under an external pressure of 6 GPa for 60 minutes, after which the heating device was turned off and the pressure was released to atmospheric levels. The SSS and HPS alloys were subsequently aged at 400°C, 450°C, and 500°C in an argon atmosphere for varying durations up to 10 hours. The samples were ground using SiC paper and polished with diamond suspension. A solution with the composition of FeCl 3(2 g), HCl (3 ml), and C 2H 5OH (100 ml) was used as the etchant. The microstructure was observed using a HITACHI SU50000 field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) and an FEI Talos F200X transmission electron microscope (TEM). Image Pro Plus 6.0 software was used to measure the area fraction and size of various precipitates based on TEM images. The foil thickness in the beam direction was determined by measuring the spacing of Kossel-Mollenstedt fringes in a {111} αreflection in a < 011 > αtwo-beam convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) pattern. X-ray diffraction (XRD, X’PERT X-ray, Holland) with diffraction angle (2θ) ranging from 30° to 100° and a scanning speed of approximately 1°/min was utilized to determine the crystal structure of the alloys. The DC conductivity measurement at room temperature (300 K) was conducted using the traditional four-probe technique. The samples measured are approximately 3 mm in length, 1 mm in width, and 0.3 mm in thickness. Four platinum wires were affixed to the samples using conductive silver paste. The DC resistance of the samples was initially measured using a physical property measuring system (PPMS, Dynacool-14T, USA) and subsequently converted to DC conductivity. Vickers hardness testing of the specimens was performed using a Huayin HV-1000A microhardness tester with a load of 200 g and an indentation time of 15 seconds. The reported hardness values represent the average of eight separate measurements. The compression test was conducted using a SANS CMT6000 universal testing machine with a compression speed of 0.5 mm/min. The compression specimen measured are 2 mm in diameter and 3 mm in length. Processing Text: Argon gas atomized powder with diameters ranging from 15 to 53 μm was subjected to LPBF fabrication. The LPBF experiments were conducted using a commercial ProX DMP 200 machine (3D Systems, USA) equipped with a 300 W fibre laser. The laser spot size is 75 μm and the wavelength is 1070 nm. The optimal processing parameters were identified, which can be used to achieve the highest relative density. After the optimisation of process parameters, both cubic-shaped and dog bone-shaped samples were built with a laser power of 285 W, scan speed of 1500 mm/s, hatch space of 90 μm, and layer thickness of 30 μm. A separate-area scanning strategy was adopted with a 90° rotation between layers. The angle between the scanning direction and the X-axis is 45° for every layer. The fabrication process was performed in a high-purity argon atmosphere with an oxygen content below 200 ppm. The alloy was exposed at 250℃ for 100 h and shows no apparent decrease despite increasing the exposure time to 500 h. The tests were carried out on a material testing machine (Zwick Roell, Germany) at ambient temperature and an elevated temperature range of 200-300℃, with a strain rate of 10−3s−1. A 10 min hold before tensile testing was applied to the samples for uniform temperature. Vickers hardness tests were performed using a 10 kg load with a dwell time of 15 s. Processing Text: In this work, through the combination of austenite reversion treatment (ART) and subsequent flash austenitizing (FA), nanoscale chemical heterogeneity was successfully introduced into a low-cost UHSS prior to the aging process. The steel with a nominal chemical composition of 0.25 C-5 Ni-5 Mn-5 Co-1 Cr-2 Mo-1 Al (wt.%) was prepared through levitation melting and cast into an ingot of ∼ 5 kg. The as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1150 °C for 10 h and subsequently hot-forged into a square bar with a cross section of 20 mm × 20 mm, followed by air-cooling. The as-forged bars were hot-rolled at 1000 °C with a reduction of thickness from 20 to 5 mm. Then the hot-rolled plates were solution-treated at 900 °C for 1 h and then oil-quenched to ambient temperature, immediately subjected to cryogenic treatment (CT) at −196 °C for 2 h (denoted as CT sample). Subsequently, the CT samples were held at 580 °C for 5 h (denoted as ART sample). After ART, the ART samples were further FA at 830 °C with a heating rate of 30 °C/s and a cooling rate of 60 °C/s (denoted as FA sample). Then the FA samples were isothermally aged at 550 °C for 2 h (denoted as AG sample). During subsequent aging, a high number density of fine Ni(Al,Mn) and (Mo,Cr) 2C nanoprecipitates were concurrently introduced and the presetting austenite further grew with the consumption of substitutional Mn and Ni from the martensitic matrix. The as-cast ingot was homogenized at 1150 °C for 10 h and subsequently hot-forged into a square bar with a cross section of 20 mm × 20 mm, followed by air-cooling. The as-forged bars were hot-rolled at 1000 °C with a reduction of thickness from 20 to 5 mm. Then the hot-rolled plates were solution-treated at 900 °C for 1 h and then oil-quenched to ambient temperature, immediately subjected to cryogenic treatment (CT) at −196 °C for 2 h (denoted as CT sample). Subsequently, the CT samples were held at 580 °C for 5 h (denoted as ART sample). After ART, the ART samples were further FA at 830 °C with a heating rate of 30 °C/s and a cooling rate of 60 °C/s (denoted as FA sample). Then the FA samples were isothermally aged at 550 °C for 2 h (denoted as AG sample). During subsequent aging, a high number density of fine Ni(Al,Mn) and (Mo,Cr) 2C nanoprecipitates were concurrently introduced and the presetting austenite further grew with the consumption of substitutional Mn and Ni from the martensitic matrix. Processing state: CT-FA-AG (Cold Treatment + Flash Austenitizing + Aging); Microstructure: dual-nanoprecipitation but relatively unstable nanoscale RA with lower Mn and Ni enrichment

Processing Text: Ingots with the nominal compositions of Al 5 Cr 20 Fe 35 Co 35 Ni 5 were fabricated by induction melting under vacuum and subjected to homogenization treatment at 1373 K for 6 h. Plates with a thickness of 4 mm were cut from the ingots and rolled at room temperature to a thickness of 0.75 mm, corresponding to the final thickness reduction of 81.3 %. High-ratio differential speed rolling (HRDSR) with a rolling-speed ratio of 2 was applied (by setting the upper and lower roll speeds to 6 rpm/min and 12 rpm/min, respectively) to impose severe plastic deformation (SPD) on the materials during the rolling process. The rolled materials were annealed in an argon atmosphere at various temperatures ranging from 923 K to 1373 K, along with different annealing duration times ranging from 10 min to 72 h. After each annealing treatment, the samples were subjected to rapid cooling by immersing them in water. Processed by High-ratio differential speed rolling (HRDSR); Limited ductility of 2.2 ± 0.6%

Samples used for subsequent experiments were obtained by directly cutting heat-treated wires using electrical discharge machining (EDM). The three types of aged wires, namely Ti6554, Ti6554-0.05B and Ti6554-0.1B ones, were machined into dumbbell-shaped tensile samples with a gauge portion of 3 mm in diameter and 15 mm in length along the rolling direction (RD). Uniaxial tensile tests were conducted on an INSTRON 1195 testing machine at a strain rate of 5 × 10−4s−1at ambient temperature. To ensure experimental repeatability, at least three samples for each alloy were measured. Tensile properties such as yield strength (σy), ultimate tensile strength (σb) and total elongation at fracture (εf) were recorded after testing. The samples for microstructural characterization were mechanically ground using a series of SiC abrasive papers and subsequently electropolished in a solution of 10 % HClO4and 90 % CH3COOH (vol%). Then, the metallographic samples were etched in a Kroll's reagent of 2 vol% HF, 8 vol% HNO3, and 90 vol% H2O. Phase constitution analysis of the aged samples was examined utilizing a Rigaku D/MAX-RB X-ray diffractometer (XRD) with Cu-Kαradiation source at an acceleration voltage of 40 kV and a current of 100 mA. Metallographic analysis was performed on Nikon MA200 optical microscope (OM) and Hitachi SU6600 scanning electron microscopy (SEM). Crystallographic information in both initial and deformed samples were captured by employing Oxford electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detector mounted on Zeiss GEMINI 500 field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM). Transmission electron microscope (TEM) foils were thinned to approximately 50 μm through mechanical grinding. Processing Text: The as-cast Mg-9 wt.% Li-5 wt.% Al-4 wt.% Zn alloy (LAZ954) plate was prepared using pure Mg (99.9 wt.%), Al (99.9 wt.%), Zn (99.9 wt.%), and Li (99 wt.%). Melting was performed in a vacuum mid-frequency induction furnace under an Ar gas shield to produce an ingot casting. The cast alloys underwent heat treatment at 450 °C for 1 h, followed by quenching in ice water. Subsequent annealing was conducted at 200 °C for 1 h, producing the base metal (“BM”). Plates for FSP, measuring 200 mm × 70 mm × 3 mm, were cut from the annealed alloys using an electrical discharge machine. The FSP employed a tool with shoulder and probe diameters of 15 mm and 6 mm, respectively, and a probe length of 2.8 mm (Fig. S1) [23]. Tool rotation speeds of 100, 200, and 400 rpm yielded different strain and heat input combinations, while maintaining a consistent processing speed of 100 mm/min. The range of the FSP parameters was selected based on previous research and process window assessment [31]. Samples from the base metal and those with tool rotation speeds of 100, 200, and 400 rpm were labeled “FSP-100”, “FSP-200”, and “FSP-400”, respectively. Processing Text: Gas-atomized IN718 powder, supplied by Renishaw plc (Staffordshire, United Kingdom), was utilized for the LPBF production with a particle size range between 15 and 35 μm. LPBF was performed using a Renishaw AM250 SLM system (Staffordshire, United Kingdom) with a Ytterbium fiber laser. Two bulk IN718 samples with dimensions of 60×60×40 mm 3were LPBF-ed. A single laser beam was utilized in continuous mode with a wavelength of 1070 nm, a spot size of 100 µm, a power of 300 W, a scanning speed of 1050 mm/s, a hatching distance of 90 µm, and a layer thickness of 0.04 mm, which led to the energy density of 71.4 J/mm 3. The substrate temperature was set at 80 ˚C. A striped scanning strategy using a hatch angle of 67° was chosen to minimize the microstructure anisotropy in perpendicular transverse directions. A bi-directional scanning method was implemented to ensure efficient melt-pool fusion and minimize residual stresses. Subsequently, vertical sheets with dimensions of 60×60 mm were wire-cut with a thickness of 3 mm to cut the tensile and fatigue specimens. Each sheet yielded either six tensile or three fatigue samples. For sample preparation, specimens were ground using a 2000# SiC sandpaper, then polished and vibration polished with a 0.03 µm alumina suspension. The TD-BD cross-section was chosen for the EBSD mapping to show the anisotropic microstructure along these two directions. EBSD maps were collected using the NOVA NanoSEM 230 scanning electron microscope (SEM) device with the Oxford Instruments® AZtec™ system at a voltage of 20 keV, a tilt angle of 70˚, a working distance of 13 mm, and a step size of 1 µm. The surface was polished similarly to the EBSD sample preparation before the XRD tests. Tensile tests were conducted according to the ASTM E8/E8M standard using the engineering strain rate of 0.001 s −1. Moreover, stress-controlled fatigue tests were carried out based on the ASTM E466/E466M with maximum stress values ranging from 550 MPa to 750 MPa, a stress ratio of 0.1, and a frequency of 15 cycles per second. Processing Text: The GH4099 superalloy was fabricated using the laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) technique. An optimal parameter combination was established using the response surface method (RSM) design and the variance method, resulting in the optimal parameter combination of PLP= 317 W, vSS= 900 mm/s, and HS =0.08 mm. The as-deposited GH4099 alloy is primarily composed of columnar crystals grown epitaxially and M23C6 carbides without the generation of the γ′-phase. After solution treatment, recrystallization and grain growth occurred, with the alloy remaining as large, irregularly shaped polygonal columnar crystals. The aging process precipitated substantial γ′-phase, which internally existed as a mixture of equiaxed and columnar crystals. Subsequently, the partial samples were subjected to solution and aging treatments. Specifically, solid solution S1130 (1130 ℃ × 2 h and then water-cooling) and solid solution-aging treatment SA800 (1130 ℃ × 2 h and then water-cooling + 800 ℃ × 9 h and then air-cooling) were carried out for part of deposited samples. The samples were separated from the matrix using a wire-cutting method. An ultrasonic cleaning device JP-010 was used to clean the as-deposited samples to remove adherent powder and impurities. The polished samples were etched using Kalling's No.2 reagent (5 g CuCl 2, 100 mL HCl and 100 mL ethanol). Electrolytic polishing was performed at 12 V in a 10% perchloric acid solution for 30 s. Room temperature and high-temperature (800 ℃ and 900 ℃) mechanical tests were conducted using a CMT5105 electronic universal testing machine at a strain rate of 1 mm/min, with three repeated tests for each sample under different conditions. Processing Text: Laser directed energy deposition (LDED) has attracted as a progressive additive manufacturing technique in fabricating the stainless steel components. The rapid melting and solidification velocity under LDED process induces the appearance of pores and the columnar dendritic, which degrades the strength of alloys. Here, a self-developed LDED-UR (ultrasonic rolling) synchronous manufacturing equipment is developed to fabricate the 316L stainless steel, and the characterization of microstructure and mechanical properties are studied. Results show that the size and fraction of pores are significantly reduced by LDED-UR processing, and fine equiaxed grains are obtained under the combined effects of ultrasonic vibration and roller pressure. With the severe plastic deformation, the average grain size of LDED-UR sample is decreased from 76.10 μm to 26.23 μm (LDED sample), and high angle grain boundaries transforms to low angle grain boundaries. Meanwhile, the dislocation density in LDED-UR sample is increased compared to the LDED sample. Owing to the grain refinement and dislocation strengthening, the average microhardness, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength and elongation of the LDED-UR sample reach 268.18 ± 13.90 HV0.2, 442 MPa, 771.2 MPa, and 49.8 %, respectively, which are larger than those of LDED sample (214.13 ± 13.76 HV0.2, 396 MPa, 682 MPa, and 45.5 %). 316L stainless steel, as a structural metallic material, has been extensively utilized in various industrial sectors for its superior mechanical properties, including aerospace and marine facilities. 316L stainless steel plate with dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm × 16 mm is fabricated as the substrate. The 99.99 % Ar gas is employed as the shielding gas to prevent oxidation of deposition layers. 316L stainless steel powders (Avimetal Powder Metallurgy Technology Co., Ltd, China) is employed in this study, and it is manufactured by gas atomization method. Processing state: LDED-UR; Microstructure: grain refinement and dislocation strengthening

Processing Text: The steel was melted in a high-frequency vacuum induction melting furnace with a capacity of 50 kg and casted into a mold with a diameter of 110 mm. Thereafter, the casting ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for a duration of 3 h. Then the ingot was cooled down to 1100 °C and directly radial forged into bars in a diameter of 16 mm with downward pressure of about 20 % per forging stroke. The starting and final forging temperatures were 1100 °C and 950 °C, respectively, and the forging temperature range was in the dual phase region. This was followed by cooling down to room temperature (RT) in air circumstance. Quasi-static uniaxial tensile were carried out using the specimens cut from the forged bars by electrical discharge machining (EDM). The uniaxial tensile tests were performed on a universal material testing equipment (Shimadzu AG-100 KN) at a strain rate of 5×10−4s −1and at RT. Standard miniaturized compact tension (CT) specimens for the fracture toughness tests were cut from the forged bars by EDM. A miniature CT specimen with a width W of ∼12.0 mm and a thickness B of ∼3.0 mm was used. In order to obtain a sharp initial crack front, the CT specimens were first notched to a depth of ∼4.0 mm by electrical discharge machining, and then fatigue pre-cracked in a tension-tension mode at a frequency of 2 Hz until an initial total crack length a0of ∼6.0 mm was reached. In order to improve the surface stress constraint and make the crack extend straightly, side grooves with a total depth of 0.2B were additionally machined on both surfaces of the fatigue pre-cracked CT specimens. The fracture tests were carried out on an Instron 5982 testing machine with a load capacity of 5 kN under displacement control at a speed of about 0.1 mm/min to stimulate crack extension. The hardness of the specimens was measured by a Shimadzu HMV-G 31DT Vickers hardness testing machine and both the loads applied to ferrite and martensite were 98.07 mN with a 15 s dwell time. All surfaces of the samples for tests and characterizations were mechanically ground by SiO 2papers and electrically polished in a solution of 20 % perchloric acid and 80 % ethanol (vol%) performed at −25 °C with a potential of 30 V and corroded in a solution of 5 % nitric acid and 95 % ethanol (vol%). Condition: RD samples; Offset: 0.2%; Associated with high strength and ductility

Processing Text: The alloys were cast using arc melting under the protection of Ar atmosphere. The raw materials used were pure metals (purity>99.9 wt%). The dimensions of the ingots were 60 × 12 × 8 (length × width × thickness) mm³. Each ingot was kept at 1200 °C for 4 h followed by water quenching. After that, a multi-pass hot rolling process was conducted at 1100 °C with a total reduction in thickness of 50 %. Then the hot-rolled plates were homogenized at 1200 °C for 4 h, followed by water quenching. The obtained alloys were denoted as the homogenized (HOMO) materials. To achieve the refined microstructure, the HOMO materials then underwent multi-pass cold rolling with a total thickness reduction of 60 %, and the cold-rolled (CR) materials were obtained. The materials in the CR state were then annealed for 3 min in a salt bath furnace and water-quenched. The materials annealed at 750 °C and 900 °C were denoted as the partially recrystallized (PRX) and the fully recrystallized (FRX) materials, respectively. Processing Text: The Al-5.0Mn-1.5Mg-0.82Sc-0.76Zr (wt.%) alloy powder with a standard composition was prepared by gas atomization (Panxing New Alloy Materials Co., Ltd., China). The powder was spherical in shape, with the particles less than or equal to 22.3 µm accounting for 10% while 90% of the particles were less than or equal to 63.4 µm, as shown in Fig. 1(a, b). All the LPBF samples investigated in this work were manufactured using a BLT S210 LPBF machine equipped with a 400 W fiber laser. Constant laser power (350 W), scanning spacing (90 µm), and layer thickness (30 µm) were used with scanning velocities ranging between 450 and 1450 mm/s. Two different substrate temperatures, 25 and 200 °C, were used for each condition. The samples with the optimized process parameters had a relative density higher than 99.8 %. A bilinear scanning strategy with a scan rotation of 67° was used between the layers. The samples were printed in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the samples were heat-treated at 200 °C for 1 h to remove residual stresses before evaluating their microstructures and mechanical properties. The LPBF samples were prepared for microstructural characterization by mechanical grinding and polishing following a standard metallographic procedure recommended in ASTM E3-11. After polishing, the microstructural features were revealed using an etchant consisting of HNO 3(2.5 mL), HCl (1.5 mL), HF (1.0 mL), and distilled water (95 mL). The wire-cut electro-discharge machine was used to slice samples with the following dimensions: ∼5 mm long, ∼5 mm wide, and ∼1 mm thick. Prior to the EBSD characterization, the sheet samples were first mechanically polished with 400 #, 1000 #, 2000 #, and 3000 # SiC water abrasive paper, then electropolished to remove the surface deformation layer generated by mechanical grinding. Electropolishing was performed at −30 °C, with: 7 % perchloric acid, 93 % ethanol; a voltage of 25 V, and a current density of 450 mA/cm 2for about 1 min. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed using the CMT4105 universal testing machine. The gauge length and cross-sectional area of the tensile specimens were 22 mm and 1.5 mm × 4 mm. All the tensile samples were tested perpendicular to the build direction at a constant strain rate of 1 mm/min, following the standard ASTM E8. Fatigue test samples with the dimensions 60 mm × 12 mm × 1.5 mm were tested on an MTS370.02 fatigue testing machine. All samples were mechanically ground and polished prior to fatigue testing to ensure similar surface roughness. The uniaxial fatigue tests were conducted in a load control mode at a frequency of 40 Hz and stress ratio of R= 0.1, following the standard ASTM E466. The samples were tested until fracture or exhaustion till 10 7cycles. Laser power: 300 W; Scanning speed: 1600 mm/s

Processing Text: The LPBF samples were prepared using a self-developed HP-LPBF300 system which possesses a continuous wave IPG YLR-2000 single-mode fiber laser (near-Gaussian mode laser beam; 2000 W maximum output power; 1070 nm wavelength). Spherical 300M steel powders with a particle size ranging from 15 μm to 56 μm, which were produced by gas atomization, were used as the feedstock for sample building. A series of cuboid samples and tensile test samples designed according to ISO 6892-1-2009 standard were deposited using the process parameters listed in Table 2. The as-built sample reveals a microstructure composed of tempered martensite and a minor amount of residual austenite. Before heat treatment, the phase transition temperatures of the LPBF-fabricated 300M samples were verified by using a NETZSCH DIL402C thermal dilatometry (TD) instrument with a heating rate of 10 k/min from room temperature to 1400 °C. The obtained thermal expansion curve displayed in Fig. 1 shows the start temperature of austenitization (A s) for the as-built sample was approximately 708 °C, while the finish temperature of austenitization (A f) is around 856 °C. Accordingly, the quenching temperature in this study was chosen as 870-1100 °C. The holding time (1 h) and the cooling method (oil quenching) were selected in accordance with the conventional quenching process applied to 300M forged components. In terms of selecting the tempering temperature, considering that tempering treatment for 300M forgings is commonly carried out at approximately 300 °C, the chosen tempering temperature range for this study spans from 200 °C to 400 °C. Furthermore, because two times of tempering treatment leads to more thorough release of residual stresses in the microstructure and thus more improved toughness and more enhanced stability of the workpiece compared to a single tempering treatment, the tempering treatment was conducted twice for every tempered sample in this study. The LPBF-fabricated samples were heat treated in a KSL-1400×-A2 muffle furnace with a heating rate of 10 K/min. The details of the different heat treatment conditions are summarized in Table 3. To investigate the evolution of microstructural morphological and crystallographic textures of the LPBF-fabricated samples with the heat treatment conditions, the bulk specimens were first ground and polished according to the standard metallographic preparation procedure and then etched by using an etchant of 4% nital solution before being observed with a Nikon Epiphot-300 optical microscope (OM) and a GeminiSEM-300 scanning electron microscopy (SEM) equipped with an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detector. In addition to mechanical polishing, the samples used for EBSD analysis were further electrolytic-polished in a mixture of 6 mL perchloric acid and 94 mL ethanol at 18 V for 2 min. Phase identification was conducted employing a PANalytical X'Pert PRO X-ray diffraction (XRD) using Cu Kα radiation with a scan step size of 0.02°. Moreover, a Tecnai G2 F30 transmission electron microscope (TEM) was used to characterize the dislocations, deformation twins, stacking fault and other substructures like carbide precipitation. TEM samples with a diameter of 3 mm were ground using 2000-grit SiC abrasive paper until the thickness reaches approximately 50 μm, and then electropolished in a 10/90% perchloric acid/ethanol solution at −20 °C using an automatic twin-jet electropolisher. Room temperature microhardness and tensile properties were characterized to assess the mechanical performance of LPBF-fabricated 300M steel before and after different heat treatments. Microhardness measurements of the samples were carried out via an HVS-1000 tester using a 4.9 N load and a 20 s dwell time. Tensile properties tests were conducted using a Shimadzu AG-100 kN tester with a strain rate of 10 −3/s, and the tensile load was perpendicular to the build direction of LPBF-fabricated samples. Processing Text: A novel high entropy shape memory alloy (HESMEA) was developed using in-situ alloying laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) by introducing a moderate amount of silicon (10 % atomic percent) to a metastable Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 HEA matrix. The HEA powders and Si powders were then weighed according to a molar ratio of 90:10 to obtain the designed composition (Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10) 90Si 10(at%) and mechanically mixed using a three-dimensional shaker mixer (Turbula) for 10 hours at a spindle speed of 30 r/min to ensure a uniform powder mixture. After three remelting passes, with sufficient diffusion time to promote the blending of the mixed pure Si in the Fe 50Mn 30Co 20Cr 20HEA matrix, the printed HESMA exhibits an outstanding recoverable strain of 5.2 % combined with a high yield stress of 500 MPa. Processing Text: The lattice constants of a= b= 2.932 Å and c= 4.684 Å are employed to construct the unit cell of Ti-7Al. Afterward, ∼12 % Al atoms are randomly located on the crystal to ensure a perfectly substitutional alloy. The consequent alloy structure takes the form of a cuboid, as depicted in Fig. 1, with final dimensions of 80.63 Å× 85.49 Å× 81.97 Å. Utilizing a consistent approach, 160 different samples are prepared for MD studies by keeping the indistinguishable dimension while introducing random variations in the positions of Al atoms on the α-structure. The force field of the atoms of the single-crystal structure has been defined by 2NN MEAM potential parameters. In each computation, the periodic boundary conditions are applied to all three directions of the samples, effectively diminishing the influence of the boundary/edge effect on the structure. Before subjecting the structures to a constant strain rate, a comprehensive energy minimization process is undertaken to achieve equilibrium among all atoms. The minimization involves a two-stage combined optimization method. First and foremost, the NVT (stands for the number of atoms, volume, and temperature of the structure) canonical ensemble is conducted for a total time of 5 picoseconds. This is aimed at the determination of the positions and velocities of each atom using non-Hamiltonian equations in the Nose-Hoover method at every time step. Following this, the simulation is extended for an additional 50 picoseconds, utilizing the NPT (stands for the number of atoms, pressure, and temperature of the structure) isothermal-isobaric ensemble where the objective of this phase is to resolve the kinematics parameters, such as linear/angular positions, orientations, and velocities of all atoms at every time step. The NPT ensemble is employed to keep constant temperature and pressure in conjunction with the imposition of uniaxial deformation along the [ 10 0] direction, featuring a specified strain rate of 10 10s −1at a temperature of 300 K. Prior to going through the NPT tension process, the samples are completely stable in terms of temperature and pressure; 5 ps of NVT ensemble has been employed to settle down the temperature at 300 K and successively 50 ps of NPT ensemble relaxed the samples to keep the zero pressure. At a constant strain rate of 10 10s −1(= ε˙11=dε11/dt), the main stress-strain simulation is conducted in [1 0 0] direction ( ε¨11= 0, ε22≠ 0, ε33≠ 0) at previously achieved constant pressure and temperature through next 30 ps. Processing Text: The button ingot of Ni38Co25Fe13Cr10Al7Ti7 (atomic percentage) MPEA was obtained by arc melting in an argon atmosphere and remelted multiple times to ensure chemical uniformity, raw materials are commercially pure metals with a purity higher than 99.95% wt. The plate sample with the size of 8 mm × 12 mm × 50 mm was produced by copper mold casting technology in high purity argon atmosphere. The heat treatment of all samples is carried out in vacuum sealed quartz tubes. The sample was first dissolved at 1200 °C for 2 h, as shown in the Fig. S1, the primary L12 precipitates could be completely dissolved at 1200 °C, and then quenched with water. The samples were then single-stage aging at 700 °C, 800 °C and 900 °C for 16 h, or double-stage aging at 1050 °C for 2 h and 780 °C for 4 h. The uniaxial tensile test of the flat dog bone (0.8 mm × 2.5 mm × 16 mm) was carried out on the electronic universal testing machine (Instron5582) to evaluate the tensile properties of the samples. The tensile test was carried out at a constant strain rate of 10−3s−1, and the actual strain was measured by a contact extensometer. Characterization of the microstructure of the sample using a scanning electron microscope (SEM；XL30-FEG) with a working voltage of 20 kV. Electrolytic etching of SEM samples with 10% perchloric acid and 90% ethanol electrolyte at a voltage of 20 V and a temperature of −20 °C for 60 s to display L12 precipitation. Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) characterizations were conducted by the SEM with Oxford C-Nano acquisition system. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM; Talos F200X) equipped with super-energy dispersive X-ray analysis (Super-EDX) was used to characterize the microstructure and composition in more detail. TEM samples were prepared by double-jet electropolishing mechanism, using 10% perchloric acid ethanol solution electrolyte, voltage 25 V, temperature −30 °C. Gas atomized Fe (purity 99%) and Si (purity 99.95%) powders, with a particle size ranging from 63 to 150 µm, obtained from American Elements (United States) and Tosoh SMD Inc (United States), were used in an Optomec Laser Engineered Net Shaping (LENS 150) equipment. The Fe-Si samples were printed by a LENS 150 equipment equipped with an IPG YLR-400 laser with a maximum laser power of 400 W and a laser beam diameter of 0.4 mm. This system was equipped with multiple powder feeders (PF), of which 2 feeders were used. Argon (Ar) was used as the inert carrying gas to transport powder from the powder feeder through the pipeline system to the powder delivery nozzle. Ar was also used as a shielding gas to control the environment during deposition. Three batches of samples were printed vertically along the z-axis. The first batch consisted of samples of Fe-5Si, Fe-10Si and Fe-20Si, each with dimensions of 5 mm ×5 mm ×6 mm, for density, hardness, and magnetic property measurements. The second batch included samples of Fe-3.5Si, Fe-5Si, Fe-10Si and Fe-20Si, each with dimensions of 5 mm ×5 mm ×25 mm, printed for tensile test measurements. The third batch comprised of samples of Fe-10Si and Fe-20Si, both with dimensions of 5 mm ×5 mm ×15 mm, printed for the compression tests. All samples were printed using optimized parameters from our previous work, i.e., laser power of 350 W, layer thickness of 0.20 mm, hatch spacing of 0.20 mm, stage speed of 8.4 mm/s, a protective gas centre purge of 20 litre per minute (lpm) and a powder supply gas flow of 4 lpm. The powder flow rates used on each powder feeder (PF1: Fe powder only, PF2: Fe+20% Si) were as follows: PF1: 3.75 rpm, PF2: 1.25 rpm for Fe-5Si. The printed samples were separated from the substrate using an electric discharge wire-cut equipment. Subsequently, the columnar sample was sectioned parallel to the build axis into two halves. Cross-sectioned surfaces were mechanically polished progressively, from Grit500, Grit2000, Grit4000 to a 0.03 µm polishing suspension, for characterization and property measurements. Measured Si content: 4.3%; Tensile test; AM (DED)

Processing Text: The Al-5.0Mn-1.5Mg-0.82Sc-0.76Zr (wt.%) alloy powder with a standard composition was prepared by gas atomization (Panxing New Alloy Materials Co., Ltd., China). The powder was spherical in shape, with the particles less than or equal to 22.3 µm accounting for 10% while 90% of the particles were less than or equal to 63.4 µm, as shown in Fig. 1(a, b). All the LPBF samples investigated in this work were manufactured using a BLT S210 LPBF machine equipped with a 400 W fiber laser. Constant laser power (350 W), scanning spacing (90 µm), and layer thickness (30 µm) were used with scanning velocities ranging between 450 and 1450 mm/s. Two different substrate temperatures, 25 and 200 °C, were used for each condition. The samples with the optimized process parameters had a relative density higher than 99.8 %. A bilinear scanning strategy with a scan rotation of 67° was used between the layers. The samples were printed in a high-purity argon atmosphere. Subsequently, the samples were heat-treated at 200 °C for 1 h to remove residual stresses before evaluating their microstructures and mechanical properties. The LPBF samples were prepared for microstructural characterization by mechanical grinding and polishing following a standard metallographic procedure recommended in ASTM E3-11. After polishing, the microstructural features were revealed using an etchant consisting of HNO 3(2.5 mL), HCl (1.5 mL), HF (1.0 mL), and distilled water (95 mL). The wire-cut electro-discharge machine was used to slice samples with the following dimensions: ∼5 mm long, ∼5 mm wide, and ∼1 mm thick. Prior to the EBSD characterization, the sheet samples were first mechanically polished with 400 #, 1000 #, 2000 #, and 3000 # SiC water abrasive paper, then electropolished to remove the surface deformation layer generated by mechanical grinding. Electropolishing was performed at −30 °C, with: 7 % perchloric acid, 93 % ethanol; a voltage of 25 V, and a current density of 450 mA/cm 2for about 1 min. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed using the CMT4105 universal testing machine. The gauge length and cross-sectional area of the tensile specimens were 22 mm and 1.5 mm × 4 mm. All the tensile samples were tested perpendicular to the build direction at a constant strain rate of 1 mm/min, following the standard ASTM E8. Fatigue test samples with the dimensions 60 mm × 12 mm × 1.5 mm were tested on an MTS370.02 fatigue testing machine. All samples were mechanically ground and polished prior to fatigue testing to ensure similar surface roughness. The uniaxial fatigue tests were conducted in a load control mode at a frequency of 40 Hz and stress ratio of R= 0.1, following the standard ASTM E466. The samples were tested until fracture or exhaustion till 10 7cycles. Condition: aged at 300 °C; Strengthening mechanisms: precipitation strengthening, solid solution strengthening, and grain boundary strengthening; Microstructure: precipitation of highly coherent Al3Sc nanoparticles (2-3 nm)

Processing Text: NbTaTiZrX RHEAs with BCC structure constructed by SQS method. The relationship between the elastic constant, elastic modulus, hardness, strength, and plasticity of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs with elements is systematically analyzed both by SQS and VCA methods. The calculated results show that alloying of Mo, W and Re with high elastic modulus can enhance the strength and the hardness of RHEAs. For alloying of V and Hf, the ductility of RHEAs is improved. The reduction of pseudo energy gaps and the formation of Hf-Hf strong metallic bonds further confirm its metallic ductility from the electronic density of states and charge density. The lattice constants (Å) of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs are calculated. Elastic constants (GPa) of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs are calculated by SQS method. Yield strength (GPa) of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs is calculated. Energy factors of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs are calculated by SQS method including screw dislocation (Ks) and edge dislocation (Ke); mixed dislocation (Km). Total density of states for NbTaTiZrX RHEAs is calculated by SQS method. Charge density contour of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs along the crystal plane (1 1 0) is analyzed. Common parameters of NbTaTiZrX RHEAs are calculated. Calculated using SQS method; Notably higher than other considered high-entropy alloys

Processing Text: In the present work, cold rolling and subsequent high-temperature annealing processes were employed to the Cu1.2NiMnFe0.5Cr0.5Al0.2 high-entropy alloy. After subsequent aging treatment at 400 °C, spinodal decomposition occurred within the matrix, leading to enhanced strength. High-entropy alloy ingots of Cu 1.2NiMnFe 0.5Cr 0.5Al 0.2(at.%) were prepared by induction melting of commercial purity metals (>99%) and casting into a cylindrical steel mold (Φ35 × 275 mm). To minimize elemental loss, the furnace chamber was evacuated and filled with argon gas. The as-cast ingots were heat-treated at 950 °C for 24 h to enhance chemical homogeneity. Subsequently, samples measuring 100 × 10 × 5 mm 3were cut from the ingots and cold-rolled with a 60% rolling reduction ratio, reducing their thickness from 5 to 2 mm. The cold-rolled plates were annealed at 950 °C for 2 h (depicted as the AN sample) and then water-cooled to obtain fully recrystallized microstructure, and sequential aging at 400 °C for xh (x = 2,4,6,8,10) and then air-cooled (designated as the 2H, 4H, 6H, 8H, and 10H samples, respectively), were conducted to acquire spinodal-decomposed microstructure. The samples for TEM were grounded to a thickness of 50 μm and then ion-milled. And the samples for electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) analysis underwent electropolishing in a solution containing perchloric acid and ethanol with a volume ratio of 9:1, the polishing process was conducted at 26.5 V for a duration of 5 s. Sharp tip specimens for atom probe tomography (APT) were made by a two-step electrochemical polishing. The 0.3 mm × 0.3 mm blanks were cut by low-speed diamond saw, followed by electrochemical polishing using 10% perchloric acid at a direct voltage of 15 V, the tips were then polished by using weaker electrolyte (2%) of perchloric acid at a direct voltage of 8 V. Processing Text: The samples were cut along the rolling direction (RD) and transverse direction (TD) and then subjected to a sequential annealing process in an air-circulating furnace, involving a temperature increase to 350 °C at 10 °C/min followed by a 50-min hold at this temperature, followed by rapid quenching in water. Surface finishing was achieved through sequential grinding with sandpapers of increasing fineness (800#, 1000#, 1500#, and 2000#), polishing with a 3 μm diamond suspension, and electropolishing at −20 °C in a solution of 10 % perchloric acid and 90 % anhydrous ethanol. Tensile specimens, designed in a flat dog-bone shape, were extracted from the plate centers in RD and TD orientations. These specimens were prepared with dimensions of 20 mm in gauge length, 2 mm in thickness, and 6 mm in width, consistent with quasi in-situ tensile testing specifications. The tensile behavior was assessed at room temperature (298K) and low temperature (77K) using an MTS C43.105 full-temperature field tensile testing machine equipped with extensometer at a strain rate of 1.2 × 10−3s−1. To achieve and maintain the desired low-temperature environment, the chamber was filled with liquid nitrogen, ensuring that the sample was completely submerged and constantly exposed to liquid nitrogen throughout the test. Prior to initiating the tensile test, the setup was equilibrated for approximately 25 min. Quasi in-situ EBSD testing was conducted to monitor the evolution of grain orientation at strain levels of 0 %, 5 %, 10 %, 15 %, and 20 %.
