The platinum, gold, and nickel sheets with high purity (99.99%) were used as the raw materials to prepare Pt-5Au-5Ni alloy. The ingots were melted by a vacuum arc melting furnace under the protection of argon gas, and followed by being cast into a graphite mould. The as-cast ingots were chemically analyzed by X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF, ZSX Primus IV). Subsequently, the ingots were homogenized at 900 °C for 1 h and quenched in water. The as-homogenized ingots were then cold rolled and cold drawn to wires with the diameter of Φ 0.5 mm. During the process of cold deformation, the intermediate annealing at 900 °C for 1 h was performed. The deformation of each pass was controlled at 15%, and the deformation accumulation of 90% was gained. Alloy wires with the diameter of Φ 0.5 mm were cut from the 90% cold-deformed sample for artificial aging treatment. The isochronous aging treatment was performed at the temperature range of 200°C-600 °C for 1 h, and the isothermal aging treatment was carried out at 300 °C and 400 °C for various durations from 1 h to 5 h. To avoid the oxidation during aging, vacuum tube furnaces were used for protection. Condition: after aging at 400 °C for 1 h following cold deformation

Processing Text: The experiment utilized 15-5 PH stainless steel powder produced by using vacuum atomization method (Oerlikon Metco., Switzerland). The powder exhibited excellent sphericity, presenting a smooth and fully formed structure ( Fig. 1(a)). The particle size distribution was mostly within 15∼53 μm, with D10, D50, and D90 being 19.4 μm, 33.2 μm, and 50.9 μm, respectively ( Fig. 1(b)). The primary chemical composition of the powder was Fe-12.48Cr-3.55Ni-3.04Cu-0.18Nb-0.48Mn-0.46Si-0.0509C (wt. %). Subsequently, the 64 sets of small square samples (10 × 10 × 10 mm 3) with different process parameters were fabricated using the L-PBF equipment (HBD 280 Metal 3D Printer). The chosen process parameters included a range of Pat 200 W, 260 W, 320 W, and 380 W, Vat 800 mm/s, 1200 mm/s, 1600 mm/s, and 2000 mm/s, Hat 0.06 mm, 0.09 mm, 0.12 mm, and 0.15 mm, respectively, and a fixed scanning layer thickness ( T) of 0.04 mm. The printing strategy involved rotating the current printing layer by 67° compared to the previous layer. Subsequently, well-formed (no visible defect) process parameters were selected for the fabrication of tensile and impact samples. The particle size of the powder was determined using a laser particle size analyzer (Better Size 2600), while the chemical composition was analyzed through inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy. Subsequently, the ground and polished samples underwent corrosion in a 15 % HF aqueous solution at a voltage of 25 V for 15 s. Microstructural observations were conducted using optical microscope (OM, Leica DMI3000 M) and scanning electron microscope (SEM, Gemini SEM300). The electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) samples were prepared using a mixed solution of 5 % HClO 4+95 % CH 3COOH (vol%) at a voltage of 25 V for 30 s. The crystal structure and texture of the samples were examined and the EBSD data were further analyzed using the software of OIM. The phase structure was analyzed by X-ray diffractometer (Smart Lab) carrying Cu Kα. Utilized the Archimedes drainage method for precise determination of the density of the formed samples. The bar shaped tensile test sample (gauge length specification: φ5 mm × 25 mm) was subjected to room temperature tensile performance testing on a universal tensile testing machine (DN200), with a strain rate of 1.3 × 10 −3s −1. The samples were subjected to HRC testing using the hardness tester (HRS-150), applying a loading force of 1470 N for a duration of 10 s. Additionally, the V-notch impact samples (size 55 × 10 × 10 mm 3) were subjected to Charpy impact testing on the metal pendulum impact testing machine (JBN500), featuring a notch depth of 2 mm and a root radius of 0.25 mm. The morphology of both tensile and impact fractures was observed under the SEM. Sample 21#, processed via L-PBF with P = 260 W, H = 0.06 mm, V = 1200 mm/s; Exhibits a heterogeneous layered structure of FCC + BCC dual-phase, fine-grain and coarse-grain layers.
Processing Word: Sample 21#, processed via L-PBF with P = 260 W, H = 0.06 mm, V = 1200 mm/s; Exhibits a heterogeneous layered structure of FCC + BCC dual-phase, fine-grain and coarse-grain layers.

The production process of the bar involved several steps, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Initially, a casting ingot with dimensions of 530 mm in width and 410 mm in thickness was heated at a temperature of 1210 °C ± 30 °C for a duration of 11 h. Subsequently, the ingot was rolled into a square middle billet measuring 240 mm × 240 mm. The middle billet was further hot-rolled into a cylindrical bar with a diameter of 130 mm, within a temperature range of 900 °C-950 °C. Before the isothermal heat treatment, the bainitic transition temperature of sample steels were obtained by the thermal expansion experiment. The thermal expansion experiment was carried out on the thermal simulation testing machine Gleeble-3500, the experiment process and the sample size are shown in Fig. 2(a). The thermal expansion curves obtained from the thermal expansion experiment are shown in Fig. 2(b). The bainite transformation temperatures range of 0Nb-steel and 0.015Nb-steel measured by the tangent method were 400∼521 °C and 381∼505 °C, respectively. For the isothermal quenching experiment, several cylinder rods with a diameter of 15 mm and a length of 70 mm were extracted from the low carbon bainitic microalloying steel rods. The isothermal process parameters and route are depicted in Fig. 3 and presented in Table 1. In the first step, the samples were austenitized in a KSL-1400X box-type high-temperature furnace. The austenite temperature (AT) was set at 950 °C, and the soaking time was 60 min. Subsequently, the samples were removed from the high-temperature furnace and directly placed into a salt bath furnace for isothermal treatment, where the salt used was nitrate salt. The temperature range of bainitic transformation, calculated by JMatPro, was determined to be 370∼550 °C. Consequently, the IT were set at 400 °C, 450 °C, and 500 °C, respectively, with each isothermal time set at 10 min. Finally, the samples were removed from the furnace and air-cooled to room temperature. Furthermore, two additional experiments were conducted with different austenitizing temperatures. The samples were austenitized at 900 °C and 1000 °C, respectively. Following the austenitization process, the samples were transferred from the high-temperature furnace to the salt bath furnace for isothermal treatment at 450 °C for 10 min. The ASTM grain size grades after austenitizing at 900 °C, 950 °C, and 1000 °C were determined to be 6, 7.5, and 8, respectively. Thermal expansion experiments were performed using the DIL 805A dilatometer, with specimen dimensions of φ4 × 10 mm. The heat treatment process involved an austenitizing temperature of 900 °C for 30 min followed by a 10-min soaking at 450 °C, as depicted in Fig. 3. The optimal isothermal quenching process for achieving a balance between strength and toughness is as follows: the steels were austenitized at 900 °C for 30 min and then subjected to an isothermal treatment at 450 °C for 10 min. Processing Text: Nearly equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi alloy samples were prepared by induction melting and mechanical alloying (MA) combined with spark plasma sintering (SPS). Pure powders of each element (Co 99.8%, Cr 99%, Fe 99.9%, Ni 99.5%, Al 99.7%) were used in appropriate amounts to prepare the equiatomic alloy. A total amount of 20 g of the powder mixture was put in the jar along with milling balls, both made from AISI 420 stainless steel. The balls-to-powder weight ratio was 1:15. To decrease the undesired cold welding, 4 wt% of n-heptane was used as the process control agent (PCA). The sealed vessel was then flushed with argon of 99.996 purity (2 l min−1 for 2 min) to prevent any oxidation during the alloying process. The MA was carried out in 30 min intervals followed by 10 min breaks between them until the straight time of the MA reached 8 h. The rotation speed was 400 rpm. The prepared powder alloy was sintered in SPS device FCT Systeme HP D 10. An amount of 10 g of the powder was put in a graphite mould with a diameter of 20 mm and sealed with graphite paper. The sintering temperature was set to 1000 °C with a heating speed of 200 °C min−1 and a pressure of 48 MPa being applied after reaching the sintering temperature. The sample was held under these conditions for 10 min, which prevents excessive coarsening of the microstructure. Eventually, the sample was cooled down to laboratory temperature with the maxima cooling speed of the machine, which is determined by the temperature gradient between the mould and both the water-cooled pistons of the SPS machine. The other AlCoCrFeNi specimen was prepared by induction melting. Small chunks of the individual base metals in precise weight ratios were melted in an Al2O3 crucible at 1800 °C under an argon atmosphere. The melted alloy was homogenized by eddy currents for several minutes before casting. Afterwards, the alloy was cast in a steel mould 14 mm in diameter. Thin foils from the cast material were electropolished (T = −30 °C, U = 15 V) in a TENUPOL 5 (Struers) unit filled with a solution of 20% HNO3 in methanol, a lamella from the sintered alloy was prepared by a Ga+ focused ion beam (FIB, FEI Quanta DualBeam). The mechanical properties were examined by Vickers hardness and compressive stress-strain tests. The hardness was measured with a load of 30 kg and a load time of 10 s. The average value was calculated after measuring 10 indents. The compressive tests were performed on the LabTest 5.250SP1-VM machine using block-shaped specimens with a height corresponding to 1.5 times the side of the base. The deformation speed was set to 10−3 s−1, and each alloy was tested using at least three samples to provide sufficient statistical reliability. The compressive tests were performed at room temperature, at 800 °C, and at room temperature after being annealed at 800 °C for 100h. Processing Text: The steel was designed to have a low stacking-fault energy (SFE, 17.8 mJ/m²) to introduce high density of nanotwins through pre-deformation. The steel was prepared by arc-melting high-purity metals in argon. The ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for 1 h, then hot-rolled to 4 mm in thickness and water quenched (labeled as HR). The HR samples were then cold-rolled 40% at room temperature to 2.4 mm in thickness (labeled CR40). Finally, the CR40 samples were annealed at 100-600 °C for 10 min, followed by water quenching. The samples annealed at 300 °C and 400 °C are respectively denoted as ANN300 and ANN400. A subsequent intermediate annealing was applied to control the reverse phase transformation from ε-martensite to austenite to enhance the deformation ability of the nanotwinned steel (rising tensile elongation from 5 to 16%). The microstructures of samples CR40, ANN300, and ANN400 were characterized in the plane containing rolling direction (RD) and normal direction (ND) of the sheets by transmission electron microscopy (TEM), electron backscattering diffraction (EBSD), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). Thin foils for TEM examinations were prepared by mechanical polishing down to 100 μm in thickness, followed by ion thinning using a Gatan 695 instrument, and observed using a 200 kV TEM (FEI Talos F200X). The samples for EBSD and X-ray diffraction were electropolished in a solution of 10% perchloric acid and 90% acetic acid at room temperature. X-ray diffraction (XRD) with Cu-Kα radiation (Bruker D8 Advance) was used to determine the phase composition. The scanning range was 35-95°, with a scan rate of 1°/min. The volume fractions of austenite ( Vγ) and ε-martensite ( Vε) were measured by a direct-comparison method. The microhardness of the samples was measured using an HVS-1000Z micro-Vickers hardness tester, with a loading force of 9.80 N and a loading time of 15 s. Tensile testing was performed at a strain rate of 10−3s−1 using a SUNS testing machine with a contact extensometer. Condition: CR40 (Cold-Rolled); Microstructure: Nanotwins and ε-martensite
Processing Word: Condition: CR40 (Cold-Rolled); Microstructure: Nanotwins and ε-martensite

For EBSD analyses, the surfaces of the polished samples need to be electrochemically polished in a mixture of 10 % HClO 4and 90 % C 2H 5OH (volume fraction) at a voltage of 20 V for 45 s. The detailed microstructure information was further conducted using transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI Tecnai G2 F30). The TEM specimens were first mechanically ground to a thickness of approximately 20 μm and then thinned using an ion milling machinery (Gatan 691). Processing Text: Ti-30Zr-5Mo alloy was triply melted by consumable vacuum arc-melting sponge Ti, sponge Zr, and Ti-32Mo master alloy. The ingot was homogenized at 1100 °C for 6 h in vacuum and then forged at 1100 °C and air cooled to room temperature. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, Netzsch STA449F3) measurements were carried out at 20 °C/min. According to the DSC results, the α to β phase transformation temperature of Ti-30Zr-5Mo alloy was determined to be approximately 700 °C. To obtain body-centered-cubic Ti-30Zr-5Mo materials with different β grain sizes, different heat treatment processes were conducted. The samples were solution treated at varied temperatures (700-950 °C) in β phase region with different annealing times (30-60 min) in vacumm and followed by water quenching. SIMRT was used to obtain finer grain sizes. The ingots were cold rolled with a reduction ratio of 30%, and then solution treated at 700 °C for 2 min. The above process is one loop, and all the processes are shown in Fig. 2b. Tensile specimens with a total length of 40 mm, gauge a length of 13 mm, a width of 3 mm, and a thickness of 1.5 mm were prepared by electrical discharge wire cutting. The SHIMADZU AG-XPLUS 100 KN tensile testing machine was used for tensile tests at room temperature with a strain rate of 3 × 10 -4s -1. Three samples of each grain size were prepared to minimize errors. Before optical microscopy observation using an optical microscope (OM, ZESS AXIO), the materials were mechanically polished and then chemically etched using a solution of 3.5 pct hydrofluoric acid (HF), 10 pct nitric acid (HNO3) and 86.5 pct distilled water (H2O). The phase constitutions of the tensile materials before and after deformation were determined by X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Smart Lab). The samples after deformation for XRD acquisition are taken near the fracture of the tensile specimens after fracture. In-situ tensile tests in scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL JSM-7001F) and electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD, Oxford instrument Symmetry) systems were used to analyze the microstructural evolution of materials during tensile deformation. Grain size: 15 μm

Processing Text: The Fe30Mn10Co10Cr2.5V1.5C MPEA was produced by ingot casting followed by solution annealing under an argon atmosphere for 5 h at 1150 °C. Subsequently, hot-rolling was applied at 1150 °C to reduce the material thickness to 4 mm. After air cooling, the material was cold-rolled to a thickness of 2 mm (50 % cold-rolling degree). Two different annealing strategies were performed: (a) recrystallization and aging route (RX+A), (b) aging treatment after cold-rolling (CR+A). In the second annealing strategy (CR+A), the aging treatments were performed after cold-rolling without recrystallization for 15 min to 16 h at temperatures in the range between 500 and 1000 °C. Processing Text: Non-equiatomic Al x-Cr-Fe-Ni MEAs (where x is the feeding speed of Al wire) were prepared using three commercial wires (ER1070, ER304L, and Ni80Cr20 wire). High-purity Ar (99.99%) was used as the shielding gas. To ensure the uniform fusion of various elements, the Al, 304 L and Ni 80Cr 20wires were loaded in feeders 1, 2 and 3 respectively ( Fig. 1(a)). Processing Text: A hot-draw stick of commercial Inconel 718 alloy with a diameter of ∼40 mm was utilized. The friction welding experiments were carried out using an HWI-IFW-130 friction welding machine developed by Harbin Welding Institute. One IN718 stick was fixed at the center of the flywheel in the welding machine and then rotated by a constant speed of 2500 r/min during the later friction welding process. Another IN718 stick was applied to tightly contact with the MCA intermedium along the axial direction of the fixed stick. The forge pressure was controlled at 400 MPa, as well as the first friction pressure at 300 MPa. The moment of inertia was kept to be constant at 1.18 kg m 2. For comparison, another friction weld joint was directly produced on two directly contacted IN718 sticks without the in-between MCA intermedium layer under identical welding conditions. The contact surfaces of the used IN718 stick were initially ground by sandpapers and polished using diamond paste, to remove any possible contaminants or oxides for better contact of the following welding. A two-step ageing treatment was performed, namely heated to 720 °C and hold for 8 h, then slowly cooled to 620 °C inside the furnace by 50 °C/h and held for another 8 h, followed by air cooling to room temperature. Flat dog-bone-shaped tensile specimens with a thickness of 1.5 mm were machined from the center part of the weld joints by using electrical discharge machining (EDM). Uniaxial tensile tests were then carried out at room temperature of ∼20 °C using an MTS landmark testing system at a constant strain rate of 1 × 10 −3s −1. The surfaces of the specimens before and after the tensile experiments were mechanically ground with silicon carbide abrasive paper (from P180 to P5000), and then fine polished using 3 μm diamond suspensions. Last polishing with ∼100 nm SiO2 suspension was carried out to remove the strained layer induced by prior mechanical grinding for a better resolution of electron microscopic characterization. The microstructural examination was conducted on a TESCAN CLARA scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) detector microscope at different regions of the attained specimens. Transmission electron microscopic (TEM) investigations including high-resolution atomic imaging and the selected area electron diffraction (SAED) analysis were conducted by using a FEI Talos F200X microscope operated at 200 kV. The elemental distribution of the weld joint was also investigated using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) instrumented in the Talos TEM device. Thin foils for the above TEM study were prepared from the zone near the interface boundary between the IN718 and IN178 or MCA intermedium, and they are produced using the Helios 600i Focus ion beam (FIB)-SEM system. The transverse distribution of nano-hardness values in the weld zone was also measured on the polished specimens using a KLA G200X nano-indenter. The indentation tests were performed under a load-control mode with a maximum force of 4 mN with a loading rate of 0.04 mN/s (i.e., a nominal strain rate of 0.01/s) at room temperature. For higher reliability, three indents were repeated at each location under identical conditions. Condition: as-weld; Compared with counterpart without MCA intermedium layer (~530 MPa)

The heterostructured Al-Mg-Si-Cu alloy profile modified by TiB2-TiC particles was prepared by conventional extrusion and solution treatment. The solution treatment was performed at 560 °C for 3 h, followed by rapid quenching to room temperature in cold water, and then the sample was artificially aged (AA) at 175 °C for different times to explore the age hardening response. The gauge section of the tensile specimens were controlled to be 15 mm (width) × 6 mm (thickness), and the gauge length was determined by 5.65 S0 (Where S0 represents the cross-sectional area of the gauge section). The tensile tests were performed on the CMT5105 tensile test machine at room temperature. The tensile speed was controlled to be 1 mm/min first and then 10 mm/min after yield. Three parallel tensile specimens for each sample were tested to obtain reproducible tensile properties. In addition, the loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tensile test at room temperature was carried out on instrument LD26.105 electronic universal test machine. The gauge dimension of the LUR specimens is 10 mm (length) × 3 mm (width) × 3 mm (thickness). Five loading-unloading loops were performed in the LUR test. The strain rate is controlled to be 5 × 10−4 s−1 to the specified strain (such as 1%). Next, it is unloaded to 50 N in a stress-controlled mode with an unloading rate of 400 N min−1. Repeat the above operation for the next cyclic tensile tests. The standard grinding and polishing processes were employed to prepare the samples for optical microstructure, which was analyzed with a ZEISS Axioskop. The microstructure of the alloy profile was also analyzed by Zeiss ∑IGMA field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS) and electron backscattering diffractometer (EBSD). After grinding with fine emery paper and polishing with diamond powder, the EBSD samples were electrolytically polished for 10 s at 21 V using a solution of 10 vol% perchloric acid and 90 vol% ethanol. The HKL Channel 5 software was used to analyze EBSD results. The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) observations were performed by an FEI Tecnai G2 F20 transmission electron microscopy operating at 200 kV. The TEM samples were prepared by standard mechanical grinding process to a thickness of around 80 μm and then punched into disks with a diameter of 3 mm. The twin-jet electro-polishing was employed to prepare the TEM samples using a solution of 30 vol% nitric acid and 70 vol% methanol at the temperature range of −25 to −40 °C. Processing Text: The 316LSS samples were produced via SLM (DiMetal-100H) using gas-atomized powders with the powder size distribution of 15-53 μm. Tensile and cubic samples of 316LSS were printed two times under various laser powers (70 W, 140 W, 210 W, and 280 W) at fixed scanning speed (200 mm/s), layer thickness (0.03 mm) and hatch spacing (0.1 mm). A combined stripe and meander pattern within each layer, along with a 67° scan angle between adjacent layers, was employed to minimize the impact of printing strategies on anisotropy. The laser energy density E was determined as follows: E = P / (v * h * t) where P refers to the laser power, v is the scanning speed, and h and t are the hatch spacing and layer thickness, respectively. The laser energy density in this work fell in the range from 116.7 to 466.7 J/mm³. Once the laser power increased from 70 to 280 W, the relative density of SLM316LSS parts initially increased and then subsequently decreased. The peak value of relative density (nearly 99.0%) was attained at a laser power of 140 W. The porosity of the SLM316LSS parts gradually disappeared as the laser power increased, which was due to the powder fusion. However, once the laser power increased to 210 W, gas pores and crack defects began to form. In the present work, the AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 EHEA was hot rolled in multiple passes at different temperatures and reductions. The hot rolling process of as-cast AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA is shown in Fig. 1(b) , involving four rolling temperatures (800 °C, 900 °C, 1000 °C and 1200 °C). Among them, the condition of 1200 °C and 60% reduction was tested as a control group to further explore the improvement of the mechanical properties. Taking the deformation of hot rolling at 1000 °C as an example, the sheet is heat-treated by annealing for 10 mins at 1000 °C, and then hot rolling operated at ∼10% reduction. Upon successful completion of the rolling process (i.e., absence of sheet edge cracking and uniform sheet thickness), the 10% reduction sample is reintroduced into the furnace and annealing for 10 mins again. Subsequently, the ∼20% reduction rolling stage is initiated, and the process is repeated. The deformation achieved during the final successful rolling represents the hot rolling reduction at this temperature. After completing all the hot rolling tests, sheets with 10% reduction at 800 °C, 40% reduction at 900 °C, 60% reduction at 1000 °C and 60% reduction at 1200 °C are obtained (denoted as H81, H94, H106 and H126, respectively). The specific samples of SEM were first polished to 3000-grit SiC abrasive paper, and then electrolytically polished for 50 s in a reagent mixture (electrolyte is a mixed solution of 10% perchloric acid, 30% n-butanol and 60% methanol). After polishing, the samples were etched in a solution (etching solution is a mixed solution of 3% hydrofluoric acid, 7% nitric acid and 90% deionized water) for 3 s to complete the SEM sample preparation. The TEM specimens were prepared by means of ion milling on a GATAN 691. High purity elements (Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni with purity above 99.9%) were used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA ingots in a vacuum induction magnetic levitation melting furnace under high purity argon atmosphere. To ensure the chemical homogeneity of the ingots, the melting process was repeated for more than five times. The melt was cast into the water-cooled copper mold, and finally AlCoCrFeNi 2.1EHEA ingots were obtained. The material with Φ74 × 100 mm was cut from the center of the ingot as the raw material used in the experiment. Subsequently, a circular sheet with a diameter of 74 mm and a thickness of 4 mm was fabricated as a hot-rolled specimen. Processing Text: FeCoNiCrMnTix (x = 0, 2, 4, 6 wt%) HEAs were prepared using vacuum arc melting. The FeCoNiCrMnTix HEAs were melted using a ZHF30-3 vacuum arc furnace under high-purity argon protection and conditions with a vacuum degree of 3 × 10-3 Pa. The process was repeated three times to avoid the presence of any other impurity gases in the cavity. The initial arc current is restricted to a maximum of 500 A, and the arc is initiated within approximately 10 min. The alloy particles are melted into a liquid state within water-cooled copper molds before being cast into ingots with a button-like shape. Strictly following the operational procedures, the alloy ingot melts back five times, with every subsequent melting requiring the ingot to be turned over. This process ensures the alloy composition remains uniform, thus preventing the segregation phenomenon. Since the mass loss of the alloy ingot during melting is less than 0.5%, the alloy composition is assumed to be the nominal composition, and the size of the ingot is approximately 30 mm × 30 mm × 15 mm. Cubic specimens measuring 8 mm × 8 mm × 6 mm (OM/SEM/HV test), 6 mm × 6 mm × 1 mm (XRD), 10 mm × 5 mm × 1.5 mm (Tensile test), and 6 mm × 8 mm × 3 mm (Wear test) were sequentially cut using the DK7720 EDM CNC wire cutting machine and grinded using metallographic sandpaper ranging from 400 to 2000 grit. After polishing treatment with diamond abrasive paste on a polishing machine and cleaning with isopropyl alcohol, the specimens for OM/SEM/HV test were electrolytically corroded in a 10% oxalic acid solution. All observations and tests were conducted on the upper surface of the cut material. Alloy A2, dual FCC + BCC phase

The multidirectional forging (MDF) experiments of Mg-Gd-Y-Zn-Zr alloy were performed. The MDF process step is shown in Fig. 1. Surface A of sample was first forged and then turned over 90° to forge the surface B of sample. Finally, the surface was again turned over 90° to forge surface C. Each press underwent one pass at initial forging temperatures of 400 °C, 450 °C, and 500 °C, respectively. In addition, a no-load pressing rate of 10 mm/s was set, such that the temperature of the sample gradually reduced from contact with air during forging. The heating temperature of the upper and lower chopping boards was measured to be 450 °C. The chopping boards were continuously heated during deformation, and the sample was air-cooled after deformation. The effects of temperature and cumulative strain on microstructure and mechanical properties of multi-directional forged Mg-Gd-Y-Zn-Zr alloy were studied. The results showed that the recrystallization ratio of the alloy gradually increased with the initial forging temperature after 3 passes of MDF. Under the condition of the initial forging temperature of 500 °C, the grain size was gradually refined with increasing MDF passes, and the average grain size was refined to 1.49 μm after 12 MDF passes. With the increase in MDF passes, the maximum texture density of the alloy gradually decreased. The mechanical properties gradually increased with the MDF passes. In the first 6 MDF passes, the mechanical properties greatly increased, but after that, the increase gradually slowed down with additional MDF passes. The optimal mechanical properties were obtained after 12 MDF passes, and the tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation after fracture were 362 MPa, 294 MPa, and 14.5%, respectively. Surface A of sample was first forged and then turned over 90° to forge the surface B of sample. Finally, the surface was again turned over 90° to forge surface C. Each press underwent one pass at initial forging temperatures of 400 °C, 450 °C, and 500 °C, respectively. In addition, a no-load pressing rate of 10 mm/s was set, such that the temperature of the sample gradually reduced from contact with air during forging. The heating temperature of the upper and lower chopping boards was measured to be 450 °C. The chopping boards were continuously heated during deformation, and the sample was air-cooled after deformation. The effects of temperature and cumulative strain on microstructure and mechanical properties of multi-directional forged Mg-Gd-Y-Zn-Zr alloy were studied. Processing Text: Novel biodegradable Zn-xCu-xTi (Cu: x = 0.001-2.72 and Ti: x = 0.03-1.21) alloys were designed and fabricated using a gradient continuous casting method followed by homogenization and rolling. The Zn-Cu-Ti alloy rod was first cut lengthwise to expose its internal structure for analysis. The test surfaces of these sections were then prepared through a two-step process: grinding and polishing. The grinding was performed sequentially starting with a coarser 240# sandpaper and progressing to a much finer 3000# sandpaper. Following the grinding, the test surfaces were polished using diamond sprays, first with a 3 μm spray and then with a finer 0.5 μm spray. Hot-rolled samples were sourced from six regions of the Zn-Cu-Ti alloy rod and then homogenized at 370 °C for 2 h. For post-homogenization, these samples underwent hot rolling at 350 °C, resulting in a 75% thickness reduction from the initial 10 mm. With each pass, the thickness was reduced by 1.5 mm. After the final pass, samples were quenched in water. The SEM and EBSD samples were cutting by electric discharging machine along the rolling direction (RD), ground with 240# to 3000# sandpaper, polished with 0.5 μm diamond sprays, and then etched using a Keller's reagent (95 ml H2O, 2.5 ml HNO3, 1.5 ml HCl, 1.0 ml HF). The EBSD samples were similarly prepared but underwent ion polishing. Processing state: as-cast

The Ni-20Co-20Cr-2Al-1Si-xSc (x = 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 1 wt%) alloys used in this experiment were prepared by melting the constituent ratios in an argon atmosphere using a vacuum arc melting furnace (WK-Ⅰ*). After melting, the resulting raw materials were vacuum-sealed in quartz tubes and subjected to annealing for 7 days in a 1000°C box-type furnace (KBF1400) for homogenization. The materials were then cut into thin slices measuring 10mm × 5mm × 2 mm using an electrical discharge machining (EDM) wire cutting machine (DK-7720). The Ni-20Co-20Cr-2Al-1Si-xSc (x = 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5,1 wt %) alloys were placed in a furnace at 1000°C for high-temperature cyclic oxidation experiments to assess their high-temperature oxidation resistance. Processing Text: Powder bed fusion (PBF), along with subsequent heat treatment, plays a crucial role in enhancing the impact toughness of FeCoNiCrMo0.2 high-entropy alloys (HEAs). In this study, the dynamic-mechanical properties and microstructure of the as-built PBF-FeCoNiCrMo0.2 HEAs and quenched PBF-FeCoNiCrMo0.2 HEAs heated at 600-750 °C for 8 h were investigated. As the heating temperature increases, the columnar grains and cellular structures undergo coarsening and the dislocation density gradually decreases. Moreover, higher heating temperatures facilitate the precipitation of Mo-rich second phases. The μ phases are predominantly distributed along the boundaries of the cellular structures. In the quenched Q700 specimen (heated at 700 °C for 8h), the size and volume fraction of the μ phases are measured to be 63.4 nm and 3.59%, respectively. Additionally, under the same condition, the Q700 specimens also exhibited a relatively slight increase in the size of the cellular structures. The preparation method for the pre-alloyed powder involved initially melting pure metal powders in a vacuum induction furnace to form pre-alloyed ingots. Subsequently, the pre-alloyed ingots were subjected to high-speed airstream in an atomization chamber, resulting in their fragmentation into small droplets that solidified to form fine powder. The cylindrical specimens were placed inside a vacuum glass tube. Then, the vacuum tube was purged with argon gas for a minimum of three cycles to remove any residual air inside the glass tube. Later, the glass tubes containing the specimens underwent a high-temperature sintering process for 10 min to ensure an airtight seal, thus providing an inert gas protective environment during the heating process. The treatment was carried out at temperatures of 600, 650, 700, and 750 °C with specimens labeled as Q600, Q650, Q700, and Q750, respectively, using the DZSX2-10-12NP (Yun Yue, P.). These specimens were heated for 8 h, then quenched with industrial oil to prevent the growth of grains and second phases. Hot-rolled STSs 308 L plates with thicknesses of 20 mm were used. A V-shaped groove was cut from the base metal along a 45° diagonal with a root gap of 10 mm. The all-weld metals were prepared using 12 flux-cored arc weld passes. The welding process involved a welding current of 240 A and arc voltage of 32 V. The specimens for the FE-SEM and EBSD observations were prepared through mechanical polishing using colloidal silica. The polished specimens were etched using a solution with 40 ml of HCl, 50 ml of nitric acid, and 100 ml of ethyl alcohol. All specimens were mechanically ground using #2000 grit SiC sandpaper, followed by electropolishing in an etchant solution (10% HCLO 4+ 90% CH 3OH) at 9 V for 100 s at −30 °C. Hydrogen was electrolytically charged for 48 h in a 3% NaCl + 0.3% NH 4SCN solution. A direct-current power supply was connected to the specimen as the cathode, and a Pt sheet was used as the anode. For the H-charging process, the current density and temperature were 100 A/m 2and 90 °C, respectively, to promote hydrogen diffusion into the specimen. After H-charging, the specimens were promptly immersed in liquid nitrogen to ensure hydrogen retention prior to subsequent analysis. Condition: Air; Temperature: 25 °C

Processing Text: The Co 35 Cr 20 Fe 15 Mn 15 Ni 15 HEA ingot was prepared by arc melting high-purity elements (with a purity greater than 99.9% in weight percentage) in an Ar gas atmosphere and repeatedly melted 5 times to ensure the uniformity of chemical composition. The ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h and then rolled at room temperature for a reduction of 40%, followed by annealing at 900 °C for 20 min and then rolled at room temperature for 40% reduction, followed by annealing at 1000 °C for 30 min to obtain recrystallized microstructure, all by water quenching to room temperature. Then, the specimens were rolled with a reduction of 10% at room temperature (denoted by 10% RR), 10% (denoted by 10% CR), 20% (denoted by 20% CR) and 30% reduction (denoted by 30% CR) at cryogenic temperature (−196 °C), respectively. Then, heat treatment (HT) of the 20% CR sample was conducted at 600 °C for 1 h (denoted by 20% CR + HT). Condition: as-recrystallized, before CR

Samples were manufactured using EOS Ti-6Al-4V grade 23 powder on an EOS M290 (EOS GmbH, Germany) LPBF machine housed at the ISO 13485 certified Centre for Rapid Prototyping and Manufacturing (CRPM) of the Central University of Technology in South Africa. Specimens were produced in three batches, and a representative portion of each batch and specimen type was selected to measure the oxygen content to ensure this was kept below 0.013 wt%. The base plate was preheated to 80 °C, and a high-speed steel blade was used as a scraper. The process parameters consisted of a 40 μm layer thickness, 280 W laser power, 1300 mm/s scan speed, 100 μm spot size and a hatch distance of 120 μm. Bidirectional scanning was used, and the scan direction was rotated by 67° between layers. This set of process parameters results in a material with less than 0.01 % porosity [ 23 ]. For tensile specimens, cylinders with a diameter of D = 10 mm and a length of L = 100 mm were produced in the vertical (Z) and horizontal (X) directions relative to the axis of the LPBF machine (and according to ASTM 59200) that is aligned with the direction in which the load is applied. For fracture toughness specimens, Compact Tension (C(T)) specimens were produced as rectangular blocks to allow for the final dimensions of a width of W = 25 mm. C(T) specimens were produced in three orientations, with the first letter indicating the direction in which the load is applied and the second letter indicating the direction in which the crack propagates, that is, ZX, XZ and XY [ 6 ], as shown in Fig. 1 . After printing, the specimens were stress-relieved (SR) at 650 °C for 3 h in a TSH 15/50/180 vacuum furnace (Elite Thermal Systems, England) and then wire-cut from the build plate. The SR treatment was chosen to allow comparison with the literature [ 15 ]. Subsequent heat treatments were conducted at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in atmospheric air using a box furnace (Ultrafurn, South Africa). Therefore, at least 1 mm was removed by wire cutting or machining from all the heat-treated specimen surfaces to remove any α-case and oxide scale that may have formed. The heat treatment schedules, detailed in Table 1 , included the SR, an anneal (AN) heat treatment, chosen due to its simplicity combined with good tensile properties, and a duplex anneal (DA) heat treatment, chosen based on optimal tensile properties reported in the literature [ 6 , 25 ]. Furthermore, the heat treatments above T β (selected based on values available in the literature [ 9 , 15 ]) were combined with the stress relief (BtSR) and anneal (BtAN) heat treatments to mimic how SR or AN specimens would perform if the PBGs were equiaxed c . c It is acknowledged the above T β heat treatment is at the cost of PBG growth. Comparison to specimens with elongated PBGs is only based on orientation effects. After heat treatment, the specimens were machined and wire-cut to their final dimensions. Condition: as-received

Processing Text: The material used in this work is cold-rolled 316L austenitic SS seamless tubes with an outside diameter of 12 mm and a thickness of 2 mm. The 316L SS tubes were bright annealed at 1080 °C followed by rapid water quench and subsequently machined into specimens. The surface of the specimens was mechanically ground and polished to obtain a smooth surface by uniformly distributing the machining marks in the longitudinal direction, thus reducing the effect of surface quality. Multiaxial non-proportional cyclic pre-hardening (CPH) treatment was performed in a circular path, with a 90° phase shift between the axial and torsion loads, over 10 cycles at the strain amplitude of 0.4 %. At the end of the CPH process, the axial strain is at its peak value (0.4 %) and the equivalent shear strain is controlled to 0. Subsequently, the axial strain reaches the minimum value of the corresponding uniaxial fatigue tests to start the uniaxial stage while the equivalent shear strain is controlled at 0 throughout the whole uniaxial stage. Monotonic tensile tests were carried out under displacement control mode at a displacement rate of 0.06 mm/s. Strain-controlled uniaxial fatigue tests at the strain amplitudes of 0.2 % and 0.4 % were performed on AR and CPH materials in a fully-reversed triangular waveform (R = -1) with a fixed strain rate of 5 × 10 -3s −1. Processing Text: C and N were added into the base alloy by using pure carbon and Fe 2N, and the two alloys were referred to as C-HEA and N-HEA, respectively. The two alloys were cast in a vacuum induction furnace, followed by wet chemical analysis to control the exact composition after casting. The nominal composition of the interstitial contents is 0.5 at%. However, doping N is more difficult to maintain, and the actual composition of N doping is 1 at%. The cold-rolled HEAs were notated as C-CR and N-CR for carbon-doped and nitrogen-doped HEA, respectively. To minimize significant grain growth during recrystallization and compare the effect of grain refinement and interstitial types with previous work [8,15], short-duration annealing was performed under three conditions: 800 °C for 5 minutes, 800 °C for 10 minutes, and 900 °C for 5 minutes, respectively. Henceforth, the carbon-doped TRIP alloys after annealing are designated as C800-5, C800-10, and C900-5, corresponding to the annealing conditions at 800°C for 5 minutes, 800°C for 10 minutes, and 900°C for 5 minutes, respectively. A polycrystalline ingot of MnCu2Al was prepared using a combination of arc melting and furnace annealing according to previous investigations. Elemental Mn (Sigma Aldrich, chips, 99%) was cleaned of its native oxides by annealing in an evacuated silica ampule for 8 h at 1000 °C. Starting materials of cleaned Mn, Cu (Alfa Aesar, wire, 99.99%), and Al (Alfa Aesar, wire, 99.9995%) were weighed with a 1:2:1 stoichiometry, totaling a mass of 3.0 g. An additional excess of Mn (10 mg) was added to compensate for volatilization during melting. The materials were arc melted four times in an Ar atmosphere, flipping the ingot between melts for homogeneity, with a total mass loss of 1.3%. The resulting ingot was wrapped in Ta foil, sealed in an evacuated silica ampule, and homogenized at 850 °C for 7 days to create a large-grained microstructure, then quenched into water. To ensure structural homogeneity, the ingot was divided and pieces were sampled from opposing faces of the ingot, ground into a fine powder, and sieved through a 140 mesh (106 μm particle size) for a synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) sample. The powder sample was again sealed within an evacuated fused silica ampule and tempered at 320 °C for 1 h to resolve any pre-existing crystallographic defects. Microscopy and mechanical testing were performed on pieces of the ingot that were tempered under the same conditions. Specifically, the nanoindentation test specimen was created from a tempered piece of the arc melted ingot that was mounted to an aluminum puck using crystal bond, ground using SiC paper, polished using diamond suspensions down to 1 μm, and vibratory polished using colloidal silica to a mirror finish. While mounted to the aluminum puck, the polished surface was imaged using SEM and mapped using EBSD, to characterize the crystallographic orientation of visible grains. Nanoindentation experiments were performed to test the mechanical properties of each grain orientation using a Nanomechanics iMicro Nanoindenter equipped with a 1000 mN load cell and Berkovich tip diamond indenter. All nanoindentation data were collected using a continuous stiffness method operating at a frequency of 100 Hz, to a total depth of 1000 nm, and each data point reported in this investigation is representative of at least 10-20 indents per crystallographic orientation, collected between depths of 400 nm-1000 nm. Data recorded during the initial 400 nm of each indentation were excluded to account for surface roughness and possible surface artifacts introduced by polishing. To create an accessible base for micro-pillar experiments, the polished specimen was remounted to an angled polishing puck and polished into a wedge-shaped geometry. Using EBSD mapping near the edge of the wedge-shaped specimen, several grains of interest were identified, and were femtosecond laser machined in situ into single-crystalline pedestals using the TriBeam microscope, a laser-equipped TFS Versa 3D FIB-SEM. Micro-compression pillars were produced directly from the single-crystalline pedestals using the FIB to mill the pillar tops and sides perpendicular to the wedge surface with a slight taper, before removing all material from the faces to create pillars with a 1:1:2 aspect ratio to mitigate the potential impact of buckling. A square pillar cross-section was employed to aid in the identification of active slip systems. Micro-compression experiments were performed in situ in an TFS Apreo S SEM equipped with a Femto-tools FT-NMT04 Nanomechanical Testing System designed to optimize alignment during small-scale mechanical testing. Each pillar was loaded in a series of load vs. displacement tests until the point of yield using a displacement-controlled method. Following SEM imaging, a detailed microstructural investigation was performed on an electron-transparent lamella micro-machined from the [11 8 2]-oriented pillar, using STEM imaging and a g⋅b analysis in the TEM. As the deformed material had high internal strains, the foil was prepared with three electron-transparent windows, framed by thicker regions for stabilization. Processing Text: The ingots were prepared via vacuum induction melting furnace under 10 −3Pa. The purity of the raw materials is 99.9%. The quality of the ingot obtained by smelting is between 20 and 25 kg. After annealing at 1473 K for 1 h, the ingots were forged into a 6 mm thick plate at 1373 K, and then hot rolled to plates with a thickness of 3 mm at 1373 K, and quenched in an ice brine solution. The plates were then cold-rolled to 0.35 mm thick strip with a reduction of 90%. The samples were electric-discharge machined from the rolled strip. Following this, the cold-rolled samples were annealed in a dry 5% hydrogen/95% argon mixed atmosphere at 1123 K for different durations ranging from 0.5 h to 3 h. After annealing, specimens were water quenched. Tensile tests were conducted at a speed of 0.0017/s on the AG-X plus instrument. The axial directions of all the tensile specimens are perpendicular to the rolling direction (RD) of the cold-rolled strip. Soft magnetic properties for the as-rolled and annealed samples were measured using MATS-2010SD loop tracer. Microstructure characterization was performed by Zeiss SUPRA55 scanning electron microscope (SEM) and FEI Tecnai G 2F30 transmission electron microscope (TEM) equipped with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS). SEM specimen was etched by a mixture solution of 4 vol.% nitric acid and 96 vol.% alcohol. TEM samples were thinned by twin-jet electropolishing using an electrolyte of 10 vol.% perchloric acid and 90 vol.% alcohol around −20 °C. Electrolytic extraction technique was employed to dissolve the matrix, 50% nitric acid solution was used for the electrolyte and after vacuum filtration the content of element remaining in the matrix was tested using ICP-AES. XRD fine-scan measurements were carried out on the finely polished samples to measure the dislocation density using a Cu-Kα radiation source. Annealed at 1123 K for 3 h

Processing Text: In this work, selective laser melting (SLM) process is used to prepare the AlNi6TiZr alloy. By analyzing the printing quality and mechanical properties of the printed specimens with different process parameters, the SLM forming window of AlNi6TiZr is obtained. The relative density of the sample printed with 270 W-1100 mm/s (laser energy density: 82 J/mm3) reaches 99.7%, exhibiting excellent mechanical properties (yield strength (YS): 421.7 MPa; ultimate tensile strength (UTS): 480.4 MPa). After an aging treatment of 325 °C-12 h, the YS and UTS of the sample increased to 494 MPa and 550.7 MPa, respectively. The hard-shell structure (HSS) formed by the Al3Ni phase at the grain boundary significantly strengthened the grain boundary strength. The precipitated Al3(Ti, Zr) phases at the grain boundaries prevent grain growth and dislocation movement. The Al3Ni and Al3(Ti, Zr) phases have good thermal stability that can still maintain excellent enhancement effects at high temperature. The raw material was a gas-atomized 6060 aluminum alloy powder (2.5-50 μm) produced by Jiangxi Baohang Advanced Materials Co., Ltd. Some microalloying powders including Ni powder (0.5-2 μm), Ti powder (70-90 nm), and high-purity Zr powder (3-7 μm) were mixed with the raw material by ball milling method, and the optimized parameters (ball powder ratio (wt%): 5:1, milling speed: 280 rpm, milling time: 10 h, protection gas: argon (> 99.99%)) of powder mixing process was according to Refs. [ 32, 44]. The mixed alloy powder was dried at 10 Pa and 120 °C for 8 h in a DZ-201 vacuum drying oven (Changsha Mitr Instrument Equipment Co., Ltd., China), and then cooled in the equipment to room temperature. The bulk and tensile specimens were printed using a LiM-X150A SLM device (Tianjin LiM Laser Technology Co., Ltd., China), which is equipped with an IPG 500 W fiber laser (wavelength: 1064 nm, spot diameter: 40-60 μm). First, the substrate ( Table 2) was fixed on the printing platform and preheated to 35 °C. Then, the printing process started under argon protection, in which the oxygen content was below 100 ppm. To optimize the printing parameters of AlNi6TiZr alloy, several sets of laser power and scanning speed were selected. The aging treatment (AT) process was conducted in an SX-B07123 electric box furnace (Tianjin Zhonghuan Electric Furnace Co., LTD, China), and the AT parameters were 325 °C for 6, 12, and 24 h, respectively. After aging treatment, the AT-ed specimens were air-cooled. The bulk specimens with a size of 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm were mechanically polished using a 2.5 μm diamond grinding paste on a polishing machine to obtain a mirror surface. Then, it was chemically etched with the Kellar reagent (HF:HCl:HNO 3:H 2O = 2:3:5:195) for 20 s. Condition: as-printed (AB); Relative density: 99.7%; Laser energy density: 82 J/mm³

Processing Text: In this work, a full composition with different mixing proportions (100 % Cu to 100 % Ni) was fabricated in a single printing process through in-situ alloying based on our process of micro laser powder bed fusion. The powder feeding system was designed to facilitate the smooth transfer of powder materials from 100 % Cu to 100 % Ni. In our system, we place a flat partition along the longer diagonal of the powder hopper, creating separate spaces for filling powders, Cu and Ni, according to their respective allocation areas. Below this hopper is a cylindrical powder mixer, with the axis of the cylinder aligned in the X direction. The mixer mixes the powders along the width of the hopper (Y direction) and maintains the desired gradient of the composition along the X direction. The gradient powders then fall into the powder recoater and are spread onto the substrate. This method enabled the fabrication of functionally gradient materials comprising Cu-Ni alloy with continuous composition variation in the X direction perpendicular to the spreading direction. Dog-bone-shaped samples with gauge dimensions of 15 mm ( L) × 4 mm ( W) × 1.5 mm ( H) were used for tensile tests. Rectangular bars measuring 30 mm ( L) × 2 mm ( W) × 2 mm ( H) were used for electrical conductivity testing. Cubes with a side length of 5 mm were prepared for microstructure inspection. For metallographic observations, 10 equally spaced specimens were cut from the fabricated Cu-Ni alloy parts along the direction of the composition gradient variation and prepared in accordance with ASTM E3-11 standards. The morphology and compositions of the received powders and chemical compositions of the as-printed samples were measured and analysed via scanning electron microscopy (JCM-6000PLUS) using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray fluorescence spectrometry (XRF, Bruker M4 Tornado). The particle size distributions of the as-received powders were measured using a laser particle size analyser (Bettersize3000). The apparent densities of the powders were measured by a loose densitometer (HR-S3 Scott volumeter). The powders of Cu and Ni had similar material densities, while the mixed powders had an acceptable apparent density that was not notably affected by the similar particle size distributions of pure Cu and Ni powders. The compositions of GA were characterised via EDS. Measurements were made at positions with element ratios (Cu/Ni) designed at 0 %, 5 %, 15 %, 25 %, …, and 100 % to validate the accuracy of gradient element distribution along the GD. An X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of components was conducted using a high-resolution Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diffractometer. The 2θ scan angle ranged from 20° to 90° and the scanning speed was 5°/min. The microstructure and grain texture studies were conducted using an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) system (EDAX Velocity Plus) with a step size of 0.5 μm and a scan area of 200 μm × 200 μm. The EBSD data were analysed using an open-source Matlab toolbox (MTEX 5.7.0). The corresponding misorientation angles were measured to calculate the grain boundaries (GBs). Misorientation angles in the range of 2°-15° were defined as low-angle GBs (LAGBs) whereas misorientation angles exceeding 15° were defined as high-angle GBs (HAGBs). The grain size was calculated according to the HAGBs, and the Williamson-Hall method was adopted to determine the dislocation density. The electrical resistance ( ρ) was evaluated using a micro-ohmmeter (YP2511) and calculated according to the equation ρ= RA/ L, where R is the measurement made by the micro-ohmmeter, A is the cross-sectional area of the bar, and L is the measurement length. Before the cross-sectional area was measured, the bars were polished with SiC sandpaper (1200 and 2500 grit) to ensure measurement accuracy. Five lengths (15, 18, 21, 24, and 27 mm) were measured to calculate the final mean values. The coefficient of linear thermal expansion (CTE) was measured using a thermal mechanical analyser (TMA 7, Perkin Elmer) following ASTM E831-19. Microhardness was measured with a hardness tester (Decca HV-1000) adopting a load force of 200 g and a hold time of 10 s. Measurements were made at 10 points, and the average values were recorded as the final microhardness. Tensile properties were evaluated by conducting uniaxial tensile tests at a constant speed of 0.96 mm/min on a tensile machine (Tinius Olsen H5KS). Three tensile bars were tested for each sample to minimise measurement errors. Cu content: 30 % (Cu 0.3Ni 0.7)

Dog-bone-shaped samples with gauge dimensions of 15 mm ( L) × 4 mm ( W) × 1.5 mm ( H) were used for tensile tests. Rectangular bars measuring 30 mm ( L) × 2 mm ( W) × 2 mm ( H) were used for electrical conductivity testing. Cubes with a side length of 5 mm were prepared for microstructure inspection. For metallographic observations, 10 equally spaced specimens were cut from the fabricated Cu-Ni alloy parts along the direction of the composition gradient variation and prepared in accordance with ASTM E3-11 standards. The morphology and compositions of the received powders and chemical compositions of the as-printed samples were measured and analysed via scanning electron microscopy (JCM-6000PLUS) using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and X-ray fluorescence spectrometry (XRF, Bruker M4 Tornado). The particle size distributions of the as-received powders were measured using a laser particle size analyser (Bettersize3000). The apparent densities of the powders were measured by a loose densitometer (HR-S3 Scott volumeter). The powders of Cu and Ni had similar material densities, while the mixed powders had an acceptable apparent density that was not notably affected by the similar particle size distributions of pure Cu and Ni powders. The compositions of GA were characterised via EDS. Measurements were made at positions with element ratios (Cu/Ni) designed at 0 %, 5 %, 15 %, 25 %, …, and 100 % to validate the accuracy of gradient element distribution along the GD. An X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis of components was conducted using a high-resolution Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diffractometer. The 2θ scan angle ranged from 20° to 90° and the scanning speed was 5°/min. The microstructure and grain texture studies were conducted using an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) system (EDAX Velocity Plus) with a step size of 0.5 μm and a scan area of 200 μm × 200 μm. The EBSD data were analysed using an open-source Matlab toolbox (MTEX 5.7.0). The corresponding misorientation angles were measured to calculate the grain boundaries (GBs). Misorientation angles in the range of 2°-15° were defined as low-angle GBs (LAGBs) whereas misorientation angles exceeding 15° were defined as high-angle GBs (HAGBs). The grain size was calculated according to the HAGBs, and the Williamson-Hall method was adopted to determine the dislocation density. The electrical resistance ( ρ) was evaluated using a micro-ohmmeter (YP2511) and calculated according to the equation ρ= RA/ L, where R is the measurement made by the micro-ohmmeter, A is the cross-sectional area of the bar, and L is the measurement length. Before the cross-sectional area was measured, the bars were polished with SiC sandpaper (1200 and 2500 grit) to ensure measurement accuracy. Five lengths (15, 18, 21, 24, and 27 mm) were measured to calculate the final mean values. The coefficient of linear thermal expansion (CTE) was measured using a thermal mechanical analyser (TMA 7, Perkin Elmer) following ASTM E831-19. Microhardness was measured with a hardness tester (Decca HV-1000) adopting a load force of 200 g and a hold time of 10 s. Measurements were made at 10 points, and the average values were recorded as the final microhardness. Tensile properties were evaluated by conducting uniaxial tensile tests at a constant speed of 0.96 mm/min on a tensile machine (Tinius Olsen H5KS). Three tensile bars were tested for each sample to minimise measurement errors. Processing state: as-printed

The (NiCoV) 100-XGa x(x = 0, 5, 7) series alloys (purity >99.9 %) were prepared by arc melting furnace. Processing Text: A series of HfNbTaTiV x alloys with various V contents (x= 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 and 1.00 in molar ratio) were fabricated from high purity (>99.95 %) metals by using vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper crucible under argon atmosphere. The cast ingots were flipped and remelted at least six cycles to achieve chemical homogeneity. Ultimately, several button-shaped ingots were prepared with about 7 mm in thickness and 30 mm in diameter. The cast ingots were subjected to a series of cold rolling using a precision rolling mill (JH-RZH-110, China) to forming sheets about 1 mm in thickness (thickness reduction >85 %). Multiple dog-bone-shaped specimens were extracted from the rolled sheets utilizing an electrical spark erosion wire cutting machine (DK77, China). The dimension of the dog-bone-shaped specimens was 16 mm in length, 12 mm in width, and 1 mm in thickness, respectively. The obtained specimens were annealed at 1200 °C for 45 min inside an evacuated quartz tube maintained about 0.67 Pa vacuum. Subsequently, the specimens were promptly quenched in water. Afterward, tension tests were conducted on the dog-bone specimens at a strain rate of 0.001 s −1, using a universal testing machine (ETM205D, China). The tensile axis was aligned parallel to the rolling direction. The hardness of the alloys was evaluated using a Vicky MHV-1000 tester under 0.3 kgf load with duration of 15 s. Processing Text: TaMoNbCrTix (x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) RHEAs were fabricated through mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The mechanical alloying process was performed using a planetary ball mill (QM-3SP4, Nanjing Nanda Instrument Co., Ltd., China) under an argon atmosphere. The milling duration was set to 50 h, while the milling speed was maintained at 350 rpm. The powders were sintered under vacuum conditions using spark plasma sintering equipment (SPS-825, Sumitomo Coal Mining Co., Ltd., Japan) with a sintering temperature of 1200 °C, a sintering pressure of 40 MPa and a holding time of 10 min. By employing severe deformation of the ball-milled powder, short sintering time, and the inhibition of precipitated phases on grain growth, the resulting RHEAs exhibited ultrafine grains measuring less than 1 μm. MEA ingots with a nominal composition of Co33.33Ni33.33V33.34(at.%) were produced by the vacuum arc melting technique in a high-purity argon atmosphere, in which a mixture of pure metals (purity over 99.9 %) was used. The samples were first remelted a minimum of four times to ensure chemical homogeneity. Following the hot rolling deformation at 1000 °C (0.5 h of treatment at this temperature before rolling resulted in a 40 % decrease in rolling volume), the ingots were annealed at 1000 °C for 2 h before being quenched in water. After reducing the samples from 10 mm to 2 mm via cold rolling, they were annealed at 1000 °C for 10 min followed by water quenching. The electrical discharge machining method was employed to obtain samples measuring 1 × 1 × 200 mm, which were then subjected to subsequent cold-drawing processes. CoNiV fibers, with a diameter of 300 μm, were produced through multipass cold-drawing at room temperature, with approximately a 10 μm reduction in diameter in each drawing step. To precisely control the content of precipitated phases, the CoNiV fibers underwent further annealing at temperatures of 1000, 900, 880, 865, and 850 °C for 10 min each. Subsequently, water quenching was performed after all the aforementioned drawing steps. The aforementioned samples were designated as 1000-10, 900-10, 880-10, 865-10, and 850-10 for convenience. Processing Text: Mg-9.5Gd-4Y-2Zn-0.3Zr alloy wires with a diameter of 1.2 mm were fabricated by a multistage drawing process with a cumulative area reduction (CAR) of 96% at 500 °C using as-extruded rods with a diameter of 6 mm as the raw material. The extrusion was carried out at 500 °C, with an extrusion ratio of 23:1, using cylindrical billets with a diameter of 70 mm and length of 400 mm. Then, cylindrical rods with a diameter of 6 mm were obtained. Mg-9.5Gd-4Y-2Zn-0.5Zr alloy wires were fabricated using a multi-pass drawing process at 500 °C. The drawing speed was between 20 mm/s and 35 mm/s. The strain of the drawing process was calculated by area reduction using Eq. (1): (1)AR=A0−AfA0where A 0and A fdenote the initial and final cross-sectional areas of the wires, respectively. The strain was between 10% and 12% per pass. Finally, the Mg-9.5Gd-4Y-2Zn-0.3Zr alloy wires with a diameter of 1.2 mm were obtained with a CAR of 96%. Samples for transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Thermofisher Talos F200X at 200 kV) were mechanically thinned to a 50-60 μm thickness, followed by electrolytic polishing in a 5% HClO 4and 95% C 2H 5OH solution at −30 °C and 30 V, then ion milling (Gatan 695) at 3°-6° incidence angle and 3-4 kV voltage. Samples for TEM were prepared using a focused ion beam (FIB, Thermo Scientific Scios 2 SEM) and an Omniprobe manipulator. The mechanical properties were evaluated through Vickers hardness (HVS-1000Z) and tensile testing (Instron 5582). The Vickers hardness tests were conducted with an applied force of 2 N for a duration of 10 s, in accordance with the ISO 6507-1 standard. Tensile testing proceeded at a uniform extension rate of 1 mm/min at ambient temperature, following the ISO 6892-1 standard. Processing state: as-extruded wire

MEAs of nominal compositions FeCr2V and FeCr2VWx (x = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5) were fabricated by arc melting using raw powders that are readily available in the market, including FeV alloy powder and commercially pure (>99 wt%) Cr, W elemental powders (all sourced from Beijing Ranbond Technology Co., China). The raw powders were mixed according to the designed nominal compositions and then placed into a water-cooled copper mold for arc melting with a vacuum arc furnace under an argon atmosphere. The ingots were flipped over and remelted three times to enhance the homogeneities of the final microstructure and chemical distribution of the obtained materials. A button-shaped ingot with the weight of approximately 30 g and dimensions of about Φ20 mm x 12 mm was obtained for each composition (referred to as W0, W0.1, W0.3, W0.5 hereinafter, based on their W composition). Vickers microhardness was measured four times for each sample of as-cast alloys under a load of 1 kg and a duration of 10 s using a Struers Durascan-70 automatic hardness tester. Processing Text: The alloys employed in the current study were prepared by vacuum arc melting using powder with purity above 99.95 wt%. Finally, NiFe 20 was obtained. The sandpaper and SiO 2polishing solution were used to polish the experimental samples to a mirror-like surface. To eliminate processing defects and maintain the "mirror" state, NiFe 20 was annealed at 800 °C for 1 h. Electrochemical charging with 0.1 mol/L NaOH and 0.5 g/L CH 4N 2S heavy water solutions under identical experimental conditions were conducted. All samples were charged at a constant current of 50 mA/cm 2for 24 h at room temperature in a heavy aqueous solution containing 0.1 mol/L NaOH and 0.5 g/L CH 4N 2S. The deuterium charged samples were put into TDS within 24 h for deuterium concentration measurement. The TDS measurements were heated from room temperature to 800 °C under high vacuum (10 −5Pa) at a constant heating rate of 1 °C/s. Slow strain tensile tests were performed for pristine and the deuterium-charged samples using an Instron 5565 tensile testing machine equipped with a video extensometer, with a strain rate of 4 × 10 −4/s and a loading rate of 0.12 mm / min at room temperature. All samples were analyzed using EBSD along the normal direction (ND), with a scanning step size of about 0.25 µm. The TEM thin sample were prepared using standard electropolishing techniques. Firstly, a disk with a diameter of 3 mm was cut near the fracture surface using electrical discharge machining (EDM). The 3 mm disk was thinned to a thickness of about 80 µm using mechanical polishing. Finally, the sample thickness was further reduced to electron transparency using a 5% perchloric acid and 95% ethanol solution on a TJ100-SE twin-jet polisher with an instrument voltage of 20 V and a temperature of − 20 ± 4 °C. Deuterium charged conditions: 24 h

The original ingots of MP159 alloy were produced by vacuum induction melting. After homogenization, the ingots were subsequently cold rolled with reduction in thickness by 90 %, recrystallized at 1000 °C for 5 min, and aged at 750 °C for 24 h. All the heat treatments were carried out in the air condition, followed by water cooling. Dog-bone-shaped samples were machined by electro-discharge machining with the stretching axis aligned with the rolling direction. The gage dimensions of the quasi-static and dynamic tensile samples were 12.5 × 3 × 1 mm 3 and 10 × 3 × 1 mm 3 (length × width × thickness), respectively. Quasi-static tensile tests were conducted by using an Instron 5969 testing machine at strain rates (10 −4, 10 −3, 10 −2 and 10 −1 s −1). Dynamic tensile tests were performed at strain rates (1200 s −1 and 1500 s −1), employing a split Hopkinson tensile bar (SHTB). MP159 alloys are recrystallized at 1,000, 1,100, and 1200 °C for 5 min to obtain grains with different sizes. Condition: quasi-static; Strain rate: 10^-4/s

Pure copper (99.995 wt. %) with an average grain size of ∼201 μm was deformed to a strain of 1.8 by dynamic plastic deformation (DPD) at liquid nitrogen temperature, and then annealed at 180℃ and 500℃, respectively, to obtain samples with average grain sizes of 1 μm and 11 μm. The deformation strain is defined as ε= ln (H 0/H f), where H 0and H fare the initial and final thicknesses of the deformed sample, respectively. Information of DPD setup and procedure has described in detail in our previous publication [20]. Samples with grain sizes of 201, 11 and 1 μm were subjected to DPD with a strain of ∼1.0 at liquid nitrogen temperature to obtain UFS samples (hereafter referred to as UFS-x, x is the corresponding grain size). Subsequently, the UFS-201, UFS-11 and UFS-1 samples were annealed at 155°C, 165°C and 205°C for 10 min, respectively. This process produced heterostructures consisting of the remaining UFS and SRX grains. These heterostructures are hereafter named HS-201, HS-11 and HS-1. Volume fraction of UFS: 30%

To obtain γ″ precipitates, the as-cast samples were annealed at 1200 °C for 5 h, followed by furnace cooling. Processing Text: Pre-alloyed powders (Ti 41V 27Hf 13Nb 13Mo 6in at%) were fabricated by the plasma rotating electrode-comminuting process (PREP) in Sailong Metal Materials Co., Ltd. The process was conducted in a Ytterbium Laser System (YLS-10000) with a 10 KW laser, a coaxial powder feeding device, and a real-time monitoring camera. The laser scanning direction was set as X with a rotation angle of 90° between adjacent layers, and the deposition direction was Z. The process parameters were set as follows: laser power of 1800-2000 W, scanning speed of 6-8 mm/s, powder delivery rate of 11 g/min, layer thickness of 0.5 mm, and laser beam diameter of 5 mm. Low line energy density (η) under 2000 W-8 mm/s (η= 250 J/mm) and high line energy density (η= 300 J/mm) under 1800 W-6 mm/s were adopted ultimately. The processing chamber was filled with argon and purged at a constant flow rate of 4 liters per minute to avoid oxidation, forming bulk specimens (12 mm × 12 mm × 35 mm). The RHEAs with grain-size graded microstructure were successfully created using the optimized processing conditions (laser power: 1800 W, scanning speed: 6 mm/s). The ambient-temperature tensile specimens with a gauge geometry of 4.0 mm × 1.5 mm × 1.0 mm were sectioned using electrical discharging. All specimens were mechanically polished to ensure surface regularity and tested along the Z direction. The uniaxial tensile testing was conducted on a Kammrath & Weiss mechanical testing platform at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. Before being tested for digital image correlation (DIC) analyses, the speckle patterns were coated on the surface of tensile specimens, and the resulting deformed characteristics were captured by a high-speed camera (frame rate, 1 Hz). In-situ tensile tests were conducted under EBSD. The tensile rate was 3 μm/s, and the gauge dimensions of the in-situ tensile samples were 3.0 mm × 1.2 mm × 0.8 mm. The samples for transmission electron microscope (TEM) observation were mechanically ground to ∼40 μm thickness, followed by ion milled, and finally identified by a double Cs corrector TEM (Themis Z). Processing Text: Pre-alloyed powders (Ti 41V 27Hf 13Nb 13Mo 6in at%) were fabricated by the plasma rotating electrode-comminuting process (PREP) in Sailong Metal Materials Co., Ltd. The process was conducted in a Ytterbium Laser System (YLS-10000) with a 10 KW laser, a coaxial powder feeding device, and a real-time monitoring camera. The laser scanning direction was set as X with a rotation angle of 90° between adjacent layers, and the deposition direction was Z. The process parameters were set as follows: laser power of 1800-2000 W, scanning speed of 6-8 mm/s, powder delivery rate of 11 g/min, layer thickness of 0.5 mm, and laser beam diameter of 5 mm. Low line energy density (η) under 2000 W-8 mm/s (η= 250 J/mm) and high line energy density (η= 300 J/mm) under 1800 W-6 mm/s were adopted ultimately. The processing chamber was filled with argon and purged at a constant flow rate of 4 liters per minute to avoid oxidation, forming bulk specimens (12 mm × 12 mm × 35 mm). The RHEAs with grain-size graded microstructure were successfully created using the optimized processing conditions (laser power: 1800 W, scanning speed: 6 mm/s). The ambient-temperature tensile specimens with a gauge geometry of 4.0 mm × 1.5 mm × 1.0 mm were sectioned using electrical discharging. All specimens were mechanically polished to ensure surface regularity and tested along the Z direction. The uniaxial tensile testing was conducted on a Kammrath & Weiss mechanical testing platform at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3s−1. Before being tested for digital image correlation (DIC) analyses, the speckle patterns were coated on the surface of tensile specimens, and the resulting deformed characteristics were captured by a high-speed camera (frame rate, 1 Hz). In-situ tensile tests were conducted under EBSD. The tensile rate was 3 μm/s, and the gauge dimensions of the in-situ tensile samples were 3.0 mm × 1.2 mm × 0.8 mm. The samples for transmission electron microscope (TEM) observation were mechanically ground to ∼40 μm thickness, followed by ion milled, and finally identified by a double Cs corrector TEM (Themis Z). Processing Text: The PBF-LB process was implemented using an SLM Solutions 125HL machine with a 400 W continuous 1060 nm wavelength (CW) fiber laser. The manufacturing process was conducted in a high Ar-content atmosphere with less than 0.1% oxygen to protect the samples from oxidation. Build plate preheating at 200 ℃ was used to reduce thermal stresses. A bidirectional scanning strategy was used in this work with a 45° angle between scanning direction and the normal direction (ND, X axis) on the first layer and a 90° rotation for each subsequent layer. Laser power and scanning speed were considered as processing variables while hatch spacing and layer thickness were held constant. Volume energy density (VED) of each process parameter set was calculated according to: (1)VED=Pv⋅h⋅twhere P, v, hand trepresent the laser power, laser scanning speed, hatch distance, and layer thickness, respectively. CoCrNi cubes with dimension of 5 × 5 × 5 mm 3and 2 mm support structure were printed with the range of processing parameters. Vickers microhardness testing was conducted on both the XY and XZ planes for 5 indents using a Struers Duramin-40 automated hardness tester with a 10 kg indent force, 10 seconds dwell time and 1 mm spacing. Tensile samples with a cross-section of 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm and a gauge length of 4 mm were cut from each PBF-LB/CoCrNi cube (15 mm × 15 mm × 15 mm) using electrical discharge machining (EDM) in both the vertical orientation (long axis parallel to the build direction) and horizontal orientation (long axis perpendicular to the build direction). The example graph of a tensile sample after EDM cutting is shown in Fig. S1eto reveal the surface quality. Two samples per orientation were characterized for six sets of PBF-LB processing parameters. Tensile tests were carried out using a Deben micro-tester equipped with a 2 kN load cell with a 0.4 mm/min displacement rate. A black and white color speckle pattern was spray painted on the surface of each sample before testing to measure the strain using digital image correlation (DIC). A video of the speckle painted sample surface was taken to record the tensile deformation for each sample. Strain data was obtained by analyzing the videos using the GOM correlation software package (Zeiss). In-situ tensile tests were conducted under an optical microscope (OM) for samples in both orientations for the E106 processing parameters. This testing method allowed a correlation between the deformation mechanisms and microstructural features. For in-situ testing, the surface of each tensile specimen was mirror polished and etched to reveal the microstructural features (melt pool and grain boundaries) under the optical microscope. The samples were step-loaded to failure with 0.6 mm displacement-controlled intervals at a displacement rate of 0.4 mm/min. After each interval step, testing was paused and OM images of the entire gauge section were taken to evaluate the deformation characteristics and microstructure evolution. The gauge area was marked by indents to perform EBSD analysis of the same location before and after deformation to reveal the texture and deformation relationship. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were conducted to analyze the melt pool shapes, temperature distributions, and cooling rates (T′) for the various PBF-LB processing parameters. Single track PBF-LB simulations were carried out using the commercial CFD solver Flow-3D which simulates both the powder bed and the laser printing process. Thus, powder particle motion and the recoating process were considered in the powder bed model establishment. Additionally, mass, momentum, and energy conservation were maintained during each simulation. Sample: E144; Orientation: Horizontal; Energy Density: Highest; Texture: <111>//LD

Processing Text: Although equiatomic CoCrFeNi medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) show excellent ductility, their strength is not high enough for the use in various engineering applications. Interestingly, the LPBF-fabricated CoCrFeNi MEAs have been found to exhibit both poor ultimate tensile strength (UTS) (∼582 MPa) and uniform elongation (δu) (∼11.7 %), attributed to the formation of hot cracks. In order to investigate the effect of TiC particles on the microstructure and mechanical properties of CoCrFeNi MEAs, pure CoCrFeNi MEAs (named as as-built MEAs) are fabricated by using the parameter iv. The relative density of as-built MEAs is measured as 99.4 %, and the microstructure of as-built MEAs is examined. Their metallographic microstructure is shown in Fig. 3(a), which presents the MPs with a typical “fish scale” shape, and the boundaries of semi-elliptical MPs can be clearly found. Fig. 3(b) displays that the cellular, cellular/columnar dendritic and elongated cellular sub-grains are formed in MPs. As-built MEAs are composed of some columnar grains which grow along the building direction (BD). Furthermore, some hot cracks occur and propagate along the boundaries of columnar grains in as-built MEAs. To explore the distribution of elements around hot cracks, the EDS characterization is carried out. The results can indicate that Co, Cr, Fe and Ni elements are evenly distributed in the columnar grains, and no obvious element segregation is found. For as-built MEAs, based on the IPFs of FCC phase and the orientation map of the IPFs of FCC phase in BD, they show an apparent preferred orientation (<110>) which is parallel to BD. As shown in Fig. 3(h), the fractions of low angle grain boundaries (LAGBs) and high angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) in as-built MEAs are 75.7 % and 24.3 %, respectively.
