Quaternary RMPEAs of Cr25Mo25Nb25V25 were prepared from pure elements of Cr, Mo, Nb, V, with 99.9% purity feedstock (American Elements, Los Angeles, USA). Using an Arcast 200 (Arcast, Maine, USA) arc melter, 10 mL buttons were melted on an actively cooled Cu hearth in an ultra-high purity (UHP) Ar environment. The melt chamber was evacuated to a vacuum level of 10 mTorr and purged three times with UHP Ar before every melt. Electromagnetic stirring enhanced mixing of the melt, and the buttons were flipped and remelted 5 times to avoid dead zones and improve mixing to achieve an overall homogenous melt. The buttons were then remelted on a vacuum arc suction cast mold into multiple cylindrical rods of 70 mm length and 8 mm diameter to achieve a more homogenous solidification. Temperature: 1250 °C; Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: Gas-atomised spherical 316 steel powder (size: 20-65 µm), sourced from SLM Solution Group AG, was used as the standard material for assessing the effectiveness of TiN in refining γ-austenite grains. Three different addition levels of TiN nanoparticles, i.e. 0.5 wt.%, 1 wt.% and 2 wt.%, were mixed with the 316 steel powder to prepare the TiN inoculated 316 steel (i.e. TI-316) feedstocks. The vibrative agitation approach enables the uniform distribution of TiN nanoparticles (less than 100 nm) on the surfaces of 316 steel particles despite a few agglomerations being observed. During L-PBF process, when the subsequent layer was deposited, previously built layer was partially remelted and the new grains tend to nucleate and grow epitaxially on the existing columnar grains due to the low nucleation barrier (i.e. low ΔTn). To overcome this limitation, we have successfully designed a strong and stiff magnesium-lithium alloy (LAZWMGT) by using Sn and RE (Gd, Y) nuclei to refine HCP α-Mg grains and forming secondary Mg2Sn inside primary Mg grains. All raw materials were melted in a fully automatic vacuum melting furnace under an argon protective atmosphere and kept at 730 °C for 10 min before pouring the melt into a copper mold to obtain cast ingots whose diameter was 150 mm, and the height was 30 mm, as shown schematically in Fig. 1. To obtain higher strength and Young′s modulus, the cast ingots were subjected to a heat treatment (solid solution (T4): 350 °C-4 h+ 400 °C-1 h, aging (T6): 85 °C-3 h). The microstructure, morphology, and elemental compositions and their distributions of the specimens were characterized by using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, S4800, Japan) equipped with an energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS, QUANTAX) and optical microscope (OM, ZEISS). The phase analysis was carried out using an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, RigakuD/max-2500) with a copper foil target and a scanning speed of 4°/min. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB 250Xi, Thermo Scientific, USA) with an Al K α source was used to determine the surface chemical composition of the Mg-Li alloy, and the C (1 s) line of the amorphous carbon with a binding energy of 284.8 eV was used to standardize the absolute binding energy. According to the Williamson-Hall method, the grain size and microstrain were also quantified for LAZWMG and LAZWMGT specimens [17]. The full width at half-maximum of the peak was obtained as a measurement of peak broadening by fitting the peaks to the XRD using the Pearson-VII software. To evaluate the strength of the specimens under different heat treatments, the samples in cast and heat treatment states of 48 mm in length and 10 mm in width, and 1.5 mm in thickness were stretched at an initial strain of 1 × 10 -3S -1using an electronic universal tensile tester (CMT5205, MTS Systems Corporation, USA) according to ASTM E8/E8M-2011. Under each condition, four specimens were tested to ensure the accuracy of the experimental data. The samples (size: 60 mm × 10 mm ×2 mm) were evaluated on an IET-01 non-destructive test instrument for the dynamic elastic modulus of solid materials using the pulse excitation method following ASTM E 1876-2009. Processing state: Solid solution

Experimental procedure Commercial Ti6Al4V powder with the size range of 45∼ 120 µm and pure Ta powder with the size range of 15–50 µm were used in this study. Ti6Al4V and Ta powders were mixed by the ball milling process with rotational speed of 150 r/min for 3 h, then dried in a vacuum furnace at 120 ℃ for 2 h to remove residual moisture. The Ti6Al4V-xTa alloys were prepared using a laser cladding system, including a 6 kW ﬁber laser cladding head equipped with the coaxial powder feeding. The substrates plates were made of forged Ti6Al4V alloy with the geometric size of 100 × 100 × 20 mm. The surface of the substrates was ground using 800 grit SiC papers then cleaned with alcohol before cladding. The laser power, scan speed and powder feed rate were chosen as 2000–2200 W, 480 mm/min and ∼5.4 g/min, respectively. The diameter of laser beam was estimated to be around 3 mm. The working chamber was ﬁlled with argon gas and the oxygen level was kept less than 20 ppm to prevent oxidation of alloy during LAM process, and argon could also provide shielding to prevent contamination of the laser lens. During the multi-layer deposition process, the layer thickness was set as 0.6 mm in the depositing direction. The overlapping fraction between the two parallel tracks was set as 30 % to achieve a continuous building. Condition: room temperature; Processing state: LAMed; Microstructure: finest uniform basketweave microstructure, weakened α-variants selection

A new Co-rich Co50Cr20Ni20Fe5Mn5 HEA was synthesized by vacuum arc remelting and processed through homogenization, cold rolling, and recrystallization. The Co 50Cr 20Ni 20Fe 5Mn 5and Co 20Cr 20Ni 20Fe 20Mn 20high entropy alloys were prepared using vacuum arc remelting (VAR) in a water-cooled copper crucible using the commercially pure metals of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Mn with a purity greater than 99.9%. In addition, pure Ti was melted and utilized as an oxygen-getter within the VAR chamber. The arc was formed in a high-purity Ar atmosphere (99.999%) using a non-consumable tungsten electrode. Each ingot was sliced into 5-6 pieces and the pieces were flipped over and underwent six remelting cycles to promote thorough mixing. To ensure reasonable homogenization, the as-cast ingots were hot-forged to a 54% height reduction across their width and subsequently homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h in a vacuum, followed by water-quenching. The homogenized alloys were analyzed for their chemical composition using inductively coupled plasma-optical emission spectrometry (ICP -OES). Following the homogenization treatment, the alloys were hot rolled at 1000 °C with a 68% thickness reduction. To ensure nearly isothermal hot deformation, the specimens were heated at 1000 °C for 15 min before the first and for 5 min before each subsequent rolling pass. After hot rolling, the samples were annealed at 1000 °C for 5 min, followed by water quenching. Further grain refinement of the alloys was achieved through cold-rolling at room temperature with a thickness reduction of 68%, followed by recrystallization annealing at 900 °C in a vacuum for 7 min, followed by water quenching. Processing Text: The 4032 aluminum alloy (12.74 wt% Si, 0.33 wt% Fe, 1.29 wt% Cu, 1.00 wt% Mg, 1.15 wt% Ni, 0.059 wt% Ti, residual Al) was melted in a 60 kg capacity crucible using a resistance furnace. During the melting process, the temperature of the resistance furnace was controlled at 720 °C. A total of 30 kg of the alloy melt was prepared, and this melt was homogenized for 1 h. Subsequently, the Al-10Sr intermediate alloy was added, and the alloy melt was subjected to outgassing and smelting for 15 min. After resting for 15 min, the desired alloy melt was obtained. The casting process was carried out using an injection speed of 0.1 m/s, a squeeze pressure of 150 MPa, a pouring temperature of 710 °C, and a mold temperature of 220 °C. Subsequently, standard sample blocks were cut from the test bar for T6 heat treatment according to the following procedure: heating of the solid-solution at 525 °C for 2.5 h, water quenching to room temperature, aging at 175 °C for 10 h, and air cooling to room temperature. The yield strength of the refiner-free 4032 aluminum alloy (hereinafter referred to as alloy CS1) in the as-cast state was determined to be 169 MPa, the tensile strength was 249 MPa, and the elongation was 1.55 %. Subsequently, alloy CS1 was subjected to T6 heat treatment, according to the following parameters: solid-solution temperature of 525 °C, solid-solution heating insulation time of 2.5 h, aging temperature of 175 °C, aging insulation time of 10 h. After the T6 heat treatment (hereinafter referred to as alloy AS1), the tensile strength of the alloy increased to 364 MPa, the yield strength increased to 334 MPa, and the elongation remained relatively constant at 1.56 %. a developed multi-step hot deformation process was employed to regulate the grain boundaries (GBs), hetero-phase boundaries (PBs) and dislocation structure for dual-phase titanium alloy. The effects of accumulative thermal deformation ratios from 33% to 75% (2-8 cycles) on the microstructure and mechanical properties have been investigated. The sintered sample shows a typical Widmanstätten structure without obvious pores and micro-cracks. However, with the increase of the deformation ratio, for the hexagonal close packed (HCP) Ti, the crystal orientations of { 01 1 ‾ 0 } and { 1 ‾ 2 1 ‾ 0 } were gradually transformed into {0001}, with the change of high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) to low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs). The density of stored geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) density raised dramatically from 1.95 × 1014 m−2 to 6.5 × 1014 m−2, and various types of dislocations have been characterized. For the β phase, in the thermal deformation process, high density α-precipitates with an average thickness below 20 nm had formed with Burgers relationship of {110}BCC//{0001}HCP and < 1 ‾ 11 > BCC//< 2 1 ‾ 1 ‾ 0 > HCP. Finally, the yield strength of the dual-phase titanium alloy increased dramatically from 881 MPa to 1178 MPa, and the ductility can still maintain at above 8.5%. The enhanced strength was mainly contributed by the increase of geometrically necessary boundaries (GNBs) and nano-lamellae boundaries (NLBs). Deformation ratio: 33%; UTS: 1200 MPa; Ductility: 11.7%

Processing Text: The substrate employed in this study is a Q235 steel plate measuring 70 mm × 70 mm × 30 mm. One is spherical 316 L stainless steel powder, with a particle size ranging from 50 μm to 150 μm. The chemical composition of the 316 L stainless steel powder is provided in Table 1. The mixed powder was subsequently placed in a vacuum drying oven and preheated at 150 °C for 2 h to remove moisture and enhance flowability. The powder was then deposited as desired coating using a self-built LDED equipment equipped with a laser of 4 KW and 1060 nm wavelength (Raycus RFL-C4000). The LDED technology utilizes a coaxial powder feeding method to ensure the stability of coating properties. The optimal parameters were identified as a laser power of 1700 W, a scanning speed of 10 mm/s, a spot diameter of 4 mm, a powder feed rate of 1.2 r/min, and an overlap ratio of 50 %. With these optimized parameters, the 316 L composite coating was fabricated via multi-layer, multi-track laser processing, yielding a well-formed surface. After completing the coating process, the uneven top surface of the coating was removed using an electrical discharge wire cutting, and then cut into samples measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm and 5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm for subsequent tests. The metallographic samples were sequentially ground with SiC sandpaper with grades from 240# to 2000#, followed by polishing with 2.5μm diamond polishing paste. Aqua regia (HCl:HNO 3=3:1 V:V) was employed to etch the sample surface for 10-15 s, followed by ultrasonic cleaning with alcohol. The polarization test samples were mechanically polished and subsequently ultrasonically cleaned with alcohol to remove any residual polishing paste and surface impurities. In this study, 316 L stainless steel specimens with 0 and 2 wt% Nb were fabricated using direct energy deposition, and heat treatment was performed at various temperatures. All the specimens were additively manufactured in a cubic shape (30 mm × 30 mm × 30 mm) using a DED machine (MX-3, Instek). The process parameters were as follows: a laser power of 400 W, scan speed of 0.85 m/min, overlap of 0.5 mm, powder feed rate of 3 g/min, hatching distance of 0.5 mm, and layer thickness of 0.25 mm. The scan strategy involved the use of a cross-snake-hatching method in which each layer was rotated by 90°. The additively manufactured 316 L stainless steel specimens were maintained at 800 °C and 900 °C, respectively, for 1 h for heat treatment, and then water quenched. The specimens that were not heat treated were denoted by “As,” and those treated at the lower and higher temperatures were denoted by “LHT” and “HHT,” respectively. The specimens were mechanically polished using SiC paper and a 1 μm cloth. The polished specimens were etched with Vilella's etchant (glycerol 45 mL + hydrochloric acid 30 mL + nitric acid) to observe their microstructure using an optical microscope (OM, Axio Observer D1m, Carl Zeiss) and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM, JSM-7900F, JEOL). Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed on non-mechanically polished specimens using a 0.04 μm colloidal solution. Laser aided additive manufacturing (LAAM) of stainless steel 316L (SS 316L) in a controlled argon environment was investigated. The controlled argon environment can significantly reduce the oxidation and fundamentally change the process conditions. It was found that after inhibiting oxidation, the surface of the deposited SS 316L showed remarkably high reflectance (71%) to laser radiation, which minimised heat accumulation. Subsequently, stable melt pool temperature and high cooling rate (4.1 × 10^4 K/s) were also observed. Furthermore, nano-sized oxides were found to be nucleated owing to excessively low internal oxygen content (220 ppm). The unique process condition resulted in enhanced strengthening effect due to cellular structure refinement and dispersed nano-sized oxides. Gas-atomised SS 316L powders were employed as the feedstock material. The SEM photo in Fig. 1(a) depicts a near-spherical morphology of the SS 316L powders, with observable satellite attachments on the surfaces. Some irregularly shaped powders can also be observed. A median particle size of 69.4 μm was characterized using laser scattering particle size analyzer. The oxygen content of the deposited SS 316L was measured through inert gas combustion method with an oxygen/Nitrogen/Hydrogen elemental analyzer (LECO ONH836). Quasi-static tensile test at the strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 was conducted on Instron 5982 universal tensile test machine at room temperature. Dynamic tensile tests with an average strain rate of 3150 s^-1 were conducted using a Spilt Hopkinson Tensile Bar (SHTB) apparatus. The microhardness of the deposited SS 316L was measured using a HVS1000 microhardness tester, with the load set as 500 g and the dwell time 15 s. The specially designed Ar chamber in this paper successfully minimizes the oxidation level to achieve a very low oxygen content of 220 ppm. The oxide particles obtained are fine, with an average size of 131.4 ± 68.5 nm. Reduction of oxidation not only influences the surface condition of the deposited material, but also leads to high reflectance of laser energy. The resulting shiny and smooth surface exhibits a reflectance of 71%. This, combined with controlled Ar environment, resulted in significantly reduced thermal accumulation, stable melt pool temperature, and high cooling rate during the LAAM process. Consequently, refined grains (24.8 μm) and cellular structures (2.4 μm) can be achieved. Quasi-static tension at strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1; As-deposited material

It was found that after inhibiting oxidation, the surface of the deposited SS 316L showed remarkably high reflectance (71%) to laser radiation, which minimised heat accumulation. Subsequently, stable melt pool temperature and high cooling rate (4.1 × 10^4 K/s) were also observed. Furthermore, nano-sized oxides were found to be nucleated owing to excessively low internal oxygen content (220 ppm). The unique process condition resulted in enhanced strengthening effect due to cellular structure refinement and dispersed nano-sized oxides. Gas-atomised SS 316L powders were employed as the feedstock material. The SEM photo in Fig. 1(a) depicts a near-spherical morphology of the SS 316L powders, with observable satellite attachments on the surfaces. Some irregularly shaped powders can also be observed. A median particle size of 69.4 μm was characterized using laser scattering particle size analyzer. The oxygen content of the deposited SS 316L was measured through inert gas combustion method with an oxygen/Nitrogen/Hydrogen elemental analyzer (LECO ONH836). Quasi-static tensile test at the strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 was conducted on Instron 5982 universal tensile test machine at room temperature. Dynamic tensile tests with an average strain rate of 3150 s^-1 were conducted using a Spilt Hopkinson Tensile Bar (SHTB) apparatus. The microhardness of the deposited SS 316L was measured using a HVS1000 microhardness tester, with the load set as 500 g and the dwell time 15 s. The specially designed Ar chamber in this paper successfully minimizes the oxidation level to achieve a very low oxygen content of 220 ppm. The oxide particles obtained are fine, with an average size of 131.4 ± 68.5 nm. Reduction of oxidation not only influences the surface condition of the deposited material, but also leads to high reflectance of laser energy. The resulting shiny and smooth surface exhibits a reflectance of 71%. This, combined with controlled Ar environment, resulted in significantly reduced thermal accumulation, stable melt pool temperature, and high cooling rate during the LAAM process. Consequently, refined grains (24.8 μm) and cellular structures (2.4 μm) can be achieved. Fabricated using L-PBF process with superior combination of strength and ductility

Material Name: near-α Ti alloys with BM (bimodal structure)
Processing Text: The Ti-5.7Al-3.2Sn-5.4Zr-0.5Mo-1.0Nb-0.4Si-0.2Er (all in wt%) alloy (IMI834) was procured from Yunnan Titanium Industry Co., Ltd (CHN), which ingot with a diameter of 200 mm and length of 400 mm was produced by vacuum arc remelting (VAR) technology triple times. The β/(α + β) transus-temperature of the Ti alloy was measured as 1005 °C by differential scanning calorimetry. The ingot is first forged at 1150 °C to obtain a cubic billet with a cross section of 50 mm. Then, forged at 980 °C to obtain a rectangular billet with a lengthwise cross-sectional side length of 40 mm. The forged bar was solution treated at 990 °C for 1 h to obtain a bimodal structure with equiaxed primary α phase. The second step is to obtain the LPS-HS by hot rolling in the α+β phase region (920,960 and 990 °C) this Ti alloy after solution treated. The sheets with a BM are annealed at a specified temperature for 15 min. During the rolling process, the reduction was 15% per pass, with annealing 5 min after per pass. This rolling process is repeated for 8 passes, and a total rolling reduction of 81%. Subsequently, the aging treatment was carried out at 700 °C for 5 h. The cooling method is air cooling(AC). We conducted a 990 °C/1h/AC heat treatment on the alloy after forging. To ensure experimental consistency, the deformation amount during rolling was kept the same, with rolling performed at temperatures of 920, 960 and 990 °C in the (α+β) phase region. The alloy after rolling is subjected to a 5 h aging treatment at 700 °C. Room Temperature tensile properties

Processing Text: Copper matrix composites reinforced by copper-coated graphite and Ti3AlC2 were fabricated using the hot-pressing sintering. The preparation of copper matrix composites mainly includes three stages. Firstly, a ball milling process was used to mix raw materials. The powder mixture of Ti3AlC2, electrolytic copper, and copper-coated graphite powders was put into 304 stainless steel jars and mixed using a planetary ball mill at 180 rpm for 8 h with weight ratio of ball to powder of 5:1. Secondly, the powders mixture was poured into a Cr12MoV die of Φ 30 mm and was cold pressed into a green compact at a pressure of 300 MPa for 5 min. Thirdly, the green compact was sintered at 1223 K below 1× 10−2 Pa by a vacuum hot-pressing under the pressure of 25 MPa followed by furnace cooling. Condition: As-prepared; Density: 98.2±0.60%; Hardness: 112±2.7 HV; Tensile Strength: 285.4±1.5 MPa; Elongation: 7.2±0.21%

Processing Text: In the present work, a Ni3(Al, Ti)-type multicomponent alloy of Ni43.9Co22.4Fe8.8Al10.7Ti11.7B2.5 was successfully fabricated using laser metal deposition (LMD) technique. Mixed powders of Ni, Co, Fe, Al, Ti and B with purity ≥99.99% were used as raw materials. The mixed powders were mechanically mixed for 3 h and dried at 393 K for 3 h. An in-house developed LMD printing system was employed, and the powder was fed into the laser melt pool on the GH4169 high-temperature alloy substrate using a coaxial nozzle under a high-purity argon gas atmosphere (≥99.99%). The variables that followed were the applied optimal process parameters: laser power of 1400 W, laser scanning speed of 400 mm/min, gas flow rate of 3 L/min and powder feed rate of 1.4 rad/min. The Ni43.9Co22.4Fe8.8Al10.7Ti11.7B2.5 alloy prepared by LMD consists of dendrite γ + γ′ phases, γ′ envelopes and interdendritic γ + γ′ phases, with discontinuous acicular TiB2 precipitates in the interdendritic γ + γ′ region. During the solidification process, TiB2 and γ dendrites preferentially precipitate, and the residual liquid phase reacts with γ dendrites to form γ′ envelope layer. Subsequently, γ and γ′ phases are co-precipitated from the residual interdendrite liquid phase. During the deposition process, the interdendrite γ′ phase coarsened and merged, and the cubic γ′ phase precipitated inside the γ dendrite. Condition: maximum value at 973 K

Processing Text: Be/Al composites containing varying volume fractions of beryllium were fabricated via the pressure infiltration method. Under pressure infiltration conditions, the molten aluminum successfully repaired the defects in the beryllium swarf. Be/Al composites with volume fractions of 30%-60% were prepared using the pressure infiltration method, and the process flow diagram is shown in Fig. 1. The treated beryllium swarf was compressed to a predetermined volume content in a steel mold with a diameter of 52 mm to obtain a preform. Subsequently, the steel mold containing the Be preform was kept at 600 °C for about 3 h. At the same time, Al was heated to above 800° and kept warm, and molten Al liquid was obtained under argon (Ar) protection. Subsequently, the prepared preform and mold were placed on the press table, and the molten Al liquid was poured into the mold cavity for mechanical pressing. According to the preparation of Be/Al composites with different body parts, the pressure range is between 50 and 100 MPa, the infiltration speed is 1-50 mm/s, and the holding time is 5min. With the full immersion of molten Al liquid into the cracks of the beryllium swarf and the gaps between the swarf, residual gas in the pores is simultaneously discharged, greatly improving the density of composite materials, and finally preparing Be/Al composites with beryllium volume fractions of 30%, 40%, 50%, and 60% respectively. Processing Text: The bulb flat steel with a yield strength of 1292 MPa, elongation of 18.5 % and an impact energy of 53 J at − 196 °C is obtained by quenching and tempering process. In order to reveal the tempering response and strengthening mechanism during the quenching and tempering process of bulb flat steel, multi-scale characterization is carried out to explore the microstructural evolution and nano-precipitation behavior of the ultralow temperature bulb flat steel under different tempering processes. After holding the cast ingot at 1200 °C for 3 h, it is forged into a rectangular billet of 150 mm * 150 mm * 2000 mm. The billet is heated and held in a three-stage heating furnace (600 °C in the preheating section, 1130 °C in the heating section and 1250 °C in the soaking section) and hot rolled after descaling. The opening rolling temperature is 1150 °C and the final rolling temperature is 920 °C. The bulb flat steel of HP140*11 specification is prepared by 12 passes of groove rolling and air cooled to room temperature. The temperature parameters of QT process are selected based on the results of phase transformation temperature determination. In this study, the quenching temperature was taken as 830 °C, and the holding time was 30 min to make the specimens fully austenitized, and then water quenched to room temperature. Subsequently, the specimens were tempered at 450 °C, 500 °C, and 550 °C for 5 h respectively. Finally, the specimens were removed and air cooled to room temperature. The QT process route is shown in Fig. 2(b). The mechanical properties of the bulb flat steel were tested by tensile and impact tests, respectively. The tensile tests at room temperature were performed on an electronic tensile testing machine with an extensometer at a strain rate of 10 -3s −1. The low temperature impact tests were performed on a TB50 impact testing machine using liquid nitrogen as the cooling medium. The sampling positions and dimensional diagram are shown in Fig. 3. The microstructures of the ultralow temperature resistant bulb flat steel after heat treatment were characterized using a SUPRA55 SEM. The samples are cut from the sampling position in Fig. 3, and the longitudinal section of the sample is polished and etched (HNO 3: alcohol = 1 ml: 10 ml). The diffraction peak profile of the specimen was measured by a German Bruker D8 ADVANCE XRD. The measurement range is 20°-140°, the measurement step is 0.02°, and the test speed is 2°/min. The crystal structure of the blub flat steel was characterized by EBSD. The specimen was ground with abrasive paper, followed by electropolishing with 5 % perchloric acid alcohol solution. The parameters of electropolishing were: voltage = 30 V, polishing time = 40 s. The microstructure of the bulb flat steel was characterized using an FEI Titan themis G2 60-300 TEM. For TEM observation, the thin foils were prepared by twin-jet electropolishing. Needle samples for APT analysis were prepared by two-step electropolishing method. The data were collected by the atom probe under vacuum of < 10-8 Pa in the analysis chamber, the sample was cooled to 50 K, the pulse voltage frequency was 200 kHz, and the pulse fraction was 20 %. Condition: tempered at 500°C for 5 h; Additional properties: maximum elongation of 18.5%

The Ni 40Co 18Cr 18Fe 14Al 5Ti 5HEA was fabricated using an FS273M SLM machine (Hunan Farsoon High-Technology Co., Ltd, China). The fiber laser of this SLM instrument has a spot diameter of 55 μm and a maximum output power of 500 W. Before printing, the chamber of the SLM device was vacuumed and then filled with high-purity argon gas to ensure the oxygen content remained below 1000 ppm. The build substrate was preheated to 100 °C to reduce thermal stress. A wide range of printing parameters including adjustments in laser power ( P), scanning speed ( V), and scanning pitch ( h), were explored. Specifically, Pranged from 260 to 300 W, Vranged from 800 to 1200 mm·s −1, and hranged from 60 to 140 μm, all while maintaining a consistent layer thickness ( t) of 40 μm. The laser beam scanned each layer in a unidirectional manner, with the scanning direction altered by 67° for each subsequent layer (as shown in Fig. 1b), aiming to minimize defects and residual stress [26]. The densities of the SLM-produced samples were determined using Archimedes' drainage method. Phase analysis of the powders and as-printed samples was conducted using a Cu Kα radiation X-ray diffractometer (XRD, 7000SX, Shimadzu). The microstructure was characterized using optical microscopy (OM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Nova Nano SEM 450), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Tecnai G20, 300 kV). For the TEM analysis, the samples were initially mechanically polished to a thickness of approximately 30 μm and then further thinned using an ion polishing system (Gatan PIPS II 695). Tensile testing was conducted on seven representative SLM-produced HEA samples, each prepared with varying printing parameters (denoted as P1, P2, …, P7) encompassing a wide range of laser power, scanning speed, and scanning pitch. SLM parameters: P = 300 W, V = 1000 mm·s−1, h = 0.08 mm

CrMnFeCoNi HEA with 5 at.% SiC nanoparticles addition was fabricated by LMD. The size of the pre-alloyed spherical equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi powder and SiC powder that were analyzed using laser particle size analyzer (Microtrac s3500) are approximately 120 μm and 40 nm, respectively. Two powders were fully mixed and dried in a vacuum environment at 120 °C for 2.5 h prior to additive manufacturing. Under the protection of argon gas, the mixed powders were delivered into the chamber through a coaxial nozzle at an argon gas flow 15 L/min and a feeding rate of 7-9 g/min. Successive layers were deposited on a 316L steel substrate, ultimately forming walled-samples. The heat treatment processes of the samples were carried out in a vertical vacuum tube quenching furnace, which quenched immediately after 2-h heat treatment at different temperatures (700/900/1100 °C). The tensile tests of the samples were performed at an engineering strain rate of 10 −3s −1 in an Instron 5982 static testing machine. Each group of samples was retested three times to obtain their average value. The tensile samples with a gauge length of 10.0 mm, gauge width of 2.0 mm, and thickness of 1.6 mm were cut from to the center of LMD-fabricated wall, and the tensile direction was parallel to deposition direction (DD). The samples under different heat treatment temperature were subjected to corrosion treatment in equal proportion of FeCl 3-HCl-H 2O solution for 30 s before SEM observation. Condition: Room Temperature (25°C)

Heterostructured (HS) 2024Al alloys with various heterogeneity levels, consisting of soft domains (CGs) and hard domains (FGs, Al3Tip, and eutectic compounds), were fabricated via adjusting the mold temperature of powder thixoforming. A powder mixture was produced by combining 3.5 wt% Ti p and 96.5 wt% 2024Al p in a planetary ball-milling machine (ND7-21). The ball-milling process was carried out for 8 h at a speed of 135 rpm/min with a ball-to-powder ratio of 5:1. To prevent overheating, the ball milling was stopped for 10 min after running for 10 min. Following ball milling, the resulting powder mixture was subjected to hot-pressing in a steel mold using a vacuum hot-pressing furnace (GWL-VSF-1200RY) to form Φ 45 mm × ∼16 mm green compacts. The process was carried out under uniaxial pressure of 224 MPa at 300 °C for 40 min. Then, the compacts were heated at 655 °C for 80 min in a tubular vacuum resistance furnace (SKG08123K-HD). Finally, the resultant semisolid ingots were promptly transferred into a steel mold and thixoforged using a pressure machine (Y32-60T) under a pressure of 196 MPa for 20 s to produce Φ 50 mm × ∼10 mm cakes. Various mold temperatures ranging from 150 °C to 300 °C were utilized and the resulting alloy samples were denoted as HS-150, HS-200, HS-250, and HS-300 for ease of reference. Mold temperature: 250 °C; Microhardness discrepancy: 1.23 GPa; Volume fraction discrepancy: 0.04

Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA powder (Beijing Yanbang New Material Technology Co., Ltd., China) was purchased and used as a feedstock for cold spray deposition. The powder size distribution was 15-53 μm (a d50 value of 29.351 μm). Al 6061 alloy substrate (5 mm thickness) was used for CS deposition. Processing Text: The W-W interatomic interactions were described using the embedded atom method (EAM) interatomic potential developed by Marinica et al., 2013. This potential was specifically designed for studying the irradiation effects and dislocations in tungsten and has undergone extensive validation through ab initio and experimental values. The simulation box with dimensions of 40.0 nm × 22.3 nm × 23.1 nm, containing approximately 1.4 million atoms, was used. The x-, y-, and z-axes of the simulation box were oriented as [111], [-110], and [-1-12], respectively. To create the edge dislocation along the z-axis whose normal direction of the slip plane is along the x-axis, the ATOMSK software package was employed. This edge dislocation, characterized by the x slip direction and a Burgers vector of a/2<111>, was introduced, where a represents the lattice constant, measuring 3.14 Ȧ. The construction of the dislocation model referred to the method developed by Osetsky and Bacon (2003). Two types of dislocation loops with Burgers vectors of a<100> and a/2<111> were introduced at the center of the simulation box, referred to as ‘perfect loop’, to account for all possible dislocation loop scenarios. The construction process involved the insertion of the dislocation, and then the energy minimization. Subsequently, the dislocation loop was inserted, and another energy minimization step was launched to obtain the initial static equilibrium configuration. Subsequent to these steps, dynamic relaxation was carried out. Initially, all atoms were assigned random velocities to produce the desired initial temperature, T. With two vacuum regions at the edge of simulation box along the y-direction, an isobaric-isothermal (NPT) ensemble was employed to obtain thermal equilibration configuration. The time step employed for dynamic relaxation was set at 1.0 fs. In this simulation, the velocity-load mode for shear strain was applied, with a corresponding strain rate of 1 × 10^7 s−1. The timestep for the dynamic shearing process remained consistent at 1.0 fs. The major simulations were conducted at a temperature of 318 K. Additionally, temperatures range is from 100 K to 900 K with the aim of improving the applicability of the study. The study focuses on dislocation loop sizes ranging from 1.0 to 10.0 nm. Additionally, the Burgers vectors of the dislocation loops, including 1/2<111> and <100>, were also taken into consideration to explore their effect on the interactions in this study. The sample was firstly annealed at 1273 K for one hour to remove the damage associated with the electric discharge machine cutting and to recrystallize the grains. An EBSD scan is performed over an area of 800 μm × 600 μm where the mean size of grain is 37.5 μm. Condition: unirradiated; Temperature: 300 K

Processing Text: The LDX 2101 material was prepared in an electric arc furnace, with an argon oxygen decarburizer, ladle refining furnace and continuous casting process. After casting, the LDX 2101 material was homogenized by heat treatment at 1250 °C for 1 h. After heat treatment, three samples were cut (10 mm thick) from LDX 2101 material for hot rolling at 1250 °C. In order to study the influence of different distributions of hot rolling reduction on the microstructure and mechanical properties, a reduction of 50 % is distributed in the first pass, and the thickness decreases to 10 mm→5 mm→4 mm→3 mm. In addition, a reduction of 50 % was distributed in the middle pass, and the thickness decreased to 10 mm→8 mm→4 mm→3 mm. Finally, the 50 % reduction is distributed in the last pass, and the thickness decreases to 10 mm→8 mm→6 mm→3 mm. After the rolling experiment, each sample was quenched in water to retain the deformed structure. After rolling, samples were prepared along the rolling direction (RD) for microscopy and mechanical testing. The microstructure of the specimens was analyzed by DM2500 optical microscope (Quanta FEG 450), and the specimens were etched in 10 % oxalic acid solution for 25 s. The dog bone-shaped tensile specimens with length of 15 mm, width of 5 mm and thickness of 3 mm were machined (by electric discharge machining) from the rolled plate along the RD. The tensile test at room temperature at a displacement rate of 1 mm/min was carried out on mTS810 tensile machine. The phase structure after deformation was determined by XRD. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was used to analyze the grain, stress-strain distribution and deformation mechanism of the phases. In order to remove the surface stress, electrolytic polishing was performed in 10 % perchlorate ethanol at 30 V for 20 s. Lastly, transmission electron microscopy (TEM, 200 kV JEM-2200FS field emission electron microscope) was performed to investigate the microstructure of LDX 2101 material after different rolling distribution. Additionally, taking into account the highest temperature of BCC phase separation (802 °C) and the eutectoid temperature (673 °C), specimens were annealed respectively at 650, 750, and 850 °C for 2 h. Processing Text: The elemental powders used in this investigation -Titanium (Ti), Aluminum (Al), and Vanadium (V)-were purchased from Alfa Aesar, USA, with an average size of 45 µm and a purity of more than 99%. The elemental powder was weighed using a digital weighing balance in the weight percentages of Ti (89 wt%), Al (6 wt%), and V (5 wt%). Milling was performed at different durations to drastically modify the internal structure (achieve more grain refinement) and investigate the influence of particle size on microstructure and mechanical performance. A powder sample of 5 g was taken from the vial at intervals of 20 h for characterization during the synthesis of Ti-6Al-5 V alloy powders. XRD analysis was performed using a Philips PANalytical instrument with a CuKα radiation source (λ = 0.1541 nm). The mean crystal size and strain were determined by X-ray peak profile analysis, taking into account the major reflection peaks in the 2θ range of 30° to 90°. HR-SEM (FEI Quanta FEG 200 microscope) and HR-TEM (JEOL Japan, JEM-2100 Plus microscope) were used for microstructural observations of the milled powder samples. SPS was used to make bulk samples using the M/s FCT Systeme GmbH machine at 1050 °C with 50 MPa pressure. A heating rate of 100 °C/min was used, and the SPS was performed under a vacuum atmosphere. Each sample was taken around 6 min during SPS, and the samples were consolidated inside a graphite die-set, producing φ 15 mm and 10 mm (height). Quanta FEG 650 FE-SEM attached with an EBSD detector was used for detailed microstructural analyses. HR-TEM was also carried out on the spark plasma-sintered sample after making the sample a thin foil with a size of around 120 nm. Vickers micro-hardness tests were conducted on sintered specimens. A 50gf load was applied with a dwell duration of 5 s. Testing was performed at 10 different locations, and the average result was used for interpretation. Cylindrical samples with dimensions of ϕ 8 mm and 10 mm (height) were fabricated from the spark plasma-sintered sample, following the ASTM E9 standard. Ti-6Al-5 V-0 h and Ti-6Al-5 V-120 h samples were subjected to compression tests. Three trials were conducted for each alloy in the compression test, and the average result was used for investigation. Processing route: MA+SPS; Mechanical Testing: Compression; Ref: [19]

Ti and Zr powder were manufactured by gas atomization, Nb and Ta powder were manufactured by plasma rotation electrode process (PREP). The powder granules are spherical. Powder composition is shown in Table 1. The metal powders were mixed in a mixer (GSM) for 12 h and dried for 8 h under vacuum condition of 100 °C. The SEM image of the powder is shown in Fig. 1(a), EDS analysis showed that the powder was homogeneous and can be used for SLM (Fig. 1(b)). NbTa0.5TiZrx RHEA was fabricated by DiMetal-150 laser powder bed melting system (China Lejia). A 500 W fiber laser with a spot diameter of 20 μm was used to fabricate NbTa0.5TiZrx RHEA. High purity Ar was used as a protective atmosphere, oxygen content <100 ppm, build platform using pure titanium substrate, which was preheated to 200 °C. Processing Text: Ingots of Ni34Co28Cr28Al10 MPEA were fabricated by vacuum arc melting (VAM) in Ar protecting atmosphere. High-purity elemental metal powders of Ni, Co, Cr and Al, > 99.99% purity for each, were mixed to achieve the targeted composition. The mixtures were melted and then solidified in a button-shaped water-cooled copper mold to obtain bulk ingots. To ensure uniform distribution of each element, all ingots were flipped and remelted at least five times. Additionally, electromagnetic stirrer was used during the last two remelting to further enhance elements homogeneous distribution of elements. Finally, these ingots were obtained by molding in copper mold with baguette shape, each measuring approximately 60 × 25 × 10 mm3. To eliminate the possible segregation of elements, as-cast samples were homogenized at 1200 ℃ for 4 h followed by water-quenching, and these samples were named HT. Subsequently, selected HT samples were aged at 700 ℃ for 2 h respectively and then quenched in water, and the corresponding samples were termed as Aged700. In the end, three types of samples were obtained: AC (as-cast), HT, Aged700. All the heat treatment was carried out under argon gas protection to prevent excessive oxidation of the samples. Sample: HT; Microstructure: Absence of precipitates

Processing Text: Cylindrical ingots (110 mm diameter; 90 mm high) of the vanadium-free MEA Ni43.4Co25.3Cr25.3Al3Ti3 (at.%) were cast by a magnetic suspension melting technique, using the same melting parameters. A 10 mm thick piece of each MEA was cut off via electrical discharge machining and homogenized at 1150 °C for 4 h. Subsequently, the pieces were cold rolled to a total thickness reduction of 80 % with a 5 % reduction in thickness for each pass. The vanadium-free MEA was aged at either 700 °C for 24 h or 900 °C for 24 h, which are referred to as V07 and V09, respectively. In addition, both the cold-rolled vanadium-free MEA were annealed at 1100 °C for 24 h to compare the microstructure with the aged MEA. All the heat treatments (i.e. homogenization, annealing, and aging) are conducted in an argon atmosphere, all of which are followed by water quenching. Temperature: 298 K

Gas atomized Haynes 282 alloy powder manufactured by Praxair® Co., with standard composition ( Table 2) was used in this study. The samples were fabricated using EOS M290 machine. The important parameters used for LPBF are given in Table 3. These optimized parameters were obtain from our previous work [12]. These parameters were used to build 15 mm ×15 mm ×15 mm cubes and flat ASTM E8 sub-specimen tensile samples as shown in Fig.S1 in supplementary data. Some of the samples were vacuum sealed in quartz tubes and subjected to two-stage standard heat treatment (as prescribed by Haynes International [24]) for γ′and grain boundary carbides precipitation. In the first step, the samples are heated to 1283 K (1010 °C) and held for 2 h, then air cooled to room temperature. In the second step, the samples are heated to 1061 K (788 °C) and held for 8 h, then air cooled to room temperature. As-built samples were subjected to standard two step ageing treatment to precipitate γ′and grain boundary carbides. The room temperature uniaxial tensile tests were carried out on sub-sized flat specimen as per ASTM E8 standard utilizing a universal tensile testing equipment (Instron 3370) with a strain rate of 10 −2s −1. Condition: As-built; Scan rotation: 67°

Ti 1.5 NbVAl x (0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1) RMEAs were prepared by vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper crucible under argon atmosphere, referred to as Al0.25, Al0.5, Al0.75 and Al1, respectively. After placing the raw material in the crucible, the chamber was evacuated to 3*10 −3 Pa. Subsequently, high purity argon gas (99.999 %) was repeatedly used to purge the air for five times. The argon gas is pressurized to 0.05Mpa before the melting alloy. During melting, the Ti ingot is first melted to absorb any residual oxygen and other impurities in the furnace chamber. To prevent the volatilization of the Al element and the segregation of the Nb element, a two-step approach was adopted. First, Ti–Al and Nb–V intermediate alloys were prepared(low-melting-point metal materials were placed at the bottom of the crucible). Each intermediate alloy ingot was remelted by inversion three times. Subsequently, the intermediate alloys were combined, flipped and remelted for five times. Each melting time lasted for 2 min to ensure a more homogeneous composition of the alloys, and then cast into a 150 mm × 15 mm × 15 mm cuboid using copper mold flip casting technology. Test: Tensile; Condition: Room Temperature; Processing state: as-cast

Processing Text: Ti 1.5 NbVAl x (0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1) RMEAs were prepared by vacuum arc melting in a water-cooled copper crucible under argon atmosphere, referred to as Al0.25, Al0.5, Al0.75 and Al1, respectively. After placing the raw material in the crucible, the chamber was evacuated to 3*10 −3 Pa. Subsequently, high purity argon gas (99.999 %) was repeatedly used to purge the air for five times. The argon gas is pressurized to 0.05Mpa before the melting alloy. During melting, the Ti ingot is first melted to absorb any residual oxygen and other impurities in the furnace chamber. To prevent the volatilization of the Al element and the segregation of the Nb element, a two-step approach was adopted. First, Ti–Al and Nb–V intermediate alloys were prepared(low-melting-point metal materials were placed at the bottom of the crucible). Each intermediate alloy ingot was remelted by inversion three times. Subsequently, the intermediate alloys were combined, flipped and remelted for five times. Each melting time lasted for 2 min to ensure a more homogeneous composition of the alloys, and then cast into a 150 mm × 15 mm × 15 mm cuboid using copper mold flip casting technology. Test: Compression; Condition: Room Temperature; Processing state: as-cast

High-purity Ti, Zr, V, and Ta (purities are all higher than 99.95 wt.%) were used as raw materials, and Ti 1.5ZrV 0.5Ta 0.5 alloy was fabricated by arc melting which was repeated at least 5 times in a water-cooled copper crucible to improve the chemical homogeneity. The as-cast samples were homogenized at 1200 °C for 6 h and then quenched in water. The homogenized samples were subsequently aged at 400 and 600 °C for 6 h, respectively, and the corresponding samples are named T400 and T600. Tensile tests were performed on a Zwick Z2.5 TH testing machine at room temperature with a strain rate of 5 × 10 -4s -1, using rectangular dog-bone-shaped tensile plate specimens with a gage dimension of 5 mm × 2 mm × 1 mm. The compression tests at room temperature were performed using WDW-200D universal testing machine at a strain rate of 1 × 10 -3s -1. The high-temperature mechanical properties of the alloy were tested by the Gleeble-3500 simulation machine with a strain rate of 1 × 10 -3s -1. The heating rate of the test temperature was 10 °C s -1 and held for 5 min. The compression tests, including room temperature and high temperature, were performed on cylindrical specimens with dimensions of φ6 mm × 9 mm. Condition: Room Temperature; Microstructure: Single-phase solid solution bcc1 phase

In this study, we fabricated a ductile Ti42Hf21Nb21V16 RHEA for additive manufacturing using a directed energy deposition (DED) technique, with a focused laser serving as the energy source. The feedstock powders used for RHEA fabrication include plasma rotation electrode atomized spherical titanium (Ti, purity> 99.95%), niobium (Ti, purity> 99.95%), hafnium (Hf, purity> 99.95%) and vanadium (V, purity> 99.95%) powders， ranging in size from 50 µm to 100 µm (D 50=75 µm). The powders exhibit a perfect spherical shape, indicating good flowability. Initially, the powders were blended in a powder mixer (Turbula, T2F) at room temperature for 2 h, with a revolving speed of 200r/min, within a sealed container. The bulk RHEA sample of size 12 × 70 × 4 mm was fabricated on a pure Ti substrate by additive manufacturing in the form of LENS (Optomec LENS MR-7). The LENS MR-7 is a coaxial powder feeding 3D printer that utilizes a high-powered laser system within a closed chamber filled with argon. The laser, with a spot size of ∼ 600 µm, was used to form the melt pool and remelt the previous path. To ensure a uniform elemental distribution, a remelting procedure was employed in our study. The scanning strategy for the fabrication process is as follows, 1)Layer building: The first layer was scanned in a zigzag strategy, with a powder feed rate of 4 g/min and a laser power of 550 W;2)Remelting procedure: After the first laser stopped, the powder delivery nozzle moved upward by 200 µm (offset value) and the remelting process began. The procedure involved a 45°rotation compared to the previous layer. No powder was delivered to the molten pool during this step and the laser power was increased to 800 W;3)Layer building: Once the remelting process was completed, the powder delivery nozzle was immediately raised by 200 µm, and the powder feed rate was initiated. The working laser power was set to 550 W, and a 45°rotation was applied for layer building;4)Remelting procedure: A scan rotation of 45°, compared to the previous layer, was applied, and a similar remelting procedure (2) was applied to remelt the previously built layer. Layer building: The first layer was scanned in a zigzag strategy, with a powder feed rate of 4 g/min and a laser power of 550 W; Remelting procedure: After the first laser stopped, the powder delivery nozzle moved upward by 200 µm (offset value) and the remelting process began. The procedure involved a 45°rotation compared to the previous layer. No powder was delivered to the molten pool during this step and the laser power was increased to 800 W; Layer building: Once the remelting process was completed, the powder delivery nozzle was immediately raised by 200 µm, and the powder feed rate was initiated. The working laser power was set to 550 W, and a 45°rotation was applied for layer building; Remelting procedure: A scan rotation of 45°, compared to the previous layer, was applied, and a similar remelting procedure (2) was applied to remelt the previously built layer. The four steps were repeated periodically until a bulk specimen with a thickness of ∼ 4 mm was built. The other parameters used in this study remained constant, including a working distance of 10 mm, a scanning speed of 5 mm/s, and a hatching space of 381 µm. Before the experiment, flowing argon was used to reduce the oxygen level to ∼ 200 ppm in the atmospheric chamber which was maintained throughout the entire printing process. After a whole procedure, the actual composition of LENS-fabricated RHEA was determined by energy disperse spectroscopy (EDS). Due to the application of high remelting laser power during the fabrication of the LENS-fabricated sample, severe residual stress was produced. To mitigate this stress and enhance the mechanical performance of the LENS-fabricated sample, a vacuum annealing approach was employed, referred to as-HT state. The annealing process involved heating the samples to 1273 K for 4 h, with a heating rate of 10 K/min and subsequent furnace cooling. The LENS process involves high cooling rates (∼10 3- 10 4K/s), which deviates the microstructure from the equilibrium calculations. Processing state: as-LENS; Fracture strain: 22.5%

Processing Text: Pure Fe, Cr, and Ni powders were used as raw materials. A high-throughput in-situ alloying technique based on Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) was employed to synthesize 80 Fe-Cr-Ni alloys. In-situ alloyed Fe-Cr-Ni samples were fabricated using a self-developed High-Throughput Additive Manufacturing System (HTAMS) developed by the CISRI Group. HTAMS is a modified LPBF machine equipped with automated powder mixing and spreading capabilities. It uniformly deposits powders of varying compositions in a pre-defined ratio on a build platform with four composition-variable zones. The build process was conducted in a high-purity Ar 2 atmosphere, with an oxygen level maintained below 100 PPM. Each sample measured 12 × 10 × 2 mm (XYZ) and featured bevels at the border for facilitating identification of the interface between samples. Samples were divided into two parts using distinct process parameters. For the top and bottom parts of the sample, low power and speed were used to sinter the powders, aiding in distinguishing sample boundaries during subsequent tests, such as microhardness. For the middle part of the sample, sintering + triple remelting strategy was used to promote element diffusion. The laser scan strategy was 'No pattern, zig-zag'. High laser energy (240 W) and a small spot diameter (60 µm) were employed to increase the melt pool temperature; slow laser scanning speed (700 mm/s) was utilized to extend the melting time of the melt pool; multiple remelting strategies were employed to subject individual positions of the sample to repeated melting and solidification cycles. All samples were cut along the YZ plane and then mounted in epoxy resin for subsequent characterization. The sample matrix was ground with 180# to 1500# sandpaper and subsequently polished with 5 µm and 0.5 µm diamond polishes. Four compositions of 2Cr, 12Cr, 12Cr6Ni, and 20Cr7Ni were selected for tensile property testing and top melt pool morphology analysis. Three rectangular specimens, measuring 7 × 40 × 7 mm (XYZ), were fabricated utilizing the sintering + triple remelting processing parameters listed in Table 3. These specimens were subsequently machined according to the dimensions depicted in Fig. 3 prior to undergoing tensile property testing. Additionally, a rectangular specimen with dimensions of 7 × 10 × 7 mm (XYZ) was fabricated and cut along the YZ plane to facilitate analysis of the top melt pool morphology. The tensile tests for the 2Cr, 12Cr, 12Cr6Ni, and 20Cr7Ni were carried out at room temperature with an elongation rate of 0.05 mm/s. Processing Text: The samples were prepared using Co, Ni, Al, Ta, and Cr of high purity (99.9 wt%). The raw materials underwent ultrasonic cleaning with anhydrous ethanol. To achieve a homogeneous composition, the metal material was melted at least 8 times in an arc-melting furnace. For heat treatment, the samples were encapsulated in a quartz tube under vacuum conditions and filled with a small amount of argon gas as a protective atmosphere. They were then quenched in cold water to obtain the desired microstructure at the target temperature. All alloy samples underwent solid solution treatment at 1250 °C for 12 h, and then were aged at 800 °C for 24 h ∼ 200 h to obtain fine γ/γ′ microstructure. To determine the oxidation rate of the sample, the bulk samples were cut into small regular geometries and then placed in a tube furnace at the appropriate temperature under an air atmosphere. During the oxidation tests, the specimens were placed in alumina crucibles, allowing for the measurement of the total weight gain, including any oxide products that may have spalled off. Various specimens were subjected to oxidation for 50 h, 100 h, 200 h, 300 h. The weight gain of each specimen was determined with a high level of accuracy, up to 10−4g. Subsequently, each specimen, along with its respective crucible, was removed from the furnace and weighed together to obtain the mass change by subtracting the initial weight of crucibles. Condition: room temperature

Processing Text: In this paper, we present a straightforward method for fabricating graphene/Cu composites with an oriented bimodal structure through an in-situ synthesis process combined with hot rolling. Dendritic copper powder, mechanical exfoliation graphene and polyacrylonitrile were used as the raw materials. The graphene/Cu composite with oriented bimodal grains achieves a good balance between strength, ductility and electrical conductivity. Both the fine grains arising from the raised fine particles of dendritic copper powder and the graphene coated on the surface of fine grains facilitate the load transfer, resulting in improved strength of the composites. Furthermore, the formation of coarse grains during sintering and hot rolling deformation contributes to enhanced ductility. Simultaneously, the oriented structure of these coarse grains and graphene sheets establishes an efficient charge transport pathway, ensuring high electrical conductivity. The tensile yield strength of the oriented bimodal composite measures 315 MPa with 0.073 wt% carbon content, while its fracture elongation is 12.4%, and the electrical conductivity remains at 95.7% IACS. This study not only sheds light on the synergistic effects between graphene and copper in a bimodal composite system but also introduces a methodology for tailoring the microstructure to achieve a desired balance between mechanical strength, ductility, and electrical conductivity. Dendritic copper powder, mechanical exfoliation graphene and polyacrylonitrile (PAN) were used as the raw materials. PAN is a common raw material for the preparation of carbon fiber, which is easy to obtain and can be uniformly coated with copper powder and has a significant tendency to graphitization. We obtain bimodal structure by preserving the small raised fine copper particles by transforming PAN to graphene on the surface of dendritic copper powder during heat treatment and sintering process, and then obtain oriented structure by hot rolling. Copper powder (200 mesh electrolytic copper powder), Polyacrylonitrile (PAN) and N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF) were purchased from Aladdin Company. The mechanical exfoliation graphene (G M) was purchased from Xiamen Kaina Graphene Technology Co., Ltd. The amounts of raw materials used for each sample is shown in Table 1. G Mand the PAN were added to DMF for magnetic stirring for 12 h, and then 33 g of copper powder was added to continue stirring for 1 h. The obtained slurry was filtered and put into a copper boat for heat treatment. Heat treatment was performed at 250 °C for 2 h and at 800 °C for 5 min at a heating rate of 10 °C/min under H 2/Ar atmosphere (with a H 2volume fraction of 17%) for all samples. The composite powders were sintered using Spark plasma sintering furnace (SPS) at 700 °C for 5 min under a pressure of 40 MPa and a heating rate of 100 °C/min. The resulting composites had dimensions of 30 mm in diameter and 5 mm in height. Subsequently, the composites were rolled at 500 °C with a total down-rolling of 70%. The schematic representation of the composite material preparation process is illustrated in Fig. 1(a). Carbon content: 0.073 wt%; Fracture elongation: 12.4%; Electrical conductivity: 95.7% IACS

Processing Text: χZr-Ti-5Al-2.5Sn (χ = 0, 10, 20, 30 and 35, wt%, χZTAS) ingots used in this study were prepared by utilizing raw materials of sponge Ti (99.9 wt%), sponge Zr (Zr + Hf ≥ 99.5 wt%), industrially pure Al (99.9 wt%) and Sn (99.9 wt%). The as-cast ingots were prepared by a vacuum non-consumable electro-arc furnace with a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere. To ensure the chemical homogeneity, the ingots were flipped and remelted at least six times. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC, NETZSCH-STA449C) was carried out at a heating rate of 10 °C/min by following ASTM: F2004-05(2010) standard to confirm the temperature range of α + β phase region of TiZrAlSn alloys ( Fig. 1a ). According to the DSC curves of as-cast TiZrAlSn alloys, a medium hot-rolling temperature of 920 °C was selected. The TiZrAlSn ingots were put in a vacuum furnace with an argon atmosphere for 30 min at 920 °C before rolling. The 15 mm button-ingots were rolled five passes by using two-high mill rolls to obtain final 5 mm thin plates, and the plates were placed in the furnace for 1 min to keep the sample temperature at 920 °C and water quenched. A holding time of 5 min was also carried out between every two rolling passes. The rolling reduction was ∼2 mm per pass (rolling velocity: 0.4 m/s) and the total deformation was ∼65%. Detailed hot-rolling processing route was given in Fig. 1b. Base material property; No special conditions mentioned

Processing Text: Elements of equal mass and purity of 99.97 % Pt, 99.99 % Au, 99.99 % Cu and 99.99 % Ni were selected and loaded into a cylindrical alumina crucible of Φ 16 mm after ultrasonic cleaning, and then the alumina crucible was placed in a cylindrical graphite crucible of Φ 18 mm. Then the DHL-400 high vacuum arc melting furnace produced by Shenyang Scientific Instrument Research Center of Chinese Academy of Sciences is used to cast Φ 16 mm × 50 mm Pt-25Au-25Cu-25Ni (wt. %) alloy ingots, in which the vacuum in the furnace is 3 × 10 −3Pa, the melting time is 60 s and the melting temperature is 1800 °C. The ingot of length 50 mm is cut off 5 mm by DK7735 EDM, and then cold rolled into thin sheets with thickness of 0.5 mm. Twenty 5 × 5 mm sheets were cut from the middle of the cold rolled sheet alloy as annealed samples, which were used to observe the microstructure and XRD analysis of the alloy after annealing at different temperatures. The remaining alloy ingots are drawn into Φ0.6 mm alloy wire for tensile tests. The total deformation is 90 %, less than 5 % each time for the rolling and drawing process. In order to prevent the alloy wire from slipping in the tensile test, copper sheets should be clamped and fixed at both ends of the chuck. In the experiment, the alloy samples were annealed in an SK-G08123K vacuum tube annealing furnace. The annealing temperature range is 250-950 °C, and the holding time is 1 h. Condition: Post-aging at 350°C for 1 hour

Herein, we report a LPBFed multiphase Fe-18Mn alloy (γ-austenite, ε-martensite, and α-ferrite) fabricated from pre-alloyed powders. After annealing at 650 °C, the alloy with a uniform microstructure displays a high 1 GPa tensile strength, a good fracture elongation of 16 %, and an extremely high work-hardening rate of 8500 MPa. The grain size of a few hundred nanometers provided the excess Gibbs free energy, resulting in an increase in the stacking fault energy (SFE) to 23.9 mJ/m2. Gas atomized pre-alloyed Fe-18Mn (nominal, wt%) powders with a size range from 15 to 53 μm were used for the LPBF processing. The powder's morphology is shown Fig. 1a. Prior to LPBF experiments, the powders were dried at 80 °C for 4 h. The chemical compositions of the powder and processed part are shown in Table 1. The Fe and Mn contents were measured using inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES, Agilent 720, USA), while the O was measured using an oxygen-nitrogen analyzer (ON-3000, NCS, China). The LPBF processing was carried out using a FS271 M LPBF system (Farsoon, Inc., China) under a protective Ar atmosphere, in which the O content was kept below 0.2 vol.%. The laser parameters were a hatch spacing of 80 μm, and a layer thickness of 30 μm, a laser power of 210 W and a scanning speed of 700 mm/s. Inter-layer rotation between scans of 67° was employed to prevent excessive heat accumulation, as shown in Fig. 1c. The heat-treatments were carried out in a SX2-12TS high-temperature vacuum atmosphere furnace, with a heating rate of ∼10 °C/min. To investigate the effects of a simple stress-relieving anneal, samples were annealed at 450 °C, 550 °C, or 650 °C. To investigate the effects of solution annealing, samples were annealed at 750 °C, 850 °C or 1050 °C. All samples were annealed for 2 h, followed by furnace-cooling to room temperature. Processing state: as-built

316L ASS powders and Ti nanoparticles were employed as deposition materials. The powder morphology and composition of 316L ASS were investigated with a ZEISS Merlin SEM, as illustrated in Fig. 1, with a size distribution between 15 and 53 μm. Ti nanoparticles were incorporated into the base powders at varying concentrations: 0.0 wt%, 0.5 wt%, and 1.0 wt%. To ensure the formation of a homogeneous mixture, 316L ASS powders and Ti particles were mechanically blended via ball milling for 3 h under an inert argon (Ar) atmosphere. The ball milling procedure was conducted with a ball-to-powder weight ratio of 5:1 and a rotational speed of 125 rpm. All the laser processing parameters involved were optimized as follows: the laser power is 600 W, the scanning speed is 4 mm/s, the lifting increment is 0.5 mm, the overlapping rate of 50 % between each track, and the laser beam diameter of 0.5 mm. During the LMD-processed, high purity argon gas was utilized as a protective gas to minimize oxidation as it carried the powders. For microstructural analysis, the specimens were etched with aqua regia, a mix of HCI and HNO 3 in a ratio of 3:1 by volume, for 30 s. They were then examined with an optical microscope (OM). Phase analysis was conducted using a Bruker D8 ADVANCE XRD instrument. The diffraction experiments were carried out in a continuous mode, spanning a 2θ range from 5° to 90° with a scanning speed of 3°/min. Following this, the grain boundary and the phase distribution of the samples were examined using EBSD at an accelerated potential of 15 kV. The sample preparation process involved an electro-polishing procedure in a 9:1 vol ratio mixture of perchloric acid and ethanol at a DC current of 25 V for 50 s, in which the process temperature was maintained at −30 °C. To obtain a more detailed view of the microstructure, thin foils for TEM were obtained using a Struers TenuPol-5 twin-jet electrolytic thinning system. Subsequently, the test was examined using a JEOL JEM-F200 TEM. Processing state: A700-60 sample; Microstructure: nano-scale sigma precipitates, nano/ultrafine-grained microstructure

Processing Text: Both sides of the welded plate were machined into an X-groove, and anchor welds were deposited. The area in the middle of the welded plate for prefabricating cracks was machined into a Y-groove, with a root gap of 2 ± 0.2 mm. Anchor welds were welded before the area for pre-cracking. According to the GB50661-2011 standard [ 26], carbon dioxide arc welding with an electrode YCJ501-1 whose nominal radius equals to 1.2 mm can be used for the anchor weld. Carbon dioxide arc welding with the same electrode YCJ501-1 as the anchor weld was also used for the pre-cracking area, but the welding conditions and interval time were different. The welding process was divided into two steps: first, only the priming weld was deposited for pre-cracking. And then 10 days later, the remaining weld was continuously filled by multi-layer and multi-pass welding. The priming weld was deposited without preheating or drying of the electrode to increase the amount of diffusible hydrogen in the weld. And the priming weld was located at the position of the change in the cross section dimensions where the stress concentration was prominent. Cracked Area Ratio: 22.21%; Fractured at Weld Metal

Processing Text: The cast ingot with an actual composition of Mg-10.15Gd-2.88Dy-2.15Sm-1.51Ag-0.24Zr (wt.%) was prepared from highly pure Mg (99.99 wt%), Ag (99.9 wt%), Mg-22Gd (wt.%), Mg-21Dy (wt.%), Mg-25Sm (wt.%), and Mg-30Zr (wt.%) master alloys in an electric resistant furnace under the atmosphere of pure argon by the water-cooled permanent mold casting method. After standing at ∼750 °C for 20 min and reducing the temperature to 730 °C, the alloy melt was poured into the mold with diameter of ∼90 mm to obtain the as-cast ingot. The ingot was solid solution-treated at 510 °C for 7.5 h, cooled in air for 2 min and then quenched into warm water of ∼80 °C to avoid the generation and propagation of cracks caused by stress during direct quenching in cold water. The solution-treated ingot was machined into the cylindrical-shaped billets with diameter of 80 mm, and then extruded into bars at 350 °C with an extrusion ratio of 28 under an extrusion ram speed of 0.3 mm s−1. The as-extruded sample was named as E. One part of the specimens was heat treated at 480 °C for 2 min (i.e. ESHT) and the other for 20 min; they were both subsequently quickly quenched into warm water of ∼80 °C, which were named as ES2 and ES20, respectively. The aging treatment of the extruded and heat treated samples were aged at 190 °C, and the age-hardening curves were obtained. The samples in peak-aged condition of ES2 and ES20 were named as ES2A and ES20A, respectively. Sample: ES2; Processing state: after extreme short-time heat treatment (ESHT)

Processing Text: The Iron-based MEA was fabricated using a vacuum arc melting furnace, and each raw material was sourced from pure commercial elements with a purity of at least 99.9 %. The master alloy was turned upside down five times during melting to ensure chemically homogenized alloy. During the melting process, the alloy was melted upside down five times to ensure a uniform chemical composition. The as-cast ingots were sealed in an evacuated quartz tube, homogenized at 1150 °C for 24 h, and then water quenched to room temperature. The homogenized ingots were subsequently cold-rolled to 87 % reduction in thickness using laboratory-scale rolling equipment. To obtain various grain sizes of the MEA, the tensile specimens were sealed in a quartz tube and annealed at different temperatures for various durations. The specimens were annealed at 950 °C for 100 s, 25 min, and 1 h, respectively. Additionally, in order to achieve a larger grain size within a shorter annealing time, some specimens were subjected to annealing at 1050 °C for 5 h. Processing Text: PM-HIPed GH3535 specimens were prepared via a typical PM-HIP process. Argon atomized powder with chemistry listed in Table 1 was used, and the HIPing scheme used was 1175 °C/150 MPa/4 h, and the samples extracted from the PM-HIPed block was not subjected to any further heat treatments. Forged GH3535 specimens were extracted from a forged bar with diameter of 50 mm, and this bar was annealed at 1180 °C after the forging process. Samples with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 1 mm were cut from the forged/PM-HIPed material blocks using a wire-cutting machine. One side of each specimen was polished to mirror finish using SiC paper from 600 grit to 1600 grit and 50 nm Al2O3 powder. Finally, specimens were electropolished at 36 V for 10 s using an electrolyte (50 % H2SO4, 40 % glycerol, and 10 % deionized water) at 0 °C. The polished specimens were irradiated by 1 MeV He+ ions with a dose of 3 × 1016 ions/cm2 at both room temperature and 650 °C. The damage profile was predicted using Stopping Range of Ions in Matter (SRIM) 2013 software in the 'Quick Calculation' Kinchin-Pease mode with displacement energies of 40 eV for Ni, Cr and Fe elements, and 60 eV for Mo element. The specimens for microstructure characterization were prepared using the same methods the samples for irradiation. The general microstructure of the materials was examined using an optical microscope (OM) and a Zeiss Merlin Compact SEM equipped with an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detector. The samples for OM observation were etched with a solution consisted of 3 g CuSO4, 10 ml H2SO4, 40 ml HCl and 50 ml H2O. Electron back-scattered diffraction (EBSD) was performed on the electro-polished specimens to analyze the orientations distribution and grain boundary characteristics. The He bubbles and dislocation loops in the irradiated samples were observed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Tecnai G2 F20) with a maximum accelerating voltage of 200 kV. Focus ion beam (FIB) was employed to prepare the cross-sectional TEM samples, thickness of the samples was measured using convergent beam electron diffraction (CEBD). Size and distribution of the helium bubbles in the irradiated samples were characterized using the through focus technique. The dislocation loops were characterized under bright field (BF) mode and dark field (DF) mode. Both the as-received and irradiation specimens were subjected to uniaxial tensile experiments, which were conducted at a constant strain rate of 8.3 × 10−4 s−1 in a uniaxial tensile testing machine (Zwick/Roell Z100) at room temperature. The yield strength of specimens was defined as the stress of 0.2 % strain, and the ultimate tensile strength was derived from the maximum stress. An MTS G200 nano-indentation device with a Berkovich indenter was used to measure the hardness of the samples before and after irradiation both at room temperature. The indent penetration depth was set at 2000 nm and no less than 10 indentation tests were performed on each sample to confirm the statistical significance and the correctness of the test results. Irradiation Temperature: RT; Calculated based on He bubbles and dislocation loops

Processing Text: An ingot of the Fe 50Ni 25Cr 15Al 10 HEAs was produced using an arc-melting furnace. The purity of the raw materials for each element was above 99.95 wt %, and the metal mixture was loaded into a Cu crucible cooled with water. To ensure chemical homogeneity, the HEA ingot was remelted six times. Subsequently, the HEA was drop-casted onto a sheet with dimensions of 25 mm × 4 mm × 80 mm. The sheet was subjected to homogenisation treatment at 1100 °C for 2 h, followed by CR until the thickness was reduced by 60%. The deformed sheet was annealed at 1000 °C for 1 h, after which aging treatment was performed for 10 h at different temperatures (550, 600, 700, and 800 °C); this process was termed as cold rolling and aging (CRA). Before SEM and EBSD, the samples were polished to a mirror surface and then electropolished in a solution of 10 vol% HClO 4 and 90 vol% C 2H 5OH (volume fraction) at a cryogenic temperature of −25 °C. The TEM samples were mechanically ground to a thickness of approximately 40-50 μm and then twin-jet electropolished. Processing state: after 600°C CRA

Laser shock peening (LSP) was implemented to treat aircraft landing gear 50CrVA alloy to improve mechanical properties. The LSP treatment was carried out on the LSP experimental equipment with a wavelength of 1064 nm, a pulse width of 20 ns, and a repeat rate of 10 Hz. In the present work, the laser energy was 7.3 J, the spot diameter was 3 mm, an S-shaped loading path was selected, and the overlap was 50 %. The LSP treatment was carried out on an area of 72 mm × 45 mm in the center of the sample, and the pulse laser beam was always perpendicular to the surface of the sample. The absorbing layer applied was a 0.1 mm thick black tape and the confining layer was a transparent running water layer approximately 1-2 mm thick. The phase composition before and after the LSP treatment were examined by the X-ray diffraction (XRD, X'Pert3 MRD, Malvern Panalytical, Netherlands) using the Co-Kα radiation. The residual stresses in the depth direction were measured by the X-Ray Residual Stress Analyzer following the GB/T 7704-2017 standard. Material Name: CoCrFeNiMn HEA with the addition of Y2O3
Processing Text: The bulk CoCrFeNiMn high entropy alloy with the addition of Y2O3 is fabricated by directed energy deposition, and its microstructures and mechanical properties were investigated in relation to laser power. The substrate is Q235 steel (Mn < 1.4 %, Si < 0.35 %, S < 0.05 %, P < 0.045 %, C < 0.22 %) with dimensions of 12 cm × 15 cm × 10 cm. It was polished using sandpaper, and afterwards, was washed employing alcohol prior to the laser process. Based on the pre-experiments, it has been observed that the deposited layer showed excellent quality when using a powder feeding speed of 0.2 r/min and a spot diameter of 2 mm. During the laser printing process, high-purity argon gas with a flow rate of 15 L/min was used as a shielding gas to prevent oxidation in the melting pool. The deposition strategy was designed to minimize cracks caused by the disparity in thermal expansion coefficients between the substrate and CoCrFeNiMn HEA. The bottom layer, serving as a transition area, was prepared using a laser power of 300 W. This was followed by deposition at gradually increasing laser power. The vertical axis was adorned with an alternating 90-degree crosshatch pattern. The process parameters are as follows: laser power of 700 W, 800 W and 1000 W, scanning speed of 10 mm/s, and an overlapping rate of 50 %. The bulk samples with dimensions of 38 mm × 10 mm × 12 mm were prepared to utilize the same processing parameters and deposition strategy for material characterization and mechanical tests. The samples for material characterization and mechanical test were removed from the Q235 substrate by employing wire electrical discharge machining (EDM). Then, the samples were polished and washed prior to the test. The sample was ground using SiC sandpaper (400#, 800#, 1200#), and then further ground with 2000# sandpaper in water. Then, the samples were electro-polished in a mixed solution prepared with 45 mL absolute alcohol and 5 mL perchloric acid. During the process, the process parameters were set as follows: a voltage of 30 V, a temperature of -30℃, and an etching time of 30 s. The raw materials for CoCrFeNiMn HEA consist of five powders with non-spherical shapes. The Y2O3 powder with a size of about 50-150 um is employed to enhance the strength of HEA. The powders were blended with a ball crusher for 12 h and then dried at a temperature of 120 °C for a minimum of 2 h. Sample: AM-700; Laser Power: 700 W

Processing Text: Four alloys with a nominal composition of Fe-13Cr-4.5Al-1Nb-2Mo- xSi ( x= 0, 0.5, 1, and 2 wt.%) were prepared by arc-melting and cast in the copper moulds with a size of about 55 mm × 22 mm × 15 mm. All cast ingots were first homogenized at 1300 °C for 1 h, followed by air cooling (AC) to room temperature. For the conventional processing route, the alloy ingots were heated to 1300 °C at a heating rate of ∼30 °C/s and rolled at this high temperature to avoid the formation of coarse Laves precipitates. Then, the plates after hot rolling (HR) were further subjected to 300 °C warm rolling (WR) and recrystallization annealing (RX). To introduce the nanoprecipitates into the alloy matrix, a novel processing route was designed. The 15-mm thick alloy plates were first heated to 1100 °C at a heating rate of ∼30 °C/s and hot rolled to 10 mm, and then thinned to 5 mm at 800 °C to refine the coarse grain of the homogenized alloys and produce Laves submicron precipitates, followed by AC to room temperature (RT). The 5 mm-thick alloy plates underwent 300 °C WR with 70% thickness reduction to further refine the layered grain obtained by HR but also introduce more substructures such as dislocation cells. The WR samples experienced fast annealing (FA) to 1150 °C at the heating rate ∼100 °C/s for ∼3 s to promote RX and regression of Laves precipitates obtained in the HR process, followed by water quenching (WQ) to RT. To enhance the density of nucleation sites of Laves nanoprecipitates and promote their uniform distribution in grain interiors during aging, 15% pre-rolling at RT was applied to the alloys to introduce more nucleation sites (e.g. dislocations) before aging with the thickness reduction to ∼1.25 mm. The aging treatment at 600 °C for 1 h was finally performed, followed by AC to RT, rendering a high density of Laves nanoprecipitates prepared uniformly in grain interiors.
