A novel L12 precipitation-strengthened Co51.3Ni19.5Cr19Al6.4Ti3.4Nb0.4 medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with excellent combination of large ductility and high strength was prepared via direct casting. The Co 51.3Ni 19.5Cr 19Al 6.4Ti 3.4Nb 0.4ingot was prepared using the mixtures of high-purity constituent elements in an arc-melting machine within an argon-filled atmosphere. The ingot was inverted and remelted at least four times with electromagnetic stirring to ensure chemical homogeneity. The molten liquid was subsequently drop-cast into a copper mold with dimensions of 70 × 10 × 10 mm 3by gravity. Subsequently, the as-cast alloy was subjected to solution treatment at 1200 °C for 15 h to ensure the uniform composition. HEAs are generally categorized into two elements, as depicted in Fig. 6. Recently, HEAs have more potential in many industries than typical alloys. High entropy alloys (HEAs) are hard, strong, and have many properties, including thermostability and corrosion resistance. HEAs also had exceptional chemical and mechanical characteristics. As a result, these alloys offer enormous development potential [ 34]. Till Jan. 2022, more than 300 high entropy alloys have been processed along with more than 35 principal elements. The concept of HEAs is different from traditional alloys because HEAs are not made up of just one or two components. HEAs have been defined in two ways by researchers: the first is based on composition, while the second is based on entropy [ 35]. So, based on composition, high entropy alloys contain a minimum of 5 main elements in the equimolar or near equimolar ratios, as depicted in Fig. 7. The atomic % of each element for these alloys lies between 5 % to 35 %. Although several additional elements were included in the high entropy alloys, the overall percentage of these elements are <5 % [ 36]. However, based on entropy, the HEAs are defined as the random blending of distinct features that yields configurational entropy (ΔSconf.). Further, these alloys are categorized into three types of alloys, as shown in Fig. 8. These materials are termed as high entropy alloys owing to the fact that their random solid & liquid state has basically higher entropies as compared to those in conventional alloys. The evolution of HEAs from conventional alloys is shown in Fig. 9. The main properties of HEAs are as given below: a) High hardness and strength. In the case of HEAs, the uneven atomic radius of distinct elements causes an intensive lattice distortion effect. These types of effects obstruct the dislocation movement, leading to very high hardness and strength [ 34]. The lattice distortion of HEA containing chromium is shown in Fig. 10. Li et al. [ 35] also reported that severe lattice distortion could occur in the high entropy alloy, and each element has its unique and specific atomic size. Fig. 11represents the schematic representation of a dislocation motion by overcoming a periodic Peierls-Nabarro energy field in HEAs. Elongation to fracture (%) is 31.428571428571423

The Fe51 CCA ingot (2 kg) with a nominal composition of Fe-35.5Ni-4Cr-6.3Al-3.2Ti (at.%) was vacuum induction cast using pure elemental metallic ingots (99.9 wt% purity) and a high-purity argon atmosphere. The cast ingot was homogenised at 1100 °C for 4 h in a muffle furnace purged with argon. The plates with a dimension of 40 mm × 60 mm × 25 mm were cold rolled (CR) to an engineering thickness reduction of 60%. Cold rolling comprised several passes with 5% true strain at each pass to achieve the required reduction in thickness. The recrystallisation temperatures of 900, 950, and 1000 °C were selected from the γ-only phase field (relatively low temperature with single-phase FCC structure to minimise grain growth and to achieve recrystallisation). The cold rolled ingot was subjected to recrystallisation annealing at three different temperatures (900, 950 and 1000 °C) for various durations (5-200 min) followed by water quenching to analyse the kinetics of recrystallisation and grain growth. They were then aged at 630 °C for 16 h to form a γ+γ′-only phase structure with the precipitation of a significant volume fraction of γ′ phase (24%; Fig. 1). The chemical composition of the Fe51 CCA was measured using SEM-EDS and the actual composition was found to be Fe-35.6Ni-4.3Cr-6.1Al-3.5Ti (at.%). d^-0.5 (µm^-0.5) is 0.0280269058295964

Representative structures of Ti xTa 2-xNbZrMo (x= 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) RHEAs were generated by following the SQS method using the Alloy-Theoretic Automated Toolkit (ATAT). The ground state total energies, equilibrium Winger-Seitz radii, the equilibrium bulk moduli, linear elastic constants, polycrystalline moduli and hardness of the alloys were theoretically calculated using the ‘thermo_pw’ and the Quantum Espresso package. The nature of the chemical bonding was analyzed by the LOBSTER package. Then equilibrium phase fraction plots were extracted by CALPHAD with Thermo-calc software. Further, to validate computational results RHEAs were prepared by TIG arc melting and microstructural and phase analysis was done by SEM and XRD. The elastic and mechanical properties were measured by Vickers hardness tester and ultrasound phase spectroscopy. The nominal composition of Ti xTa 2-xNbZrMo (x= 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) RHEAs were prepared by using Ti, Ta, Nb, Zr, and Mo elemental powders with a purity of more than 99 wt%. Arc-melted ingots were fabricated under a Ti-gettered high-purity argon atmosphere in a water-cooled copper hearth. The melted ingots were subjected to several runs of remelting and flipping to ensure chemical homogeneity. The master alloy ingots were fabricated to square (5×5×5 mm 3) shape samples using wire-cut electrical discharge machining (WEDM). Crystalline phases of the as-cast RHEAs were examined by X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis using a Bruker D8 Advanced X-ray diffractometer with Cu K α (wavelength, λ=1.54 Å) radiation and the 2Ɵ range of 30-90˚. Step-scanning mode was used for scanning with a scan rate of 4˚ per minute. The operating voltage and current of 40 kV and 40 mA, respectively, was used for XRD. Moreover, lattice parameters of both the phases were determined using (220) diffraction line. Microstructural characterization and chemical composition of as-casted ingots was carried out by the energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) equipped scanning electron microscopes (SEM FEI Quanta 400 made). The elastic constants such as the longitudinal (C11) and the shear (C44) wave velocities were measured along all three directions of the sample using an Ultrasound phase spectroscopy (UPS) (RAM-5000, RITEC Inc., USA) instrument. The hardness of the as-casted alloys was measured using a LECO® LV700 Vickers hardness tester equipped with a 136˚ Vickers diamond pyramid under 200 g load and a dwell time of 15 s. A minimum of 20 indentations were taken at random sites of the ingots and the average values of hardness as well as corresponding standard deviations were reported in the results section. Moreover, the residual imprints of the indents were imaged using optical microscopy (AXIO Imager.A2m) in the differential interference contrast (DIC) mode. Ta is 1.0118670886075949

Green pellets with a diameter of 10 mm were produced using a 25-ton manual press (Kimaya Engineers, India) at a pressure of 520 MPa. The compacts were sintered in a tube furnace (Swam Equip, India) under a continuous flow of 99.99 % pure argon gas. The green samples were subjected to a sintering temperature range of 560-650 °C, with a 30 °C interval, at a heating rate of 5 °C/min. The duration of sintering was 90 min, followed by controlled cooling within the furnace. Bulk density measurements were performed using the Archimedes principle with a Sartorius Secura YDK03 instrument. Phase analysis was conducted using a Panalytical X-pert powder X-ray diffractometer (Make: Panalytical, Model: X-pert powder). The instrument was equipped with Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm) for data profile acquisition. The process involved a voltage of 45 kV and a current of 30 mA, with a step size of 0.02 and a duration of 25s/step. Optical microscopy (Quasmo ISI Microscope) and scanning electron microscopy (VEGA 3 LMU TESCAN) were employed to characterize the microstructure. Quantification and mapping of elements were performed using a Field Emission Gun Scanning Electron Microscope (FEGSEM) (JEOL, model: JSM 7800F) equipped with an Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS) detector. For TEM analysis, specimens were obtained by cutting 300-micron-thick discs from the sintered samples, followed by metallographic polishing to a thickness of less than 100 μm. Subsequently, ion beam milling was applied to the specimens. The crystal structure and lattice imperfections, such as stacking faults, dislocations, and precipitation and their boundaries at the atomic scale, were investigated using a High Resolution- Transmission Electron Microscope (HR-TEM) (Model: JEOL JEM 2100, at an operating voltage of 200 kV). Nanoindentation measurements were performed using a Berkovich diamond indenter with a radius of 150 nm, featuring an included angle of 142.30° and a half angle of 65.27°, within a NANOINDENTER device (BRUKER'S HYSITRON TI PREMIER). A 2 mN load was used for the nanoindentation study and the distance between the two consecutive indentations was 3 μm to evaluate the hardness and modulus. The load-displacement curves were used to generate hardness and elastic modulus profiles across the matrix, intermetallic, and particle interfaces. The room temperature and isothermal compressive strength (at 200 °C, 250 °C, and 300 °C) of the composite were assessed using cylindrical samples (φ10mm x l = 15 mm) with an aspect ratio (l/d) of 1.5. The test was performed using a Universal Testing Machine (Jinan, WDW-100S) following the ASTM E−09standard. For the isothermal compression test, a furnace setup was employed. All samples were sintered at 620 °C due to its verified superior density in line with our previous findings. All samples were subjected to a strain of 0.5 and then water-quenched to facilitate microstructural observation. The strain rate for both room temperature and isothermal tests was set at 10 −4S −1. Ni (Wt %) is 2

Spherical 1060 pure aluminum (Al) powders (purity＞99.6 %) and CuO powders (purity＞99.9 %) were used as raw powders, whose average diameters were 5 μm and 1 μm, respectively. The mass ratio of Al: CuO powders was 95:5. The Al/CuO blended powders were mixed by a planetary ball milling machine (QM-3SP2, Nanjing University Instrument Plant) with a rotation velocity of 200 rpm. The milling time and ball-to-powder ratio were 10 h and 10:1, respectively. The milled powders were pre-compacted at 200 MPa for 60 s by a cold tubular mold. Then, the round preform was placed in the Al mold and was sheared and stirred by a processing tool. This severe plastic deformation (SPD) process was named deformation-driven metallurgy (DDM) [20,21], which is derived from friction stir welding [22]. The rotational velocity of the tool was varied during the preparation process to introduce more substructure in materials. The rotational velocity was initially set at 500 rpm and changed to 100 rpm when the sample was only 1.5 mm (h 1in Fig. 1) in thickness. Then, keep it until 1 mm (h 2in the Fig. 1) and hold for 10 s. The detailed schematic of the whole preparation process is given in Fig. 1. Al-5wt.%CuO prepared with a constant rotational velocity of 500 rpm was used as the control group. Total strain (%) is 13.308823529411764

Pure metals Al, Co, Cr, Fe and Ni with a purity of 99.5% were weighed according to the nominal composition, and the pre-alloyed ingots were melted by non-consumable vacuum arc furnace. Each pre-alloyed ingot was melted 5 times, and the ingot was turned over before each re-melting to ensure homogeneous composition. Metal rods with a diameter of 7 mm were cut from the pre-alloyed ingot by spark machining, and the surface was polished and cleaned to serve as a material for directional solidification. The metal rods with a total length of about 10 cm were placed in the ceramic tubes and then placed in the Bridgeman directional solidification furnace, where the rods were melted by radiative heat transfer through graphite and held for 50 min to ensure complete melting and uniform temperature distribution. The alloy melt was withdrawn into the Ga In liquid using a pulling system with withdrawal speeds of 5 μm/s, 50 μm/s, 100 μm/s, 150 μm/s and 200 μm/s, respectively. When the withdrawal distance reached 4 cm, the alloy melt was rapidly pulled into the Ga In liquid and quenched to retain the solid-liquid (S-L) interface morphology. Finally, a directional solidification rod with a length of about 10 cm was obtained, including non-directional solidification zone, directional solidification zone and quenching zone. Directional solidification rods were cut along the direction parallel to the heat flow to prepare specimens for microstructure observation and mechanical property testing. The phase composition was analyzed by X-ray diffraction (XRD, MXP21V AHF) using Cu Ka radiation in the range of 20°-100° at a rate of 8°/min. The microstructure and element distribution were analyzed by scanning electron microscope (SEM, TM4000) and transmission electron microscope (TEM FEI Talos F200). Electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD, Zeiss Super55) was used to determine the phase structure and strain distribution. The EBSD samples were electro-polished in a mixture of 90% alcohol and 10% perchloric acid with an applied voltage of 15 V for 10-12 s at room temperature. The mechanical properties were tested using an Instron 5569 universal tensile testing machine at a tensile speed of 1 mm/min. The tensile specimen is dog-bone shaped, with a gauge length of 16 mm, a thickness of 1.8 mm, and a width of 2 mm. The specimens under each directional solidification condition were tested three times to ensure the accuracy of the data. The nano-hardness of different phases was tested by G200 nanoindentation, and the maximum depth was set to 300 nm. Solidification rate(µm/s) is 4.838709677419345

All specimens were manufactured by an EOS M290 L-PBF machine, equipped with a 400 W Yb-fiber laser with a laser spot size of 80μm in diameter. The printing laser power was 210 W and the laser moved in a stripe printing pattern with a 50μm hatch distance. The printing head scanning speed was 1750 mm/s and the powder layer thickness was 20μm. After each layer was printed, the subsequent layer was rotated by 67 ∘ as indicated in Fig. 1a for the coherence of microstructure through whole specimens. After the printing process, several heat treatments were implemented on all specimens. The first step was hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C for 4 h under 200 MPa. The following step was standard solution heat treatment at 1120 °C for 2 h. The final step was aging at 850 °C for 24 h. After heat treatments, all specimens were machined in dog-bone shaped tensile bars as shown in Fig. 1c. The gauge length was 24.5 mm and the gauge diameter varied from 3 mm to 5 mm in Fig. 1d. Uniaxial tensile tests were carried out on an Instron 5982 universal testing system with a 100 kN loading capacity and crosshead movement speed ranging from 0.0001 to 1016 mm per minute. The temperature was measured by three temperature sensors at three zones of the furnace. An extra sensor was attached to the middle of specimens for accurate measurement of temperatures at the surface. The testing temperature ranged from 650 °C to 950 °C for different specimens. A dwell time of 2 h after reaching the target temperature was used before the start of tests to achieve a homogeneous thermal distribution as well as for stabilizing the thermal expansion of the specimens. The strain rate was 10 −3, that is, a displacement rate of 1.47 mm/min. The strain was measured by means of a 7361C extensometer attached to the middle of the specimens. Once the strain measured by the extensometer reached 2%, the strain data was read from the crosshead displacement. Pristine specimen’s surfaces and cross sections from the near fracture surface were mechanical polished. For the phase identification, the surfaces were etched in a 10% phosphoric acid solution. A field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Hitachi SU70) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was occupied for morphology observation at an acceleration voltage of 20 kV. The corresponding chemical composition was determined by EDS and analyzed in the Oxford Instruments’ INCA software. EBSD was measured via an Oxford NORDLYS EBSD detector and acquired by Flamenco software. nan is 650.8403361344538

For the ANN alloys, the aging treatments were conducted at 550 °C by varying holding time, i.e. 1.5 h, 3 h, and 24 h, respectively. Subsequently, the alloy was rolled with a reduction ratio of 75 % (final thickness ∼2.5 mm) and then annealed at 800 °C for 15 min followed by water quenching. For the ANN alloys, the aging treatments were conducted at 550 °C by varying holding time, i.e. 1.5 h, 3 h, and 24 h, respectively. It was found that the partial recrystallization occurs and precipitates BCC particles by performing cold-rolling, annealing and aging treatments. Uniform elongation (%) is 54.38073394495413

The equimolar CoCrFeNi HEA ingot used in this work was prepared by vacuum induction levitation melting from pure Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni metals with 99.9 wt.% purity constituent elements. The ingot was remelted four times to promote chemical homogeneity and then dropped into a rectangular cross-section copper mold with a length of 300 mm and an inner diameter of 25 mm. The ingot was cut to a rod of diameter 20 mm and length 200 mm, which was then homogenized at 1473 K for 24 h. The rod was first hot-rotary swaged to 8 mm in diameter along the longitudinal direction after preheating at 1173 K for 1 h, and then hot-drawn to 1 mm in steps at 1023 K. Subsequently, the HEA wires of diameter 1 mm was subjected to multi-pass cold-drawing at ambient temperature with an areal reduction of ∼10% followed by annealing at 1173 K for 1 h in each step, resulting in a final diameter of ∼70 µm with a length of more than 300 m. The CoCrFeNi microfibers were further treated by ECT. The electric current was applied parallel to the length direction of the treated microfiber using a precision direct current (DC) power supply for 480 s with various current densities of j= 100, 120, 140, 160, 180, 200 A/mm², and the corresponding specimens are labeled as ECT100, ECT120, ECT140, ECT160, ECT180 and ECT200, which reach a stable temperature of 623 K, 747 K, 850 K, 943 K, 1013 K, and 1075 K during the ECT, respectively, as measured by an FLIR A325sc infrared camera. Engineering strain (%) is 46.05809128630705

The Inconel 718 superalloy was fabricated using spark plasma sintering (SPS) technology with varying sintering temperatures and heating rates. The raw Inconel 718 superalloy powders were sourced from Jiangsu Vilory Advanced Materials Technology Co., Ltd., China. The powders primarily consist of Ni (51.5 %), Cr (22.48 %), Fe (19.67 %), Nb (3.78 %), Al (1.31 %), Ti (1.25 %), etc. The powders were provided in sizes ranging from 30 to 70 µm. In order to decrease particle size, increase contact area, and enhance interparticle integration during the sintering process, ball milling was employed. The parameters used for ball milling can be found in Table 1. Cylindrical sintered specimens were then prepared using a spark plasma sintering system (SPS-mini, Shanghai Chenhua Science and Technology Co., Ltd., China). The sintering system had a maximum current of 3000 A, a maximum voltage of 30 kV, a maximum heating rate of 300 °C/min, and a minimum vacuum of 10 −4Pa. Sintering tests were carried out using various temperatures and heating rates under a sintering pressure of 50 MPa and a holding time of 5 min, as indicated in Table 2. The resulting 5 sets of sintered specimens were named S-1 to S-5, respectively. To investigate the effect of pulse current on the sintering neck formation process in the heating stage, 4 specimens were sintered with a heating rate of 100 °C/min, and the sintering time is listed in Table 3. When the target sintering time was reached, the sintering process was immediately halted, obtaining a sintering specimen with the characters of that time. The Inconel 718 superalloy powders after ball-milling were weighed using a balance, and loaded into graphite molds. Before filling the powders into the mold, the graphite spray was evenly sprayed on the inner wall of the mold cavity and the surface of the punches, to prevent the powder from sticking to the mold cavity and the punches when sintering, improving the dimensional accuracy of the sintered specimens. The experimental molds and punches are composed of hot-pressed graphite material (type GTTKG347) with a compressive strength of 100 MPa, supplied by Shanghai Chenda Company, China. A miniature temperature-measuring hole is located at the center of the outer surface of the mold, which is aligned with the temperature-measuring device during installation to facilitate real-time measurement of the sintering temperature. nan is S-1

Ti2NbVAl0.3Zrx (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) LRHEAs were prepared by the vacuum arc melting furnace under the protection of high-purity argon gas. Metal particles with purity >99.95 % were used as raw materials. In order to avoid melting losses and melting segregation, Ti-Al and Zr-V-Nb intermediate alloys were prepared. Finally, the intermediate alloys were combined and melted six times repeatedly. Before melting, the air pressure in the chamber was reduced to 3*10−3Pa and the chamber underwent five purging cycles with high-purity argon gas. This was followed by melting Ti ingots to remove residual oxygen in the chamber and prevent sample contamination. SEM samples were polished using a 0.3 μm alumina suspension, followed by metallographic etching using a solution of HCL, HNO3, and HF in a ratio of 10:3:1. TEM samples were mechanically ground to 50 μm and subsequently thinned using an ionic thinning machine (Gatan 695). Tensile tests were conducted on the specimens using an electronic universal testing machine (Instron 68 MT-55) at a quasi-static strain rate of 1*10−3S−1. The tensile samples were identified with a section size of 5mm × 2mm × 1.5 mm and were mechanically ground to 2000 mesh prior to the commencement of the experiment. Vickers hardness of the samples was measured using TMHV-1000Z with a load of 200g and a force holding time of 15s. The corrosion behavior of the current alloy system was tested using an electrochemical workstation (VersaSTAT 3F) in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. The sample size was 10mm × 10mm × 4 mm, with a test area 1 cm2, and was mechanically ground to 2000 mesh prior to testing. Electrochemical tests were conducted in a three-electrode electrolytic cell setup, with the sample serving as the working electrode, the saturated calomel electrode (SCE) as the reference electrode, and the platinum electrode as the auxiliary electrode. The open circuit potential was initially stabilized for 1800s, followed by potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) tests. The PDP test was conducted at a scan rate of 0.333 mV/s, starting from an initial potential of −0.3V SCE(vs. OCP) and ending at 2V SCE(vs. OCP). EIS measurements were carried out with an amplitude of 5 mV/s and a frequency range from 105Hz to 10−2Hz. Each sample underwent three tests under identical conditions to ensure result accuracy. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; Thermo Scientific K-Alpha) analyzed the oxide film formed on the sample surface. Engineering Strain (%) is 5.998217468805704

In present study, a 30 kg ingot of Fe-17Mn alloy was cast by using a high-frequency vacuum-induction furnace. Fabrication of CrCoNi alloy by pulsed-wave laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). (a)A schematic of pulsed-LPBF of pre-alloyed CrCoNi powder with an inserted crystalline lattice structure of the MEA. (b)A schematic showing the comparison of emission mode between pulsed-wave and continuous-wave lasers. (c)As-built microstructural features of the pulsed-LPBF CrCoNi alloy at various length scales from the cross-section view. The pulsed-wave laser induces extra thermal cycles, generating additional pre-existing dislocations that are uniformly distributed within the interiors of solidification cells, a phenomenon distinct from conventional AM. The first batch of CrCoNi alloy samples was printed by a customized LPBF machine equipped with a 200 W SPI fiber laser source, as schematically shown in Fig. 1a. In contrast with the continuous-wave lasers used in typical LPBF processes, the laser in this work was emitted in repeated pulses at a frequency of 1000 kHz ( Fig. 1b). The working duration of each pulse was ∼250 ns. The wavelength and the spot size of the laser were 1060 nm and 100 µm respectively. The prints employed gas-atomized CrCoNi powder with a nominal composition shown in Table S1. The particle size of the spherical powder ranged from 20 to 53 µm. The pulsed-LPBF prints were conducted in a nitrogen atmosphere and maintained at a constant parameter set including a laser power of 200 W, a powder layer thickness of 40 µm, and a scan rotation of 90° between layers. Initial optimization of process parameters was conducted with cubic CrCoNi samples (6 mm × 6 mm × 6 mm) using scanning speeds of 400-1000 mm/s and hatch spacings of 40-100 µm. After observations of polished cross-section surfaces by optical microscopy, the optimized pulsed-LPBF process window was refined to scanning speeds of 500-800 mm/s and hatch spacings of 60-100 µm, ensuring the relative density of the printed MEA is higher than 99.8% ( Fig. S1a). The surface roughness generated within this refined process window is in a range of 10-20 µm ( Fig. S1b). These cubic samples were printed starting with a 0° laser scan followed by a 90° rotation. The samples (30 mm length × 10 mm width × 6 mm height) for mechanical tests were printed starting with a 45° laser scan followed by a 90° rotation. To compare the effect of continuous-wave and pulsed-wave lasers on microstructure and mechanical properties, a second batch of CrCoNi samples was printed with the same geometric size using a commercial LPBF machine (EOS M290). The continuous-wave laser used in this batch had the same wavelength (1060 nm) and spot size (100 µm) as the pulsed-wave laser used in the first batch. To decouple the influence of other factors, the print parameters were selected from the process window optimized in the first batch print: a laser power of 200 W, a scanning speed of 500 mm/s, a hatch spacing of 80 µm, a layer thickness of 40 µm, and a scan rotation of 90°. The relative density of the fabricated sample was also higher than 99.8% ( Fig. S1c). Uniform elongation (%) is 1.6252390057361374

A Ti6242 bar was employed in the as hot-rolled condition with a chemical composition of Ti-6.31Al-1.95Sn-4.12Zr-1.91Mo-0.1Si (wt.%), and its β transition temperature ( Tβ) was measured to be approximately 1006 °C by a DIL805A/D type dilatometer. The samples were subjected to three-step heat treatment to obtain heterogeneous structure. Firstly, the samples were solution treated at 950 °C for 1 h, and then quenched in the water (WQ), designated as Step 1. Secondly, the samples were rapidly up-quenched to the single β phase region for 12 s by high-frequency induction heating to transform the equiaxed α pphase to β phase, but maintained the solute partition in the two phases as the limited solution time was not enough for the homogenization of alloying elements (Step 2). Finally, the samples were aged at 590 and 620 °C for 8 h, respectively, and then cooled in air (AC) to precipitate heterostructure with different thicknesses of α lamella (Step 3). The two samples after three-step heat treatment were called HS-590 and HS-620. For comparison, the EM samples with homogeneous microstructure were prepared using the same treatments in steps 1 and 3, and designated as EM-590 and EM-620. Elongation (%) is 3.19225037257824

A series of Hf xNbTaTiV ( x= 0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00 in molar ratio) alloy ingots with different Hf content were synthesized from high purity (>99.95%) metals by vacuum arc melting within a Ti-gettered ultra-high purity Ar (>99.99%) atmosphere. The as-cast ingots were flipped and remelted at least six cycles to ensure chemical homogeneity. The button-shaped ingots were rolled into thin sheets approximately 1 mm in thick at room temperature using a precision rolling mill (JH-RZH-110, China). More than three dog-bone-shaped samples were sliced from the rolled sheets for each alloy component along the rolling direction using an electrical spark erosion wire cutting machine (DK77, China). The size of the dog-bone samples was about 16 mm in length, 12 mm in width, and 1 mm in thickness. Processing Text: In-situ titanium boride (TiB) reinforced titanium matrix composites (TMCs) were fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) technique. The Ti6Al4V alloy powders were mechanically mixed with 0.5 wt% and 1 wt% TiB 2nanoparticles, respectively, using a three-dimensional mixer (JXHY-2L). The mixing process included a speed of 80 rpm/min and a duration of 4 h. To avoid the adverse effect of energy on the properties of the alloy powders during the mechanical mixing process, the machine was paused for cooling at room temperature for 10 min after every 20 min of mixing, ensuring mixed uniformly. The process parameters for fabricating samples with Ti6Al4V powders and 0.5 wt% TiB 2/Ti6Al4V powders, respectively, were as follows: a laser power of 180 W, a scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, a hatching spacing of 120 µm, and a layer thickness of 30 µm; additionally, a short linear scanning strategy was implemented with an interlayer rotation angle of 67°. To alleviate residual stress accumulation during processing, the substrate was preheated to 180 °C. Prior to processing, the powders underwent drying in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 8 h; high-purity argon gas was introduced to maintain oxygen levels below 100 ppm to prevent oxidation within the melt pool. Additional content of TiB2 (wt.%) is 0.0

The ingots of Al 5Ti 8(FeCoNi) 86.9B 0.1(at. %) HEA were fabricated from metals with purity exceeding 99.9 wt.% in a vacuum arc melting furnace. Each ingot underwent five remelting cycles to ensure chemical homogeneity before being cast into a water-cooled copper mould measuring 50 × 15 × 10 mm 3. Subsequently, the cast ingots were homogenized at 1200 °C for two hours and then subjected to multi-pass rolling at room temperature to achieve a 50 % reduction in thickness (from 10 mm to 5 mm). Following rolling, the samples were heat-treated at 1165 °C for 10 min to achieve a recrystallized FCC-type grain microstructure (abbreviated as HT alloy). Afterwards, the samples underwent further multi-pass rolling to achieve an 80 % reduction in thickness (from 5 mm to 1 mm), abbreviated as the CR alloy. The cold-rolled samples were then annealed in the FCC+L1 2two-phase region ( Fig. 1) at 760 and 800 °C for two hours and were designated as CR760 and CR800 alloys, respectively. All heat treatments were followed by quenching in water. Elongation (%) is 32.175141242937855

Processing Text: The Ti54Nb14Zr15Mo17 alloys were prepared by arc-melting. The Ti54Nb14Zr15Mo17 alloys, with high Mo Eq, Bo, and Md values, fall within the range of β-titanium alloys. The crystal structures were identified by an X-ray diffractometer (XRD, Bruker D8 Advance, Germany). To study the hot processing behavior and microstructure evolution of the Ti54Nb14Zr15Mo17 alloys, single-pass compression tests on small bars were conducted using the THERMECMASTOR-Z100KN thermal simulation machine. Prior to the tests, graphite plates coated with tantalum sheet lubricant were placed between the specimens and the dies to reduce friction. Four different testing temperatures (950 ℃, 1000 ℃, 1050 ℃, and 1100 ℃) and four different strain rates (0.001 s⁻¹, 0.01 s⁻¹, 0.1 s⁻¹, and 1 s⁻¹) were utilized. After the hot compression tests, the deformed alloys were water-quenched immediately to maintain the deformation microstructure. True stress-strain curves were obtained through hot compression tests, and a constitutive equation was derived to relate flow stress to hot deformation parameters. A hot processing map was constructed based on the dynamic material model and verified by deformation microstructure. The mechanical properties of the alloys were tested by selecting the optimal hot processing parameters from the map, and the orientation distribution function (ODF) method was employed to quantitatively investigate the texture evolution under different deformation conditions. The DRX mechanisms were analyzed in detail by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Compressive Modulus (GPa) is 48.034188034188034

Four different testing temperatures (950 ℃, 1000 ℃, 1050 ℃, and 1100 ℃) and four different strain rates (0.001 s⁻¹, 0.01 s⁻¹, 0.1 s⁻¹, and 1 s⁻¹) were utilized. After the hot compression tests, the deformed alloys were water-quenched immediately to maintain the deformation microstructure. True stress-strain curves were obtained through hot compression tests, and a constitutive equation was derived to relate flow stress to hot deformation parameters. A hot processing map was constructed based on the dynamic material model and verified by deformation microstructure. The mechanical properties of the alloys were tested by selecting the optimal hot processing parameters from the map, and the orientation distribution function (ODF) method was employed to quantitatively investigate the texture evolution under different deformation conditions. The DRX mechanisms were analyzed in detail by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Compressive Modulus (GPa) is 93.76068376068376

A eutectic high-entropy alloy powder, AlCoCrFeNi 2.1, was prepared using spray atomisation. The powder exhibited a typical spherical structure with particle sizes of 23.4-55.6 μm. The average particle size was determined to be 36.103 μm, as shown in Fig. 1(a). The experiment employed the EP-M260 selective laser melting additive manufacturing system, with a power of 500 W and a laser spot diameter of 76-100 μm. Steel was selected as the substrate material, and the process involved continuous linear scanning under the protection of high-purity Ar gas ( Fig. 1(b) and (c)). The scanning path was specifically designed for laser melting and additive manufacturing of cubic specimens. The process parameters for the chosen laser melting equipment were as follows: laser scanning spacing of 100 μm, powder layer thickness of 30 μm, and scanning speed of 900 mm/s. The input laser power was adjusted by modifying the laser power. Where, the opotimizal parameters can be obtained with the denisity of specimans by selective laser melting additive manufacturing, previously. The sample was prepared by stamping the sample into circular pieces with a diameter of 3 mm and manually grinding them to below 100 μm. Before characterisation, the sample was mechanically polished to a mirror-like state and then chemically etched for 5-15 s using a diluted acidic solution (concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl) and concentrated nitric acid (HNO 3) in a volume ratio of 3:1). An HV-1000Z micro-hardness tester was used to conduct hardness tests on the samples printed using various parameters. These tests were performed under a load of 500 g for a residence time of 10 s, and the upper and lower surfaces of the samples were polished before testing. Each sample surface was tested five times at different positions to obtain an average value. The tensile strength tests were used a 5982B18430 universal tensile testing machine operated at a strain rate of 0.1 mm/min. According with the standard ISO 6892, the specimen was prepared via wire cutting to obtain a tensile sample with dimensions of 50 × 30 × 3 mm 3. Before testing, all the samples were subjected to surface polishing. To investigate the anisotropy of the mechanical properties of the additive-manufactured specimens at room temperature, the tensile loading directions were selected as parallel (X-Y) and perpendicular (X-Z) to the printing direction. Before testing, the 1 × 1 × 1 cm 3square sample was cut from the substrate using wire cutting. Standard tensile specimens with lengths of 50 mm, widths of 30 mm, and thicknesses of 3 mm were processed via wire cutting. All the samples were polished before testing. The electrochemical impedance of each sample was measured using a PARSTAT2273 electrochemical workstation, and the Tafel polarisation curves of the samples were obtained using a Coaster CS310 electrochemical workstation. The test was terminated when the current density exceeded 10 mA·cm −2, and the duration of testing was 1 h. In the electrochemical impedance test, a 3.5 % NaCl solution was selected as the corrosion solution with a scanning potential of 0.5-1.2 V. VED (J/mm³) is 166.99658703071674

Total elongation (%) is 26.2992125984252,MPa,A 50 kg ingot of lightweight steel with a composition of Fe-18Mn-8Al-1C-5Ni (wt%) was prepared in a vacuum induction melting furnace (chemical composition analyzed by spark optical emission spectroscopy: Fe-18.20Mn-7.98Al-1.03C-5.02Ni wt%). The as-forged steel was hot rolled to 5 mm at 1200°C with a total reduction of 93 %, followed by water quenching (referred to as "WQ"). The hot-rolled steels were homogenized at 1200°C for 1 hour and then cold-rolled to a final thickness of 1 mm with a total reduction of 80 %. Three types of heat treatment schedules were applied to the cold rolled specimens in the present study, as illustrated in the Fig. 1. The cold-rolled strips were at 1000°C for 50 minutes to obtain full recrystallization (referred to as "AN50"), and annealed at 850 °C for 5 minutes to induce partial recrystallization (referred to as "AN5"), followed by WQ. Pre-straining was conducted in the AN5 specimen with several tensile strains of 0 %, 5 %, and 15 %. Subsequently, these AN5 specimens with different pre-strains were annealed at 850°C for 7 minutes with WQ. These pre-strained and sequent annealed specimens were denoted as "0 %-AN7", "5 %-AN7", and "15 %-AN7," respectively.The AN5 specimen with a total elongation of approximately 26.3% was tested under conditions that included partial recrystallization after annealing at 850°C for 5 minutes, followed by water quenching.

Processing Text: The spherical pre-alloy powders of the CoCrNi HEA and Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10HEA were prepared by vacuum induction melting gas atomization. The laminated HEAs were printed by a direct energy deposition method. During printing, the CoCrNi HEA and the Fe 50Mn 30Co 10Cr 10HEA were alternately deposited up to a desired height. The scanning path follows a zigzag pattern, where the scanning direction is rotated by 90° between each adjacent layer to minimize residual stress. Here, the laminated HEAs were successfully fabricated with three different layer spacings of 0.1 mm, 0.3 mm, and 0.5 mm, denoted as LH0.1, LH0.3 and LH0.5, respectively. The laser diameter is 1 mm, and the powder feeding airflow and protective airflow are fixed at 5 and 10 L/min, respectively. Sample is LH0.1

Elemental powders of tungsten (W), niobium (Nb), tantalum (Ta), and vanadium (V) with purities exceeding 99.5 % were employed to fabricate the equal-atomic ratio WNbTaV RHEA samples. A planetary ball-mill (QM-3SP2, Nanjing Chishun Technology Co., Ltd.) was utilized to mix raw powders for 24 h at 300 rpm with tetrafluoroethylene tank, ZrO 2balls and ball-to-powder ratio of 5:1. Following ball milling, the powders were consolidated using SPS (LABOX-350, Sinterland, Japan) apparatus. As observed, the prepared powders were loaded into a graphite mold, and sequentially heated to target temperatures (1300, 1400, 1500, and 1600 ℃) at a rate of 100 ℃/min. Each temperature was sustained for 5 min under a uniaxial pressure of 30 MPa, followed by cooling to room temperature in the furnace. Specifically, the powder body was held at 1200 ℃ for 10 min during heating to facilitate the solid solution formation among the powders. After the SPS process, the samples underwent grinding and polishing for subsequent observation and experiments. Sintering temperature (°C) is 1300

This work utilizes a consolidation technique that uses high-pressure & high-temperature (HPHT) to produce an ultrafine-grained (UFG) FeCrCoNi HEA. The high consolidation pressure has two effects: 1) reducing interparticle distances due to the enforced plastic deformation of individual granules, making for high bulk density, and 2) reducing the diffusivity, thereby reducing the growth speed of grains. The high strain is primarily the result of a reduction in the diameter and content of Cr-Mn-O-rich oxides - which reduce the interface area between the soft matrix and hard oxides, thereby suppressing the sources of crack generation - due to the utilization of high pressure. UFG FeCoNiCr HEA was prepared by MA and HPHT techniques. Applying a substantial consolidation pressure (4 GPa) leads to the UFG FeCoNiCr HEA achieving a relative density near 99 %. The consolidated UFG FeCoNiCr HEA exhibits an average grain diameter of approx. 181 nm and displays exceptionally high yield strength of approx. 1526 MPa - significantly higher than the yield strength (162 MPa) of CG FeCoNiCr HEA - and a high fracture of 35 %. The high yield strength is predominantly brought about by the UFG matrix. The achievement of the UFG matrix can be attributed primarily to the application of a high consolidation pressure, which has two effects: 1) reduces interparticle distances because of the enforced plastic deformation of the individual powder particles and 2) reducing the diffusivity, thereby reducing the rate of grain growth. The high strain is predominately induced by fine diameter and low content of coarse Cr-Mn-O-rich oxide. High sintering pressure suppresses the oxides to grow, reducing the interface area between soft matrix phases and hard oxides, and thus decreasing the sources of crack generation. Strain (%) is 4.959349593495936

Material Name: RHEAs containing both W and C
Processing Text: Raw materials with purities higher than 99.95 wt.% were used to prepare the W-Ta-Ti-V-C RHEAs by vacuum arc melting under a Ti-gettered, high-purity argon atmosphere. Here, the C element was introduced by adding WC particles. To ensure the homogeneity of RHEAs, W-Ta and Ti-V-WC middle-alloys were firstly prepared by 4 melting times respectively. The middle-alloys were then merged to fabricate ingot, which was flipped and remelted 12 times, and maintained a liquid state for about 5 min in each melting. The compressive samples with dimensions of 3 mm × 3 mm × 6 mm were cut from the prepared ingots by wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) and the mirror-like surfaces were achieved by mechanical polishing for the following microstructural observation. The phase structure of prepared RHEAs was inspected by performing standard X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observation on an X-ray diffractometer (PANalytical X-Pert PRO MPD, Netherlands) and high-resolution transmission electron microscope (Talos F200X G2, China), respectively. The TEM foils were prepared by ion milling (Gatan 695, USA) and focused ion beam (FIB, Crossbeam 350, Germany) lift-out technology. The phase stability of the RHEAs was inspected by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) using a simultaneous thermal analyzer (Netzsch STA449F3, Germany) under an argon atmosphere with a heating rate of 10 °C/min from 25 °C to 1400 °C. Annealing treatment was also performed to examine the phase stability of the RHEAs in a muffle furnace (KSL-1100X, HF-Kejing, China) under an argon atmosphere with a heating rate of 10 °C/min from 25 °C to 1000 °C and a soaking time of 24 h. The microstructure of RHEAs was observed on the field-emission scanning electron microscopes (SEM, Hitachi SU8020, Japan and Gemini 500, Germany), and the element distribution was detected using the equipped energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS). Fracture strain (%) is 7.303609341825904

Following this, the cold-rolled plates were subjected to various annealing treatments with different temperatures and cooling rates. A subset of cold-rolled plates was annealed at temperatures of 300 °C, 325 °C, 350 °C, 375 °C, and 400 °C for 2 h, followed by faster cooling (FC) down to 250 °C at a cooling rate of approximately 3.65 °C/min, and then air cooled to room temperature. These samples were labeled as X-FC, with “X” indicating the specific annealing temperature. Another subset of the cold-rolled plates was annealed at 400 °C for 2 h and subsequently cooled with a slower cooling rate (SC) of about 0.5 °C/min down to room temperature, which is designated as 400°C-SC. All annealed specimens were underwent a solid solution treatment (SST) at 505 °C for 60 min before being quenched in ambient water. To determine the engineering mechanical properties, the materials were ultimately aged at 152 °C for 38 h following a 5 % pre-stretch deformation. Both cold-rolled and APC specimens were annealed at 300 °C-400 °C for 30 s-3600 s. Subsequently, rapid quenching in ambient water and HV testing were performed. For the HV testing, a 500 g load was applied for 15 s with an average of 10 measurements per sample. The Al 5Ti 8(FeCoNi) 86.9B 0.1 (at.%) ingots were fabricated by melting high-purity (>99.9 wt.%) raw materials (Al, Ti, Fe, Co, Ni, and B) in a vacuum arc furnace under a protective argon atmosphere. Each ingot underwent 5 melting cycles and was then cast into a copper mold with dimensions of 50×15×10 mm 3. The samples were subsequently heated to 1200 °C and held for 2 hours to achieve homogenization. Next, they were cut using an electrical discharge machine (EDM) to dimensions of 50×15×5 mm 3 along the thickness direction. Using powder metallurgy and hot extrusion techniques, Al5083 MMCs were then created with differing amounts of SiC/RGO. The current study used Al5083 powder for the matrix material. Initially, SiC/RGO reinforcing particles were combined with 5083 aluminum alloy powder in varying mass fractions of 0.1 %, 0.3 %, and 0.5 %. The resulting mixture was transferred to a ball milling tank, followed by the addition of 1 g of stearic acid. Afterward, the tank was flushed with argon gas, and the materials underwent milling in an ND7-1L ball mill using a ball-to-material ratio of 5:1, a rotational speed of 200 rpm, for a duration of 10 h. The 10-hour ball milling converted spherical 5083 aluminum alloy powder into flakes, enhancing sintering performance through increased surface area and mechanical interlocking. The uniformly mixed powder was subsequently transferred to a SK2-2-12TPB2 vacuum tube furnace for heating at 400 °C, the process that facilitates the removal of stearic acid from the powder. Thereafter, the SiC/RGO/Al5083 powder was placed into the cylindrical mold and use a hydraulic press to obtain the φ40 × 4 mm 3shape. Then, the mold and the cold-extruded billet were placed into the hot extrusion equipment together. Subsequent to a 30-minute hold at 500 °C, the aluminum matrix composite rods were hot-extruded according to an extrusion ratio of 1:16. Content of SiC/RGO (wt.%) is 0.0

The RHEAs of NbTaTiV were prepared by MA and SPS. The process was shown in Fig. 1. First, the raw powders of a specific mass were weighed by an equal atomic ratio ( Fig. 1a). In the next step, the raw powders were ball-milled according to the specific ball milling process ( Fig. 1b). Following, the pretreated NbTaTiV powders were dried at 30 °C for 1 hour ( Fig. 1c). Finally, as shown in Fig. 1(d), graphite dies with a diameter of 24 mm filled with the ground powders was placed in the SPS chamber between two graphite electrodes and the powders were sintered. Mechanical alloying of powders was achieved by vertical planetary grinding (LC-PBM-6L, Shanghai Lichen Instrument Technology Co., LTD). The parameters of ball milling were formulated as follows: The ZrO 2vials and balls were utilized as the milling media with balls to powders mass ratio of 10:1. The powders were milled in planetary ball millers for 30, 40 and 50 h at 300 rpm in a vacuum atmosphere, and some anhydrous ethanol (30 ml) was added in the vials. To prevent the grain growth of NbTaTiV RHEAs, the samples (with the cylindrical shape of Φ 24 ×7 mm) of NbTaTiV alloys were fabricated by spark plasma sintering technique (SPS, SPS-PM-20/60, Shanghai Jinghua Technology Co., LTD, China). The sintering parameters were formulated according to the literature reports [30]. The composite powders were sintered under a pressure of 50 MPa at a sintering temperature of 1200 °C, 1300 ℃ and 1400 ℃ with a heating rate of 100 °C/min, and the gradient heating method was used to prevent temperature overshoot ( Fig. 2a). The pressure was held all time in the hole process, and the vacuum degree was 0.2 × 10 −5Pa. Then, the samples were cooled to room temperature in the furnace. Engineering strain (%) is 2.298657718120806

Ingots with the nominal compositions of CoCrFeNi and Al 0.3CoCrFeNi HEAs were fabricated from Al, Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni pure elements (purity >99.9 wt %), using the vacuum-arc-melting facility. The melting chamber was initially evacuated to a pressure of 10 -5torr. Then, the mixed elements were melted, remelted, superheated, and poured into a high-purity graphite crucible with an inner length of 200 mm, upper inner diameter of 65 mm, and bottom inner diameter of 50 mm. After casting, the resultant CoCrFeNi and Al 0.3CoCrFeNi HEAs were cut into several disks with identical dimensions (diameter of 30 mm and thickness of 1.0 mm). To obtain a uniform surface roughness and a strong interfacial bonding, both surfaces of the CoCrFeNi and Al 0.3CoCrFeNi sheets were brushed with steel wool pads to remove surface oxides and contaminants, and they were then cleaned in an ultrasonic acetone bath for 5 min. After the surface cleaning treatment, ten Al 0.3CoCrFeNi sheets and nine CoCrFeNi sheets were stacked alternatively to form a stacked laminate (with the outermost layers being Al 0.3CoCrFeNi). The stacked laminates were placed in a graphite die for confinement and pressed under a pressure of 40 MPa at 1100 °C for 2 h in a vacuum hot-pressing furnace to obtain hot-pressed Al 0.3CoCrFeNi/CoCrFeNi laminated composites. Subsequently, the laminated composites were cold rolled to achieve a total thickness reduction of 90 % after multiple passes. To determine the best annealing temperature for optimizing the properties of the multilevel HLSed HEAs, the rolled Al 0.3CoCrFeNi/CoCrFeNi laminated composites were annealed in Ar atmosphere at a series of temperatures in the range between 500 °C and 700 °C for 24 h, and they were subsequently water-quenched. The thermo-mechanical processing triggers Al element diffusion from the Al 0.3CoCrFeNi layer into the adjacent CoCrFeNi layers, resulting in the formation of numerous fine-scale B2 and σ precipitates adjacent to the layer interfaces in both the CoCrFeNi and Al 0.3CoCrFeNi constituent layers and thus enhancing the interface bonding. Fracture Elongation (%) is 62.408477842003855

HEAs are generally categorized into two elements, as depicted in Fig. 6. Recently, HEAs have more potential in many industries than typical alloys. High entropy alloys (HEAs) are hard, strong, and have many properties, including thermostability and corrosion resistance. HEAs also had exceptional chemical and mechanical characteristics. As a result, these alloys offer enormous development potential [ 34]. Till Jan. 2022, more than 300 high entropy alloys have been processed along with more than 35 principal elements. The concept of HEAs is different from traditional alloys because HEAs are not made up of just one or two components. HEAs have been defined in two ways by researchers: the first is based on composition, while the second is based on entropy [ 35]. So, based on composition, high entropy alloys contain a minimum of 5 main elements in the equimolar or near equimolar ratios, as depicted in Fig. 7. The atomic % of each element for these alloys lies between 5 % to 35 %. Although several additional elements were included in the high entropy alloys, the overall percentage of these elements are <5 % [ 36]. However, based on entropy, the HEAs are defined as the random blending of distinct features that yields configurational entropy (ΔSconf.). Further, these alloys are categorized into three types of alloys, as shown in Fig. 8. These materials are termed as high entropy alloys owing to the fact that their random solid & liquid state has basically higher entropies as compared to those in conventional alloys. A CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with gradient hetero-structure (GHS) composing of gradient nanostructured surface layer and hetero-structured matrix was prepared via a two-step process: pre-cold rolling (CR) deformation and subsequent annealing followed by surface mechanical grinding treatment (SMGT) and secondary annealing. The equiatomic CrCoNi MEA was electromagnetic levitation melted under a high-purity argon atmosphere and cast into ingot with dimensions of 10 × 70 × 800 mm 3. The chemical composition of the trial alloy is 32.05Cr-35.85Co-32.1Ni, in at.%. The 5 kg ingot was homogenized in an argon atmosphere at 1150 °C for 2h, followed by water cooling. The homogenized ingot was then cold rolled (CR) for multiple passes into sheets of 1.5 mm thickness with a total reduction of about 82%. The CRed sheets were then annealed at 650°C-800 °C to obtain HS samples, which were designated as HS650, HS700 and HS800 samples, respectively. The HS700 sample was selected for SMGT processing. A polished WC/Co ceramic ball with a diameter of 8.0 mm was pressed into the surface of the HS700 plate sample to obtain a gradient structured SL. The room-temperature SMGT processing was conducted under lubricating oil, with a pressing amount of 25 μm per pass and a total processing number of 15 passes. Both the surfaces of the plate sample were processed by SMGT, with the plates itself undergoing a synchronous alternation of positions in both the up-and-down and forward-and-backward directions at each processing interval. The sample obtained from the SMGT processing of the HS700 sample is designated as the GHS sample. In order to optimize the surface grain size gradient structure to maintain high strength and further restore intragranular dislocation plasticity in SL, the GHS sample was subjected to an additional annealing treatment at 625 °C for 1h, resulting in an optimized GHS sample, which is designated as the GHS625 sample. The designed Ti-4.5Al-4.5Mo-7V-1.5Cr-1.5Zr alloy was fabricated by a vacuum arc melting furnace. After casting, the ingot was subjected to two different forging processes. The first one takes place in the β-phase region, followed by water quenching (WQ). By contrast, the second one was performed with a starting temperature slightly above Tβ and a finishing temperature below it (β trans forging), followed by air cooling (AC). The single reduction for both processes was set to be ∼40 %. After the forging process, the alloy underwent an aging treatment at 480 °C for 6 h, followed by AC. The whole thermomechanical process is shown schematically in Fig. 2. The present forged and aged Ti alloys were subjected to various microstructure characterization facilities, including scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi-SU6600), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, Oxford instrument), transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-F200), and scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM, Hitachi-HF5000). The specimens for SEM and EBSD were prepared following standard metallographic procedures. For TEM analysis, the samples were ground to a foil with a thickness of ∼50 μm and punched into 3 mm discs. To produce electron-transparent regions in these punched disks, twin-jet polishing was conducted at -30 °C and 50 V in a solution of 65 % methanol, 30 % butyl alcohol, and 5 % perchloric acid. The X-ray diffraction (XRD, PANalytical X'Pert-PRO diffractometer) pattern was obtained using a Cu anode at 45 kV, the diffraction angular is in a range from 30° to 90°. The flat dog-bone tensile specimens with a gauge length of ∼12 mm and gauge width of ∼5 mm were cut using an electrical discharge machine (EDM). Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests were performed on an INSTRON 1195 testing machine with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min (corresponding to an initial strain rate of 1.4 × 10 -3) at room temperature. Tensile properties such as yield strength ( σ0.2), ultimate tensile strength ( σUTS), and total elongation at fracture ( ɛf) were measured using standard operation. Loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) cycles were conducted to measure the back stress evolution. In each cycle, the specimen was first stretched with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min to a designated strain ε, and then it was unloaded using the load-control mode to 20 N at a rate of 200 N/min, followed by reloading at a rate of 1 mm/min again to the next designated strain. At least three samples were performed to ensure the repeatability of the testing. Processing state: aged

The high strain is predominately induced by fine diameter and low content of coarse Cr-Mn-O-rich oxide. Processing Text: Powder assembly and alloying process including elemental alloying and shift-speed ball milling is applied in fabrication of CNT/Al-xMg (x = 0, 2.5, 5, wt.%). Pure Al powders (mean diameter ∼30 μm), pure Mg powders (mean diameter ∼10 μm) and graphitized raw CNTs powders (30-50 nm in diameter and <10 μm in length, 1.5 wt.% added, Chengdu Organic Chemistry Co., Ltd.) are mixed together and then ball milled at 135 rpm for 10 h and 270 rpm for 2 h, respectively. The mass ratio of stainless-steel milling balls to powders is controlled to be 20:1. Low speed ball milling (LSBM) at 135 rpm flake the powders and provides sufficient surface areas for uniform dispersion of CNTs. High speed ball milling (HSBM) at 270 rpm assembles the powder flakes by cold welding. To avoid massive oxidation and cool down the planetary ball milling system, the ball milling jars are filled with Ar atmosphere and take rest for 30 min after every 2 h of working. The cold-welded particles and pure Al powders (∼10 μm in diameter) with mass ratio of 7:3 is further ball milled together at 135 rpm for another 2 h and then assembled under pressure of 70 T to form green compacts. Subsequent vacuum sintering at 813 K promotes their densification and the diffusion of Mg in Al matrix. The heating rate of the sintering furnace is 4 K/min. After cooling down at ∼0.67 K/min to room temperature, the as-sintered samples are preserved in Muffle furnace of 653K for 2h and then extruded at 653 K under pressure of 80 T. The extrusion ratio is 25:1 and the diameter of the extruded rods are ∼8 mm. After cooling down by water quenching, the extruded rods showing surface temperature of ∼300 K are preserved in freezers (∼273 K). Specimens for tensile tests, EBSD, XRD, TEM and Raman tests are cut from the extrusion rods of CNT/Al, CNT/Al-2.5 Mg and CNT/Al-5Mg. The AA 2024 alloy was melted using susceptor-assisted microwave heating, and the molten alloy was then directionally solidified in-situ at five solidification rates (50, 100, 150, 200, and 250 μm/s) under microwave irradiation. The target alloy was exposed to microwave at 900 W for 1200 s with a 300 s stabilization period; duty cycle was adjusted as shown in Table 3. Upon melting, the target alloy gets self-poured in-situ into the preheated mould which is adequately connected to the cooling and withdrawal system. The mould withdrawal system was equipped with a CNC controller to effectively maintain the targeted solidification rate by providing the physical movement to the mould using a stepper motor arrangement. The cooling system was designed to extract heat from the bottom of mould using a water jet at 30 °C. Initially, water jet cooling was applied at the bottom of the mould to induce nucleation, followed by withdrawing the mold from the applicator to the ambient environment at a predetermined rate to facilitate the growth of the nuclei. The Al-Mg alloy plates used for the study were prepared by depositing AA5087 wire (1.2 mm in diameter) onto AA5A06 plates via the WADED system. The WADED system mainly includes an ABB six-axis robot and a Fronius CMT Advanced 4000R welding system. During the WADED process, the filler wire was melted by the arc in a protective atmosphere (99.99 % Ar), and the CMT torch moved horizontally (Y-depositing direction) with the molten wire to form a deposited layer. Deposition of the next layer was performed on the previous layer by raising the torch height (Z-building direction). The WADED Al components were finally removed from the substrate using electrical discharge machining (EDM) and double-side milling to 6 mm thickness. The LSP experiment was carried out in a self-built LSP system, which mainly included a Nd: YAG pulsed laser (with a wavelength of 1064 nm and a pulse duration of 15 ns) and a six-axis robot. WADED Al plate was ground and polished before LSP, and then fixed on six-axis robot to adjust position. The Al foil with a thickness of 100 µm and the flowing water layer were covered on the surface of WADED Al plate as absorbing layer and constraining layer, respectively. The front and back sides of the WADED Al plate were strengthened in turn. The pulsed laser with energy of 5 J was focused by a convex lens into a circular spot with a diameter of 2 mm. Both sides of sampling region were treated twice by LSP at a 50 % overlapping rate to prevent the distortion and obtain the unform residual stress distribution. The as-deposited samples after LSP treatment were further annealed at 200 °C for 1 h to study the effect of the LSP + annealing process on the WADED Al alloy. Various mold temperatures ranging from 150 °C to 300 °C were utilized and the resulting alloy samples were denoted as HS-150, HS-200, HS-250, and HS-300 for ease of reference. The SPD processes can be classified as bulk-SPD, surface-SPD and powder-SPD methods. In bulk-SPD, the goal is to modify the bulk microstructure of a material with reasonably large sizes. In surface-SPD, only surface and sub-surface layers are modified. In powder-SPD, the material is in the form of powder, and strain is introduced on the surface layer and core of the powder particles usually by ball milling methods. Different methods based on rolling, torsion, forging and extrusion can satisfy the required conditions for SPD processing of bulk material. The most known method for inducing SPD in powders is high-energy ball milling. Recent trends in SPD methods include hydrostatic pressure methods, upscaling disc samples to rods using HPTE, pipe sample processing using t-HPS, sheet processing using IF-HPS, cryogenic-SPD, and ultra-SPD. Before printing, the chamber of the SLM device was vacuumed and then filled with high-purity argon gas to ensure the oxygen content remained below 1000 ppm. The build substrate was preheated to 100 °C to reduce thermal stress. A wide range of printing parameters including adjustments in laser power ( P), scanning speed ( V), and scanning pitch ( h), were explored. Specifically, Pranged from 260 to 300 W, Vranged from 800 to 1200 mm·s −1, and hranged from 60 to 140 μm, all while maintaining a consistent layer thickness ( t) of 40 μm. The laser beam scanned each layer in a unidirectional manner, with the scanning direction altered by 67° for each subsequent layer (as shown in Fig. 1b), aiming to minimize defects and residual stress [26]. The densities of the SLM-produced samples were determined using Archimedes' drainage method. Phase analysis of the powders and as-printed samples was conducted using a Cu Kα radiation X-ray diffractometer (XRD, 7000SX, Shimadzu). The microstructure was characterized using optical microscopy (OM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Nova Nano SEM 450), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM, FEI Tecnai G20, 300 kV). For the TEM analysis, the samples were initially mechanically polished to a thickness of approximately 30 μm and then further thinned using an ion polishing system (Gatan PIPS II 695). Tensile testing was conducted on seven representative SLM-produced HEA samples, each prepared with varying printing parameters (denoted as P1, P2, …, P7) encompassing a wide range of laser power, scanning speed, and scanning pitch. Processing Text: AA7075 is widely utilized in aerospace and transportation due to its high specific strength, specific stiffness, and corrosion resistance. Hot forging is an efficient and cost-effective method for manufacturing AA7075 cylindrical rings. During hot forging, AA7075 cylindrical ring undergoes complex metal flow, resulting in anisotropy in both microstructure and mechanical properties. The present study investigated the anisotropic behaviors of microstructure and mechanical properties in AA7075 cylindrical rings along three directions: rolling direction (RD), transverse direction (TD), and normal direction (ND). The results indicated that the microstructural anisotropy contributed to anisotropy in mechanical properties both before and after hot forging. In the present study, an AA7075 extruded bar ( Table 1), measuring ø300 × 520 mm, was held at 435°C for 12 h before the initial upsetting was completed. Following the first upsetting, the material was held at 435°C for 1 h prior to the second upsetting. Following the second upsetting, the bar diameter was adjusted to ø415 mm after another hour at 435°C. Finally, the material underwent hot forging in a hot forging mold after being held at 435°C for one more hour. Fig. 1shows the hot forging die and the resulting AA7075 cylindrical ring. The tensile strength and elongation at break of AA7075 cylindrical ring were evaluated in RD, TD, and ND using uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature. Fig. 2a illustrates the relative positions of the tensile samples within the cylindrical ring, while Fig. 2b provides the detailed dimensions of these samples. Each tensile testing was performed according to the same standard procedure. Three tensile tests were conducted for each group of samples at room temperature, using a strain rate of 2 mm/min, to obtain the average values of the samples' tensile strength and elongation at break. The microstructures of three planes - RD-TD, RD-ND, and TD-ND - were examined using a scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. Before microscopic analysis, the samples were ground and polished to achieve a suitable surface finish. This process involved three stages: grinding with sandpaper with roughness of 800, 1200, 1500, 2000, and 2500, respectively; polishing with a 1μm diamond suspension; and electrolytic polishing with electrolyte (10 % HClO 4+90 % C₂H₅OH). The SEM and EBSD test were conducted on the JSM-7800F electron microscope equipped with the EBSD detector at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV and a scanning step of 1.4 μm. Processing Text: The alloys were manufactured using vacuum induction melting (VIM) from high-purity industry grade melt stock. The melt charges weighted 8 kg and were loaded in an alumina crucible for VIM under 200 Torr (26.7 kPa) partial pressure of argon. Once melted, the liquid metal was brought to a 50 °C superheat and poured into a cylindrical graphite mold to form 75 mm diameter ingots. The ingots were homogenized in a vacuum heat-treatment furnace with high-vacuum capabilities and utilizing a 50 Torr (6.7 kPa) argon partial pressure once the heat treatment temperature reaches 800 °C. A computationally optimized heat treatment schedule was determined based on chemistry and microstructure to reduce residual elemental inhomogeneity to below 1 %. Hot working was performed at 1100 °C and consisted of steps of forging followed by hot rolling with reheating between each step. Doing so, the ingots were processed into ∼10 mm thick plates. Processing Text: The alloys employed in the current study were prepared by vacuum arc melting using powder with purity above 99.95 wt%. Finally, NiCoCrFeMn (equal atomic ratio) was obtained. The sandpaper and SiO 2polishing solution were used to polish the experimental samples to a mirror-like surface. NiCoCrFeMn was annealed at 1000 °C for 1 h. Electrochemical charging with 0.1 mol/L NaOH and 0.5 g/L CH 4N 2S heavy water solutions under identical experimental conditions were conducted. All samples were charged at a constant current of 50 mA/cm 2for 24 h at room temperature in a heavy aqueous solution containing 0.1 mol/L NaOH and 0.5 g/L CH 4N 2S. The NiCoCrFeMn alloy was subjected to additional 6 h and 12 h electrochemical deuterium charging experiments to compare the effect of charging time. The deuterium charged samples were put into TDS within 24 h for deuterium concentration measurement. The TDS measurements were heated from room temperature to 800 °C under high vacuum (10 −5Pa) at a constant heating rate of 1 °C/s. Slow strain tensile tests were performed for pristine and the deuterium-charged samples using an Instron 5565 tensile testing machine equipped with a video extensometer, with a strain rate of 4 × 10 −4/s and a loading rate of 0.12 mm / min at room temperature. All samples were analyzed using EBSD along the normal direction (ND), with a scanning step size of about 0.25 µm. The TEM thin sample were prepared using standard electropolishing techniques. Firstly, a disk with a diameter of 3 mm was cut near the fracture surface using electrical discharge machining (EDM). The 3 mm disk was thinned to a thickness of about 80 µm using mechanical polishing. Finally, the sample thickness was further reduced to electron transparency using a 5% perchloric acid and 95% ethanol solution on a TJ100-SE twin-jet polisher with an instrument voltage of 20 V and a temperature of − 20 ± 4 °C. Powder assembly and alloying process including elemental alloying and shift-speed ball milling is applied in fabrication of CNT/Al-xMg (x = 0, 2.5, 5, wt.%). Pure Al powders (mean diameter ∼30 μm), pure Mg powders (mean diameter ∼10 μm) and graphitized raw CNTs powders (30-50 nm in diameter and <10 μm in length, 1.5 wt.% added, Chengdu Organic Chemistry Co., Ltd.) are mixed together and then ball milled at 135 rpm for 10 h and 270 rpm for 2 h, respectively. The mass ratio of stainless-steel milling balls to powders is controlled to be 20:1. Low speed ball milling (LSBM) at 135 rpm flake the powders and provides sufficient surface areas for uniform dispersion of CNTs. High speed ball milling (HSBM) at 270 rpm assembles the powder flakes by cold welding. To avoid massive oxidation and cool down the planetary ball milling system, the ball milling jars are filled with Ar atmosphere and take rest for 30 min after every 2 h of working. The cold-welded particles and pure Al powders (∼10 μm in diameter) with mass ratio of 7:3 is further ball milled together at 135 rpm for another 2 h and then assembled under pressure of 70 T to form green compacts. Subsequent vacuum sintering at 813 K promotes their densification and the diffusion of Mg in Al matrix. The heating rate of the sintering furnace is 4 K/min. After cooling down at ∼0.67 K/min to room temperature, the as-sintered samples are preserved in Muffle furnace of 653K for 2h and then extruded at 653 K under pressure of 80 T. The extrusion ratio is 25:1 and the diameter of the extruded rods are ∼8 mm. After cooling down by water quenching, the extruded rods showing surface temperature of ∼300 K are preserved in freezers (∼273 K). Specimens for tensile tests, EBSD, XRD, TEM and Raman tests are cut from the extrusion rods of CNT/Al, CNT/Al-2.5 Mg and CNT/Al-5Mg. Processing Text: Nanocrystalline NiTi SMAs are frequently made into the components by experiencing plastic deformation at moderate temperatures in order to prevent nanocrystalline grains from growing up at high temperatures. Nanocrystalline NiTi SMAs are fabricated by means of local canning compression and subsequent appropriate annealing, where the average diameters of nanocrystalline grains are 66.7, 88.2 and 98.5 nm, respectively. In particular, nanocrystalline Ni 50·3Ti 49.7SMA exhibits a strong size effect during plastic deformation at 400 °C, where yield stress increases with the decrease of grain size. A CPFEM is employed for studying strengthening mechanism of nanocrystalline Ni 50·3Ti 49.7SMA during hot deformation at 400 °C, where SSD and GND densities are integrated into the crystal plasticity constitutive model to account for strain gradients based on dislocation slip. Processing Text: In-situ titanium boride (TiB) reinforced titanium matrix composites (TMCs) were fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) technique. The Ti6Al4V alloy powders were mechanically mixed with 0.5 wt% and 1 wt% TiB 2nanoparticles, respectively, using a three-dimensional mixer (JXHY-2L). The mixing process included a speed of 80 rpm/min and a duration of 4 h. To avoid the adverse effect of energy on the properties of the alloy powders during the mechanical mixing process, the machine was paused for cooling at room temperature for 10 min after every 20 min of mixing, ensuring mixed uniformly. The process parameters for fabricating samples with Ti6Al4V powders and 0.5 wt% TiB 2/Ti6Al4V powders, respectively, were as follows: a laser power of 180 W, a scanning speed of 1000 mm/s, a hatching spacing of 120 μm, and a layer thickness of 30 μm; additionally, a short linear scanning strategy was implemented with an interlayer rotation angle of 67°. To alleviate residual stress accumulation during processing, the substrate was preheated to 180 °C. In comparison to Ti6Al4V, TiB 2exhibits a higher melting point and enhanced laser absorption characteristics, necessitating increased laser energy densities when fabricating samples with elevated TiB 2content. Consequently, when the TiB 2addition reached 1 wt%, adjustments to the process parameters were made: specifically, increasing the laser power to 200 W while reducing the scanning speed to 800 mm/s and modifying the hatching spacing to 100 μm. Prior to processing, the powders underwent drying in a vacuum oven at 80 °C for 8 h; high-purity argon gas was introduced to maintain oxygen levels below 100 ppm to prevent oxidation within the melt pool. The Ni 50Cr 20Co 15Al 10V 5(at. %) HEAs in this work were synthesized using an arc-melting furnace in a Ti-getter, high-purity Ar atmosphere. High-purity Ni, Cr, Co, Al, and V metals (>99.9 wt %) were melted to cast the alloys. To ensure compositional uniformity, the alloys underwent more than seven repeated melting cycles under electromagnetic stirring. The alloys were then cast into a water-cooled copper mold, producing ingots measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 80 mm. Subsequently, homogenization treatment was carried out at 1200 °C for 24 h in an Ar atmosphere, followed by water quenching. The homogenized ingots underwent cold rolling, resulting in an 80 % reduction in thickness. Following cold rolling, the alloys were recrystallized at 1100 °C for 10 min and then water-quenched to room temperature. After that, the recrystallized samples were subjected to aging treatments at 700 °C for 1 h and 12 h, respectively. These alloys for the study were named as aged-1h, aged-12 h, and recrystallized samples, respectively. The samples for examination underwent initial sanding with SiC sandpapers ranging from 400# to 2000#, followed by polishing with a 50 nm oxide polishing suspension (OPS) solution to remove surface stress. Samples for TEM analysis were first ground with SiC sandpapers to a thickness of less than 100 μm. Following this, the samples were further thinned using a precision Ar ion-beam milling system (Gatan 691) to achieve electron transparency. Samples for tensile tests were obtained with a gauge length of 10 mm and width of 2 mm using electric spark cutting. Before testing, the surface of all samples was sanded with SiC sandpapers ranging from 400# to 2000#. For analyzing the deformed microstructure, samples were additionally polished with OPS solution for EBSD and ECCI measurements. Processing state: Aged-12 h (summary mention)

The materials used in this study were commercial CuCrZr alloys (grade C18150). The commercial copper alloys had undergone cold deformation and annealing treatment, resulting in mostly deformed grains and a large number of precipitates. Cryogenic treatment was conducted using the SLX-30B cryogenic treatment box, developed by the Institute of Physics and Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, with nitrogen supplied from a pressure tank. As-sintered Ti2AlNb intermetallic mainly contained the O phase and a little of B2 and α2 phases, showing brittle characteristics. A solution treatment at 950℃ for 2 h and then water quenching was conducted. The brittle α2 at the grain boundaries transformed into O phase and the O phase dissolved into the soft B2 phase partially, resulting in a much higher increase in elongation with 10.4 % and its yield strength still remained at 867.3 MPa compared with the sintered ones. Along with the EBSD analysis, this strength-ductility matching mechanism was mainly attributed to the decrease of the brittle hexagonal α2 and orthorhombic O phase, and the increase of the soft cubic B2 phase. HEAs are generally categorized into two elements, as depicted in Fig. 6. Recently, HEAs have more potential in many industries than typical alloys. High entropy alloys (HEAs) are hard, strong, and have many properties, including thermostability and corrosion resistance. HEAs also had exceptional chemical and mechanical characteristics. As a result, these alloys offer enormous development potential [ 34]. Till Jan. 2022, more than 300 high entropy alloys have been processed along with more than 35 principal elements. The concept of HEAs is different from traditional alloys because HEAs are not made up of just one or two components. HEAs have been defined in two ways by researchers: the first is based on composition, while the second is based on entropy [ 35]. So, based on composition, high entropy alloys contain a minimum of 5 main elements in the equimolar or near equimolar ratios, as depicted in Fig. 7. The atomic % of each element for these alloys lies between 5 % to 35 %. Although several additional elements were included in the high entropy alloys, the overall percentage of these elements are <5 % [ 36]. However, based on entropy, the HEAs are defined as the random blending of distinct features that yields configurational entropy (ΔSconf.). Further, these alloys are categorized into three types of alloys, as shown in Fig. 8. These materials are termed as high entropy alloys owing to the fact that their random solid & liquid state has basically higher entropies as compared to those in conventional alloys. In the case of HEAs, the uneven atomic radius of distinct elements causes an intensive lattice distortion effect. [ 35] also reported that severe lattice distortion could occur in the high entropy alloy, and each element has its unique and specific atomic size.
