Processing Text: AA7075 is widely utilized in aerospace and transportation due to its high specific strength, specific stiffness, and corrosion resistance. Hot forging is an efficient and cost-effective method for manufacturing AA7075 cylindrical rings. During hot forging, AA7075 cylindrical ring undergoes complex metal flow, resulting in anisotropy in both microstructure and mechanical properties. The present study investigated the anisotropic behaviors of microstructure and mechanical properties in AA7075 cylindrical rings along three directions: rolling direction (RD), transverse direction (TD), and normal direction (ND). The results indicated that the microstructural anisotropy contributed to anisotropy in mechanical properties both before and after hot forging. In the present study, an AA7075 extruded bar ( Table 1), measuring ø300 × 520 mm, was held at 435°C for 12 h before the initial upsetting was completed. Following the first upsetting, the material was held at 435°C for 1 h prior to the second upsetting. Following the second upsetting, the bar diameter was adjusted to ø415 mm after another hour at 435°C. Finally, the material underwent hot forging in a hot forging mold after being held at 435°C for one more hour. Fig. 1shows the hot forging die and the resulting AA7075 cylindrical ring. The tensile strength and elongation at break of AA7075 cylindrical ring were evaluated in RD, TD, and ND using uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature. Fig. 2a illustrates the relative positions of the tensile samples within the cylindrical ring, while Fig. 2b provides the detailed dimensions of these samples. Each tensile testing was performed according to the same standard procedure. Three tensile tests were conducted for each group of samples at room temperature, using a strain rate of 2 mm/min, to obtain the average values of the samples' tensile strength and elongation at break. The microstructures of three planes - RD-TD, RD-ND, and TD-ND - were examined using a scanning electron microscope (SEM) equipped with an electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) detector. Before microscopic analysis, the samples were ground and polished to achieve a suitable surface finish. This process involved three stages: grinding with sandpaper with roughness of 800, 1200, 1500, 2000, and 2500, respectively; polishing with a 1μm diamond suspension; and electrolytic polishing with electrolyte (10 % HClO 4+90 % C₂H₅OH). The SEM and EBSD test were conducted on the JSM-7800F electron microscope equipped with the EBSD detector at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV and a scanning step of 1.4 μm. CR was performed between two stainless steel plates to protect the rolls. Then, aging temperatures of 550-600 °C, typical for Fe-Mn-Al-C alloys were applied. The samples were also aged at 200-300 °C. After homogenization, DAF and cold rolling, the chemical composition of the produced alloy was verified by the inductively coupled plasma emission spectroscopy with ARCOS FHM22 MV130 spectrometer made by SPECTRO Analytical Instruments (for metallic elements), combustion infrared absorption method with LECO CS-844 analyzer (for carbon) and helium transport melting infrared absorption method with LECO ONH836 (for oxygen). This work utilizes a consolidation technique that uses high-pressure & high-temperature (HPHT) to produce an ultrafine-grained (UFG) FeCrCoNi HEA. The high consolidation pressure has two effects: 1) reducing interparticle distances due to the enforced plastic deformation of individual granules, making for high bulk density, and 2) reducing the diffusivity, thereby reducing the growth speed of grains. The high strain is primarily the result of a reduction in the diameter and content of Cr-Mn-O-rich oxides - which reduce the interface area between the soft matrix and hard oxides, thereby suppressing the sources of crack generation - due to the utilization of high pressure. UFG FeCoNiCr HEA was prepared by MA and HPHT techniques. Applying a substantial consolidation pressure (4 GPa) leads to the UFG FeCoNiCr HEA achieving a relative density near 99 %. The consolidated UFG FeCoNiCr HEA exhibits an average grain diameter of approx. 181 nm and displays exceptionally high yield strength of approx. 1526 MPa - significantly higher than the yield strength (162 MPa) of CG FeCoNiCr HEA - and a high fracture of 35 %. The high yield strength is predominantly brought about by the UFG matrix. The achievement of the UFG matrix can be attributed primarily to the application of a high consolidation pressure, which has two effects: 1) reduces interparticle distances because of the enforced plastic deformation of the individual powder particles and 2) reducing the diffusivity, thereby reducing the rate of grain growth. The high strain is predominately induced by fine diameter and low content of coarse Cr-Mn-O-rich oxide. High sintering pressure suppresses the oxides to grow, reducing the interface area between soft matrix phases and hard oxides, and thus decreasing the sources of crack generation. Plastic deformation at room temperature followed by post-annealing is one of the best methods to achieve fine-grained metals and alloys. In this research, the high-temperature annealing behavior of cold-rolled electrolytic tough-pitch (ETP) copper sheets was studied. 90 % asymmetric cold rolling followed by high-temperature post-annealing at 673 K for 1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 60, and 120 min were applied on the copper. The microstructure was significantly changed with increasing annealing time from 1 to 2 min owing to full recrystallization. With increasing the annealing duration, the grain size is increased. The formation of equiaxed grains with a smaller size (∼9 μm) compared to the full-annealed (initial) sample (∼68 μm) is observed after the longest time of post-annealing (120 min) due to the pinning effect of Cu2O particles. The post-annealed copper sheets processed by asymmetric rolling (in this work) exhibited a more homogeneous microstructure through the thickness compared to the symmetric rolling due to more uniform stored strain energy. The results showed that the first deformed grains that undergo recrystallization during post-annealing are Goss-oriented grains. With an increase in the post-annealing time, the S and Copper components were eliminated and a strong Cube and P texture orientations were formed. Interestingly, after 1 min of post-annealing, the yield and tensile strength enhanced to 410.2 MPa and 418.6 MPa owing to the annealing hardening phenomenon. The hardness and strength reached a constant value after the post-annealing for 10 min and above. With the increase of post-annealing time from 1 min to 120 min, the electrical conductivity was increased from 77.6 to 97.5 %IACS. From the obtained results, it can be concluded that the asymmetric cold rolling followed by high-temperature post-annealing is capable of strength improvement and maintaining electrical conductivity in copper. Processing Text: A polycrystalline ingot of MnCu2Al was prepared using a combination of arc melting and furnace annealing according to previous investigations. Elemental Mn (Sigma Aldrich, chips, 99%) was cleaned of its native oxides by annealing in an evacuated silica ampule for 8 h at 1000 °C. Starting materials of cleaned Mn, Cu (Alfa Aesar, wire, 99.99%), and Al (Alfa Aesar, wire, 99.9995%) were weighed with a 1:2:1 stoichiometry, totaling a mass of 3.0 g. An additional excess of Mn (10 mg) was added to compensate for volatilization during melting. The materials were arc melted four times in an Ar atmosphere, flipping the ingot between melts for homogeneity, with a total mass loss of 1.3%. The resulting ingot was wrapped in Ta foil, sealed in an evacuated silica ampule, and homogenized at 850 °C for 7 days to create a large-grained microstructure, then quenched into water. To ensure structural homogeneity, the ingot was divided and pieces were sampled from opposing faces of the ingot, ground into a fine powder, and sieved through a 140 mesh (106 μm particle size) for a synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) sample. The powder sample was again sealed within an evacuated fused silica ampule and tempered at 320 °C for 1 h to resolve any pre-existing crystallographic defects. Microscopy and mechanical testing were performed on pieces of the ingot that were tempered under the same conditions. Specifically, the nanoindentation test specimen was created from a tempered piece of the arc melted ingot that was mounted to an aluminum puck using crystal bond, ground using SiC paper, polished using diamond suspensions down to 1 μm, and vibratory polished using colloidal silica to a mirror finish. While mounted to the aluminum puck, the polished surface was imaged using SEM and mapped using EBSD, to characterize the crystallographic orientation of visible grains. Nanoindentation experiments were performed to test the mechanical properties of each grain orientation using a Nanomechanics iMicro Nanoindenter equipped with a 1000 mN load cell and Berkovich tip diamond indenter. All nanoindentation data were collected using a continuous stiffness method operating at a frequency of 100 Hz, to a total depth of 1000 nm, and each data point reported in this investigation is representative of at least 10-20 indents per crystallographic orientation, collected between depths of 400 nm-1000 nm. Data recorded during the initial 400 nm of each indentation were excluded to account for surface roughness and possible surface artifacts introduced by polishing. To create an accessible base for micro-pillar experiments, the polished specimen was remounted to an angled polishing puck and polished into a wedge-shaped geometry. Using EBSD mapping near the edge of the wedge-shaped specimen, several grains of interest were identified, and were femtosecond laser machined in situ into single-crystalline pedestals using the TriBeam microscope, a laser-equipped TFS Versa 3D FIB-SEM. Micro-compression pillars were produced directly from the single-crystalline pedestals using the FIB to mill the pillar tops and sides perpendicular to the wedge surface with a slight taper, before removing all material from the faces to create pillars with a 1:1:2 aspect ratio to mitigate the potential impact of buckling. A square pillar cross-section was employed to aid in the identification of active slip systems. Micro-compression experiments were performed in situ in an TFS Apreo S SEM equipped with a Femto-tools FT-NMT04 Nanomechanical Testing System designed to optimize alignment during small-scale mechanical testing. Each pillar was loaded in a series of load vs. displacement tests until the point of yield using a displacement-controlled method. Following SEM imaging, a detailed microstructural investigation was performed on an electron-transparent lamella micro-machined from the [11 8 2]-oriented pillar, using STEM imaging and a g⋅b analysis in the TEM. As the deformed material had high internal strains, the foil was prepared with three electron-transparent windows, framed by thicker regions for stabilization. HEAs are generally categorized into two elements, as depicted in Fig. 6. Recently, HEAs have more potential in many industries than typical alloys. High entropy alloys (HEAs) are hard, strong, and have many properties, including thermostability and corrosion resistance. HEAs also had exceptional chemical and mechanical characteristics. As a result, these alloys offer enormous development potential [ 34]. Till Jan. 2022, more than 300 high entropy alloys have been processed along with more than 35 principal elements. The concept of HEAs is different from traditional alloys because HEAs are not made up of just one or two components. HEAs have been defined in two ways by researchers: the first is based on composition, while the second is based on entropy [ 35]. So, based on composition, high entropy alloys contain a minimum of 5 main elements in the equimolar or near equimolar ratios, as depicted in Fig. 7. The atomic % of each element for these alloys lies between 5 % to 35 %. Although several additional elements were included in the high entropy alloys, the overall percentage of these elements are <5 % [ 36]. However, based on entropy, the HEAs are defined as the random blending of distinct features that yields configurational entropy (ΔSconf.). Further, these alloys are categorized into three types of alloys, as shown in Fig. 8. These materials are termed as high entropy alloys owing to the fact that their random solid & liquid state has basically higher entropies as compared to those in conventional alloys. The evolution of HEAs from conventional alloys is shown in Fig. 9. The main properties of HEAs are as given below: a) High hardness and strength. In the case of HEAs, the uneven atomic radius of distinct elements causes an intensive lattice distortion effect. These types of effects obstruct the dislocation movement, leading to very high hardness and strength [ 34]. The lattice distortion of HEA containing chromium is shown in Fig. 10. Li et al. [ 35] also reported that severe lattice distortion could occur in the high entropy alloy, and each element has its unique and specific atomic size. Microstructure and mechanical properties remain important indicators for large-scale structural components in aerospace ( Ren et al., 2017). For the high-power/high-efficiency LDED process of titanium alloys, research hotspots mainly focus on the microstructural and properties ( Zhang et al., 2019), including the non-uniformity of microstructure, grain refinement mechanism, anisotropy of properties, and the improvement of mechanical properties ( Song et al., 2023). Through the use of the pulsed LDED process, it has become possible to produce a fully equiaxed grain structure in TC4 titanium alloy, with an average grain size of 139 μm ( Zhang et al., 2023). However, the drawback is that the tensile elongation is only 4.09%, indicating insufficient toughness ( Chen et al., 2024). Meanwhile, the introduction of external energy fields also contributes to grain refinement ( Tan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2022, 2023). Applying high-frequency ultrasonic vibration during the deposition process can transform coarse columnar grains into fine equiaxed grains, thereby refining the grain structure and effectively enhancing tensile properties ( Todaro et al., 2020). In the LDED deposition of TC4 titanium alloy, the introduction of a transverse static magnetic field can refine the primary β grains and produce a discontinuous grain boundary α phase, thereby improving tensile ductility and reducing the anisotropy of tensile properties ( Yuan et al., 2021). The present study investigated the anisotropic behaviors of microstructure and mechanical properties in AA7075 cylindrical rings along three directions: rolling direction (RD), transverse direction (TD), and normal direction (ND). Following the first upsetting, the material was held at 435°C for 1 h prior to the second upsetting. Finally, the material underwent hot forging in a hot forging mold after being held at 435°C for one more hour. Fig. 1shows the hot forging die and the resulting AA7075 cylindrical ring. Three tensile tests were conducted for each group of samples at room temperature, using a strain rate of 2 mm/min, to obtain the average values of the samples' tensile strength and elongation at break. By conducting the parameters optimization process, the optimal combination (laser power: 120 W, scanning speed: 1100 mm/s, hatch spacing: 0.07 mm, layer thickness: 0.02 mm, VED: 77.92 J/mm3) was then decided based on the sample having the highest density of 99.73 %.
